# Photographic Emulsion and Film-Base Technical Knowledge Base

**Purpose.** This document is a self-contained technical reference on photographic emulsions,
their sensitometry and image structure, and on photographic film bases and their aging. It was
built by reading six sources in full and extracting the technical content — the numbers, the
definitions, the measured relations and the mechanisms — with page-level provenance, so that the
original documents can be removed from the project directory without losing what they contain.

It is written for one specific purpose: to decide what a physically-based film-simulation engine
may legitimately model, and to prevent theoretical photographic science from being converted into
unsupported simulation parameters. That is why every item carries a classification tag, and why
the sections recording what the sources **do not** say are as long as the sections recording what
they do.

**Created** 2026-08-27. **Sources read in full:** 974 PDF pages across six documents spanning
1922–2020.

---

## 0. How to read this document

### 0.1 Classification tags — on every substantive item

| Tag | Meaning | What you may do with it |
|---|---|---|
| **[F]** | **Documented fact.** Stated directly by a source. | Cite it. Do not derive a number from it. |
| **[Q]** | **Quantified fact.** Stated *and* accompanied by enough numbers to model. | Candidate for the database, subject to §25. |
| **[M]** | **Mechanism only.** The physics or chemistry is explained, but the source does not quantify it sufficiently to model. | Keep for understanding. **Do not invent the missing coefficients.** |
| **[E]** | **Engineering conclusion.** Ours, not the source's. | Treat as a design opinion that must be validated. |
| **[S]** | **Speculative / insufficiently supported.** | Recorded so it is not mistaken for a finding. |

The distinction between **[Q]** and **[M]** is the one that matters. A great deal of this material
explains *why* film behaves as it does without giving a single number that could parameterise it.
That content is genuinely valuable — it tells us which of our existing heuristics have the wrong
*shape* — but it is not a source of values.

### 0.2 Citation format

Every substantive claim carries its source, chapter or section, printed page, PDF page, and the
figure or table number where one applies:

```
[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.216 (PDF 225), Fig. 7.8]
[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.61 (PDF 65), Table 3]
[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14), Table 4]
[Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.157 (PDF 164)]
[Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.11 (PDF 11)]
[NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)]
```

Both page numbers are given because the PDF page is what a future re-check needs and the printed
page is what a citation needs. Page offsets differ per document and per range; they are recorded
in §29.

### 0.3 Rules this document follows

1. **No invented numbers.** Where a source is silent, the silence is recorded explicitly, in the
   form "no source in this set gives …". Those statements are load-bearing.
2. **Conflicts are recorded, never averaged.** Where two sources disagree, both appear with their
   dates and the disagreement is stated. Averaging two dated observations produces a number that
   describes no real material.
3. **Era is marked on everything era-dependent.** A 1966 statement of "current practice" is a
   dated data point about 1966, not a timeless fact. Presenting late-century knowledge as though it
   applied unchanged across the century is the specific failure this document is organised to
   avoid — see §2.
4. **Where the sources do not establish that something changed over time, that is stated** rather
   than a trend being inferred.
5. **OCR damage is flagged at the point of use** and the raw string quoted. Two of the six sources
   are scans; one has lost every display equation to image-only rendering (§29.3).
6. **Archaic units are preserved** with a metric conversion marked "(conv.)". A 1929 formula in
   grains and ounces is reproduced as printed, because the conversion is ours and could be wrong.

### 0.4 Structure

| Part | Sections | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Front matter | §0–§1 | Conventions; source register |
| Chronological spine | §2 | 1920 → 2020, what changed and what is not established to have changed |
| Materials and mechanism | §3–§14 | Emulsion, crystals, size, making, gelatin, sensitization, latent image, development, interimage |
| Measurement | §15–§18 | Sensitometry, characteristic curve, granularity, sharpness and MTF |
| Colour and processing | §19–§20 | Colour materials, processing effects |
| Carrier | §21–§23 | Film base, acetate degradation, carrier versus image |
| Application | §24–§27 | Property→appearance map; what we can use now; what needs future work; reference only |
| Apparatus | §28–§29 | Figures worth digitising; provenance and source-integrity register |

## 1. Source register

Six documents, read in full. The 73-year span is the reason this document is organised
chronologically rather than thematically: these are three different technology generations of the
same craft, plus two preservation assessments of the carrier, plus one first-hand manufacturing
manual.

### 1.1 The sources

**S1 — Davis & Walters 1922.**
Raymond Davis and F. M. Walters, jr., *Sensitometry of Photographic Emulsions and a Survey of the
Characteristics of Plates and Films of American Manufacture.* Bureau of Standards Scientific Paper
No. 439 (B.S. Sci. Pap. No. 439), U.S. Department of Commerce, Government Printing Office.
Dateline Washington, 6 September 1921; GPO printing marks read "-22-", i.e. issued 1922. 121 PDF
pages. Google-digitised library copy.
*Contents:* Part 1 general characteristics of photographic emulsions; Part 2 apparatus and testing
conditions at the Bureau; Part 3 measured data on "practically all brands of emulsions (made in
the United States) coated on glass and celluloid, the trade names of the emulsions being omitted".
*Why it matters:* the only source in the set that measures real, named-by-class commercial
materials and publishes the sensitometry. It is a dated snapshot of the American market circa
1920, and it defines the period's terms — inertia, H&D speed, gamma-infinity — in the period's own
words. → §15, §16.
*Integrity:* thin OCR; digits require care. See §29.3.

**S2 — Wall 1929.**
E. J. Wall, Hon. F.R.P.S., F.C.S., *Photographic Emulsions: Their Preparation and Coating on
Glass, Celluloid and Paper, Experimentally and on the Large Scale.* American Photographic
Publishing Co., Boston, 1929. 267 PDF pages.
*Contents:* emulsion types and making, ripening, washing, sensitizing, coating by hand and by
machine, drying, base preparation, baryta paper, with worked recipes and machine drawings.
*Why it matters:* first-hand manufacturing practice at the end of the 1920s, including coating
weights measured on ten commercial plates, and the earliest fixed point in this set for the film
base. → §3, §6, §21.

**S3 — Duffin 1966.**
G. F. Duffin, *Photographic Emulsion Chemistry.* Focal Press Limited, London, © 1966. The Focal
Library; General Editor Prof. Dr. W. F. Berg, Photographisches Institut der E.T.H. Zürich;
editorial board including Prof. Dr. K. V. Chibisov (Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R.) and
Prof. Dr. J. Eggert. Printed in Hungary, 1966. 250 PDF pages.
*Contents:* I Silver Halides; II Gelatin; III Photographic Base Materials; IV Emulsion
Preparation; V Chemical Sensitization; VI Spectral Sensitization; VII Stabilizers and
Antifoggants; VIII Coating; IX Latent Image; X Colour Processes; XI Non-conventional Processes.
*Why it matters:* the mid-century industrial chemistry, stated as then-current practice — which
makes its "current" a 1966 data point. The base chapter is the numeric bridge between Wall's
celluloid and the modern polyester era. → §4, §6, §7, §19, §21.

**S4 — Tani 1995.**
Tadaaki Tani, Ashigara Research Laboratories, Fuji Photo Film Company, *Photographic Sensitivity:
Theory and Mechanisms.* Oxford University Press, New York / Oxford, 1995. Oxford Series in Optical
and Imaging Sciences, vol. 8. 263 PDF pages.
*Contents:* 1 Silver Halide Photographic Materials; 2 Structure and Preparation of Silver Halide
Grains; 3 Physical Properties of Silver Halides; 4 Mechanism of Latent Image Formation;
5 Spectral Sensitization; 6 Chemical Sensitization and Stabilization; 7 Development —
Amplification of Latent Image; 8 Future Prospect of Silver Halide Photography.
*Why it matters:* the modern physical account, written from inside a manufacturer's research
laboratory after tabular-grain technology. It supplies the quantum-level constraints — the
detective-quantum-efficiency budget, the atom-count thresholds for developability, the two
development types — that tell us which of our heuristics are the wrong shape. → §5, §10, §12, §17.
*Integrity:* ⚠ every display equation is image-only in the OCR. The equations quoted in this
document were recovered by reading the rendered page images directly; see §29.3.

**S5 — Reilly, IPI 1993 (rev. 1996).**
James M. Reilly, Director, Image Permanence Institute, Rochester Institute of Technology,
70 Lomb Memorial Drive, Rochester NY 14623-5604. *IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film.* © 1993
with a minor revision 1996. 24 PDF pages.
*Contents:* the storage "Wheel", time-contour predictions, free-acidity levels and A-D strip
levels, the stages of acetate decomposition, physical consequences, storage recommendations,
nitrate, polyester, identification.
*Why it matters:* the quantitative authority on acetate base degradation, and — importantly — the
source that states plainly which parts of it do *not* reach the photographic image. → §21, §22, §23.

**S6 — NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020.**
Monique Fischer, *A Short Guide to Film Base Photographic Materials: Identification, Care, and
Duplication.* Northeast Document Conservation Center, 100 Brickstone Square, Andover MA
01810-1494. Preservation Leaflets, Photographs 5.1, © 2020. 6 PDF pages. Cites ISO 18916:2007
(Photographic Activity Test) and a 2006 Society of American Archivists title.
*Why it matters:* a second, 27-years-later account of the same material, which lets base
chronology and decomposition staging be cross-checked rather than taken from one source. Where it
differs from S5, both are recorded. → §21, §22.

**Addendum, 2026-09-01 — two later additions, read in full but not part of the six-document
chronological spine.** They are single-topic primary documents rather than surveys, so they are
registered here and treated in their own sections rather than woven through §2.

**S7 — US 4,495,277 (1985).** Becker, Klötzer and Moisar; assignee Agfa-Gevaert AG, Leverkusen;
filed 1983-08-01. Agfa's own core/shell emulsion patent, and the only document in this corpus
written from inside Agfa's emulsion laboratory. → §23e, where what it does and does **not** license
is set out in full.

**S8 — Ōue & Takano 1965.** Physical Society of Japan abstract 10p-A-2, p269, from Fuji Photo Film
Research Laboratories. Granularity Wiener spectra for five emulsions indexed by AgX **crystal
size** rather than by product — the only such source here. → §23f, §17.

**S9 — Trumpy & Gschwind 2015.** ACM JOCCH 8(2) Art. 7, Digital Humanities Lab, Basel. A
dust-and-scratch detection paper whose Fig. 5 carries the second measured Callier Q(D) in
this corpus, redrawn after Streiffert 1947. → §23g, §24.

**S10 — Flueckiger et al. 2018.** University of Zurich / DIASTOR scanner study,
88 pages. Its emulsion content — the Technicolor No. IV transfer dyes and the Dufaycolor réseau
transmittances — is treated in §23h; its scanner content is in `SCANNER_CHARACTERISTICS.md`,
deliberately kept out of this document and out of the film database.

**S11 — 日本写真学会会誌, eighteen offprints 1938–1963.** The Japanese photographic
society's journal. Two papers are load-bearing — Sayanagi's theory of the Callier Q factor and
Ooue's granularity instrument, which states the aperture behind S8 — and twelve more carry
supporting science. → §23i.

### 1.2 What the set covers, and what it does not

| Topic | Coverage in this set |
|---|---|
| Emulsion chemistry and crystal physics | Strong — S3 and S4, two eras |
| Latent image and quantum sensitivity | Strong — S4 |
| Development mechanism and kinetics | Strong — S4, with S3 for the chemistry |
| Manufacturing practice | Strong — S2 (1929) and S3 (1966) |
| Period sensitometry and real measured stocks | Strong for ~1920 — S1 only |
| Film base and its aging | Strong — S5, S6, with S3 and S2 as period snapshots |
| **rms granularity values** | ⚠ **Absent.** No source gives an rms granularity figure, a σ-versus-density relation, or a grain-size→granularity number. The Selwyn constant *G* appears only inside the DQE expression. → §17 |
| **MTF curves, f50 figures, adjacency overshoot** | ⚠ **Absent.** No source in this set plots an MTF or gives an f50. Resolving power appears; frequency response does not. → §18 |
| **Halation magnitude or radius** | ⚠ **Absent.** The 1929 source treats halation extensively as a *manufacturing problem to suppress* and never measures it. → §18 |
| Per-stock data for any stock in our current database | ⚠ **Absent.** None of the six is a datasheet for a stock we model. S1's survey materials are anonymised by the authors and are ~1920 plates. |

**The single most important thing to understand about this source set:** it is rich in mechanism
and poor in the specific per-stock numbers our schema stores. Its value is therefore mostly
*structural* — it constrains the form our models should take and identifies which of our current
parameters are physically independent and which are not. §25–§27 act on that distinction rather
than pretending otherwise.

## 2. The chronological spine: what the six sources document changing between 1920 and 1996

### 2.0 Method, and the limits of the method

This section is the document's time axis. Everything later in the knowledge base that carries a number, a mechanism or a behaviour is meant to be read against it, because almost nothing in photographic emulsion technology held still across the twentieth century, and the sources that describe the century do not describe it evenly.

Four rules govern what follows.

**First, only documented change is reported as change.** Where a source says in its own voice that something was formerly one way and is now another — "some years ago … present-day emulsions frequently have no more than 100 grams of gelatin per gram molecule of silver" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)]` — that is a documented change, and it is labelled as such. Where two sources from different decades simply describe different practice without either of them comparing the two, that is *inference from juxtaposition*, and it is labelled as the weaker evidence it is. The distinction matters constantly: a 1929 book giving iodide contents of 1–5 mol % and a 1995 book giving 3 mol % as typical do not, between them, establish that iodide content fell — neither author is speaking about the other's era.

**Second, a publication date is not the date of the practice a book describes.** Davis & Walters is printed 1922 but its survey work "was begun in the spring of 1920" and its dateline is Washington, 6 September 1921; the materials it charts are the American market of 1920, and the paper itself warns that the market had already moved: "Materials now on the market may have, therefore, higher sensitiveness than given on these charts… In a year one maker's product whose film was only slightly orthochromatic and slow in speed more than doubled in speed and color sensitiveness" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.33–34 (PDF 34–35)]`. Wall 1929 is worse in this respect and says so: much of its doctrine is quoted from Eder's *Handbuch* of 1903, and the book's own historical authority, T. Bolas, asserts that "there is nothing of fundamental importance in emulsion matters that was not published in the early eighties" `[Wall 1929, Ch. XIII, p.242 (PDF 249)]`. Duffin 1966 carries a preface dated January 1965. Tani 1995 explicitly positions itself as an account of what changed since James's *The Theory of the Photographic Process*, 4th edition, of 1977 `[Tani 1995, Preface, p.vi (PDF 7)]`, so its "recently" means post-1977 and usually post-1983. Reilly's storage guide is © 1993, minor revision 1996, and its polyester commentary is anchored to "nearly 50 years of manufacturing and keeping experience" `[Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)]`; the NEDCC leaflet is © 2020 but, as shown in §2.9, is in several respects a *narrower* chronology than the 1993 document, not a more current one.

**Third, the sources are not a continuous record.** They sample 1920, 1929, 1966 and 1995, plus a base-materials chronology reaching to 1951/1955 dates and a 2020 restatement. There are two large gaps — roughly 1930–1964 and 1967–1976 — in which the sources report events (gold sensitization, colour film, coloured couplers, DIR couplers) only retrospectively, as dated milestones inside a later book. Any statement about those decades in this document is a milestone date, not a description of practice.

**Fourth, absence is reported.** Where a source could have documented a property and did not, that silence is stated, because the alternative — silently importing a later era's value — is exactly the error this section exists to prevent.

Each thread below runs early- to late-century and closes with a one-line **state of evidence** note.

---

### 2.1 Emulsion composition and structure

#### 2.1.1 The 1920 and 1929 object: one layer, on glass

In 1920 the object under test is a single sensitive layer on glass, or the same layer on nitrate celluloid. The definition is flat: "A photographic dry plate is a sheet of glass on which is coated a thin layer of gelatin containing the light-sensitive silver bromide (or other silver halide). A film has the sensitive layer coated on celluloid" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.3 (PDF 4)]`. Of the 86 charted materials, 71 are plates on glass and only 12 are films plus 3 aerial materials `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.34 (PDF 35)]`. **[F]**

The only structural elaboration recognised in 1920 is *double coating*, used as an anti-halation device and treated as a product sub-class in its own right: charts 21–23 (ordinary), 53–60 (orthochromatic) and 67–68 (panchromatic) are captioned "Double coated (nonhalation)" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.34 (PDF 35)]`. **[F]**

Wall 1929 gives the composition numbers the 1920 paper does not. Ten commercial plates analysed by Tappen & Rekaschow yield a mean dried coating of **0.43724 g per 100 cm²**, comprising **42.6 % silver halide, 50 % gelatine and 7.5 % residual water**, i.e. a **gelatine-to-halide ratio of 1.3 : 1** `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, pp.157–158 (PDF 164–165)]`. **[Q]** Two arithmetic cautions belong with that figure. Converted, 0.43724 g/100 cm² is **43.7 g/m²** of layer solids plus bound water — a conversion of ours, not the book's. **[E]** And Wall's "mean" is the sum of nine retained values divided by ten; the true mean of the nine he keeps is **0.4858 g/100 cm² (48.6 g/m²)** `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, pp.157–158 (PDF 164–165)]`. **[E]** Use 0.437 to reproduce the book, 0.486 to reproduce its own data. ⚠ **And the composition half of that headline is not merely rounded, it is impossible**: C and D are complementary in every row, so their means must sum to 100, and Wall's "42.6 % halide / 50 % gelatine" sums to 92.6. The true pair is **42.363 / 57.637**. Only the ratio he quotes, 1.3 : 1, survives — because a ratio is immune to the divisor error that produced the rest. Full working in §3.3.1a. **[E]**

Wall also documents the 1929 layer-count situation candidly, and it is a negative result: the genuine two-layer structure patented by J. T. Sandell in 1891 (Eng. Pat. 21,381), "who actually coated first a very slow, opaque emulsion and then on top a faster and more translucent one", had by 1929 largely degenerated into a marketing term — "so-called double-coated plates on the market are merely coated with an extra quantity of emulsion, and not actually double-coated" `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]`. **[F]** This is a documented *regression* in structural sophistication between 1891 and 1929, stated by the source.

Individual composition figures for 1929: negative emulsions are silver bromide with **1–5 % silver iodide** `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.34 (PDF 42)]`, with 3–4 % preferred for landscape and 1–2 % or none for ammonia portrait emulsions `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.35 (PDF 43)]`; 10 % is "not commercially met with" `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.35–36 (PDF 43–44)]`. Positive, lantern and paper emulsions are chloride or chlorobromide, and Valenta's analyses of commercial chlorobromide plates give chloride-to-bromide ratios from **50:50 (German) to 15:85 (English)** and gelatine-to-halide ratios of **2:1 to 6:1** in English products `[Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.97 (PDF 104)]`. **[Q]** Note that the 2:1–6:1 paper/positive ratio and the 1.3:1 negative-plate ratio are different product classes, not a change over time.

#### 2.1.2 1966: the gelatin-to-silver ratio falls, and the layer stack acquires named functions

Duffin gives the single clearest documented composition change in the whole corpus, in the book's own voice:

> "Some years ago, many plate-coated emulsions had as much as **300–400 grams of gelatin per gram molecule of silver** and the same was true of some film emulsions. Such a ratio gives an emulsion layer which is far too thick for present-day standards; it would possess a slow rate of development, poor drying characteristics and low sharpness. Present-day emulsions frequently have **no more than 100 grams of gelatin per gram molecule of silver**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)]` **[Q]**

That is a stated three- to four-fold reduction in binder per unit silver, with three named image-level consequences (development rate, drying, sharpness). It is corroborated elsewhere in the same book by the coating chapter's remark that "Satisfactory performance of modern silver-halide materials stems from the correct silver/gelatin ratio and therefore the emulsion chemist is not free to vary this at will", explicitly contrasted with "earlier years… the principal consideration was that of gelatin concentration" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` **[F]**, and by the supercoat chapter's driver: "With the modern tendency to use less gelatin, leaving the grains more unprotected…" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.166 (PDF 172)]` **[F]**.

There is a floor on the reduction: "For satisfactory coating of emulsion by standard procedures and using gelatins of average viscosity and strength, the gelatin concentration cannot be permitted to drop appreciably below 5 %" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)]` **[Q]**, and the extreme case shows what the floor is for — nuclear-track emulsions run "as little as 20 g per g mole, so that there is very little free space; they are almost solid silver bromide" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.187–188 (PDF 193–194)]` **[Q]**.

Duffin's layer stack is still schematically simple — supercoat / emulsion / base / backing `[Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15), Fig. 1.1]` **[M]** — but the thickness envelope is now stated and is the first real geometry in the corpus: emulsion **30–600 µm at the coating point, 2–40 µm dry**; supercoats and filter layers **1–3 µm dry**; and, critically, "**Colour materials** frequently contain a large number of layers, **all of them 1–3 µm thick in the dry state**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]`. **[Q]** The colour tripack order is given explicitly, top down: supercoat / blue-sensitive / yellow filter layer / green-sensitive / red-sensitive / support `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.195–196 (PDF 201–202)]`. **[F]** Overall colour films are thinner than X-ray films `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.202 (PDF 208)]` **[F]**, and X-ray films are "coated at very high coating weights to increase the likelihood of absorption" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.187–188 (PDF 193–194)]` **[F]**.

One important absence: Duffin defines coating weight as the controlled quantity — "It is the silver-halide coating weight which must be controlled in order to obtain a satisfactory photographic response" — but **never prints a g/m² figure for it** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)]`. **[F]** So the corpus has a 1929 coating weight and no 1966 one; the two cannot be compared.

#### 2.1.3 1995: fourteen layers, twenty micrometres, a hundred organic compounds

Tani's description of a typical ISO 100 colour negative film is the end point of the thread and the most quantitative composition statement in the corpus:

> "On a film base there are blue-, green-, and red-sensitive layers, which are coated one over the other. Moreover, each color-sensitive layer is composed of high-speed, medium-speed, and low-speed sublayers, which are also coated one over the other. A photosensitive layer in a typical color negative film is composed of **about 14 layers** with different functions and is about **20 µm thick** in total. There are **12 million silver halide grains per square millimeter** and **more than 100 kinds of functional organic compounds** in a film." `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]` **[Q]**

Restated elsewhere with the pixel accounting: **1.2 × 10⁷ grains/mm²**, **2 × 10⁷ equivalent pixels per 36 × 24 mm² frame**, hence **≈43 µm² per equivalent pixel containing about 500 silver halide grains** `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28), Fig. 1.13]`. **[Q]** Packing density is deliberately low — "A large number of fine and well-designed silver halide grains are separately and randomly arranged in thin gelatin layers with a relatively low packing density to achieve fine imaging. However, this arrangement prevents grains in these layers from absorbing incident light efficiently" `[Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]` **[M]** — but **no numeric volume fraction is given anywhere** `[Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]`. **[F]**

Tani also makes the structural comparison across the whole 150 years explicitly, which is the corpus's only end-to-end statement on this thread:

> "The remarkable progress in silver halide photography during these 150 years is evident when we compare the composition of a Daguerreotype with a current color film. The former is a black-and-white photosensitive material with a thin layer of AgI, while the latter is a color film with many well-designed silver halide grains and many functional organic compounds." … "there have been **many changes in structure** during its long history." `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.5 (PDF 14)]` **[F]**

#### 2.1.4 Layer-count and composition summary

| Era | Layers | Layer thickness | Silver : gelatin | Coating weight | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c.1920 | 1 emulsion layer; "double coated" as a product sub-class | not stated | not stated | not stated | `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.3, 34 (PDF 4, 35)]` |
| c.1929 | 1; genuine 2-layer structure (1891) largely lapsed to a marketing term | not stated in µm; judged optically | gelatine : halide 1.3 : 1 (negative plates); 2:1–6:1 (chlorobromide) | 0.43724 g/100 cm² (≈43.7 g/m², conv. ours) | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, pp.157–158 (PDF 164–165); Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91); Ch. V, p.97 (PDF 104)]` |
| c.1966 | b&w 1 + supercoat + backing; colour "a large number" | b&w 2–40 µm dry (30–600 µm wet); supercoat/filter 1–3 µm; colour layers all 1–3 µm | ≤100 g gelatin per g-mole Ag (was 300–400); floor 5 % gelatin in coating melt; nuclear-track 20 g/mole | defined as the controlled quantity but **no value printed** | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83); Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159); Ch. IX, pp.187–188 (PDF 193–194)]` |
| c.1995 | ≈14 functional layers (3 colour records × 3 speed sublayers + interlayers) | ≈20 µm total photosensitive stack | not stated as a ratio | not stated; areal grain count 1.2 × 10⁷ mm⁻² instead | `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12); §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)]` |

**State of evidence.** Genuinely documented change on two points — the gelatin-to-silver ratio (Duffin states the before and after himself) and the single-layer-to-multilayer transition (Tani states it himself, and Duffin dates the colour tripack's commercialisation to the 1930s); everything else in this thread, including layer thickness and coating weight, is four eras' practice described independently, with no source comparing the numbers, and the 1966 coating weight is simply missing.

---

### 2.2 Grain and crystal characteristics

#### 2.2.1 1920: grain exists only as a resolution number and a speed penalty

Davis & Walters measure no grain size and print no size distribution. Grain enters the 1920 paper twice: as a resolution limit — "For ordinary photographic negatives, this limit lies between four ten-thousandths and sixteen ten-thousandths inch (one-hundredth to four-hundredths mm)" `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–31 (PDF 30–32)]`, i.e. **0.01–0.04 mm** **[Q]** — and as a class-level correlate of speed: ultra-fast plates "fog easily, and have large grain, therefore not the best resolving power"; fast plates have "slightly finer grain"; very slow plates are "thinly coated. The grain size is usually small, hence they give excellent resolution" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.4 (PDF 5)]`. **[F]** The paper qualifies the rule itself: "As a general rule, the faster a plate the larger will be its grain size and the poorer its resolution… **But this is not strictly true**" `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–31 (PDF 30–32)]`. **[F]** Two other factors are named as competing with grain for resolution: **irradiation** ("the spreading of the image due to the reflection of light in the film from one silver grain to another") and "the spreading of the image in development" `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–31 (PDF 30–32)]`. **[M]** The measured resolution numbers across the 86 materials span **12 to 28** thousandths of a millimetre, i.e. 0.012–0.028 mm `[Davis & Walters 1922, PDF 36–121]`. **[Q]**

#### 2.2.2 1929: grain as a manufacturing defect, controlled by colloid concentration and monitored by eye

Wall gives "no numerical grain sizes, no measured size distributions, and no micrograph data of his own" `[Wall 1929, Ch. III]`. **[F]** Grain in 1929 is a *manufacturing* variable, and the levers are qualitative: protective-colloid concentration, with high gelatine for fine grain and slow speed and "as low as ~1 % in the mix" for fast emulsions, below which "coarse grain and fog will ensue" `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.31, 52 (PDF 39, 60)]` **[Q]**; excess bromide, which coarsens by Ostwald ripening — "the finer particles of silver bromide are dissolved by the excess and in the course of ripening are deposited on the larger grains, thus giving increased sensitiveness" `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.33 (PDF 41)]` **[M]**; and alcohol, iodide addition order, stirring and dilution, all named without numbers `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.31–32, 39, 47 (PDF 39–40, 47, 55)]`. **[M]**

The working measurement instrument is the human eye. The **dip test** reads ripening state from transmitted colour on a glass slide: "blood-red → orange → green → blue (stop) → greyish-violet (fogged)" `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.72 (PDF 79)]`. **[F]** That is the state of grain metrology in the 1929 factory.

Two 1920s research results are cited but not reproduced: Trivelli & Sheppard's 122 photomicrographs at ×2500, which found no instance of separate hexagonal AgI and regular AgBr crystals and so established the mixed-crystal nature of iodobromide `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.38–39 (PDF 46–47)]` **[F]**; and Renwick & Sease's sedimentation study, the corpus's only pre-1966 statement about the *distribution* rather than the mean — "the percentage of silver iodide and of coarse grains in the lower strata of emulsions, allowed to settle, was much higher than in the upper strata", which Wall dismisses as "probably only due to a particular method of mixing" `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.37 (PDF 45)]`. **[F]** Carroll & Hubbard's Bureau of Standards tables of "grain size, fog and gammas" (1927) are cited as a pointer only, with no data carried over `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.27–28 (PDF 35–36)]`. **[F]**

#### 2.2.3 1966: numbers appear, monodispersity does not

Duffin supplies the corpus's first quantitative grain figures for a named commercial stock class. The archetype is "a normal fast iodobromide emulsion of the type used for **Kodak Tri-X** and similar types of film", specified as **3.1 mol % iodide** and **mean grain 1.2–1.4 µ² surface area** — note the unit is surface area, not diameter `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)]`. **[Q]** Related figures: **4 × 10¹⁴ grains per gram-mole of silver**; a triangular grain surface area of **≈2 µ²**; a fine-grain emulsion of **0.2 µ side**; AgBr crystal thickness **0.2–0.3 µ** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.142 (PDF 148); Ch. VI, p.133 (PDF 139)]`. **[Q]** Approximately **3 × 10⁸ silver ions on the surface** of one grain of the archetype emulsion `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.94–95 (PDF 100–101)]`. **[Q]**

Duffin also records the surface-area anomaly that constrains any surface-site model: "optimum quantity of sulphur sensitizer varies very little with the grain size of the emulsion. When one considers that crystals of one micron diameter will possess roughly ten times the surface area of crystals of 0.1 micron diameter, then this is a very surprising fact indeed and points undeniably to the concept that only certain selected sites on each crystal need to collect their 'coating' of silver sulphide" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.86–87 (PDF 92–93)]`. **[Q]**

What Duffin does *not* have is the vocabulary of controlled size distribution. Monodispersity is absent as a term. Continuous precipitation exists but is a frontier: continuous processes are "more modern ways of making photographic emulsions", with conditions "quite different from those of the more classical procedures" — named and not described `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.57 (PDF 61)]`. **[F]** Tabular grains do not appear.

One temperature-regime distinction in Duffin is itself a dated statement about grain growth: ammonia emulsions "ripen rapidly and frequently a temperature of 40 °C or 45 °C is quite high enough", whereas without ammonia excess bromide alone requires "much higher temperatures … frequently up to 70 °C. and **in earlier days even higher**" — hence the older name "neutral or boiled emulsions" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.66 (PDF 70)]`. **[Q]**

#### 2.2.4 1995: habit, monodispersity and tabular technology, with dates

Tani's chapter opening is the corpus's explicit claim of change on this thread:

> "The preparation of silver halide grains in photographic emulsions is one of the most important technologies … and **significant progress has been made over the last decades to make silver halide grains controllable with respect to size, shape, halide distribution, and crystal defects. Monodispersed silver halide grains with sophisticated structures are being developed.**" `[Tani 1995, Ch. 2 opening, p.24 (PDF 33)]` **[F]**

The 1995 crystallography: face-centred cubic, space group Fm3m; seven possible regular forms, of which only cube and octahedron are stable because "Only {100} and {111} faces are usually stable on the grain surface" `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33), Figs. 2.1, 2.2]` **[F]**; face fractions P₁₀₀ and P₁₁₁ summing to 1, measured via differential absorption of 9-methyl-thiacarbocyanine dyes `[Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.24–25 (PDF 33–34)]` **[F]**. Grain size: "The average size of the silver halide grains usually used is around 1 µm, ranging from less than 0.1 µm to several micrometres" `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33)]`. **[Q]** Composition set: AgBr, AgCl, and mixed crystals of AgBr with AgI and/or AgCl and of AgCl with AgBr and/or AgI `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33)]`. **[F]** Double-structured core/shell grains — AgBrI core, AgBr shell — are illustrated with an X-ray diffraction profile `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.29 (PDF 38), Fig. 2.7]` **[F]**, and their purpose is stated as inhibiting "harmful photographic effects of iodide ions such as retardation of development" `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]`. **[F]** Epitaxial grains — a cubic AgCl host with eight AgBr(Cl) guest crystals at the corners — are also 1995 practice `[Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.29–30 (PDF 38–39), Fig. 2.8]`. **[F]**

The two dated technology claims are the ones a period-aware model needs.

**Monodispersity.** "monodispersed cubic and octahedral silver halide emulsion grains were prepared and **have been refined for many years**", the primary references being Berry & Skillman **1962** and Klein & Moisar **1962–1963**, with Moisar **1991** `[Tani 1995, §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)]`. **[F]** The mechanism is stated: monodispersity requires **diffusion-controlled** growth, in which "a small grain grows faster than a large grain, and the difference in r among initially formed grains decreases"; under **reaction control** the growth-rate exponents (dr/dt ∝ r² for the mononuclear-layer mechanism, ∝ r⁰ for the polynuclear-layer mechanism) cannot produce monodispersity `[Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.34–35 (PDF 43–44), Fig. 2.14]`. **[M]** Wey & Strong's mixing experiment confirms the supersaturation dependence: the size difference "decreased under a high degree of supersaturation, whereas the difference increased under a low degree of supersaturation" `[Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.34–35 (PDF 43–44)]`. **[F]**

**Tabular grains.** The book is careful, and its care is the datum:

> "In addition to three-dimensional grains, tabular silver halide emulsion grains **have been prepared for a long time**. **Recently, much progress has been made in the preparation and sensitization of tabular grains, since the advantages of tabular grains for various photographic materials have been proposed and recognized.**" `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.25 (PDF 34)]` **[F]**

The "long time" reference is Berriman & Herz, *Nature* **180**, 293 (**1957**) — the twin-plane X-ray proof. The "recent progress" references are *Research Disclosure* Item 22534, **225**, 20 (**January 1983**); Kofron & Booms (**1986**); Sowinski & Wightman (**1987**); Jacobson, Axford & Ford (**1990**) `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.25 (PDF 34)]`. **[F]** Tabular grains are therefore, on this source's own citation trail, a **post-1983 commercial attribute**, with the underlying crystallography known since 1957. **[E]** The book states that "tabular grains are the most important for the present and in the future in photographic materials" `[Tani 1995, §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)]` **[F]**, but says **nothing about which commercial stocks adopted them or when** `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.25 (PDF 34)]`. **[F]**

Tabular geometry as given: hexagonal tabular grains carry two twin planes on {111} lattice planes parallel to the main surfaces, formed by stacking faults `[Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.25–26 (PDF 34–35), Figs. 2.3, 2.4]` **[F]**; Maskasky found an even number of parallel twin planes in large hexagonal grains and an odd number in large triangular ones, while Black et al. found "no obvious correlation between the external shape and the number of twin planes" `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.26 (PDF 35)]` **[F]**; tabular AgBr grains with a (100) surface face and no twin plane also exist (Mignot et al.) `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.26 (PDF 35)]` **[F]**. Study thickness is **0.1 µm**, characterised by equivalent circular diameter D_c `[Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.39–40 (PDF 48–49), Fig. 2.17]` **[Q]**. **No aspect-ratio figure is stated anywhere in the range** `[Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.39–40 (PDF 48–49)]`. **[F]**

Iodide's structural role is also new relative to 1966: a pure AgBr tabular grain shows no dislocation, while "the generation of dislocations at the interface between different silver halide phases" is seen in a tabular silver iodobromide grain of composition printed as `AgBr09I0 |` — decimal points lost in OCR, evidently AgBr₀.₉I₀.₁, i.e. 10 mol % iodide `[Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.31–32 (PDF 40–41), Fig. 2.10]`. **[Q]** Twinning is enhanced by, among other factors, "a high concentration of iodide ions" `[Tani 1995, §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)]`. **[F]** Iodide also acts electronically, as a shallow isoelectronic hole trap: localization energy **0.04 eV** for an isolated iodide ion, **0.1–0.15 eV** for an iodide ion pair `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.71 (PDF 80)]`. **[Q]**

Finally, the crystallite/grain distinction: "In the absence of crystal defect, the crystallite size is the same as the grain size, whereas the former is smaller than the latter in the presence of crystal defects… many regular silver halide grains in emulsions were crystallographically perfect, whereas there were also many silver halide emulsion grains that contained many crystal defects and were divided into small crystallites, forming a mosaic structure" `[Tani 1995, §2.1, p.32 (PDF 41)]`. **[F]** And Farnell's optimum: grains with few defects *and* grains with too many defects both show low efficiency, "grains with a medium number of defects showed the highest sensitivity" `[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.89–90 (PDF 98–99)]`. **[F]**

#### 2.2.5 Grain chronology summary

| Property | c.1920 | c.1929 | c.1966 | c.1995 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Size measured? | no | no | yes, as surface area (1.2–1.4 µ²) | yes, ~1 µm mean, <0.1 to several µm range |
| Habit controlled? | not discussed | not discussed | not discussed as habit | cube/octahedron/tabular/epitaxial, P₁₀₀/P₁₁₁ formalism |
| Size distribution | not discussed | one sedimentation result, dismissed | not discussed; "continuous precipitation" named only | monodispersity a design target since 1962, refined for decades |
| Iodide content | not stated | 1–5 mol % (negative) | 3.1 mol % (Tri-X archetype) | 3 mol % cited for absorption gain; up to 10 mol % in tabular study grains |
| Tabular grains | — | — | — | crystallography from 1957; technology "recent", refs 1983–1990 |
| Grain count | — | — | 4 × 10¹⁴ per g-mole Ag | 1.2 × 10⁷ per mm² of layer |
| Citations | `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.4, 29–31 (PDF 5, 30–32)]` | `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.31–39 (PDF 39–47)]` | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100); Ch. VII, p.142 (PDF 148)]` | `[Tani 1995, §2.1–2.2, pp.24–40 (PDF 33–49)]` |

**State of evidence.** One documented change stated by a source in its own voice — Tani's "significant progress … over the last decades" in size, shape, halide distribution and defect control, with tabular technology dated by its own citations to 1983–1990 and monodispersity to 1962 onward. Everything before that is four eras describing different things with different instruments: 1920 and 1929 do not measure grain at all, so no 1920→1966 size trend can be extracted, and the iodide figures across eras are product-class statements, not a documented trend.

---

### 2.3 Sensitivity and chemical sensitization technology

This is the thread where the corpus is strongest, because three of the four technical books date the milestones themselves and the fourth shows what the technology looked like before any of them existed.

#### 2.3.1 The overall gain, and the figure that shows it

Tani states the century-and-a-half result outright:

> "Judging from the exposure time needed for taking a Daguerreotype picture, photographic sensitivity was increased by **more than 10⁶ times over the past 150 years and is still increasing**, as shown in Fig. 1.1." `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12), Fig. 1.1]` **[Q]**

Fig. 1.1 is captioned "Change in sensitivity of silver halide photographic materials" and is itself an amendment of a figure in S. Ooue, *Seimitsu Kikai* **32**, 300 (1966) `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12), Fig. 1.1]`. **[F]** The anchors at the low end are given: 1826, Niépce's heliography on asphalt, whose modern reproduction by Marignier "had to expose to sunlight a photosensitive plate of heliographie for **5 days**"; and 1839, the Daguerreotype — "a thin layer of AgI was the photosensitive material, and a latent image was revealed by a development process with mercury vapor. However, it still took **many minutes** to take a picture" `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]`. **[Q]** Note carefully what this figure is and is not: it is a **10⁶ gain measured from 1839**, not from 1920, and the corpus contains no comparable curve for the twentieth century alone.

There is a second, tighter comparative snapshot: Fig. 1.7 plots "various photosensitive materials produced and studied **in 1970**", and Fig. 1.8 the same for "the various photosensitive materials **presently in use**", both on axes of sensitivity (ASA or 1/(erg/cm²)) against resolving power in line pairs per millimetre `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20), Figs. 1.7, 1.8]`. **[Q]** The envelope law of that map is stated: Ooue "derived the equation used in the preparation of this figure by making the sensitivity proportional to the reciprocal of the resolving power squared", i.e. **S ∝ R⁻²** `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20)]`. **[Q]** That is a family-level envelope for the whole field of photosensitive materials, not a within-brand rule. **[E]**

#### 2.3.2 1920: no chemical sensitization at all

The most telling fact about Davis & Walters is an absence. Its account of emulsion preparation runs: soluble halides in gelatin, silver nitrate added, ripening at "a definite temperature until it develops the desired characteristics", setting, shredding, washing in cold water, optional further ripening "by standing at ordinary temperatures", melting and coating `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.3–4 (PDF 4–5)]`. **[F]** The listed sensitive variables are "the purity of the salts used, the proportions used, the rate and temperature of mixing, the concentration of the solutions used, the character of the gelatin, the temperature and time of ripening, the character of the water used in washing the emulsion, and the rate of drying" `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.3–4 (PDF 4–5)]`. **[F]** There is **no mention of sulphur or gold chemical sensitization, no double-jet precipitation, no controlled grain-size distribution, no hardeners and no anti-halation undercoat on film** `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.3–4 (PDF 4–5)]`. **[F]** Sensitivity in 1920 is bought with ripening time and temperature and with "the character of the gelatin", and "The formulas used and most of the other conditions of manufacture are trade secrets" `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.3–4 (PDF 4–5)]`. **[F]**

The consequence is measurable. Across the 86 charted materials the Bureau of Standards speed (10/i) spans **B.S. 18 to 1050** using only unambiguous values, about 58× `[Davis & Walters 1922, PDF 36–121]`. **[Q]** Class ceilings: ordinary single-coated plates 145–1050; orthochromatic single-coated 78–600; panchromatic single-coated 80–180 and panchromatic double-coated 75–350 `[Davis & Walters 1922, PDF 36–121]`. **[Q]**

#### 2.3.3 1925–1929: Sheppard, and the discovery that gelatin was the sensitizer

Wall 1929 records the break, and calls it what it is: Sheppard's 1925 identification of "Gelatine X" as **allyl isothiocyanate** is "the most important contribution to the science and practice of emulsion making yet published" `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.25–27 (PDF 33–35)]`. **[F]** The quantities are given: **1 : 1,000,000 to 1 : 300,000** relative to the emulsion, forming a silver complex which in alkali splits to **silver sulphide** plus cyanamide, guanidine and alkaline bromide, the Ag₂S nuclei being the sensitivity centres — but they "must form nuclei discretely and not above a certain size", and "The action reaches a maximum effect for a certain quantity and then decreases as the amount of the active material is increased, with corresponding increase in fog" `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.25–27 (PDF 33–35)]`. **[Q]** Other agents of the same order are named: sodium thiosulphate, Na₂SeSO₃, K₂Te₂O₃, potassium isoselenocyanate — "all these combine with the silver halides to form decomposable complexes" `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.26 (PDF 34)]`. **[F]** Lumière's riposte the same year reports ~900 substances screened, six named sensitizers (aesculin, codeine, thebaine, diethylenediamine, thiocarbamide, guanidine sulphocyanate) already in commercial use and previously unpublished `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.27 (PDF 35)]`. **[F]**

Crucially, in 1929 this knowledge is not yet a *control* technology. Speed is still bought with **ammonia** (English practice sp. gr. 0.880 ≈ 35 % NH₃; American 0.90 ≈ 28 %, "the latter is one-fifth weaker") or with a boil at **95–98 °C**, and paid for in fog `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.11 (PDF 19); Ch. III, p.29 (PDF 37); Ch. IV, p.56 (PDF 64)]`. **[Q]** Wall states the era's unsolved problem plainly: "Of all problems in photography that of making a really fast clean-working emulsion with a decently high gamma infinity is about the hardest. Speed may be obtained but with too much fog; reduce the latter to reasonable limits and down goes the speed in the most unaccountable fashion" `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.70–71 (PDF 77–78)]`. **[F]**

The 1929 speed envelope, in H&D numbers (the only system named in the book): slow clean plate **22 H&D** with high γ∞ and D_fog 0.10 at 10 min in pyro-soda; slow/process **25 H&D at γ = 3**; "slow negative" **150–200 H&D**; fast **225 H&D** (Harris) to **250 H&D with γ∞ = 1.3** `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32); Ch. VII, p.135 (PDF 142); Ch. III, p.30 (PDF 38); Ch. XIII, p.225 (PDF 232)]`. **[Q]**

#### 2.3.4 The dated milestone table

Tani's Table 6.1 carries an "Origin" column, and it is the corpus's cleanest chronology of sensitization chemistry.

| Sensitization type | Date and event, as printed | Sensitizer | Centre | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sulfur | **1871**, introduction of gelatin (Maddox); **1925**, discovery (Sheppard) | sodium thiosulfate, allylthiourea | (Ag₂S)₂, solid-solution type | `[Tani 1995, Table 6.1, p.167 (PDF 176)]` |
| Gold | **1936**, discovery (Koslowsky) | KAuCl₄ + KSCN, Au(SCN)₂⁻, Au(S₂O₃)₂³⁻ | Au⁺ | `[Tani 1995, Table 6.1, p.167 (PDF 176)]` |
| Reduction | **1933**, sensitization by sulfite (Carroll); **1951**, concept (Lowe, Roberts & Jones) | SnCl₂, thiourea dioxide, hydrazine derivatives | Ag₂ at neutral site (R centre); Ag₂ at positive kink site (P centre) | `[Tani 1995, Table 6.1, p.167 (PDF 176)]` |

All **[F]**. The supporting text is explicit that sulfur sensitization arrived by accident: "it is believed that sulfur sensitization was introduced into silver halide photographic materials when Maddox used gelatin for these materials in 1871" `[Tani 1995, §6.2, p.167 (PDF 176)]` **[F]**; and that Sheppard found it by chasing gelatin variability — "Focusing on the fact that photographic sensitivity depended remarkably upon the kind of gelatin used, Sheppard analyzed the chemical contents of gelatin and discovered in 1925 that sulfur compounds could increase photographic sensitivity" `[Tani 1995, §6.2, p.167 (PDF 176)]` **[F]**. Gold: "In collaboration with Mueller in 1936, Koslowsky discovered gold sensitization by the use of chloroauric acid and thiocyanate" `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.176 (PDF 185)]`. **[F]** Reduction: "Carroll and Hubbard observed chemical sensitization using sodium sulfite as early as 1933. Paying attention to its difference from sulfur sensitization, the concept of reduction sensitization was introduced by Lowe et al. in 1951" `[Tani 1995, §6.4, p.180 (PDF 189)]`. **[F]**

Duffin, writing thirty years closer to the event, dates gold independently and consistently: "**About thirty years ago** a further method … was discovered by the **Agfa** workers", i.e. approximately the mid-1930s `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.91–92 (PDF 97–98)]`. **[F]** He also dates the organic stabilizer family: "Some **thirty years ago**" heterocyclic stabilizers were discovered, the parent 4-hydroxy-6-methyl-1,3,3a,7-tetrazaindene "discovered to be a stabilizer by **Birr in 1935**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.138 (PDF 144)]`. **[F]** And palladium for the fastest emulsions was raised at "a conference in **London in 1960** on the maximum sensitivity of photographic materials" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)]`. **[F]**

#### 2.3.5 1966: from operator-controlled digestion to metered addition

Duffin documents the transition from gelatin-as-sensitizer to sensitizer-as-ingredient in his own voice, and this is one of the most consequential documented changes in the corpus:

> "**Only a few years ago the behaviour of an emulsion in this digestion stage was always entirely controlled by the nature of the gelatin.** Gelatins which produced a large increase in sensitivity in a conveniently short time were referred to as fast or active gelatins while those that produced little or no change were referred to as slow or inert." … "**It is now more usual to add known amounts of these sensitizers … before the digestion stage in order to permit control of the process.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]` **[F]**

The enabling definition is dated: "inert gelatin" was "first proposed by **Kelly at the Liège Conference in 1959**", with the threshold "**less than five parts per million of both sulphur sensitizer and nucleic-acid type restrainer** would render a gelatin inert", and "**Modern practice tends far more to the use of inert gelatins**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.44–45 (PDF 48–49)]`. **[Q]** The identity of the natural sensitizer was also revised: the belief in allylthiourea gave way — "**More recently, it has been made clear** that … the sensitizing substance of normal commercial gelatins is **sodium thiosulphate**, possibly with sodium tetrathionate" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 91)]`. **[F]** That is a documented correction of Wall's 1929 statement of the same fact, by a later source, on the same question — one of the very few places in the corpus where two sources engage directly.

The 1966 process envelope and quantities:

| Quantity | 1966 value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Digestion temperature | 40–70 °C | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89)]` |
| Digestion duration | "a few minutes up to several hours" | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89)]` |
| Active sulphur in gelatin | 1–2 ppm (inert types) to 100 ppm (active types) | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.94–95 (PDF 100–101)]` |
| Added thiosulphate (Bekunov) | 25–150 ppm in the gelatin | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.94–95 (PDF 100–101)]` |
| Gold dose | 1–30 mg gold per gram-mole silver; more if added after digestion | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.91–92, 95–96 (PDF 97–98, 101–102)]` |
| Gold + sulphur speed gain over sulphur alone | 2 to 2½ times; maximum **+0.33 log E** | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.91–92, 95–96 (PDF 97–98, 101–102), Fig. 5.9]` |
| Sensitizer consumed at peak speed | "only a fraction, usually around 10 %" | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.94–95 (PDF 100–101)]` |
| Silver ions bound as Ag₂S at optimum | ≈3 % of surface silver; ~1 in 50,000 of all silver ions | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.90, 94–95 (PDF 96, 100–101)]` |
| Silver atoms per grain to make it developable | "as many as 100" (assumed) | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.90 (PDF 96)]` |
| Polyethylene oxides | "up to twice the speed" in fast iodobromides; "a fairly recent introduction" | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.165 (PDF 171)]` |

All **[Q]** except the last clause, which is **[F]**. The +0.33 log E gold figure is the corpus's one clean, dated, exposure-index offset between two sensitization generations, and it corresponds to ×2.1 in linear exposure, consistent with the stated "2 to 2½ times" **[E]**.

Two structural facts about 1966 sensitization matter for era modelling. Gold alone is useless — "**Gold sensitization alone gives a very poor effect characterized by a low contrast and is, therefore, always applied in conjunction with sulphur sensitizing**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.91–92 (PDF 97–98)]` **[F]** — and gold buys speed partly by *spending* contrast: "Examination of the curves in Figure 5.6 shows that gold increases the speed by **reducing the contrast**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.186 (PDF 192)]`. **[F]** Gold is used "mainly with fast iodobromide materials, such as those for camera use, either black-and-white or colour, or X-ray emulsions" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.91–92 (PDF 97–98)]`. **[F]** Duffin also retracts an earlier finding: "**Early work, carried out with much larger quantities** of sulphur sensitizers, showed that the digestion reaction was autocatalytic … **However, in recent years, the use of more refined methods, in particular … radiotracer techniques** … have shown a behaviour like that of the normal uncatalysed reaction" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.86–87 (PDF 92–93)]`. **[F]**

Reduction sensitization in 1966 is understood as a speed route with a contrast and fog penalty: "the contrast obtainable after treatment with a reducing agent is generally lower and there is a greater tendency to fog formation" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.88–89 (PDF 94–95)]`. **[M]**

#### 2.3.6 1995: the same three sensitizations, now measured

By 1995 nothing new has been added to the list of three, but the centres have been counted and their trap depths measured — a change in *knowledge*, not in *technology*, and the sources should not be read as claiming otherwise.

| Measured quantity | Value | Worker and date | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trap depth, sulfur centres | 0.33 eV (thermal, from temperature coefficient of red sensitivity) | Hamilton, Harbison & Jeanmaire, 1988 | `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.73–74 (PDF 82–83)]` |
| Trap depth, sulfur-plus-gold centres | 0.19 eV | same | `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.73–74 (PDF 82–83)]` |
| Trap depth, sulfur centres (independent) | 0.39 eV thermal | Kellogg & Hodes, 1987 | `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.73–74 (PDF 82–83)]` |
| Trap depth, sulfur-plus-gold (independent) | 0.17 eV | same | `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.73–74 (PDF 82–83)]` |

All **[Q]**. The mechanistic pay-off is stated: the three-atom versus four-to-five-atom threshold "is the **major contribution of gold sensitization** to the increase in photographic sensitivity" `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]`. **[F]**

Tani also reverses a received view about stabilizers, and dates the reversal to his own work: "It has generally been believed that stabilizers and antifoggants decrease photographic sensitivity, or at most do not change it. Tani has described a new photographic phenomenon…: **They actually can increase photographic sensitivity of emulsions with and without spectral sensitization**" `[Tani 1995, §6.5, p.191 (PDF 200)]`. **[F]**

#### 2.3.7 The measured sensitivity trajectory, and where the headroom went

The one quantitative trajectory in the corpus for the *late* twentieth century runs through detective quantum efficiency.

- **1969.** "Bird et al. measured, for the first time, the DQE of photographic materials and found that the DQE of a high-speed photographic film for taking pictures was **as low as about 1 %**." The cascade: reduced to **42 % by incomplete light absorption**, to **64 % (total 27 %) by the four-atom threshold**, to **16 % (total 4.3 %) by recombination losses**, to **36 % (total 1.5 %) by the distributions of grain size and sensitivity**, and to **72 % (total 1.1 %) by random grain arrangement.** "**The DQE values of photographic films have been improved to a limited degree since that time.**" `[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]` **[Q]** This is a 1969 measurement on one high-speed film, and Tani's own closing clause is the caution against treating it as current. **[E]**
- **1985.** "In 1985, Tani determined that photographic sensitivity is dependent upon light absorption, the quantum yield of latent image formation, and the size of the smallest latent image center. The fraction of incident photons absorbed … was thought to be **at most one third** and could thus be **increased by about three times**… the **quantum sensitivity … was around 10 and the theoretical limit is two**, [so] the quantum sensitivity was expected to **increase by about five times**… In total, it was predicted that there would be room for an increase in sensitivity of **about one order of magnitude**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.4, p.235 (PDF 244)]` **[Q]**
- **1985 → 1995, what actually happened.** "**Since then, remarkable progress has been made** … The **light absorption of color films was improved by the use of tabular grains**, and the possibility for increase in light absorption in the future is about two times. The **average volume of silver halide grains in color films was greatly reduced without changing their sensitivity**, indicating the achievement of an increase in quantum sensitivity of the grains." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.4, pp.235–236 (PDF 244–245); refs. Ishimaru et al. 1992; Sasaki 1994]` **[Q]** That sentence is the corpus's single clearest statement of what late-century emulsion engineering delivered: not more speed at the same grain volume, but **the same speed at smaller grain volume** — i.e. the gain was taken as image quality rather than as exposure index. **[E]**
- **1989.** "In 1989 Bird predicted that silver halide photographic systems would advance from the DQE value of **1–2 % at that time to about 10 %**", the improvement to be spent as "**either an increase in image quality by reducing the size of emulsion grains without changing their sensitivity or an increase in sensitivity without changing image quality**" `[Tani 1995, §8.1.4, p.236 (PDF 245)]`. **[Q]**
- **1995 estimate of current DQE.** "The estimated value of DQE of photographic films clusters in the range of **1–2 %**" `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25)]`. **[Q]**

Supporting absorption figures that explain why the ceiling is where it is: a **1 µm cubic AgBr grain absorbs about 10 % at 420 nm and 1 % at 460 nm**; incorporating **3 mol % silver iodide increases the 460 nm absorption fivefold**; and in the spectrally sensitized region a high-sensitivity film absorbs only **10–20 %** `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]`. **[Q]** The dye monolayer itself is the ceiling on the sensitized region: J-aggregates covering 65 % of an evaporated AgBr surface (1.3 × 10⁻⁶ mol/m²) gave a peak absorbance of only **0.09**, so "the absorbance of these dye molecules on a tabular grain is too weak to absorb all incident photons in the panchromatic range (i.e., 600–700 nm)" `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, pp.229–230 (PDF 238–239), Fig. 8.1]`. **[Q]**

Two scaling laws close the thread, both stated by Tani: "photographic sensitivity is, in principle, **proportional to the volume** of silver halide grains and the spectral sensitivity of dyes grains is **proportional to their average surface area**" `[Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)]` **[Q]**, with the proportionality breaking above a knee at the **~1 µm scale** because of the limited photoelectron diffusion length `[Tani 1995, §3.3, p.65 (PDF 74); §4.2, p.88 (PDF 97)]` **[Q]**, and the knee moving to *smaller* sizes in sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized grains `[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.88–89 (PDF 97–98), Fig. 4.3]` **[F]**.

**State of evidence.** This thread is genuinely documented change, on multiple independent sources' own testimony: Davis & Walters shows a 1920 technology with no chemical sensitization at all; Wall dates the discovery to 1925 and describes it as not yet controllable; Duffin states in his own voice that control shifted from gelatin selection to metered addition "only a few years" before 1966, dates gold to the mid-1930s, and quantifies the gold gain at +0.33 log E; Tani supplies the milestone table with dates, the 10⁶ overall gain from 1839, and the 1969/1985/1989/1995 DQE trajectory including the explicit statement that late-century gains were taken as reduced grain volume at constant sensitivity. The weakest link is the twentieth century's *middle*: no source measures a speed increase between 1929 and 1966, and the 1920 B.S. and 1929 H&D scales are not convertible (see §2.5).



---

## 3. Photographic emulsion fundamentals

### 3.1 What an emulsion is — and why the name is wrong

A photographic emulsion is not an emulsion in the physical-chemical sense. It is a dispersion of solid crystals in a hydrocolloid: "dispersions of very small solid particles, called grains, of silver-halide … prepared in a liquid medium, usually dilute gelatin solution, which can be cooled, set and dried after coating on a base" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15)]. **[F]**

The 1995 statement of the same thing is in terms of the finished device rather than the liquid: silver halide grains "are separately and randomly arranged in thin gelatin layers with a relatively low packing density to achieve fine imaging" [Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]. **[F]**

Wall's 1929 demonstration of what the gelatin actually does is worth preserving because it is the only direct observation of the colloid effect in this source set: silver nitrate poured into 10 % potassium bromide solution gives "thick white curds or flocks"; the same silver nitrate poured into 10 % gelatine containing 10 % potassium bromide gives "a perfectly smooth liquid… something like cream", and a drop viewed by transmitted light is "almost a blood-red color **without the slightest suspicion of grain**". The aqueous precipitate settles in minutes; the gelatin dispersion stays milky for hours [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.30–31 (PDF 38–39)]. **[M]**

The three sources use three different framings, and the framing itself is era-dependent:

| Era | Framing of "an emulsion" | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1929 | A batch of liquid, described by its recipe (g AgNO₃, g halide, g gelatine, ccm water) and by its factory test result (H&D speed, γ∞, K, fog) | [Wall 1929, Ch. I, p.8 (PDF 16)] | **[F]** |
| 1966 | A dispersion characterised by two concentrations — silver-halide concentration "expressed in grams of silver for a given volume thus giving a uniformity to the different halides", and gelatin concentration as weight/volume % — whose *coating weight* is the quantity that must be controlled: "It is the **silver-halide coating weight** which must be controlled in order to obtain a satisfactory photographic response" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)] | **[F]** |
| 1995 | One functional layer among ~14 in a multilayer device, each layer being "a multifunctional device" whose multifunctionality itself limits performance | [Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18); Table 1.1, p.8 (PDF 17)] | **[F]** |

### 3.2 The layer stack: 1929, 1966, 1995

**1929 — single layer on glass or celluloid.** Wall's normal product is one emulsion layer, coated on cleaned glass (plates) or on subbed celluloid (film), with an optional dyed sub between support and emulsion for antihalation, and an optional pigmented backing on the rear of the glass or the back of the film [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.83–84 (PDF 90–91); Ch. X, p.163 (PDF 170)]. **[F]**

Two-layer coatings existed but were rare and were sold for halation control, not for tone reproduction: "Some of the non-halation, so-called double-coated plates, on the market are **merely coated with an extra quantity of emulsion, and not actually double-coated**", whereas J. T. Sandell (Eng. Pat. 21,381/1891) "actually coated **first a very slow, opaque emulsion and then on top a faster and more translucent one**" [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]. **[F]** The only stated penalty is process time: "the longer time required for fixation, washing and drying" [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]. **[F]** No source in this set states any effect of double coating on contrast or latitude; Wall connects it only to halation, coating thickness and processing time. **[F]**

**1966 — a four-element stack, drawn but not dimensioned.** Duffin's Fig. 1.1 ("Representation of silver halide coating") labels, top to bottom: **Supercoat → Silver Halide Grain / Gelatin (emulsion layer) → Base → Backing**. No thicknesses appear on the figure [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15), Fig. 1.1]. **[M]** Colour materials of 1966 are explicitly multilayer: "**Colour materials** frequently contain a large number of layers, **all of them 1–3 µ thick in the dry state** and correspondingly thicker when wet" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]. **[Q]** The layer count is never given. **[F]**

**1995 — fourteen layers, three colour records, three speed sublayers each.** This is the single most usable geometry statement in the source set and is quoted in full:

> "On a film base there are blue-, green-, and red-sensitive layers, which are coated one over the other. Moreover, each color-sensitive layer is composed of high-speed, medium-speed, and low-speed sublayers, which are also coated one over the other. A photosensitive layer in a typical color negative film is composed of about 14 layers with different functions and is about 20 /xm thick in total. There are 12 million silver halide grains per square millimeter and more than 100 kinds of functional organic compounds in a film."
> [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)] **[Q]**

(OCR: `/xm` = µm.) The stock described is ISO 100 colour negative [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)]. **[Q]**

| Quantity | 1995 value | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Functional layers in a colour negative photosensitive pack | ≈ 14 | [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)] | **[Q]** |
| Colour records | 3 (blue, green, red), coated one over another | [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)] | **[Q]** |
| Speed sublayers per colour record | 3 (high, medium, low), coated one over another | [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)] | **[Q]** |
| Total photosensitive-pack thickness | ≈ 20 µm | [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)] | **[Q]** |
| Distinct functional organic compounds in the film | > 100 kinds | [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)] | **[Q]** |

3 records × 3 sublayers = 9 emulsion layers; the remaining ≈ 5 of the 14 are interlayers, filter layers and auxiliary layers. **The identity and function of those remaining layers is never enumerated by Tani** — no source in this set gives the coating order of a colour negative, the composition of the yellow filter layer, or the position of the UV layer. **[F]**

Combining Duffin's per-layer dry thickness with Tani's layer count is arithmetically consistent and is our inference, not either source's: 14 layers × 1–3 µm dry = 14–42 µm, bracketing Tani's ≈ 20 µm, i.e. the mean dry layer in a 1995 colour negative is ≈ 1.4 µm, at the thin end of Duffin's 1966 band [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159); Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]. **[E]**

**Layer thickness, the full quantitative picture (1966 only).**

> "The thickness of an emulsion layer, which varies widely with the type of material, between **30–600 µ at the coating point** which will then be **2–40 µ thick after drying**. **Supercoats and filter layers** are usually thinner than this, being **1–3 µ in the dry state**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)] **[Q]**

OCR note: the raw string reads "1-3 mu" twice. From context this is µ (microns), not mµ (millimicrons) — a 1–3 mµ supercoat is physically absurd. **[F]** Wet-to-dry ratio implied: 30/2 = 15× to 600/40 = 15×, i.e. a consistent ≈ 15:1 wet:dry thickness reduction across the whole range. **[E]**

Duffin also gives the water balance that produces that reduction: "During drying, the water content will go from **about 85%**, only **15%** being assumed to be gelatin, silver halide and other minor additives, **to about 5%**, because the gelatin will **retain 10–12% of its weight of water**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.158 (PDF 164)]. **[Q]** 85 % → 5 % water on a constant-solids basis implies a thickness ratio of (100−5)/(100−85) ≈ 6.3:1, not 15:1; the two statements are not reconcilable without assuming lateral flow or a differing solids basis. We flag the discrepancy rather than resolving it. **[E]**

Supercoat gelatin loading, 1966: "**10% or less of the amount of gelatin in the emulsion**", coated after the emulsion or "**from an additional slot during the emulsion coating**"; "**Quite commonly the bulk of the emulsion hardener is added via the supercoat**, the diffusion into the emulsion layer being relied upon to produce a sufficiently high hardening level there" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.166 (PDF 172)]. **[Q]**

**Wall 1929 gives no wet or dry layer thickness anywhere in the book.** Thickness is only ever expressed as coating weight, or judged optically: the film machine used a 10 c.p. metal-filament lamp behind a 2-inch slit safelight, and "for positive: the thickness must be such that the shape of the filament is entirely lost"; for negative "the filament should be just discernible" [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.199 (PDF 206)]. **[F]** For hand coating, judge "by looking through the plate at an electric lamp filament, or by film thickness at the plate edge; when an exact quantity of emulsion is required for a given plate surface, a graduated pipette must be used" [Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.164 (PDF 171)]. **[M]**

### 3.3 Coating weight and silver per unit area

#### 3.3.1 The measured 1929 data — Tappen & Rekaschow's ten commercial plates

This is the only set of *measured* coating weights on *commercial* material anywhere in the source set. Wall reproduces analyses of ten commercial plates. Columns as printed: **A** = weight of emulsion in grammes per 100 qcm; **B** = water as % of the emulsion; **C** = % silver halide in the anhydrous emulsion; **D** = remainder as gelatine [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.157 (PDF 164); column key p.158 (PDF 165)].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| English | 0.4246 | 42.46 | 8.30 | 41.44 | 58.56 | **[Q]** |
| English | 0.4406 | 44.06 | 8.65 | 41.93 | 58.07 | **[Q]** |
| English | 0.4770 | 47.70 | 9.52 | 41.64 | 58.36 | **[Q]** |
| English | 0.5373 | 53.73 | 8.19 | 43.22 | 56.78 | **[Q]** |
| German | 0.4838 | 48.38 | 8.74 | 40.50 | 59.50 | **[Q]** |
