| Austrian | 0.3465 | 34.65 | 9.59 | 36.38 | 63.62 | **[Q]** |

Wall's stated mean, **excluding the last (Austrian, 0.3465) plate as "obviously exceptional"**:

> "0.43724 g per 100 qcm (about **2.821 g per 100 square inches**), and this contains **7.5 per cent of water, 42.6 of silver halide and 50 per cent of gelatine, or a ratio of gelatine of 1.3 to 1 of halide**"
> [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.158 (PDF 165)] **[Q]**

Conversions (conv.): 0.43724 g/100 qcm = **4.372 mg/cm² = 43.72 g/m²**; 2.821 g/100 sq in = 43.73 g/m² (the two printed forms agree to 0.03 %). **[E]**

**Arithmetic flag — this is a book error, not OCR damage.** The nine retained values sum to 4.3722 g/100 qcm; 4.3722/9 = **0.4858**, not 0.43724. Wall's "mean" is the sum of nine divided by **ten**. Use 0.4858 g/100 qcm (**48.58 g/m²**) if you want the true mean of the nine plates he retained; use 0.4372 g/100 qcm to reproduce the book. Likewise the headline "7.5 % water / 42.6 % halide / 50 % gelatine" does not sum to 100 and mixes two bases: B is water on the whole coating, while C and D are percentages of the **anhydrous** emulsion. **[E]**

Derived areal coverages (ours, from Wall's own headline figures; Wall does not compute these):

⚠ **The table that stood here until 2026-08-27 applied an ANHYDROUS percentage to a WET coating
weight, and every mass in it was ~9 % high.** C and D are percentages of the *anhydrous* emulsion;
A is the coating weight *including* its residual water. Multiplying A by C directly double-counts the
water. The correct chain is A → remove water (× (1 − B/100)) → split by C and D. Corrected:

| Derived quantity | From Wall's mean 0.43724 g/100 qcm | From the true mean 0.48580 g/100 qcm | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total coating (solids + residual water) | 43.72 g/m² | 48.58 g/m² | **[E]** |
| Residual water, at B̄ = 8.427 % of the coating | 3.68 g/m² | 4.09 g/m² | **[E]** |
| Anhydrous emulsion | 40.04 g/m² | 44.49 g/m² | **[E]** |
| Silver halide, at C̄ = 42.363 % of the anhydrous | **16.96 g/m²** | **18.85 g/m²** | **[E]** |
| Gelatine, at D̄ = 57.637 % of the anhydrous | **23.08 g/m²** | **25.64 g/m²** | **[E]** |
| Metallic silver equivalent, assuming the halide is AgBr (Ag fraction 107.868/187.772 = 0.57450) | **9.74 g Ag/m²** | **10.83 g Ag/m²** | **[E]** |
| *(superseded)* the same rows computed on the wrong base | ~~18.52 / 25.20 / 10.64~~ | ~~20.58 / 28.00 / 11.82~~ | ❌ |

The three mass rows now sum to the coating weight exactly, which the old ones could not.

The silver figure is an engineering conclusion of ours and carries two explicit caveats: Wall never states the halide identity in these analyses, and 1–5 % of the halide is iodide (§4.4), which shifts the silver fraction by under 2 %. **[E]**

#### 3.3.1a Verification pass (2026-08-27, task A4a)

This table was on the worklist for a **page render**, because a hand-typed nineteenth-century table
recovered from OCR is exactly the sort of thing that carries a silently flipped digit, and because
its PDF page had been reached by offset arithmetic rather than by reading a folio. Both concerns are
now closed, and neither needed a render.

**The page is confirmed by its own running head, not by arithmetic.** The text layer of PDF 164
opens `PREPARATION FOR COATING    157` and PDF 165 opens `158 PHOTOGRAPHIC EMULSIONS`. The table
sits on printed p.157 and its column key on p.158, exactly as cited. (Wall's offset in this range is
+7 — see §29.1, where it is now measured per page rather than assumed.)

**The digits are confirmed by an internal identity the OCR could not have faked.** For all ten
plates, **C + D = 100.000 exactly**, with no exceptions and no rounding slack — which is what the
column key requires, since D is defined as the remainder after C. A single flipped digit anywhere in
either column would break that identity in the row it occurred. Columns C and D are therefore sound
as extracted. A and B carry no such identity and cannot be checked this way; they are used below only
in aggregate, where a single-plate error is diluted.

**A second book error, and it is larger than the first.** §3.3.1 already flags that Wall's mean
coating weight divides a sum of nine by ten. Checking the rest of the headline turns up something
worse: **Wall's stated composition is arithmetically impossible on his own table.** Because
C + D = 100 in every row, the mean of C and the mean of D must sum to 100 for *any* subset and *any*
divisor. Wall's headline gives **42.6 % halide and 50 % gelatine — 92.6, not 100.** No selection of
plates and no divisor can produce that pair.

What the retained nine plates actually give:

| Quantity | Wall's headline | True value (nine retained plates) | How Wall's number arises |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean A | 0.43724 g/100 qcm | **0.48580** | sum of nine ÷ **ten** |
| Mean B (water, % of coating) | 7.5 % | **8.427 %** | sum of nine ÷ **ten** gives 7.584 → "7.5" |
| Mean C (halide, % anhydrous) | 42.6 % | **42.363 %** | ÷ nine, then rounded up rather than down |
| Mean D (gelatine, % anhydrous) | 50 % | **57.637 %** | **unexplained by any divisor** — ÷9 gives 57.64, ÷10 gives 51.87 |
| Gelatine : halide | 1.3 : 1 | **1.3605 : 1** | ✅ correct — the ratio is invariant to the divisor, which is why this one survived |

The pattern is that A and B were divided by ten, C was divided by nine, and D was neither. Note that
the ratio Wall quotes, 1.3 : 1, is *right* — it is the one headline figure immune to the divisor
error, which is a fair warning about how little a single consistent-looking number proves. His three
percentages also sum to 100.1, which reads like a deliberate three-way split of the whole coating;
but the table does not support one, because B is a percentage of the coating while C and D are
percentages of the anhydrous emulsion. Put on a single base, the nine plates give **water 8.427 %,
silver halide 38.794 %, gelatine 52.780 %**, summing to 100.000. **[E]**

**The first thickness estimate the corpus can support, and it closes a stated gap.** §3.3.1 records
that "the corpus has a 1929 coating weight and no 1966 one; the two cannot be compared." They can be
compared through density. Taking ρ(AgBr) = 6.473, ρ(gelatin) = 1.35 and ρ(water) = 1.00 g/cm³, and
using the identity that **1 cm³ spread over 1 m² is exactly 1 µm**:

| | From the true mean 0.48580 g/100 qcm | From Wall's 0.43724 |
|---|---|---|
| Emulsion layer as coated (residual water in) | **26.0 µm** | 23.4 µm |
| Emulsion layer dry | **21.9 µm** | 19.7 µm |
| Silver-halide volume fraction of the dry layer | **13.3 %** | 13.3 % |

⚠ **[E], and the densities are assumed, not sourced** — no document in this set states the density of
a coated emulsion layer, and the halide is assumed pure AgBr where Wall never identifies it. The
value of the number is not its third digit; it is that **21.9 µm dry lands inside Duffin's stated
envelope of "2–40 µm dry" (§2.1), near its thick end**, which is where a 1929 plate should sit and is
an independent sanity check on the whole chain from Wall's grammes to Duffin's micrometres. The
13.3 % volume fraction is likewise consistent with Tani's qualitative "relatively low packing
density" (§3.3.4), which is the only statement on packing anywhere in the corpus. **Neither is
evidence for the other; they are two eras agreeing about an order of magnitude.**

**No database change follows.** Per-stock coated thickness and per-stock halide loading are Category C
(§27) — no stock in our database is a 1929 plate, and there is no route from an areal silver loading
to a rendered pixel that does not pass through granularity and Dmax, both of which we measure
directly. This is era context for §2, and it is now arithmetically clean. **Task A4a closed.**

#### 3.3.2 Wall's other 1929 coverage figures

| Fast negative film emulsion, total bulk 11,000 g, "should coat six hundred square feet of celluloid" | 11,000 g / 600 ft² | 600 ft² = 55.74 m² → **197.3 g wet emulsion/m²** | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.80 (PDF 87)] | **[Q]** |
| Gold P.O.P. formula (X), "should coat 38 meters of paper 66 cm wide" | 38 m × 0.66 m | = 25.08 m² (area only; the bulk of that formula is not summed in the text) | [Wall 1929, App., p.241 (PDF 248)] | **[Q]** |
| Baryta undercoat on paper: "1000 g of the baryta mixture… is required for every 10 square meters of paper surface **for the three coats**"; allow "roughly one-fifth more" for waste | 1000 g / 10 m² | **100 g/m² for three coats; 120 g/m² with waste allowance** | [Wall 1929, App., p.251 (PDF 258)] | **[Q]** |
| Tacky mounting layer on carrier glass | "Allow 250 ccm for every 20 × 16 sheet of glass" | 250 ccm / 2064 cm² = **0.121 ccm/cm² = 1.21 mm wet** | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.183 (PDF 190)] | **[Q]** |

Cross-check of the 197.3 g/m² wet figure against the measured plates (ours): if the wet emulsion is ~85 % water as Duffin's 1966 drying figures imply, 197.3 g/m² wet dries to ≈ 30 g/m², against Wall's own measured 43.7–48.6 g/m² on plates. Plates were coated more heavily than film; the two figures are consistent in magnitude and in the expected direction. **[E]**

#### 3.3.3 Duffin's 1966 coating figures

Duffin **never gives a silver or halide coating weight in any areal unit** — this is stated explicitly as a gap after a keyword sweep of the whole book range: coating weight "is discussed as a controlled quantity but **never given a numeric value in any areal unit**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83); range-wide absence]. **[F]** What he gives instead is the gelatin-to-silver ratio, the coatable concentration window, and two edge cases.

**The gelatin:silver ratio and its historical fall — the highest-value 1966 coating number:**

> "Some years ago, many plate-coated emulsions had as much as **300–400 grams of gelatin per gram molecule of silver** and the same was true of some film emulsions. Such a ratio gives an emulsion layer which is far too thick for present-day standards; it would possess a slow rate of development, poor drying characteristics and **low sharpness**. Present-day emulsions frequently have **no more than 100 grams of gelatin per gram molecule of silver**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)] **[Q]**

Recast onto a gelatin:halide weight basis (ours; 1 g-mole AgBr = 187.77 g):

| Era / material | g gelatin per g-mole Ag | Gelatin : AgBr by weight | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| "Some years ago" plate and some film emulsions | 300–400 | **1.60 : 1 to 2.13 : 1** | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)] | **[E]** |
| 1966 "present-day" emulsions | ≤ 100 | **≤ 0.53 : 1** | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)] | **[E]** |
| Nuclear-particle-track emulsions (extreme case) | "as little as 20 g per g mole", "almost solid silver bromide" | **0.107 : 1** | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.187–188 (PDF 193–194)] | **[E]** |
| Measured 1929 commercial plates (Wall) | — | **1.3 : 1** (Wall's own statement of the ratio) | [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.158 (PDF 165)] | **[Q]** |
| Measured commercial chlorobromide plates (Valenta, in Wall) | — | gelatine : silver halide **2 : 1 to 6 : 1** (English) | [Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.97 (PDF 104)] | **[Q]** |
| Bromide paper worked example (Wall) | — | gelatine : silver ≈ **1 : 15** | [Wall 1929, Ch. VI, p.102 (PDF 109)] | **[Q]** |

Wall's measured 1.3:1 for 1929 plates falls **below** Duffin's "some years ago" band of 1.60–2.13:1, and Valenta's chlorobromide analyses (2:1 to 6:1) fall **above** it. The sources disagree on where 1920s practice sat: Wall's own ten-plate mean and Valenta's chlorobromide analyses differ by a factor of up to 4.6 on the same quantity in the same era, and Duffin's retrospective band sits between them. Present all three; do not average. **[E]** A plausible reconciliation — that negative plates ran leaner in gelatine than positive chlorobromide plates — is consistent with Wall's rule that "slow and medium speed [emulsions] should be mixed in the presence of large quantities of gelatine and water, while fast ones should be compounded with low ratios of gelatine" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.52 (PDF 60)], but no source states it. **[S]**

**Coatable concentration limits, 1966:**

| Constraint | Value | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gelatin concentration floor for standard coating | "the **gelatin concentration cannot be permitted to drop appreciably below 5 %**" (gelatins of average viscosity and strength) | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)] | **[Q]** |
| Trough / dip coating | **5 %–8 %** gelatin for film emulsions, "lower for paper emulsions"; support contacts emulsion at **36–40 °C** | [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.153–154 (PDF 159–160), Fig. 8.1] | **[Q]** |
| Air-knife / metal-knife "doctoring" | **8 %–13 %** gelatin | [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.155 (PDF 161), Fig. 8.2] | **[Q]** |
| Slot applicator | **6 %–10 %** gelatin; coating weight set "by the volume of emulsion which is pumped onto a given area of support" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.156 (PDF 162), Fig. 8.3] | **[Q]** |
| Coating speed ceiling, 1966 | "it is **exceptional to exceed twenty-five feet per minute**" (7.62 m/min, conv.), "and in many cases not more than half of this is obtained" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.155 (PDF 161)] | **[Q]** |
| Chill-set temperature after coating | **about 10–15 °C** | [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.156–157 (PDF 162–163)] | **[Q]** |

The mechanism that couples viscosity to coating weight in trough coating is stated plainly, and it is the reason gelatin quality is a coating-weight variable rather than only a physical-properties variable: "**The amount of emulsion 'taken-up' by the base from the coating trough or similar device is controlled by the viscosity of the gelatin**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.40 (PDF 44)]; dilute emulsion → low pick-up → apparently higher speed possible, but the gel will not set fast enough in a shortened chill zone and will not dry in the available transit; concentrated emulsion → higher viscosity → higher pick-up → higher silver coating weight; net constraint: "the whole system… restricts the manufacturer to the use of gelatins with only **moderate viscosity but which give high jelly strength** on setting" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.154–155 (PDF 160–161)]. **[M]**

Duffin's own summary of the 1966 shift in what the coating engineer controls: "Satisfactory performance of modern silver-halide materials stems from the correct **silver/gelatin ratio** and therefore the emulsion chemist is not free to vary this at will", in contrast with "earlier years… [when] the principal consideration was that of gelatin concentration" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]. **[F]**

**The two areal figures Duffin does give** are both edge cases, not conventional stocks:

| Case | Value | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct X-ray recording film | "coated at **very high coating weights** to increase the likelihood of absorption" — no number | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.187–188 (PDF 193–194)] | **[F]** |
| Silver-salt diffusion-transfer positive image | "may contain only **a few milligrams of silver per sq. dm.** in an image of high density" (a few mg/dm² = a few hundred mg/m², conv.) | [Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.219 (PDF 225)] | **[Q]** |
| Relative overall thickness | "The overall thickness of a modern **colour** film is **much less than that of a modern X-ray emulsion**" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.202 (PDF 208)] | **[F]** |

#### 3.3.4 Tani 1995 on coating weight — an explicit blank, plus a tolerance

**Tani gives no silver coating weight and no grain volume fraction anywhere in the range examined.** Packing density is stated only qualitatively: silver halide grains are "separately and randomly arranged in thin gelatin layers with a **relatively low packing density** to achieve fine imaging. However, this arrangement prevents grains in these layers from absorbing incident light efficiently"; and "photographic emulsion layers have to be thin and contain silver halide grains with a low packing density to achieve fine imaging" [Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]. **[F]**

What Tani does supply is the coating **uniformity** requirement, which is the 1995 manufacturing tolerance:

> "The coating technology used with photographic materials is quite unique and is characterized by great precision, high uniformity, and high speed, as well as simultaneous multilayer coating in the dark. A precision and uniformity containing 1-2% variation is necessary to achieve the desired abilities of photographic materials."
> [Tani 1995, §1.2.5, p.10 (PDF 19)] **[Q]**

So: 1929 coating was judged by eye against a lamp filament [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.199 (PDF 206)]; 1966 coating weight was controlled through gelatin concentration and pick-up, with "restricted degree of coating-weight control" on knife coaters and direct volumetric control only on slot applicators [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.153–156 (PDF 159–162)]; 1995 coating was simultaneous-multilayer to a 1–2 % uniformity spec [Tani 1995, §1.2.5, p.10 (PDF 19)]. That is the trajectory of the coating stage across the three eras. **[E]**

### 3.4 Grains per unit area, grains per equivalent pixel, packing density

Only Tani quantifies areal grain density.

| Quantity | Value | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grains per mm², ISO 100 colour negative | **12 × 10⁶** (stated as "12 million") | [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)] | **[Q]** |
| Grains per mm², same stock, restated | **1.2 × 10⁷** | [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28), Fig. 1.13] | **[Q]** |
| Equivalent pixels per 135 frame (36 × 24 mm²) | **2 × 10⁷** | [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)] | **[Q]** |
| Area per equivalent pixel | **43 µm²** — OCR reads `43 A2` | [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)] | **[Q]** |
| Grains per equivalent pixel | **≈ 500** | [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)] | **[Q]** |

OCR flag on the pixel area: the raw string is `43 A2`, i.e. the unit glyph is corrupt. The arithmetic fixes it: 864 mm² / 2 × 10⁷ = 43.2 µm², so the printed value is **43 µm²**, mis-OCR'd as "43 A2". Quote as "43 µm² [OCR reads '43 A2']". **[Q]** Internal consistency check (ours): 1.2 × 10⁷ grains/mm² = 12 grains/µm²; × 43 µm² = 516 ≈ 500 grains per equivalent pixel. The three figures are mutually consistent. **[E]**

The stated consequence of the random, low-density arrangement is defect immunity:

> "A defective silver halide grain or a dust particle whose size is comparable to those of silver halide grains (around 1 ^m) hardly disturbs the function of an equivalent pixel in a color film, because it is only one among 500 grains…"
> [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)] **[F]**

(OCR: `1 ^m` = 1 µm.) Tani contrasts this with CCD manufacture, where "Murphy-See's model showing productive yield as a function of the frame area of CCD in the presence of **defects of 5 cm⁻¹**" makes large-area sensors uneconomic [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.18 (PDF 27), Fig. 1.11]. **[F]**

**Packing density — a derived estimate, ours, because no source states it.** Take Tani's 12 × 10⁶ grains/mm² and 20 µm pack thickness. The pack volume per mm² of frame is 10⁶ µm² × 20 µm = 2 × 10⁷ µm³. A tabular grain of equivalent circular diameter 1.0 µm and thickness 0.1 µm (Tani's own tabular thickness, §5.4) has volume ≈ 0.079 µm³; 12 × 10⁶ such grains occupy ≈ 9.4 × 10⁵ µm³, i.e. a **silver-halide volume fraction of ≈ 4.7 % averaged over the whole 20 µm pack**. Converting that to areal silver: 9.4 × 10⁵ µm³/mm² = 9.4 × 10⁻⁷ cm³/cm² × 6.473 g/cm³ (AgBr density, [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22), Table 1.4]) = 6.1 × 10⁻³ g/cm² halide = **61 g/m² halide → ≈ 35 g Ag/m²**. That figure is implausibly high against known practice, which tells us the assumed average grain volume is too large: matching a realistic 4–6 g Ag/m² requires an average grain volume of order 0.01 µm³, i.e. an average grain far smaller than 1 µm ECD — consistent with Tani's own statement that grain sizes range "from less than 0.1 µm to several micrometers" and that only the fastest sublayers carry the large grains (§5.1). **We therefore record the volume-fraction method and its sensitivity, and record that this source set does not permit a reliable silver coating weight for a 1995 colour negative.** **[E]**

For contrast, the 1929 measured plate carried **18.6 g halide/m² ≈ 10.7 g Ag/m²** in a *single* layer (§3.3.1), which is a firm measured number. **[Q]** No comparable measured number exists for 1966 or 1995 in this set. **[F]**

### 3.5 Grain counts and ion counts per unit of emulsion

Duffin works these out explicitly for two model emulsions and for the general case; they are the only per-grain inventories in the source set.

**General case, 1966:**

> "an emulsion grain is an **imperfect crystal**, possessing basically a cubic lattice structure with a large number of internal and external imperfections. These grains may be between **0.03 µ and 2.5 µ** in diameter, and assuming that they are cubes (this is only true of some products), it can be calculated that there are **about 50 silver and 50 halide ions on each edge in the smallest crystals and about 4,000 of each in the largest crystals**. In each crystal, therefore, there are approximately **1,000,000 total ions in the smallest grains and about 500,000,000,000 in the largest, or 10⁶ and 5 × 10¹¹** respectively."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.27 (PDF 31)] **[Q]**

OCR note: the two exponents print as `10°` and `5x10"`; the longhand digit strings preceding them are intact and fix the values as 10⁶ and 5 × 10¹¹. **[Q]**

### 3.6 What no source in this set gives, on emulsion fundamentals

- **Silver coating weight in g/m² or mg/dm² for any conventional stock of any era.** Wall's plate analyses permit one to be derived (§3.3.1); Duffin states the quantity matters but never numbers it; Tani never mentions it. **[F]**
- **Grain volume fraction / packing density as a number.** Tani states it is "relatively low" and nothing more [Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]. **[F]**
- **Wet or dry layer thickness in 1929.** Absent from Wall entirely. **[F]**
- **Layer count for a 1966 colour material.** Duffin says "a large number of layers" and gives their thickness, never their number [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]. **[F]**
- **Identity and function of the non-emulsion layers in the 1995 fourteen-layer pack.** [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]. **[F]**
- **Refractive index of any material — base, gelatin, or silver halide.** Not mentioned once in Duffin; absent from Wall and from Tani's range. **[F]**
- **Coating uniformity across web width (vignette).** Absent from Duffin; Tani gives only the 1–2 % global figure. **[F]**
- **rms granularity, Selwyn granularity, graininess, or any grain-noise metric.** Duffin: zero occurrences of "granularity" or "graininess" in the whole book. Tani: the Selwyn granularity constant *G* appears only as a symbol inside the DQE equation, Eq. (1.1) — whose body was lost to OCR but has been **recovered from the rendered page image** and is quoted in full in §17.2. *G* is named there and nowhere defined in this source set. Wall: never discusses print graininess at all. **[F]**

One adjacent noise figure can be constructed and is flagged as ours: 500 grains per equivalent pixel gives a Poisson-limited fluctuation of 1/√500 = **4.5 % rms per equivalent-pixel area** for a binary developed/undeveloped grain population at mid-scale [derived from Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)]. **[E]** Tani's own efficiency figure for the whole system is the detective quantum efficiency: "The estimated value of **DQE of photographic films clusters in the range of 1-2%**", against a CCD's "several tens of percentages at low temperature" [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25), Eq. (1.1)]. **[Q]** The DQE equation body is lost to OCR; its printed symbol list is "**R and R₀ are signal-to-noise ratios at the input and output**, respectively; **γ is the slope of the D-logE plot**; **E is exposure in terms of photons per unit area**; and **G is the Selwyn granularity constant**" [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25)]. **[F]**

## 4. Silver halide crystals: composition, structure, defects

### 4.1 Which halides, and their solubilities

Four halogens exist; three are used: "the last three elements are used in photographic emulsions; **silver fluoride is quite useless photographically**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.12 (PDF 16)]. **[F]** The 1995 statement of the composition set: "Silver halide grains used in photographic materials are composed of AgBr, AgCl, and mixed crystals of AgBr with Agl and/or AgCl and of AgCl with AgBr and/or Agl" [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33)]. **[F]** Note that pure AgI is *not* in the 1995 list; the only pure-iodide photographic material named in the set is the Daguerreotype: "In Daguerrotype, **a thin layer of Agl** was the photosensitive material, and a latent image was revealed by a development process with **mercury vapor**" [Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]. **[F]**

**TABLE 1.2 — SOLUBILITY OF SILVER HALIDES**, in water at 25 °C, g-moles per litre [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.12 (PDF 16), Table 1.2]:

| Halide | Solubility (mol/L) | Raw OCR string | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| AgCl | **1.33 × 10⁻⁵** | `1.33 x 1075` | **[Q]** |
| AgBr | **7.12 × 10⁻⁷** | `7.121077` | **[Q]** |
| AgI | **2 × 10⁻⁸** | `2x 1058` | **[Q]** |

OCR flag: the minus signs and superscript markup are lost in all three rows; the exponent digits themselves survive, and the internal consistency check of §4.2 confirms the AgBr reading. **[Q]** Ordering statement: "Silver chloride is sparingly soluble in water … Silver bromide is less soluble than silver chloride and silver iodide is a highly insoluble substance" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.12 (PDF 16)]. **[F]**

Ratios (ours): AgCl is **18.7×** as soluble as AgBr, which is **35.6×** as soluble as AgI. Total span AgCl:AgI = **665:1**. This is the quantity that drives every differential-precipitation and ripening effect in §6 — notably that "when silver nitrate is added to mixed bromide and iodide ions, **silver iodide is precipitated first** because of the much lower solubility" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.64–65 (PDF 68–69)]. **[E]**

**No source in this set gives the temperature dependence of any silver halide solubility or solubility product**, although every ripening operation described in §6 is carried out at 40–98 °C. This is the single most consequential numeric gap in the set for anyone modelling grain growth. **[F]**

### 4.2 Solubility product, pAg, and silver-ion concentration

**Derivation as printed, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.12–13 (PDF 16–17)]:

```
rate of solution      = k1 [AgBr]
rate of precipitation = k2 [Ag+][Br-]
At equilibrium:  k2 [Ag+][Br-] = k1 [AgBr]
Therefore:       [Ag+][Br-]    = constant
```

Symbols: `[Ag+]`, `[Br-]` = molar ion concentrations in solution; `[AgBr]` = concentration of dissolved AgBr; `k1`, `k2` = rate constants. **[Q]**

Value: "`[Agt] [Br]` = a constant which is equal to **5.08 × 10⁻¹³ at 25 °C**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.13 (PDF 17)]. **[Q]** OCR flag: the raw string is `to 5.08` / `x 10 —#8at 25°` — the exponent glyph is corrupt. The reading is fixed arithmetically: (7.12 × 10⁻⁷)² = 5.07 × 10⁻¹³, matching Table 1.2 exactly, so the printed exponent is **−13**. **[E]**

**The 1995 formalism** is the same relation written in p-notation, with the equation bodies lost to OCR. Symbols as printed: activities [Ag⁺], [X⁻] with X⁻ = Cl⁻, Br⁻ or I⁻; activity solubility product **Ksp**; and the definitions "−log[Ag⁺] = pAg, −log[X⁻] = pX, and −logKsp = pKsp". Ksp "is independent of the nature and concentration of the other electrolytes present, and is approximately obtained by considering the concentration of the ions, instead of their activities, when the ionic strength of the medium is low" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.32 (PDF 41), Eqs. (2.1)–(2.2)]. **[F]**

**pAg, defined and measured (1966):**

```
pAg = log10 ( 1 / [Ag+] )
pH  = log10 ( 1 / [H+] )     (by analogy with [H+][OH-] = constant)
```
[Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.13 (PDF 17)] **[Q]**

> "If, therefore, more bromide ions are added to an emulsion, the silver-ion concentration will decrease." "In the case of pAg, silver halides are very similar, and **there is a point of neutrality when [Ag⁺] = [Hal⁻]**; at lower pAg values there is an excess of silver ions, and at higher values an excess of halide ions."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.13 (PDF 17)] **[F]**

Measurement is potentiometric against a calomel reference (Fig. 1.2 shows the cell: KCl solution / KCl solid / Hg₂Cl₂ solid / mercury), with a Nernst-type response:

```
E = E0 + 0.06 log10 [Ag+]
```
`E` = measured potential in volts, read on "an accurate voltmeter, taking negligible current otherwise the results will be faulty"; `E0` = fixed offset set by the reference half-cell, "determined by measuring the potential of a known silver-ion concentration and plotting a calibration curve". The coefficient is **0.06 V per decade** at fixed temperature [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.13 (PDF 17), Fig. 1.2]. **[Q]**

**Derived reference values (ours).** From Ksp(AgBr) = 5.08 × 10⁻¹³ at 25 °C: pKsp = **12.29**; at the point of neutrality [Ag⁺] = [Br⁻] = √Ksp = 7.13 × 10⁻⁷ M, so **pAg = pBr = 6.15** for AgBr at 25 °C. **[E]** This lets Tani's pBr-based growth work and Duffin's bromide-normality recipes be placed on one axis:

| Source condition | Stated as | pBr | pAg = pKsp − pBr (25 °C) | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neutral point, AgBr | [Ag⁺] = [Br⁻] | 6.15 | **6.15** | **[E]** |
| Duffin octahedral emulsion, ripening | 1.0 molar bromide, 244 % excess | 0.0 | **12.29** | **[E]** |
| Duffin ammonia/cubic emulsion, ripening | 0.1 molar bromide, 24 % excess | 1.0 | **11.29** | **[E]** |
| Tani tabular growth, diffusion-controlled regime | pBr 3.3 | 3.3 | **8.99** | **[E]** |
| Tani tabular growth, lateral ≫ vertical | pBr 2.63 | 2.63 | **9.66** | **[E]** |
| Tani tabular growth, lateral rate rising with size | pBr 2.0 | 2.0 | **10.29** | **[E]** |

**Caveat on that whole table, stated because it matters:** the conversion uses a 25 °C Ksp, whereas every one of these operations runs at 40–70 °C, where Ksp is substantially larger and pAg correspondingly lower. No source in this set supplies Ksp(T). The pAg column is therefore a *relative* ordering, not an absolute one. **[E]**

The habit consequence, which both sources state and which the table above makes consistent, is in §5.3 and §6.5.

### 4.3 Lattice type, lattice constant, ionic radii, density

**Lattice type.** AgBr and AgCl "both form what is known as the **cubic lattice**: … the individual cell of a crystal is a cube with silver halide ions at opposite corners" (Figs. 1.3, 1.4) [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.17 (PDF 21)]. **[F]** The 1995 statement is more precise: "The crystal structure is face-centered cubic, belonging to the space group **Fm3m**" [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33)]. **[F]**

"The **silver-iodide lattice is totally different**, but no normal photographic materials use pure or substantially pure iodide and therefore the only lattice which is of photographic importance is the cubic one" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.17 (PDF 21)]. **[F]** No source in this set names the AgI structure type or gives its lattice constants. **[F]**

**Lattice constant.** "An important measurement is the **distance between one silver ion and the next, which is 5.755 Å in silver bromide**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.17 (PDF 21)]. **[Q]** The same quantity is used on p.68 as "**The unit cell has a side of 5.75 Å**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.68 (PDF 72)]. **[Q]** Both readings are clean OCR; the printed values differ in the third decimal. Present both. **[Q]**

Interpretation (ours): the quantity is the **cubic cell edge a**, not the Ag–Br nearest-neighbour separation — confirmed by Duffin's own use of it, "each 1.0 µ edge of a triangular grain will therefore contain `1.0 × 10,000 / 5.75` = **1,800 silver ions**", which counts like ions, i.e. cell repeats [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.68 (PDF 72)]. The Ag–Br nearest-neighbour distance is therefore a/2 = **2.878 Å**, and the Ag–Ag nearest-neighbour distance is a/√2 = **4.070 Å**. Neither derived value is printed in any source here. **[E]**

**TABLE 1.3 — IONIC RADII (Å)** [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.17 (PDF 21), Table 1.3]:

| Ion | Radius (Å) | Raw OCR | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ag⁺ | **1.26** | `Agt 1.26` | **[Q]** |
| Cl⁻ | **1.81** | `Cla 1.81` | **[Q]** |
| Br⁻ | **1.96** | `Br~ 1.96` | **[Q]** |
| I⁻ | **2.20** | `hg 2.20` | **[Q]** |

Duffin's stated interpretation, which is the whole reason the table is there: "bromide and chloride ions are similar in size and are considerably larger than silver ions but smaller than iodide ions" — the stated reason Cl/Br are fully miscible while I is size-limited [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.17 (PDF 21)]. **[F]** Ionic-radius differences (ours): Br⁻ − Cl⁻ = 0.15 Å (**8.3 %** of Br⁻); I⁻ − Br⁻ = 0.24 Å (**12.2 %** of Br⁻). **[E]**

**Internal inconsistency flag (ours):** r(Ag⁺) + r(Br⁻) = 1.26 + 1.96 = 3.22 Å, but the observed Ag–Br separation from the same book's lattice constant is a/2 = 2.878 Å — a 12 % contraction. Duffin's Table 1.3 radii are not additive to his own lattice constant. Use the lattice constant for geometry and the radii only for the qualitative size-ordering argument. **[E]**

**TABLE 1.4 — DENSITY OF SILVER HALIDES** (units not printed; g cm⁻³ implied) [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22), Table 1.4]:

| Halide | Density | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Chloride | **5.56** | **[Q]** |
| Bromide | **6.473** | **[Q]** |
| Iodide | **5.67** | **[Q]** |

Cross-check (ours): AgBr formula mass 187.77 g/mol; four formula units per fcc cell of edge 5.755 Å (volume 1.906 × 10⁻²² cm³) gives ρ = 4 × 187.77 / (6.022 × 10²³ × 1.906 × 10⁻²²) = **6.54 g cm⁻³**, against the tabulated 6.473 — agreement to 1 %. The lattice constant, the formula mass and the density in Duffin's own tables are mutually consistent. **[E]**

**Bonding.** Silver halides are of the **electrovalent** (ionic) type, but their colour "has been taken as evidence that they are not truly electrovalent … it seems very likely that the electrons linking the silver and the halide atoms are **more equally distributed than the formula Ag⁺Br⁻ suggests**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.16, 19 (PDF 20, 23)]. **[M]** The 1995 account replaces this intuition with a band-structure statement (§4.5): the valence band is "composed of np orbitals of halide ions and 4d orbitals of silver ions", with strong p–d mixing at the L point [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.47 (PDF 56)]. **[M]** The two accounts are compatible: the "more equally distributed electrons" of 1966 are the 1995 silver-4d contribution to the valence band. **[E]**

**Regular crystal forms.** "regular grains can exist in seven forms, which are the cube, octahedron, rhombic dodecahedron, icositetrahedra, trisoctahedra, tetrahexahedra, and hexaoctahedra, as shown in Fig. 2.1. Only {100} and {111} faces are usually stable on the grain surface, and thus the cube and octahedron are the shapes of stable regular grains" [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33), Figs. 2.1, 2.2]. **[F]** The non-cube/octahedron regular forms require crystal-habit modifiers; the rhombic dodecahedron has been observed for AgCl (Claes) and AgBr (Berry, Nishiyama) [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33)]. **[F]**

**Face-fraction formalism.** "the ratios of the area of the {100} face and {111} face to the total surface area (PIOo and Pin, respectively, and P100 + Plu = 1) are important" — i.e. P₁₀₀ + P₁₁₁ = 1 [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.24–25 (PDF 33–34)]. **[F]** Tani measures these fractions through the differential absorption spectra of 9-methyl-thiacarbocyanine dyes — specifically **3,3′-bis(4-disulfobutyl)-9-methyl-thiacarbocyanine** — on {100} vs {111} vs gelatin: the dye adsorbs to {100} first, then to {111} once {100} saturates, then spills into the gelatin. The method relies on the applicability of Kubelka–Munk to emulsions [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.24–25 (PDF 33–34)]. **[M]**

### 4.4 Mixed halides and the solid-solution limits of iodide

**Commercial practice, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)]:

1. "Most positive-emulsions, as well as those used for high-contrast slower films, such as films for graphic-arts purposes and microfilms, contain mixtures of **silver chlorobromide in which the bromide/chloride ratio may vary from 5 % to 50 %**." **[Q]**
2. "**All negative-emulsions, including colour and X-ray films, contain silver bromide containing a small proportion of iodide, usually between 1 % and 8 %.**" **[Q]**

Pure AgCl or pure AgBr emulsions exist for "a few special purposes … but these are unusual" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)]. **[F]**

**Solid solution, not mechanical mixture** — a load-bearing fact, because it means a single emulsion record has one halide composition, not two populations: "both chlorobromide and iodobromide emulsions do **not** consist of some crystals of one halide and some of the other, but … **all the crystals are similar and contain both halides in about the same proportion**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)]. **[F]**

The 1929 evidence for the same conclusion is microscopic and is worth keeping because it is a count: Trivelli & Sheppard examined **122 photomicrographs of as many emulsions at 2500 × magnification** and found no instance of separate hexagonal AgI and regular AgBr crystals — all highly sensitive emulsions contain the iodide in mixed crystal [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.38–39 (PDF 46–47)]. **[Q]** Wall adds a spectral argument: separately prepared AgI and AgBr, mechanically mixed, give a spectral curve showing "a drop on the more refrangible side of the G line", whereas in a true bromo-iodide "the curve is continuous" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.38 (PDF 46)]. **[F]**

**Cl/Br miscibility.** "The similarity in size of the chloride and bromide ions enables them to mix freely throughout the crystals in **all proportions**. The overall properties of a range of silver-chlorobromide emulsions **vary steadily** as the proportions are changed" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)]. **[F]** Restated in the emulsion-making chapter: "chloride and bromide are mixed in all proportions **form 1 : 0 to 1 : 1**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.74 (PDF 80)]. **[Q]** This licenses a smoothly interpolable parameterisation of chlorobromide behaviour against Br fraction; it explicitly does **not** license the same for iodide. **[E]**

**Iodide: the solid-solution limit and the photographic limit are different numbers.** This is the headline statement of the whole section:

> "It is possible to include **up to 20 % of iodide in silver-bromide crystals without interfering with the lattice**, although **the emulsion would be useless photographically before that concentration of iodide is reached**. The addition of small quantities of iodide has a very great influence on the properties of emulsions and a wide variety of emulsion types may be produced in the **iodide range 1 %–8 %**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)] **[Q]**

Reinforced twice: "Unlike iodide which is only added to bromide emulsion within a range of about **1.0 to 8.0 %**…" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.74 (PDF 80)] **[Q]**; and "If … the iodide percentage is increased **above 10 %**, the photographic sensitivity falls, which has been attributed to the formation of more internal image" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.65 (PDF 69)]. **[Q]**

**Iodide contents across the three eras, tabulated.**

| Era / context | Iodide content | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1929, general commercial | AgI = **1–5 %** of total silver halides | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.34 (PDF 42)] | **[Q]** |
| 1929, "practically permissible" (Eder) | **1–6 parts KI per 100 parts bromide**, both ammonia and boiled processes | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.35 (PDF 43)] | **[Q]** |

| 1995, tabular grain used for a dislocation study | **AgBr₀.₉I₀.₁**, i.e. 10 mol % — OCR reads `AgBr09I0 |` | [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.31–32 (PDF 40–41), Fig. 2.10] | **[Q]** |

OCR flag on the 1995 figure: the caption raw string is "a thin tabular AgBr grain (right) and an **AgBr09I0 |**, showing the generation of dislocation lines that were perpendicular to its edges (left)". The decimal points are lost; the composition is AgBr₀.₉I₀.₁ (10 mol % iodide). Quote with the raw string. **[Q]**

The 1929 and 1966 practical ranges **agree**: 1–5 % (Wall) sits inside 1–8 % (Duffin), and both name ≈3–3.5 % as the sweet spot for gradation. **[E]** **Tani 1995 states no iodide solid-solution limit and no commercial iodide range** — the only iodide contents in his range are experimental (10 mol %). **[F]**

**Iodide location within the grain is a design variable, 1966:** "the location of the iodide, which may be present mainly at the centre of the crystal, distributed throughout the grain or mainly on the outside. The actual location of the iodide is determined by the preparation conditions and will clearly have an influence on the physical and chemical properties of the crystal" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)]. **[M]** Evidence that it really is non-uniform: "the **coarser grains of a broadly dispersed iodobromide emulsion contain the most iodide**, suggesting that grains containing the most iodide were probably precipitated first and tend to grow more quickly", and "some silver-bromide crystals contained a **core having quite large concentrations of iodide**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.64–65 (PDF 68–69)]. **[F]**

The 1929 counterpart observation, from sedimentation rather than analysis: Renwick & Sease sedimented emulsions and found "the percentage of **silver iodide and of coarse grains in the lower strata** of emulsions, allowed to settle, was much higher than in the upper strata" — i.e. iodide correlates with the coarse tail of the size distribution. Wall notes the result "is probably only due to a particular method of mixing" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.37 (PDF 45) and note 4, p.53 (PDF 61)]. **[F]** Duffin 1966 and Renwick & Sease (in Wall 1929) therefore report the *same* correlation — iodide-rich grains are the coarse ones — thirty-seven years apart, with Wall sceptical of it and Duffin accepting it. **[E]**

**Vegard's law and its EXAFS violation (1995).** "the average distance between a silver ion and its nearest neighbor halide ion, which is given by X-ray diffraction measurement, changes linearly with its halide composition, forming Vegard's law. However, it has recently been revealed from EXAFS measurements that the real distance between a silver ion and its nearest neighbor halide ion in a mixed crystal does not obey Vegard's law" [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.31 (PDF 40), Fig. 2.9]. **[F]** For AgBrCl, the Br–Ag distance exceeds the average X–Ag distance. **Internal inconsistency in the source:** the body text says the discrepancy "decreases with increasing temperature", but the footnote on the same page says "the deviation increased with increasing temperature" and cites "Fig. 2.7" where it means Fig. 2.9. Do not use the direction of the temperature dependence. **[F]** The stated cause is a competition of forces: the Vegard structure is most stable when determined by a long-range ionic force, and the deviation is ascribed to short-range covalent-bonding contributions, whose relative importance rises with temperature as the lattice expands and the long-range force weakens [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.31 (PDF 40), footnote]. **[M]**

**Iodide as an electronic dopant (1995), the effect Duffin and Wall could not see:** "the trapping of a positive hole at a residual iodide impurity was dominant in nominally pure AgBr at liquid helium temperature, and the localization energy of the hole trapped at iodide ion can be estimated as **0.04 eV for an isolated iodide ion** and as **0.1 to 0.15 eV for an iodide ion pair**" [Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.71 (PDF 80)]. **[Q]** Listed alongside as shallow isoelectronic (uncharged) hole traps: I⁻ in AgBr, I⁻ in AgCl, Br⁻ in AgCl [Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.71 (PDF 80)]. **[F]**

**Iodide as a structural dopant (both eras).** 1966: iodide, "being larger than bromide, will increase the size of one layer and therefore make the introduction of **edge and screw dislocations** more likely" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.25–27 (PDF 29–31)]. **[M]** 1995, with direct imaging: "Figure 2.10 is a transmission electron micrograph of thin tabular grains showing the **absence of any dislocation in a pure AgBr tabular grain** and the **generation of dislocations at the interface between different silver halide phases** in a tabular silver iodobromide grain", the dislocation lines running perpendicular to the grain edges [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.31–32 (PDF 40–41), Fig. 2.10]. **[F]** These two statements, twenty-nine years apart, are the same claim: iodide generates dislocations. Duffin infers it from ionic size; Tani photographs it. **[E]**

**Iodide's stated photographic payoff (1966), the highest-value chemistry→image link in Duffin's emulsion chapter:** "other things being similar, iodide has the following effects: **a) increased photographic speed, especially after chemical sensitization, which is much less likely to give fog with higher iodide-content emulsions. b) improved spectral sensitization**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.64–65 (PDF 68–69)]. **[F]** The 1929 list for the same additive is longer and partly different: iodobromide emulsions are "more opaque, less halation and solarization"; after sufficient digestion "more sensitive than a pure bromide emulsion and more to gaslight than to daylight"; iodide "acts as a fog preventive → permits longer digestion"; iodide **decreases development velocity**, the same gamma being reachable by longer development; iodide **prolongs the period of under-exposure**; fixation is slower; and "iodide fog" (milkiness in hypo, clearing on washing) appears [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.33–35, 42 (PDF 41–43, 50)]. **[F]** The two lists agree on speed-after-digestion and on fog restraint; only Wall reports the development-rate and fixation penalties, and only Duffin reports the spectral-sensitization benefit. **[E]**

### 4.5 Intrinsic absorption: colour, absorption edges, and the indirect transition

**The 1966 statement — colours and edges in Ångström:**

> "Silver chloride is **colourless (white)** while silver bromide is **pale yellow** and silver iodide **somewhat deeper yellow**. This means that silver chloride **does not absorb light in the visible region of the spectrum to any extent but only in the near ultra-violet**, and to some extent at the violet end of the visible spectrum. **Silver bromide, however, absorbs light up to about 4,900 Å**, while the addition of silver iodide to silver bromide deepens the yellow colour and extends the light absorption further into the visible spectrum, **up to 5,200 Å; the maximum effect is produced by about 2.0 % of iodide and higher values cause the colour to lighten**. Because only absorbed light can have any photographic effect, **silver chloride is only sensitive to u.v. and violet light, while silver bromide and iodobromide are sensitive to the violet and blue region of the spectrum**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.19 (PDF 23)] **[Q]**

Restated in nm (conv.): **AgBr absorption edge ≈ 490 nm; AgBr(I) extended to ≈ 520 nm, with the maximum extension at ≈ 2.0 mol % AgI and a *reversal* above that iodide level.** **[Q]** The non-monotonicity above 2 % iodide is a specific and unusual claim; no other source in this set states or contradicts it. **[F]**

Duffin's supporting figure, **Fig. 6.1 "Spectral sensitivity of undyed emulsions"**, has two panels, **Chlorobromide** and **Iodobromide**, on a wavelength axis of **4000–7000 Å**. The curves are lost to OCR; only the axis ticks (4000, 5000, 6000, 7000 Å) and the panel labels survive [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.99 (PDF 105), Fig. 6.1]. **[F]** The governing law is named: the Grotthus–Draper law, "only that light which is **absorbed** can be effective in producing a chemical change; the formation of a latent image is a chemical change" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.99 (PDF 105)]. **[F]**

Duffin adds one important qualification that keeps the "edge" from being a hard cut: silver sulphide or silver formed during chemical sensitization produces "appreciable long-wavelength sensitivity" — a red tail beyond the intrinsic absorption edge — "present even with the purest crystals" but stronger in chemically-sensitized emulsions [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.132 (PDF 138)]. **[F]** Tani's 1995 counterpart of this statement is quantitative in a different way: sulphur and sulphur-plus-gold centres, "being excited by red light, … can inject electrons into the conduction band of silver halide with the aid of thermal energy and **thus give rise to red sensitivity**", their trap depths having in fact been *measured* from the temperature coefficient of that red sensitivity [Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.73 (PDF 82)]. **[F]**

**The 1995 statement — indirect transitions with energies.** This is the mechanism the 1966 book could only gesture at:

| Quantity | Value | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Indirect exciton transition energy, AgCl | **3.245 eV** | [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.46 (PDF 55)] | **[Q]** |
| Indirect exciton transition energy, AgBr | **2.684 eV** | [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.46 (PDF 55)] | **[Q]** |
| Same, converted to wavelength | AgCl **382.0 nm**; AgBr **461.9 nm** (using hc = 1239.84 eV·nm, conv.) | derived | **[E]** |
| Indirect exciton binding energy, AgBr | **0.022 eV** | [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.60 (PDF 69)] | **[Q]** |
| Indirect exciton binding energy, AgCl | **0.04 eV** (estimated) | [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.60 (PDF 69)] | **[Q]** |
| Quantum yield for photoconduction of electrons, AgBr at 300 K | **> 0.960** | [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.60 (PDF 69)] | **[Q]** |
| Electron effective mass | **0.399** (AgCl), **0.282** (AgBr), single isotropic parabolic valley | [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.61 (PDF 70)] | **[Q]** |

**Reconciling the 1966 edge with the 1995 transition energy (ours).** Duffin's "AgBr absorbs up to about 4,900 Å" (490 nm, 2.53 eV) and Tani's "indirect exciton transition of AgBr is 2.684 eV" (462 nm) are **not** contradictory, because they are different quantities: Tani's is the transition energy of the indirect exciton, while Duffin's is the long-wavelength limit of the *absorption tail*, which extends below the transition energy because the transition is phonon-assisted and therefore has a temperature-broadened tail. Tani describes exactly that tail: each absorption spectrum "is composed of a low-energy, weak, and highly temperature-dependent light absorption band with an extended tail in the visible wavelength region and an intense exciton band in the UV region" [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.45 (PDF 54), Fig. 3.1]. The 28 nm difference is the tail. **[E]**

**Why blue absorption is weak — the band-structure explanation, quoted because it is the load-bearing mechanism:**

> "the minimum of the conduction band in AgBr and AgCl are located at the F point in momentum space. It has been established that the maximum of the valence band of AgBr is located along the [111] direction and at the L point. … Thus, the transition with the least energy and the longest wavelength is the indirect exciton transition from the L point to the F point, and has a small probability, since it should be accompanied with the change in momentum. On the other hand, the transition by the intense exciton band in the UV region is assigned to the direct exciton transition and has a large probability, since it is not accompanied by a change in momentum. The change in momentum is achieved by the interaction of the excitons with phonons or impurities."
> [Tani 1995, §3.1, pp.46–47 (PDF 55–56), Fig. 3.2] **[M]**

(OCR: "F point" throughout is the Γ point.) And the orbital origin:

> "the minimum of the conduction band of silver halides is mostly composed of 5s orbitals of silver ions, whereas the valence band is composed of np orbitals of halide ions and 4d orbitals of silver ions. The maximum of the valence band at the L point exhibits strong p-d mixing, whereas the valence band at the F point exhibits little p-d mixing. The repulsive interaction between halide np and silver 4d states raises the valence band in the region away from the F point, bringing about the low-energy indirect exciton transition. On the other hand, the valence bands of alkali halides are essentially composed of the np orbitals of halogen ions."
> [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.47 (PDF 56)] **[M]**

The photographic significance is stated explicitly, and it is the reason weak absorption is *not* simply a defect:

> "The absorption of visible light, which is one of the most important properties of silver halides as photosensitive elements in photographic materials, arises from this indirect transition. It is noted that this transition is brought about by the p-d mixing in the valence band of silver halides. Although the absorption is weak due to its small transition probability and is not necessarily favorable for capturing incident light, **the small transition probability also predicts a small recombination probability, which is favorable for efficient latent image formation**. It is therefore noted that the contribution of 4d orbitals of silver ions to the valence bands of silver halides is important for the application of silver halides to photography from the viewpoints of electronic structure and light absorption."
> [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.47 (PDF 56)] **[M]**

Two corroborating details: alkali halide absorption spectra consist of "only an intense exciton band in the UV region", with no low-energy tail at all — the contrast that isolates the silver-4d contribution as the cause [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.45 (PDF 54)] **[F]**; and the temperature dependence discriminates the two momentum-change routes, since "the strength of the phonon-assisted indirect-exciton transition in pure AgBr was temperature dependent, whereas that of the transition of the indirect exciton band bound at an isoelectric iodine impurity was nearly independent of temperature" [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.47 (PDF 56)]. **[F]**

Because the indirect exciton binding energies (0.022 eV AgBr, 0.04 eV AgCl) are small compared with kT at room temperature (0.0257 eV), "excitons in silver halide emulsion grains freely dissociate into an electron and a positive hole at room temperature", which is what delivers the > 0.960 photoconduction quantum yield [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.60 (PDF 69)]. **[Q]** This is the closest thing in the set to a primary-photoconversion efficiency: **> 0.96 free electrons per absorbed photon in AgBr at 300 K.** **[Q]**

**The 1929 position on the same physics** is entirely empirical and is worth recording as the baseline the other two improved on. Wall reports Carey Lea's claim that AgI is "much more sensitive to red and orange than the bromide"; that KI-bathed plates give "distinct orange and red sensitiveness"; Sheppard's finding that the action is **specific**, appearing only in emulsions already showing red sensitivity — "merely an intensification of an already existing action"; and Wall's own scepticism that the effect "is limited apparently to a particular method of emulsion making", with increasing iodide ratio "frequently seem[ing] to prevent its appearance" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.43–44 (PDF 51–52); Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 95)]. **[F]** Wall also reports that in positive cine emulsions iodide can be varied and "with greater quantities the emulsion becomes distinctly red-sensitive" [Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 95)]. **[F]**

**These sources disagree about what added iodide does to long-wavelength response.** Duffin 1966 states the absorption extension peaks at ≈2.0 % iodide and that "higher values cause the colour to lighten", i.e. the extension *reverses* [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.19 (PDF 23)]. Wall 1929 reports, from several workers, that *greater* iodide quantities produce red sensitivity [Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 95); Ch. III, pp.43–44 (PDF 51–52)]. Both are stated as observations. Wall himself doubted the generality of the 1929 claim, and the 1929 observations were on iodide-*bathed* or accidentally overdosed material rather than on precipitated solid solutions, which may be the reconciliation — but that reconciliation is ours, and neither book offers it. **[E]** Tani 1995 says nothing on the point. **[F]**

### 4.6 Point defects: Frenkel, Schottky, and interstitial silver ions

**Definitions, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.24–26 (PDF 28–30), Figs. 1.13–1.15]:

- "A defect is defined as the **absence of a component or components from the lattice** and implies no gross structural distortion as occurs with dislocations." **[F]**
- **Schottky defects** = absence of a *pair* of ions (Fig. 1.13). "it does not appear that they are of great significance in silver halide." **[F]**
- **Frenkel defects** = "the omission of one ion from its position in the lattice and, in order to maintain electrical neutrality, its appearance at a **non-lattice position, called an interstitial position**" (Fig. 1.14). "it is the **smaller silver ion** which is moved … the ions located in the interstitial positions are therefore called **interstitial silver ions**. The **appreciably larger bromide ions cannot, because of their size, be located in interstitial positions**." **[M]**
- "From recent work … it seems very likely that the **majority of the interstitial silver ions are located on the surface of emulsion grains**." **[F]**
- "**interstitial ions are not fixed** like those in lattice positions but are **free to move within the crystal lattice**." **[M]**

**The same two defect types, 1995:** "There are two types of intrinsic point defects in ionic crystals: Frenkel defect and Schottky defect, as schematically shown in Fig. 3.3. It is determined that **Frenkel defects composed of interstitial silver ions and silver ion vacancies are predominant in silver halide** and are the charge carriers for the dark conductivity (i.e., ionic conductivity) of silver halides" [Tani 1995, §3.2, p.48 (PDF 57), Fig. 3.3]. **[F]** Both books therefore agree on the essential point: Frenkel, not Schottky; interstitial silver, not interstitial halide. **[E]**

(3.10)]. **[M]** As of 1995 the defect formation parameters were still open: "defect formation parameters such as ΔGi, ΔGv, and Φs are **still under consideration**" [Tani 1995, §3.2, p.59 (PDF 68)]. **[F]**

**How much interstitial silver is actually available — a reversal of a long-held premise.** Tani records the 1995 position verbatim against Mitchell's earlier one: "It has been found that **a large number of interstitial silver ions are present and available for latent image formation in an emulsion grain**", where Mitchell had held "there would be **less than one interstitial silver ion per emulsion grain** at room temperature" [Tani 1995, §4.1.2, p.85 (PDF 94)]. **[F]** Duffin 1966 already sided with the later view, on the grounds that most interstitials sit at the surface [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.26 (PDF 30)]. **[E]**

**Impurity control of the interstitial population — the 1966 doping argument, with a stoichiometric consequence:** "a divalent metal ion, which substitutes a silver ion at a lattice position, is associated with a silver ion vacancy for the neutralization of the excess charge on the divalent metal ion" [Tani 1995, §3.2, p.49 (PDF 58)] **[M]**; and, in the same terms but with the counting made explicit, "**Polyvalent positive ions, notably the doubly-charged cadmium ion**" are "active in producing **Frenkel defects**. Maintenance of electrical neutrality means that there will be **vacancies associated with each cadmium ion and also one fewer interstitial silver ion per cadmium ion**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.25–27 (PDF 29–31), Fig. 1.15]. **[Q]**

The stated practical consequence of that stoichiometry is a real formulation rule: "it is therefore significant that **cadmium salts are more frequently mentioned in connection with silver-chloride and chlorobromide emulsions, where frequently large quantities are incorporated, whereas they are used only rarely in iodobromide emulsions where the introduction of fairly small quantities produce large effects**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.25–27 (PDF 29–31)]. **[M]** Wall 1929's use of cadmium is consistent but unexplained — cupric chloride, not cadmium, is his contrast additive for chloride emulsions, at 5–7.5 g per 500 g AgNO₃, "increases contrast", "the quantity may be varied at will" [Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 101); Ch. VI, p.104 (PDF 111)]. **[Q]** Duffin's 1966 counterpart is cadmium chloride, "used to obtain chloride and chlorobromide emulsion of **maximum contrast**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.74 (PDF 80)]. **[F]** So both eras use a divalent-cation additive to raise the contrast of chloride emulsions; the cation changed from Cu²⁺ to Cd²⁺, and only the 1966 source offers the vacancy mechanism. **[E]**

**Which divalent ions actually matter electronically (1995):** over the series Hg²⁺, Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺, Ni²⁺, Co²⁺, Cd²⁺, Fe²⁺, Zn²⁺, Ba²⁺, Sr²⁺, Mn²⁺ (ordered by redox potential), "only Hg2+ and Cu2+ could decrease the luminescence intensity and photographic sensitivity of a cubic AgBr emulsion by providing deep traps for electrons" [Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.71 (PDF 80)]. **[F]** Cd²⁺ is in that list and is *not* one of the two active ones — so its 1966 role must be the ionic/vacancy one, not an electron-trapping one, exactly as Duffin argued. **[E]**

This corresponds to `5x 107’` equivalents of rhodium and therefore only a few rhodium ions per grain" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.74 (PDF 80)]. **[Q]** OCR flag: the exponent is corrupt; the printed value is most likely 5 × 10⁻⁷ equivalents. **[F]** So the Rh³⁺-for-contrast trick is documented in **both** 1966 (as a recipe, with a dose) and 1995 (as a trap depth and a lifetime), twenty-nine years apart, and the two accounts are complementary rather than conflicting. **[E]**
