(3.23)]. **[Q]** Three (E, t) pairs are enough to fix a two-parameter Arrhenius law, and they place the sulphur-centre thermal depth of ~0.3 eV at a residence of only ~1 µs — consistent with Tani's insistence that useful electron traps must be *shallow*. **[E]**

### 4.7 Dislocations, twin planes, kinks, jogs, and mosaic structure

**Dislocations, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.20–23 (PDF 24–27), Figs. 1.6–1.11]:

- **Edge dislocations** — "displacement of the edge of a growing crystal, leading to an incomplete plane" (Figs. 1.6, 1.7); alternatively produced "by the slip of the lower planes"; "caused by strain deformation of perfect crystals". The alternating Ag/Br pattern must be maintained, which complicates the geometry (Fig. 1.7). **[M]**
- **Screw dislocations** — "caused by the slip of a piece of the growing crystal face by **one whole unit cell**" (Figs. 1.8–1.10); the irregularity appears only on the upper and lower faces, not on the front face. "If the slip goes right through the crystal it **disappears completely as a dislocation** and merely becomes an unfinished terrace of cells which will build up to give a perfect cube again." **[M]**
- **Persistence:** both types "cannot be cancelled out without some drastic treatment of the crystal … growth upwards from the crystal face will **perpetuate the dislocation**." **[M]**
- **Jogs:** two screw dislocations meeting at right angles form a **jog** (Fig. 1.12), producing "a **row of vacancies** … lattice positions will be unoccupied because of the influence of two dislocations." **[M]**
- **Kink sites:** "the actual edge ions at an incomplete part of a crystal, either internally or externally, i.e. **where an ion is not surrounded by the six ions of opposite sign**." May or may not be associated with a dislocation (Fig. 1.10). **[M]**

**Observation history of dislocations (1995):** Mitchell and coworkers observed dislocations within crystals for the first time, in AgBr, "made visible by decoration with photolytic silver"; Farnell and coworkers observed dislocation lines in silver iodobromide *emulsion grains* by the same decoration method; Hamilton and Shiozawa observed dislocation lines in transmission electron micrographs of tabular AgBr grains; and the formation and observation of dislocations was reviewed by Mitchell [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.30–31 (PDF 39–40)]. **[F]** Defect types listed as introduced into emulsion grains and playing "important roles in photographic processes": **twin planes, dislocations, and stacking faults** [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.30 (PDF 39)]. **[F]**

**Twin planes and tabular grains (1995).** "a hexagonal tabular grain has two twin planes on {111} lattice planes in parallel to its main surfaces, and uneven side surfaces with the lines of the intersection of the twin planes with them"; and "a twin plane is formed as a result of a **stacking fault**" [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.25–26 (PDF 34–35), Figs. 2.3, 2.4]. **[F]** Two conflicting observations are recorded side by side in the source itself, and must be preserved as such:

| Observation | Worker | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| "a large hexagonal tabular grain had an **even number** of parallel twin planes and a large triangular one had an **odd number** of parallel twin planes" | Maskasky | [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.26 (PDF 35)] | **[F]** |
| "there was **no obvious correlation** between the external shape and the number of twin planes in a common tabular crystal" | Black et al. | [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.26 (PDF 35)] | **[F]** |
| Tabular AgBr grains with a **(100)** face on the surface and **no twin plane at all** also exist | Mignot et al. | [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.26 (PDF 35)] | **[F]** |

These three findings are mutually inconsistent on whether twin-plane parity determines habit, and Tani presents them without resolving the question. **[F]**

**The 1966 twin-plane mechanism, which predates all of that and is geometrically explicit** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.69–72 (PDF 73–76), Figs. 4.5–4.10]: the growth-promoting AgBr₃²⁻ ion can attach to a (111) surface in a **normal position** (Fig. 4.7 — perfect extension) or in a **twin position** (Fig. 4.8 — a fault). A single twin plane yields "pockets" on one face (Fig. 4.9, marked X), giving preferential lateral extension and hence a tabular crystal. "the vast majority of crystals examined show **not just one twin plane but two**", which gives "pockets along **all six edges**" (Fig. 4.10), hence rapid edge growth and large plates. Duffin's own caveat: the confirming electron micrographs were of crystals "larger than those ever found in commercial emulsions" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.69–72 (PDF 73–76)]. **[M]** Duffin's "two twin planes are the vast majority" agrees exactly with Tani's 1995 statement that a hexagonal tabular grain "has two twin planes on {111} lattice planes in parallel to its main surfaces" — a rare instance of a 1966 mechanism surviving intact to 1995. **[E]**

**Crystallite vs grain size; the mosaic structure (1995).** X-ray diffraction line-profile analysis gives the average size of *crystallites*, the regions in which the lattice is perfect:

> "In the absence of crystal defect, the crystallite size is the same as the grain size, whereas the former is smaller than the latter in the presence of crystal defects in the grains. It was confirmed by this method that many regular silver halide grains in emulsions were crystallographically perfect, whereas there were also many silver halide emulsion grains that contained many crystal defects and were divided into small crystallites, forming a **mosaic structure**."
> [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.32 (PDF 41)] **[F]**

**Dislocations vs photolysis, with an explicit 1966 caution against over-reading large-crystal work** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.75 (PDF 81)]:

- "Compared with **transistors**, another class of crystalline substances where impurities are deliberately introduced, the published literature on silver-halide technology is **very sparse**; experiments with large doped silver-halide crystals **may not be valid** for photographic-emulsion crystals." **[F]**
- "Many workers have shown that **print-out silver in large silver-bromide slabs forms along dislocation lines** within the crystals but Swinnerton demonstrated that **quite different patterns are obtained from similar looking crystals**." **[F]**
- Mitchell: "**etch pits were formed most quickly at points where the dislocations came to the crystal surface**." **[F]**
- "**So far it has not been decided whether a perfect silver-halide crystal would be useless photographically** although most authors suggest that this would be the case. Mitchell has pointed out that dislocations as such may not be needed but the occurrence of **surface imperfections** is a part of many modern considerations of photographic sensitivity." **[F]**

Tani 1995 answers the question Duffin 1966 left open, and answers it with an optimum rather than a monotone: "Farnell examined the photographic sensitivity of emulsion grains as a function of the density of crystal defects, and found that the grains with few crystal defects as well as those with too many crystal defects suffered from low efficiency for latent image formation, and **grains with a medium number of defects showed the highest sensitivity**" [Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.89–90 (PDF 98–99)]. **[F]** So the 1929/1966 intuition that a perfect crystal would be useless is confirmed in direction, and refined: excess defects are also harmful, and there is an interior maximum. **[E]**

Wall 1929 has no concept of a dislocation or a point defect. His nearest equivalent is the observation, offered without mechanism, that "It is believed that these imperfections may play a vital part…" is entirely absent — imperfection language does not appear in Wall at all; his crystal-quality proxy is the **dip test** colour sequence (§6.4). **[F]**

### 4.8 The crystal surface, its reconstruction, and the electrical double layer

**The surface is where photography happens (1966):** "The surface of the silver-halide crystal is where the **vast majority of the photographic processes take place**, e.g. chemical sensitisation, stabilisation, dye sensitisation and development, and usually latent-image formation as well" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.19 (PDF 23)]. **[F]**

**The electrical double layer, and its direct link to fog (1966)** — quoted in full because the fog link is stated nowhere else in the set:

> "although an emulsion crystal as a whole contains equal numbers of silver and halide ions, in suspension in a solution containing excess bromide ions, there is a **layer of bromide ions closely associated with the crystal surface**. This is called the **electrical double layer** and results in the whole crystal being **negatively charged relative to its environment**. The layer is retained throughout the life of a silver-halide emulsion grain, except in certain special emulsions in the early stages of their formation, and **its disappearance will immediately make the grain developable without the action of light, i.e. a fogged grain**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.19–20 (PDF 23–24), Fig. 1.5] **[M]**

A corroborating consequence appears in the coating chapter: polyethylene oxides are believed to act "by reducing the charge of the double layer surrounding the grain, and thus facilitate the approach of the negatively-charged developing agents", giving "**up to twice the speed**" in fast iodobromide emulsions under optimum conditions [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.165 (PDF 171)]. **[Q]**

**{111} surface reconstruction (1995).** A truncated {111} face would consist of a full Ag or Br layer, carrying a large surface dipole; reconstruction gives a **half-filled** top layer instead. Two computed low-energy models exist — hexagonal and alternate-row — and **SEXAFS agrees better with the alternate-row model**. The AgBr {100} face relaxes "rumpled", with Br displaced above and Ag below the nominal plane [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.26–27 (PDF 35–36), Figs. 2.5, 2.6]. **[M]** As of 1995 this was live: "The surface structure of silver halides, in particular, the structure of the {111} surface, **has been a point of argument**" [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.26 (PDF 35)]. **[F]** The techniques: XPS, ISS, SIMS, backscattered electron imaging, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction analysis, SEXAFS ("**recently** … 1988–1992"), and "**Recently, the atomic force microscope has been successfully used for observation of each bromide ion on the surface of AgBr**" (1992–1993 references) [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.27, 31 (PDF 36, 40)]. **[F]**

**Charge state of a kink site — the number that makes the whole latent-image mechanism work.** Tani's "partially charged trap" principle:

> "the electrostatic charge of an initial electron-trapping center suitable for efficient latent image formation has a partial, preferably **+½** charge, as for the case of a surface kink site, and becomes a **−½** charge when the center traps an electron. Electron trapping by the center is followed by the ionic process, which makes the center become **+½** charged and thus 'reset' for trapping another electron. The concept of a partially charged electron trap results in an alternating sign of charge at each step … and **minimizes the recombination probability**…"
> [Tani 1995, §4.1.1, p.83 (PDF 92)] **[M]**

OCR note: the fractions render as `+\`, `-|`, `+ \`; the text elsewhere says "half a positive charge" for a kink site, confirming ±½. **[F]**

### 4.9 The stated FUNCTION of imperfections in image formation

This is the question the source set answers most directly, and the 1966 statement is the fullest. Quoted at length because it is the mechanism:

> "Apart from the **release of interstitial silver ions**, there are other important functions … In the bulk of the crystal the charges are balanced because all the ions are surrounded by a complete group of ions of opposite charge. **At these special sites, however, this is not so and, as a result, a residual charge resides on the ion in that position**; this may be a residual negative charge on a kink bromide ion or a residual positive charge on a kink silver ion. These ions will, therefore, be able to **attract and, to a limited extent, retain a charged entity of opposite sign** … and are therefore called **traps. Traps play an important part in the formation of the latent image.** Alternatively, the absence of an ion at a vacant lattice site will mean that the residual negative charge of the six surrounding ions is available to attract a positive entity. Therefore **vacant lattice sites will act as traps for positively-charged units**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.27 (PDF 31), Fig. 1.16 "Electrostatic balance in crystals" — showing the bulk situation, an Ag ion at an edge dislocation, an Ag ion at a kink site, an Ag ion at a jog, and a Frenkel defect] **[M]**

The same point, stated earlier and more cautiously: "It is believed that these imperfections **may play a vital part in giving the crystal its photographic sensitivity**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.20 (PDF 24)]. **[M]**

So the stated function decomposes into exactly three roles, all electrostatic:

| Role of the imperfection | Trapped entity | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source of mobile silver — release of interstitial Ag⁺ (Frenkel) | — (supplies the ionic half of the process) | [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, pp.26–27 (PDF 30–31)] | **[M]** |
| Kink silver ion, residual **positive** charge | electron | [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.27 (PDF 31)] | **[M]** |
| Kink bromide ion, residual **negative** charge; and vacant lattice sites | positive hole / positive entity | [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.27 (PDF 31)] | **[M]** |

Tani 1995 sharpens the first two into the alternating ±½ charge cycle of §4.8, and adds the quantitative corollary that the *number* of traps has an optimum (§4.7, Farnell) and that trap **depth** determines residence time via Marker's equation (§4.6). **[E]** Tani's own verdict on what ultimately limits sensitivity is worth recording here because it is a statement about traps: "we have learned that **dispersion of image centers** and **recombination between photoelectrons and positive holes** are the major factors limiting photographic sensitivity" [Tani 1995, §4.1.3, p.87 (PDF 96)]. **[F]**

Duffin's summary sentence for the whole chapter — the one-line answer to "what is an emulsion grain?" — is: "an emulsion grain is an **imperfect crystal**, possessing basically a cubic lattice structure with a large number of internal and external imperfections" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.27 (PDF 31)]. **[F]**

### 4.10 Gaps and unresolved points in §4

- **Ksp and solubility as functions of temperature.** Absent from all three sources, despite every ripening operation being hot. **[F]**
- **Lattice constant of AgCl and of AgI; the AgI structure type.** Absent. Only AgBr's cell edge is given (5.755 / 5.75 Å). **[F]**
- **Frenkel formation energies: the two sources disagree**, especially for AgCl (1.687 eV from Duffin/Pouradier vs 1.49 eV from Tani), and they report different thermodynamic quantities (ΔG vs ΔH). **[F]**
- **Direct exciton (UV) transition energies.** Tani gives only the indirect values numerically; the intense UV exciton band is described but not numbered. **[F]**
- **Absorption coefficients or optical constants of any silver halide at any wavelength.** Absent from all three sources. The spectra exist only as figures (Tani Fig. 3.1; Duffin Fig. 6.1), both lost to OCR. **[F]**
- **Whether a perfect crystal would be photographically useless.** Explicitly open in 1966 [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.75 (PDF 81)]; answered in direction but not in magnitude by Farnell's defect-density optimum in 1995 [Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.89–90 (PDF 98–99)]. **[F]**
- **1995 open frontiers, in the source's own words:** "**Further studies are needed** on the electronic structures of the surfaces of silver halides and the interfaces between different silver halides" [Tani 1995, §3.1, p.48 (PDF 57)]; "Further studies are needed for the clarification of the nature and role of the conductivity of silver ions on the (111) surface" [Tani 1995, §3.2, p.54 (PDF 63)]; "The studies on physical properties and photographic behavior of **AgCl emulsion grains are only beginning**" [Tani 1995, §3.4.1, p.70 (PDF 79)]. **[F]**

---

## 5. Crystal size, size distribution, habit, and tabular-grain technology

### 5.1 Grain sizes, with source and era for each figure

**1929 gives no numbers at all.** This must be stated plainly: "Wall gives **no numerical grain sizes, no measured size distributions, and no micrograph data of his own.** All grain statements are qualitative or cited second-hand" [Wall 1929, Ch. III passim]. **[F]** Wall does cite one source that had the data — Carroll & Hubbard, *J. Phys. Chem.* 1927, **31**, 906, who "published full tables as to the **grain size, fog and gammas** obtained" for various bromides — but he reproduces none of it [Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.27–28 (PDF 35–36)]. **[F]** The only quantitative grain observation in Wall is a count of micrographs, not of sizes: Trivelli & Sheppard's 122 emulsions at 2500 × (§4.4). **[Q]**

**1966 — Duffin's Table 1.1, the era's grain-size prior by stock class.**

**TABLE 1.1 — EMULSION GRAIN SIZES ("Approx. mean Diameter", µ)** [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15), Table 1.1]:

| Type of emulsion | Approx. mean diameter (µ) | Metric (conv.) | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| High Resolution Film | **0.03** | 30 nm | **[Q]** |
| Chlorobromide Paper | **0.2** | 200 nm | **[Q]** |
| Lithographic Film | **0.35** | 350 nm | **[Q]** |
| Fine Grain Pan Film | **0.7** | 700 nm | **[Q]** |
| Fast Negative Film | **2.0** | 2.0 µm | **[Q]** |
| Fast Medical X-ray Film | **2.5** | 2.5 µm | **[Q]** |

OCR notes: the "Fast Negative Film" row reads `a` then `2.0`; the "Fast Medical X-ray Film" row reads `25`, i.e. 2.5, confirmed by the prose "to 2.5µ in the coarsest-grained fast negative or X-ray emulsions". **[Q]** Supporting prose: "the sizes range from **0.03 µ diameter**, in the case of very fine-grain emulsions used for high resolution scientific work, to **2.5 µ** in the coarsest-grained fast negative or X-ray emulsions"; grains at the fine end "are in some cases too small to be detected by ordinary microscopes and can only be seen by the use of the electron microscope" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15)]. **[Q]**

The book's own unit footnote survives and is worth keeping because the archaic µ/mµ notation runs through the whole text: "The micron, µ, is one millionth of a metre (10⁻⁶ metres) and other units are the mµ or millimicron, which is a thousandth of a µ (10⁻⁹ metres) and the Angstrom unit, Å, which is a tenth of a mµ (10⁻¹⁰ metres or 10⁻⁸ cms)" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15), footnote]. **[Q]**

Span of Table 1.1 (ours): 0.03 → 2.5 µ is a **factor of 83 in linear size, 5.8 × 10⁵ in volume**. If per-grain sensitivity scales with volume (§5.6), that alone spans the entire practical speed range of photographic materials. **[E]**

**1966 — the two fully worked commercial-type emulsions.**

| Quantity | Octahedral (bromide-ripened) | Cubic (ammonia) | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean size | **0.87 µ** diameter | **1.2 µ** cube edge | **[Q]** |
| Mean volume | **0.18 µ³** | **1.75 µ³** | **[Q]** |
| Surface area per grain | **≈ 2 µ²** | **8.7 µ²** | **[Q]** |
| Thickness | **≈ 0.2 µ** (flat octahedra) | — (equiaxed) | **[Q]** |
| Thickness/diameter | "usually only about **1/10th or 1/5th** as thick as their diameter" | — | **[Q]** |
| Size distribution | "a **fairly broad range** of grain sizes"; "The **broad spread of grain sizes in this emulsion is characteristic of emulsions ripened in the presence of a large excess of bromide**" | "the grains are **much more even in size** … the **absence of either small or very large grains** will be noticed" | **[F]** |
| Citation | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.66–68 (PDF 70–72), Plate 4.1, Figs. 4.3–4.4] | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.72–73 (PDF 76, 79), Plate 4.2, Fig. 4.11] | |

Surface-to-volume ratios (ours): octahedral 2/0.18 = **11.1 µm⁻¹**; cubic 8.7/1.75 = **4.97 µm⁻¹**. The octahedral emulsion has **2.2× the surface area per unit volume**, which matters for dye-sensitized speed (§5.7) and for sensitizer coverage (§7.4). **[E]**

**1966 — a named commercial stock with a measured grain figure.** Bekunov's sensitization work used "an iodobromide emulsion containing **3.1 molar per cent of iodide** and **mean grain size 1.2–1.4 µ² surface area**; **this would be a normal fast iodobromide emulsion of the type used for Kodak Tri-X and similar types of film**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)]. **[Q]** Note the unit: **surface area in µ², not diameter**. Equivalent-sphere diameter (ours): a sphere of surface 1.2–1.4 µm² has diameter 0.62–0.67 µm; a cube of the same total surface has edge 0.45–0.48 µm. Either way, Tri-X-class grains at 1.2–1.4 µm² surface are **substantially smaller** than Duffin's own Table 1.1 entry of 2.0 µ diameter for "Fast Negative Film". The two 1966 figures for the same stock class differ by roughly a factor of three in linear size and are not reconcilable from what is printed; present both. **[E]**

**1995 — Tani's range statement and his experimental grain sizes.**

| Quantity | Value | Citation | Tag |

| Full range | **< 0.1 µm to several micrometers** | [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33)] | **[Q]** |
| Tabular AgBr used in growth studies | thickness **0.1 µm**, characterised by **Dc = equivalent circular diameter** (diameter of the circle of equal projected area) | [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.39–40 (PDF 48–49), Fig. 2.17] | **[Q]** |
| Octahedral AgBr, reduction/hypersensitization work | average diameter **0.2 µm** | [Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.98–100 (PDF 107–109)] | **[Q]** |

| Tabular AgBr, sulphur-sensitization optimum curve | equivalent circular diameter **1.1 µm** | [Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.87–88 (PDF 96–97), Fig. 4.2] | **[Q]** |
| Tabular AgBr, HIRF vs conductivity work | equivalent circular diameter **0.2 µm** | [Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.90–91 (PDF 99–100), Fig. 4.4] | **[Q]** |
| Grain size used as the reference for dust immunity | "around 1 µm" (OCR `1 ^m`) | [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)] | **[F]** |
| A hard floor on grain size | grain size "cannot be smaller than molecules/polymers" — a ceiling on resolving power relative to photopolymers | [Tani 1995, §1.2.3, p.10 (PDF 19)] | **[F]** |

**The three eras' size statements are consistent** where they overlap: Duffin's 0.03–2.5 µ (1966) and Tani's <0.1 to several µm with a ~1 µm average (1995) describe the same span, with 1995 practice using rather larger extremes at the coarse end and rather larger typical values. **[E]** Wall 1929 offers nothing to compare. **[F]**

### 5.2 Size distribution and its width

**No source in this set gives a coefficient of variation, a standard deviation, or any other numeric width for a grain-size distribution.** Tani uses "monodispersed" throughout with no CV attached [Tani 1995, §2.2 passim]. **[F]** Duffin describes distributions as "broad" or "much more even" and plots them (Figs. 4.3, 4.4, 4.11, and Fig. 4.2 for iodide dependence) without tabulating them; the plotted curves are lost to OCR. **[F]** Wall gives nothing. **[F]** This is the single largest gap in §5.

What the sources *do* establish is which process variables set the width, and what the width does to the image.

**Polydisperse vs monodisperse — the 1966 pair, with their stated image consequences.** This is the highest-value distribution statement in the set:

| Emulsion | Distribution | Stated image-level consequence | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Octahedral, bromide-ripened, 244 % Br excess | broad | "The **contrast of emulsion of this type is fairly low** and this kind of grain pattern is **most suitable for negative and colour emulsions when a wide range of light intensities must be recorded**" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.67 (PDF 71)] | **[F]** |
| Cubic, ammonia, 24 % Br excess | narrow | "The relatively **large volume of each grain** and the **fairly narrow grain-size distribution** make emulsions of this type of **high speed** to the light absorbed by the silver halide, **the sensitivity of each crystal being a volume relationship**, and of **high contrast**. This makes this kind of emulsion very suitable for medical X-ray films for use with fluorescent screens … the high contrast is required in order to give 'bright' radiographs showing good differentiation" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.73 (PDF 79)] | **[F]** |

So: **broad distribution → low contrast, wide latitude; narrow distribution → high contrast, high speed.** Duffin states the direction and the mechanism; he gives **no functional form**, so any curve fitted to this is the fitter's, not his. **[E]**

**The mechanism behind that mapping, made explicit in 1966** — this is the closest thing in the set to a first-principles derivation of the characteristic curve:

> "There are **two types of variation** which can occur between individual emulsion grains. The first is the **stopping power** of the crystals; how many quanta each will absorb, and **this depends on grain volume**. The second difference is in the **number of quanta needed to render a grain developable**. **These two effects are to a large extent additive and account for the differing grain sensitivities, which, in turn, account for the shape of the well-known characteristic curve. The number of quanta per crystal required to render a grain developable, controls the contrast.**"
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.185 (PDF 191), Fig. 9.12] **[Q]**

Fig. 9.12's provenance is stated, and matters: it "was **calculated mathematically from the random absorption of the light by the crystals and is not derived from an experiment**. Experimental results, however, show that **the faster crystals do give lower contrast**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.185 (PDF 191)]. **[Q]**

The second distribution — the per-grain quanta threshold — is quantified as a range:

> "In those grains where, for reasons of purely random movement, recombination does not occur, **4 quanta produce 4 silver atoms** and the grain becomes developable. In the other grains, **which may be identical in structure**, an amount of recombination does occur… and then more photons will be needed. **In extreme cases a large proportion of the photons recombine, and then perhaps 30 quanta are needed to produce 4 silver atoms.** These considerations have important practical implications; they mean that it is **probably not possible ever to make all the grains in an emulsion respond to just four quanta**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.185 (PDF 191)] **[Q]**

And measured directly by Farnell on a single-grain layer (an unhardened emulsion washed off with warm water so that grains adhered to glass): "there was a wide range of requirements, **some grains needing 50 or 100 quanta**, even in a sensitive emulsion, but that **four seems to be the minimum number**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.172 (PDF 178)]. **[Q]**

Putting the two together (ours): the per-grain threshold distribution in a 1966 emulsion spans **4 to 50–100 absorbed quanta**, i.e. a factor of 12–25, at **fixed grain structure**. That threshold spread is a contrast-limiting term entirely independent of the size distribution, and it means that even a perfectly monodisperse emulsion would have a finite gamma. **[E]**

**What controls monodispersity — the 1995 growth-regime answer.** This is mechanistic and is parameterised only through growth-rate exponents:

> "During grain growth in a diffusion-controlled condition, a small grain grows faster than a large grain, and the difference in r among initially formed grains decreases, finally bringing about monodispersed emulsion grains."
> [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.34–35 (PDF 43–44), Fig. 2.14] **[M]**

Wey & Strong's discriminating experiment: two AgBr emulsions of different edge length were mixed; "The difference decreased under a **high degree of supersaturation**, whereas the difference **increased** under a low degree of supersaturation" [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.34–35 (PDF 43–44)]. **[F]**

Reaction-controlled growth cannot deliver monodispersity, and the exponents say why: "it is believed that dr/dt is proportional to **r²** for the mononuclear-layer mechanism and dr/dt to **r⁰** for the polynuclear-layer mechanism" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.35 (PDF 44)]. **[Q]** Since narrowing requires dr/dt to *fall* with r, only the diffusion-controlled regime (dr/dt ∝ 1/r when r/δ → 0, §6.3) narrows the distribution; r² *widens* it and r⁰ preserves absolute spread while narrowing relative spread. **[E]**

Tabular grains grown at low supersaturation behave the wrong way: "The growth rate of tabular grains increased by increasing their size, indicating that the dispersity of grain size **increased** as the grains grew under this condition" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.39 (PDF 48)]. **[F]** And at pBr 2.63 the reverse holds: the lateral critical growth rate "still decreases with increasing Dc → dispersity of Dc decreases as grains grow" [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.39–41 (PDF 48–50), Fig. 2.17]. **[Q]** So **for tabular grains the sign of the dispersity evolution is a function of pBr**, reversing between pBr 2.63 and pBr 2.0. **[Q]**

**What controls the width in 1966 practice:**

| Variable | Effect on distribution width | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Double jet vs single jet | "the **double-jet method gives a more even grain distribution** at the end of emulsification … as the concentration of ripening agents remains fixed throughout, no initial large excess is present to cause the more rapid growth at the beginning of the process" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.63 (PDF 67)] | **[F]** |
| Large excess bromide during ripening | broad spread — "characteristic of emulsions ripened in the presence of a large excess of bromide" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.67 (PDF 71)] | **[F]** |
| Ammonia route with small (24 %) Br excess | narrow — "absence of either small or very large grains" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.73 (PDF 79)] | **[F]** |
| Iodide content | **Fig. 4.2** "Grain-size distribution with iodide content. The numbers on the curves are the molar percentage of iodide" (Trivelli & Smith). The plotted curves are lost; surviving axis labels are *"Grains per 1000"* (y, ticks 200, 300) vs *"Grain size"* (x; unit glyph OCRs as `2`, i.e. µ or µ²) | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.65 (PDF 69), Fig. 4.2] | **[F]** |
| Gelatin as protective colloid, 1929 | "prevents not only the formation of a coarse grain, but also fog" | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.30 (PDF 38)] | **[M]** |
| Controlled double-jet, 1995 | "useful for the control of the **uniformity of size and shape** of emulsion grains" | [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.32–33 (PDF 41–42), Fig. 2.11] | **[F]** |

**Historical marker on monodispersity.** "monodispersed cubic and octahedral silver halide emulsion grains were prepared and **have been refined for many years**", with the founding references being Berry & Skillman (1962) and Klein & Moisar (1962–1963, with Moisar 1991) [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)]. **[F]** So the monodisperse era begins ≈1962 — after Wall, contemporaneous with Duffin's writing (which is why Duffin describes the double-jet advantage but no monodisperse practice), and mature by 1995. **[E]** Tani's chapter-opening claim for the whole field: "**significant progress has been made over the last decades to make silver halide grains controllable with respect to size, shape, halide distribution, and crystal defects. Monodispersed silver halide grains with sophisticated structures are being developed**" [Tani 1995, Ch.2 opening, p.24 (PDF 33)]. **[F]**

### 5.3 Habit: cubic, octahedral, tabular

**The stable habits.** Only {100} and {111} faces are usually stable, so the cube and the octahedron are the stable regular shapes; the other five regular forms require habit modifiers (§4.3) [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33), Figs. 2.1, 2.2]. **[F]**

**The pAg/pBr habit rule — stated by both technical sources, in mutually consistent but oppositely-worded form.**

| Source | Statement | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Tani 1995 | "the precipitation of silver bromide grains under **low pBr** condition gives **octahedral** grains with a {111} face on their surfaces, and precipitation under **high pBr** condition gives **cubic** grains with a {100} face on their surfaces" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)] | **[F]** |
| Duffin 1966 (Moisar & Klein) | Seed crystals with "nearly equal areas of **(100)-(cubic)** and **(111)-(octahedral)** faces" were fed from a double jet at constant pAg. "At **low pAg**, that is low excess bromide concentration, the **111-faces are the site of growth** and therefore these disappear giving finally a **100-faced crystal**." "At **higher bromide-concentration** … marked adsorption of bromide-ions at these faces causing hindrance to normal growth … growth can only take place easily on the (100)-faces to produce a final crystal with **(111)-faces**." [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.59–60 (PDF 63–64)] | **[M]** |

Since pAg = pKsp − pBr, low pBr ≡ high pAg. **Both sources therefore say the same thing: high bromide → octahedral {111}; low bromide → cubic {100}.** **[E]** Duffin's own worked emulsions confirm it internally: the 1.0-molar-bromide (244 % excess) emulsion came out octahedral, and the 0.1-molar-bromide (24 % excess) ammonia emulsion came out as rounded cubes [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.66–68, 72–73 (PDF 70–72, 76, 79)]. **[E]**

**The mechanism, 1995:** "a nucleus on the flat {100} is unstable and is stabilised by adsorbed halide ions; the atomically rough {111} needs no such stabilisation — so raising halide-ion concentration preferentially accelerates {100} growth" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)]. **[M]** Growth on a face makes that face disappear, so accelerating {100} growth yields a crystal *bounded* by {111}, i.e. an octahedron. Duffin's 1966 mechanism is the same in substance — bromide adsorption on {111} hinders growth there, forcing growth onto {100} and yielding a {111}-bounded crystal. **[E]**

**AgCl is different, and both sources say so.** Duffin: "In silver chloride, however, **no (111)-planes can be observed even at very high chloride-ion concentration**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.60 (PDF 64)]. **[F]** "The vast majority of commercial chlorobromide emulsions contain crystals of an **almost perfect cubic shape**"; Agfa detected a small number of AgCl twins in early nucleation, showing (111) planes exist "at least temporarily but (100)-faced crystals were given finally" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.74 (PDF 80)]. **[F]** Tani notes the rhombic dodecahedron has been observed for AgCl under habit modification (§4.3) [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.24 (PDF 33)]. **[F]**

**1929 habit language.** Wall has no habit vocabulary — no "cubic", "octahedral" or "tabular" in the crystallographic sense. His grain-quality control is entirely by proxy: the **dip test**, in which a drop of emulsion on glass viewed by gaslight passes **blood-red → orange → green → blue** as digestion proceeds, and the operator stops at blue; "If the color reaches a **greyish-violet** the emulsion nearly always shows fog" [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.72 (PDF 79)]. **[F]** A variant instruction: "digest 40 min or till blue by transmitted light, then lower the temperature and digest 20 min till grey" [Wall 1929, Ch. XIII, pp.224–225 (PDF 231–232)]. **[F]** Wall's one recorded grain-shape observation is the "pepper" grain of chloride emulsions: "a characteristic coarse grain in chloride emulsions, reduced to metal without exposure; may be invisible to the naked eye — 'test plates should always be examined with an eyepiece'", avoided by **reducing water at the mix** or by adding the **silver nitrate dry** to the chlorized gelatine [Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.92 (PDF 99)]. **[F]**

**Habit as a controllable variable — the era boundary.** Habit control by pAg is a 1966-and-later concept. Wall 1929 controls grain *size* through gelatine quantity, temperature, time and bromide excess, but has no concept of controlling grain *shape*. **[E]**

### 5.4 Tabular grains, aspect ratio, and the technology's dates

**Tabular grains are old; tabular *technology* is not.**

> "In addition to three-dimensional grains, tabular silver halide emulsion grains **have been prepared for a long time**. **Recently, much progress has been made in the preparation and sensitization of tabular grains, since the advantages of tabular grains for various photographic materials have been proposed and recognized.**"
> [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.25 (PDF 34)] **[F]**

The citations date both halves precisely: the "long time" reference is Berriman & Herz, *Nature* **180**, 293 (**1957**) — the twin-plane X-ray proof; the "recent progress" references are Research Disclosure Item 22534, **225**, 20 (**Jan. 1983**); Kofron & Booms (**1986**); Sowinski & Wightman (**1987**); Jacobson, Axford & Ford (**1990**) [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.25 (PDF 34), refs. 8, 9(a)–(d)]. **[F]** **The tabular era is therefore dated by the source's own citations to 1983–1990.** Tabular technology is a post-1983 attribute; the book states nothing about which commercial stocks adopted it or when. **[E]** Tani's priority claim: "Among those grains, **tabular grains are the most important for the present and in the future** in photographic materials" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)]. **[F]**

**Aspect ratio — the sources split.**

| Source | Aspect-ratio information | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Wall 1929 | none; no tabular concept at all | **[F]** |
| Duffin 1966 | For the tabular fraction of the worked octahedral emulsion: flat octahedra "usually only about **1/10th or 1/5th as thick as their diameter**", i.e. **aspect ratio 5:1 to 10:1**; measured thickness ≈ 0.2 µ against 0.87 µ mean diameter [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.66–68 (PDF 70–72)] | **[Q]** |
| Duffin 1966, elsewhere | AgBr crystal thickness **0.2–0.3 µ** [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.133 (PDF 139)] | **[Q]** |
| Tani 1995 | **No aspect-ratio number is stated anywhere in the range examined.** Only the thickness (0.1 µm) and the Dc parametrisation are given [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.39–40 (PDF 48–49)] | **[F]** |

Note the internal tension in Duffin's own numbers: 0.2 µ thickness against 0.87 µ mean diameter is an aspect ratio of 4.4:1, at or just outside the low end of his stated 5:1–10:1 band; a 10:1 ratio at 0.2 µ thickness requires a 2.0 µ diameter, which is the coarse tail of that emulsion rather than its mean. The 5:1–10:1 statement is best read as covering the tabular *population*, not the mean grain. **[E]**

Combining Tani's 0.1 µm tabular thickness with his ~1 µm typical grain size gives an aspect ratio of ≈10:1 for 1995 tabular practice — but **that is our arithmetic, not his statement**, and it happens to land at the top of Duffin's 1966 band, which would imply no change in aspect ratio between the two eras. Given that the whole point of the 1983–1990 tabular programme was higher aspect ratio, we regard that implication as an artefact of combining a 1995 thickness with a 1995 *average* diameter rather than with a tabular-specific diameter. **[S]**

**Why tabular grains grow tabular — the two accounts.** Duffin 1966's twin-plane pocket mechanism is in §4.7. Tani 1995 adds the *selection* mechanism, which explains how an emulsion ends up containing **only** tabular grains:

> "a tabular grain with parallel twin planes can grow more rapidly than other grains, since its side surfaces have a rough structure with re-entrant corners, which are believed to be suitable places for incorporation of solute ions. Therefore, during the process of Ostwald ripening, the pK^ of tabular grains is larger than the pKsp of other grains, and **only tabular grains can grow with the dissolution of other grains, and finally survive to give emulsions composed of only tabular grains with parallel twin planes**."
> [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.39 (PDF 48)] **[M]**

(OCR: `pK^` = pKsp.) So tabular grains are not merely *made*; they are *selected* by Ostwald ripening because they dissolve less readily than their neighbours. **[M]**

**Conditions that promote twinning (and hence tabular grains), 1995.** Saito's conclusion, quoted because it is a complete list of levers: twinning "took place af random among grains and could be enhanced by conditions with a high degree of supersaturation, including **a high concentration of halide ion, a high addition rate of solute ions, low temperature, a high concentration of iodide ions, a low concentration of gelatin**, and so on" [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.38–39 (PDF 47–48)]. **[M]** Two competing mechanistic proposals are recorded: Berry et al. — "Since it has been commonly observed that twinning takes places at high pAg, [they] have considered that the accumulation of the complex ion **AgBrf ~** onto a growing grain brings about the formation of a twin plane" (OCR: the complex-ion subscript/charge is corrupt; from Duffin's parallel discussion the growth-active species is AgBr₃²⁻ or AgBr₄³⁻) **[M]**; and Jagannathan — twin-plane formation is ascribed to instability of the {111} face at high supersaturation [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.38–39 (PDF 47–48)]. **[M]**

Note that Saito's list includes **low gelatin concentration** as a twinning promoter, while Wall 1929 warns that too little gelatine at the mix gives "coarse granular silver salt… and thin results" and that "~1 % is a safe limit during the actual mix", more being added soon after, "otherwise coarse grain and fog will ensue" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.31, 52 (PDF 39, 60)]. **[Q]** These are not in conflict — 1929's "coarse grain" from low gelatine may well have been unrecognised tabular growth — but no source in this set makes that identification, so we mark the connection speculative. **[S]**

**Anisotropic tabular growth: the pBr-dependent lateral/vertical split (1995), Hosoya & Tani, tabular AgBr of thickness 0.1 µm** [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.39–41 (PDF 48–50), Figs. 2.17–2.19]:

| pBr | Lateral vs vertical critical growth rate | Size dependence | Interpretation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **3.3** | both small and **equal to each other** | decreasing with increasing Dc | diffusion controlled, like octahedral/cubic at the same pBr | **[Q]** |
| **2.63** | **lateral ≫ vertical** | lateral still decreases with increasing Dc → dispersity of Dc **decreases** as grains grow | intermediate | **[Q]** |
| **2.0** | lateral very high | "the lateral critical growth rate at pBr 2.0 **steeply increased** with increasing Dc" → dispersity **increases** | reaction/edge controlled | **[Q]** |

And the counterintuitive result of Fig. 2.18: as pBr decreases, the **octahedral** critical growth rate **increases** (following AgBr solubility) while the tabular **vertical** critical growth rate **decreases** — despite both faces being nominally {111}. The interpretation offered (Fig. 2.19) is that solute ions arriving at the main tabular faces are forced to diffuse onward to the side faces [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.40–41 (PDF 49–50), Figs. 2.18, 2.19]. **[Q]** This is the mechanism by which a grain can be made to grow *only* sideways, i.e. the physical basis of high-aspect-ratio tabular technology. **[M]**

### 5.5 Double-structured (core–shell) and epitaxial grains

| Structure | Description as printed | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Double-structured (core–shell) | "Fig. 2.7 illustrates a double-structured grain with **ArBrI in its core and AgBr in its shell**, and an X-ray diffraction profile of the grains" (OCR "ArBrI" = **AgBrI**) | [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.29 (PDF 38), Fig. 2.7] | **[F]** |
| Epitaxial | Cubic **AgCl host** with **eight AgBr(Cl) guest crystals at the corners** | [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.29–30 (PDF 38–39), Fig. 2.8] | **[F]** |
| Iodide-cored grains, 1966 anticipation | "some silver-bromide crystals contained a **core having quite large concentrations of iodide**"; and iodide "may be present mainly at the centre of the crystal, distributed throughout the grain or mainly on the outside" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.64–65 (PDF 68–69); Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)] | **[F]** |
| Core–shell as a *measurement* tool, 1995 | electron diffusion length in AgBr core/shell grains determined by the shell-thickness method (Matejec & Moisar): **0.5 µm** | [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.65 (PDF 74)] | **[Q]** |
| Surface vs internal image, 1966 | Digestion shifts the image from internal to surface: surface-image sensitivity rises while internal-image sensitivity falls, because surface specks out-compete internal traps, the internal trapping sites not themselves being chemically altered. "**In commercial practice, sensitization is carried out so that surface latent image is at a maximum.**" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.183–184 (PDF 189–190), Fig. 9.11] | **[F]** |

So the core–shell idea exists in 1966 as an *observed accident* of iodide distribution and as a design variable in principle, and in 1995 as a deliberately engineered heterojunction with an X-ray-diffraction signature. **[E]** The structural consequence of the heterojunction is dislocation generation at the phase interface (§4.4, Fig. 2.10) [Tani 1995, §2.1, pp.31–32 (PDF 40–41)]. **[F]** The electronic consequence — that the interfaces between different silver halides have been studied "as models of double-structured silver halide emulsion grains and epitaxial grains" by Granzer and coworkers and by Kawasaki and Hada — is recorded but not quantified [Tani 1995, §3.1, pp.47–48 (PDF 56–57)]. **[F]**

### 5.6 The size ↔ sensitivity relation

**The law, 1995:**

> "It is important to increase the growth rate to form large silver halide grains for the development of highly sensitive photographic materials, since **photographic sensitivity is, in principle, proportional to the volume of silver halide grains** and the spectral sensitivity of dyes grains is proportional to their average surface area."
> [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)] **[Q]**

**The same law, 1966:** "the sensitivity of each crystal being a volume relationship" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.73 (PDF 79)] **[F]**; and, with the reason: "The **volume** of the crystal, not merely its surface area facing the incident light, is the important property in assessing the light-trapping capacity of a crystal. This accounts, for example, for the **high speed to blue light of the thick grains of the modern high-speed X-ray emulsions**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.175 (PDF 181)]. **[F]**

**The same law, 1929 — qualitative only, and expressed as a ripening effect:** excess bromide dissolves "the finer particles of silver bromide… in the course of ripening [they] are deposited on the larger grains, thus giving **increased sensitiveness**". This is the book's only explicit grain-size→speed mechanism [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.33 (PDF 41)]. **[M]**

**Where the volume law breaks down (1995), with a number:**

> "It has been described by Farnell and is now widely observed that the sensitivity of silver halide emulsion grains to blue light (inherent sensitivity) is **proportional to their volume only under the condition that the grain size does not exceed a certain value**. Since the absorbance of a silver halide emulsion grain in the blue region is weak and nearly proportional to its volume, the inherent sensitivity of an emulsion grain should be proportional to its volume such that the **diffusion length of photoelectrons is large enough to allow them to reach a growing nucleus in the grain**."
> [Tani 1995, §4.2, p.88 (PDF 97)] **[Q]**

And numerically: "The deviation of the proportionality of sensitivity to grain size was usually observed when the **grain volume exceeded about 1 /Am** and could be attributed to the limited diffusion length of photoelectrons with respect to the size of emulsion grains" [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.65 (PDF 74)]. **[Q]** **OCR flag:** the raw string is `grain volume exceeded about 1 /Am`. "Volume" with a length unit is dimensionally wrong: the printed statement is either "grain **size** exceeded about 1 µm" or "grain volume exceeded about 1 µm³". Quote the raw string; do not silently pick one. Either way the knee is at the **~1 µm scale**. **[Q]**

The knee is set by the electron diffusion length, and Tani's own diffusion-length table makes that identification checkable [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.65 (PDF 74), Eq. (3.12)]:

| Carrier / medium | µd (cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹) | τ | Diffusion length ℓ | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Electrons, large AgBr crystal | 60 | 0.1–10 µsec | **4–40 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Electrons, AgBr emulsion grains (Hirano) | 2.1 | 0.1 µs | **2.3 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Electrons, tabular AgBr emulsion grains (Farnell, photolytic-silver method) | — | — | **0.4 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Electrons, AgBr core/shell grains (Matejec & Moisar, shell-thickness method) | — | — | **0.5 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Holes, large AgBr crystal | 1.1 | 0.1–10 µsec | **0.5–5 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Holes, large AgBr crystal (Kanzaki & Mori, photon-stimulated Br₂ desorption) | — | — | **1.4 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Holes, AgBr emulsion grains | 0.001 | 15 µs | **0.19 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Holes, AgBr emulsion grains (Tani, fog-bleaching + dye-oxidation size dependence) | — | — | **0.2 µm** | **[Q]** |
| Holes, large AgBr crystal (Luckey, escape-distance method) | — | — | `f /«n` — **OCR-lost fraction** | **[Q]** |

The electron diffusion length *in grains* is **0.4–2.3 µm**, which brackets the ~1 µm knee. That is the physical origin of the knee and the two are quantitatively consistent. **[E]** These numbers must not be used as an MTF length scale: optical scatter and halation, not carrier diffusion, dominate emulsion MTF, and no source in this set addresses either for the emulsion layer itself. **[E]**

Related carrier data, for completeness: electron drift mobilities from time-of-flight on high-quality single crystals, agreeing with photo-Hall values, are **50 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ for AgCl and 60 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ for AgBr**, mobility being limited by LO-phonon scattering rather than by shallow traps and therefore *increasing* with falling temperature [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.61 (PDF 70)]. **[Q]** For holes: the AgCl self-trapped hole is a hole on a silver ion with displaced nearest-neighbour Cl⁻ (Jahn–Teller), thermal ionization energy **0.12 eV**, unstable above ~**50 K**; AgCl hole drift mobility at RT **~10⁻¹ cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹**; AgBr hole drift and Hall mobility at RT **~1 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹**, "steeply decreasing with increasing temperature"; AgBr hole trapping level depth from Eq. (3.11) **0.44 eV**; Kanzaki's dominant hole centre is the silver ion vacancy, binding energy **0.4 eV** [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.62 (PDF 71), Figs. 3.17, 3.18]. **[Q]** Measured hole lifetimes in grains: tabular AgBr **15 µsec** (Hamilton & Brady); 0.5 µm octahedral AgBr **26 µsec at room temperature** (Kellogg, Hodes, Muenter, radiofrequency method) [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.64 (PDF 73)]. **[Q]** In AgCl emulsions "the field-decay time was as much as **40 times longer** than the electron lifetime" (Keevert) [Tani 1995, §3.3, p.64 (PDF 73)]. **[Q]**

**Table 3.1 warning.** Tani's Table 3.1 (p.61 / PDF 70) "Electronic properties of AgBr" is **column-scrambled by OCR**. The caption survives; the row labels list "Large crystal / Emulsion grains" for Electron and Positive hole; the header block reads `PD (cnf/V-sec) | T l[Eq. (10)] (/jLSec) (fwi) | Kef.` (i.e. µD, τ, ℓ[Eq. 3.12], reference). The numeric block `60 | 0.2 | 0.6 ~ 0.8 | >8 | 2.1 | 1.1 | 0.001` and `0.1 -10 | 4-40 | 3 | 1.2 | 0.1 | 2.3 | 0.4* | 0.5* | 0.1 - 10 | 0.5 - 5 | 0.33* | 15 | 0.19 | 0.2*` **cannot be reliably assigned to cells**. Asterisk footnote: "*Experimentally observed value." The prose values tabulated above are the trustworthy source. **[F]**

**Chemical sensitization moves the knee to smaller sizes:** "deviation of the sensitivity from its proportionality to grain volume appeared in **sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized grains at a smaller size than in unsensitized grains**, indicating that the diffusion length of photoelectrons was shorter in the former than in the latter" [Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.88–89 (PDF 97–98), Fig. 4.3]. **[F]** Fig. 4.3 plots log S against d (the diameter of the circle of equal projected area) for unsensitized (○) and S+Au-sensitized (●) octahedral AgBr [Tani 1995, §4.2, p.89 (PDF 98), Fig. 4.3]. **[F]** So the useful grain-size ceiling is **not a constant** — it depends on the sensitization state. **[E]**

**The measured size↔speed↔gamma family — Duffin's Table 4.1, and what it proves.**

**TABLE 4.1 — EFFECT OF EMULSIFICATION TIME ON GRAIN SIZE AND SPEED** (single-jet) [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.62 (PDF 66), Table 4.1]:

| Time of addition (raw OCR) | Mean grain area * | Relative speed | Gamma | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `031”` (≈ 0'31") | 0.14 | 12 | `2S` (unreadable) | **[Q]** |
| `4’22”` | 0.28 | 52 | 2.08 | **[Q]** |
| `ONS` (unreadable) | 0.50 | 150 | 1.50 | **[Q]** |
| `19’30”` | 0.82 | 250 | 1.36 | **[Q]** |
| `4240”` (≈ 42'40") | 1.47 | 450 | 0.94 | **[Q]** |
| `54’50’”` | 2.35 | 630 | 0.83 | **[Q]** |
| `8510’` (≈ 85'10") | 2.56 | 910 | 0.65 | **[Q]** |

**OCR flags:** the footnote defining `*` — the unit of mean grain area — **did not survive** and is absent from the page; treat the grain-area units as unknown and use ratios, not absolutes. Row-1 time is almost certainly `0'31"`; row-3 `ONS` is unreadable (a value between 4'22" and 19'30"); row-5 is almost certainly `42'40"`; row-7 almost certainly `85'10"`. Row-1 gamma `2S` is unreadable (likely 2.5 or 2.3). **[Q]**

The accompanying mechanism: "very rapid mixing of the halide and silver solution produces a large number of small nuclei and **the longer the time of the silver addition, the larger the grains will grow**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.62 (PDF 66)]. **[M]**

**This table quantitatively confirms the volume law, and that is worth spelling out because it is the only place in the source set where the law is testable against data.** Over the tabulated span, mean grain **area** rises 0.14 → 2.56 (×18.3) and relative **speed** rises 12 → 910 (×75.8). If area ∝ d² and volume ∝ d³, then volume ∝ area^1.5, so the volume law predicts a speed ratio of 18.3^1.5 = **×78.2** against the measured **×75.8** — agreement to 3 %. Fitting the log–log slope end-to-end gives **S ∝ (area)^1.49**, i.e. **S ∝ volume^0.99**. The middle rows run above the pure power law and the second-from-last below it, so the fit is not perfect row by row, but the overall exponent is 1.49 ± the row scatter. **[E]**

The same table also yields a **contrast** scaling, which no source states: fitting gamma against area from row 2 to row 7 gives Δlog γ = log(0.65/2.08) = −0.5054 against Δlog A = log(2.56/0.28) = 0.9609, i.e. **γ ∝ (area)^−0.53 ≈ (area)^−1/2 ∝ d⁻¹ ∝ volume^−0.35**. Over this single-recipe family, **doubling grain area costs a factor 1.44 in gamma and buys a factor 2.8 in speed**. **[E]** This is an inverse speed/contrast trade at fixed chemistry, produced by a single manufacturing variable (emulsification time). **[E]**

**Consistency with Tani's knee.** Duffin's table shows no roll-off of the speed–volume law over an 18× area span. If the units of column 2 are µ², the largest entry (2.56 µ²) corresponds to an equivalent-sphere diameter of 0.90 µm — i.e. the whole table sits *below* Tani's ~1 µm knee, so the absence of roll-off is exactly what Tani predicts. That reading also makes the column-2 units µ², which is consistent with Duffin's use of µ² for grain size elsewhere (the Tri-X figure, §5.1). **[E]**

**The general law relating speed to resolving power (1995), which is the size↔sensitivity relation seen from the image side:**

> "In 1970, Ooue summarized the relation between sensitivity and resolving power of various photosensitive materials that had been produced and studied by that time. This is illustrated in Fig. 1.7, in which sensitivity is expressed as **ASA** or the reciprocal of the exposure (**erg/cm²**) for imaging, and resolving power is expressed as the number of parallel **line pairs per millimeter** detected by photosensitive materials. **Ooue derived the equation used in the preparation of this figure by making the sensitivity proportional to the reciprocal of the resolving power squared.**"
> [Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20), Figs. 1.7, 1.8] **[Q]**

i.e. **S ∝ 1/(resolving power)², so S·R² = constant.** **[Q]** Tani presents it as the empirical envelope of the entire photosensitive-materials field, not as a within-brand rule: "silver halide photographic materials are the best photosensitive materials known from the viewpoint of sensitivity and resolving power, and form the **boundary region**, ranging from high sensitivity with low resolving power to low sensitivity with high resolving power" [Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20)]. **[F]** Consistency check (ours): if S ∝ V ∝ d³ and R ∝ 1/d, then S ∝ R⁻³, not R⁻². The observed R⁻² therefore implies that resolution degrades more slowly than grain size grows — consistent with resolution being limited by optical scatter and layer thickness as well as by grain size. The two laws are not contradictory but they are not the same law, and combining them is ours. **[E]**

Tani's explicit CCD analogy makes the size↔speed law a general sensor statement: "The decrease in pixel size in CCD corresponds to a decrease in the size of emulsion grains in silver halide photography, **which should always be associated with a decrease in sensitivity**" [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.17 (PDF 26)]. **[F]**

### 5.7 Photons absorbed intrinsically scale with grain VOLUME; dye-sensitized absorption scales with grain SURFACE AREA

This distinction is the single most important scaling statement in §5, and the source states both halves in one sentence:

> "photographic sensitivity is, in principle, **proportional to the volume of silver halide grains** and the spectral sensitivity of dyes grains is **proportional to their average surface area**."
> [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)] **[Q]**

The terminology is defined in the spectral chapter: "the sensitivities of the excitation of silver halides and sensitizing dyes are called **intrinsic sensitivity** and **spectral sensitivity**, respectively. The former and the latter are also called **blue sensitivity** and **minus-blue sensitivity**, respectively, in the case of AgBr and AgBrI" [Tani 1995, §5.1, p.111 (PDF 120)]. **[F]**

The reason for the split is physical and is fully stated in the source, though not assembled there:

| Absorption route | Absorber location | Scales with | Supporting statement | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intrinsic (blue) | the bulk of the crystal, via the weak indirect transition | **grain volume** | "the absorbance of a silver halide emulsion grain in the blue region is **weak and nearly proportional to its volume**" [Tani 1995, §4.2, p.88 (PDF 97)]; "The **volume** of the crystal, not merely its surface area facing the incident light, is the important property in assessing the light-trapping capacity" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.175 (PDF 181)] | **[Q]** |
| Dye-sensitized (minus-blue) | a monolayer or sub-monolayer of dye **adsorbed on the surface** | **grain surface area** | "the spectral sensitivity of dyes grains is proportional to their **average surface area**" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)]; dye at the higher commercial loadings covers "about half the surface of the grains", an average dye occupying **50–100 Å²** [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.114 (PDF 120)] | **[Q]** |

**The engineering consequence, which the source does not draw.** For a tabular grain of equivalent circular diameter D and thickness t, volume V ∝ D²t and (main-face) area A ∝ D². Therefore A/V ∝ 1/t. Making a grain tabular — large D, small t — at **constant volume** leaves intrinsic (blue) speed unchanged while **raising** dye-sensitized (green/red) speed in proportion to the aspect ratio. Equivalently, at constant *silver*, going from a 1:1 to a 10:1 aspect ratio multiplies the dye-bearing surface by ≈ 10^(1/3) ≈ 2.15 for a fixed volume, or by 10 for a fixed main-face diameter. That is the standard rationale for tabular grains in the green and red records, it follows directly from the source's own two proportionalities, and **the source does not state it in the range examined.** **[E]**

Two corroborating facts, both from the source set, that make the inference safer:

- The 1966 emulsions bear it out numerically: the octahedral (flatter, aspect 5:1–10:1) emulsion has surface/volume = 11.1 µm⁻¹ against 4.97 µm⁻¹ for the cubic emulsion — a 2.2× advantage in dye-bearing surface per unit silver (§5.1). **[E]**
- The 1966 statement that finer-grain emulsions have "a larger surface area per mole" and therefore "**a smaller percentage of their surface covered and … fewer sulphur atoms per grain**" at fixed sensitizer dose per mole [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)] confirms that surface-area-per-mole, not volume, is the relevant budget for anything adsorbed. **[F]**

**A caution on the surface-area law.** Duffin records a result that limits how literally "proportional to surface area" can be taken for *chemical* sensitizers: "One very surprising fact … is that **optimum quantity of sulphur sensitizer varies very little with the grain size of the emulsion**. When one considers that **crystals of one micron diameter will possess roughly ten times the surface area of crystals of 0.1 micron diameter**, then this is a very surprising fact indeed and **points undeniably to the concept that only certain selected sites on each crystal need to collect their 'coating' of silver sulphide**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.86–87 (PDF 92–93), Figs. 5.2–5.4]. **[Q]** (Ours: the "roughly ten times" is per *unit mass*, since surface/volume ∝ 1/d; per grain the ratio is 100×.) **[E]** So **chemical** sensitizer demand scales with neither surface nor volume but with a site count; **dye** demand scales with surface. These are different budgets and should not be conflated. **[E]**

The 1995 counterpart figure for site density: "the number of sulfur sensitization centers were as many as **2800/[µm]²of the (100) face** of AgBr emulsion grains when the grains were optimally sulfur sensitized" [Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.74 (PDF 83)]; restated as "2800//mi2 on cubic AgBr grains" [Tani 1995, §4.1.3, p.86 (PDF 95)]. **[Q]** For a 1 µm cube (6 µm² surface) that is ≈ **1.7 × 10⁴ centres per grain** — ours, and to be contrasted with Duffin's 1966 estimate of "about `5 x 104` sulphur atoms per grain" (exponent OCR-destroyed) for a similar emulsion [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)]. The two are the same order of magnitude. **[E]**

### 5.8 The size ↔ granularity relation

**No source in this set relates grain size, or grain count, to granularity.** This must be stated flatly, because it is the relation a reader will most expect to find here.

| Source | Position | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Wall 1929 | "**Grain size → graininess**: no statement anywhere in the book. Wall discusses grain only as it affects speed, fog ('pepper'), image colour and density — never print graininess" | **[F]** |
| Duffin 1966 | Zero occurrences of "granularity" or "graininess" in the whole book. No rms measure, no Selwyn area, no sigma-vs-density relation, no grain-size dependence of noise | **[F]** |
| Tani 1995 | No statement relating grain size or grain count to rms granularity, Selwyn granularity, graininess, or Print Grain Index. The Selwyn granularity constant *G* appears only as a symbol inside the DQE equation; that equation's body was image-only in the OCR and has been recovered from the rendered page image (§17.2, §29.3), but *G* itself is named and never defined anywhere in this source set | **[F]** |

The *adjacent* statements, which are the most that can honestly be extracted:

- **Clumping, not size, is Duffin's stated noise source.** "All these precipitation methods … require **very efficient redispersion** … Without this, the grains will tend to **clump together which will produce aggregates of developed silver on processing**. Even if these are not serious enough to degrade the image, they will give a **coarser-grained result** than in a completely dispersed system" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.80 (PDF 86)]. **[M]**
- **Covering power, not grain noise.** "Filamentary silver has higher **covering power** than compact silver, beneficial in terms of speed, contrast and maximum density" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.173 (PDF 179)]. **[F]**
- **Developer effect on grain.** Diethyl-p-phenylenediamine "[acts] as a fairly low-energy developer giving **fine-grain results**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.191 (PDF 197)]. **[F]**
- **Chromogenic images decouple from grain geometry.** "there is little connection between the grain pattern of the original silver-halide emulsion and that of the developed dye image"; and substantive couplers show "a pronounced tendency to clump" — a *dye*-clumping noise source, unquantified [Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.194, 201 (PDF 200, 207)]. **[M]**
- **Wall's one relevant negative result.** A sodium-halide-plus-sulphite formula was claimed by its originator to give the finest grain of any process; "Wall tested it repeatedly and '**no extra fineness of grain could be detected**'" — though it gave very clean plates with high gamma infinity [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.61 (PDF 69)]. **[F]**
- **Wall's one positive result on decoupling speed from grain.** Valenta, working on Lippmann emulsions, added **0.1 g Na₂SO₃ per 300 ccm emulsion** and digested at 35 °C for **5, 15 and 30 min**, obtaining "**increase of speed without coarsening of the grain**" [Wall 1929, Ch. VI, p.131 (PDF 138)]. **[Q]**
- **Wall on grain size and image colour** — a different relation, often confused with graininess: "Chapman Jones has also proved that the color of the image is dependent on the size of the silver particles." Wall's own series (pure AgCl → 5, 10, 20 % … → pure AgBr; exposures 1:1 to 1:1024 under a step plate of densities 1–3.01; constant metol-hydroquinone developer) showed image colour is set by **rate of development / rate of silver deposition**, not by exposure or by emulsion composition [Wall 1929, Ch. V, pp.95–96 (PDF 102–103)]. **[Q]**

**The only quantitative grain-count statement in the set that a noise model can use** is Tani's **500 grains per equivalent pixel** at 43 µm² [Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)]. **[Q]** From it, a Poisson-limited fluctuation of 1/√500 = **4.5 % rms per equivalent-pixel area** follows — ours, not the source's (§3.6). **[E]** Tani's related grain-count figures — 1.2 × 10⁷ grains/mm², ~14 layers over 20 µm — imply that the effective grain count in a *single* layer of a colour record is roughly 1/9 of the total, i.e. ≈ 1.3 × 10⁶ grains/mm² per emulsion sublayer and ≈ 56 grains per equivalent pixel per sublayer, giving ≈ 13 % rms per sublayer before any inter-sublayer averaging. Both figures are ours and rest on the assumption that the nine emulsion sublayers carry equal grain numbers, which no source states. **[S]**

### 5.9 Explicitly asserted without numbers — the register for §5

The brief requires these to be flagged, so they are collected here:

| Relation asserted | Numbers given? | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intrinsic sensitivity ∝ grain volume | **Yes** — testable, and confirmed at exponent 1.49 on area by Duffin's Table 4.1 (§5.6) | [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46); Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.62 (PDF 66), Table 4.1] | **[Q]** |
| Spectral (dye-sensitized) sensitivity ∝ average grain surface area | **No number, no measured family, no proportionality constant.** Asserted once, in one clause | [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)] | **[F]** |
| Broad size distribution → low contrast / wide latitude; narrow → high contrast / high speed | **No functional form and no distribution width.** Direction and mechanism only | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.67, 73 (PDF 71, 79)] | **[F]** |
| Diffusion-controlled growth narrows the distribution | Parameterised only through growth-rate exponents (r⁻¹, r², r⁰); no rate constants, no resulting CV | [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.34–35 (PDF 43–44)] | **[M]** |
| Tabular grains are advantageous | The *advantage* is never stated numerically anywhere in the range examined; no aspect ratio, no speed gain, no granularity gain | [Tani 1995, §2.1, p.25 (PDF 34); §2.2, p.38 (PDF 47)] | **[F]** |
| Grain size → granularity | **No statement at all in any of the three sources** | — | **[F]** |
| Sensitivity ∝ 1/(resolving power)² | Exponent stated; the constant is not, and it is a cross-material envelope rather than a within-family law | [Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20)] | **[Q]** |
| Optimum defect density exists | Direction and existence of an interior maximum stated; no defect densities, no sensitivity magnitudes | [Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.89–90 (PDF 98–99)] | **[F]** |
| Aspect ratio of 1966 flat octahedra | **5:1 to 10:1** — the only aspect-ratio number in the set | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.66–68 (PDF 70–72)] | **[Q]** |
