## 6. Emulsion making and grain growth

### 6.1 The stage sequence, and what each era called it

| Stage | 1929 name (Wall) | 1966 name (Duffin) | 1995 name (Tani) | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Make-up of the halide/gelatine solution | "bromized gelatine" | "reaction solution" / solution A | "aqueous gelatin reaction solution" | **[F]** |
| Silver addition | **the mix**, emulsification | **emulsification**, precipitation | **precipitation** (single-jet, double-jet, controlled double-jet) | **[F]** |
| Hot hold that grows the grains | **digestion**, boiling, ripening | **ripening**, **physical ripening**, Ostwald ripening | **Ostwald ripening**, grain growth | **[F]** |
| Removal of soluble salts | **washing** (noodle/worm washing) | **washing** (noodle) or **coagulation washing** | not covered in the range examined | **[F]** |
| Second hot hold that raises sensitivity | **after-ripening**, redigestion, cold ripening | **digestion**, chemical ripening, after-ripening | **chemical sensitization** / digestion | **[F]** |
| Final additions and coating | final gelatine, "doctors", alcohol, bromide | final gelatin, addenda, hardener | coating (multilayer, simultaneous) | **[F]** |

Duffin gives the three historic synonyms explicitly for the second hot hold — "**digestion, chemical ripening, after-ripening**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)] **[F]** — and distinguishes the two ripenings: "the emulsion is given a heat treatment, during which time the crystals grow … This is called **ripening, or physical ripening** to distinguish it from chemical ripening, or **Ostwald ripening** after Ostwald who first recorded the change of fine precipitates of silver iodide into coarser ones on heat treatment where a proportion of the crystals grew at the expense of the rest. This process is continued until the crystals have attained the **desired grain size and grain-size distribution**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.58 (PDF 62)]. **[F]**

The terminology is a trap: Wall's "digestion" is usually the *physical* ripening (the boil or the hot ammonia hold that grows grains), while Duffin's "digestion" is usually the *chemical* ripening after washing. Wall's second hot hold is "after-ripening" or "redigestion". Read every temperature/time figure in context. **[E]**

### 6.2 Precipitation

**Single-jet and double-jet, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.57 (PDF 61), Fig. 4.1 "Representation of precipitation methods. Left: single-jet method; right: double-jet method"]:

- **Single jet:** silver-nitrate solution run through a jet at a carefully controlled rate into a stirred solution containing halide + gelatin. **[F]**
- **Double jet:** silver-nitrate and an equivalent halide solution added simultaneously through two separate jets into stirred gelatin/halide. **[F]**
- Solution strengths "frequently around normal solution strength, in other words they contain of the order of **one gram molecule of silver salt or halide per litre**". **[Q]**
- "Except with very special emulsions, the quantities of halide and silver are never equivalent; in the vast majority of photographic emulsions, particularly those of a negative type, **excess halide is always present**." **[F]**
- A 1966 marker of then-emerging industrial practice: "Apart from more modern ways of making photographic emulsions by **continuous precipitation processes** in which the conditions are quite different from those of the more classical procedures…" **[F]** Continuous precipitation is named but never described — a named-but-unexplained frontier as of 1966 [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.57 (PDF 61)]. **[F]**

**The same two methods, 1995, plus the controlled variant:** "In single-jet precipitations, an aqueous solution of water-soluble silver salt is poured into an agitated aqueous reaction solution, which contains gelatin and water-soluble halide salt(s). In double-jet precipitations, aqueous solutions of a water-soluble silver salt and a water-soluble halide salt(s) are simultaneously poured into an agitated aqueous gelatin reaction solution. A double-jet precipitation in which **the concentration of silver ions in the reaction vessel can be controlled is called controlled double-jet precipitation**, and is useful for the control of the uniformity of size and shape of emulsion grains" [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.32–33 (PDF 41–42), Fig. 2.11 "Block diagram of an apparatus for controlled double-jet precipitation"]. **[F]** Tani adds: "This technique is of great importance for understanding the physical properties and photographic behavior of silver halide grains and for the development of new emulsion technologies" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.32 (PDF 41)]. **[F]** The founding references are Berry & Skillman and Klein & Moisar, i.e. 1962–63 (§5.2). **[F]**

**Order of addition and its stated consequences, 1929** — Wall's treatment is the most detailed in the set, because in 1929 the order *was* the process:

| Method | Stated consequence | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Single jet** — silver into gelatine holding all the halide | Later silver forms in a decreasing bromide excess: "primarily a very slow form of silver halide followed by successive portions of more rapid"; if the silver is run slowly, the first-formed halide gets longer ripening | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.45–46 (PDF 53–54)] | **[M]** |
| **Double jet** — silver and halide run simultaneously into gelatine, bromide kept in excess | "always formed in the presence of increasing quantities of excess halide… extremely useful… tendency to give fast emulsions and yet **without want of density in the high-lights**… **very little tendency to the formation of the period of over-exposure**" | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.46 (PDF 54)] | **[F]** |
| **Split silver** — successive portions at stages of digestion | Adding only **one-fourth** of the silver first and the remainder later "gives rather a **higher gamma infinity**" | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.75 (PDF 82)] | **[F]** |
| **Nucleation** | "Run a little silver in first… stir well for about a minute before running in the bulk… **as this gives nuclei for the formation of further crystals**" | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.48 (PDF 56)] | **[M]** |
| **Iodide placement** | Iodide into bromized gelatine ("primary") vs into a finished bromide emulsion ("secondary") vs mixing separate emulsions ("tertiary"). Adding iodide after the mix **delays ripening**, but "provided digestion be prolonged, an equally fast emulsion can be obtained… and **there is less fog**." Iodide added just before setting "**appears to slow the emulsion considerably**" | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.39–40, 44–45 (PDF 47–48, 52–53)] | **[F]** |
| **Ammonia placement** | Ammonio-nitrate route: free ammonia rises through the mix. Constant-ammonia variant: ammonia added to the bromized gelatine — "**less ammonia used, there may be less chance of fog**." Both give higher initial speed than an acid mix | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.46 (PDF 54); Ch. IV, p.78 (PDF 85)] | **[M]** |
| **Reversed precipitation (chloride/chlorobromide), 1966** | "either the entire halide is added to the silver, or more frequently the silver is added to insufficient halide, and the extra halide is then added. Whichever variation is used, **the emulsion environment is on the silver side of 'neutrality' for some time during the emulsification, a situation never mentioned in connection with iodobromide emulsions**" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.74 (PDF 80)] | **[F]** |

**Wall's process constants for the mix:**

| Item | Value | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard batch | **500 g AgNO₃**; larger demands met by repeating the batch (10 × 500 g rather than one 5000 g mix) | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 59)] | **[Q]** |
| Rate of mixing | Acid process **~1000 ccm in 10 min**; ammonia process may be double that; some formulas up to **2 h** | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 59)] | **[Q]** |
| Stirring | Continuous throughout mix and digestion, **~60 r.p.m.**; without it the halide settles into "a coarse-grained hard cake" | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.46–48 (PDF 54–56)] | **[Q]** |
| Summary rule | "**Slow and medium speed ones should be mixed in the presence of large quantities of gelatine and water, while fast ones should be compounded with low ratios of gelatine and considerably less water.**" | [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.52 (PDF 60)] | **[F]** |

**Duffin's 1966 process constants for emulsification:** the time "may vary from a very rapid addition in **5 secs** (very difficult to achieve and control industrially) to a slow mixing in **up to one hour**; addition times **around one minute are most common**"; temperature "usually in the range **40° to 70 °C**"; "Generally, increasing the emulsification temperature causes faster crystal growth and therefore gives a **coarser grained emulsion**. This is not always the case, and in some situations alteration of the emulsification temperature may **affect grain pattern** considerably" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.61, 63 (PDF 65, 67)]. **[Q]**

Wall's 1929 mixing rate of ~1000 ccm in 10 min is *slow* by Duffin's 1966 standard (~1 minute typical), which is consistent with 1929 relying on the mix itself to do part of the grain-growth work. **[E]**

**The ten emulsion variables — Duffin's own list, printed as a numbered set, which is the most compact statement of what an emulsion maker actually controls** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.61–62 (PDF 65–66)]:

1. Mode of emulsification (single or double jet). **[F]**
2. Emulsification time (5 s – 1 h; ~1 min typical). **[Q]**
3. Emulsification temperature (40–70 °C). **[Q]**
4. **Excess halide**, uniform or decreasing, quoted as percentage excess over the silver equivalent:
   - **Iodobromide: 20 %–250 % excess bromide** during precipitation and ripening; "those for **negative purposes commonly containing the highest amounts** while **X-ray emulsions have the lowest**." **[Q]**
   - **Chlorobromide and chloride: rarely more than about 10 % excess halide, but may be as low as 1 % or 2 % where very little growth is desired.** **[Q]**
   - "the vast majority of emulsions are formed at roughly the same concentration, **around 2,000 ml. per g. mole of silver**", so % excess and normality are near-interchangeable descriptions. **[Q]**
5. Quantity of ammonia and its position in the formulation. **[F]**
6. pH of the solution. **[F]**
7. Quantity and nature of the gelatin — "Account must be taken also of the presence of **microimpurities** which may have a marked effect in some emulsions, particularly those of fine grain." **[F]**
8. Proportion of the different halides and their mode of introduction — "**iodide in an iodobromide emulsion; the latter, in particular, very critically influences the growth and sensitivity of the grains.**" **[F]**
9. Cation of the halide (K, ammonium, alkaline-earth e.g. CaCl₂; **lead and cadmium salts specifically claimed**). **[F]**
10. Deliberate organic restrainers/accelerators of grain growth — named as **iminazoles, thiazoles, thioglycollic acid** (Glafkides) [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.62 (PDF 66)]. **[F]**

**Wall's 1929 bromide-excess table** — six named workers' recommendations, per 100 g AgNO₃, NH₄Br assumed [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.33 (PDF 41)]:

| Worker | Bromide (g per 100 AgNO₃) | Excess (%) | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Abney | 73 | **15.4** | **[Q]** |
| Bennett | 63.6 | **6.03** | **[Q]** |
| Burton | 59.5 | **1.9** | **[Q]** |
| Debenham | 115.2 | **57.6** | **[Q]** |
| Eder | 66 / 125 / 133 / 150 | **8.4 / 67.4 / 75.4 / 92.4** | **[Q]** |
| Newberry | 72.17 | **14.57** | **[Q]** |

Wall's gloss: "That a fairly large excess of bromide is favorable for the attainment of a high speed is now generally acknowledged", with the stated mechanism "the finer particles of silver bromide are dissolved by the excess and in the course of ripening are deposited on the larger grains, thus giving increased sensitiveness" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.33 (PDF 41)]. **[M]**

**Comparing the two eras' bromide excesses (ours).** Wall's 1929 recommendations span **1.9 %–92.4 %**; Duffin's 1966 iodobromide range is **20 %–250 %**, with negative emulsions at the top. So 1966 practice used *substantially larger* bromide excesses than any of Wall's six authorities, and Duffin's own worked octahedral emulsion at **244 %** excess is nearly three times Eder's most extreme 1929 figure. **The direction of change from 1929 to 1966 is toward much higher bromide excess during ripening.** **[E]** Both eras agree on the sign of the effect (more excess bromide → more ripening → larger grains → more speed, at the cost of a broader distribution), and both attribute it to the same dissolution-and-redeposition mechanism. **[E]**

### 6.3 Nucleation and growth theory (1995 only)

Neither 1929 nor 1966 has a nucleation theory; Wall has the empirical trick of pre-nucleation (§6.2) and Duffin has the qualitative "rapid mixing → many small nuclei" rule (§5.6). Tani supplies the framework.

**The LaMer-type diagram.** Three solute concentrations are defined: **Cs** (solubility), **C*min** (the critical supersaturation above which rapid spontaneous nucleation occurs), and **C*max** (the critical limiting supersaturation). Regions I / II / III of Fig. 2.12 are "the period before nucleation, nucleation, and growth, respectively". In the silver halide case "the product of the concentrations of silver and halide ions can be applied to the ordinate" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.33 (PDF 42), Fig. 2.12]. **[F]**

The process narrative, quoted because it is the design rule for monodispersity:

> "the spontaneous nucleation of silver halide begins to take place rapidly when the concentration exceeds C£in, and then ceases shortly thereafter, since the concentration begins to decrease and becomes lower than C*in. **In order to control the uniformity of size of emulsion grains, it is important to keep the concentration lower than C*min after the initial nucleation is finished in order to prevent the occurrence of further nucleation.** Thus, all the reactants added after the initial nucleation are used for the growth of the nuclei formed in the initial nucleation stage. The growth rate at C*min is called the **critical growth rate**."
> [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.33–34 (PDF 42–43)] **[M]**

**The one quantified threshold:** "Several investigators reported a C*in/Cs above which the spontaneous nucleation of silver halide takes place. Those values ranged from **1.075 through 1.67**, depending upon the experimental conditions used" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.34 (PDF 43)]. **[Q]** So the supersaturation ratio required to nucleate silver halide is only **7.5 %–67 % above saturation** — a remarkably low barrier, and the reason nucleation control needs the reaction-vessel silver-ion concentration to be servo-controlled (the controlled double jet). **[E]**

**Nuclei sizes, and the exclusion of heterogeneous nucleation:**

> "By observing that the nucleation of AgBr could be enhanced neither by CuS grains with a radius of about **25 A** nor by Agl grains with diameter of about **150 A**, Berry and Skillman concluded that the **heterogeneous nucleation process was negligible** for the precipitation of silver halide." … "The sizes of the critical stable nuclei, which were reported by several investigators, ranged from **140 A through 600 A**."
> [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.34 (PDF 43)] **[Q]**

Critical stable nuclei are therefore **14–60 nm** (conv.), i.e. **0.014–0.060 µm** — smaller than the smallest finished grain in Duffin's Table 1.1 (0.03 µ = 30 nm) by a factor of about 2 at the low end, and comparable at the top. **[E]** A 140 Å AgBr nucleus contains, at a = 5.755 Å and 4 formula units per cell, ≈ (140/5.755)³ × 4 ≈ **5.8 × 10³ AgBr units**; a 600 Å nucleus ≈ **4.5 × 10⁵ units**. Both are ours. **[E]**

**The diffusion-controlled growth law.** Equation (2.3)'s body is lost to OCR; the printed symbol list is: **dr/dt** = one-dimensional growth rate; **D** = diffusion constant of solutes; **Vm** = volume of 1 mole of silver bromide; **δ** = width of the diffusion layer; **r** = grain radius; **C** = bulk concentration, **Ci** = surface concentration, **Cs** = solubility. "The difference between C and Ci is the driving force for diffusion, and the difference between Ci and Cs is the driving force for reaction" [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.34–35 (PDF 43–44), Eq. (2.3), Figs. 2.13, 2.14]. **[F]**

Stated behaviour, which is all that survives and all that is needed:
- "Equation (2.3) shows that the growth rate **increases with decreasing r and δ**." **[Q]**
- "When **r/δ is nearly zero**, it is regarded that **dr/dt is proportional to the reciprocal of r**." **[Q]**
- Agitation and overlapping diffusion layers reduce δ and so raise dr/dt; Jagannathan & Wey observed a growth-rate increase with increasing grain population, ascribed to δ reduction by diffusion-layer overlap. **[F]**

Reaction-controlled exponents (§5.2): dr/dt ∝ r² (mononuclear-layer mechanism), dr/dt ∝ r⁰ (polynuclear-layer mechanism) [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.35 (PDF 44)]. **[Q]**

The 1929 empirical counterpart of the "agitation reduces δ" result is striking and should be recorded: Cajal, working on Lippmann emulsions, found gentle stirring gave a slow emulsion and vigorous agitation in a bottle a faster one — "**the speed might thus be varied as 1 : 3**" [Wall 1929, Ch. VI, p.132 (PDF 139)]. **[Q]** A 3× speed change from agitation alone is a factor of 3 in volume, i.e. 1.44× in linear grain size (ours), and is exactly the sign Tani's δ argument predicts. **[E]**

**Which pBr regime is diffusion controlled.** "both solubility and critical growth rates are steeply dependent upon pBr, and the larger the solubility is, the higher is the critical growth rate. **In the range where the solubility is small, the growth rates of the {100} and {111} faces are small and are equal to each other, indicating that the growth of AgBr in this region is diffusion controlled. In the range in which pBr is small and the solubility is high, the critical growth rates of the {100} and {111} faces are high and differ from each other**" [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.36–38 (PDF 45–47), Figs. 2.15, 2.16]. **[Q]** So diffusion control — the only regime that narrows the size distribution — occurs at **low solubility, i.e. high pBr, i.e. low bromide excess**. This is the physical reason Duffin's low-bromide ammonia emulsion was monodisperse and his 244 %-excess emulsion was polydisperse. **[E]**

**Protective colloid is required for monodispersity:** gelatin in most cases, some synthetic polymers usable; "**In the absence of a protective colloid, monodispersed silver halide grains could be prepared only in a extremely diluted solution**" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.41 (PDF 50)]. **[F]**

### 6.4 Physical ripening and Ostwald ripening

**The mechanism, 1966 — the clearest statement in the set:**

> "the larger the surface area of a crystal, relative to its volume, the higher will be the energy state of that crystal. In general terms, therefore, the silver-halide emulsion will tend to a state containing a small number of larger crystals because this system is in a lower energy state."
> Growth is "by **cannibalism**": surface ions dissolve under the ripening agent, migrate, and reprecipitate on a neighbour. "an emulsion must be regarded as a **dynamic system** since in the presence of ripening solvents this process is always continuing."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.60 (PDF 64)] **[M]**

**The 1929 statement of the same mechanism**, which predates any thermodynamic framing: excess bromide dissolves "the finer particles of silver bromide" and "in the course of ripening [they] are deposited on the larger grains, thus giving increased sensitiveness" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.33 (PDF 41)]. **[M]** Wall attributes the effect to Ostwald only implicitly; Duffin names him: "**Ostwald ripening** after Ostwald who first recorded the change of fine precipitates of silver iodide into coarser ones on heat treatment where a proportion of the crystals grew at the expense of the rest" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.58 (PDF 62)]. **[F]**

**The 1995 statement, and its use as a *selection* mechanism** rather than merely a coarsening one: during Ostwald ripening the pKsp of tabular grains exceeds that of other grains, so "**only tabular grains can grow with the dissolution of other grains, and finally survive**" (§5.4) [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.39 (PDF 48)]. **[M]** This is the conceptual advance between 1966 and 1995: Ostwald ripening is not just how grains get bigger, it is how a *habit* is purified. **[E]**

**The ripening agents — the complex-ion chemistry that makes the silver mobile, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.59 (PDF 63)]:

```
AgBr    + Br- = AgBr2-
AgBr2-  + Br- = AgBr3--
AgBr3-- + Br- = AgBr4---
```
(OCR of the third and fourth: `Ag&r>~ + GSr- = AgBr>--`, charge superscripts corrupt.) **[Q]**

- "The most predominant of these complex ions, in the range of excess bromide concentrations used in photographic emulsions, is the **AgBr₄³⁻** complex ion." **[F]**
- "it has been suggested that the important complex from the point of view of **crystal growth** is **AgBr₃²⁻**." **[F]**
- Ammonia complex: **Ag(NH₃)₂⁺**. **[F]**
- Other ripening agents in the literature: **thiocyanate** in place of bromide; the amines **morpholine** and **N-hydroxyethylpiperidine** instead of ammonia. **[F]**

Note the distinction Duffin draws and which matters: the *most abundant* complex (AgBr₄³⁻) is not the *growth-active* one (AgBr₃²⁻). **[F]** Tani's twinning mechanism invokes the same family of species, with the subscript OCR-lost (§5.4) [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.38–39 (PDF 47–48)]. **[F]**

**Ammonia conversion equations, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.61 (PDF 65)]:

```
2 AgNO3 + 2 NH4OH = Ag2O + 2 NH4NO3 + H2O
AgNO3   + 2 NH4OH = Ag(NH3)2NO3 + 2 H2O
```
"At this stage the silver is said to be *converted* and *ammoniacal emulsions* are those in which this quantity of ammonia has been added." **[Q]** Tani's 1995 note on the same agent: "Among those agents, **ammonia is most popular and has been used for the preparation of large silver halide grains for a long time**" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)]. **[F]** Wall's 1929 ammonia specification, which matters because the strengths differed by country: England used sp. gr. **0.880 ≈ 35 % NH₃**; the USA used sp. gr. **0.90 ≈ 28 %** — "the latter is one-fifth weaker" [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.11 (PDF 19)]. **[Q]** The ammonia method "gives the highest sensitiveness", and silver halide formed in the presence of ammonia has an "initial speed … greater than when an acid mix is used" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.29 (PDF 37); Ch. IV, p.78 (PDF 85)]. **[F]**

**Chloride emulsions cannot use ammonia freely, 1966:** ammonia "is little used here because the very high solubility of silver chloride in ammonia restricts its use to small quantities and even these have a drastic effect on the grain growth" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.74 (PDF 80)]. **[F]**

**Neutral (boiled) vs ammonia — the temperature-regime distinction, 1966:** ammonia emulsions, "particularly those using converted silver, ripen rapidly and frequently a temperature of **40 °C or 45 °C** is quite high enough". Without ammonia, excess bromide alone requires "much higher temperatures … frequently **up to 70 °C. and in earlier days even higher**" — hence the names "neutral or boiled emulsions" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.66 (PDF 70)]. **[Q]**

Wall confirms the "even higher" from the inside: "the emulsion **does not actually boil**; its temperature ranges from **95° to 98 °C (203° to 208 °F)**" [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.56 (PDF 64)]. **[Q]** And he states the contrast consequence: acid-boiled formulas "have rather a **low gamma infinity**", while the boil-then-ammonia modification gives "not only faster plates but a **higher gamma**" [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.56 (PDF 64)]. **[F]**

**The effect of gelatin quantity on growth, 1966:** "Generally speaking, **more gelatin produces slower grain growth**. It is fairly certain that this is not just a viscosity effect … This is a function of the basic peptide structure and due to the influence of **ripening restrainers** in the gelatin." "the use of **inert gelatin** enables the emulsion chemist to have **more control of the grain-growth stage**." "It may well be that the most important function of the gelatin is merely to **keep the emulsion grains apart**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.65 (PDF 69)]. **[M]**

**Why gelatin permits growth at all, 1966** — a result that reframes the colloid's role: "Recent measurements of the **heat of adsorption of gelatin to silver bromide** have shown it to be **very low indeed** … it may be that the important property of gelatin is its **very weak adsorption** to the grain surface which permits grain growth without interference while at the same time maintaining the crystals in suspension; **other colloids more powerfully adsorbed do inhibit grain growth**." Plate-like grains are *not* attributable to the gelatin layer, since they also form in other colloids or in colloid-free hydrobromic acid [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.65–66 (PDF 69–70)]. **[M]**

**Effect of iodide on growth, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.64–65 (PDF 68–69), Fig. 4.2]:
- "when silver nitrate is added to mixed bromide and iodide ions, **silver iodide is precipitated first** because of the much lower solubility." **[F]**
- "the **coarser grains** of a broadly dispersed iodobromide emulsion **contain the most iodide**, suggesting that grains containing the most iodide were probably precipitated first and **tend to grow more quickly**." **[F]**
- Iodide introduces **defects** into the AgBr lattice, whence increased speed after chemical sensitization and improved spectral sensitization (§4.4). **[F]**
- Above 10 % iodide, sensitivity falls (internal image). **[Q]**

Wall's 1929 view of the same variable is that iodide **retards** ripening: adding iodide after the mix "delays ripening", and iodide added just before setting "appears to slow the emulsion considerably" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.39–40, 44–45 (PDF 47–48, 52–53)]. **[F]** Also, "iodide alone [is] very apt to form a coarse granular precipitate, hence adding it after the bromide" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.39 (PDF 47)]. **[M]** **The two sources disagree in emphasis:** Duffin 1966 reports iodide-rich grains growing *faster*; Wall 1929 reports iodide additions *delaying* ripening. They may be describing different things — the growth rate of an already-iodide-rich nucleus versus the ripening rate of the population when iodide is introduced late — but neither source makes that distinction, so both statements stand as printed. **[E]**

### 6.5 pAg/pBr control of growth rate and habit

Covered mechanistically in §5.3 (habit) and §6.3 (regime). The quantitative content is collected here.

| Solubility and critical growth rate vs pBr | both "steeply dependent upon pBr, and the larger the solubility is, the higher is the critical growth rate" | [Tani 1995, §2.2, pp.36–38 (PDF 45–47), Fig. 2.15] | **[Q]** |
| Diffusion-controlled regime | small solubility (high pBr): {100} and {111} growth rates small **and equal** | [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)] | **[Q]** |
| Reaction-influenced regime | small pBr, high solubility: {100} and {111} critical growth rates high **and unequal** | [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)] | **[Q]** |

| Habit rule, 1966 form | low pAg → cubic (100)-faced; high bromide → (111)-faced | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.59–60 (PDF 63–64)] | **[M]** |

| Face-specific size dependence | Fig. 2.14 gives the size dependence of critical growth rates for cubic AgBr, cubic AgCl and octahedral AgBr | [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.36 (PDF 45), Fig. 2.14] | **[F]** |

All citations in the table are [Wall 1929, Ch. III–IV, at the printed/PDF pages given].

**Patterns visible in the 1929 table (ours).**
- **Gelatine at the mix is the primary speed lever, inversely.** Slow negative: 250 g; fast negative: 50 g; fast stepped: 100 g soft; ammonium-nitrate fast: 80 g; slow contrast (process): **625 g**; sodium-halide fine-grain: 675 g; "ordinary" landscape: 675 g. The fast emulsions run at **50–120 g** and the slow/contrast emulsions at **250–675 g** per 500 g AgNO₃ — a **5–13× span**, and the single sharpest recipe discriminator in the set. **[E]**
- **Digestion time is the secondary lever.** Slow negative boils 30 min; fast negative boils 75 min — a 2.5× difference in the hot hold at the same nominal chemistry class. **[E]**
- **Iodide tracks speed weakly.** 9 g (slow) to 25 g (fast) per 500 g AgNO₃, i.e. ≈ 1.8 %–5.1 % molar on the silver (ours, using KI 166 and AgNO₃ 169.87), consistent with the 1–5 % commercial range of §4.4. **[E]**
- **Total water at the mix tracks the gelatine.** Fast emulsions use 1125–2500 ccm; slow and contrast emulsions 3500–5680 ccm — exactly Wall's own stated rule (§6.2). **[E]**

**Wall's gelatine-quantity rules, stated rather than implied** [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.31–32, 52 (PDF 39–40, 60); Ch. IV, pp.62, 82 (PDF 70, 89)]:

| Statement | Effect | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Gelatine is a protective colloid — "prevents not only the formation of a coarse grain, but also fog" | grain ↓, fog ↓ | **[M]** |
| Slow/transparency emulsions: high gelatine proportion in the mix | grain ↓ (speed not required) | **[F]** |
| Fast emulsions: "the less gelatine used, within certain limits, the better"; **~1 % is a safe limit during the actual mix**, more added soon after, "otherwise coarse grain and fog will ensue" | speed ↑; below the limit, grain ↑ and thin results | **[Q]** |
| Early rule: gelatine at mix = **1/5 of AgNO₃ weight**; in the boiling process add **1/4 of that** every half hour; at the end of digestion add gelatine = **2 × silver weight** | grain-carrying | **[Q]** |
| Minimum ever used (W. K. Burton): **1/800 of the total bulk of mixing liquids** | — | **[Q]** |
| Higher gelatine content ⇒ **less ripening and less increase in fog** during cold after-ripening | speed ↓, fog ↓ | **[F]** |
| Alcohol added at the mix to prevent coarse grain when gelatine is reduced (e.g. **375 ccm per 5000 ccm water**) | grain ↓ | **[Q]** |
| Gelatine in the final cine positive emulsion: **8–9 % of final bulk** | — | **[Q]** |

Note the internal consistency check (ours): Wall's "~1 % gelatine during the actual mix" against a fast-negative recipe of 50 g gelatine in 2500 ccm gives 2.0 % — twice his stated safe limit, though 50 g in the full 4250 ccm after the silver is added gives 1.2 %. The rule and the recipes agree if the percentage is taken on the *final* mix volume. **[E]**

**Multiple/double-addition (nucleation) emulsification — two published 1966 formulae**, both of which are recognisably Wall's split-silver trick formalised [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.63–64 (PDF 67–68)]:

*(a) Agfa formula for a very fast emulsion "used for night photography, the details of which were published after the war":*

| Solution | Component | Amount | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Water | 70 ml. | **[Q]** |
| | Potassium bromide | 8.0 g. | **[Q]** |
| | Potassium iodide | 0.5 g. | **[Q]** |
| | Gelatin | 1.0 g. | **[Q]** |
| B | Water | 90 ml. | **[Q]** |
| | Silver nitrate | **OCR lost** (raw `Shing:`) | **[Q]** |

"Solutions A and B were both heated to **65 °C** and then **half of B was added to A in one minute. The second half was then added over 29 minutes**, enabling the first half of the silver halide to ripen and act as nuclei for the second." **[Q]** Iodide fraction (ours): 0.5 g KI (166) vs 8.0 g KBr (119) = 3.01 mmol I vs 67.2 mmol Br → **4.3 mol % iodide**. **[E]** Gelatin is 1.0 g against ~11–12 g of silver halide, i.e. gelatin:halide ≈ **0.09:1** — far leaner even than Duffin's 1966 "≤100 g per g-mole" (0.53:1), consistent with an extreme-speed formula. **[E]**

*(b) Glafkides formula (numbers partly OCR-damaged — treat with care):*

| Solution | Component | Amount (raw OCR where damaged) | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Gelatin | 6.0 g. (raw `60g.`) | **[Q]** |
| | Ammonium bromide | 19.0 g. | **[Q]** |
| | Potassium iodide | 0.7 g. | **[Q]** |
| | Ammonia (S.G. 0.910) | 4 ml. | **[Q]** |

| B | Water | 140 ml. | **[Q]** |
| | Silver nitrate | 20.7 g. (raw `207>g:`) | **[Q]** |
| C | Water | 70 ml. | **[Q]** |
| | Silver nitrate | 10 g. (raw `1Oige:`) | **[Q]** |
| D | Gelatin | 35 g. (raw `35° 1g.`) | **[Q]** |

"At a temperature between **42°–70 °C** depending on the nature of the gelatin, (this is a very wide range and a modern emulsion formula using inert gelatin would require this factor to be better defined). Solution B was added to Solution A in **1–5 minutes**. The emulsion was then ripened for **10–60 minutes** before the second silver solution C was added, followed by more gelatin D and a **second physical ripening for 15 minutes**." **[Q]** Duffin's parenthetical criticism of the 42–70 °C latitude is itself the era marker: by 1966 an inert-gelatin formula was expected to pin the temperature. **[F]** Also: "a recent Japanese ammonia formula uses **only one third of its silver iodobromide as nuclei** for the remainder" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.64 (PDF 68)]. **[Q]**

Nucleus fraction across the three documented split-addition formulae (ours): Wall's split-silver **1/4**; Agfa night-photography **1/2**; the Japanese ammonia formula **1/3**; Glafkides **20.7/(20.7+10) = 0.67**. The nucleus fraction is evidently a free design parameter in the range **0.25–0.67**. **[E]**

These are the most complete emulsion specifications in the source set, and they bracket the polydisperse/monodisperse divide.

**The two recipes side by side — this is the cleanest controlled comparison in the source set.**

| Variable | Octahedral | Ammonia/cubic | Ratio | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silver | 85 g AgNO₃ (0.5 mole) | 85 g AgNO₃ (0.5 mole) | 1 : 1 | **[Q]** |
| Gelatin at mix | 12.5 g (25 g/mole) | 12.5 g (25 g/mole) | 1 : 1 | **[Q]** |
| Ripening volume | 2500 ml/mole | 2500 ml/mole | 1 : 1 | **[Q]** |
| Ripening temperature | 50 °C | 50 °C | 1 : 1 | **[Q]** |
| Addition time | 60 s | 60 s | 1 : 1 | **[Q]** |
| **Bromide excess** | **244 %** | **24 %** | **10 : 1** | **[Q]** |
| **Free bromide** | **1.0 M** | **0.1 M** | **10 : 1** | **[Q]** |
| **Ammonia** | none | **1.0 M** | — | **[Q]** |
| Iodide | <3.0 % | 1.0 % | 3 : 1 | **[Q]** |
| **Habit** | octahedral, tabular fraction | rounded cubes | — | **[F]** |
| **Mean volume** | 0.18 µ³ | 1.75 µ³ | **1 : 9.7** | **[Q]** |
| **Distribution** | broad | narrow | — | **[F]** |
| **Contrast** | "fairly low" | "high" | — | **[F]** |

So with silver, gelatin, volume, temperature and addition time all held constant, changing the free bromide by 10× and adding 1.0 M ammonia changes the mean grain volume by ≈10×, inverts the habit, and inverts the distribution width and the contrast. **[E]** Note that the ammonia emulsion achieved the *larger* grains on the *smaller* bromide excess — because ammonia, not bromide, is doing the solvent work, and it is a far more powerful silver solvent. Neither source states this comparison; it is ours. **[E]**

**Wall's 1929 counterpart of the chlorobromide trend** agrees exactly: "The more bromide… the faster it is, as a rule, the longer the scale of gradation and the less easy to obtain warm tones"; "Speed and contrast are functions of bromide content"; nomenclature: chloro-bromide = chloride in excess, bromo-chloride = bromide predominates [Wall 1929, Ch. V, pp.94–96 (PDF 101–103)]. **[F]** Valenta's analyses of commercial chlorobromide plates put the Cl:Br ratio at **50:50 (German) to 15:85 (English)** [Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.97 (PDF 104)]. **[Q]** Duffin's 1966 chlorobromide range is quoted as a "bromide/chloride ratio [that] may vary from **5 % to 50 %**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.18 (PDF 22)]. **[Q]** These two ranges are stated on different bases and are not directly comparable; Valenta's 15:85 Cl:Br (i.e. 85 % bromide) lies outside Duffin's "5 % to 50 %" bromide band, so either the bases differ or 1929 English chlorobromide plates were far more bromide-rich than 1966 practice. Present both. **[E]**

### 6.8 Washing

**1929 — noodle/worm washing, with all the apparatus numbers.**

| Item | Value | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shredding cloth | canvas of **not less than ¼ in mesh** (≈6.4 mm, conv.); the jelly broken to walnut size, then shredded under water | [Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, pp.139–141 (PDF 146–148)] | **[Q]** |
| Power press | phosphor-bronze cylinder **27 in long × 6 in bore, 24 in piston travel** (≈68.6 cm × 15.2 cm, 61 cm, conv.), silver-lined (≥ **6 oz deposit** ≈ 170 g, conv.), silver die with **3/8 in** (9.5 mm, conv.) holes and **1/16 in** (1.6 mm, conv.) clearance; hydraulic, water pressure **≥ 20 lb/in²** (≈1.4 bar, conv.) | [Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, pp.139–141 (PDF 146–148)] | **[Q]** |
| Wash-water temperature | "should not exceed **15 °C (59 °F)** while **10° to 12 °C** is better. The warmer the water, the more rapid the diffusion of the salts, but the more water the worms pick up" | [Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, p.144 (PDF 151)] | **[Q]** |
| Historic vs 1929 durations | "as late as **1892**, from **twelve to eighteen hours**… of recent years… in some cases to **four to six hours** and in others even to **half these latter times**" (i.e. 2–3 h) | [Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, p.145 (PDF 152)] | **[Q]** |
| Amateur scale | ~1 litre, bagged, water changed every 5–10 min for **1 h** = properly washed; the jar method washes 2 litres in 1 h | [Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, pp.142–143 (PDF 149–150)] | **[Q]** |
| Endpoint test | Volhard sulphocyanide titration for bromide | [Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, p.149 (PDF 156)] | **[F]** |
| Draining and store-melt | worms drained ~1 h; store-melt at **not more than 40 °C (104 °F)** for an hour to release occluded air | [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.150 (PDF 157)] | **[Q]** |

**The 1929 statement that washing itself changes the photographic properties** — this is the one that matters:

> "**That the duration of washing can exert considerable action on the emulsion is an accepted fact**" — long washing or too-warm water gives "**washing fog**"; but "**it is possible for an increase in speed to take place without increase of fog, and this is sometimes reckoned on by the emulsion maker as an essential part of the process**" — dangerous unless the temperature is controlled.
> [Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, p.145 (PDF 152)] **[F]**

So in 1929 the wash was, deliberately, part of the ripening. **[F]**

**1966 — noodle washing described, and superseded.**

- Method: the emulsion is set to a soft jelly, shredded to noodles, and suspended in frequently changed water; ions diffuse out osmotically. Progress is monitored by (1) **conductivity** of the aqueous phase or of the melted emulsion, or (2) **pAg** by potentiometry with a silver electrode against a standard calomel reference. Duffin argues **pAg is "much to be preferred"** because two emulsions of equal excess halide but different total ionic strength reach different halide concentrations at the same conductivity [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.76 (PDF 82)]. **[M]**
- The dilution penalty, quantified: "it is quite common for the **emulsion concentration to have dropped to almost half its initial value**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.76 (PDF 82)]. **[Q]**
- The historical verdict: noodle washing is "**The earliest, and until recently the commonest**, method" and "has very largely been replaced by more modern methods"; "if it is satisfactory to coat fairly dilute emulsions, **as was the case when coating was carried out on glass** … then this dilution effect can be tolerated. **Modern high-speed film-coating methods commonly require more concentrated emulsion**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.75–77 (PDF 81–83)]. **[F]**
- Plate-side aid: **magnesium sulphate** wash liquor to suppress noodle swelling [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.76 (PDF 82)]. **[F]**

**1966 — coagulation washing, the replacement, with a worked number:**

> "if **0.5 molar excess bromide** is used during the ripening stage as in the octahedral formula given above, then the removal of **95 %** of the aqueous phase, which is readily achievable, results in a **bromide normality of 0.05** if the emulsion were reconstituted to half of its original volume, which is a concentration at which digestion could be carried out."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.78 (PDF 84)] **[Q]**

One precipitation/separation is "virtually adequate"; a second is common [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.78 (PDF 84)]. **[F]** Arithmetic check (ours): 0.5 M reduced by removing 95 % of the aqueous phase gives 0.025 M in the residue's original volume; reconstituting to half the original volume doubles it to **0.05 M** ✓. The printed figure is consistent. **[E]**

**The coagulation methods, with their numbers** [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.78–80 (PDF 84–86), Plate 4.3]:

| Method | Reagent and quantity | Conditions | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Solvent precipitation | industrial **ethanol**, "frequently around **1 litre per gram molecule of silver**" | — ; "probably the **earliest method of coagulation** commonly used in production but **has now been largely displaced**" | **[Q]** |
| Salt precipitation | **ammonium sulphate** | "at a pH value just below the isoelectric point, e.g. at a **pH value below 4** according to a Kodak patent". Residual salt in an emulsion at the end of ripening "rarely exceeds **1.0 molar** in total content" | **[Q]** |
| Sulphonic-acid precipitation | naphthalene disulphonic acids, long-chain alkyl sulphates | "usually at a **pH value below 4**" | **[F]** |
| Acylated (e.g. **phthalated**) gelatin | — | precipitates on acidifying to "about **4**"; **redisperses again if the pH is lowered further, for example to 3**, because guanidino (arginine) and iminazole (histidine) groups protonate. Plate 4.3 compares unmodified vs phthalated gelatin; "there seems to be little evidence of such differences although some Russian authors have reported that **benzene-sulphonated gelatin produced slower grain growth**" | **[Q]** |

**The image-level consequence of getting redispersion wrong** — the only granularity-adjacent statement in Duffin's emulsion-making chapter: "All these precipitation methods … require **very efficient redispersion** … Without this, the grains will tend to **clump together which will produce aggregates of developed silver on processing**. Even if these are not serious enough to degrade the image, they will give a **coarser-grained result** than in a completely dispersed system" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.80 (PDF 86)]. **[M]**

**Tani 1995 does not cover washing at all** in the range examined — there is no washing, no coagulation, and no salt-removal discussion. **[F]** This is a real gap: by 1995 the washing/coagulation step must still have existed, but this source set contains no post-1966 information on it. **[F]**

### 6.9 After-ripening / digestion / chemical ripening

**The 1966 process envelope, and the speed-vs-fog race that defines it:**

> "a treatment, often after the addition of a chemical sensitizer, at an elevated temperature, **from 40° to 70 °C**, which may vary in duration **from a few minutes up to several hours**, when **speed and fog are increased** … if the conditions used were not optimum in terms of **pH, nature of the gelatin or the quantities of various additions**, then the **speed increase might be much smaller or the onset of fog might take place sooner** (indicated by the dotted line) … **as this reaches its maximum value the onset of fog occurs**, that is some of the silver-halide crystals become developable without exposure."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89), Fig. 5.1 "Growth of speed and fog in digestion: iodobromide emulsion"; y-axis "Fog and Relative Log Speed" 0–2.0, x-axis "Digestion Time"] **[Q]**

Fig. 5.1 is the source's own picture of the manufacturing speed/fog trade-off, and its axes are worth recording because it means fog and speed are two outputs of one process variable, not two independent knobs. **[E]**

**The 1966 dating statement on who controlled digestion** — the pivot of the whole gelatin story (§7):

> "**Only a few years ago the behaviour of an emulsion in this digestion stage was always entirely controlled by the nature of the gelatin.** Gelatins which produced a large increase in sensitivity in a conveniently short time were referred to as **fast or active** gelatins while those that produced little or no change were referred to as **slow or inert**." … "**It is now more usual to add known amounts of these sensitizers … before the digestion stage in order to permit control of the process.**"
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)] **[F]**

**Sulphur sensitization during digestion — the dominant route, 1966.** "**Sulphur sensitization is the most widely-used method of conferring speed and contrast on a silver-halide emulsion**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]. **[F]** The three types of chemical sensitization are **1. sulphur, 2. reduction, 3. precious metal**; "The first two types … may be produced by chemicals **naturally present in gelatin**, but it is necessary to **add special compounds** to the emulsion for the third type" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]. **[F]**

Reactions as printed [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.84–85 (PDF 90–91)]:
```
Ag(+) + Ag—S—C(=NH)(NH2) + OH(-)  ->  Ag2S + NH2CONH2      (urea)
Ag(+) + [Ag(S2O3)2]       + OH(-)  ->  Ag2S + 3 HSO3(-)
```
(Charge superscripts are OCR-mangled; species and coefficients are legible.) **[Q]**

- The active class is the thiourea skeleton `>N.CS.N<`; "Active compounds of this class usually possess the **unsubstituted H atom**, to make the formation of a silver-sulphur link possible. The fully substituted **1,1,3,3-tetramethylthiourea (CH₃)₂N.CS.N(CH₃)₂ is reported as being substantially inert**." **[F]**

- Adsorption to the crystal surface "is a **basic requirement** for sulphur sensitization." **[F]**

The 1966 "only certain selected sites need their coating of silver sulphide" (Duffin's surface-area anomaly, §5.7) and the 1995 measured density of 2800 centres/µm² of (100) are the same finding at two levels of precision: the sites are specific, and they are numerous but far fewer than the surface silver ions. Ours: 2800 centres/µm² against ≈ 1.2 × 10⁷ surface silver ions per µm² (from a = 5.755 Å, i.e. (10⁴/5.755)² ≈ 3.0 × 10⁶ cells/µm² × 4 ions) is **1 centre per ≈ 4300 surface silver ions**, against Duffin's "3 % of surface silver associated with sulphur" — which is a statement about the *silver bound in the sulphide*, not about the number of centres, so the two are not in conflict. **[E]**

**Reduction sensitization during digestion, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.88–89 (PDF 94–95), Fig. 5.5]:

> "The addition to the emulsion of **very small quantities of reducing substances** followed by a heat treatment, also produces an increase of emulsion speed similar to that obtained by sulphur sensitization, **except that the contrast obtainable after treatment with a reducing agent is generally lower and there is a greater tendency to fog formation**. **Sodium sulphite and stannous chloride** are examples … may be carried out at the same kind of pAg and pH values as are used for sulphur sensitization."
> **[M]**

- Alternative route: "heat treatment carried out **in excess silver ions**; bromide ions are then added to give the usual coating pAg." **[F]**
- "**The reduction process has been shown to be autocatalytic**" (Fig. 5.3 shape). **[F]**
- Why it fogs: "a process in which a **distribution of silver atoms** is formed on the grain could easily give rise to fog, because **when any one nucleus becomes as large as a latent-image speck it will be able to initiate development** of the crystal." **[M]**
- Evidence the centres are weakly attached: "**stripping of the gelatin film from large silver-bromide crystals, which had been reduction sensitized, removed the bulk of the surface sensitivity**." The same loss occurs on adsorbing dyes. Mitchell inferred "the sensitizing substance was **a small group of silver-atoms surrounded by gelatin molecules and therefore attached to, but slightly separate from, the grain**." **[M]**
- Sulphite's effect (Bekunov, Fig. 5.5, curves "sulphite added" / "without sulphite"): "the presence of sulphite can **increase the sensitivity given by sulphur sensitization although no increase in the rate of growth of sensitivity** was obtained. **The rate of fog growth was found to be higher in the presence of sulphite, but only after maximum speed had been obtained.**" **[Q]**

**Wall's 1929 sulphite result is the same additive, measured sensitometrically** — and it is one of only two complete sensitometric records in his book: **0.25 g Na₂SO₃ per 100 g AgNO₃**, in a slow emulsion converted to ammonio-nitrate, digested **1 h at 43 °C (110 °F) + 2 h at 27 °C (80 °F)**, set on ice, gave "regular, very clean… **speed of 22 H. & D.** with **high gamma infinity**, the **fog reading with ten minutes development with the standard pyro-soda developer being only 0.1**" [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]. **[Q]** A counter-example is also recorded: 4 parts anhydrous sulphite to 10 AgNO₃ plus ammonia (Wellington) reduced the AgBr and formed a silver mirror — though Wall notes this was effectively an ammoniacal silver sulphite [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]. **[Q]** So the usable sulphite dose spans **0.25 parts per 100 AgNO₃ (works) to 40 parts per 100 AgNO₃ (destroys the emulsion)**, a 160× window. **[E]**

**The 1995 view of gold, and of the ultimate limit:** "Hamilton and Logel, by analyzing the ability of evaporated metal clusters to initiate physical development, estimated that **the smallest latent image center is composed of four silver atoms or two gold atoms**" [Tani 1995, §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101)]. **[Q]** And "the smallest latent image center is composed of **three atoms** on sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized emulsion grains and of **four to five atoms** on sulfur-sensitized emulsion grains" [Tani 1995, §4.1.1, p.83 (PDF 92)]. **[Q]** So the 1966 statement that gold raises speed "by reducing the number of quanta needed to form a stable development centre" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.186–187 (PDF 192–193)] **[M]** is confirmed in 1995 with numbers: the threshold falls from 4–5 atoms to 3 atoms. **[E]** A 4→3 atom threshold reduction gives roughly the observed 2–2.5× speed gain if the nucleation is a multi-photon coincidence process; that inference is ours. **[E]**

**Other metals, 1966:** "there are a number of references to the enhanced sensitivity produced by **cadmium** salts, and many of the metals with variable valency, such as **mercury, iron, palladium and platinum** have been mentioned in the patent literature. **At a conference in London in 1960 on the maximum sensitivity of photographic materials, reference was made to the use of palladium, in particular in the sensitization of the fastest emulsions.**" "The amounts of other rare metals added for sensitization are of a **similar order to those of gold**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.94, 96 (PDF 100, 102)]. **[F]**

V, p.87 (PDF 93)]. **[Q]**

This after-digestion may vary… **from one to two hours to days**. "**The difference in speed may be as much as one hundred per cent with the ammonia process.**" The crock retains ammonia; the open pan loses it | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.81 (PDF 88)] | **[Q]** |

"This method gives rapid emulsions with high gamma infinity, and **the colder the solutions during the mix the less the fog**" | [Wall 1929, Ch. XIII, pp.222–223 (PDF 229–230)] | **[Q]** |

**The change in after-ripening duration between the eras is dramatic and worth stating as such (ours).** 1929: after-ripening at 32–35 °C for **three days to ten days**, tested daily, five days minimum before coating. 1966: digestion at 40–70 °C for "**a few minutes up to several hours**", with the sensitizer dosed to a known amount. That is a reduction in cycle time of roughly **two orders of magnitude**, achieved by raising the temperature and by replacing the gelatin's uncontrolled natural sensitizer with a weighed addition. **[E]**

**Restrainers in digestion, 1966 — why the same recipe digests differently in different gelatins** [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.96–97 (PDF 102–103)]:

> "in the presence of the **same quantity of sensitizing substance** … **the same emulsion will digest at quite different rates with different gelatins**." "**adenine slows, and in large quantities curtails, chemical sensitization.** This is believed to be due to the fact that the restrainer functions by **controlling the manner in which the silver sulphide is laid down on the grain surface**, and thus its effectiveness in producing sensitivity and fog. Analytical evidence shows that **silver-sulphide formation continues in spite of the presence of the adenine** and its effect on sensitization. The opinion has been expressed that the influence of the adenine may be to cause the **silver sulphide to be located in the adsorbed gelatin layer instead of on the grain surface**."
> **[M]**

Caveats and corollaries as printed: the adenine assay "uses drastic treatment which would break down any fragile molecule. There is, therefore, **no real support for the assumption that adenine itself is the restraining substance**; it is much more likely to be a **derivative of adenine, probably of high molecular weight**" **[F]**; pyrimidine fragments (**cytosine, uracil, thymine**) "have been shown to be **far less active restrainers than the fused ring compounds**" **[F]**; 1966 practice: "**Reference is frequently made to 'the addition of artificial restrainers' and it seems likely, therefore, that at least some manufacturers make such additions to their emulsions**" **[F]**; and the interaction with dose: "**Since the rate of digestion is controlled by the content of both restrainer and sensitizer, it is likely that the use of very small quantities of sensitizer would result in the onset of fog before useful sensitivity is obtained. This may well be the controlling factor.**" **[M]**

**The nature of the sensitivity speck and of digestion fog — explicitly unresolved in 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.89–91 (PDF 95–97)]. Two most-discussed views: (1) **silver sulphide in a layer form, e.g. islands on the grain surface** (James & Vanselow); (2) **silver only**, Ag₂S being merely a step or a parallel reaction (Chibisov *et al.*, who "even postulate that silver sulphide has an **adverse** effect"). **[F]** Duffin's arbitration: Chibisov's fine-structure evidence "has been queried by Western workers, **none of whom have been able to repeat it**"; and "Chibisov himself showed that **the presence of gold salts during digestion prevented the formation of non-halide silver** … this is **strong evidence against the silver-speck theory**". **[F]** A third proposal (Sauvenier & Hautot): the **adsorbed silver-thiosulphate complex** is the speck, and "an **etching reaction**, arising from the silver-halide solvent action of the thiosulphate, is necessary to create the correct surface condition for sensitization. The formation of silver sulphide in appreciable quantity is believed to produce fog." **[F]**

Digestion fog: three candidate centre types are listed — Ag₂S aggregates of different shape (e.g. a three-dimensional lattice); over-large Ag₂S specks ("**recent work has shown that even large quantities of silver sulphide are unlikely to render the grain developable**"); or a slower/selective silver-forming reaction within or adjacent to an Ag₂S speck. **[F]** A discriminating experiment: "digestion of emulsions containing **only very small quantities of sensitizer, e.g. thiourea, for prolonged periods produces fog which can be almost completely bleached by dilute chromic-acid solutions** while a **similar level of fog, produced by a large quantity of sensitizer, is very resistant to bleaching**"; gold post-treatment makes Ag₂S-type fog **lower** in density and silver-type fog **higher**. **[F]** pH effect: "**Thiourea forms silver sulphide very slowly at pH 6.0 whereas at pH 8.0 it reacts very rapidly**"; starting at pH 8.0 and dropping to 6.0 mid-reaction, "the formation of fog continues at a fair speed". **[Q]** Duffin's conclusion: "**it seems possible that fog is probably silver in many cases, certainly in commercial emulsion**, and it is only with large quantities of sulphur sensitizers that silver-sulphide fog is really important." **[F]**

**1995 on reduction-sensitization centres, with absolute numbers** — the resolution of the 1966 speck argument, at least for reduction sensitization [Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.96–104 (PDF 105–113), Figs. 4.9–4.18]:

| Item | Value / statement | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Two centre types | **P centre** = electron-trapping; **R centre** = hole-trapping. "an electron-trapping silver cluster is formed at a **positively charged site**, while a hole-trapping center is formed at an **electrically neutral site**" | **[M]** |
| MO confirmation | Hamilton & Baetzold: "**Ag₂ at a positively charged kink site is an electron trap, while Ag₂ at a neutral kink site is a positive hole trap**" | **[M]** |
| Absorption peaks | **474 nm** = P centres; **540 nm** = fog centres | **[Q]** |
| P-centre stoichiometry | "the absorption coefficient of P centers was proportional to the **square** of the amount of reduction sensitizer, indicating that a P center was **Ag₂**" | **[Q]** |
| Fog-centre stoichiometry | with more sensitizer, "the absorption coefficient of P centers was saturated and the absorption coefficient of fog centers increased **in proportion** to the amount of reduction sensitizer" | **[Q]** |
| Emulsion and sensitizer | octahedral AgBr, average diameter **0.2 µm**; reduction sensitizer **DMAB (dimethylamine borane)**; sensitivity at **10 s exposure** | **[Q]** |
| Method | Kubelka–Munk, **(1 − R)²/2R ∝ absorption coefficient**, R = diffuse reflectance of a thick emulsion layer | **[Q]** |
| Redox positions | "the oxidation potential of P centers was more positive by about **0.4 V** than that of R centers, indicating that the HOMO level of P centers was about 0.4 eV lower than that of R centers. The oxidation potential of R centers in the interior of the grains was **0.05 V** less positive than that of P centers." Method: emulsions equilibrated in redox buffers, Eox taken as the potential eliminating **half** the sensitizing effect, **17 and 41 hours at 25 °C** | **[Q]** |
| Photographic effects | Tani: electron-trapping centres raise surface sensitivity (otherwise in competition with internal sensitivity); hole-trapping centres raise surface sensitivity (otherwise reduced by recombination). **Moisar disagrees in detail:** "hole-trapping reduction sensitization centers increased **both** surface and internal sensitivities, while electron-trapping centers increased surface sensitivity and **decreased** internal sensitivity" | **[F]** |
| Fog centre identity | "a fog center is identical to or similar to a latent image center" | **[F]** |

Citations for the block: [Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.96–104 (PDF 105–113), Figs. 4.9–4.18]. Note the recorded disagreement between Tani's and Moisar's accounts of what R centres do to *internal* sensitivity; both are printed side by side. **[F]**

Duffin's 1966 fog mechanism for reduction sensitization — "when any one nucleus becomes as large as a latent-image speck it will be able to initiate development" — is exactly Tani's 1995 finding that a fog centre "is identical to or similar to a latent image center", and Tani's dose-response (P centres ∝ [sensitizer]², fog centres ∝ [sensitizer]¹, P saturating first) supplies the quantitative form Duffin lacked. **[E]**

### 6.10 Consolidated stage-by-stage effect table

Each row states the stage, the variable, and its documented effect on grain size, speed, contrast and fog, with the numbers where the sources give them. Era is marked on every row.

The raw string is `is pro- portional to the fourth power of the wavelength`; the words are intact, so this is a book/typesetting error, not an OCR artefact. Use **λ⁻⁴** [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.164 (PDF 170)]. **[F]**

### 6.11 What changed between the eras — summary

| Aspect | 1929 (Wall) | 1966 (Duffin) | 1995 (Tani) | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Precipitation mode | single jet dominant; double jet known and praised | single and double jet; **continuous precipitation** named as emerging | **controlled** double jet with servo pAg | **[F]** |
| Nucleation | empirical pre-nucleation trick | "rapid mixing → many small nuclei" | LaMer diagram, C\*min/Cs = 1.075–1.67, critical nuclei 140–600 Å | **[Q]** |
| Growth control | temperature, time, bromide excess, gelatine quantity | the ten variables; pAg for habit | pBr for habit **and** for the growth-control regime; face-specific critical growth rates | **[Q]** |
| Size distribution | not measured; recognised only through "coarse grain" faults | described (broad vs narrow) and photographed, not quantified | "monodispersed" as a design target, still not quantified | **[F]** |
| Habit control | no concept | pAg controls (100) vs (111) | pBr controls habit; twinning conditions enumerated; tabular grains selected by Ostwald ripening | **[F]** |
| Washing | noodle washing, 2–18 h, itself part of the ripening | noodle washing superseded by coagulation washing | not covered | **[F]** |
| Digestion control | "**entirely controlled by the nature of the gelatin**" | "**more usual to add known amounts** of these sensitizers" | trap depths and centre densities measured; sensitizer level treated as a designed parameter | **[F]** |
| Digestion duration | 3–10 days at 32–35 °C | minutes to hours at 40–70 °C | 30 min at 60 °C in the cited experimental recipe | **[Q]** |
| Speed measure | Hurter & Driffield; works record of "standard speed, gamma infinity, K and fog reading" | relative, unitless | ISO; and a DQE of 1–2 % | **[F]** |
| Sensitizer identity | allyl thiocarbamide ("Gelatine X") believed to be *the* natural sensitizer | "**More recently, it has been made clear**" that it is **sodium thiosulphate** | Ag₂S dimers at kink sites, 2800 per µm² of (100) | **[F]** |
| Gold | not mentioned | discovered "about thirty years ago"; ×2–2½ speed | threshold falls from 4–5 to 3 atoms | **[Q]** |
| Tabular grains | no concept | twin-plane pocket mechanism described; flat octahedra at 5:1–10:1 present but not sought | deliberate technology, 1983–1990 | **[F]** |

## 7. Gelatin

### 7.1 Why gelatin at all — the historical break

Gelatin is not merely the medium; its introduction is what made dry photography possible.

> "It was **not until gelatin was introduced** into the preparation of photographic materials that really satisfactory sensitivity was obtained and it became possible to make '**dry plates**' … Previously other suspending substances were used, notably **collodion**, but emulsions prepared in this medium **only retain their light sensitivity for a short while** and, therefore, coatings were **bathed in a sensitising silver-nitrate solution just before use, and often exposed wet**. Also, it was necessary to **develop these coatings very shortly after exposure**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.29 (PDF 33)] **[F]**

Wall 1929 confirms the collodion era was already over for general work: "Except for photomechanical work, the use of collodion emulsion has completely died out" [Wall 1929, Ch. VI, p.110 (PDF 117)]. **[F]** He still gives collodion recipes and one collodion specification worth recording as an archaic control parameter — the required **viscosity 1.57–1.60**, defined as the ratio of the collodion efflux time to the water efflux time [Wall 1929, Ch. VI, pp.110–112 (PDF 117–119)]. **[Q]**

### 7.2 Role as protective colloid

The primary role is stated most directly by Wall, and demonstrated by him (§3.1): "Gelatine is a protective colloid — [it] **prevents not only the formation of a coarse grain, but also fog**" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.30 (PDF 38)]. **[M]**

The 1966 view is that the protection is *weak adsorption*, and that this is precisely what makes it useful: "Recent measurements of the **heat of adsorption of gelatin to silver bromide** have shown it to be **very low indeed** … it may be that the important property of gelatin is its **very weak adsorption** to the grain surface which permits grain growth without interference while at the same time maintaining the crystals in suspension; **other colloids more powerfully adsorbed do inhibit grain growth**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.65–66 (PDF 69–70)]. **[M]** And, with a shrug: "It may well be that the most important function of the gelatin is merely to **keep the emulsion grains apart**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.65 (PDF 69)]. **[M]**

The 1995 view adds one hard requirement and one caveat: gelatin "in most cases", some synthetic polymers usable, and "**In the absence of a protective colloid, monodispersed silver halide grains could be prepared only in a extremely diluted solution**" [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.41 (PDF 50)]. **[F]** So by 1995 the colloid is required not merely for suspension but for *monodispersity at working concentration*. **[E]**

**Gelatin also controls habit, not just size — a 1966 statement that goes beyond mere protection:**

> "gelatin, and other substances of synthetic origin, with a similar chemical structure … **are adsorbed to the silver-halide surface**. This action has two effects: first, it enables gelatin to **suspend the silver-halide grain** … secondly, it has a **very important role in controlling the growth of the silver-halide crystal and enables octahedral and cubic crystals to be formed within a narrow range of grain sizes**. Generally, **regularity of habit is only possible in the presence of gelatin** and other substances closely related to it. The use of many other polymeric substances, for example, polyvinyl alcohol and polyacrylamide, although acting effectively as suspending agents … **causes them to grow in a more random fashion or else tends to inhibit the growth to such an extent that only small ill-defined grains are produced**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.35 (PDF 39)] **[M]**

The specific active group is named: the **guanidino unit in arginine** is "shown to possess outstanding activity" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.35 (PDF 39)]. **[F]** Note that this claim — regular habit requires gelatin — sits in tension with Duffin's own statement in the emulsion chapter that plate-like grains form "in other colloids or in colloid-free hydrobromic acid" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, pp.65–66 (PDF 69–70)]. Both are printed; the reconciliation is presumably that *tabular* growth needs no gelatin while *monodisperse regular* growth does, but Duffin does not say so. **[E]**

### 7.3 The nine functions of gelatin (1966), quoted in full

Duffin's numbered list is the most complete statement of gelatin's job in the source set [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.29–30 (PDF 33–34)]:

1. Suspends the grains during emulsion-making, particularly during precipitation, "thus preventing **clumping and settling-out**". **[F]**
2. "Gelatin **influences the rate at which the silver-halide crystals grow**." **[F]**
3. "facilitates subsequent chemical treatments to **increase the sensitivity** of the grains." **[F]**
4. "The **reversible gelling properties** … are of great value in the coating process." **[F]**
5. "Gelatin contains **minor constituents which affect the light sensitivity** of the emulsion." **[F]**
6. Physical properties of the coated layer can be modified by additions to the gelatin medium. **[F]**
7. "Gelatin **interacts with some of the products of the photolysis thus stabilizing the latent image**." **[F]**
8. "Gelatin plays a vital part in **rendering the unexposed grains relatively less developable than the exposed ones**." **[F]**
9. "Coated and dried gelatin layers **swell in aqueous solutions and allow the diffusion of water-soluble substances** enabling processing of emulsion layers to take place." **[F]**

Items 5, 7 and 8 are the ones that make gelatin a *photographic* variable rather than a mechanical one: 5 is the root of stock-to-stock speed and fog variation (§7.5–7.7), 7 bears on latent-image keeping, and 8 is the physical basis of the fog floor. **[E]** Note that function 7 (latent-image stabilisation) is asserted and never quantified anywhere in the set. **[F]**

**Substitutes — an explicitly negative result.** "there has also been a very large amount of research into the possibility of replacing gelatin but **few of the many substitutes proposed have been used commercially**." Named as **partial** replacements in patents: polyacrylamide, acrylamide/acrylic-acid copolymers, polyvinylpyrrolidone. Named as less gelatin-like: polyvinyl alcohol and its esters and acetals, polyvinylpyridines, water-solubilised cellulose derivatives [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.30 (PDF 34)]. **[F]** For the supercoat specifically the same families reappear — polyvinyl alcohol and partial esters, polyvinylpyrrolidone, acrylamide/maleic acid and acrylamide/acrylic acid copolymers — "but the amount of commercial usage of these agents is not known" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.166–167 (PDF 172–173)]. **[F]**

### 7.4 Manufacture, composition, and the constants that follow from it

**Sources and process, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.30–32 (PDF 34–36)]:

| Stage | Numbers as printed | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Raw materials | **bones** (cattle, from slaughterhouses or "in a suitable dry clean form from India") or **hide and skin** (usually cattle hide, sometimes pigskin, from leather-trade trimmings) | **[F]** |
| Bone preparation | broken to "about an inch cube or a little smaller" (≈25 mm, conv.); inorganic matter, mainly calcium phosphate, "makes up about **two-thirds of the total weight of the bone**"; removed with dilute HCl at "about **15 °C**, for a few days". Organic residue = **ossein**, rich in **collagen** | **[Q]** |
| **Liming** | "a very long treatment, which may go **up to a hundred days**, with dilute lime … at room temperature". End product: fragments of **molecular weight of the order of 70,000** | **[Q]** |
| **Isoelectric point** | lime process → **pH 4.8–5**; acid process (much shorter) → **pH ≈ 8.5**. "**Gelatins normally used for photographic purposes are those of the lower isoelectric point and, therefore obtained by the lime treatment.**" | **[Q]** |
| **Extraction** | a series of hot-water extracts "commencing at **50–60 °C**" rising to boiling; extraction-water pH "generally around **6.5**" | **[Q]** |
| Extract quality | concentration "usually around **6 %**"; "each successive fraction is of higher viscosity. The very last extract will be of very poor quality gelatin with low physical strength in the gel, and rather similar to glue" | **[Q]** |
| **Evaporation and drying** | film evaporator under reduced pressure concentrates "up to **35 %**"; chilled drum → gelled sheets "a few millimetres thick"; tunnel-dried to a product "still containing about **15 % of moisture**" | **[Q]** |

**The manufacturer's hidden lever.** "there is **no doubt that individual gelatin manufacturers can control the properties of the gelatin by variation at this stage** [extraction pH, generally around 6.5], **but these remain industrial secrets**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.31 (PDF 35)]. **[F]**
