The surviving residues sum to 907.6 per 1,000, so the five OCR-lost entries (hydroxylysine, glutamic acid, methionine, isoleucine) account for ≈92 residues per 1,000 between them — a useful constraint if the table is ever reconstructed. **[E]**

The general formula printed with the table is `NH2 CH(R) CO2H`, with an R-group column giving each side chain: e.g. Lysine `NH2 CH2 CH2 CH2 CH2—`, Glycine `H—`, Alanine `CH3—`, Serine `HO CH2—`, Aspartic `HO CO—CH2—`, Glutamic `HO CO—CH2 CH2—`, Cysteine `HS CH2—` [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.33 (PDF 37)]. **[Q]** The table footnote survives: "Some authors refer to the disulphide, **cystine**, containing the `—CH2—S—S—CH2—` link in a double molecule. However, the conversion between these is very simple and it is difficult to say which is the truly naturally occurring substance" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.33 (PDF 37)]. **[F]**

Two stated interpretations: "The presence of **hydroxy proline is almost characteristic of collagen** and thus of the gelatin derived from it"; and, importantly for how much of gelatin chemistry was actually understood in 1966, "Although the constituent amino acids are known, **the way in which these units are joined together in space … is not known**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.33 (PDF 37)]. **[F]**

**Backbone chemistry as printed** [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.32 (PDF 36)]:
```
(1)  NH2 CHR CO2H                         (amino-acid residue; R = variable side chain)
(2)  —CO—NH—CH(R)—CO—NH—CH(R')—CO—NH—     (peptide chain)
(3)  Cn(H2O)m                             (carbohydrate general formula, "m and n … commonly equal")
```
**[Q]**

**The single most consequential number in Table 2.1 is the cysteine content, < 0.1 residues per 1,000** — because cysteine is the precursor of the natural sulphur sensitizer (§7.5). At <0.1 per 1,000 residues and a fragment molecular weight of ~70,000 (≈700 residues), that is **fewer than 0.07 cysteine residues per gelatin molecule on average**, i.e. most molecules contain none. The natural sensitizer therefore derives from a trace constituent, which is exactly why its concentration is so variable and so hard to control. That inference is ours. **[E]**

**Isoionic vs isoelectric point — both defined, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.35 (PDF 39)]:
- **Isoionic point:** "the pH value of a solution of gelatin possessing no other non-colloidal ion than hydrogen or hydroxyl, in other words the pH of a solution of pure gelatin. It will be noted that **no reference is made to the charged state** of the gelatin." **[F]**
- **Isoelectric point:** "the pH value of a gelatin solution when, under the influence of an electric field, the gelatin molecule **moves towards neither** the positive nor the negative electrode, in other words **its total charge is nil**." **[F]**

**Gelling — the hydrogen-bonding mechanism, 1966.** Hydrogen bonds form between C=O groups and H atoms "in another chain or another part of the same chain", and are "particularly strong when the hydrogen atom is associated either with the **free amino group of lysine** or with the **guanidino groups of arginine**". Both intramolecular (helical) and intermolecular bonding exist simultaneously and "are responsible for the gelling". "In dilute solution above the gelling temperature these coils are perfectly random … but when setting occurs a **regular helical arrangement** is set up" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.36, 41 (PDF 40, 45), Fig. 2.2]. **[M]**

Two confirming chemical experiments are recorded, attributed to Janus: hypobromite destruction of the guanidino groups gives a **non-gelling** gelatin, and O-methylisourea conversion of the lysine amino groups **into** guanidino groups gives "higher rigidity and much higher setting rate" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.157–158 (PDF 163–164)]. **[Q]** So arginine's guanidino group is simultaneously the habit-control group (§7.2) and the gelling group. **[E]**

**Cross-linking / hardening, 1966.** Hardening of the coated layer is either by inorganic salts (**chromium**, reacting with **carboxyl** groups) or by an organic bifunctional reagent (**formaldehyde**, reacting with **free amino** groups, "in particular the terminal amino group of lysine"). "It is clear that the **relative action of a given gelatin to hardening depends upon the balance between free amino and free carboxyl groups** which … will be related to the **isoelectric point** of the gelatin" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.36 (PDF 40)]. **[M]** The quantitative hardening data are in §6.10.

**Chemical modification of the gelatin itself, 1966.** Acylation of free amino groups (most probably the ε-amino of lysine) with an acid chloride or anhydride → `RCONH—`; also aryl sulphonyl chloride → `ArSO2NH—`; or condensation with an active double bond (acrylic acid) → `HOCOCH2—CH2—NH—`. "generally speaking, this is **not influenced by the preparation** as is the presence of sensitizers and restrainers. It is related to the number and reactivity of the free amino groups" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.39–40 (PDF 43–44)]. **[F]** The phthalated variant is used for coagulation washing (§6.8). **[F]**

### 7.5 Natural sulphur sensitizers, and the concentrations involved

This is where gelatin stops being an inert binder. The two eras name **different substances**, and the change of identification is itself a documented event.

**1929 — allyl thiocarbamide, "Gelatine X".**

> **Allyl isothiocyanate / allyl thiocarbamide ("Gelatine X")** — Sheppard/Punnett. Concentration **1 : 1,000,000 to 1 : 300,000**. This is *the* stated cause of high sensitivity in "active" gelatine. The silver complex is written `(AgBr)ₘ·(CS·NHR·NH₂)ₙ` with m, n "probably 2 and 1"; in alkali it splits to **silver sulphide** + cyanamide + guanidine + alkaline bromide — the Ag₂S nuclei being the sensitivity centres, but they "**must form nuclei discretely and not above a certain size**". And the dose–response: "**The action reaches a maximum effect for a certain quantity and then decreases as the amount of the active material is increased, with corresponding increase in fog.**"
> [Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.25–27 (PDF 33–35)] **[Q]**

Converted to parts per million (conv.): **1 : 1,000,000 = 1 ppm; 1 : 300,000 = 3.3 ppm**. **[E]**

Other 1929 sulphur/selenium/tellurium sensitizers, "of the same order" (i.e. 1–3.3 ppm implied): **sodium thiosulphate (hypo)**, **Na₂SeSO₃**, **K₂Te₂O₃**, **potassium isoselenocyanate** — "all these combine with the silver halides to form decomposable complexes" [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.26 (PDF 34)]. **[F]** Note that Wall lists sodium thiosulphate as *one of several* candidates; he does not identify it as the actual natural sensitizer of commercial gelatine. **[F]**

Wall also records the industrial screening effort and a set of non-sulphur sensitizers: the Lumière list of **900 substances screened**, of which "aesculin, codeine, thebaine, diethylenediamine, thiocarbamide, guanidine sulphocyanate" were said to be usable, used commercially but unpublished [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.27 (PDF 35)] **[F]**; and the historic organics — Newton's tea plus mustard-seed infusion giving increased sensitiveness over tea alone, and codeine and narcotine "well known as sensitizers for washed collodion emulsion" — with the pointed observation that these **contain no sulphur** [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.27 (PDF 35)]. **[F]** A dose for one of them: narcotine at **0.5 g per ~1 L** of collodion emulsion [Wall 1929, Ch. VI, p.114 (PDF 121)]. **[Q]**

**1966 — thiosulphate, and the retraction of the thiourea identification.**

> "the presence of small quantities of sulphur-containing substances, **usually 10–200 parts per million of thiosulphate**, which have a marked influence on the sensitivity of the emulsion. These are most likely to be produced during the liming processes by degradation of the sulphur-containing amino acid, **cysteine**. This, after oxidizing to the disulphide, **cystine**, will break down to give **polysulphides** which are then oxidized eventually to **thiosulphate**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.36 (PDF 40)] **[Q]**

And explicitly as a change of view: "the belief in allylthiourea gave way — **More recently, it has been made clear** that … the sensitizing substance of normal commercial gelatins is **sodium thiosulphate**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 91)]. **[F]**

**The two sources disagree on the identity of the natural sensitizer, and the disagreement is dated.** Wall 1929 states it is allyl thiocarbamide at 1–3.3 ppm (Sheppard/Punnett). Duffin 1966 states it is sodium thiosulphate at 10–200 ppm, arising from cysteine degradation during liming, and records that the thiourea identification was superseded. Both are printed as the settled view of their time; do not average the concentrations, which are for different substances and differ by roughly a factor of 30–60 in any case. **[F]**

**The independent 1966 figure for total active sulphur**, which is the number to use for stock-to-stock variation: "**The active sulphur quantity present in gelatin varies from 1 to 2 parts per million for the inert types to 100 parts per million for active gelatins**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)]. **[Q]**

Collected concentration figures, all eras:

| Quantity | Value | Era | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Allyl thiocarbamide in "active" gelatine | **1 : 1,000,000 to 1 : 300,000** (= 1–3.3 ppm, conv.) | 1929 | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.25–27 (PDF 33–35)] | **[Q]** |
| Thiosulphate in gelatin | **10–200 ppm** | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.36 (PDF 40)] | **[Q]** |
| Active sulphur, inert gelatins | **1–2 ppm** | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)] | **[Q]** |
| Active sulphur, active gelatins | **100 ppm** | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)] | **[Q]** |
| Added thiosulphate for a Tri-X-class emulsion (Bekunov) | **25–150 ppm in the gelatin** | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)] | **[Q]** |
| Threshold for "inert" (both sensitizer and restrainer) | **< 5 ppm** | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.44–45 (PDF 48–49)] | **[Q]** |

Note the internal consistency of the 1966 figures (ours): if an active gelatin carries 100 ppm of active sulphur and a maker wants the Bekunov dose of 25–150 ppm, then an *active* gelatin already supplies most or all of the required sensitizer — which is exactly why 1929 and pre-1960 practice let the gelatin do the sensitizing, and why an inert gelatin at 1–2 ppm requires a weighed addition. **The whole shift from "gelatin-controlled" to "chemist-controlled" digestion follows arithmetically from these two numbers.** **[E]**

**How a maker deliberately tunes the natural sensitizer level** — the process levers, 1966 [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.36 (PDF 40)]:

| Objective | Lever | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimise** sensitizer | "vigorous washing and acid deliming after the liming treatment; **nitric acid is particularly suitable** for the removal of these substances" | **[F]** |
| **Maximise** sensitizer | "only a few changes of lime during the liming period together with the minimum of washing during the subsequent purification" | **[F]** |
| **Synthesise** it | treating the gelatin liquor with **sulphur dioxide** forms thiosulphates, giving "a gelatin … very similar to the natural sensitized product" | **[F]** |
| Source dependence | "**Hide gelatins usually contain more sensitizer than those from ossein**; this is derived mainly from the treatment used to remove the hair from the skins" | **[F]** |

**Bromine acceptors — a third gelatin function, 1966.** "three amino acids have been considered as possible acceptors in gelatin. These are **tyrosine, histidine and methionine** … all of which possess groups able to react with bromine; **by substitution** as do the first two acids, or **indirectly by being easily oxidized** as occurs with methionine" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.37 (PDF 41)]. **[M]** From Table 2.1, tyrosine is 4.6 and histidine 4.8 residues per 1,000, with methionine OCR-lost — so the acceptor capacity rests on ~1 % of the residues. **[E]** No source in this set quantifies the acceptor capacity or relates it to a photographic effect. **[F]**

### 7.6 Restrainers

**1966 identifies them as nucleic-acid breakdown products, assayed as adenine, and gives two sets of concentrations.**

> "the **breakdown products of the nucleic acids** are most likely to be present in gelatin and that these are, if not identical with the restrainers, very important components of them. It has been demonstrated that **gelatins from hide contain substantial amounts (10–220 parts per million) of these products, as determined by adenine content, but ossein gelatins show a much lower content**. **Gordon and Swann** were able to show a **direct relationship between the adenine content of a gelatin and its restraining action on the rate of digestion**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.37 (PDF 41)] **[Q]**

Restated with tighter numbers in the sensitization chapter: "gelatins from hide contained an average of **30–50 parts per million, sometimes even 200 p.p.m.** of **adenine** … but gelatins from ossein were found to contain only **4–6 p.p.m. of adenine**" (guanine is also present) [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.96 (PDF 102)]. **[Q]**

| Gelatin source | Adenine content | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hide, as a range | **10–220 ppm** | [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.37 (PDF 41)] | **[Q]** |
| Hide, as an average | **30–50 ppm**, "sometimes even 200 ppm" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.96 (PDF 102)] | **[Q]** |
| Ossein | **4–6 ppm** | [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.96 (PDF 102)] | **[Q]** |

The hide:ossein ratio is therefore roughly **7:1 to 50:1** in restrainer content (ours) — and hide gelatins simultaneously carry *more* sulphur sensitizer (§7.5). Hide gelatin is thus high in both accelerator and restrainer, ossein low in both, which is why ossein is the base for inert gelatin (§7.8). **[E]**

**Process levers for restrainer level, 1966:** low restrainer ← frequent lime changes during a prolonged treatment plus thorough washing and deliming; maximum restrainer ← short liming with few changes, and it "may further be maintained by prolonging the preliminary acid treatment" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.37 (PDF 41)]. **[F]**

**The restrainer/growth controversy — explicitly unsettled in 1966, with a hard number that separates two effects:**

> "**The whole position of growth retarders is a confused one.** Wood has postulated that the small quantities of restrainers in the quantities of gelatin used for commercial emulsions do not affect the crystal growth. He points out that while **100 parts per million of adenine … affects sensitization, 10,000 parts per million have no influence on the crystal growth**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.37–38 (PDF 41–42)] **[Q]**

That is a **100× separation between the concentration at which adenine restrains sensitization and the concentration at which it would restrain crystal growth** — i.e. within the commercial range the restrainers act on *digestion*, not on *physical ripening*. **[E]** Duffin's caution on the whole literature: "much of the evidence produced is scanty and not generally applicable, for example, work on fine-grain emulsions under conditions very different from those existing in commercial emulsions" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.38 (PDF 42)]. **[F]**

**A competing school, recorded as such.** **Steigmann** attaches "great significance to sulphur-containing amino acids, **cysteine, methionine and histidine**"; cysteine "is said to be a **powerful crystal-growth restrainer**" and reacts with gelatin aldehydes to give **thiazolidines** "which are themselves very powerful restrainers" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.38 (PDF 42)]. **[F]** **This directly contradicts Wood's position** that the gelatin's restrainers do not affect crystal growth at commercial concentrations. Both views are printed side by side and Duffin does not adjudicate. **[F]**

**"Gradation bodies" — a documented contrast/desensitisation link, 1966:**

> "there seems little doubt from a survey of the literature that the **nucleic-acid or sulphur-containing amino-acid constituents greatly affect the behaviour of fine-grain emulsions used for positives**. Reference is made to their **effect on contrast and their desensitizing action**; **Steigmann uses the term 'gradation bodies'**. However, no positive chemical identification has been made although they are most likely to be **thiazolidines**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.38 (PDF 42)] **[M]**

This is the only place in the source set where a gelatin constituent is tied directly to *contrast* rather than to speed or fog. It is asserted without numbers. **[F]**

**How restrainers act during digestion** — see §6.9: adenine controls the *manner* in which the silver sulphide is laid down, possibly locating it in the adsorbed gelatin layer rather than on the grain surface, while silver-sulphide formation continues unabated [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.96–97 (PDF 102–103)]. **[M]**

**Wall 1929 has no restrainer concept in the gelatin.** His restrainers are deliberate additions to the finished emulsion — soluble bromide at 0.1–3 parts per 1000, hydrobromic acid at 0.005 %, etc. (§6.10) [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, pp.154–155 (PDF 161–162)]. **[Q]** What Wall attributes to the gelatine is the *sensitizer* (Gelatine X) and the *impurities* (§7.7), not a restrainer. **[F]** So the discovery that gelatin carries its own restrainers, and that they are nucleic-acid derivatives, belongs to the period between 1929 and 1966. **[E]**

### 7.7 Batch variability and impurity limits

**Wall 1929's impurity specification** — the earliest quantitative gelatine spec in the set, and it is a fog spec:

| Impurity | Limit | Purpose | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ash | **≤ 2 %** | fog/speed control | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.25 (PDF 33)] | **[Q]** |
| Metallic salts (Fe, Cu, Pb, Zn) | **≤ 50 ppm** | fog/speed control | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.25 (PDF 33)] | **[Q]** |
| Aluminium | **> 0.106 %** indicates alum-hardening (i.e. a disqualifying marker, not a limit) | detection of adulteration | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.25 (PDF 33)] | **[Q]** |
| Sulphur as SO₂ | **≤ 0.1 %** | fog/speed control | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.25 (PDF 33)] | **[Q]** |

Note the scale mismatch (ours): Wall's sulphur-as-SO₂ limit of 0.1 % is **1,000 ppm**, three orders of magnitude above the 1–3.3 ppm of active allyl thiocarbamide he identifies as the sensitizer, and ten times Duffin's 100 ppm for an "active" gelatin's total active sulphur. Wall's SO₂ figure is therefore a *total* sulphur measure, not a measure of photographically active sulphur; the two must not be compared directly. **[E]**

**Related 1929 raw-material limits**, because gelatine was not the only variable impurity source:

| Material | Test / limit | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ammonia | test 3.5 ccm NH₃ into 20 ccm HNO₃, evaporate; the residue must be colourless. Pyridine/pyrrole/aniline are "almost certain to cause fog" | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.12 (PDF 20)] | **[Q]** |
| Silver nitrate | silver nitrite in the AgNO₃ "not only causes fog, but also reduction in speed" | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.12 (PDF 20)] | **[F]** |
| Ammonium bromide | dissociation "at 30 °C (86 °F) noticeable"; **0.4 g HBr from 100 g NH₄Br per half-hour boiling**; KBr does not dissociate — the reason NH₄Br is preferred for the acid/boiling process | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.10 (PDF 18)] | **[Q]** |

**The 1966 statement of the problem — "an almost magical quality":**

> "For many years the chemical principles underlying the behaviour of photographic gelatins were **very ill understood**. Indeed, even some fairly recent text books consider that there is an **almost magical quality in the 'nature of the gelatin'** in advocating the view that **only gelatins from certain manufacturers will function in certain types of emulsion formulae**."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.29 (PDF 33)] **[F]**

And the admission that the problem was not solved even in 1966: "For many years the likely behaviour of a particular gelatin in a particular emulsion formula could not have been predicted at all and **even today this cannot be undertaken with confidence** since an understanding of the problems is still incomplete" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.42 (PDF 46)]. **[F]**

**Why gelatin was the dominant source of stock-to-stock variation — the causal chain, assembled from the source's own statements:**

1. The active sensitizer content varies **1–2 ppm (inert) to 100 ppm (active)**, a **50–100× range** [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.94 (PDF 100)]. **[Q]**
2. The restrainer content varies **4–6 ppm (ossein) to 220 ppm (hide)**, a **~40× range** [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.37 (PDF 41); Ch. V, p.96 (PDF 102)]. **[Q]**
3. Speed and fog during digestion are *both* driven by the same process, so the sensitizer/restrainer balance sets where the batch lands on the speed-vs-fog race [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89), Fig. 5.1]. **[Q]**
4. "in the presence of the **same quantity of sensitizing substance** … **the same emulsion will digest at quite different rates with different gelatins**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.96–97 (PDF 102–103)]. **[F]**
5. And the interaction is not merely additive: "**Since the rate of digestion is controlled by the content of both restrainer and sensitizer, it is likely that the use of very small quantities of sensitizer would result in the onset of fog before useful sensitivity is obtained. This may well be the controlling factor.**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.97 (PDF 103)]. **[M]**

The composition of the chain: a 50–100× swing in sensitizer against a 40× swing in restrainer, both uncontrolled and both acting on the same speed/fog race, is a complete explanation of why a recipe that worked on one gelatin delivery failed on the next. **[E]**

**A third, less-discussed variable constituent — the carbohydrates and aldehydes, with a very wide concentration range** [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.38–39 (PDF 42–43)]:

| Item | Value / statement | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| True carbohydrates in collagen | **glucose and galactose**. "These materials are **inert photographically in the quantities present** in gelatin, but in the isolation of the gelatin they are further degraded to simpler materials … **three-carbon fragments** are the most likely products" | **[F]** |
| Identified degradation products | **reductone, methyl glyoxal, dihydroxyacetone, pyruvic acid** (Landucci *et al.*). Bound to terminal amino groups, possibly via proline/hydroxyproline; "the **amino acid–aldehyde link is a weak one and the first to break** in the degradation of gelatin" | **[F]** |
| Assay | reaction with **thiobarbituric acid** in acetic acid gives coloured products "which possess a number of absorption maxima, notably at about **4,500 and 5,300 Å**" (450 and 530 nm, conv.) | **[Q]** |
| **Concentration range** | "By standardisation with known substances, the aldehyde content can be determined and **may be between 300 and 15,000 p.p.m.**" | **[Q]** |
| Speculative image link | "these substances, most of which are aldehydes … are therefore **quite strong reducing substances** … it is very likely that the **formation of fog and sensitivity are connected with the presence of silver atoms on the crystal surface**. Of all the substances present as minor constituents in photographic gelatins, the **aldehyde-like sugar-derived compounds appear to be the most likely to behave in this manner**" | **[S]** |
| Honest limitation | "Our present-day understanding of the presence and action of these carbohydrates is **not sufficient for any detailed discussion of the effect of processing changes** on the proportion present in the final gelatin" | **[F]** |

The aldehyde content — **300–15,000 ppm**, a **50× range** — is one to two orders of magnitude *larger* than either the sensitizer or the restrainer content, and Duffin himself flags it as the most likely reduction-sensitizing constituent, while conceding it is unquantified in effect. **This is the largest uncontrolled compositional variable in a 1966 photographic gelatin, and its photographic consequence was unknown.** **[E]** Duffin's own labelling of the aldehyde–fog link as "very likely" rather than demonstrated is why we tag it speculative. **[S]**

**The Ammann(-Brass) test — the industry's gelatin classifier, 1966** [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.42–43 (PDF 46–47), Figs. 2.3–2.6]:

- Method: "A **silver-chloride emulsion** is prepared using **cadmium chloride** as the source of halide and emulsifying in the presence of **different quantities of the gelatin** … At a fixed temperature, the **rise of turbidity** is measured over a range of times and **turbidity is then plotted against gelatin concentration, with a curve for each time**. The experimental details are **very critical**." **[M]**
- Diagnostic curve shapes: **high sensitizer → curves rising with increasing gelatin concentration (Fig. 2.3)**; **high restrainer → curves falling (Fig. 2.4)**; most gelatins are mixed (Fig. 2.5); **an inert gelatin gives a series of parallel lines (Fig. 2.6)**. **[F]**
- Duffin's criticism, recorded because it matters for how much weight the test can bear: "it is a **long step from the nucleation and growth of these particular chloride emulsions to the digestion behaviour of commercial iodobromide emulsions** and there seem to be **no convincing theoretical arguments to justify such an extrapolation**. Also the intervention of other agents, apart from sensitizers and restrainers, such as reducing substances, is ignored. Nevertheless the general relation established by the Ammann test does seem to hold." **[F]**

**Wall's 1929 equivalent of the Ammann test does not exist.** His gelatine assessment is entirely by physical constants (§7.9) plus the chemical impurity limits above; there is no photographic-response classifier in the book. **[F]** His in-process proxy is the **dip test** on the emulsion itself (§5.3), not a test on the gelatine. **[F]**

### 7.8 "Inert gelatin", and when the variability was brought under control

**The definition, its author, and its date:**

> "This definition for an inert gelatin was **first proposed by Kelly at the Liège Conference in 1959** and has been widely accepted." … "On present-day knowledge, **less than five parts per million of both sulphur sensitizer and nucleic-acid type restrainer would render a gelatin inert**." … "Photographically therefore, an inert gelatin is one which **does not confer additional photographic sensitivity on digesting an emulsion on its own but gives the maximum response in the presence of added sensitizer**." … "**Modern practice tends far more to the use of inert gelatins and these are obtained most readily from ossein. Hide gelatin … normally contains considerable quantities of both sulphur-sensitizers and restraining substances and these are difficult to remove to give an inert product.**"
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.44–45 (PDF 48–49)] **[Q]**

Two caveats printed with the definition, both of which limit it: the definition "requires a **lower limit in the detection** of such impurities. It is not possible to say that none of a certain impurity is present, merely that its concentration is below a certain value"; and "as more and more is understood … no doubt **other compounds will be added to the list of impurities**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.44–45 (PDF 48–49)]. **[F]**

**The answer to "when was it brought under control", assembled from the dated statements in the set:**

| Date | Event | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1929 | Gelatine's sensitizing action attributed to allyl thiocarbamide at 1–3.3 ppm (Sheppard/Punnett); the *practical* control is to buy gelatine by physical constants and impurity limits and to test each batch's emulsion by H&D sensitometry. Batch behaviour is not predictable | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.7–9, 25–27 (PDF 15–17, 33–35)] | **[F]** |
| **1959** | **Kelly proposes the "inert gelatin" definition at the Liège Conference** — the threshold being < 5 ppm of both sulphur sensitizer and nucleic-acid restrainer | [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.44–45 (PDF 48–49)] | **[Q]** |
| "Only a few years ago" (relative to 1965/66) | Digestion behaviour "was always **entirely controlled by the nature of the gelatin**"; gelatins were classed *fast/active* or *slow/inert* by how they digested | [Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)] | **[F]** |
| By 1966 | "**It is now more usual to add known amounts of these sensitizers … before the digestion stage in order to permit control of the process**"; "**It is normal practice today to use a gelatin which is substantially free from this kind of additive and then to introduce it in the desired quantity**"; "**Modern practice tends far more to the use of inert gelatins**"; "the tremendous emphasis, in the past on the nature of the gelatin **is slowly giving way**" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.44–45 (PDF 48–49); Ch. IV, p.65 (PDF 69); Ch. V, pp.84–85 (PDF 90–91)] | **[F]** |
| 1966, residual uncertainty | "even today this cannot be undertaken with confidence since an understanding of the problems is still incomplete"; and the aldehyde constituent (300–15,000 ppm) remains unquantified in effect | [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.38–39, 42 (PDF 42–43, 46)] | **[F]** |
| 1995 | Gelatin variability **is not discussed at all** in the range examined. Gelatin appears only as "a protective colloid", with synthetic polymers noted as alternatives, and as the ε₁ dielectric constant in the emulsion dielectric-loss analysis | [Tani 1995, §2.2, p.41 (PDF 50); §3.2, p.51 (PDF 60), Eqs. (3.3)–(3.4)] | **[F]** |

**The engineering reading of that sequence.** Gelatin variability was brought under control in two moves, not one. The first was **substitution of an inert base** — ossein-derived gelatin purified below 5 ppm of both active constituents, defined in 1959 and standard practice by the mid-1960s. The second was **transfer of the sensitizing function from the gelatin to a weighed addition** — dosing thiosulphate and gold deliberately before digestion, also standard by the mid-1960s. Together these convert the gelatin from an active reagent with a 40–100× compositional swing into a nominally passive binder. The residual uncertainty Duffin flags in 1966 is the aldehyde/carbohydrate fraction, whose 300–15,000 ppm range was still uncontrolled and whose effect was still unknown. That Tani 1995 does not discuss gelatin variability at all is the strongest available indication that by 1995 it was no longer a live engineering problem — but its absence is not a positive statement, and no source in this set says when or how the aldehyde question was settled. **[E]**

### 7.9 Setting point, melting point, viscosity, gel strength

**Wall 1929's gelatine test constants** — the properties an emulsion maker actually bought against:

| Property | Value and method | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Melting point of a gel** | "varies from about **24 °C (75 °F)** upwards"; the Child Bayley apparatus is repeatable to **0.5 %**; the Gamble capillary method is readable to **0.3 °C** | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.17–19 (PDF 25–27)] | **[Q]** |
| **Melting vs setting point** | melting is "**from eight to ten degrees higher** than the setting point" | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.20 (PDF 28)] | **[Q]** |
| **Water absorption** | good gelatine absorbs **5–10 × its own weight**; test 5 g in 100 ccm distilled water, 12 h in an ice room | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.20 (PDF 28)] | **[Q]** |
| **Jelly strength** (Lipowitz / Valenta) | good hard emulsion gelatine: breaking strain **1500 g**; 50 ccm jelly, 12–24 h at room temperature then to **15 °C (59 °F)**; disc 16 mm diameter, 5 mm deep; mercury sp. gr. **13.56** | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.21–23 (PDF 29–31)] | **[Q]** |
| **Classes** | **hard / medium / soft**, differentiated by setting point, melting point and water absorption | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.14 (PDF 22)] | **[F]** |
| **Degradation during processing** | small: setting point falls **≈2 °C** after 1–2 h boiling with a little acid; **3 °C** after 5 h ammonia digestion at 50 °C | [Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.32 (PDF 40)] | **[Q]** |

The melting-point-minus-setting-point gap of 8–10 °C is the physical basis of the whole coat-then-chill process: the emulsion can be held liquid at 33–40 °C (§3.3.3) and set by chilling to 10–15 °C, with hysteresis preventing it from re-melting on the drying run. **[E]**

**Wall's specification for the baryta-layer gelatine** shows how tightly these constants were held in practice: hard and medium gelatine mixed 2:1, 1:1 or 1:2 by season (harder in summer); a 10 % solution "must not melt below **32°–34 °C (90°–93 °F)**"; setting point "not below **22°–26 °C (72°–79 °F)**"; and "mix 2–3 gelatine batches for regularity" [Wall 1929, App., p.249 (PDF 256)]. **[Q]** The instruction to blend batches deliberately, to average out variability, is itself the 1929 answer to the batch-variation problem. **[E]**

**Duffin 1966 on viscosity and gel strength** [Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.40 (PDF 44), Fig. 2.1]:

- "**The amount of emulsion 'taken-up' by the base from the coating trough or similar device is controlled by the viscosity of the gelatin.**" — the direct coating-weight link (§3.3.3). **[M]**
- Longer alkaline treatment → higher viscosity; low-pH extraction → lower viscosity; extensive degradation → low-molecular-weight fragments → lower viscosity, which "must be avoided". **[M]**
- "The viscosity of a gelatin solution is **highly dependent on pH and is at a minimum at the isoelectric point, increasing either side** of this value" (Fig. 2.1: y-axis "Viscosity in Centipoises", x-axis "pH" with ticks at ≈2, 5, 8, 10, 12; annotation "**Gelatin—Isoelectric Point pH 4.8**"). **[Q]**
- Gel strength: "It is very important that, in the coating process, the gelatino-silver halide layer shall **set to a strong gel very shortly after it has moved away from the coating position**. The extent to which this occurs will influence its **susceptibility for physical distortion in the machine during drying** and its ultimate strength in the final layer." The manufacturer "must prevent degradation … because this can reduce the jelly strength." **[M]**
- The resulting constraint on gelatin selection: "moderate viscosity but … high jelly strength" (§3.3.3) [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.154–155 (PDF 160–161)]. **[F]**

Note that Duffin's Fig. 2.1 isoelectric point of pH 4.8 matches his own stated lime-process isoelectric range of 4.8–5 (§7.4), confirming that photographic gelatin is lime-processed. **[E]** Note also that the emulsion coating pH is ≈6.0 [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.158–159 (PDF 164–165)] **[Q]** — i.e. **above** the isoelectric point, so the gelatin carries a net negative charge in the coating and the viscosity sits on the rising limb of Fig. 2.1. Both facts are printed; the inference that this places coating on the rising limb is ours. **[E]**

**Drying and molecular order, 1966:** "Generally speaking the more slowly drying is carried out, the more orderly will be the array of the gelatin molecules… maximum order is obtained by **drying at room temperature**; this is economically impossible and may not be desirable anyway" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.157–158 (PDF 163–164)]. **[F]**

**Setting temperatures in practice, both eras:**

| Item | Value | Era | Citation | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand plate coating temperature | "convenient temperature… about **35 °C (95 °F)**" | 1929 | [Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.164 (PDF 171)] | **[Q]** |
| Roll-film coating temperature | "the emulsion is usually at a coating temperature of **33 °C (92 °F)**" | 1929 | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.190 (PDF 197)] | **[Q]** |
| Hot-water box under the film trough | held "two to three degrees higher than that of the emulsion"; thermometer range needed **27°–40 °C (81°–104 °F, conv.)** | 1929 | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.196 (PDF 203)] | **[Q]** |
| Paper (gold P.O.P.) coating | **37° to 40 °C (99° to 104 °F)** | 1929 | [Wall 1929, App., p.241 (PDF 248)] | **[Q]** |
| Baryta coating | melt **45–50 °C (113–122 °F)** "to give the correct coating temperature of about **41 °C (105 °F)**"; coating speed **28 m/min** | 1929 | [Wall 1929, App., p.251 (PDF 258)] | **[Q]** |
| Experimental setting box | iron top **1/16 in (1.6 mm, conv.)**, **3 in deep (76 mm, conv.)**, filled with cracked ice and cold water; "kept cold enough for any number of coatings" | 1929 | [Wall 1929, Ch. X, pp.165–166 (PDF 172–173)] | **[Q]** |
| Support-contact temperature, trough coating | **36–40 °C**, "above the setting point of the gelatin but… sufficiently near to it to permit ready setting" | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.153–154 (PDF 159–160)] | **[Q]** |
| Chill-set temperature | **about 10–15 °C** | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.156–157 (PDF 162–163)] | **[Q]** |
| Store-melt of washed emulsion | "not more than **40 °C (104 °F)**" for an hour, to release occluded air | 1929 | [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.150 (PDF 157)] | **[Q]** |
| Emulsion storage before coating | "**below 5 °C**"; stable finished emulsion keeps "several months", undigested material "only a few days" | 1966 | [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.81 (PDF 87)] | **[Q]** |

The two eras' coating temperatures agree closely — 33–40 °C in 1929 and 36–40 °C in 1966 — which is expected, since both are set by the same gelatin melting/setting hysteresis. **[E]**

**Wall's chilling-length argument** is worth preserving because it converts the setting kinetics into a machine dimension: the film-machine "run" from trough exit to first turn "should not be less than **thirty-six inches**" (914 mm, conv.), depending on gelatine content, emulsion temperature and room temperature; the chilling/setting surface runs "from **ten to twelve feet** or longer if desired" (3.0–3.7 m, conv.); and a 3 ft drum coater gives only "two and one-third feet" (0.71 m) of chilling surface, "very close to the danger line", with a maximum usable arc of "about 67°" ≈ 3½ ft (1.07 m) [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.189–192 (PDF 196–199)]. **[Q]** The stated reason: "mere setting or gelling… is not the only desideratum. It must be thoroughly chilled, and the colder it is when it leaves the setting surface, the less chance for it to subsequently melt and run" [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.191–192 (PDF 198–199)]. **[M]**

### 7.10 Gelatin against the dye and against the developer

Two further gelatin behaviours are quantified in the set and belong here because they are both competitions for the grain surface.

**Gelatin is displaced by sensitizing dye, 1966:**

> "In the absence of gelatin, the adsorption of the dye is very fast indeed but … although an adsorbed gelatin layer may **retard** dye adsorption, the dye is **more powerfully held**. Measurements, by direct analysis of nitrogen content, of the amount of gelatin remaining on dyed emulsions, have shown clearly that **gelatin is readily displaced from the grains. At sufficiently high dye concentrations, higher than those used commercially, the gelatin may be completely removed.** The heat of adsorption of a dye is higher with emulsions of low gelatin content. This suggests that the measured heat of adsorption, **around 7,000 calories per gram-mole in the case of an emulsion with 7 % gelatin**, is the difference between that of the dye and that of the gelatin."
> [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.115 (PDF 121)] **[Q]**

7,000 cal/g-mole = **0.30 eV per molecule** (conv.), and it is a *difference* of two adsorption energies, not the dye's own [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.115 (PDF 121)]. **[E]** Dye coverage at the top of commercial loading is "about half the surface of the grains", an average dye molecule occupying **50–100 Å²** [Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.114 (PDF 120)]. **[Q]** So at commercial dye loadings roughly half the gelatin shell is displaced — which bears directly on the "gelatin as protective colloid" story, since the protection is only partial on a fully dyed grain. **[E]**

**Gelatin's shell impedes the developer, 1966.** The adsorbed shell is 20–60 Å thick (§3.5) [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.66 (PDF 70)] **[Q]**, and excessive hardening of the layer "will interfere with developer penetration" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.160–161 (PDF 166–167)]. **[F]** Glyoxal's different cross-link geometry "changes the balance of properties, for example, hardness, toughness … and factors such as **developer penetrability** and **the influence of the hardened gelatin on the developed state of the image and thus its covering power**" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.160–161 (PDF 166–167)]. **[F]**

**Wall 1929's counterparts** are the "doctors" — additions made to the finished emulsion to control its behaviour at the coating machine, all of which act on or through the gelatine [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, pp.151–157 (PDF 158–164)]:

| Addition | Quantity | Stated effect | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alcohol (methyl / "Columbian spirits", or acetone; ethyl being dutiable) | **~8 %** of the emulsion | flow; anti-coarse-grain at the mix | **[Q]** |
| Chrome alum ("blue doctor", basic) | 1 part chrome alum, or 10 parts of the basic solution, per **250–300 parts dry gelatine** | hardening; prevents frilling | **[Q]** |
| Tannin (Wratten) | **1 : 286 of gelatine** | hardening; excess gives a yellow stain | **[Q]** |
| Quillaia / saponin ("brown doctor") | 75 : 1000; or 1 : 1000; or 125 : 1000; saponin as a 13 % solution at 7.5 : 1000 | coating flow; prevents "comets" | **[Q]** |
| Phenol / thymol | 5 parts per 1000 / 0.25 parts | antiseptic; "It is an open question whether they are of any practical value, as probably they are entirely lost in the drying process" | **[Q]** |
| Alcohol seal (0.5 % phenol, ½–¾ in deep) over stored set emulsion | — | seals the surface, checks bacteria; rapid emulsions kept a month (Homolka) | **[Q]** |
| Glycerine for suppleness | — | "a dangerous trick, as glycerine is hygroscopic and may eventually cause trouble"; prefer golden syrup at **6.5 ccm/litre**, "but it is better to avoid even this" | **[Q]** |
| Matting powder | rice starch (finest grain) 25 parts + gelatine 25 parts in 250 water, added to 1000 emulsion | matt surface for retouching; particles must be fine and uniform. Precipitated BaSO₄ "gives a finer matt surface to the film, but when dry is **too translucent**" | **[Q]** |

The 1966 equivalents are the wetting agents — "**20 mg–1.0 g of pure wetting agent per 100 g of gelatin**", in classes anionic (sodium laurylsulphate), non-ionic (dodecylphenol polyethylene oxide ether, **n = 5 to 10**) and cationic (hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide), with **saponin** still "a natural non-ionic still widely used, while at one time it was almost the only known product for this purpose" [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.163–164 (PDF 169–170)]. **[Q]** Saponin therefore appears in both books, 37 years apart, doing the same job — the single longest-lived addendum in the source set. **[E]** Anti-foaming agents, 1966: aliphatic alcohols of intermediate chain length, **amyl (C₅) and nonyl (C₉)** (raw OCR "amyl (C,) and nonyl (C,)" — the subscripts are lost but recoverable from the names), plus glycerol monolaurate [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.164 (PDF 170)]. **[Q]** Wall's antifoam for the baryta coat was **fresh milk, 100 ccm, boiled three times** [Wall 1929, App., pp.249–251 (PDF 256–258)]. **[Q]**

**Wall's hardener prohibition, which contradicts 1966 practice head-on.** Wall: "**Under no circumstances should formaldehyde be used as a hardener**" — it "inevitably… leads eventually to **fog on keeping**" [Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.152 (PDF 159)]. **[F]** Duffin 1966 uses formaldehyde as a standard hardener at **1–3 g per 100 g of gelatin**, while conceding the same fault: formaldehyde "probably because of its strong reducing action, is very prone to produce **fog during storage**", and its volatility can contaminate other materials [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.159–161 (PDF 165–167)]. **[Q]** **The two sources agree on the defect and disagree on whether it is tolerable.** By 1966 the fault was managed rather than avoided — with alternatives available (glyoxal, glutaraldehyde, mucochloric acid, bis-hydroxymethylurea) and hardening accelerators (resorcinol, resorcylaldehyde, 4-chloroacetyl catechol) at **0.1–1.0 g per 100 g gelatin** [Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.159–162 (PDF 165–168)]. **[Q]**

### 7.11 What no source in this set gives, on gelatin

- **Any gelatin data after 1966.** Tani 1995 treats gelatin only as "a protective colloid" and as a dielectric constant symbol. There is no 1995 statement on gelatin grades, sensitizer or restrainer content, inert-gelatin practice, or synthetic replacement in production. **[F]**
- **A quantified relation between any gelatin constituent and any characteristic-curve parameter.** "Gradation bodies" affect contrast; adenine curtails sensitization; aldehydes are "very likely" connected with fog and sensitivity — all asserted, none numbered against a gamma, a Dmin, or a speed point. **[F]**
- **The molecular weight distribution of a photographic gelatin.** Only the single figure "of the order of 70,000" after liming. **[F]**
- **The temperature dependence of gelatin viscosity.** Fig. 2.1 gives viscosity against pH at one unstated temperature; no viscosity–temperature curve appears. **[F]**
- **Any refractive index for gelatin**, which would be needed for a scattering model of the layer. Not mentioned in any of the three sources. **[F]**
- **Quantification of gelatin function 7 (latent-image stabilisation).** Asserted in the list of nine and never returned to. **[F]**
- **How and when the aldehyde/carbohydrate variability (300–15,000 ppm) was brought under control.** Open in 1966 and unmentioned in 1995. **[F]**
- **Gelatin's own contribution to the fog floor, separated from the sensitizer's.** Function 8 states that gelatin renders unexposed grains "relatively less developable"; no source quantifies the effect or the resulting Dmin. **[F]**


---

## 8. Chemical sensitization

### 8.1 Definition and the three classes

Chemical sensitization is the deliberate placing of chemical species on or in the silver halide grain, by reaction during a heat treatment after precipitation and washing, so that the grain makes more efficient use of the light it already absorbs. It is distinguished from spectral sensitization, which extends the *wavelength range* over which the grain responds. Duffin states the split explicitly: the two routes to sensitivity are (1) "cause emulsion grains to make the most efficient use of the light they absorb; i.e. **chemical sensitization**"; (2) "cause the grains to be able to use light in a region of the spectrum in which they would normally not absorb, i.e. **spectral sensitization**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89)]` **[F]**

Duffin's three types: "**1. Sulphur sensitization. 2. Reduction sensitization. 3. Precious metal sensitization.** The first two types … may be produced by chemicals **naturally present in gelatin**, but it is necessary to **add special compounds** to the emulsion for the third type." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]` **[F]**

Tani's terminology, three decades later, separates the *process stage* rather than the chemistry: **chemical sensitization** = placing chemical species on/in grains by reactions during **ripening** (agitation at elevated temperature for a time period); **hypersensitization** = treating coated layers **before** exposure; **latensification** = treating coated layers **after** exposure, before development, to increase the developability of subimage and small image centres. `[Tani 1995, §6.1, pp.165–167 (PDF 174–176)]` **[F]**

The heat treatment itself has three interchangeable historical names, all for the same operation: **digestion, chemical ripening, after-ripening**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]` **[F]**

### 8.2 Tani's summary table of sensitizer / centre / function, with dates

| Type | Sensitizers named | Centre formed | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sulfur | sodium thiosulfate, allylthiourea | **(Ag₂S)₂**, solid-solution type | shallow electron trap for preferential formation of a latent image centre |
| Gold | KAuCl₄ + KSCN, Au(SCN)₂⁻, Au(S₂O₃)₂³⁻ | **Au⁺** | increase developability of image centres; modify the sulfur sensitization centre |
| Reduction | SnCl₂, thiourea dioxide, hydrazine derivatives | **Ag₂ at a neutral site (R centre)**; **Ag₂ at a positive kink site (P centre)** | R: hole trap preventing recombination, plus supply of an extra electron. P: electron trap, precursor of a latent image centre |

`[Tani 1995, §6.1, Table 6.1, p.167 (PDF 176)]` **[Q]**

Dates from the "Origin" column of the same table and its supporting text:

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1871 | Sulfur sensitization enters photographic materials with Maddox's introduction of gelatin — "it is believed that **sulfur sensitization was introduced into silver halide photographic materials when Maddox used gelatin for these materials in 1871**" |
| 1925 | Sheppard, analysing why sensitivity depended on the kind of gelatin, "**discovered in 1925 that sulfur compounds could increase photographic sensitivity**" |
| 1933 | "**Carroll and Hubbard observed chemical sensitization using sodium sulfite as early as 1933**" |
| 1936 | "**In collaboration with Mueller in 1936, Koslowsky discovered gold sensitization by the use of chloroauric acid and thiocyanate**" |
| 1951 | "the concept of reduction sensitization was introduced by **Lowe et al. in 1951**" |

`[Tani 1995, §§6.1–6.4, pp.165–180 (PDF 174–189), Table 6.1 p.167 (PDF 176)]` **[F]**

Duffin dates gold independently and less precisely: "**About thirty years ago** a further method … was discovered by the **Agfa** workers", i.e. the mid-1930s, consistent with Tani's 1936. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.91 (PDF 97)]` **[F]**

Duffin also dates the organic-stabilizer field: "Some **thirty years ago**" heterocyclic stabilizers were found, and the parent 4-hydroxy-6-methyl-1,3,3a,7-tetrazaindene "was discovered to be a stabilizer by **Birr in 1935**". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.138 (PDF 144)]` **[F]**

Wall, writing in 1929, dates Sheppard's identification of the active gelatin constituent to 1925 and calls it "the most important contribution to the science and practice of emulsion making yet published". `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.25–27 (PDF 33–35)]` **[F]**

### 8.3 The 1929 understanding (Wall)

**1929.** Wall has no electronic theory whatever. There is no band structure, no electron trap, no photoelectron; the word "latent" does not occur anywhere in the book (zero occurrences in the full text). Sensitization in 1929 is a matter of nuclei of silver sulphide formed from sulphur-bearing impurities in gelatine, established empirically. **[F]** `[Wall 1929, whole text]`

Wall's account of the active principle, following Sheppard:

- The sensitizing agent in "active" gelatine is **allyl isothiocyanate / allyl thiocarbamide**, marketed conceptually as "Gelatine X", present at **1 : 1,000,000 to 1 : 300,000** (i.e. 1–3.3 ppm). `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.25–27 (PDF 33–35)]` **[Q]**
- The intermediate is a silver complex `(AgBr)ₘ·(CS·NHR·NH₂)ₙ`, with m and n "probably 2 and 1"; in alkali it splits to **silver sulphide** plus cyanamide, guanidine and alkaline bromide. The Ag₂S nuclei are the sensitivity centres, but they "must form nuclei discretely and not above a certain size." `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.25–27 (PDF 33–35)]` **[M]**
- The optimum-then-decline law, stated in 1929 in essentially its modern form: "**The action reaches a maximum effect for a certain quantity and then decreases as the amount of the active material is increased, with corresponding increase in fog.**" `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.27 (PDF 35)]` **[F]**
- Chemically equivalent agents, "all these combine with the silver halides to form decomposable complexes": sodium thiosulphate (hypo), **Na₂SeSO₃**, **K₂Te₂O₃**, potassium isoselenocyanate. Selenium and tellurium sensitization is therefore already known in 1929, at the same order of concentration. `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.26 (PDF 34)]` **[F]**
- Lumière's riposte to Sheppard: ~900 substances screened, of which aesculin, codeine, thebaine, diethylenediamine, thiocarbamide and guanidine sulphocyanate "could be advantageously used"; already in commercial use, previously unpublished. `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.27 (PDF 35)]` **[F]**
- Sulphur-free historic sensitizers are noted as an anomaly: Newton's (1874) tea plus mustard-seed infusion; codeine and narcotine, "well known as sensitizers for washed collodion emulsion" and containing **no sulphur**. Narcotine dose for collodion emulsion: **0.5 g per ~1 litre of emulsion**. `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.27 (PDF 35); Ch. VI, p.114 (PDF 121)]` **[Q]**

Wall's one worked reduction-sensitization recipe with sensitometric outcome — the only place in the 1929 book where a sensitization treatment is tied to measured speed, gamma and fog together:

| Quantity | Digestion | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium sulphite **0.25 : 100 AgNO₃** (slow emulsion, converted to ammonio-nitrate) | **1 h at 43 °C (110 °F)** then **2 h at 27 °C (80 °F)**, set on ice | "regular, very clean … **speed of 22 H. & D.** with **high gamma infinity**, the **fog reading with ten minutes development with the standard pyro-soda developer being only 0.1**" |

`[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]` **[Q]**

A second sulphite datum, from Lippmann-plate practice, separates the speed gain from grain coarsening: Valenta added **0.1 g Na₂SO₃ per 300 ccm emulsion** and digested at **35 °C for 5, 15 and 30 min**, obtaining "**increase of speed without coarsening of the grain**". `[Wall 1929, Ch. VI, p.131 (PDF 138)]` **[Q]**

A negative control on the same chemistry: **4 parts anhydrous sulphite : 10 AgNO₃ with ammonia** (Wellington, 1885) reduced the AgBr outright and formed a silver mirror — though Wall notes this was effectively an ammoniacal silver sulphite. `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]` **[F]**

Wall's fog-control specification for gelatine, i.e. the 1929 way of controlling the sensitization/fog balance by raw-material purity rather than by dosing:

| Impurity | Limit stated |
|---|---|
| Ash | ≤ **2 %** |
| Metallic salts (Fe, Cu, Pb, Zn) | ≤ **50 ppm** — "Most to be feared" |
| Aluminium | > **0.106 %** indicates alum-hardening |
| Sulphur as SO₂ | ≤ **0.1 %** |

`[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.25 (PDF 33)]` **[Q]**

Ammonia strength is the other 1929 speed lever, and the book flags a transatlantic unit trap: England uses sp. gr. **0.880 ≈ 35 % NH₃**, the USA sp. gr. **0.90 ≈ 28 %** — "the latter is one-fifth weaker". The ammonia method "gives the highest sensitiveness". Impurity test: 3.5 ccm NH₃ into 20 ccm HNO₃, evaporate; the residue must be colourless, since pyridine, pyrrole or aniline are "almost certain to cause fog". `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.11–12 (PDF 19–20); Ch. III, p.29 (PDF 37); Ch. IV, p.78 (PDF 85)]` **[Q]**

Wall gives **no gold sensitization at all**, and no precious-metal sensitization of any kind: gold appears in his book only as a *toner* in self-toning print-out papers, with Spiller's 1869 priority noted. This is a hard era boundary — gold sensitization did not exist in 1929 practice. `[Wall 1929, Ch. VI, p.119 (PDF 126)]` **[F]**

### 8.4 The 1966 understanding (Duffin)

**1966.** The digestion envelope, stated as a process window:

> "a treatment, often after the addition of a chemical sensitizer, at an elevated temperature, **from 40° to 70 °C**, which may vary in duration **from a few minutes up to several hours**, when **speed and fog are increased** … if the conditions used were not optimum in terms of **pH, nature of the gelatin or the quantities of various additions**, then the **speed increase might be much smaller or the onset of fog might take place sooner** … **as this reaches its maximum value the onset of fog occurs**, that is some of the silver-halide crystals become developable without exposure."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89), Fig. 5.1 "Growth of speed and fog in digestion: iodobromide emulsion"; ordinate "Fog and Relative Log Speed" 0–2.0, abscissa "Digestion Time"]` **[Q]**

The dated practice statement that marks the 1966 transition: "**Only a few years ago the behaviour of an emulsion in this digestion stage was always entirely controlled by the nature of the gelatin.** Gelatins which produced a large increase in sensitivity in a conveniently short time were referred to as **fast or active** gelatins while those that produced little or no change were referred to as **slow or inert**." And: "**It is now more usual to add known amounts of these sensitizers … before the digestion stage in order to permit control of the process.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]` **[F]**

#### 8.4.1 Sulphur sensitization, 1966

- "**Sulphur sensitization is the most widely-used method of conferring speed and contrast on a silver-halide emulsion.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]` **[F]**
- The natural agent: "the sensitizing substance of normal commercial gelatins is **sodium thiosulphate, Na₂S₂O₃, possibly with sodium tetrathionate, Na₂S₄O₆**." (OCR prints the latter as `Na,S,O,`.) `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]` **[F]**
- Reaction schemes as printed (charge superscripts OCR-mangled; species and stoichiometric coefficients legible):
```
Ag(+) + Ag—S—C(=NH)(NH2) + OH(-)  ->  Ag2S + NH2CONH2   (urea)
Ag(+) + [Ag(S2O3)2]       + OH(-)  ->  Ag2S + 3 HSO3(-)
```
`[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.84–85 (PDF 90–91)]` **[Q]**
- Structural requirement on thiourea-class sensitizers `>N.CS.N<`: "Active compounds of this class usually possess the **unsubstituted H atom**, to make the formation of a silver-sulphur link possible. The fully substituted **1,1,3,3-tetramethylthiourea (CH₃)₂N.CS.N(CH₃)₂ is reported as being substantially inert.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.84 (PDF 90)]` **[F]**
- Rate laws, with exponents: "**The rate of the reaction is directly proportional to the silver-ion concentration**", i.e. rate ∝ [Ag⁺]¹. The hydroxyl-ion dependence is disputed in the source: "**James and Vanselow** found a dependence to a **power greater than unity** with allylthiourea, methylthiourea and other derivatives whereas **Sutherns and Loening** found the rate with allylthiourea to be **proportional to the 0.7th power of the hydroxyl-ion concentration**." Duffin does not resolve it, and neither do we: both exponents stand. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 91)]` **[Q]**
- Habit dependence: "recent work has indicated **very different rates on 100-faces of silver bromide, relative to those of 111-faces**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 91)]` **[F]**
- Product identity and its location: the silver sulphide "is **part of the crystal surface, formed by the displacement of bromide ions and the replacement of every two of them by one doubly-charged sulphide ion**" — not bulk precipitated Ag₂S. "**Silver sulphide formed elsewhere, for example in the gelatin medium, usually gives yellow or dichroic fog.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 91)]` **[M]**
- Reaction-order history: early work with much larger sensitizer quantities found the digestion reaction **autocatalytic** (Fig. 5.3); "However, in recent years, the use of more refined methods, in particular the application of **radiotracer techniques** … have shown a behaviour like that of the **normal uncatalysed reaction** of Figure 5.2." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.86–87 (PDF 92–93), Figs. 5.2, 5.3]` **[F]**
- Preferential sites: Sutherns and Loening found "the initial stage of the breakdown of allylthiourea on silver-bromide sols is **more rapid** than that of the greater fraction of the reaction … This important result suggests that **reaction takes place at certain sites on the crystal surface**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.87 (PDF 93), Fig. 5.4]` **[M]**
- pH sensitivity of Ag₂S formation from thiourea: "**Thiourea forms silver sulphide very slowly at pH 6.0 whereas at pH 8.0 it reacts very rapidly.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.91 (PDF 97)]` **[Q]**

#### 8.4.2 The surface-area anomaly — the strongest structural argument in the 1966 account

> "One very surprising fact which concurs with this view is that **optimum quantity of sulphur sensitizer varies very little with the grain size of the emulsion**. When one considers that **crystals of one micron diameter will possess roughly ten times the surface area of crystals of 0.1 micron diameter**, then this is a very surprising fact indeed and **points undeniably to the concept that only certain selected sites on each crystal need to collect their 'coating' of silver sulphide**."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.87 (PDF 93)]` **[Q]**

Restated later: "**Finer grain emulsions, possessing a larger surface area per mole, will have a smaller percentage of their surface covered and … fewer sulphur atoms per grain; there is no indication from the literature that such emulsions require more sensitizer per mole of silver.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.95 (PDF 101)]` **[F]**

| Item | Value | Note |

| Active sulphur in gelatine, active types | **100 ppm** | same |

| Grains per gram-mole in the reference iodobromide | raw string `4x10"`; recoverable as **4 × 10¹⁴** because the author's own arithmetic only closes at 10¹⁴ | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.95 (PDF 101); Ch. VII, p.142 (PDF 148)]` |

| Fraction of surface silver associated with sulphur | "**only about 3 %** of this silver (2 silver ions per sulphur atom)" | ratio survives; usable |
