| Fraction of silver involved, if 100 silver atoms per grain are needed for developability | "**only one silver atom in every 10,000,000**" | same |
| Sensitizer actually consumed at peak speed | "only a fraction, usually around **10 %**, of the sulphur sensitizer has been broken down by the time that the speed has reached its maximum" | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.95 (PDF 101)]` |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.90, 94–95 (PDF 96, 100–101)]` **[Q]** — with the caveat that four of the absolute atom counts are unusable because the OCR destroyed their exponents; the *ratios* (10 %, 3 %, 1 in 50,000, 1 in 10⁷) are intact and are the modellable content.

Note the internal tension in Duffin's own numbers: on p.90 he assumes "**as many as 100 silver atoms per grain are necessary in order to render the grain developable**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.90 (PDF 96)]`, whereas his own Chapter IX puts the minimum at **four** silver atoms `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.172 (PDF 178)]`. The p.90 figure is an order-of-magnitude bound used in an illustrative calculation, not a measurement; the Chapter IX figure is the measured one. The two are not reconciled in the book. **[F]**

Reducing the dose to the ~10 % that actually reacts does not work: using only that fraction "does not give, after a long digestion, as high a photographic sensitivity; **fog formation is increased**." Sutherns and Loening therefore invoke "the need for **sufficient surface coverage of adsorbed unreacted sensitizer**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.95 (PDF 101)]` **[F]**

Over-dosing: "some of Bekunov's data, given in Figure 5.8, show that **larger quantities produce lower maximum speed**. With other gelatins, not specified, Bekunov obtained a **constant maximum speed over a wide range of values of added thiosulphate**." Fig. 5.8 axes: ordinate "Speed" 0–0.6 (ticks 0, 0.3, 0.6), abscissa "Digestion Time in hours" 1–5, two curves labelled **40** and **80** parts per million in gelatin. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.95 (PDF 101), Fig. 5.8]` **[Q]**

Emulsions needing no separate digestion at all: "**silver-chloride emulsions made using fast gelatins** … and physically ripened in only a **small excess (1–3 %) of chloride**. The **relatively low pAg** of these emulsions, even before washing, enables the silver sulphide to be formed during physical ripening and in melting treatments so that the emulsion is fully sensitized by the time it is melted after washing." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.87 (PDF 93)]` **[Q]**

#### 8.4.4 Gold sensitization, 1966 — the headline speed gain

- "**Gold sensitization alone gives a very poor effect characterized by a low contrast and is, therefore, always applied in conjunction with sulphur sensitizing.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.92 (PDF 98)]` **[F]**
- **"Under optimum conditions, the speed obtainable by the combination of gold and sulphur sensitization is 2 to 2½ times that obtainable by sulphur sensitizing alone."** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.92 (PDF 98)]` **[Q]**
- Measured as a log-exposure shift: "the **maximum increase in this case over speed from sulphur sensitization alone is 0.33 log E units**." Fig. 5.9 ("Quantity of gold — sodium aurothiocyanate iodobromide emulsion"; ordinate "Relative Log Speed", abscissa "Quantity of Gold, moles × 10⁵"(?), ticks 2, 4, 6, 8, 10). 0.33 log E ≈ ×2.1 in linear exposure, consistent with the "2 to 2½ times" statement above. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.96 (PDF 102), Fig. 5.9]` **[Q]**
- Dose: "**from 1 to 30 mg. of gold**, either as chloroauric acid or a more complex gold salt, being used **per gram mole of silver**. **If a gold sensitizer is added at the completion of digestion, then larger quantities are needed.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.96 (PDF 102)]` **[Q]**
- Sensitizers: "**potassium aurothiocyanate or potassium aurochloride**"; the aurothiocyanate, "the original gold sensitizer, is formed by treating gold chloride with an equivalent quantity of an alkali thiocyanate." Used "in amounts comparable to the sulphur sensitizer." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.91 (PDF 97)]` **[F]**
- Application, as 1966 practice: "effective on **both negative and positive** emulsions but is **used mainly with fast iodobromide materials, such as those for camera use, either black-and-white or colour, or X-ray emulsions**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.92 (PDF 98)]` **[F]**
- Free-gold-ion requirement, with the two equilibria as printed:
```
AuCl4-   =  Au(3+) + 4 Cl-
Au(CN)2- =  Au(+)  + 2 CN-      ("very heavily displaced towards the left-hand side")
```
"the very stable gold cyanide complex salt, **K Au(CN)₂, does not sensitize at all**." A patent claim uses **N-methylbenzothiazole-2-thione** to give a gold complex with "just the optimum free gold-ion concentration." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.92–93 (PDF 98–99)]` **[Q]**
- Fog liability: "**gold-sensitized emulsions are very susceptible to the action of small quantities of reducing substances** … there are many indications that **reducing substances produce fog very easily in gold-sensitized emulsions**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.93 (PDF 99)]` **[F]**
- Product identity unresolved in 1966: "Whether the sensitizing substance is **aurous sulphide Au₂S** … **or gold metal** … have not been satisfactorily decided." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.93 (PDF 99)]` **[M]**
- Effect on digestion rate is emulsion-dependent: "gold salts may **either accelerate digestion or retard it**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.93 (PDF 99)]` **[F]**
- Figures for digestion and curve shape: Fig. 5.6 "Effect of gold on digestion: iodobromide emulsion" (ordinate "Fog and Relative Log Speed" 0–2.0, abscissa "Digestion Time", ticks 20', 30', 40', 50'; two curves "with gold" / "without gold"). Fig. 5.7 "Effect of gold on D-log E curve: iodobromide emulsion" (ordinate 0–2.0, abscissa "Relative Log E" 0–2.0; curves "with gold" / "without gold") — the only D–log E figure in Duffin's chemical-sensitization chapter. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.91–92 (PDF 97–98), Figs. 5.6, 5.7]` **[Q]**

The mechanism-level statement of what gold buys, from Duffin's latent-image chapter rather than his sensitization chapter, is a direct contrast statement: "**Examination of the curves in Figure 5.6 shows that gold increases the speed by reducing the contrast.**" Gold acts "in the secondary stages of latent-image formation by reducing the number of quanta needed to form a stable development centre" — not by increasing light absorption. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.186–187 (PDF 192–193)]` **[F]**

And gold's fog penalty, mechanistically: Mitchell's argument is that gold sensitization "is always more prone to run into fog than that produced by sulphur sensitizers alone", because **Au⁺–Ag is more stable than Ag⁺–Ag**, so the first sub-image or sub-fog speck is stabilized and more likely to collect further silver. Gold-bearing image and fog specks are harder to bleach; Spracklen's mercuric-chloride treatment showed gold-sensitized emulsions contain a fraction of grains very resistant to that oxidant, and **the resistant fraction increased with longer exposures**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.186–187 (PDF 192–193)]` **[M]**

#### 8.4.5 Reduction sensitization, 1966

> "The addition to the emulsion of **very small quantities of reducing substances** followed by a heat treatment, also produces an increase of emulsion speed similar to that obtained by sulphur sensitization, **except that the contrast obtainable after treatment with a reducing agent is generally lower and there is a greater tendency to fog formation**. **Sodium sulphite and stannous chloride** are examples … may be carried out at the same kind of pAg and pH values as are used for sulphur sensitization."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 94)]` **[F]**

- Alternative route: "heat treatment carried out **in excess silver ions**; bromide ions are then added to give the usual coating pAg." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 94)]` **[F]**
- "**The reduction process has been shown to be autocatalytic**" — Fig. 5.3 shape, in contrast to the uncatalysed shape now accepted for sulphur. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 94)]` **[F]**
- The centres "comprise **silver atoms** … reside on the grain surface but **may not be an integral part of the surface** as are the silver sulphide entities." Evidence: "**stripping of the gelatin film from large silver-bromide crystals, which had been reduction sensitized, removed the bulk of the surface sensitivity**. The same loss occurs with the adsorption of dyes in similarly sensitized emulsions." Mitchell's inference: "the sensitizing substance was **a small group of silver-atoms surrounded by gelatin molecules and therefore attached to, but slightly separate from, the grain**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.88–89 (PDF 94–95)]` **[M]**
- Why it fogs, stated as a threshold argument: "a process in which a **distribution of silver atoms** is formed on the grain could easily give rise to fog, because **when any one nucleus becomes as large as a latent-image speck it will be able to initiate development** of the crystal." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.89 (PDF 95)]` **[M]**
- Sulphite as an adjunct to sulphur sensitization (Bekunov, Fig. 5.5, curves labelled "sulphite added" / "without sulphite"): "the presence of sulphite can **increase the sensitivity given by sulphur sensitization although no increase in the rate of growth of sensitivity** was obtained. **The rate of fog growth was found to be higher in the presence of sulphite, but only after maximum speed had been obtained.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.89 (PDF 95), Fig. 5.5]` **[Q]**

#### 8.4.6 What the sensitivity speck *is* — 1966's open question

Duffin presents this as unresolved and names the parties. Two most-discussed views: (1) **silver sulphide in a layer form, e.g. islands on the grain surface** (James and Vanselow); (2) **silver only**, Ag₂S being merely a step or a parallel reaction (Chibisov *et al.*, who "even postulate that silver sulphide has an **adverse** effect"). Duffin's arbitration: Chibisov's fine-structure evidence "has been queried by Western workers, **none of whom have been able to repeat it**"; and "Chibisov himself showed that **the presence of gold salts during digestion prevented the formation of non-halide silver** … this is **strong evidence against the silver-speck theory**." A third proposal (Sauvenier and Hautot): the **adsorbed silver-thiosulphate complex** is the speck, and "an **etching reaction**, arising from the silver-halide solvent action of the thiosulphate, is necessary to create the correct surface condition for sensitization." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.89–91 (PDF 95–97)]` **[M]**

Duffin's own summary: silver sulphide is formed "at certain reactive sites"; "If it is necessary that this must be accompanied by the formation of an even smaller quantity of another sensitizing substance, e.g. silver, then this occurs in a way which, at the moment, we cannot detect." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.91 (PDF 97)]` **[M]**

**Digestion fog** — three candidate centre types listed: Ag₂S aggregates of different shape (e.g. a three-dimensional lattice); over-large Ag₂S specks, with the caution that "**recent work has shown that even large quantities of silver sulphide are unlikely to render the grain developable**"; or a slower, selective silver-forming reaction within or adjacent to an Ag₂S speck. A bleach discrimination experiment separates the two fog chemistries: "digestion of emulsions containing **only very small quantities of sensitizer, e.g. thiourea, for prolonged periods produces fog which can be almost completely bleached by dilute chromic-acid solutions** while a **similar level of fog, produced by a large quantity of sensitizer, is very resistant to bleaching**." Gold post-treatment discriminates the same way: Ag₂S-type fog "becomes **lower** in density"; silver-type fog is **enhanced**. Duffin's conclusion: "**it seems possible that fog is probably silver in many cases, certainly in commercial emulsion**, and it is only with large quantities of sulphur sensitizers that silver-sulphide fog is really important." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.90–91 (PDF 96–97)]` **[M]**

#### 8.4.7 Other metals, and restrainers in digestion, 1966

- "there are a number of references to the enhanced sensitivity produced by **cadmium** salts, and many of the metals with variable valency, such as **mercury, iron, palladium and platinum** have been mentioned in the patent literature. **At a conference in London in 1960 on the maximum sensitivity of photographic materials, reference was made to the use of palladium, in particular in the sensitization of the fastest emulsions.**" "The amounts of other rare metals added for sensitization are of a **similar order to those of gold**", i.e. 1–30 mg per gram-mole Ag. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.94, 96 (PDF 100, 102)]` **[Q]**
- Restrainer action: "in the presence of the **same quantity of sensitizing substance** … **the same emulsion will digest at quite different rates with different gelatins**." "**adenine slows, and in large quantities curtails, chemical sensitization.** This is believed to be due to the fact that the restrainer functions by **controlling the manner in which the silver sulphide is laid down on the grain surface** … Analytical evidence shows that **silver-sulphide formation continues in spite of the presence of the adenine**. The opinion has been expressed that the influence of the adenine may be to cause the **silver sulphide to be located in the adsorbed gelatin layer instead of on the grain surface**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.96–97 (PDF 102–103)]` **[M]**
- Duffin doubts adenine is the actual agent: the assay "uses drastic treatment which would break down any fragile molecule. There is, therefore, **no real support for the assumption that adenine itself is the restraining substance**; it is much more likely to be a **derivative of adenine, probably of high molecular weight**." Pyrimidine fragments (**cytosine, uracil, thymine**) "have been shown to be **far less active restrainers than the fused ring compounds**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.97 (PDF 103)]` **[M]**
- Coupling of the two dosages: "**Since the rate of digestion is controlled by the content of both restrainer and sensitizer, it is likely that the use of very small quantities of sensitizer would result in the onset of fog before useful sensitivity is obtained. This may well be the controlling factor.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.97 (PDF 103)]` **[M]**

Restrainer concentrations, from the gelatin chapter, since in 1966 these are the numbers that actually set the digestion rate:

| Gelatin source | Adenine-equivalent restrainer |
|---|---|
| Hide | **10–220 ppm**; restated tighter as an average of **30–50 ppm, sometimes even 200 ppm** |
| Ossein (bone) | "much lower content"; restated as **4–6 ppm** |
| Inert-gelatin threshold | "**less than five parts per million of both sulphur sensitizer and nucleic-acid type restrainer would render a gelatin inert**" (definition first proposed by Kelly, Liège Conference **1959**) |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.37, 44–45 (PDF 41, 48–49); Ch. V, p.96 (PDF 102)]` **[Q]**

Note the internal disagreement on whether restrainers act on growth at all: "**The whole position of growth retarders is a confused one.** Wood has postulated that the small quantities of restrainers in the quantities of gelatin used for commercial emulsions do not affect the crystal growth. He points out that while **100 parts per million of adenine … affects sensitization, 10,000 parts per million have no influence on the crystal growth**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.37–38 (PDF 41–42)]` **[Q]**

### 8.5 The 1995 understanding (Tani)

**1995.** The 1995 account is electronic and quantitative: sensitization centres are characterised by their **electron- or hole-trap depth in eV**, their **number density per µm² of a named crystal face**, their **oxidation potential in mV**, and the **stoichiometry of the cluster** (monomer vs dimer). This is the substantive change from 1966.

#### 8.5.1 Sulfur sensitization, 1995 — trap depths

| Quantity | Value | Method / source as cited |
|---|---|---|
| Thermal depth, sulfur centre, octahedral AgBr | **0.33 eV** | Hamilton, Harbison & Jeanmaire — temperature coefficient of red sensitivity (λ > 620 nm) |
| Thermal depth, sulfur-plus-gold centre, octahedral AgBr | **0.19 eV** | same |
| Thermal depth, sulfur centre, octahedral AgBr | **0.39 eV** | Kellogg & Hodes — thermally stimulated current |
| Thermal depth, sulfur-plus-gold centre, octahedral AgBr | **0.17 eV** | same |
| **Optical** depth, sulfur centre, AgBr emulsion grains | **0.5 eV** | Kanzaki & Tadakuma — transient absorption band of the localized electron, luminescence-modulation spectroscopy at liquid-helium temperature |
| Thermal depth inferred from that band's low-energy threshold | **about 0.3 eV** | same |

`[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.73–74 (PDF 82–83); §4.1.3, p.86 (PDF 95); §6.2, pp.170–171 (PDF 179–180)]` **[Q]**

The two independent thermal determinations of the sulfur centre disagree — 0.33 eV (Hamilton, Harbison & Jeanmaire) versus 0.39 eV (Kellogg & Hodes) — and Tani reports both without reconciling them. Likewise for S+Au: 0.19 eV versus 0.17 eV. Do not average; the spread 0.17–0.19 eV for S+Au and 0.30–0.39 eV for S is the honest statement. **[Q]**

The trap-depth figures are the whole point of gold: **sulfur-plus-gold centres are shallower than sulfur centres**, 0.19 eV against 0.33 eV. Tani's rationalisation: Au⁺ is larger than Ag⁺, so the two Coulombic orbitals of the dimer sit further apart, their splitting is smaller, and the bonding (deeper) orbital is raised — the trap is shallower. `[Tani 1995, §6.3, pp.178–179 (PDF 187–188)]` **[M]**

Hailstone's simulation states the trade this implies: "the **number of electron traps per grain needed to achieve the maximum quantum sensitivity should increase by decreasing their trap depths**, and the **maximum quantum sensitivity increased with decreasing the trap depth** within the conditions examined." `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.179 (PDF 188)]` **[M]**

There is also a spectral consequence of chemical sensitization that is easy to miss: "being excited by red light, these centers can inject electrons into the conduction band of silver halide with the aid of thermal energy and **thus give rise to red sensitivity**." The trap depths above were measured *by* the temperature coefficient of exactly that red sensitivity. So an undyed sulfur-sensitized emulsion has a weak, temperature-dependent red response that is not dye-derived. No spectral curve is given. `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.73 (PDF 82)]` **[F]**

#### 8.5.2 Sulfur sensitization, 1995 — centre stoichiometry and number density

| Quantity | Value | Source as cited |
|---|---|---|
| Composition of the effective sulfur centre | a **dimer of silver sulphide**, (Ag₂S)₂, solid-solution type | Kanzaki & Tadakuma; Keevert |
| Centre density, optimally sulfur-sensitized, on the (100) face of AgBr | **2800 centres per µm²** | Tadakuma, Yoshida & Kanzaki, from quantitative Ag₂S assay plus Smoluchowski's equation |
| Centre density, alternative estimate | "as many as **1000 per µm²**" | Keevert |
| Centres on a 0.8 µm cubic grain | **11,000 dimers** | Tadakuma *et al.* |
| Scaling law confirming the dimer | number of centres ∝ **(amount of Ag₂S)²** | same |

`[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.74 (PDF 83); §6.2, p.171 (PDF 180); repeated §8.1.1, p.232 (PDF 241)]` **[Q]**

The two density estimates, 1000/µm² and 2800/µm², disagree by a factor of 2.8; Tani reports both. **[Q]**

**[E]** The 2800/µm² figure applied to a 1 µm cube (6 µm² of surface) gives ≈1.7 × 10⁴ competing electron traps per grain. That is the quantity that sets the nucleation-versus-growth competition, and therefore the balance between low- and high-intensity reciprocity failure discussed in §10.7. It is the natural single "trap density" parameter if a physical reciprocity model is attempted, but the source does not use it that way.

#### 8.5.3 Sulfur sensitization, 1995 — kinetics, activation energies, and the two-step mechanism

| Quantity | Value | Source as cited |
|---|---|---|
| Thiosulfate adsorption to grains | **reversible, Langmuir-type** | Spracklen, ³⁵S tracer |
| Decomposition of adsorbed thiosulfate | **first-order, activation energy 22 kcal/mol** | same |
| Sensitometric activation energy of the whole sulfur-sensitization *process* | **32–35 kcal/mol**, "nearly independent of the kind of sensitizers" | Ridgeway & Hillson |

Because the sensitometric activation energy (32–35 kcal/mol) exceeds that of Ag₂S *formation* (22 kcal/mol), the rate-determining step of sensitization is **not** the formation of Ag₂S but the subsequent **rearrangement / aggregation** of Ag₂S — a two-step mechanism. `[Tani 1995, §6.2, pp.168–170 (PDF 177–179)]` **[Q]**

Habit dependence, now with the reaction order attached: Ag₂S formation from thiosulfate is **faster on octahedral than cubic** grains; from **triethylthiourea, faster on cubic than octahedral**. Moisar: first-order on (111), **self-catalyzed on (100)**. `[Tani 1995, §6.2, pp.168–169 (PDF 177–178)]` **[F]**

The two steps resolved sensitometrically: with uniformly distributed **Na₂S at 40 °C for 15 min**, sensitivity rises in **two steps**; the second step coincides with a **drop in photoconductivity** (so the species formed in step 2 is an electron trap — the **dimer**), while the first step does not (so step 1 forms **hole traps — monomers**). Digestion at **60 °C for 60 min** blurs the two steps together. Photoconductivity measured as **35 GHz microwave** peak height. `[Tani 1995, §6.2, pp.171–172 (PDF 180–181), Fig. 6.4]` **[Q]**

Oxidation potentials of the centres, by Frei's redox buffers, vs SCE, at **pBr 3, 25 °C, 17 and 41 hours** equilibration:

| Function | Assignment | Cubic AgBr | Octahedral AgBr |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensitization centre acting as **hole trap** | (Ag₂S)₁, solid solution | **280 mV** | **360 mV** |
| Sensitization centre acting as **electron trap** | (Ag₂S)₂, solid solution | **240 mV** | **345 mV** |
| **Fog centre** | Ag₂S cluster | **> 400 mV** | **> 400 mV** |

`[Tani 1995, §6.2, Table 6.2, p.174 (PDF 183), Fig. 6.5]` **[Q]**

Fog centres "could be oxidized, **not by Frei's redox buffer solutions, but by much stronger oxidizing solutions such as bromine water**"; their oxidizability resembles that of **Ag₂S powder**. `[Tani 1995, §6.2, p.174 (PDF 183)]` **[F]**

Structural model: two configurations of Ag₂S on AgBr — **solid-solution type**, in which S²⁻ replaces Br⁻ at a lattice site and is charge-compensated by an **interstitial Ag⁺** whose Coulombic orbital is a very shallow electron trap (two such orbitals in a dimer interact to give bonding and non-bonding combinations, the **bonding orbital giving the deeper trap**), and **cluster type**, an isolated Ag₂S on the surface. **Effective sensitization centres are Ag₂S dimers of the solid-solution type; fog centres are Ag₂S clusters.** The HOMO is the 3d orbitals of S²⁻. `[Tani 1995, §6.2, pp.174–175 (PDF 183–184), Fig. 6.6]` **[M]**

Note that this is the 1995 resolution of the 1966 open question of §8.4.6: Duffin could not decide between "Ag₂S islands" and "silver only", and could not distinguish sensitizing Ag₂S from fogging Ag₂S. Tani's answer is that both are Ag₂S but in **different configurations** — solid-solution dimer sensitizes, surface cluster fogs — and that this is why "even large quantities of silver sulphide are unlikely to render the grain developable" (Duffin's own observation) while some Ag₂S certainly does fog. **[E]**

#### 8.5.4 The fog margin — the single hardest number on sensitization dosing

> "The amount of Na₂S₂O₃ for the formation of **fog centers was two orders of magnitude larger** than that for maximum sensitivity."

Conditions: octahedral AgBr **0.2 µm**; digestion **60 °C for 60 min**; exposure **10 s** to tungsten at **2854 K**; developer **MAA-1**. `[Tani 1995, §6.2, p.171 (PDF 180), Fig. 6.3]` **[Q]**

That is a **100× margin in sensitizer dose** between peak speed and the onset of fog centres, for that emulsion and that digestion. It is not a general constant — Duffin's Fig. 5.1 shows the fog onset arriving *at* the speed maximum for a fast iodobromide, and Duffin explicitly warns that non-optimum pH, gelatin or additions bring the fog onset forward `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89)]`. The two sources are describing different systems (0.2 µm octahedral AgBr model emulsion versus a commercial fast iodobromide) and they do not contradict each other on mechanism, but they give very different practical margins: **100× dose margin (Tani, model emulsion) versus effectively no margin (Duffin, commercial emulsion)**. Both stand. **[Q]**

#### 8.5.5 Gold sensitization, 1995

- **Au⁺, not Au³⁺, is the sensitization centre.** Gelatin and thiocyanate both reduce Au³⁺ → Au⁺; gelatin binds Au⁺ so strongly that it blocks incorporation into grains; Pd ions bind gelatin harder still and thus **release Au⁺**. `[Tani 1995, §6.3, pp.176–177 (PDF 185–186), Fig. 6.7]` **[F]**
- Stability constants β of aurous complexes, which set whether a gold salt sensitizes at all:

| Complex | β | Sensitizing behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Au(SCN)₂⁻ | **9.6 × 10¹⁶** | good sensitizer |
| Au(S₂O₃)₂³⁻ | **10²⁶** | good sensitizer; "**S₂O₃²⁻ was more suitable than SCN⁻**" for releasing Au⁺ from gelatin |
| Au(CN)₂⁻ | **0.2 × 10³⁹** | **too stable to release Au⁺; not a sensitizer** |

`[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.176 (PDF 185), Fig. 6.7]` **[Q]** — this is the quantitative version of Duffin's 1966 statement that "the very stable gold cyanide complex salt, K Au(CN)₂, does not sensitize at all" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.93 (PDF 99)]`, and it is the same physical argument with numbers attached: too labile and the gold never leaves the gelatin, too stable and it never leaves the complex.
- **Electron affinities: gold 2.4 eV versus silver 1.1 eV.** This is the evidence that gold atoms are actually *incorporated* into latent image centres — the oxidation potential of gold-sensitized image centres is more positive. `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.177 (PDF 186)]` **[Q]**
- **Gold latensification proceeds by plating, not replacement:** Agₙ → AgₙAu_m, not Agₙ → Ag₍ₙ₋ₘ₎Au_m, concluded from the absence of any loss of developability after removal of gold with KCN. `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.178 (PDF 187)]` **[F]**
- Sensitometric consequences, confirmed independently of mechanism: **improvement in high-intensity reciprocity law failure** with gold latensification (James); and a **narrower distribution of development rate** of latent image centres in gold-plus-sulfur than in sulfur-only emulsions (Spencer). `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.177 (PDF 186)]` **[F]**
- Gold as a fog source: Au⁺ disproportionates (Tani's Eq. 6.7, body lost in the OCR); **Au₂ is a development (fog) centre**; candidate fog centres include Au₂S or mixed Au₂S/Ag₂S clusters. But "the developability of Au₂S clusters is **smaller** than that of Ag₂S clusters", so applying gold to *over*-sulfur-sensitized grains converts Ag₂S clusters into Au₂S clusters — which is why "**gold sensitization could reduce the fog density of excessively sulfur-sensitized emulsions**." `[Tani 1995, §6.3, pp.179–180 (PDF 188–189)]` **[M]**

That last point is a genuine reversal of the naive expectation and it is worth stating plainly: gold normally *raises* fog liability (Duffin 1966, Mitchell's Au⁺–Ag stability argument, §8.4.4), but on an emulsion that has already been over-sulfur-sensitized, gold can *lower* fog by converting the fogging clusters to a less developable form. The two statements are not in conflict — they apply on opposite sides of the sulfur optimum. **[E]**

#### 8.5.6 Reduction sensitization, 1995 — the R/P distinction

The 1995 account splits reduction sensitization into two centre types with opposite functions, a distinction absent from 1966:

| Centre | Site | Species | Trap type | Photographic function |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **R centre** | electrically **neutral** kink/site | Ag₂ | **positive-hole** trap | retards recombination; and liberates an **extra free electron** on trapping a hole |
| **P centre** | **positively charged** kink or jog site | Ag₂ | **electron** trap | precursor of a latent image centre |

`[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.96–99 (PDF 105–108), Figs. 4.9–4.12; §6.4, pp.181–182 (PDF 190–191)]` **[Q]**

The site-charge rule, stated generally: "an electron-trapping silver cluster is formed at a positively charged site, while a hole-trapping center is formed at an electrically neutral site." Hamilton and Baetzold's MO calculations on Ag₂/AgBr models: "**Ag2 at a positively charged kink site is an electron trap, while Ag2 at a neutral kink site is a positive hole trap.**" `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, p.97 (PDF 106), Fig. 4.11]` **[M]**

Discriminated experimentally by photoconductivity: "**R centers increase sensitivity without an influence on photoconductivity, whereas P centers increase sensitivity with decreasing photoconductivity**." The HOMO of R lies **higher** than that of P and higher than the AgBr valence-band top. `[Tani 1995, §6.4, pp.181–182 (PDF 190–191)]` **[Q]**

Absolute absorption identification of the centres, from diffuse reflection spectra of thick layers of reduction-sensitized emulsion (octahedral AgBr, average diameter **0.2 µm**; sensitizer **DMAB, dimethylamine borane**; sensitivity by **10 s** exposure), Kubelka–Munk analysis with (1 − R)²/2R ∝ absorption coefficient:

| Absorption peak | Assignment |
|---|---|
| **474 nm** | **P centres** |
| **540 nm** | **fog centres** |

Dose–response: "the absorption coefficient of P centers was proportional to the **square** of the amount of reduction sensitizer, indicating that a P center was **Ag2**"; and "With a further increase in the amount of reduction sensitizer, the absorption coefficient of P centers was **saturated** and the absorption coefficient of fog centers increased in **proportion** to the amount of reduction sensitizer." `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.98–100 (PDF 107–109), Figs. 4.12, 4.13, 4.14]` **[Q]**

So the fog channel is **first order** in reduction sensitizer while the useful channel is **second order and saturating** — which is the quantitative statement of why over-reduction-sensitization is all fog and no speed. **[E]**

Redox potentials of the reduction centres: emulsions equilibrated in redox buffer solutions, E_ox taken as the redox potential eliminating **half** the sensitizing effect, **17 and 41 hours at 25 °C**, octahedral AgBr 0.2 µm. "the oxidation potential of P centers was more positive by about **0.4 V** than that of R centers, indicating that the HOMO level of P centers was about 0.4 eV lower than that of R centers. The oxidation potential of R centers in the interior of the grains was **0.05 V** less positive than that of P centers." Fig. 4.18 compares P centres against latent image centres on **unsensitized (U)**, **sulfur-sensitized (S)** and **sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized (S+Au)** grains: E_ox(P) is more positive than E_ox(latent image centres), so HOMO(Ag₂) lies below HOMO(Agₙ, n > 2) and LUMO(Ag₂) above — **which is why a P centre cannot itself initiate development.** `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.102–104 (PDF 111–113), Figs. 4.17, 4.18]` **[Q]**

Sensitizers named in 1995: **SnCl₂, dimethylamineborane (DMAB), aminoiminomethanesulfinic acid (thiourea dioxide), hydrazine derivatives**; also **silver digestion at low pAg** and **hydrogen gas**. Reduction centres are **removable by ferricyanide**, whereas sulfur centres require bromine water — a clean chemical discrimination. Reduction centres are made developable by **gold latensification**. `[Tani 1995, §6.4, pp.180–181 (PDF 189–190)]` **[F]**

Surface-versus-internal effects, with two conflicting reports given side by side. Tani's own reading: "the electron-trapping centers increased the surface sensitivity of the AgBr grains, which was otherwise in competition with internal sensitivity, and … hole-trapping centers increased the surface sensitivity of the AgBr grains, which was otherwise reduced by recombination". Moisar's: "hole-trapping reduction sensitization centers increased both surface and internal sensitivities, while electron-trapping centers increased surface sensitivity and decreased internal sensitivity." `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, p.97 (PDF 106)]` — the two accounts agree on electron-trapping centres and disagree on whether hole-trapping centres help the internal image. **[F]**

Crystal-habit dependence: reduction centres on **octahedral** AgBr contain **more electron-trapping (P) centres** than on cubic, judged from photoelectron lifetimes; and **neutral fog centres form more easily on cubic than on octahedral grains**. The fog centre's charge then affects developer choice: "The developability of the [positively charged] was larger with a **negatively charged developing agent** than with a neutral agent, while the developability of the [neutral] was not dependent upon the charge of the developing agent." `[Tani 1995, §6.4, pp.181–182 (PDF 190–191), Figs. 6.8, 6.9]` **[Q]**

#### 8.5.7 Cooperation and incompatibility between sensitization types

- "**Sulfur-plus-gold sensitization is particularly effective and is widely used in practical photographic materials.**" **[F]**
- "Sulfur sensitization and reduction sensitization can effectively cooperate…" **[F]**
- "However, there is some difficulty with cooperation between **gold sensitization and reduction sensitization, since reduction sensitization centers are inclined to be converted into development centers (i.e., fog centers) by gold sensitization.**" **[F]**

`[Tani 1995, §6.1, pp.165–166 (PDF 174–175)]`

#### 8.5.8 Hydrogen hypersensitization — the most efficient combination reported

> "Hydrogen hypersensitization was invented by Babcock et al. and enabled the most efficient latent image formation thus far on fine AgBr grains in combination with sulfur-plus-gold sensitization. Babcock and James found that only **two to three absorbed photons per grain** were required to make more than half of the grains developable."

`[Tani 1995, §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101)]` **[Q]**

Further properties: effective for sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized emulsions **without severe fog**; "hardly forms P centers"; and — the only humidity dependence anywhere in the Tani material — "**The rate of hydrogen hypersensitization decreased markedly with increasing relative humidity**", the reaction occurring in **dry** emulsion layers. Fig. 6.10 conditions: **0.15 µm cubic AgBr**, optimum S+Au, held in **room air / vacuum / hydrogen at 23 °C for 6 h**, exposed to **400 nm for 100 s**. `[Tani 1995, §6.4, pp.182–183 (PDF 191–192), Fig. 6.10]` **[Q]**

#### 8.5.9 Dopants: Ir, Rh, Ru, and the divalent-ion screen

These are not "chemical sensitization" in the classical sense (they are incorporated during precipitation, not during digestion) but they are the 1995 way of buying reciprocity behaviour and contrast, and the numbers are the only ones in the material:

| Dopant | Centre | Thermal trap depth | Lifetime | Photographic effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ir³⁺ | `[(IrCl₆)⁴⁻V]⁰` | **0.46 eV** | **~20 msec at room temperature** | shallow trapping, thermal re-excitation and repeated retrapping delays annihilation → "the addition of Ir3+ **reduces high-intensity reciprocity law failure** of emulsions when this decay mechanism predominates" |
| Rh³⁺ | `[(RhCl₆)⁴⁻]⁰` | **~0.8 eV** | **> 10⁵ sec at 300 K** | "The sensitivity of the emulsion is reduced as a result of Rh3+ doping, but **the contrast is increased**, making it suitable for applications in printing industries" |
| Both Rh³⁺ and Ir³⁺ | — | — | — | "reduce the photoelectron lifetime to about **10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁹ sec**" |
| `[Ru(NO)Cl₅]²⁻` → `[Ru(NO)Cl₅]³⁻` | — | "in excess of **1.2 eV**" | raw string "**1.6 X 109 sec**" | **OCR flag: 1.6 × 10⁹ s ≈ 50 years is implausible for a trap lifetime; a negative exponent or a broken superscript is suspected. Quote the raw string; do not use the value.** |

`[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.72–73 (PDF 81–82)]` **[Q]**

The divalent-ion screen, over the series Hg²⁺, Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺, Ni²⁺, Co²⁺, Cd²⁺, Fe²⁺, Zn²⁺, Ba²⁺, Sr²⁺, Mn²⁺ (ordered by redox potential): "only Hg2+ and Cu2+ could decrease the luminescence intensity and photographic sensitivity of a cubic AgBr emulsion by providing deep traps for electrons". `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.71 (PDF 80)]` **[F]**

### 8.6 The key quantitative result: gold lowers the minimum developable centre from 4–5 atoms to 3

This is the single most important number in the chemical-sensitization literature covered here, because it converts a chemistry into a threshold, and a threshold into a speed.

> "the smallest latent image center is composed of **three atoms** on sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized emulsion grains and of **four to five atoms** on sulfur-sensitized emulsion grains."

`[Tani 1995, §4.1.1, p.83 (PDF 92)]` — attributed to Hailstone and Hamilton, by computer simulation of sensitometry. **[Q]**

Corroborating, from evaporated metal clusters tested for their ability to initiate physical development: "Hamilton and Logel, by analyzing the ability of evaporated metal clusters to initiate physical development, estimated that the smallest latent image center is composed of **four silver atoms or two gold atoms**." `[Tani 1995, §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101); restated §6.3, p.177 (PDF 186)]` **[Q]**

And in Tani's own schematic of the sensitization types, the smallest latent image centre drawn for the gold case is "**three atoms containing a gold atom**". `[Tani 1995, Fig. 6.1, p.166 (PDF 175)]` **[Q]**

The chain of reasoning that makes this a *speed* statement rather than a curiosity is Duffin's, from 1966, before the numbers existed: gold acts "in the secondary stages of latent-image formation by reducing the number of quanta needed to form a stable development centre", and "**gold increases the speed by reducing the contrast**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.186–187 (PDF 192–193)]`. Duffin's Chapter IX also supplies the population argument: "**The number of quanta per crystal required to render a grain developable, controls the contrast.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.185 (PDF 191), Fig. 9.12]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Put together: dropping the threshold from 4–5 atoms to 3 atoms is worth roughly the observed 0.33 log E (×2 to ×2½) that Duffin measured for S+Au over S alone `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.92, 96 (PDF 98, 102)]`, and it must simultaneously *reduce* gamma, because a lower per-grain threshold narrows nothing about the grain-volume distribution but does move every grain's threshold down by the same integer step, compressing the spread of effective grain sensitivities less than it shifts them. Speed and gamma from gold are therefore not independent knobs; the sources assert the coupling (speed ↑, gamma ↓, fog liability ↑) but give no transfer function.

### 8.7 The optimum-then-decline behaviour

Every era states it; only 1995 explains it.

**1929:** "**The action reaches a maximum effect for a certain quantity and then decreases as the amount of the active material is increased, with corresponding increase in fog.**" `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.27 (PDF 35)]` **[F]**

**1966:** Fig. 5.1 is the picture — speed rises through digestion and "**as this reaches its maximum value the onset of fog occurs**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89)]`; and on dose rather than time, "**larger quantities produce lower maximum speed**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.95 (PDF 101), Fig. 5.8]`. Duffin also gives the competition explanation for the dose side: higher speed from *smaller* quantities of sulphur sensitizer is attributed to **decreased competition between multiple sensitivity specks on one grain** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.185 (PDF 191)]`. **[Q]**

**1995:** "…it is usually observed that photographic sensitivity increases, reaches a maximum, and then decreases by increasing the number of electron-trapping sensitization centers." The mechanism: added centres **enhance nucleation** but **disturb growth**, because they "further enhance nucleation by **decreasing the mobility and diffusion length of photoelectrons**", raising the chance that a subsequent electron starts a *competing* nucleus rather than growing the existing one. The formation of more than one image centre on a grain "wastes photoelectrons and is called **dispersion of image centers**." `[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.87–88 (PDF 96–97), Fig. 4.2; §8.1.1, p.232 (PDF 241)]` **[Q]**

Fig. 4.2 is the source's own optimum curve: surface sensitivity (a) and internal sensitivity (b) of sulfur-sensitized tabular AgBr grains against amount of **sodium thiosulfate**, **10 s exposure**, equivalent circular diameter **1.1 µm**. `[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.87–88 (PDF 96–97), Fig. 4.2]` **[Q]**

The same non-monotonic law holds for crystal defects, not just sensitizer: "Farnell examined the photographic sensitivity of emulsion grains as a function of the density of crystal defects, and found that the grains with few crystal defects as well as those with too many crystal defects suffered from low efficiency for latent image formation, and grains with a **medium number of defects showed the highest sensitivity**." `[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.89–90 (PDF 98–99)]` **[F]**

And for interstitial silver ion concentration: "**dispersion decreases then increases with interstitial-Ag⁺ concentration**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.232 (PDF 241)]` **[F]**

The factors Tani names as controlling the nucleation rate, and therefore the position of the optimum: **number, cross-section and depth of the electron traps**, plus the **interstitial-Ag⁺ concentration**. `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.232 (PDF 241)]` **[M]**

**Over-sensitization raises fog without raising speed** because the two channels have different dose orders (§8.5.6: fog ∝ dose¹, useful centres ∝ dose² then saturating) and because the useful channel has an internal competition (dispersion) that the fog channel does not. **[E]**

### 8.8 A note on the efficiency range that sensitization spans

Two figures bound it, both from Tani:

| Emulsion state | Photons absorbed per grain required |
|---|---|
| Unsensitized octahedral AgBr, 0.2 µm, high-pressure mercury lamp in a photochemical reactor | **about 5000 photons/grain**, with latent-image centre concentration **1 per grain** (OCR reads "(I/grain)") |
| H-hypersensitized + sulfur-plus-gold, fine AgBr | **2–3 absorbed photons/grain** to make more than half the grains developable |

`[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, p.101 (PDF 110), Figs. 4.15, 4.16; §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** That is roughly three decades of quantum sensitivity attributable purely to sensitization state, on grains of comparable size. It is the strongest single quantitative statement about what chemical sensitization is worth. The two measurements are not on identical emulsions (0.2 µm octahedral versus "fine AgBr") so the ratio is indicative, not a controlled comparison.

### 8.9 Stabilizers and antifoggants

#### 8.9.1 Definitions

Tani's definitions are precise and should be used:

> "**Stabilizers** are agents that decrease the changes in developable fog and/or other sensitometric characteristics of emulsion layers that occur **during storage**. **Antifoggants** are agents that **decrease the rate of fog density growth during development to a larger degree than they decrease the rate of development of latent images.**"

`[Tani 1995, §6.5, p.184 (PDF 193)]` **[F]** — note that the antifoggant definition is an explicit statement of *differential rate selectivity*: two competing rate constants, and the agent must slow the fog one more than the image one.

Duffin's version of the same distinction, and his own doubt about it: antifoggants are "substances which combat fog formation under **vigorous conditions of processing**", but the stabilizer/antifoggant split "is rather an artificial one". Because a fog grain is "one which will develop without light exposure", "**the nature of the development influences the fog**" — so sensitometric testing must use the processing the material will actually receive. "An emulsion may be acceptably low-fog in a conventional developer yet foggy, when aged, in a developer of very high activity." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.148–149 (PDF 154–155)]` **[F]**

#### 8.9.2 Compound families and their concentrations, 1966

All per **gram-mole of silver** unless stated:

| Agent | Quantity | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Most active organic mercapto compounds, e.g. **1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole** | **1–10 mg** | "completely and rapidly adsorbed; none left in aqueous phase" |
| Older types, e.g. **5-nitrobenziminazole** | **up to 100 mg** | |
| **Tetrazaindenes** | **up to several grams** | only "a few per cent" / "about 10 %" adsorbed; adsorption slow. Similar quantities of *other* heterocyclics "would desensitize an emulsion completely, largely by making it undevelopable" |
| **Benzenesulphinic acid** | **up to 10 g** | "apparently not adsorbed to the crystal surface… functions in the bulk of the emulsion" |
| Water-soluble **cadmium** salt (chloride or nitrate) | **5–25 g** | good stability on chlorobromides, "where it may increase the speed", and on iodobromides. "Many modern lithographic emulsions, all chlorobromides, contain large quantities of cadmium salts" |
| **Mercuric chloride HgCl₂** | **0.02–0.25 mg** | effective in iodobromide emulsions |
| Complex mercury derivatives — 8-chloromercuriquinoline, bis(2-amino-5-iodopyridine hydroiodide)mercuric iodide | **up to 25 mg** | |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.142–143 (PDF 148–149)]` **[Q]**

Note the **five-decade span** of effective dose across this table, from 0.02 mg (HgCl₂) to 10 g (benzenesulphinic acid) per gram-mole of silver — because the mechanisms differ: strongly adsorbed species work at monolayer-fraction coverage on the grain, weakly adsorbed ones work in the gelatin bulk. **[E]**

The named compound inventory, structures lost to OCR but names intact: tetrazaindenes/triazaindolizines and a 6-substituted series; pyrimidines — 2-mercapto-4-hydroxypyrimidine, 2-amino-4-hydroxypyrimidine, 2-mercapto-4-methylpyrimidine; benziminazoles — 5-nitrobenziminazole, 2-mercaptobenziminazole; 2-mercaptobenzothiazole; 2-mercapto-4-methylthiazole; 2-mercaptobenzoxazole; 4,5-diphenyl-2-mercapto-oxazole; 2-mercapto-1,3,4-oxadiazoles; 2-mercapto-1,2,4-triazoles; 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole; benzotriazole and 6-nitrobenzotriazole; 3,3′-dipyrazolyl ("a recently described stabilizer"); benzene sulphinic acid. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.139–141 (PDF 145–147)]` **[F]**

#### 8.9.3 The surface-coverage calculation, 1966 — fully reconstructible

Duffin's worked example, for the reference iodobromide emulsion of his Chapter IV:

| Step | Value |
|---|---|
| Grains per gram-mole Ag | **4 × 10¹⁴** (raw OCR `4x 104`; the exponent is recoverable because the author's arithmetic only closes at 10¹⁴) |
| Dose of 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole (M = 178) | **5 mg per gram-mole Ag** |
| Molecules per grain | ≈ **0.5 × 10⁵ = 50,000** |
| Area occupied per stabilizer molecule | **about 60 Å²** (printed as "0.60/10⁸ µ²" — an OCR/typesetting error; 60 Å² = 0.60 × 10⁻⁶ µ², and only that value closes the author's own arithmetic) |
| Surface area of one triangular grain in this emulsion | **≈ 2 µ²** |
| Room available on one grain | **about 3 × 10⁶** molecules |
| Resulting coverage | **about 1 % of the grain surface** |

"A fine-grain emulsion for example of **0.2 µ side**, will possess an even higher surface area per gram molecule of silver and the coverage will be still lower… **a selective function is demanded rather than blanket action**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.142 (PDF 148)]` **[Q]**

Duffin explicitly rejects blanket-coverage explanations on exactly these grounds, and also rejects a pH explanation: "Rejected: hydroxyl-ion-concentration effect (pH experiments negative); complete surface blanketing (quantities too small)." What he does accept as a prerequisite is **adsorption to the grain, usually via silver-salt formation**. Silver salts of the older stabilizers are "exceedingly insoluble, commonly approaching the insolubility of silver iodide", so pAg rises; but tetrazaindenes "have less effect on the silver-ion concentration than that produced by the added bromide", so silver-ion reduction alone cannot explain them. Removing the hydroxy group from a tetrazaindene destroys both antifoggant power and silver-salt formation. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.143–146 (PDF 149–152)]` **[M]**

#### 8.9.4 Effect on speed — a genuine disagreement across eras

**1966, Duffin, on tetrazaindenes:** "The outstanding advantage of this class of compounds is that as well as conferring great stability upon emulsions of many kinds, particularly those of high speed, **no speed loss occurs** when they are added; on the contrary **a slight speed increase is frequently detectable**… either on the addition of the stabilizer or after a short heat treatment." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.139 (PDF 145), Fig. 7.1]` **[F]**

**1966, Duffin, on mercapto compounds:** "Many of these mercapto derivatives, 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole is a well-known example, cause a **marked speed loss particularly in iodobromide emulsions**… they are quite useless in many high-speed commercial emulsions. On the other hand, 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole has far less effect on the speed of **chloride and chlorobromide** emulsions, at the quantities found to be effective, and is therefore commonly used in **paper** emulsions." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.141 (PDF 147)]` **[F]**

**1995, Tani, generalising the speed increase:** "It has generally been believed that stabilizers and antifoggants decrease photographic sensitivity, or at most do not change it. Tani has described a new photographic phenomenon…: **They actually can increase photographic sensitivity of emulsions with and without spectral sensitization.**" `[Tani 1995, §6.5, p.191 (PDF 200)]` **[F]**

So the received view Tani is arguing against (stabilizers cost speed) is *not* the view Duffin held in 1966 for tetrazaindenes specifically — Duffin already reported a slight gain there. The 1995 novelty is the generality of the claim and the mechanisms measured for it. **[E]**

Tani's measured mechanisms for the speed increase, all for **TAI** = 4-hydroxy-6-methyl-1,3,3a,7-tetraazaindene:

1. **TAI increased surface sensitivity and decreased internal sensitivity** of sulfur-sensitized octahedral (1.2 µm) and cubic (0.7 µm) AgBr. Fig. 6.16 conditions: exposure **1 s**; **D19** for surface development; **D19 + KI at 0.5 g/l** for internal development after bleaching surface centres. **[Q]**
2. Photoelectron lifetimes: τ(S) < τ(U); **both increase** with added TAI, and the **fraction of photoelectrons captured by sulfur sensitization centres F_s increases** with TAI (Fig. 6.17; trapping probabilities 1/τ(S), 1/τ(U), 1/τ(Ag₂S); the Eq. 6.14-set bodies are lost in the OCR). **[Q]**
3. TAI **raises the Dember photovoltage**, hence photoelectron mobility, by lowering the interstitial-Ag⁺ concentration (Fig. 6.18). **[Q]**
4. Possibly reduced band bending in the space-charge layers. **[S]**
5. **TAI reduces hole-trapping desensitization by cyanine dyes.** **[F]**
6. TAI **retards dispersion of latent image centres** — "sensitization by TAI was pronounced with **high-intensity exposures** and almost disappeared after **gold latensification**"; and "Sensitization by stabilizers and antifoggants was **pronounced for emulsions with added cyanine dyes**." **[Q]**

`[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.192–194 (PDF 201–203), Figs. 6.16–6.18]`

Also from Tani: **all the agents studied decreased the ionic conductivity** (hence the interstitial-Ag⁺ concentration) of AgBr grains, and the capability tracked adsorptivity. Fig. 6.15 plots the ionic conductivity of **0.5 µm cubic AgBr** against amount of benzotriazole, measured by **Dember photovoltage decay**. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.189, 191 (PDF 198, 200), Fig. 6.15]` **[Q]**

Duffin's 1966 inorganic analogue of exactly this: cadmium ions greatly decrease the concentration of interstitial silver ions (Brady & Hamilton, *J. app. Phys.* **35**, 1565 (1964)), and "a considerable parallel" is suggested with the organic stabilizers. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.148 (PDF 154)]` **[F]**

#### 8.9.5 The physical-chemical constants of the three stabilizer families, 1995

These are the only tabulated acidity and silver-salt-solubility data in the material, and they are what makes adsorptivity predictable.

| Compound | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pKa | 6.27 | 5.86 | 5.32 | 3.38 | 6.41 | 6.10 | 6.53 |
| pK_sp | 10.5 | 10.0 | 9.3 | — | — | 10.2 | 10.8 |

**Table 6.4 — benzotriazoles (compounds 8–12; R = Bz, Cl, H, CH₃, NO₂)**

| Compound | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pKa | 7.49 | 7.54 | 8.30 | 8.50 | 6.40 |
| pK_sp | 12.8 | 12.9 | 13.6 | 13.7 | 11.9 |

**Table 6.5 — mercaptoazoles (compounds 13–19)**

| Compound | 13 | 14 | 15 | 16 | 17 | 18 | 19 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pKa | 2.95 | 7.68 | 7.28 | 4.81 | 6.94 | 10.07 | 4.31 |
| pK_sp | 16.1 | 16.1 | 15.9 | 16.5 | 16.5 | 16.5 | 16.8 |

`[Tani 1995, §6.5, Tables 6.3–6.5, pp.184–185 (PDF 193–194)]` **[Q]**

Structure–property relations: pKa is **linear in Hammett σ_m** for the tetraazaindenes and benzotriazoles (Fig. 6.11); **pK_sp is linear in pKa with slope ≈ 1** for those two families; but mercaptoazole pK_sp is **very large and independent of pKa** (Fig. 6.12). Adsorptivity order: **mercaptoazoles > benzotriazoles > 4-hydroxy-tetraazaindenes** — which is precisely the order of Duffin's 1966 dose table in reverse (the most adsorbed need the least). `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.186–189 (PDF 195–198), Figs. 6.11, 6.12]` **[Q]**

pH-dependent reversals of adsorptivity are predicted by Tani's Eq. (6.12) (body lost) plotted against pH in Fig. 6.13, and confirmed by measured isotherms: **nitrobenzotriazole (12) adsorbs less than compounds 8–11 at pH 10 but more at pH 5**. Isotherms measured at **pH 5, 7 and 10, at 30 °C**, on AgBr of **specific surface area 0.271 m²/g** (Fig. 6.14). `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.186–189 (PDF 195–198), Figs. 6.13, 6.14]` **[Q]**

#### 8.9.6 Alkyl-chain length versus stabilizing efficiency — Duffin's Table 7.1

Birr varied the side chain R on a 6-substituted tetrazaindene from H through carbon groups of 1 to 17 atoms and "found that there was a general relationship between the amount adsorbed to the crystal surface and the stabilizing efficiency, **which dropped as the carbon chain became longer and the quantity adsorbed increased**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.144 (PDF 150)]` **[F]**

**TABLE 7.1 — EFFECT ON SENSITIVITY AND STABILIZATION OF A SERIES OF COMPOUNDS** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.145 (PDF 151)]`

The header row survived OCR only as fragments — raw strings, in file order: `Number / of / Foo: / carbon / atoms / uantit / uantit / uantit / rie / es / inside-chainSe / Ane / hsmee / Sensitivityiat bigoe / R / incubation*`. Six columns are identifiable: (1) number of carbon atoms in side-chain R; (2)(3)(4) three "Quantity" columns; (5) "Sensitivity at …"; (6) "Fog after incubation\*". **The three sub-headings distinguishing the Quantity columns, the units of Quantity, the qualifier on "Sensitivity at …", and the footnote \* are all lost.**

| R carbons | Qty A | Qty B | Qty C | Sensitivity | Fog after incubation\* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | — | — | — | **unreadable** (raw `INS)`) | 1.66 |
| 0 | 2.18 | 1.0 | 1.18 | 21.5 | 1.42 |
| 1 | 15.65 | 1.0 | 14.65 | 21.5 | 0.05 |
| 2 | 2.63 | 1.0 | 1.63 | 21.5 | 0.59 |
| 3 | 17.89 | 1.0 | 16.89 | 21.5 | 0.0 |
| 4 | 1.34 | 1.0 | 0.34 | 20.5 | **1.32** (raw reads `1632`; the column context makes it 1.32, a lost decimal point) |
