| 11 | 1.00 | 1.0 | 0 | 19.0 | 0.06 |

Two of the "21.5" entries appear in the raw OCR as `DAES`, `21S`, `Dib`. **[Q]**

Arithmetic check that survives independently of the headers: in every complete row Qty A = Qty B + Qty C exactly, and Qty B is constant at 1.0 — consistent with an experiment in which enough compound was added (Qty A) to leave a *fixed* amount adsorbed (Qty B = 1.0, arbitrary units) with the balance free in solution (Qty C). **That column assignment is our inference from the arithmetic, not the book's text.** **[E]**

The modellable part is the Sensitivity column: **21.5 → 20.5 → 19.0** as R grows from 0–3 to 4–7 to 11 carbons, i.e. progressive desensitization with alkyl chain length; "the same relation between desensitizing action and the size of the alkyl substituent has been confirmed by Russian workers." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.147 (PDF 153)]` **[Q]**

#### 8.9.7 Antifoggants against specific fog channels, 1966

A whole antifoggant class exists specifically against fog caused by **long-chain polyethylene oxides**, a fog "particularly pronounced with gold-sensitized emulsions because gold and polyethylene oxides are frequently used together." Active against it: cadmium and mercury compounds; acidic heterocyclics — 3,5-dihydroxy-1,2,4-triazole, 2-guanidobenziminazole, 4,5-diphenyl-2-mercapto-oxazole, 5-mercapto-3-methyl-1,2,4-thiadiazole; non-salt-forming heterocyclics — 2,4,6-triethylthio-1,3,5-triazine, the ester of 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole; **phenols** — p-substituted phenols, a bis-phenol, and phenolic aldoximes such as salicylaldoxime; **polymers** — polyvinylpyrrolidone and its vinyl-acetate copolymers, iodine complexes of polyvinyl oxazolidone. "Probably because of their fairly recent introduction, **there is no published work on how these substances function**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.149–151 (PDF 155–157)]` **[F]**

Good general-purpose antifoggants, 1966: **benzotriazole** and **5-nitrobenziminazole** — low restraining activity for digestion but effective in both black-and-white and colour developers; a mercapto tetrazaindene is "very active". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.149 (PDF 155)]` **[F]**

One mechanistic caution on sulphinic acids, worth keeping because it reverses the expected sign: "oxidation is not usually regarded as a common cause of fog; **reduction is much more likely to produce fog**. Oxidation would more likely cause **loss of sensitivity** and it is in preventing this that these sulphinic acids could be effective although they are referred to as anti-foggants." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.141 (PDF 147)]` **[M]**

Also: fog need not be neutral. "Fog produced under these conditions may not result in the formation of a **neutral** overall density; **sulphide contamination** of films… can cause the formation of **yellow fog**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.149 (PDF 155)]` **[F]** Duffin's Chapter V gives the same for the manufacturing side: "**Silver sulphide formed elsewhere, for example in the gelatin medium, usually gives yellow or dichroic fog.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 91)]` **[F]**

#### 8.9.8 The 1929 equivalent of a stabilizer: soluble bromide, and Wall's warnings

Wall has no heterocyclic stabilizers — the class was discovered in 1935, six years after his book. His restrainer is soluble bromide, and he reports it as being on its way out:

| Addition | Quantity | Stated effect |
|---|---|---|
| Soluble bromide (Eder) | **0.1 to 3 parts KBr or NH₄Br per 1000** (larger for foggy emulsions) | restrains fog; "if added in anything like large quantities it certainly slows the plates, that is **increases the inertia** of the plate with normal time of development" |
| Hydrobromic acid | 5 parts of a 1 % solution per 1000 = **0.005 % HBr** | "probably a negligible quantity" |
| Sodium carbonate | **0.1 to 5 g per litre** | "more details in the shadows and making the plates faster"; Wall calls it dangerous and "not likely to improve the keeping power" |
| Phenol / thymol | 5 parts per 1000 / 0.25 parts | antiseptic |
| Formaldehyde | — | "**Under no circumstances should formaldehyde be used as a hardener**" — "this inevitably… leads eventually to **fog on keeping**" |

`[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, pp.152–155 (PDF 159–162)]` **[Q]**

And the dated obsolescence note: bromide restrainer in the emulsion is "an heirloom from the early days when a clean-working emulsion was practically an exception. **The practice has fallen to a great extent into disuse**, except possibly for transparency and paper emulsions." `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.154 (PDF 161)]` **[F]**

Wall's 1929 antifoggant practice is therefore essentially *raw-material purity control* (§8.3) plus bromide, plus process hygiene: fog is attributed to pyridine/pyrrole/aniline in the ammonia, silver nitrite in the silver nitrate, metallic salts above 50 ppm in the gelatine, silver in excess of the halide, warm or long washing ("washing fog"), combustion products in the drying air, and static discharge during stripping. `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, pp.12, 25 (PDF 20, 33); Ch. III, pp.32–33 (PDF 40–41); Ch. VIII, p.145 (PDF 152); Ch. XI, p.185 (PDF 192); Ch. XII, pp.211, 215 (PDF 218, 222)]` **[F]**

### 8.10 What changed between the three eras

| Question | 1929 (Wall) | 1966 (Duffin) | 1995 (Tani) |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is the sensitivity centre? | Ag₂S nuclei from gelatine sulphur, "discrete and not above a certain size" | **Unresolved**: Ag₂S islands (James & Vanselow) vs silver only (Chibisov) vs adsorbed thiosulphate complex (Sauvenier & Hautot). Duffin leans to Ag₂S at reactive sites | **(Ag₂S)₂ dimer, solid-solution type** — S²⁻ on a lattice site, charge-compensated by an interstitial Ag⁺; distinct from the fogging **Ag₂S cluster** |
| How is it characterised? | not at all | by chemistry, adsorption and reaction rate | by **trap depth (eV)**, **number density (per µm² of a named face)**, **oxidation potential (mV)**, **cluster stoichiometry** |
| Is the sensitizer dosed deliberately? | No — controlled by gelatine selection; "active" vs "inert" gelatines | **Transitional**: "It is now more usual to add known amounts of these sensitizers … before the digestion stage in order to permit control" | Yes, throughout |
| Gold sensitization | **does not exist** (gold is a toner only) | ×2 to ×2½ speed, 0.33 log E, 1–30 mg Au per mole Ag, always with sulphur; product identity unresolved | **Au⁺** centre; trap depth 0.19 eV vs 0.33 eV for S; complex stability constants govern availability; plating not replacement; lowers threshold to **3 atoms** |
| Reduction sensitization | sulphite and stannous chloride known; speed gain reported | recognised as a third class; lower contrast, more fog; centres are silver atoms loosely attached, autocatalytic formation | split into **R centres** (neutral site, hole trap, supplies an extra electron) and **P centres** (charged site, electron trap); absorption at **474 nm** (P) and **540 nm** (fog); P ∝ dose², fog ∝ dose¹ |
| Minimum developable centre | not discussed (no latent-image concept) | **4** silver atoms (Farnell; ultracentrifuge and ultrasonic methods give 3–4); a separate illustrative calculation uses 100 | **3** atoms on S+Au; **4–5** on S; 4 Ag or 2 Au from evaporated clusters |
| Stabilizers | soluble bromide (0.1–3 parts per 1000), and it is falling out of use; raw-material purity limits | three organic families with doses spanning 0.02 mg to 10 g per mole Ag; tetrazaindenes give **no speed loss, often a slight gain**; mercaptos cost speed in iodobromide | pKa/pK_sp tables for 19 compounds; adsorptivity order and its pH reversals; stabilizers **can increase speed**, with six measured mechanisms |
| Fog theory | impurity- and process-driven; empirical | two fog chemistries (silver-type vs Ag₂S-type) discriminated by chromic-acid bleach and by gold post-treatment; "fog is probably silver in many cases" | fog centres are Ag₂S **clusters** (E_ox > 400 mV, oxidizable only by bromine water); storage fog has a named kinetic mechanism (aggregation step 2) |

### 8.11 Where the sources are silent, and where they disagree

**Silences a reader would expect filled:**

- **No source gives a sensitization recipe tied to a measured D–log E curve with numbers on both axes.** Duffin's Figs. 5.6, 5.7 and 5.9 are the closest — the only D–log E figure in his sensitization chapter — but their curves did not survive OCR; only axis labels and tick values are recoverable, and the gold-quantity abscissa unit is itself uncertain ("moles × 10⁵"(?)). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, pp.91–92, 96 (PDF 97–98, 102), Figs. 5.6, 5.7, 5.9]` **[F]**
- **No source gives a fog-density-versus-storage-time curve with axes in days and density.** Duffin gives the expectation ("**Modern photographic materials are expected to keep for at least two years**") and Tani gives the mechanism, but neither gives D_fog(t). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.137 (PDF 143)]` **[F]**
- **Tani gives no digestion time/temperature envelope of his own** comparable to Duffin's 40–70 °C / minutes-to-hours; only individual experimental conditions (60 °C/30 min, 60 °C/60 min, 40 °C/15 min). `[Tani 1995, §3.4.1, p.70 (PDF 79); §6.2, pp.171–172 (PDF 180–181)]` **[F]**
- **Selenium and tellurium sensitization**, present in Wall 1929, does not reappear in the 1966 or 1995 material covered here. **[F]**
- Tani's numbered display equations were images in the PDF and did not survive text extraction. For chemical sensitization this affects **Eqs. (6.1)–(6.13)** (including Eq. 6.7, the Au⁺ disproportionation; Eq. 6.12, the pH-dependent adsorptivity relation; and the Eq. 6.14-set for photoelectron trapping probabilities). The symbol definitions survive and are given above where relevant; **the functional forms are not recoverable from this material.** `[Tani 1995, §0 caveat; §§6.1–6.5, pp.165–199 (PDF 174–208)]` **[F]**

**Disagreements, presented unaveraged:**

1. **Sulfur centre thermal trap depth:** 0.33 eV (Hamilton, Harbison & Jeanmaire) vs 0.39 eV (Kellogg & Hodes) vs ~0.3 eV (Kanzaki & Tadakuma, from the optical band threshold). `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.73–74 (PDF 82–83); §6.2, pp.170–171 (PDF 179–180)]`
2. **S+Au centre thermal trap depth:** 0.19 eV vs 0.17 eV, same two groups. Same citation.
3. **Sulfur centre number density:** 1000/µm² (Keevert) vs 2800/µm² (Tadakuma, Yoshida & Kanzaki). `[Tani 1995, §6.2, p.171 (PDF 180)]`
4. **Hydroxyl-ion order of the sulphur-sensitization rate:** > 1 (James & Vanselow) vs 0.7 (Sutherns & Loening). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 91)]`
5. **Whether hole-trapping reduction centres raise internal sensitivity:** Tani says surface only; Moisar says both surface and internal. `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, p.97 (PDF 106)]`
6. **Fog margin on sulphur dose:** 100× between peak speed and fog onset (Tani, 0.2 µm octahedral AgBr) vs fog onset coincident with peak speed (Duffin, commercial fast iodobromide). `[Tani 1995, §6.2, p.171 (PDF 180), Fig. 6.3; Duffin 1966, Ch. V, p.83 (PDF 89), Fig. 5.1]`
7. **Minimum silver atoms for developability, within Duffin:** 4 (Chapter IX, measured) vs "as many as 100" (Chapter V, illustrative calculation). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.172 (PDF 178); Ch. V, p.90 (PDF 96)]`
8. **Whether restrainers affect crystal growth:** Wood says 10,000 ppm adenine has no influence on growth while 100 ppm affects sensitization; Steigmann attributes powerful growth restraint to cysteine and its thiazolidines. Duffin calls the position "confused". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.37–38 (PDF 41–42)]`

---

## 9. Spectral sensitization and sensitizing dyes

### 9.1 Definition, discovery, and the two sensitivities

Spectral sensitization renders silver halide responsive at wavelengths longer than those it absorbs intrinsically. "Spectral sensitization was discovered by Vogel in **1873** and is now widely used to render silver halides sensitive to wavelengths longer than that of blue light, such as green, red, and infrared…" `[Tani 1995, §5.1, p.111 (PDF 120)]` **[F]**

Tani's terminology, which should be used because it keeps the two contributions separate: "In this chapter the sensitivities of the excitation of silver halides and sensitizing dyes are called **intrinsic sensitivity** and **spectral sensitivity**, respectively. The former and the latter are also called **blue sensitivity** and **minus-blue sensitivity**, respectively, in the case of AgBr and AgBrI." `[Tani 1995, §5.1, p.111 (PDF 120)]` **[F]**

Duffin's version of the discovery, with the dye's own date: "**In 1873 Vogel**, seeking to obtain a filtering effect by the use of dyes, **discovered that silver-halide crystals could be spectrally sensitized**. This was quickly exploited commercially and one of the early dyes which was suitable was **Cyanine, which had been discovered by Greville Williams, as long ago as 1856**." He places the whole business in "the '**dyestuff era**' of organic chemistry, **between 1850 and 1910**". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.100–110 (PDF 106–116)]` **[F]**

The governing law is Grotthus–Draper, stated by Duffin as the reason spectral sensitization is even necessary: "only that light which is **absorbed** can be effective in producing a chemical change; the formation of a latent image is a chemical change." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.99 (PDF 105)]` **[F]**

### 9.2 The intrinsic absorption edges the dye has to work beyond

| Halide | Colour | Intrinsic absorption limit |
|---|---|---|
| AgCl | "colourless (white)" | "does not absorb light in the visible region of the spectrum to any extent but only in the near ultra-violet, and to some extent at the violet end of the visible spectrum" |
| AgBr | "pale yellow" | "absorbs light up to about **4,900 Å**" (≈490 nm) |
| AgBr + AgI | "somewhat deeper yellow" | "extends the light absorption further into the visible spectrum, **up to 5,200 Å**" (≈520 nm); "**the maximum effect is produced by about 2.0 % of iodide and higher values cause the colour to lighten**" |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.19 (PDF 23)]` **[Q]** — note the non-monotonicity above 2.0 mol % iodide, an unusual and specific claim.

Duffin's Fig. 6.1 "Spectral sensitivity of undyed emulsions" has two panels, **Chlorobromide** and **Iodobromide**, both on a wavelength axis **4000–7000 Å**; the curves were lost to OCR and only the axis ticks (4000, 5000, 6000, 7000 Å) and the panel labels survive. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.99 (PDF 105), Fig. 6.1]` **[F]**

Duffin also notes a long-wavelength tail beyond the intrinsic edge that is *not* dye-derived: silver sulphide or silver formed in chemical sensitization produces "appreciable long-wavelength sensitivity", present "even with the purest crystals" but stronger in chemically sensitized emulsions. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.132 (PDF 138)]` **[F]** This is the same phenomenon Tani quantifies as the red sensitivity of sulfur centres, from which their trap depths were measured (§8.5.1). `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.73 (PDF 82)]` **[F]**

The energy requirement, stated in calories by Duffin: to form a latent image by absorption *in the crystal*, light must have energy equivalent to **5,000 Å in silver bromide, corresponding to 57,000 cal per gram-mole**; in dye sensitization the light energy "can be less than half of this". No systematic difference between AgBr and AgCl, nor between green and infrared sensitization. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.131 (PDF 137), Figs. 6.10, 6.11]` **[Q]**

### 9.3 Mechanism: electron transfer, settled by 1995

**1995.** "After many debates by many groups of workers over the electron transfer versus energy transfer mechanism, it is now accepted that spectral sensitization in silver halide photographic materials takes place according to the **electron transfer mechanism** proposed by Gurney and Mott (i.e., the transfer of electrons from optically excited dye molecules to the conduction band of silver halides)." The dye must therefore do two things: absorb at the desired wavelength **and** transfer an electron to the AgX conduction band from its excited state. `[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.111 (PDF 120)]` **[F]**

**1966.** Duffin cannot settle it: both electron transfer and energy transfer are supported; "they both can function; one dye may sensitize by both mechanisms simultaneously or under different conditions". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.133 (PDF 139)]` **[M]** This is a genuine era difference: the mechanism was open in 1966 and closed by 1995.

The 1995 experimental disposal of the energy-transfer alternative: Kuhn *et al.* used Langmuir–Blodgett fatty-acid spacers in **27 Å steps** and found that energy transfer does operate under some conditions, "however, its rate was **considerably smaller than that of the electron transfer mechanism, even for the dyes that were in contact with silver halide**." The rival **semiconductor-junction model** (Meier, Levy) is contradicted by UV photoelectron spectroscopy showing that the **AgX Fermi level is lower than the dye's before contact**. `[Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.149–150 (PDF 158–159)]` **[F]**

The transfer is fast. Duffin 1966: transfer from dye to substrate "is achieved in a period of no more than `10-"` sec" — **OCR-damaged exponent; raw string is `10-"`; almost certainly 10⁻¹¹ s (West)**. "In terms of all normal photographic exposures [this] is instantaneous." Only a very short-lived excited state is responsible. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.130 (PDF 136)]` **[Q]** Tani 1995 gives the rate constant: the raw OCR reads "the rate constant of electron transfer from an excited dye molecule to the conduction band of a silver halide grain is on the order of **1(T10 to 1CT11 sec**" — **OCR garble; read as 10⁻¹⁰–10⁻¹¹ sec** as a *time*, i.e. k_s ≈ 10¹⁰–10¹¹ s⁻¹, consistent with the Marcus-fit maximum k° = 10¹¹ s⁻¹ below. "the values of k_s and k_L are **widely variable**, depending on the condition of spectral sensitization." `[Tani 1995, §5.6, pp.142–143 (PDF 151–152), Figs. 5.22, 5.24]` **[Q]**

The 1995 refinement of the mechanism is that the excited dye can inject **either** carrier. Fig. 5.31, the "modified electron transfer mechanism": an excited dye can inject an electron (forming latent image) **or** a hole (destroying latent image); "Spectral sensitization can be observed only when the formation of latent image centers due to electron transfer overcomes the destruction of centers due to hole transfer." Rate constants k_s1a/k_s1b (electron) and k_s2a/k_s2b (hole) enter through Eqs. (5.28)–(5.30) with constants β₁, β₂; when β₁ = β₂ the governing quantities become **(ε_LU + ε_HO)/2**, which Tani calls the "**quasi-Fermi level**", and **(E_R + E_ox)/2**, the "**hyper-redox potential**". "For practical sensitizing dyes, k_s1/k_s2 ≫ 1". And a design consequence: "The difference in sensitizing capability between **infrared-sensitizing dyes and desensitizing dyes** comes **not from the difference in ε_LU, but from the difference in (ε_LU + ε_HO)/2**." `[Tani 1995, §5.8, p.150 (PDF 159), Fig. 5.31]` **[M]** — the equation bodies are lost; only the symbol set and these stated conclusions survive.

Where does the injected electron go? Duffin 1966 supplies one number that is often misread: "photoelectrons induced by light absorbed by sensitizing dyes have been shown to **diffuse 40–50 microns in large sheet crystals**, i.e. as far as photoelectrons produced by light absorption by the halide." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.131 (PDF 137)]` **[Q]** This is a large-single-crystal laboratory result, orders of magnitude larger than any emulsion grain (0.2–2 µm); it establishes that dye-injected electrons are ordinary conduction-band electrons, and nothing more. **[E]**

### 9.4 Energy-level requirements, with the two threshold potentials

The dye's LUMO must lie above the AgX conduction-band bottom for electron injection; the direct spectroscopic demonstration is on evaporated AgBr: the LUMO of merocyanines with n = 0 and 1 (Dyes 42, 43) lie **above** the AgBr conduction-band bottom, while n = 2 and 3 (Dyes 44, 45) lie **below** it — consistent with their sensitizing ability. And: "the **vacuum level of each dye was considerably shifted to match its Fermi level with that of AgBr** when they were in contact." `[Tani 1995, §5.4, p.131 (PDF 140), Fig. 5.14]` **[Q]**

The two threshold reduction potentials are the most quantitative statement of the energy-level requirement in the material:

| Threshold | Value (E_R, V vs SCE) |
|---|---|
| Threshold E_R for **spectral sensitization** | **−1.42 V** |
| Threshold E_R for **electron-trapping desensitization** | **−1.25 V** |

The ~**0.2 V (0.2 eV)** difference between them is "the **first experimental evidence** of the difference in the electronic energy level between Dye\* and Dye⁻". `[Tani 1995, §5.5/§5.8, pp.139, 152 (PDF 148, 161), Fig. 5.20]` **[Q]**

*OCR note:* the Fig. 5.20 caption gives the thresholds as "−1.42 and −1.25 **eV**" while the body text uses **V vs SCE**; treat them as V vs SCE. **[F]**

Those two thresholds partition all dyes into three classes, which is also the classification that predicts whether supersensitization will help:

| Class | E_R | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Dye I** | more negative than **−1.42 V** | sensitizes; no supersensitization needed |
| **Dye II** | between **−1.42 and −1.25 V** | supersensitization helps |
| **Dye III** | less negative than **−1.25 V** | barely helped by supersensitization |

`[Tani 1995, §5.8, p.152 (PDF 161)]` **[Q]**

Substituent design rules on the energy levels, 1995: the π-electron in the HOMO is localised on **odd**-numbered atoms counting from the ends of the polymethine chain, and in the LUMO on **even** atoms. Therefore "the attachment of an electron-withdrawing substituent to an odd atom in the polymethine chain mainly lowers ε_HO and thus **increases E_TR**, and the attachment of an electron-withdrawing substituent to an even atom … mainly lowers ε_LU and thus **decreases E_TR**." `[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.117 (PDF 126), Fig. 5.3]` **[M]** More generally, **Hammett σ** is a good measure: electron-withdrawing substituents lower both ε_LU and ε_HO, electron-donating raise them, and the magnitude is proportional to the electron density in the LUMO/HOMO at the substituted atom (Fig. 5.11, for 5,5′-substituted 9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanines). `[Tani 1995, §5.4, pp.128–129 (PDF 137–138), Fig. 5.11]` **[Q]** No nm-per-substituent numbers are given.

Measurement technique matters here: **phase-selective second-harmonic voltammetry** (Lenhard, *J. Imaging Sci.* **30**, 27, **1986**) gives more accurate E_R and E_ox than conventional polarography, which is corrupted by secondary reactions of the oxidised or reduced dye. There is a linear relation between E_ox and the ionization energy I from UV photoelectron spectroscopy for Dyes 5–8 (Fig. 5.13). `[Tani 1995, §5.4, pp.129–130 (PDF 138–139)]` **[F]**

### 9.5 The transition energy and the medium shift — a usable one-parameter law

Tani's Eqs. (5.1) and (5.2) relate λ_max to the HOMO→LUMO transition energy; the equation bodies were images and are lost, but the symbol set survives: **λ_max** = wavelength of the absorption maximum; **E_TR** = transition energy from HOMO to LUMO; **ε_HO, ε_LU** = energy levels of HOMO and LUMO. Fig. 5.2 correlates calculated against observed E_TR, with the abscissa in units of **β**, "the resonance integral between 2p orbitals of two adjacent carbon atoms in a conjugated system", for **thiacyanine** and **2,2′-quinocyanine** series of varying polymethine chain length. "The agreement between them is fairly good, except for monomethine dyes with steric effects." `[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.113 (PDF 122), Eqs. (5.1), (5.2), Fig. 5.2]` **[F]**

The medium shift is the one place a fully stated functional form survived:

> "The value of E_TR of a molecule is usually a function of both the electrostatic dielectric constant (D) and the optical dielectric constant (n², where n is the refractive index) of its surrounding according to the theory of solvent effects of absorption spectra, as described by MacRae's equation. However, it was found that E_TO of symmetrical cyanine dyes in solutions, and even on the surface and in the interior of silver halide, was a **linear function of only (n² − 1)/(2n² + 1)** of solvents and silver halide."

`[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.117 (PDF 126)]` **[Q]** — the shift therefore arises solely from electronic polarization, and the dye–medium interaction is van der Waals. Merocyanines additionally show dipole and hydrogen-bonding effects superimposed. **[M]**

**[E]** This is a genuinely usable one-parameter model for moving a symmetrical cyanine's peak between media (gelatin versus adsorbed on AgX): E_TR is linear in (n² − 1)/(2n² + 1). The source states the form and its validity domain but does not give the slope.

| n | Longest absorption maximum (Å) |

| 0 | 2,520 |
| 1 | 3,180 |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.103 (PDF 109), Table 6.1]` **[Q]**

Reading given: "as the chain becomes longer, the **wavelength increase produced by each successive increase is less**." **[F]**

#### 9.6.2 Duffin's Table 6.2 — a series of related cyanines

| n | Wavelength of absorption maximum (Å) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 4,230 |
| 1 | 5,570 |
| 2 | 6,500 |
| 3 | 7,580 |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.106 (PDF 112), Table 6.2]` **[Q]**

Reading given: "the **same increment in the conjugated chain length produces a larger increase in the wavelength of the maximum than occurs with the hydrocarbons of Table 6.1**" — "**this is fortunate otherwise infra-red photography would not have been possible**." The absorption maximum depends on two things: (1) the **basicity of the nitrogen atoms** — "generally speaking the more basic the nitrogen, the longer is the wavelength of the first absorption band"; (2) the **length of the carbon chain**, "the most important influence". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.106 (PDF 112)]` **[F]**

Comparing the two tables directly: at n = 3 the polyene sits at 3,770 Å and the cyanine at 7,580 Å — a factor of two in wavelength for the same chain increment count. That is the whole reason cyanines, and not polyenes, are the sensitizer class. **[E]**

#### 9.6.3 Duffin's other named absorption wavelengths, as a calibration ladder

| Compound / class | Wavelength |
|---|---|
| Ethane | **1,300 Å** |
| Ethylene | **1,800 Å** |
| Butadiene | **2,100 Å** |
| Benzene | **2,590 Å** |
| Naphthalene | **2,750 Å** |
| Anthracene | **3,700 Å** |
| Cyanine dye (37) with **thirteen carbon atoms** between the two rings | absorption maximum **11,000 Å in solution**; **sensitizes in the far infra-red at 11,800 Å** |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.100–110 (PDF 106–116)]` **[Q]**

Spectral-region framing: "Radiation from the U.V. and visible region (**1,000–10,000 Å**) is of appropriate energy to cause changes in the energy levels of the bonding electrons"; whereas "**infra-red light, just beyond the visible spectrum (20,000–150,000 Å), causes vibration of the molecule … but these changes cannot be put to any photographic use in silver halide.**" Photon relations as printed: `E = h ν`; "every form of radiation consists of electromagnetic waves, which are propagated at the same speed, **3 × 10¹⁰ cm per second**"; `wavelength × frequency = velocity`; "**the energy is inversely proportional to wavelength**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.100–102 (PDF 106–108)]` **[Q]**

Dye classes with seven-carbon chains "were amongst the **first good sensitizers to the infra-red**." And a categorical exclusion: "**no azo dyes act as spectral sensitizers**" — though azo dyes are used elsewhere in colour photography. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.106–110 (PDF 112–116)]` **[F]**

#### 9.6.4 The λmax library that did not survive

Tani's **Table 5.1 ("Absorptions of vinylogous dyes", p.112 / PDF 121)** and **Table 5.2 ("Dyes used in this chapter", pp.114–116 / PDF 123–125)** were image-only in the PDF. The captions survive; the contents do not. These are the tables that would hold λ_max per dye for the ~46 numbered dyes Tani uses throughout Chapter 5. **This is the single largest numeric loss in the spectral-sensitization material, and it cannot be recovered from the extracted text.** Consequently: every "Dye n" reference in Tani that appears below is a bare identifier — the structure and λ_max behind it are not available here, and Duffin's Tables 6.1/6.2 (§9.6.1–9.6.2) plus Wall's dye inventory (§9.9) are the only wavelength tables this document can carry. `[Tani 1995, §5.2, Tables 5.1, 5.2, pp.112–116 (PDF 121–125)]` **[F]**

### 9.7 Dye chemistry: classes and structural taxonomy

**1995, Tani.** "The essential structure of sensitizing dyes is the **polymethine chain, with an odd number of methine groups and hetero atoms at its ends**." Three chromophore systems — **amidinium ion**, **carboxyl ion**, **amidic** — exemplified by his Groups (1), (2), (3):

| Group | Class | Members by chain length |
|---|---|---|
| (1) | **cyanines** | n = 0, 1, 2, 3 → **cyanine, carbocyanine, dicarbocyanine, tricarbocyanine** |
| (2) | **oxonols** | — |
| (3) | **merocyanines** | — |
| (4), (5) | non-sensitizing controls | — |

The sensitizing groups' bands are "stronger and appear at a longer wavelength … in terms of their chain length" than the non-sensitizing controls. `[Tani 1995, §5.2, pp.111–113 (PDF 120–122), Fig. 5.1]` **[F]**

**1966, Duffin.** "**The dyes used exclusively today for spectral sensitization are the cyanine dyes.**" Two classes: **true cyanines** and **merocyanines**; the commonest merocyanines are **dimethin** (two-carbon chain). "the **best dyes are those containing sulphur or oxygen in these rings** as well as carbon." Ring systems in use: quinoline, thiazole, thiazoline, triazole, pyrroline, indolenine, benzoselenazole, benziminazole, benzoxazole, benzothiazole. Ketomethylene partners for merocyanines: **N-ethylrhodanine, 2-phenyl-5-oxazolone, 1-phenyl-3-methyl-5-pyrazolone**. Duffin also flags the cross-connections: "the **pyrazole ring, present in almost all magenta colour couplers**" and "**pyrimidine present in so many stabilizers**". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.104–110 (PDF 110–116)]` **[F]**

Duffin's general lesson on colour, worth keeping because it corrects a common misconception: "there is **no essential difference in structure between a coloured substance and a non-coloured one**. Indeed, **all substances will absorb light**; some appear coloured because the transmitted or reflected light is deficient in some of those wavelengths comprising white light." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.103 (PDF 109)]` **[F]**

**Planarity is the structural requirement.** "**all the bonds must lie in one plane** because conjugation through the whole π bonded system requires that all the chain atoms, including the nitrogen, must participate … **Failure to achieve this overall planarity due to the geometry of the whole molecule, results in a decrease of light absorption and sensitization** by the molecule." For distorted cyanines "usually **three effects** will be observed. **1. The absorption maximum shifts to a longer wavelength. 2. The intensity of the absorption decreases. 3. The sensitizing efficiency decreases.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.105, 111 (PDF 111, 117)]` **[M]**

Exception, and a nice one: "**cruciform**" molecules (Brooker) — extreme crowding relieved by the bulky middle substituent turning perpendicular to the rest — "possess the **typical light absorption and sensitizing properties of the simple trimethincyanines**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.111 (PDF 117)]` **[F]**

**Brooker's shape classification** appears in both sources, and both connect it to J-aggregation:

- Tani: "Brooker classified the molecular structures of cyanine dyes into three groups, that is, **loose, compact, and crowded**, and found that **compact** cyanine dyes were the most likely to form J-aggregates." `[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.121 (PDF 130)]` **[F]**
- Duffin: "loose" dyes associate poorly; "crowded" dyes (compact molecules over-substituted so the plane must twist) are usually very poor sensitizers; "compact" dyes aggregate readily and sensitize well. "Cruciform" dyes are good compact molecules and behave typically as J-aggregates. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.120 (PDF 126)]` **[F]**

A useful negative: "The size of the anion plays no part at all in the shape of the dye molecule… The nature of this anion has no spectral effect either on the light absorption or the spectral sensitization of the dye." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.120 (PDF 126)]` **[F]**

Substituent effects on sensitizing power specifically (as distinct from on wavelength): nitro, cyano, acetyl and propargyl groups "**depress the sensitizing power to a marked extent**" even when introduced where they cause no crowding. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.125–126 (PDF 131–132)]` **[F]**

And a non-additivity that argues against simple structure–activity reasoning: the pyrazolone–indolenine merocyanine (50) sensitizes well although both parent halves — pyrazolone dye (70) and indolenine trimethin cyanine (71) — "**are both very poor sensitizers**". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.125–126 (PDF 131–132)]` **[F]**

### 9.8 Adsorption: only adsorbed dye sensitizes, and the numbers that go with it

The governing pair of statements, 1966, and the most consequential facts in this section:

> "1. **Only the dye adsorbed to the silver-halide grain is effective in conferring sensitivity** upon it, since only the intimate contact of an adsorbed molecule can transfer the effect of the light. **Dye in the gelatin phase will only cause a filtering action** … **and thus reduce speed in the region in which the dye absorbs light.**
> 2. **The wavelength of this conferred sensitivity is that of the light absorption of the dye in the adsorbed state.** This may be very different from that of the simple dye in dilute solution as individual free molecules."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.114 (PDF 120)]` **[F]**

#### 9.8.1 Adsorption isotherms, orientation and energetics

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Isotherm type | **monomolecular, Langmuir-type**, for many sensitizing dyes | `[Tani 1995, §5.3, p.123 (PDF 132), Fig. 5.7]` |
| Orientation | occupied area per molecule ≈ **length × thickness** of the molecule → **edge-on** (not flat-on, not end-on) | same |
| Heat of adsorption, general | **≈ 10 kcal/mole** | same |
| Heat of adsorption, Dye 14 on AgBrI | **9 kcal/mole (octahedral)**, **11 kcal/mole (cubic)** | `[Tani 1995, §5.3, pp.123–124 (PDF 132–133), Fig. 5.8]` |
| Heat of **desorption** from octahedral | **26 kcal/mole** — desorption is the rate-determining step of rearrangement | same |
| Desorption order for J-aggregates on octahedral grains | **zero-order** — only end molecules can leave, implying **linear** aggregates | same |
| Adsorption equilibration time (transfer octahedral → cubic) | **several hours at 40 °C; ~10 min at 60 °C; < several minutes at 70 °C** | same |
| Heat of adsorption, 1966 figure | **10,000 to 12,000 calories per mole**, "less than half the heats of formation of conventional chemical bonds", "**higher for the first fraction of the dye to be adsorbed**" — implying **special preferential sites** | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.114–115 (PDF 120–121)]` |
| Heat of adsorption in a 7 % gelatin emulsion | "**around 7,000 calories per gram-mole**" — interpreted as the *difference* between the dye's and the gelatin's heats of adsorption | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.115 (PDF 121)]` |

**[Q]** for the whole table.

Nature of the binding, 1966: not covalent, not primarily electrostatic — "a cyanine dye may be equally well adsorbed whether the molecule carries a net negative or positive charge or no charge at all" — and therefore ascribed to **van der Waals forces**, with the dye's π electrons interacting with the halide surface. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.114–115 (PDF 120–121)]` **[M]**

Tani agrees and adds the spectroscopic test: adsorption is **physical** (van der Waals plus Coulombic), not chemisorption, for cyanines — IR spectra are unchanged on adsorption, and the monomer absorption peak on grains is "2CM-0 nm longer" than in solution — **OCR garble; read as "20–40 nm longer"**, consistent with the surrounding argument that the bathochromic shift lies within the solvent-effect range of §9.5. The exception is merocyanines bearing **C=S**, which *do* interact chemically: the XANES 1s→π\* feature at the sulphur K-edge disappears on adsorption to AgCl, indicating a coordinate S–Ag bond. `[Tani 1995, §5.3, pp.124–126 (PDF 133–135)]` **[Q]**

Molecular geometry of the adsorbed layer, 1966, from X-ray and other methods on 2,2′-quinoline cyanine: "The dye molecules are **stacked edge-on**, the nitrogen atoms being nearest the plane of adsorption, **about 4–5 Å apart**, which … is **within the range of van der Waals forces**, the stacking being at **an angle of about 30° from the vertical**; the molecules are like a pack of cards stood on their long edges on the crystal and then tilted slightly." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.117–118 (PDF 123–124), Fig. 6.6]` **[Q]** Tani's orientation statement is compatible: "**upright, with their long sides on the grain**, possibly with the nitrogen atoms nearest the crystal surface" — with Carroll's caution that "**for only partial surface coverage, the situation existing in most commercial emulsions, the position is very unclear at present**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.115 (PDF 121)]` **[M]**

#### 9.8.2 Adsorption is competitive with gelatin, and effectively irreversible in practice

"In the absence of gelatin, the adsorption of the dye is very fast indeed but … although an adsorbed gelatin layer may **retard** dye adsorption, the dye is **more powerfully held**. Measurements, by direct analysis of nitrogen content, of the amount of gelatin remaining on dyed emulsions, have shown clearly that **gelatin is readily displaced from the grains. At sufficiently high dye concentrations, higher than those used commercially, the gelatin may be completely removed.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.115 (PDF 121)]` **[Q]**

Desorption is slow, "particularly when the surface was only partially covered and, therefore, it has been generally assumed that the adsorption of a dye under practical conditions in a photographic emulsion **has a high degree of irreversibility**." But there is a specific commercial counterexample worth remembering: "the **cyan colour coupler of substantive couplers … can strip off the sensitizer from the surface and remove the red sensitivity**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.115 (PDF 121)]` **[F]**

#### 9.8.3 Dye adsorption changes the grain's ionic conductivity

This is the mechanism by which a spectral sensitizer becomes a *reciprocity* variable, and it belongs here rather than in §10 because it is a property of the adsorbed dye.

> "…the adsorption of **cyanine dyes with a positive charge** on their chromophore to the grains **increased** the conductivity by repelling silver ions at surface sites into interstitial positions, and the adsorption of a dye with a **negative charge** on their chromophore and a **merocyanine** dye with affinity to a silver ion to the grains **decreased** the conductivity by stabilizing silver ions at surface sites."

`[Tani 1995, §3.2, p.53 (PDF 62), Figs. 3.7, 3.8]` **[M]** Cyanine adsorption is additionally **enhanced at elevated pAg**, and **J-aggregation strengthens adsorption**; raising agitation temperature or time grows the aggregates. `[Tani 1995, §5.3, pp.124–126 (PDF 133–135)]` **[F]**

The photographic consequence: "Tani and Ihama found that cyanine dyes brought about **desensitization due to enhancement of HIRF** (i.e., dispersion of image centers) on sulfur-sensitized cubic AgBr grains, and attributed it to the increase in concentration of interstitial silver ions caused by adsorption of the dyes onto the grains." `[Tani 1995, §4.2, p.91 (PDF 100)]` **[F]**

### 9.9 Aggregates: M, D, H, J, and the double band

This is where the *shape* of a spectral-sensitivity curve comes from.

#### 9.9.1 The aggregate ladder, 1966

Duffin sets out the sequence on rising dye concentration: monomer **M-band** → **D-band** (dimer; a short-wavelength shoulder that becomes a peak) → **H-band** (a further, higher-intensity short-wavelength polymer) → **J-band**, "suggested… one of increasing size of aggregation". "**Dyes in the H-aggregate form are rather poor sensitizers**" (with exceptions). Illustrated for benzothiazole dye (66). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.121–122 (PDF 127–128), Figs. 6.7, 6.8]` **[M]**

The two bands defined with wavelength shifts:

- **M-band:** at low dye concentration ("only a few per cent of the crystal surface is covered"), dilute-solution absorption and emulsion sensitisation are "spectrally very similar", i.e. sensitisation by individually adsorbed molecules — "the **molecular or M-band**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.116 (PDF 122)]` **[F]**
- **J-band:** "At low concentrations, most dyes giving adsorption curves like curve (2) in Figure 6.4 confer spectral sensitization at a **longer wavelength, usually 200–300 Å longer**, than the maximum of light absorption in dilute solution. **Larger additions of dye introduce another sensitizing peak at longer wavelengths which is enhanced as the quantity increases.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.116–117 (PDF 122–123)]` **[Q]**

#### 9.9.2 Adsorption shifts the peak: Duffin's specific number

> "In a large number of cyanines, this shift is **about 200–400 Å towards longer wavelengths**. Thus the **N,N′-diethyl benzothiazole dye (51) absorbs at 5,590 Å in solution but sensitizes at 5,820 Å.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.116 (PDF 122)]` **[Q]** — a 230 Å shift in the worked example, at the low end of the quoted 200–400 Å band.

Merocyanines behave differently: the solution maximum is strongly solvent-polarity dependent and "**no general rule can be given** of the changes that occur." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.116 (PDF 122)]` **[F]**

#### 9.9.3 Aqueous aggregation in solution — the one three-concentration series

For a quinoline cyanine (53) in water: "the characteristic maximum at **5,250 Å**, the usual maximum in ethanol, but more concentrated solutions exhibit first a change in the relative heights of the **5,250 Å and 4,900 Å** bands and then the appearance of **a totally new and very intense band at 5,700 Å**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.116–117 (PDF 122–123), Fig. 6.5]` **[Q]**

Fig. 6.5's three concentrations are given as **1.3 × 10⁻⁵ molar, 7.1 × 10⁻³(?) molar, 1.4 × 10⁻³(?) molar**; raw OCR strings `1:3x10°°Molar`, `7-1.x107?Molar`, `1-4x10° Molar` — **exponents destroyed; do not quote the concentrations.** The three wavelengths (5,250 / 4,900 / 5,700 Å) are clean. **[F]**

So for this dye: monomer at 5,250 Å, H-type band at 4,900 Å (−350 Å), J-type band at 5,700 Å (+450 Å). **[E]**

#### 9.9.4 The J-band's key property for modelling: it does not shift on adsorption

> "One important difference between J-band and M-band sensitization is that **the absorption maximum, and therefore the sensitizing maximum, of the J-band is not changed when it is adsorbed to the grain surface.** Apparently, the high stability of the J-aggregate maintains the same electron levels within itself regardless of the substrate."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.117–118 (PDF 123–124)]` **[F]**

The aggregate is large — "possibly with **hundreds of dye molecules linked together**" — and "**electronic excitation can be transferred through the group of molecules comprising a J-aggregate**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.117–118 (PDF 123–124)]` **[M]**

#### 9.9.5 J-aggregates, 1995 — band position, band width, and why colour photography needs them

> "Many cyanine dyes form aggregates in aqueous solutions, and especially in silver halide emulsions, producing large spectral shifts and distinct changes in band shape. Figure 5.4 shows the absorption spectrum of Dye 11 in methanol and those of Dye 11 in photographic emulsions composed of octahedral AgBr grains that were agitated at **40°C and 70°C for 20 min**, respectively. The dye showed an **M-band** corresponding to its monomeric state in methanol and a sharp and bathochromatically shifted **J-band** corresponding to its J-aggregate. The **J-band became sharper**, indicating the increase in aggregate size with increasing agitation temperature. **J-bands are especially important for color photography, since they make photographic emulsions sensitive to specialized narrow wavelength regions.** It is also known that some cyanine dyes showed a hypsochromatically shifted **H-band** corresponding to their H-aggregates."

`[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.118 (PDF 127), Fig. 5.4]` **[F]** — the numeric peak wavelengths and half-widths exist only in Fig. 5.4, which is image-only. **The nm values for this figure are not recoverable from this material.** **[F]**

**[E]** The load-bearing statement is that the aggregate *state*, not merely the dye identity, sets both band position and band half-width, and that the half-width narrows as aggregate size grows with digestion temperature. It follows that a spectrally sensitized emulsion's green or red band is narrow and asymmetric rather than Gaussian, and that its width is a manufacturing/processing-dependent parameter (agitation temperature and time) rather than a constant of the dye.

#### 9.9.6 Molecular exciton theory of the aggregate shift

Tani's Eqs. (5.3)–(5.8) treat this; the bodies are lost. The symbol set as printed: **H, H₁, H₂, H₁₂** = Hamiltonians of molecules 1, 2 and their interaction; **Φ_G** = ground-state wavefunction; **Φ₊, Φ₋** = excited-state wavefunctions; **E_G, E₊, E₋** = corresponding energies; **M₊, M₋** = transition moments; **α** = "the angle between the long axis of a dye molecule and that of an aggregate", i.e. the **slip angle**; **ε\*** = monomer excited-state energy; **E_TR(M), E_TR(H), E_TR(J)** = transition energies of monomer, H-aggregate, J-aggregate. `[Tani 1995, §5.2, pp.118–121 (PDF 127–130), Fig. 5.5]` **[M]**

The rules stated in the prose, which do survive:

- "**J-aggregates have a small α, while H-aggregates have a large α.**"
- The dominant shift term is `(φ*₁φ₂|H₁₂|φ₁φ₂)`.
- "The transitions to the excited states of aggregates with transition dipoles in **parallel** and **opposite** directions give **M** and **0** as M₊ and M₋, respectively, and are therefore **allowed** and **forbidden**."
- "The energy of the allowed transition (i.e., E₊ − E_G) is **larger** than ε\* for the aggregate with large α (i.e., H-aggregate), and **smaller** than ε\* for the aggregate with small α (i.e., J-aggregate)."

`[Tani 1995, §5.2, pp.118–121 (PDF 127–130)]` **[M]** — this is the mechanism for why H-aggregates are hypsochromic and J-aggregates bathochromic, but the functional form is not recoverable.

#### 9.9.7 The double band (herringbone aggregate)

> "There is another important aggregate that gives a so-called **double band** with two absorption peaks… both J- and H-aggregates have a molecular arrangement with **one molecule in a unit cell**, and are composed of an allowed transition and a forbidden transition. On the other hand, the aggregate that gives the double band has a molecular arrangement with **two molecules in a unit cell** and is composed of **two allowed transitions**. A **herringbone** structure … has been proposed… It is known that **9-methyl-thiacarbocyanine** dye derivatives, such as Dyes 14 and 15, adsorbed on the **(100)** face of silver halide exhibit the double band."

Fig. 5.6 conditions: Dye 14 monomeric in a gelatin layer (a) versus the herringbone double band in an emulsion layer of **cubic AgBr, edge length 0.65 µm**, Dye 14 at **0.23 mmole/mole AgBr** (b). `[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.121 (PDF 130), Fig. 5.6]` **[Q]** — the peak positions themselves are in the figure and are not recoverable. **[F]**

#### 9.9.8 Mixed-dye J-aggregates — a design lever

"J-aggregates may also be formed from mixtures of two different dyes which must be of closely-related structure. For example, two benzothiazole dyes with different substituents in the benzene rings may form a joint aggregate, **the sensitizing maximum of which is intermediate between the two individual maxima**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.121 (PDF 127)]` **[F]**

Also: merocyanines give J-aggregates less often; the pyrazolone dye (50) is a notable exception and "**only shows J-band sensitization**". Symmetrical end-groups favour J-band formation (Anderson's four end-group arrangements; the fully crowded form is impossible). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.120–121 (PDF 126–127)]` **[F]**

And the commercial weighting, 1966: "The J-band sensitization, particularly that given by the **benzothiazole dyes with a trimethin chain**, is very important in **modern panchromatic and colour films**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.121 (PDF 127)]` **[F]**

### 9.10 Quantum yield of spectral sensitization

#### 9.10.1 Definition — and the two sources define it the same way

**1966, Duffin.** *Relative quantum yield* = (number of absorbed quanta required to produce a given density at **4,000 Å**) ÷ (number of quanta similarly required at the wavelength of sensitization). 4,000 Å is chosen "because the sensitivity at that point is due entirely to the silver halide". "The value of the relative quantum yield **can never exceed 1.0** and is only brought near to that value by the very best dyes." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.122–123 (PDF 128–129)]` **[Q]**

**1995, Tani.** **φ_r** = relative quantum yield of spectral sensitization = ratio of quanta absorbed by AgX alone (measured at **400 nm**, "unabsorbed by most dyes") to quanta absorbed by dye alone at λ, both to produce the same developed density; symbols E_400, A_400, E_λ, A_λ in Eq. (5.14). φ_r equals the electron-transfer efficiency φ_s only when φ_LI,λ = φ_LI,400 (Eqs. 5.15–5.16; bodies lost; φ_s = electron-transfer efficiency, k_s / k_L = electron-transfer and deactivation rate constants, k_r / k_nr = radiative and non-radiative recombination). `[Tani 1995, §5.5, pp.132–133 (PDF 141–142)]` **[Q]**

The reference wavelength is the same (4,000 Å = 400 nm) and the definition is the same. But Tani documents **two cases where φ_r exceeds unity**, contradicting Duffin's flat "can never exceed 1.0":

1. with **Ag₂ (reduction) centres** present and high-HOMO dyes;
2. in **grains too large** for interior holes to reach the surface — there φ_r "**increased and even exceeded unity**" with increasing edge length (Fig. 5.16: cubic AgBr prepared at pH 2.5, dye surface coverage **0.1**, Dye 35).

`[Tani 1995, §5.5, pp.133–134 (PDF 142–143), Figs. 5.15, 5.16]` **[Q]**

The two statements do not average. Duffin's bound is correct for the quantity he defines *if* the latent-image-forming efficiency per conduction electron is the same at both wavelengths; Tani's cases are exactly the cases where that assumption fails, and Tani says so explicitly (φ_r = φ_s only when φ_LI,λ = φ_LI,400). The physical reason φ_r can exceed 1 is the extra electron liberated by hole capture at a reduction centre — see §10.5.4. **[E]**

*Inconsistency to flag inside Tani:* the text says Fig. 5.15 uses "cubic AgBr emulsion grains (**edge length of 0.6 µm**)" while the Fig. 5.15 caption says "cubic AgBr grains (**0.2 µm**)". `[Tani 1995, §5.5, p.133 (PDF 142), text vs caption]` **[F]**

Example E_ox values quoted alongside those experiments: Dye 11 **+0.89 V vs SCE** ("moderate"), Dye 27 **+0.97 V** ("low"), Dye 35 **+0.575 V**, Dye 26 **+0.70 V** ("extremely high" HOMO). `[Tani 1995, §5.5, p.134 (PDF 143)]` **[Q]**

#### 9.10.2 The Marcus-theory fit — the one real quantitative model of sensitization efficiency

φ_r plotted against the energy gap (expressed as E_R in V vs SCE) fits Tani's Eqs. (5.17)–(5.19) with:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **k°**, maximum electron-transfer rate constant | **10¹¹ sec⁻¹** |
| **λ**, solvent/rearrangement energy | **0.05 eV** |

Other symbols: ΔG\* = activation energy; E_R = the reduction potential at which ΔE = 0. `[Tani 1995, §5.5–5.6, pp.135–137 (PDF 144–146), Figs. 5.17, 5.18]` **[Q]**

*OCR flag:* the Fig. 5.17 caption raw string reads `where k° and A are 10'' sec"1 and 0.05 eV` — the `10''` is **10¹¹**, confirmed by the body text "with k° of 1011 sec"1". **[F]**

The fit reproduces the steep rise, but the experimental points **depart from the predicted "inverted region"** — i.e. **no inverted region is observed**. Tani's explanation: the conduction band is a *continuum* of acceptor levels, so some final-state curve always crosses at the bottom of the initial-state curve. For comparison, electron transfer in solutions has **λ > 0.3 eV** and does show an inverted region. `[Tani 1995, §5.6, pp.135–137 (PDF 144–146), Fig. 5.18]` **[Q]**

Temperature dependence: the temperature dependence of k_s **decreases with increasing ΔE and becomes nearly zero** at large ΔE. Frieser found that the efficiency of spectral sensitization is usually reduced at low temperature, but is **maintained at low temperature in dye–supersensitizer combinations** (Dyes 1 + 46). Tani confirmed by Dember photovoltage plus sensitometry that the supersensitizer **both increases efficiency and extinguishes its temperature dependence** (Fig. 5.32: octahedral AgBr **0.7 µm**, Dye 1 at **1.2 × 10⁻⁴ mole/mole AgBr**, Dye 46 at **3 × 10⁻⁵ mole/mole AgBr**, exposure **10 s**). `[Tani 1995, §§5.6, 5.8, pp.137–139, 151 (PDF 146–148, 160)]` **[Q]**

Duffin's low-temperature datum, from 1966, is compatible: dye sensitization is "still quite measurable at liquid-air temperatures, **−196 °C**", but the sensitivity loss at that temperature is much greater in the dye-sensitized region than in the region of natural sensitivity; the loss "is **no greater with red sensitizers than with blue**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.132 (PDF 138)]` **[Q]**

#### 9.10.3 Aggregate size versus quantum yield — and a direct conflict in the literature

Tani, Fig. 5.22, Dye 11 on octahedral AgBr: growing the J-aggregate (by higher agitation temperature) **decreases φ_r**, via **increased k_L** *and* **decreased k_s**. k_nr decreases with aggregate size but k_r increases per Eq. (5.22), whose symbols are k_r(J), k_r(M) = radiative rate constants in the J-aggregate and the monomer, **N** = number of molecules per aggregate, **α** = the slip angle. `[Tani 1995, §5.6, pp.141–142 (PDF 150–151), Fig. 5.22]` **[Q]**

But: "Muenter et al. found k_s **increases** with aggregate size" (diluting the aggregates with a structural analogue), attributing the competition instead to **energy transfer to defects in aggregates**. `[Tani 1995, §5.6, p.142 (PDF 151)]` **[F]** The two results are opposite in sign on the same variable, and Tani reports both. Do not reconcile.

Duffin's 1966 statement of the same trade is qualitative and agrees with Tani's sign: J-bands, despite high sensitizing power and commercial importance, "generally possess **lower** relative quantum yields than do the same dyes in the molecular band" (energy wasted inside the aggregate); their advantage is "the high light absorption of the J-band and the much larger amount of dye present". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.124 (PDF 130)]` **[F]**

**[E]** So the J-aggregate is a *net* win bought at the cost of per-quantum efficiency: it absorbs far more light in a narrow band, at a lower yield per absorbed quantum. That is the trade behind narrow-band colour records.

#### 9.10.4 A methodological caution on published fluorescence lifetimes

k_s and k_L are obtained from the fluorescence lifetime **τ_F** together with φ_r (Eqs. 5.20–5.21, bodies lost). Streak-camera measurements are corrupted by **singlet–singlet exciton annihilation** (S₁ + S₁ → S₀ + S_n), because a single strong pulse excites nearly all the molecules in an aggregate; photon counting avoids that but accumulates **sample damage**. The fix is continuously **moving the sample** so each area receives less exposure, with the measured lifetime converging as the movement rate increases. `[Tani 1995, §5.6, pp.140–141 (PDF 149–150)]` **[M]** — methodological, but a real caution about any published τ_F for a dyed emulsion.

#### 9.10.5 Extinction and the planarity penalty, 1966 — quantified

- Within a dye family, light-absorption intensity varies little and generally increases with chain length; for non-planar crowded dyes it "can drop to as low as **a third** of the value of a closely related non-crowded dye". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.122 (PDF 128)]` **[Q]**
- The case that separates absorption from yield: the crowded tertiary-butyl cyanine (67) retains **70 %** of the light-absorbing power of the chain ethyl derivative (68) yet is "almost devoid of sensitizing power **because of its negligible relative quantum yield**". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.123–124 (PDF 129–130)]` **[Q]**

### 9.11 Dye quantity per mole of silver, and the monolayer coverage limit

#### 9.11.1 Duffin's dose figures — the most directly usable numbers in this section

> "The cyanine dyes are usually introduced into the emulsion **at a late stage in the making process, normally at the conclusion of the digestion**, in the form of dilute solutions, **normally of 1 in 1,000 or less**, in a water-miscible organic solvent, such as ethanol or acetone, or in water if the dyes are salts …
> The spectral sensitizers are added at the rate of **0.02 to 0.2 g of dye per g mole of silver**, corresponding to about **0.05 to 0.5 millimoles per mole** or **1 : 20,000 to 1 : 2,000 relative to the silver halide**, which are **larger quantities than those of the chemical sensitizing substances** usually used. In the case of the emulsion considered earlier, with `4x10"` grains of silver halide per gram mole, these concentrations provide `10°` to `10` **dye molecules per grain** [*exponents OCR-destroyed*], mostly adsorbed on the grain surface … **An average dye occupies 50–100 Å², so that in this emulsion the higher quantities would cover about half the surface of the grains.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.114 (PDF 120)]` **[Q]**

Consolidated:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Dye stock solution strength | **1 in 1,000 or less**, in ethanol, acetone, or water for dye salts |
| Addition point | **at the conclusion of digestion** |
| Dose, mass basis | **0.02–0.2 g dye per gram-mole Ag** |
| Dose, molar basis | **0.05–0.5 mmole per mole Ag** |
| Dose, ratio basis | **1 : 20,000 to 1 : 2,000** relative to silver halide |
| Area per adsorbed dye molecule | **50–100 Å²** |
| Coverage at the top of the dose range | "**about half the surface of the grains**" |
| Molecules per grain | exponents destroyed by OCR — **not quotable** |
| Comparison with chemical sensitizers | dye dose is **larger** than chemical-sensitizer dose |

Duffin adds a process note: "in emulsions which have already been **stabilized with large quantities of tetrazaindene stabilizer, a period of heat treatment facilitates the interaction**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.114 (PDF 120)]` **[F]**

Cross-check against Duffin's own grain-scale statement elsewhere: a latent-image speck needs "e.g. **4–25**" silver atoms in a grain carrying "**10⁵–10⁸ dye molecules** on its surface" (raw `105-108`); and "One thousandth of the normal dye quantity still corresponds to `10-104` dye molecules per grain" — **OCR-damaged; by consistency with 10⁵–10⁸ this should read 10²–10⁵.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.131–133 (PDF 137–139)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** The 10⁵–10⁸ dye molecules per grain against a 4–25 atom latent-image threshold is the ratio that makes spectral sensitization work at all: a vast light-harvesting antenna feeding a four-atom target.

#### 9.11.2 Tani's dye loadings, as used in his experiments

These are not recommended doses; they are the loadings at which the 1995 measurements were made, and they bracket Duffin's range:

| Experiment | Dye loading |
|---|---|
| Herringbone double band, cubic AgBr 0.65 µm | Dye 14 at **0.23 mmole/mole AgBr** |
| Supersensitization temperature study, octahedral AgBr 0.7 µm | Dye 1 at **1.2 × 10⁻⁴ mole/mole AgBr**; Dye 46 at **3 × 10⁻⁵ mole/mole AgBr** |
| Latent-image decay, octahedral AgBr 0.24 µm | Dye 11 at **5.5 × 10⁻⁴ mole/mole AgBr** |
| Arrhenius study, octahedral AgBr 0.25 µm | **0.57 µmole Dye 11 per m² of grain surface** |
| Aggregate-size desensitization split, octahedral AgBr 0.25 µm | **0.35 µmole Dye 11 per m² of grain surface** |
| φ_r versus grain size, cubic AgBr | dye **surface coverage 0.1** (fractional) |
| Absorbance-ceiling measurement, evaporated AgBr | **65 % surface coverage = 1.3 × 10⁻⁶ mol/m²** |

`[Tani 1995, §5.2, p.121 (PDF 130); §§5.5–5.8, pp.133–158 (PDF 142–167); §8.1.1, pp.229–230 (PDF 238–239)]` **[Q]**

Note the last row: **65 % coverage = 1.3 × 10⁻⁶ mol/m²** implies full monolayer ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol/m², i.e. about 1.2 × 10¹⁸ molecules/m² = 83 Å² per molecule — squarely inside Duffin's 50–100 Å² range. The two sources are consistent on the monolayer areal density. **[E]**

#### 9.11.3 Why dye-sensitized absorption is limited by grain SURFACE AREA

This is the central scaling law and Tani states both halves of it explicitly:

> "photographic sensitivity is, in principle, **proportional to the volume** of silver halide grains and the spectral sensitivity of dyes grains is **proportional to their average surface area**."

`[Tani 1995, §2.2, p.37 (PDF 46)]` **[Q]**

And the reason, stated as a mechanism: "Blue absorption is weak because it is an **indirect transition**; photons absorbed by a grain ∝ **grain volume**; photons absorbed by adsorbed dye ∝ **grain surface area** (dye is a **monolayer**)." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` **[F]**

The dye cannot be piled up: it is adsorbed, adsorption is monomolecular and Langmuir-type (§9.8.1), and dye that is not adsorbed does not sensitize but does filter (§9.8). Therefore the total dye-absorbing cross-section available per grain is fixed by the grain's surface area, and the *only* ways to increase dye-sensitized absorption are to increase total surface area per unit silver, or to increase the absorbance per unit area of the dye layer — and the second is bounded (§9.12). **[E]**

**[E]** For a tabular grain of thickness t and diameter D: V ∝ D²t while A ∝ D². Going tabular (large D, small t) raises A/V and therefore raises *minus-blue* speed per unit silver while holding *blue* speed. This is derivable from Tani's two proportionalities above, and it is exactly the standard rationale for tabular grains in the green- and red-sensitive records, but **Tani does not draw this conclusion in the material examined.** Tani does record the outcome: light absorption "was improved by the use of **tabular grains**" and "**increased to a considerable degree when a high-speed color negative film was designed using tabular grains instead of conventional grains**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242); §8.1.4, pp.235–236 (PDF 244–245)]` **[F]**

#### 9.11.4 The dose optimum and the penalty for exceeding it

**1966.** The speed-versus-dye-quantity curve has a maximum, which Duffin labels point "X", and "X" "is reached **before total coverage** of the emulsion crystals takes place, and… a **rapid loss of useful speed occurs if too much dye is added**." "For many commercial purposes, the balance of other properties makes desirable the use of **smaller quantities of dye than that giving maximum speed**." The position of X depends on dye and emulsion; increasing the iodide content of an iodobromide increased J-band sensitization. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.125 (PDF 131), Fig. 6.9]` **[Q]**

Chain length shifts X: mono- and trimethin cyanines are frequently good sensitizers; the five- and seven-carbon benzothiazoles are poorer despite **higher** light absorption, because of desensitization — point "X" occurs at low dye concentration for them, "therefore, they are added in much smaller amounts than customary for their shorter-chain analogues". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.125–126 (PDF 131–132), Fig. 6.8]` **[F]**

**1995.** The same optimum, stated as a failure of the material rather than of the speed: "the degree of **desensitization and stain of films caused by sensitizing dyes steeply increases when the amount of adsorbed dye molecules approaches the value for saturation of the grain surface**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.230 (PDF 239)]` **[F]**

Adsorption isotherm shapes that matter for where X falls — Duffin's **Fig. 6.4 "Adsorption isotherm for cyanine dyes"** (ordinate "Quantity of Dye Adsorbed", abscissa "Quantity of Dye added"): curve (1) a **Langmuir isotherm**, merocyanine (48), with a dotted line B marking the saturation level; curve (2) benzoxazole trimethincyanine (52) — **sigmoidal**, "adsorption is slow until a certain dye concentration is reached when a **rapid increase** occurs"; curve (3) pyrazolone merocyanine (50). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.117–118 (PDF 123–124), Fig. 6.4]` **[Q]** The sigmoidal shape of curve (2) is the aggregation signature: the rapid rise is cooperative J-aggregate formation. **[E]**

### 9.12 Absorbance actually achieved — the ceiling on dye-sensitized absorption

This is the hardest quantitative limit in the spectral-sensitization material.

**Fig. 8.1 measurement.** J-aggregates of **3,3′-disulfopropyl-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine** covering **65 % of an evaporated AgBr surface** (= **1.3 × 10⁻⁶ mol/m²**) gave a **peak absorbance of 0.09** with a **half-width of 283 cm⁻¹**. Conclusion: "the absorbance of these dye molecules on a tabular grain is **too weak to absorb all incident photons in the panchromatic range (i.e., 600–700 nm)**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, pp.229–230 (PDF 238–239), Fig. 8.1]` **[Q]**

*Discrepancy to flag:* the figure caption names the dye as 3,3′-disulfopropyl-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine while the body text names the panchromatic dye as **5,5′-dichloro-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine**. `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, pp.229–230 (PDF 238–239)]` **[F]**

Percent absorbance of real film, and of bare grains:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Percent absorbance of a high-sensitivity film, **intrinsic (blue) region** | **[NUMBER LOST IN OCR]** — raw string reads `is as low as` followed by a blank, then `in the intrinsic (blue) region and 10-20% in the spectrally sensitized region.` The blue figure is not recoverable from this material |
| Percent absorbance of a high-sensitivity film, **spectrally sensitized region** | **10–20 %** |
| Cubic AgBr grain, **1 µm edge**, at **420 nm** | **about 10 %** |
| Cubic AgBr grain, **1 µm edge**, at **460 nm** | **about 1 %** |
| Effect of **3 mol % AgI** in AgBr on percent absorption at **460 nm** | **increases it by five times** |

`[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Reading these together: a spectrally sensitized layer absorbs 10–20 % of the light in its own band, and a single 1 µm grain absorbs 1 % at 460 nm rising to five times that (≈5 %) with 3 mol % iodide. Incomplete light absorption is therefore the *largest single* efficiency loss in the whole photographic chain, and the DQE budget of §10.8 confirms it quantitatively at 42 % retained (i.e. 58 % lost) at that first stage. The dye monolayer cannot fix it, because the peak absorbance of a 65 %-covered monolayer is only 0.09 (≈19 % absorption in a single pass) and the half-width is only 283 cm⁻¹, far narrower than the 600–700 nm panchromatic band it has to cover.

Duffin's 1966 statement of the same limit, without numbers: "The high speed in the dye region [is] obtained by **less than monomolecular coverage** of dye, while a **silver-bromide crystal 0.2–0.3 µ thick** will give no greater response in the region of natural sensitivity." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.131–132 (PDF 137–138)]` **[Q]**

And Tani's structural reason a layer cannot simply be made thicker: "When the packing density is constant, the **fraction of incident light absorbed by the layers increases, and the image quality decreases with increasing thickness** of the layers." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242)]` **[F]** Together with "A large number of fine and well-designed silver halide grains are separately and randomly arranged in thin gelatin layers with a **relatively low packing density** to achieve fine imaging. However, **this arrangement prevents grains in these layers from absorbing incident light efficiently.**" `[Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]` **[F]** — **no numeric grain volume fraction is given anywhere.** **[F]**

### 9.13 Supersensitization

#### 9.13.1 Definitions and magnitudes

**1995, Tani.** **Supersensitization** = "phenomena in which φ_r is **increased** on addition of a second substance"; **antisensitization** = φ_r decreased. `[Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.151–152 (PDF 160–161)]` **[F]**

**1966, Duffin.** Supersensitization is the enhancement of a dye's sensitizing power by a small quantity of a second substance, "frequently **1 % of the dye quantity**"; "in some cases an increase in sensitized speed of as much as **twenty times** is produced." And a hard structural restriction: "**Only dyes showing polymer (usually J-band) sensitization are capable of supersensitization.**" Many supersensitizers are colourless, so "the position of the absorption maximum of the supersensitizer is not important". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.127–128 (PDF 133–134)]` **[Q]**

Active supersensitizer classes, 1966: acylmethylene derivatives of heterocyclic bases (72); cyanine dye **bases** (73) with trivalent N in both rings, hence incapable of cyanine mesomerism; ketones such as **p-dimethylaminobenzalacetone** (74); and dyes similar to the 2,2′-quinoline dyes (53), e.g. (75), which supersensitize trimethine dyes such as (66). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.127–128 (PDF 133–134)]` **[F]**

What supersensitization is *not*: "measurement shows **neither light absorption nor dye adsorption is increased**, although in some cases the wavelength of the sensitisation maximum is changed slightly." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.128 (PDF 134), Fig. 6.12]` **[F]**

#### 9.13.2 The two mechanisms, 1995

1. **Hole-trapping supersensitization** (Gilman; Fig. 5.21). The supersensitizer donates an electron to Dye\*, giving **Dye⁻**, whose electron sits about **0.2 eV higher** — now above the AgBr conduction-band bottom; and Dye⁻ is also **longer-lived** than Dye\*. `[Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.151–152 (PDF 160–161), Fig. 5.21]` **[M]** This is precisely why the two thresholds of §9.4 are 0.2 V apart, and why the Dye II class (E_R between −1.42 and −1.25 V) is the class supersensitization helps. **[E]**
2. **Aggregate-partitioning / exciton-trapping supersensitization** (West & Carroll; Fig. 5.23). Supersensitizer molecules **split large aggregates**, increasing the number of aggregate-end **exciton traps** where charge separation occurs. Bird's alternative reading of the same data: bigger aggregates incorporate more **antisensitizers**, which partitioning then isolates. `[Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.151–152 (PDF 160–161), Fig. 5.23]` **[M]**

Duffin's 1966 mechanism proposal is mechanism 2 in embryo: the supersensitizer is incorporated into the J-polymer "as an irregularity providing a transfer point", and/or "**chopping the polymer into smaller, more efficient pieces**". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.128, 133–134 (PDF 134, 139–140), Fig. 6.12]` **[M]**

Picosecond confirmation that the gain is purely in the transfer step: for hole-trapping supersensitization (Fig. 5.24), **k_s increases with φ_r while k_L is independent of φ_r**. `[Tani 1995, §5.6, p.142 (PDF 151), Fig. 5.24]` **[Q]**

E_R and E_ox in V vs **Ag/AgCl**; φ_r = relative quantum yield for sensitization by Dye 1 in the presence of each compound.

| Compound | E_R (V) | E_ox (V) | φ_r | ESR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dye 36 | −1.32 | 1.00 | 0.04 | − |
| (Dye 1, alone) | −1.03 | 0.99 | 0.03 | − |
| Dye 27 | −1.26 | 0.94 | 0.03 | − |
| Dye 37 | −1.06 | 0.88 | 0.07 | − *(raw shows "--")* |

`[Tani 1995, §5.8, Table 5.3, p.152 (PDF 161)]` **[Q]**

The stated conclusion: "**only the compounds with ε_HO much higher than that of Dye 1 could supersensitize.**" That is visible in the table as the E_ox column: the four supersensitizers all have E_ox ≤ 0.78 V while the four non-supersensitizers all have E_ox ≥ 0.88 V, and the boundary is sharp. The ESR column (a light-induced Dye⁺ signal) switches sign at the same boundary. `[Tani 1995, §5.8, p.152 (PDF 161)]` **[Q]**
