Note that E_R does **not** predict supersensitizing ability in this table — Dye 36 at −1.32 V does not supersensitize while Dye 6 at −1.00 V does. It is E_ox (the HOMO) that separates them. **[E]**

### 9.14 Desensitization and antisensitization

#### 9.14.1 Tani's three desensitization mechanisms

> "**Three desensitization mechanisms:** (1) **electron-trapping**, (2) **hole-trapping**, (3) **dispersion of image centres caused by dyes**."

`[Tani 1995, §5.8, p.153 (PDF 162)]` **[F]**

**(1) Electron-trapping desensitization** is fast: it "took place **as rapidly as several tens of nanoseconds**". Both the intrinsic sensitivity and the 35 GHz microwave photoconductivity are **unaffected** for dyes with E_R more negative than **−1.25 V**, and both fall sharply for less negative E_R (Figs. 5.33–5.35; cubic AgBr **0.82 µm**, Dyes 11 and 8). Lewis and James: **evacuation reduces** electron-trapping desensitization, so transfer of dye-trapped electrons **to oxygen** is the main cause; hydrogen hypersensitization removes the residual, so **recombination** is the other cause; and it is **not observed on grains containing Ir³⁺** (which provide strong interior electron traps). `[Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.153–156 (PDF 162–165), Figs. 5.33–5.35]` **[Q]**

**(2) Hole-trapping desensitization** depends on **ε_HO, not ε_LU** (Fig. 5.26), and is **not** detectable in tens-of-nanoseconds photoconductivity, so it is slower. It is improved by the stabilizer **TAI** (see §8.9.4, mechanism v). `[Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.156–157 (PDF 165–166), Fig. 5.26]` **[Q]**

**(3) Dispersion of image centres**: dyes **accelerate high-intensity reciprocity-law failure**. Fig. 5.36 gives **reciprocity-law curves** of sulfur-sensitized cubic AgBr **0.58 µm** with Dye 14 at several dye levels (labelled in mmole/mole AgBr) under minus-blue exposure; Fig. 5.37 shows the dye **increased the number of undevelopable relative to developable image centres per grain** (arrested development, with and without gold latensification). `[Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.157–158 (PDF 166–167), Figs. 5.36, 5.37]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Fig. 5.36 is the only reciprocity-law *family* in the Tani material, and it says HIRF depends on **dye loading**. That makes reciprocity behaviour a per-record property: the heavily dyed green and red records of a multilayer should show worse HIRF than the lightly dyed or undyed blue record of the same emulsion. The magnitudes are in the figure and not in the text.

#### 9.14.2 The 1966 account: desensitization is unavoidable and it is a ground-state property

> "In almost every case, even with the best commercial sensitizers, the addition of sensitizing dye to an iodobromide emulsion **causes a speed decrease in the region of natural sensitivity**. In other words, **the dye is behaving as a sensitizer and a desensitizer at the same time.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.124 (PDF 130)]` **[F]**

The worked case that separates absorption, yield and desensitization: the 4-phenylthiazole dye (69) has light absorption very similar to benzothiazole dye (51) and slightly *higher* relative quantum efficiency, but is such a powerful desensitizer at 4,000 Å that in **effective** sensitizing power (51) rates "good" and (69) "very poor" (Spence and Carroll). Good sensitizers (25) and (48) combine high relative quantum yield with only slight desensitizing action. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.124 (PDF 130)]` **[Q]**

Duffin identifies desensitization as a **ground-state** property (electron acceptance) and therefore **wavelength-independent** — and flags a rival explanation: "It has recently been pointed out that this so-called desensitization may be due to **interference with development** rather than lower efficiency in latent image formation." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.134 (PDF 140), Fig. 6.13; ref. Borginon & Van Veelen, J. Phot. Sci. 13, 273 (1965)]` **[F]** That alternative is not raised in the 1995 material.

#### 9.14.3 Antisensitization — 1966, with the one wavelength criterion

Antisensitization: similar small quantities of a foreign substance cause a great reduction in spectral sensitization *without* affecting blue speed (hence it is not desensitization). **Only J-band sensitizers show it.** The classic pair is the 2,2′-quinoline dye (53) with its crowded, twisted dimethyl analogue (76) — useless as a sensitizer, powerful as an antisensitizer.

The criterion, which is the one quantitative rule in the antisensitization material:

> "**If a non-planar, crowded dye absorbs at a much shorter wavelength (more than 700 Å difference) than the sensitizing dye, then it can act as a slight supersensitizer but is an antisensitizer for another dye where no such difference exists.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.128–129 (PDF 134–135)]` **[Q]** — i.e. a **700 Å separation** flips a molecule from antisensitizer to weak supersensitizer.

#### 9.14.4 Dye-induced fog — a dated statement

"Many of the **older** cyanine dyes, particularly those with a quinoline ring, caused an increase in fog when added to digested emulsions and this imposed a limit on the amount of dye which could be added. This has been attributed to the reducing properties of the dye resulting in the formation of free silver. **Modern dyes rarely show this behaviour.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.124 (PDF 130)]` **[F]** — 1966 marking a pre-1966 problem as solved.

### 9.15 Contrast effects of spectral sensitization

> "In addition to affecting the speed, a sensitizing dye also influences the **contrast** of a photographic emulsion. Usually, the contrast in the sensitized region is **higher** than that of the natural blue sensitivity."

Duffin's explanation: at incomplete coverage, small grains carry more dye molecules per unit *volume* than large grains, whereas intrinsic (undyed) sensitivity is proportional to grain volume; the dye therefore **narrows the large/small grain sensitivity spread**, and a narrower spread means higher contrast. A rival explanation via the iodide content of large versus small grains "is at variance with Dickinson's findings". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.124–125 (PDF 130–131)]` **[M]**

**[E]** This is internally consistent with Duffin's own grain-population theory of the characteristic curve (§10.10): intrinsic speed scales as V, dye-sensitized speed as A ∝ V^(2/3), so the dye-sensitized sensitivity distribution is a compressed version of the intrinsic one. It follows that the minus-blue records of a given emulsion should carry higher gamma than its blue record, from grain statistics alone. Duffin asserts the effect and its sign; neither source gives a Δgamma.

### 9.16 Chloride and chlorobromide emulsions — where spectral sensitization pays most

> "Very little has been published on the spectral sensitization of silver-chloride or chlorobromide emulsions, although this is of technological importance." The outstanding difference from iodobromide: "a powerful sensitizer can increase the **total speed** of a chloride or chlorobromide emulsion by as much as **thirty times**, probably because of the **low light-absorbing power of silver chloride** and also because **very little desensitization occurs** in the region of natural sensitivity." Contrast this with iodobromide, where dyeing "rarely confers an increased total sensitivity".

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.127 (PDF 133), Fig. 6.9]` **[Q]**

**[E]** The ×30 figure is a direct consequence of §9.2: AgCl has essentially no visible absorption to lose speed *from*, so the dye's contribution is nearly all gain. On an iodobromide, whose intrinsic blue absorption already extends to 520 nm, the dye's gain in the minus-blue is largely offset by its desensitization in the blue, and the *total* speed barely moves.

### 9.17 The 1929 dye inventory (Wall) — a dated snapshot

**1929.** Wall's practice is bathing or late addition of a handful of named commercial dyes, dosed in ccm of 1:1000 alcoholic solution per litre of emulsion, with spectral performance quoted against **Fraunhofer lines** rather than in nm. Erythrosine dominates for orthochromatic work; panchromatic work uses a pair of isocyanines.

| Dye | Quantity per unit emulsion | Spectral data as Wall gives it |
|---|---|---|
| **Erythrosine**, extra-bluish (potassium tetra-iodofluoresceinate) | General practice **0.07–0.1 g per 100 g dry AgNO₃**. In formulas: **1.875 g per 500 g AgNO₃** (medium and rapid isochromatic); **0.5 g** late addition; **0.8 g** (cine negative); Harris: **53 ccm of a 1 % solution per 500 g AgNO₃** | leaves "the marked gap between **b and F**" |
| **Pinaflavol** (Meister, Lucius & Brüning, Höchst; introduced 1921, D.R.P. 395,666) | gelatine strength not reported by Wall; for **collodion, 0.02 per 1000** of emulsion; collodion ortho use, **20 ccm of 1:1000 alcoholic per litre** | "sensitizes up to the **D lines, wave-length 5893**, with a **maximum at E, wave-length 5270**, joining on to the individual sensitiveness of bromo-iodide of silver, **without the marked gap between b and F** given by erythrosin and other eosin dyes" |
| **2-p-dimethylaminostyrylpyridine methiodide** (Mills & Pope, 1922; "probably the same as or closely allied to pinaflavol") | plates **bathed 1 : 30,000 to 1 : 40,000** | absorption bands at **about 4750 and 4600 Å**; bathed plates "showed almost uniform sensitiveness to all wave-lengths from the blue to **5600**, there being **no gap in the blue-green**" |
| **Sensitol green** (= **ortho-chrom T**) | **20 ccm of 1:1000 alcoholic solution per litre of emulsion**, added just before coating, into the alcohol | no λ given by Wall |
| **Sensitol violet** (= **pinachrom violet**) — the panchromatizing dye | **10 ccm of 1:1000 per litre** (gelatine); collodion **1:1000, same strength**; Lippmann collodion **1 ccm of 1:1000 per 100 ccm emulsion** | no λ given by Wall |
| **Cyanine**, alone or with **glycin red** | — | "the earlier color sensitizers used"; superseded by the isocyanines |
| **Isocol (Ives)** | **1 ccm of 1:1000 alcoholic per 100 ccm** | Lippmann and colour work |

`[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.66–70 (PDF 74–77); Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 95); Ch. VI, pp.114, 117, 134 (PDF 121, 124, 141); Ch. XIII, p.226 (PDF 233)]` **[Q]**

The Fraunhofer-line wavelengths Wall relies on, so the table above can be read without them: **D = 5893 Å**, **E = 5270 Å**; **b** and **F** are the magnesium b group (~5170 Å) and hydrogen F (4861 Å) respectively, and "the marked gap between b and F" is therefore a **blue-green sensitivity notch around 4900–5170 Å**. Wall states the D and E wavelengths explicitly; **he does not state numeric wavelengths for b or F**, so the notch position is only as precise as the line identifications. `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.69 (PDF 76)]` **[F]**

Panchromatic recipe, 1929, in full: "For making panchromatic emulsions the best dyes to use are **ortho-chrom T or sensitol green and sensitol violet (pinachrom violet)**, and these dyes should be added to the emulsion **just before coating**. It should be noted that **the emulsions must not be acid**. The dye solutions should be mixed with the alcohol usually employed and added with constant stirring to the fluid filtered emulsion. **About 20 ccm of sensitol green solution, 1 : 1000 alcohol, and 10 ccm sensitol violet, same strength, should be added to every liter of emulsion.**" `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.70 (PDF 77)]` **[Q]**

Erythrosine practice, 1929, with the timing rule: "the ordinary commercial isochromatic emulsions are prepared by the addition of erythrosin to the emulsion, and **the best result, that is the most marked color-sensitivity, is obtained when the dye is present at the moment of mixing**. Ammonia emulsions are most suitable for this process, as the insoluble tetra-iodofluorescein is precipitated by acids. The dye may be added to the bromized gelatine or to the silver solution; in the latter case there is first formed a deep red precipitate of **silver erythrosinate**, insoluble in water but readily soluble in ammonia, therefore an ammoniacal solution must be used. **There is no practical difference in the results of these two methods of mixing.**" `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.65–66 (PDF 73–74)]` **[Q]**

Note the era contrast: Wall's best result comes from dye present **at the moment of mixing**, whereas Duffin's 1966 practice is addition **at the conclusion of digestion** and Wall's own panchromatic recipe says **just before coating**. Wall's dye-at-the-mix rule applies specifically to erythrosine in ammonia emulsions and reflects its precipitation as silver erythrosinate; it is not a general rule and the later sources do not follow it. **[E]**

Wall also refutes a standing 1929 axiom: "It has been accepted as an axiom that emulsions intended for ortho-chromatizing should contain **little or no iodide**; but the writer has not found that the presence of larger quantities of iodide is prejudicial; **certainly as high as five per cent has been successfully used.**" `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.66 (PDF 74)]` **[F]** — Duffin's 1966 position is stronger still: increasing the iodide content of an iodobromide **increased** J-band sensitization `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.125 (PDF 131)]`. **[F]**

**Self-screened / non-filter plates**, 1929 — yellow dyes added just before coating to build the yellow filter into the emulsion:

| Dye | Concentration |
|---|---|
| Naphthol yellow S | **0.16 %** |
| Tartrazine or "filter yellow" | **0.075 %** |
| Thiazol yellow, nitrophenine or canary yellow | **0.1–0.2 %** |

`[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.69 (PDF 76)]` **[Q]**

**Iodide as a "red sensitizer"** — a 1929 phenomenon reported and then largely disowned. KI-bathed plates give "distinct orange and red sensitiveness"; Carey Lea (1875) proved AgI "much more sensitive to red and orange than the bromide"; Sheppard (1922) found the action **specific**, appearing only in emulsions *already* showing red sensitivity — "merely an intensification of an already existing action". Wall's own view: the effect "is limited apparently to a particular method of emulsion making," and increasing the iodide ratio "**frequently seems to prevent its appearance**." An accidental overdose (Archey) is cited as the discovery route. `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.43–44 (PDF 51–52); Ch. V, p.88 (PDF 95)]` **[F]**

A related 1929 observation on mixed crystals, which bears on the shape of an undyed emulsion's blue cut-off: bromo-iodide prepared as a true mixed crystal gives a **continuous** spectral curve, whereas separately prepared AgI and AgBr mechanically mixed give a curve with "**a drop on the more refrangible side of the G line**". `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.38 (PDF 46)]` **[F]**

Wall's antihalation and backing materials, included because in 1929 they are the only spectral control other than the sensitizing dyes themselves: dyed 5 % gelatine subbing using an acid red dye (fuchsin, Congo red, carmine L, lanafuchsin SB, tolan red, with or without naphthol yellow or tartrazine); or Oakley's (1895) **0.6 % potassium permanganate in gelatine**, reduced in situ to colloidal manganese hydroxide, which "cannot diffuse into the emulsion" and is therefore "a better protection for panchromatic emulsions". Backing for panchromatic plates: yellow dextrin 80 g / water 85 ccm / **ivory sienna black 900 g** / phenol 15 g; burnt sienna instead for ortho and ordinary plates. `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.83–84 (PDF 90–91); Ch. XIII, p.241 (PDF 248)]` **[Q]**

**What Wall does not have.** No aggregate concept of any kind — no M-, D-, H- or J-band, no dimer, no monolayer coverage calculation, no quantum yield, no supersensitization, no desensitization as a distinct phenomenon, no adsorption isotherm, no energy levels, no mechanism beyond the bare statement that dyes confer sensitivity. There is no wavelength given for sensitol green or sensitol violet, the two dyes his panchromatic recipe actually depends on. **[F]**

### 9.18 The 1966 inventory in summary form

Consolidating §§9.6–9.16 into what a 1966 emulsion maker actually had:

| Item | 1966 position |
|---|---|
| Dye classes in commercial use | "**The dyes used exclusively today for spectral sensitization are the cyanine dyes**" — true cyanines and merocyanines |
| Commercially dominant J-band dyes | **benzothiazole dyes with a trimethin chain**, "very important in modern panchromatic and colour films" |
| Ring systems | quinoline, thiazole, thiazoline, triazole, pyrroline, indolenine, benzoselenazole, benziminazole, benzoxazole, benzothiazole |
| Merocyanine ketomethylene partners | N-ethylrhodanine, 2-phenyl-5-oxazolone, 1-phenyl-3-methyl-5-pyrazolone |
| Excluded class | **azo dyes** — "no azo dyes act as spectral sensitizers" |
| Dose | **0.02–0.2 g per gram-mole Ag** = 0.05–0.5 mmole/mole = 1:20,000 to 1:2,000 |
| Addition point | at the conclusion of digestion, as a 1:1000-or-weaker solution in ethanol/acetone/water |
| Coverage at top of dose range | about **half** the grain surface; **50–100 Å²** per molecule |
| Adsorption shift | **200–400 Å** to longer wavelengths for a large number of cyanines |
| J-band shift over dilute-solution maximum | usually **200–300 Å** longer |
| Longest-wavelength dye reported | 13-carbon chain cyanine: absorbs **11,000 Å**, sensitizes **11,800 Å** |
| Supersensitizer dose | frequently **1 % of the dye quantity**; up to **×20** sensitized speed |
| Antisensitizer criterion | **> 700 Å** shorter absorption ⇒ weak supersensitizer instead |
| Speed gain on chloride/chlorobromide | up to **×30** total speed |
| Unavoidable cost | speed decrease in the region of natural (blue) sensitivity, in almost every case |
| Contrast effect | contrast in the sensitized region usually **higher** than in the natural blue region |
| Mechanism | **unsettled** — electron transfer and energy transfer both held to operate |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.99–135 (PDF 105–141)]` **[Q]**

### 9.19 What changed across the eras, and what remains unquantified

**1929 → 1966.** The dye class narrows to the cyanines and merocyanines exclusively; the aggregate ladder (M/D/H/J) is discovered and becomes the controlling concept for band position and band shape; adsorption is recognised as the necessary condition, quantified as a Langmuir isotherm with 50–100 Å² per molecule and a heat of 10–12 kcal/mole; dose is specified per mole of silver rather than per litre of emulsion; supersensitization, antisensitization and desensitization become named, dosed, quantified phenomena; and relative quantum yield becomes the efficiency metric, referenced to 4,000 Å. Wavelengths move from Fraunhofer lines to Ångströms. **[E]**

**1966 → 1995.** The mechanism closes: electron transfer, with energy transfer measured and found "considerably smaller" even in contact. Energy levels become the design variables, measured by second-harmonic voltammetry and UV photoelectron spectroscopy, with two sharp threshold potentials (−1.42 V for sensitization, −1.25 V for electron-trapping desensitization) that classify dyes and predict whether supersensitization will help. Marcus theory is fitted (k° = 10¹¹ s⁻¹, λ = 0.05 eV) and the absence of an inverted region explained. Aggregate shift gets a molecular-exciton treatment with the slip angle α as the controlling geometric variable. Adsorption gets desorption enthalpies and a zero-order desorption law implying linear aggregates. And the absorbance ceiling is measured: peak absorbance 0.09 at 65 % coverage, half-width 283 cm⁻¹, film absorbance 10–20 % in the sensitized region. **[E]**

**Silences a reader would expect filled:**

- **There is no spectral-sensitivity curve for any real film stock anywhere in this material** — no λ, no relative sensitivity, no half-width for any commercial product, in any of the three sources. `[Wall 1929; Duffin 1966; Tani 1995]` **[F]**
- **Tani's dye λ_max library (Tables 5.1, 5.2) is image-only and unrecoverable** (§9.6.4), so no wavelength can be attached to any of Tani's numbered dyes. **[F]**
- **The J-band peak wavelengths and half-widths of Tani's Figs. 5.4 and 5.6 are in the figures only.** The only surviving absolute half-width anywhere is **283 cm⁻¹** for the Fig. 8.1 aggregate. `[Tani 1995, §§5.2, 8.1.1, pp.118–121, 229–230 (PDF 127–130, 238–239)]` **[F]**
- **No nm-per-substituent numbers** exist for the Hammett/substituent design rules, in either source. **[F]**
- **No dye extinction coefficient in absolute units** (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹ or cm²/molecule) appears anywhere; absorption strength is always relative or expressed as an absorbance at a stated coverage. **[F]**
- **The percent absorbance of a high-sensitivity film in the intrinsic blue region is lost to OCR** (§9.12); only the spectrally sensitized figure (10–20 %) survives. **[F]**
- Tani's numbered display equations in Chapter 5 were images and did not survive extraction. This affects **Eqs. (5.1)–(5.30)**, including the λ_max/E_TR relations (5.1–5.2), the molecular exciton treatment (5.3–5.8), Kubelka–Munk (5.9), the φ_r definition (5.14) and its identity conditions (5.15–5.16), the Marcus expressions (5.17–5.19), the k_s/k_L extraction from τ_F (5.20–5.21), the radiative-rate/aggregate-size relation (5.22), the back-reaction channels (5.24)–(5.27), and the two-carrier injection model (5.28)–(5.30). **The symbol definitions given throughout §9 above are what survived; the functional forms are not recoverable from this material.** `[Tani 1995, §0 caveat; Ch. 5, pp.111–158 (PDF 120–167)]` **[F]**

**Disagreements, presented unaveraged:**

1. **Mechanism:** 1966 holds electron transfer *and* energy transfer both operate; 1995 holds electron transfer is established and energy transfer is much slower even in contact. This is a dated change, not a standing dispute. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.133 (PDF 139); Tani 1995, §5.8, pp.149–150 (PDF 158–159)]`
2. **Whether relative quantum yield can exceed unity:** Duffin says never; Tani documents two cases where it does and explains why. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, pp.122–123 (PDF 128–129); Tani 1995, §5.5, pp.133–134 (PDF 142–143)]`
3. **k_s versus aggregate size:** Tani finds k_s *decreases* with aggregate size; Muenter *et al.* find it *increases*. `[Tani 1995, §5.6, pp.141–142 (PDF 150–151)]`
4. **What "desensitization" is:** Duffin flags a 1965 proposal that it may be **interference with development** rather than reduced latent-image efficiency; Tani's three mechanisms are all latent-image-side and do not consider the development-side explanation. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.134 (PDF 140); Tani 1995, §5.8, p.153 (PDF 162)]`
5. **Fig. 5.15 grain size inside Tani:** text says 0.6 µm, caption says 0.2 µm. `[Tani 1995, §5.5, p.133 (PDF 142)]`
6. **Fig. 8.1 dye identity inside Tani:** caption names 3,3′-disulfopropyl-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine, text names 5,5′-dichloro-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine. `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, pp.229–230 (PDF 238–239)]`
7. **Iodide and orthochromatic sensitization:** the 1929 received axiom was that ortho emulsions should contain little or no iodide; Wall himself refutes it (5 % used successfully) and Duffin reverses it outright (more iodide increased J-band sensitization). `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.66 (PDF 74); Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.125 (PDF 131)]`

## 10. Latent-image formation, quantum sensitivity, and reciprocity

### 10.1 The Gurney–Mott framework and its 1966 status

**1966.** "The first theory which came anywhere near explaining the facts, on a modern solid-state basis, is that due to **Gurney and Mott in 1938**." Duffin sets out the sequence:

1. Two entities pre-exist in the crystal: **(a)** a **sensitivity speck**, "the chemical entity produced during the sensitization process and which may be silver or silver sulphide", which "confers the sensitivity by acting as a **nucleating centre** for the latent-image formation"; **(b)** **interstitial silver ions**, i.e. silver ions not at lattice positions.
2. On exposure, **electrons and positive holes** are formed. The electrons "rapidly move through the crystal and locate themselves at the sensitivity speck." The mobility ordering is stated as a fact: "**electrons > positive holes > interstitial Ag ions**."
3. "Sufficient interstitial silver ions will therefore be attracted to the now negatively-charged sensitivity speck to cause the **neutralization of this charge** and thus form an **aggregation of silver atoms, the latent image**."
4. "The positive holes escape to the surface, and, **as bromine atoms, react with the gelatin**. **If, on the other hand, the positive hole gets to the sensitivity centre before the silver ion it will recombine with the electron and the results of the absorption of the photon will be lost.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.176–177 (PDF 182–183), Figs. 9.1–9.4]` **[M]**

What Duffin says is settled about it: "The most important of these is the **separation of the mechanism of latent-image formation into electronic and ionic steps**; all subsequent theories have accepted this concept." Two independent supports are given: (i) the latent image forms **very inefficiently at very low temperatures** — "although the trapping of the very mobile electrons takes place at the low temperature, the subsequent completion of the second stage is retarded because **ionic movement is 'frozen'** and can only occur on warming. This increases the chances of recombination with a positive hole"; (ii) Hamm, Hamilton and others, exposing large silver-halide grains in an applied electric field, showed **the silver is formed nearest the positive pole** — i.e. the electrons moved first and the silver ions discharged them subsequently. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.176–178 (PDF 182–184), Fig. 9.5]` **[Q]**

Duffin's verdict, with its dated caveat: "**Overall, the present day form of the Gurney—Mott theory is probably the best explanation of the facts**", but one of his own objections is itself period-marked — "The very important part played by imperfections in the formation of internal image in large slab crystals **was not appreciated in 1938** and is completely ignored by the theory." And: "**Most authors today still regard the question as unsolved.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.176, 178, 188 (PDF 182, 184, 194)]` **[F]**

The rival Mitchell stepwise mechanism, and Duffin's objection to it: six stages, requiring a kink-site Ag⁺ (electron trap, giving an unstable Ag atom) and a kink Br⁻ or S²⁻ sensitivity centre (hole trap, which releases an interstitial Ag⁺); repeated three times this gives an "uncharged latent-image speck" of **three** silver atoms, and a fourth interstitial ion then gives the stable, positively charged **Ag₄⁺** speck which "will now actually **repel positive holes**". Duffin's criticism: it requires a **triple collision**, "very rare in chemistry… and it is necessary for this to occur three times". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.179–182 (PDF 185–188), Figs. 9.6–9.10]` **[M]**

**The concentration principle** — Duffin's name for the requirement that makes a sensitivity speck necessary at all:

> "The products of the photolysis must be **concentrated at a single point** if they are to initiate development efficiently. If they are distributed randomly over the crystal surface, **no real latent image would be present; any situation producing such a dispersion of photolysis products will increase the total number of silver atoms required to initiate development.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.177 (PDF 183)]` **[F]** — this is the 1966 statement of what Tani calls dispersion of image centres (§8.7), and it is the shared root of high-intensity reciprocity failure and of the sensitization optimum.

Supporting measurement, 1966: the ionic conductivity of emulsion crystals "has shown it to be **about 1,000 times as high as for pure crystals**", and Brady and Hamilton's work shows this conductivity is produced by **surface** ions — evidenced by its sensitivity to added chemicals known to affect silver-ion mobility, and to the pAg of the environment. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.179 (PDF 185)]` **[Q]** Tani's figure for the same comparison is consistent in direction and magnitude: grain σᵢ is "**2–3 orders of magnitude above large-crystal σᵢ**". `[Tani 1995, §3.1, p.49 (PDF 58)]` **[Q]**

### 10.2 The 1995 mechanism: alternating electronic and ionic steps, with the charge-alternation principle

**1995.** The sequence: light absorption → photoelectron plus hole → photoelectron trapped (**electronic** process) → the trapped electron attracts and reacts with an interstitial Ag⁺ (**ionic** process) → a silver atom, the **latent preimage centre** → repetition at the same centre → the **latent image centre**.

> "Although a latent preimage center is unstable, it is capable of trapping a free electron and then capturing a second interstitial silver ion to form **Ag2, which is fully stable** and is called a latent subimage center… a latent image center forms in **two distinct stages, which are termed nucleation and growth**."

`[Tani 1995, §4.1.1, pp.81–83 (PDF 90–92), Fig. 4.1]` **[M]**

The **charge-alternation (partially charged trap) principle**, which is the 1995 explanation of why an efficient trap must be a *kink site* and not a deep trap:

> "…the electrostatic charge of an initial electron-trapping center suitable for efficient latent image formation has a partial, preferably **+½** charge, as for the case of a surface kink site, and becomes a **−½** charge when the center traps an electron. Electron trapping by the center is followed by the ionic process, which makes the center become **+½** charged and thus 'reset' for trapping another electron. The concept of a partially charged electron trap results in an **alternating sign of charge** at each step … and **minimizes the recombination probability**…"

`[Tani 1995, §4.1.1, p.83 (PDF 92)]` **[M]** — the OCR renders the fractions as `+\`, `-|`, `+ \`; the text elsewhere says "half a positive charge" for a kink site, confirming ±½. **[F]**

### 10.3 Nomenclature and the three thresholds

> "A single silver atom, a dimer, and a tetramer of silver atoms are called the latent **preimage**, **subimage**, and **image** centers, respectively. A **preimage center is unstable**, and **subimage and image centers are stable**. A **latent image center can initiate development, whereas a subimage center cannot**."

`[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.8 (PDF 17), Fig. 1.6]` **[F]**

| Centre | Composition | Stability | Developable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Latent **preimage** | Ag₁ | unstable | no |
| Latent **subimage** | Ag₂ | stable | **no** |
| Latent **image** | Ag₄ (tetramer, as named here) | stable | **yes** |

A parallel threshold exists on the fog side, and Tani makes it the reason silver halide materials can be both fast and stable: "A **threshold also exists in the steps for the formation of a fog center**, and photographic emulsions are stable for a long time during both their production and storage due to the existence of this threshold. This is the reason why silver halide photographic materials can achieve both high sensitivity and stability." A fog centre "is identical to or similar to a latent image centre", and absorbs at **540 nm**. `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.8 (PDF 17); §4.3.2, pp.98–99 (PDF 107–108), Fig. 4.13]` **[F]**

### 10.4 The amplification factor

> "Figure 1.5 shows the case of a cubic AgBr grain with an edge length of 1 µm in which there are **20 billion silver ions**. The photolytic reduction and clustering of only **four** silver ions are needed to change the fate of 20 billion silver ions in a grain. The degree of amplification in this case is as large as **five billion**, and is one of the most important reasons why silver halide photographic materials achieve their high sensitivity."

Restated: "Photographic development is a unique amplification process that can amplify as much as **> 10⁹**." `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.7 (PDF 16), Fig. 1.5; §4.1.1, p.83 (PDF 92)]` **[Q]**

Duffin's 1966 version of the same statement: "The capture of a small number, frequently only four, photons can result in a permanent record of four silver atoms. By the development step, these can be converted… into **10⁶ to 10⁹ silver atoms**" — but the raw OCR reads `10° to 10”`, so **the exponents are not reliably recoverable and the range as printed should not be quoted from this material**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.173 (PDF 179)]` **[F]**

### 10.5 The minimum number of silver atoms, and quantum sensitivity

#### 10.5.1 Definition of quantum sensitivity

Tani's definition, verbatim: quantum sensitivity is "the number of absorbed photons per grain required to make **half** of the grains developable". `[Tani 1995, §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101)]` **[F]** Note that this is a *population median*, not a per-grain threshold; the two are different quantities and the literature values below mix them.

#### 10.5.2 Every estimate in the material, in one table

| Quantity | Value | Emulsion / method | Source as cited |
|---|---|---|---|

| Smallest latent image centre, **S**-sensitized AgBr | **4–5 atoms** | same | same |
| Smallest latent image centre, from evaporated metal clusters initiating physical development | **4 Ag atoms** or **2 Au atoms** | evaporated clusters | Hamilton & Logel, in `[Tani 1995, §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101); §6.3, p.177 (PDF 186)]` |
| Smallest latent image centre in Tani's own sensitization schematic, gold case | **three atoms containing a gold atom** | — | `[Tani 1995, Fig. 6.1, p.166 (PDF 175)]` |

IX, p.172 (PDF 178)]` |

| Latent-image speck, Mitchell's uncharged speck then stable speck | **3 atoms** uncharged → **Ag₄⁺** stable | theory | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.179–182 (PDF 185–188)]` |

The surrounding text and the Fayet *et al.* context make Ag₄⁺ the intended reading, but **the raw string does not resolve it**; quote as `Ag^J+ [subscript lost in OCR]`. #### 10.5.3 How the minimum varies with sensitization — the key result

The threshold is **not** a constant of silver halide; it is a function of the sensitization state:

| Sensitization state | Minimum developable centre |
|---|---|
| Sulfur-sensitized AgBr | **4–5 silver atoms** |
| Sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized AgBr | **3 atoms** (one of them gold) |
| Pure gold clusters | **2 gold atoms** |

`[Tani 1995, §4.1.1, p.83 (PDF 92); §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101); §6.3, p.177 (PDF 186); Fig. 6.1, p.166 (PDF 175)]` **[Q]**

The physical basis is the electron affinity difference: **gold 2.4 eV versus silver 1.1 eV**, which is why gold-sensitized image centres have a more positive oxidation potential, and why the gold-bearing cluster reaches developability at a smaller size. `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.177 (PDF 186)]` **[Q]**

The oxidation-potential ladder that pins down where developability begins, measured against a Gibbs–Thompson calibration (ΔE, the redox potential of silver clusters relative to a large silver crystal, ∝ 1/d):

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Extrapolated ΔE for **Ag₄** | about **−380 mV** |
| Extrapolated ΔE for **Ag₇** | about **−340 mV** |
| Measured E_ox of the smallest latent image centres | **−185 mV** (Cramp & Hillson) |
| Measured E_ox, alternative | **about −100 mV** (Hillson) |
| Threshold for physical development | **0 mV** (Pontius *et al.*) |

`[Tani 1995, §4.3.1, p.93 (PDF 102), Fig. 4.6]` **[Q]** — Tani's own warning is that the Gibbs–Thompson line does not extrapolate cleanly to Ag₄, so the −380 mV figure is a extrapolation, not a measurement. **[F]**

And the reason a P centre (Ag₂ at a charged site) cannot itself develop, expressed in the same terms: E_ox(P) is more positive than E_ox(latent image centres), so HOMO(Ag₂) lies below HOMO(Agₙ, n > 2) and LUMO(Ag₂) above — the dimer is both harder to oxidise and a poorer electron donor than the tetramer. `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.102–104 (PDF 111–113), Fig. 4.18]` **[Q]**

There is also headroom below the threshold: latent subimage centres are stable and become developable after **latensification** or under **enforced development**; "there is some possibility for a further increase in photographic sensitivity if one could find the development condition that could detect and discriminate image centers composed of **two atoms** … from fog formation." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` **[Q]**

#### 10.5.4 One photon, two electrons — Lowe's hypothesis

The mechanism by which the effective threshold can be beaten, and the reason relative quantum yield can exceed unity (§9.10.1):

Sequence as printed: light absorption → hole trapped by an R centre, `Ag₂(R)` → ionic relaxation (release of a silver ion into an interstitial position) → dissociation of a single silver atom and **liberation of an extra free electron**.

> "Thus, in the presence of R centers, **one absorbed photon can produce two free electrons** available for latent image formation."

Restated: "an absorbed photon can create **at most two free electrons** in a grain in the presence of hydrogen hypersensitization centers or reduction sensitization centers". `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, p.104 (PDF 113), Eqs. (4.4)–(4.8); §4.3.1, p.92 (PDF 101)]` **[Q]**

Also stated as a *double* function of hole capture: "the capture of a positive hole by an R center achieves **not only the prohibition of the recombination, but also the creation of an extra free electron** available for the formation of a latent image center." `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, pp.74–75 (PDF 83–84), Eqs. (3.20)–(3.22)]` **[M]**

**[E]** This is why the "theoretical limit is two" photons per grain quoted in §10.5.2 sits below the three-atom minimum centre: two photons yield up to four electrons in the presence of R centres, enough for a three- or four-atom centre. The factor of two is the whole margin between the observed practical quantum sensitivity (~10) and the theoretical floor (2).

### 10.6 Carrier generation, transport, lifetimes and diffusion lengths

#### 10.6.1 Primary conversion efficiency

> "Since the binding energies of indirect excitons are as small as **0.022 eV for AgBr** and **0.04 eV (estimated value) for AgCl**, excitons in silver halide emulsion grains freely dissociate into an electron and a positive hole at room temperature. The **quantum yield for the photoconduction of electrons in AgBr at 300 K is therefore greater than 0.960** and favorable for photographic sensitivity."

`[Tani 1995, §3.3, p.60 (PDF 69)]` **[Q]** — i.e. **η > 0.96 free electrons per absorbed photon in AgBr at 300 K**. This is the closest thing in the material to a primary-photoconversion quantum efficiency, and it is nearly unity: essentially none of the DQE loss happens at this step.

#### 10.6.2 Effective masses and mobilities

| Quantity | AgCl | AgBr |
|---|---|---|
| Electron effective mass (single isotropic parabolic valley) | **0.399** | **0.282** |
| Electron drift mobility μ_D (time-of-flight, high-quality single crystals; in agreement with Hall mobility from the photo-Hall effect) | **50 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹** | **60 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹** |
| Hole drift mobility at room temperature | **~10⁻¹ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹** | **~1 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹**, "steeply decreasing with increasing temperature" |

`[Tani 1995, §3.3, pp.61–62 (PDF 70–71), Figs. 3.17, 3.18]` **[Q]**

The mobility "is limited **not by shallow electron traps, but by scattering on LO phonons**, whose probability is proportional to the LO phonon density. The mobility thus **increases with decreasing temperature**." `[Tani 1995, §3.3, p.61 (PDF 70)]` **[M]**

Hole self-trapping, AgCl: the self-trapped hole is a hole on a silver ion with displaced nearest-neighbour Cl⁻ (Jahn–Teller); its thermal ionization energy is **0.12 eV** and it is unstable above about **50 K**. For AgBr the hole trapping level depth from Tani's Eq. (3.11) is **0.44 eV**; Kanzaki finds the silver ion vacancy is the dominant hole centre, with a binding energy of **0.4 eV**. `[Tani 1995, §3.3, pp.62 (PDF 71), Fig. 3.18]` **[Q]**

#### 10.6.5 Why the electron diffusion length matters: the size–sensitivity knee

> "It has been described by Farnell and is now widely observed that the sensitivity of silver halide emulsion grains to blue light (inherent sensitivity) is proportional to their **volume** only under the condition that the grain size **does not exceed a certain value**. Since the absorbance of a silver halide emulsion grain in the blue region is weak and nearly proportional to its volume, the inherent sensitivity of an emulsion grain should be proportional to its volume **such that the diffusion length of photoelectrons is large enough to allow them to reach a growing nucleus in the grain**."

And numerically: "The deviation of the proportionality of sensitivity to grain size was usually observed when the **grain volume exceeded about 1 /Am** and could be attributed to the limited diffusion length of photoelectrons with respect to the size of emulsion grains."

**OCR flag:** the raw string is `grain volume exceeded about 1 /Am`. "Volume" carrying a length unit is dimensionally wrong: this is either "grain **size** exceeded about 1 µm" or "grain volume exceeded about 1 µm³". **Quote the raw string; do not silently pick one.** Either way the knee is at the **~1 µm scale**, consistent with the in-grain electron diffusion lengths of 0.4–2.3 µm above. **[F]**

Chemical sensitization moves the knee: "deviation of the sensitivity from its proportionality to grain volume appeared in **sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized grains at a smaller size** than in unsensitized grains, indicating that the diffusion length of photoelectrons was **shorter** in the former than in the latter." Fig. 4.3 plots log S against d (diameter of the circle of equal projected area) for unsensitized (○) and S+Au-sensitized (●) octahedral AgBr. `[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.88–89 (PDF 97–98), Fig. 4.3]` **[F]** — this is the same mechanism as the sensitization optimum: added traps shorten the electron's range.

#### 10.6.6 Trap depth and residence time — Marker's equation

Berry, via Marker's equation (Tani's Eq. 3.23; body lost; symbols E = trap depth, t = resident time of the electronic charge carrier):

| Trap depth E | Residence time t |
|---|---|
| **0.3 eV** | **1 µsec** |
| **0.7 eV** | **10 sec** |
| **1.2 eV** | **10 years** |

`[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.75 (PDF 84)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** These three (E, t) pairs are enough to fix a two-parameter Arrhenius law, and they bracket every trap depth quoted elsewhere in this document. Note the consequence: at 0.3 eV — the sulfur centre's thermal depth (§8.5.1) — residence is only about 1 µs. That is consistent with Tani's insistence that a *useful* sensitization trap must be shallow: the electron must be held long enough for the ionic step (interstitial Ag⁺ arrival) but not so long that the trap becomes a recombination site. The Ir³⁺ dopant at 0.46 eV with ~20 ms lifetime and the Rh³⁺ dopant at ~0.8 eV with > 10⁵ s lifetime (§8.5.9) sit on the other side of that boundary, which is why they cost speed.

### 10.7 Reciprocity: the two-stage picture, the I² law, and the two failures

#### 10.7.1 Definitions, stated verbatim because they matter

> "Photographic sensitivity (S) is usually expressed by the reciprocal of the exposure required to make a certain proportion of emulsion grains developable, and exposure (E) is the product between light intensity (I) and exposure time (t). **The reciprocity law means that S is solely given by 1/E, regardless of I and t.** Failure of the reciprocity law is usually observed in the ranges of **high I with short t** [i.e., **high-intensity reciprocity law failure (HIRF)**] and/or **low I with long t** [i.e., **low-intensity reciprocity law failure (LIRF)**]."

`[Tani 1995, §4.2, p.89 (PDF 98)]` **[F]**

#### 10.7.2 The I² statement — the source's own reciprocity argument

> "Since a latent subimage center is composed of **two** silver atoms, the rate of formation of subimage centers is proportional to the **square of the number of photons absorbed per second** and thus to the **square of the light intensity**. Thus, a threshold exists between a latent preimage center and a subimage center in steps for the formation of a latent image center in terms of light intensity. Thus, **any illumination whose intensity is not strong enough to form a latent subimage center does not change silver halide grains, even when it is repeated many times over a long period.**"

Restated in the sensitivity chapter: "…it is considered that **the rate of the nucleation is proportional to the square of the concentration of photoelectrons (i.e., proportional to the square of light intensity)**, and is therefore **larger for high intensity and short exposure than for low intensity and long exposure under the condition with constant exposure**."

`[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.8 (PDF 17); §4.2, p.87 (PDF 96)]` **[Q]**

This is the **only exponent-bearing reciprocity law in the material**: nucleation rate ∝ I². **There is no Schwarzschild exponent, no threshold intensity in absolute units, and no temperature dependence of reciprocity failure anywhere in the material examined.** **[F]**

**[E]** Nucleation ∝ I² at fixed E = I·t means nucleation ∝ I·E, i.e. the *number of nuclei* rises linearly with intensity at constant exposure. That is simultaneously the correct sign for LIRF (too few nuclei at low I, and the unstable preimage reverts before a second electron arrives) and for HIRF (too many nuclei at high I, dispersed over the grain, so no single one reaches the developable size). A two-sided reciprocity model with an intensity-dependent nucleus-count term is therefore supported in *form* by the source; **every coefficient would have to come from measured LIRF/HIRF data, not from this material.**

The same threshold argument is what makes very weak illumination photographically inert: if I is too low to build a subimage centre before the preimage reverts, no amount of repetition accumulates anything. This is the mechanism behind the stability side of the "high sensitivity and stability" claim of §10.3. **[E]**

#### 10.7.3 The accepted mechanisms of the two failures

> "It is accepted that **LIRF arises from inefficiency in formation of the nucleus due to instability of a latent preimage**, and that **HIRF arises from inefficiency of latent image formation due to dispersion of the nuclei (i.e., formation of more than one image center per grain)**. Hamilton and Hailstone have proposed that **dispersed image centers are likely to enhance recombination of trapped electrons with positive holes**."
> "Thus, it is generally observed that **LIRF could be increased and HIRF decreased by increasing the number of electron-trapping sensitization centers**. For example, increase in the number of sulfur sensitization centers usually results in **improvement in LIRF and deterioration of HIRF**."

`[Tani 1995, §4.2, p.89 (PDF 98)]` **[F]**

The first sentence of that second quotation is internally awkward ("LIRF could be increased and HIRF decreased"); the second sentence disambiguates it. **Read as: more sulfur sensitization centres → LIRF improves, HIRF worsens.** **[F]**

Duffin's 1966 statements of the same two failures, independently arrived at:

**LIRF (long-time reciprocity failure):** "**if the total three photons are not absorbed in a certain minimum time, then the sub-image or pre-image specks will break down and nullify the effect of the exposure.**" Mitchell's stepwise mechanism accounts for it, but "**any process which entails a number of steps before stability must possess the same ability to explain long-time exposure reciprocity failure.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.182 (PDF 188)]` **[M]**

**HIRF:** "A special case of competition is high-intensity reciprocity-failure. The loss in speed at very short exposure is believed to be due to the **formation of a multiplicity of silver-specks instead of one of sufficient size to initiate development**. At high intensities many photo-electrons will be formed in a very short interval. If one of these moves to an appropriate trapping-site but the slower-moving silver-ion cannot neutralize the electron… before a second electron arrives, that **second electron will be repelled to another location**. The additive effect will therefore be partly lost, with a consequent loss in effective speed. **There is good evidence that more latent-image sites are formed by high-intensity exposures.**" The electron/hole-recombination alternative is "**a less widely accepted explanation**" in 1966 — the reverse of the 1995 weighting, where Hamilton and Hailstone attribute the loss precisely to recombination at the dispersed centres. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.186 (PDF 192)]` **[M]**

Duffin's timing framing, which is the only stated "normal operating range" in the material: "During an exposure, say **between 1/50th and 1 sec, the usual range for normal photographic materials**, a lot of time is available for many atomic processes, each needing **10⁻⁸ secs or less**" (raw `10 ~®secs`, exponent ambiguous; most likely 10⁻⁸). "However, the time interval over which the absorption of the four photons… is very important; **if these photons arrive too quickly or too slowly then they are less effectively used.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.172 (PDF 178)]` **[Q]**

And a categorical exclusion: "**Reciprocity failure does not exist with exposures to X-rays.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.187 (PDF 193)]` **[F]** — consistent with §10.11 below, where a single X-ray quantum delivers hundreds of silver atoms and no accumulation over time is required.

#### 10.7.4 The measured HIRF optimum in ionic conductivity

The most model-relevant reciprocity result in the material, because it has a defined metric:

> "Takada prepared silver halide emulsion grains with variations of ionic conductivity (i.e., variation of concentration of interstitial silver ions) by changing their **halide composition and crystal habit**. He then sulfur-sensitized the grains and examined the degree of their HIRF. It was observed that the **smallest degree of HIRF was observed in the grains with medium ionic conductivity**, and that **severe HIRF was observed in the grains with low ionic conductivity, such as AgCl grains, as well as in grains with high conductivity, such as octahedral AgBrI grains**."

The metric, verbatim from Fig. 4.5: "the degree of HIRF as expressed by the **difference between sensitivities with exposures for 10⁻⁴ sec [S(10⁻⁴ s)] and for 1 sec [S(1 s)]**… The degree of sulfur sensitization of each emulsion was **optimized for a 1 sec exposure**." Fig. 4.4 grains: equivalent circular diameter **0.2 µm**.

`[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.90–91 (PDF 99–100), Figs. 4.4, 4.5]` **[Q]**

The mechanism on both sides of the optimum:

- **Low σᵢ:** "electron trapping by a sensitization center cannot be followed rapidly enough by the ionic process for the center to be **reset**", so a *new* nucleus forms under high intensity. **[M]**
- **High σᵢ:** excessive interstitial Ag⁺ gives an enhanced ionic process and hence **enhanced nucleation**, and "since the rate of nucleation is proportional to the square of light intensity, this enhancement of nucleation is **more significant for high-intensity exposures**" — again dispersing the image centres. **[M]**

`[Tani 1995, §4.2, pp.90–91 (PDF 99–100)]`

**[E]** ΔlogS between 10⁻⁴ s and 1 s exposure is exactly the form a reciprocity-failure specification takes. The source gives the metric and its qualitative dependence on halide composition and habit (AgCl worst at low σᵢ, octahedral AgBrI worst at high σᵢ, a minimum in between) but **no absolute ΔlogS values appear in the text** — they exist only in Fig. 4.5. **[F]**

### 10.8 Detective quantum efficiency

#### 10.8.1 Eq. (1.1), recovered from the page image

Tani's numbered display equations were images in the PDF and did not survive text extraction. **Eq. (1.1) is the only one available verbatim, recovered from the page image:**

```
Eq. (1.1)  DQE = R_o^2 / R^2 = (log e)^2 * gamma^2 / (E * G^2)
```

where R and R_o are signal-to-noise ratios at the input and output respectively; gamma is the slope of the D-logE plot; E is exposure in photons per unit area; G is the Selwyn granularity constant. DQE of photographic films clusters at 1-2%.

`[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25), Eq. (1.1)]` **[Q]**

The surrounding prose, as printed: "The efficiency of color films as well as CCDs as photoreceptors can be evaluated by detective quantum efficiency (DQE), defined as follows: … where **R and R₀ are signal-to-noise ratios at the input and output**, respectively; **γ is the slope of the D-logE plot**; **E is exposure in terms of photons per unit area**; and **G is the Selwyn granularity constant**." And: "The estimated value of **DQE of photographic films clusters in the range of 1-2%**. … The quantum efficiency of a CCD could be as large as **several tens of percentages at low temperature**." `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25)]` **[Q]** — the printed text carries a stray footnote marker, "per unitf area". **[F]**

#### 10.8.2 What Eq. (1.1) constrains

**[E]** Eq. (1.1) ties the characteristic-curve slope γ, the Selwyn granularity constant G, and the photon exposure E into one relation, so **γ, granularity and speed are not independently free.** Reading the equation:

- DQE ∝ γ² — steeper curves convert a given input signal-to-noise ratio into more output modulation.
- DQE ∝ 1/G² — granularity enters squared and with the opposite sign, so any gain in γ that is bought by widening the grain-sensitivity distribution (and hence raising G) can be wholly cancelled.
- DQE ∝ 1/E — for a fixed γ and G, the DQE falls as the exposure required rises; equivalently, at fixed DQE, speed (1/E) is set by (γ/G)².

The practical consequence is that a stock's gamma, its rms granularity and its speed form a constrained triple: given any two and a DQE figure, the third follows. Since measured DQE for photographic films clusters in a narrow band (1–2 %, §10.8.1) and had improved only "to a limited degree" between 1969 and 1995 (§10.8.3), that constraint is tight in practice, not merely formal. Note this is our reading of the relation; **Tani states the equation and the DQE range but does not draw this conclusion.**

Tani does, however, assert the underlying trade in words: "Most photographic materials need appropriate **gradation and exposure latitude**, and therefore photographic emulsion layers contain silver halide grains whose sensitivity is distributed over an appropriate range." And: "When the **distribution of sensitivity among grains is expanded, the DQE value becomes lower at the maximum and more wide ranging** in the plot of DQE versus exposure." Bird's criterion: the **integral of DQE over exposure** is largest "when the **smallest number of monodispersed emulsions** was used to make pictures with the desired gradation." Tani's assessment of the state of the art: "the grain sizes of emulsions used for products are **still widely distributed** and leave much room for future improvement." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242)]` **[Q]**

#### 10.8.3 The DQE loss budget — Bird et al., reproduced by Tani

Bird *et al.* measured, for the first time, the DQE of photographic materials and found the DQE of a high-speed photographic film for taking pictures was as low as about 1%. The chain of losses, as Tani reproduces it:

incomplete light absorption reduces DQE to 42%; the four-atom threshold for latent-image formation to 64% (cumulative 27%); recombination losses in latent-image formation to 16% (cumulative 4.3%); the distributions of grain size and sensitivity to 36% (cumulative 1.5%); random grain arrangement to 72% (cumulative 1.1%).

`[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]` **[Q]**

Tabulated, with the stage factors and running product:

| Stage | Stage factor | Cumulative DQE |
|---|---|---|
| Incomplete light absorption | **42 %** | **42 %** |
| Four-atom threshold for latent-image formation | **64 %** | **27 %** |
| Recombination losses in latent-image formation | **16 %** | **4.3 %** |
| Distributions of grain size and sensitivity | **36 %** | **1.5 %** |
| Random grain arrangement | **72 %** | **1.1 %** |

`[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237); primary source Bird, Jones & Ames, Appl. Optics 8, 2389 (1969)]` **[Q]**

Tani's own gloss: "The DQE values of photographic films have been improved to a **limited degree** since that time." `[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]` **[F]**

**[E]** This is a complete multiplicative efficiency budget with five named stages, and it locates the losses unambiguously. The single largest loss is the first — incomplete light absorption, 58 % gone before any photochemistry happens — which is exactly what the absorbance numbers of §10.9 and §9.12 predict. The largest *internal* loss is recombination at 16 % retained (84 % lost), which is why the entire 1995 mechanism (charge alternation, R centres, hole traps, space-charge band bending) is organised around suppressing recombination. Note also that the 36 % factor for grain size and sensitivity distribution and the 72 % factor for random arrangement together bound how much of a material's granularity can be attributed to placement statistics versus sensitivity spread. The budget is a **1969 measurement on one high-speed film**; it must not be treated as a current-stock value.

Tani gives a direct verdict on trying to recover the last factor: "the random arrangement of large numbers of silver halide grains in emulsion layers brings about the **insensibility of photographic materials to small numbers of inferior silver halide grains and dust particles** … and enables the mass production of photographic materials with a large area. This advantage is liable to deteriorate when grains are regularly arranged… Taking into account the facts that the regular arrangement of the grains has a poor prospect of success at present and would **increase DQE by at most 40 %** according to the analysis by Bird et al., it seems that the regular arrangement of silver halide grains in emulsion layers is **not necessarily promising**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242)]` **[Q]** — 1/0.72 = 1.39, so "at most 40 %" is exactly the reciprocal of the last stage factor. **[E]**

The defect-insensitivity that random arrangement buys, quantified: "A defective silver halide grain or a dust particle whose size is comparable to those of silver halide grains (around 1 µm) hardly disturbs the function of an equivalent pixel in a color film, because it is only **one among 500 grains**…" — the 500 figure coming from an ISO 100 colour negative with **1.2 × 10⁷ grains/mm²** and **2 × 10⁷ equivalent pixels per 36 × 24 mm² frame**, giving **43 µm² per equivalent pixel** (raw string reads `43 A2`; 864 mm² / 2 × 10⁷ = 43.2 µm², so this is 43 µm², mis-OCR'd). `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28), Fig. 1.13; §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]` **[Q]**

#### 10.8.4 The dated DQE trajectory

| Year | Statement |
|---|---|
| **1969** | Bird, Jones & Ames measure film DQE for the first time: **about 1 %**, with the five-stage budget above |
| **1985** | "**In 1985, Tani determined that photographic sensitivity is dependent upon light absorption, the quantum yield of latent image formation, and the size of the smallest latent image center.**" The absorbed fraction was thought to be "**at most one third**" and could be "**increased by about three times**"; quantum sensitivity of camera films was "**around 10**" against a "**theoretical limit [of] two**", so "**increase by about five times**" was expected; "In total, it was predicted that there would be room for an increase in sensitivity of **about one order of magnitude**" |
| **1989** | "**In 1989 Bird predicted that silver halide photographic systems would advance from the DQE value of 1–2 % at that time to about 10 %**" and that any such improvement "would be reflected in all silver halide systems". The gain "will be used to achieve **either an increase in image quality by reducing the size of emulsion grains without changing their sensitivity or an increase in sensitivity without changing image quality**" |
| **1992–1994** | "**Since then, remarkable progress has been made** … The **light absorption of color films was improved by the use of tabular grains**, and the possibility for increase in light absorption in the future is **about two times**. The **average volume of silver halide grains in color films was greatly reduced without changing their sensitivity**, indicating the achievement of an increase in quantum sensitivity of the grains. It is therefore reasonable to consider that there will be room for a **several times improvement** in the efficiency of image formation in the future." (refs. Ishimaru *et al.*, *Fujifilm Res. Dev.* **37**, 1 (1992); Sasaki, *Fujifilm Res. Dev.* **39**, 1 (1994)) |

`[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237); §8.1.4, pp.235–236 (PDF 244–245)]` **[Q]**

Tani's assessment of the author's own two dominant limits: "…we have learned that **dispersion of image centers** and **recombination between photoelectrons and positive holes** are the major factors limiting photographic sensitivity". `[Tani 1995, §4.1.3, p.87 (PDF 96)]` **[F]** — which matches the budget: the 64 % and 16 % stages together are the internal photochemical losses, and the 16 % recombination stage is by far the worse of the two.

### 10.9 Light absorption — the numbers behind the first stage of the budget

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Percent absorbance of a high-sensitivity film, **spectrally sensitized region** | **10–20 %** |
| Percent absorbance of a high-sensitivity film, **intrinsic (blue) region** | **[LOST IN OCR]** — raw string reads `is as low as` then a blank, then `in the intrinsic (blue) region and 10-20% in the spectrally sensitized region.` |
| Cubic AgBr grain, **1 µm edge**, at **420 nm** | **about 10 %** |
| Cubic AgBr grain, **1 µm edge**, at **460 nm** | **about 1 %** |
| Effect of **3 mol % AgI** in AgBr on percent absorption at **460 nm** | **increases it by five times** |

`[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` **[Q]**

The two structural reasons: blue absorption is weak because it is an **indirect transition**; and photons absorbed by a grain scale as **grain volume**, while photons absorbed by adsorbed dye scale as **grain surface area**, because the dye is a monolayer. `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Reading the 42 % first-stage factor of the budget together with these numbers: 42 % retained means 58 % of incident photons were not absorbed, which is consistent with the "at most one third" absorbed fraction quoted in the 1985 assessment (§10.8.4) only if the two figures refer to different quantities — Bird's 42 % is a DQE-weighted stage factor, not a raw absorbed fraction. The two should not be conflated. What is unambiguous is that a 1 µm cubic AgBr grain absorbs ~1 % at 460 nm, that 3 mol % iodide takes that to ~5 %, and that a whole high-speed film absorbs only 10–20 % in its dye-sensitized band. Absorption is the dominant loss and it is a geometric and optical problem, not a photochemical one.

The design bind Tani states plainly: "A large number of fine and well-designed silver halide grains are separately and randomly arranged in thin gelatin layers with a **relatively low packing density** to achieve fine imaging. However, **this arrangement prevents grains in these layers from absorbing incident light efficiently.**" And: "When the packing density is constant, the **fraction of incident light absorbed by the layers increases, and the image quality decreases with increasing thickness** of the layers." **No numeric grain volume fraction is given anywhere in the material.** `[Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18); §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242)]` **[F]**

Duffin's 1966 version of the volume-not-area rule: "The **volume** of the crystal, not merely its surface area facing the incident light, is the important property in assessing the light-trapping capacity of a crystal. This accounts, for example, for the **high speed to blue light of the thick grains of the modern high-speed X-ray emulsions**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.175 (PDF 181)]` **[F]**

### 10.10 From grain populations to the characteristic curve — Duffin's derivation

This is the clearest statement in the material of why the characteristic curve has the shape it does, and it belongs in this section because both of its inputs are latent-image quantities.

> "There are **two types of variation** which can occur between individual emulsion grains. The first is the **stopping power** of the crystals; how many quanta each will absorb, and **this depends on grain volume**. The second difference is in the **number of quanta needed to render a grain developable**. **These two effects are to a large extent additive and account for the differing grain sensitivities, which, in turn, account for the shape of the well-known characteristic curve. The number of quanta per crystal required to render a grain developable, controls the contrast.**"

Provenance of the figure that illustrates it, stated by Duffin himself: Fig. 9.12 "was **calculated mathematically from the random absorption of the light by the crystals and is not derived from an experiment**. Experimental results, however, show that **the faster crystals do give lower contrast**."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.185 (PDF 191), Fig. 9.12]` **[Q]**

And the mechanism that generates the *threshold* distribution, as distinct from the volume distribution — a recombination lottery:

> "In those grains where, for reasons of purely random movement, recombination does not occur, **4 quanta produce 4 silver atoms** and the grain becomes developable. In the other grains, **which may be identical in structure**, an amount of recombination does occur… and then more photons will be needed. **In extreme cases a large proportion of the photons recombine, and then perhaps 30 quanta are needed to produce 4 silver atoms.** These considerations have important practical implications; they mean that it is **probably not possible ever to make all the grains in an emulsion respond to just four quanta.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.185 (PDF 191)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Together these give a first-principles account of the characteristic curve from two distributions: (i) an absorbed-quanta distribution set by the grain-volume distribution, Poisson given even illumination (the book states the calculation assumes "a purely random distribution of photons"); and (ii) a per-grain quanta-threshold distribution running from 4 to about 30, set by recombination luck and by multiple-speck competition. Contrast is then a *derived* quantity: a higher threshold raises contrast, and faster grains give lower contrast (which Duffin says is experimentally confirmed). Gold sensitization moves the threshold down and therefore moves speed up and gamma down together, exactly as §8.6 records. Tani's DQE statement (§10.8.2) is the same coupling seen from the noise side: widening the grain-sensitivity distribution to buy gradation lowers peak DQE. Neither source gives a transfer function.

Duffin's related statement on where the internal/surface split goes during digestion, which sets which population is being counted: digestion shifts the image from internal to surface — surface-image sensitivity rises while internal-image sensitivity falls, because surface specks out-compete internal traps, the internal trapping sites not themselves being chemically altered. "**In commercial practice, sensitization is carried out so that surface latent image is at a maximum.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.183–184 (PDF 189–190), Fig. 9.11]` **[F]**

The assay methods that make the split measurable, 1966: surface image only, with "a strictly **non-solvent** developer, that is a developer containing **no bromide or sulphite**"; internal image, by a brief **potassium ferricyanide** bleach then a developer containing thiosulphate sized to etch the grains; total image, by solvent development without prebleach. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.183–184 (PDF 189–190)]` **[F]** Tani's equivalent, 1995: **D19** for surface development and **D19 + KI at 0.5 g/l** for internal development after bleaching the surface centres. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.192–194 (PDF 201–203), Fig. 6.16]` **[F]**

### 10.11 High-energy quanta and charged particles — where the model breaks

Duffin's Table 9.2 is the only quantitative comparison of visible-light and X-ray photochemistry in the material.

**TABLE 9.2 — NUMBER OF SILVER ATOMS PER QUANTUM FOR VISIBLE LIGHT AND X-RAYS**

| Wavelength (Å) | Silver atoms per quantum absorbed |
|---|---|
| 4936 | **0.96** |
| 4047 | **0.92** |
| 3658 | **0.93** |
| 1.54 | **148** |
| 1.09 | **210** |
| 0.63 | **363** |
| 0.24 | **920** |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.187 (PDF 193), Table 9.2]` **[Q]** — the first three entries are visible/near-UV mercury lines, the last four X-ray wavelengths; the yield is dimensionless silver atoms per absorbed quantum. Reconstruction confidence is high: the OCR emitted a strict alternating wavelength/value stream, and the physics (≈1 atom per visible quantum, hundreds per X-ray quantum, rising as λ falls) is self-consistent. **[F]**

The accompanying text: high-energy radiation "gives a whole series of secondary changes, releasing a **flood of electrons and positive holes**"; "**In extreme cases, more than one silver-halide grain may be affected, something which never occurs with visible light**"; and the same applies to charged particles, so "**every grain struck by the radiation or a particle becomes developable**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.187 (PDF 193)]` **[F]**

**[E]** The visible-light column of Table 9.2 is itself a significant result: 0.92–0.96 silver atoms per absorbed quantum, i.e. essentially one silver atom per photon, which is the direct sensitometric confirmation of the >0.96 photoconduction quantum yield Tani quotes from exciton binding energies (§10.6.1). The two sources, thirty years apart and by entirely different methods, agree to within their stated precision. The X-ray column explains the absence of reciprocity failure under X-rays (§10.7.3): a single quantum delivers 148–920 silver atoms, far above any threshold, so no temporal accumulation is required and neither LIRF nor HIRF can arise.

Duffin also records the developed-silver form as a separate variable: "The form of this final silver-image is also important and can consist of compact or **bulky filamentary** silver-metal; the latter gives the **higher covering power** and is therefore beneficial in terms of **speed, contrast and maximum density**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.173 (PDF 179)]` **[F]**

## 11. Latent-image stability and keeping

Two quite different things are called "keeping" in this literature and the sources do not always separate them. They must be kept apart:

1. **Latent-image keeping** — the fate of an *exposed* but undeveloped image over time. Its failure mode is **latent-image fading** (also called regression), a loss of developable centres.
2. **Raw-stock keeping** — the fate of an *unexposed* coated material in storage. Its failure mode is **fog growth**, the spontaneous appearance of developable grains.

The two have opposite signs (one loses centres, one gains them) but share chemistry: both turn on the stability of small silver and silver sulphide clusters against oxidation and against further growth.

### 11.1 Why a latent image can fade at all: the stability ladder

The thermodynamic basis is the threshold structure of §10.3. The preimage centre (Ag₁) is **unstable**; the subimage (Ag₂) and image (Ag₄) centres are **stable**. `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.8 (PDF 17), Fig. 1.6]` **[F]** So a *completed* latent image is not spontaneously unstable — fading requires an external agent, most obviously a positive hole or an oxidant.

Duffin's Mitchell-mechanism account makes the hole-attack sensitivity explicit and stage-dependent:

- The **pre-latent-image speck** (one silver atom) is unstable and "acts as a convenient location point for another photoelectron and interstitial silver ion". **[M]**
- The **latent sub-image speck** (two silver atoms) is "**relatively unstable in that it has no resistance to attack by positive holes**". **[M]**
- After a third electron/hole-trapping sequence, the **uncharged latent-image speck** of three silver atoms forms; "It is now large enough to act as a development [centre]". **[M]**
- A fourth interstitial ion gives the stable, positively charged **Ag₄⁺** speck, which "**will now actually repel positive holes**". **[M]**

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.179–182 (PDF 185–188), Figs. 9.8–9.10]`

**[E]** The Ag₄⁺ charge reversal is the structural reason a fully formed latent image is far more stable than a partial one: the completed speck electrostatically repels the very species that would destroy it. That makes fading a phenomenon of *underexposed* grains — those carrying subimage or small image centres — rather than of well-exposed ones, and therefore predicts that latent-image fading should attack the toe of a characteristic curve more than the shoulder. Neither source states this consequence.

Duffin's own use of the same ladder is for reciprocity, not keeping: "**if the total three photons are not absorbed in a certain minimum time, then the sub-image or pre-image specks will break down and nullify the effect of the exposure.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.182 (PDF 188)]` **[M]** — i.e. in 1966, sub-image reversion is invoked as the mechanism of *low-intensity reciprocity failure*, and it is the same reversion that would appear as latent-image fading if it happened after the exposure rather than during it. Duffin does not make that connection.

Duffin's stated **minimum time** is never given a value. "In a certain minimum time" is as quantitative as it gets. **[F]**

### 11.2 The one quantified fading mechanism: dye-hole attack (Tani)

The only latent-image fading measured with time constants, kinetic order and activation energy anywhere in this material is the fading caused by **positive holes trapped on adsorbed sensitizing dyes**.

#### 11.2.1 The bidirectional result — fading without R centres, growth with them

> "Latent subimage and image centers are formed rapidly. When positive holes migrate on the grain surface in the presence of many sensitizing dyes acting as deep positive hole traps, it takes a long time (e.g., **several minutes** depending upon the dyes used) for positive holes to bleach latent image centers as well as to bleach R centers…"
> "It was then observed that, in the presence of a sensitizing dye, **the number of latent image centers decreased after exposure to light in the absence of R centers, while the number of latent image centers increased after exposure to light in the presence of R centers**… Thus, positive holes reacted with latent image centers with a **time constant of several minutes** to bring about their **fading** in the absence of R centers, while positive holes mostly reacted with R centers with a similar time constant to create extra electrons, which were used for the **growth** of subimage centers to latent image centers."

The time constants of the growth and fading reactions "were similar to each other and to the time constant of the **decay of Dye⁺** as measured by means of an electron paramagnetic spectrometer."

`[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.104–105 (PDF 113–114), Fig. 4.19]` **[Q]**

Fig. 4.19 conditions, verbatim: "Time-dependent characteristic curves of unsensitized (solid line) and hydrogen-hypersensitized (broken line) octahedral AgBr emulsion grains (**0.2 µm**) with **3,3′-disulfopropyl-5,5′-dichloro-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine** adsorbed. The emulsions were exposed for **10⁻³ sec**, were kept for **t sec**, were **immersed in water to deactivate positive holes trapped by the dye**, and were developed by **MAA-1 surface developer**." `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, p.105 (PDF 114), Fig. 4.19]` **[Q]**

**[E]** The sign reversal is the important part and is easy to get backwards: with reduction sensitization (R centres) present, density **rises** over minutes after exposure; without them, it **falls**. The same hole population does both, depending on what it finds first. Any account of post-exposure behaviour that assumes a single sign is wrong for one of the two cases. Note also the experimental trick — water immersion terminates the process, which means the effect is confined to the dry coated layer and is quenched the moment processing begins.

#### 11.2.2 Kinetics and activation energies

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Kinetic order of Dye⁺ decay | **second-order** |
| Kinetic order of latent-image-centre decay in the presence of such dyes | **second-order** |
| Relation between the two | "rate constant and activation energy **comparable**" — the two are the same process |
| Rate-constant dependence on dye HOMO | "rate constant **increases as HOMO is lowered**" |
| Activation enthalpies of dye-positive-hole decay, for aggregates formed at 40, 50, 60, 70 °C | **0.53, 0.51, 0.53, 0.52 eV** respectively |
| Dependence of the activation enthalpy on aggregate size | **none** — "enthalpy independent of aggregate size" |
| Dependence of the rate constant on aggregate size | rate constant **decreases with increasing aggregate size**, so "the **entropy** of holes in the aggregate increases with size" |

`[Tani 1995, §5.7, pp.144–148 (PDF 153–157), Figs. 5.25, 5.27, 5.28, 5.30]` **[Q]**

Fig. 5.30 conditions (the Arrhenius set): octahedral AgBr **0.25 µm**, **0.57 µmole Dye 11 per m² of grain surface**, aggregates formed by agitation at **40 / 50 / 60 / 70 °C for 20 min**. `[Tani 1995, §5.7, p.148 (PDF 157), Fig. 5.30]` **[Q]**

Fig. 5.27 protocol (the time-dependent curves): octahedral AgBr **0.24 µm**, Dye 11 at **5.5 × 10⁻⁴ mole/mole AgBr**, exposure **10⁻³ s** to blue and to minus-blue, held **t seconds**, **immersed in water to terminate decay**, developed with **MAA-1**. `[Tani 1995, §5.7, pp.144–146 (PDF 153–155), Fig. 5.27]` **[Q]**

**This 0.51–0.53 eV set is the cleanest activation-energy determination anywhere in the material** — four independent aggregate sizes giving the same enthalpy to within 0.02 eV. **[Q]**

**[E]** An activation enthalpy of 0.52 eV with a several-minute time constant at room temperature implies a strong temperature dependence: by the Arrhenius relation this corresponds to roughly a factor of 2 in rate per 8–9 K near 300 K. The source does not state that, and the Fig. 5.30 Arrhenius plot is the only temperature data — so the *coefficient* is available in principle from that figure but not from the text.

#### 11.2.3 Which dyes do this — the observability threshold

The light-induced ESR signal of Dye⁺ is structureless and sharp; its half-width **decreases with increasing aggregate size** and with increasing measurement temperature, which Tani reads as **motional narrowing** by hole movement within the aggregate. Critically, the signal is observable "**only for dyes whose HOMO lies more than 0.3 eV above the AgBr valence-band top**." `[Tani 1995, §5.7, p.144 (PDF 153)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** The 0.3 eV HOMO criterion is therefore also the criterion for a dye to cause this mode of latent-image fading: a dye whose HOMO lies within 0.3 eV of the valence-band top does not hold the hole long enough to trap it, so no Dye⁺ accumulates and no slow post-exposure attack occurs. Dye selection is thus simultaneously a latent-image-keeping decision. The source states the ESR observability threshold but does not draw the keeping consequence.

The hole's fate is set out as competing channels — Tani's Eqs. (5.24)–(5.27), bodies lost: **(5.24) rapid**; **(5.25) generally slow**; **(5.27)** = the reaction of Dye⁺ with Agₙ, available when holes can move within the aggregate and reach the latent-image centre. `[Tani 1995, §5.7, p.143 (PDF 152)]` **[M]**

#### 11.2.4 The aggregate-size split between fast and slow desensitization

This is the cleanest separation of "sensitivity lost at exposure" from "sensitivity lost after exposure":

| Channel | What it looks like | Dependence on aggregate size |
|---|---|---|
