| **Fast** channel (5.24) | loss of sensitivity **immediately** after exposure | **increases** with aggregate size — nearly absent for 40 °C aggregates |
| **Slow** channels (5.25)–(5.26) | sensitivity decaying **with time** after exposure | **decreases** with aggregate size |

Fig. 5.29 conditions: octahedral AgBr **0.25 µm**, **0.35 µmole Dye 11 per m² of grain surface**, aggregates formed at **40 °C versus 70 °C for 60 min**, exposure **10⁻³ s**. `[Tani 1995, §5.7, pp.147–148 (PDF 156–157), Fig. 5.29]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Growing the J-aggregate therefore *improves* latent-image keeping while *worsening* immediate desensitization. Since aggregate size is set by digestion agitation temperature and time (§9.9.5), the same manufacturing variable that sets the spectral band's half-width also trades immediate speed against post-exposure stability. The source gives both dependences and their signs; the magnitudes are in Fig. 5.29 only.

### 11.3 Latent-image fading versus latent-image *growth* by latensification

**Definitions.** From Tani: **hypersensitization** = treating coated layers **before** exposure; **latensification** = treating coated layers **after** exposure, before development, to increase the developability of subimage and small image centres. `[Tani 1995, §6.1, pp.165–167 (PDF 174–176)]` **[F]**

Latensification is the deliberate, chemical version of the R-centre growth effect of §11.2.1: it converts sub-threshold centres into developable ones. The material's statements about it:

- **Latent subimage centres "are stable"** and become developable with latensification or under forced development. `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` **[F]**
- The headroom this represents: "there is some possibility for a further increase in photographic sensitivity if one could find the development condition that could detect and discriminate image centers composed of **two atoms** … from fog formation." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` **[Q]**
- **Gold latensification** works by **plating** (Agₙ → AgₙAu_m), not by replacement (Agₙ → Ag₍ₙ₋ₘ₎Au_m), concluded from the absence of any loss of developability after removal of the gold with KCN. `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.178 (PDF 187)]` **[F]**
- Gold latensification gives an **improvement in high-intensity reciprocity law failure** (James) — consistent with its being a threshold-lowering treatment applied to the dispersed sub-threshold centres HIRF produces. `[Tani 1995, §6.3, p.177 (PDF 186)]` **[F]**
- Reduction sensitization centres, which are non-developable silver clusters, are **made developable by gold latensification** — which is exactly why gold sensitization and reduction sensitization are hard to combine (§8.5.7): the same treatment that rescues a subimage centre also converts a reduction centre into a fog centre. `[Tani 1995, §6.4, pp.180–181 (PDF 189–190); §6.1, pp.165–166 (PDF 174–175)]` **[F]**
- Gold latensification is used as an *assay* in the material as well as a treatment: it renders arrested-development speck populations countable. Fig. 4.9 (reduction-sensitized AgBr, **4 s exposure**, gold latensification, arrested development) distinguished small specks present before exposure and **disappearing during exposure** (hole traps = reduction sensitization centres) from large specks absent before exposure and **appearing during exposure** (electron traps = latent image centres). Fig. 5.37 used arrested development with and without gold latensification to count **undevelopable versus developable image centres per grain**. `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.96–99 (PDF 105–108), Fig. 4.9; §5.8, pp.157–158 (PDF 166–167), Fig. 5.37]` **[Q]**

**[E]** The existence of a working latensification treatment is itself evidence about latent-image keeping: it establishes that a substantial fraction of the exposure's product sits *below* the developability threshold as subimage centres, and that those centres persist long enough after exposure to be rescued chemically. That is a lower bound on subimage stability, though the sources put no time on it.

**No source in this material gives a time limit on latensification** — no statement of how long after exposure the treatment remains effective, and no fading of latensifiability with hold time. **[F]**

### 11.4 Latent-image destruction by light and by heavy exposure

Two phenomena in the 1966 material destroy an existing latent image, and both are quantified in wavelength if not in rate.

#### 11.4.1 The Herschel effect

Definition: "the **bleaching of a latent image by exposure to light of longer wavelength** than that used to form it." Discovered by **Sir John Herschel in 1840** (bleaching of printed-out silver chloride where red light fell). "Complete in silver chloride, only **partial** in silver-bromide emulsions."

| Response maximum | Material | Source as cited |
|---|---|---|
| "a **broad maximum at 6500 Å**" | exposed silver bromide | Carroll & Kretchman |
| "quite a strong maximum at **6900 Å**" | large single crystals of exposed silver bromide | Hilsch & Pohl |
| "the most effective wavelength … is **5200 Å**" | silver chloride | reported, source unnamed |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, pp.220–223 (PDF 226–229)]` **[Q]** — note that the two AgBr maxima, 6500 Å and 6900 Å, are from different workers on different specimens (emulsion versus large single crystal) and Duffin reports both without reconciling them.

The practical exploitation, which requires *deliberately* fogging the material first and then bleaching image-wise: the emulsion "is fogged either by the action of light or by a chemical fogging agent, e.g. **formamidine sulphinic acid**, and is then treated with the Herschel sensitizer, **quantities from 10 mg to 2.0 g per gram-mole of silver** are specified for various compounds." A **yellow filter absorbing all light below 5000 Å** is preferred for the imaging exposure, "presumably because the image in silver chloride is very efficiently bleached by light of 5200 Å and the use of a yellow filter will ensure that no U.V. light reaches the film and reforms the latent image by the usual negative-imaging process." Light sources: mercury vapour and arc lamps. Product cited: **Kodak Autopositive paper**, on "a fairly fine-grain silver-chloride emulsion". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, pp.221–224 (PDF 227–230), Fig. 11.4]` **[Q]**

Desensitizing dyes that enhance the effect, giving a **spectrally sensitized Herschel effect** whose maximum sits "at the absorption maximum of the dye": **pinakryptol yellow** and **phenosafranine**. Additional sensitizers are cyanine/merocyanine-like, and a further group are stabilizer-like and all nitro-bearing, "therefore latent-image oxidants". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, pp.221–224 (PDF 227–230)]` **[F]**

Why the process is high contrast and low speed — a genuinely instructive pair of statements about latent-image-centre optics:

> "The **light-absorbing entity is removed during the exposure**. This makes the process one of **very high contrast**, because as each silver speck becomes smaller it presents less area for light absorption and therefore **all the centres are likely to reach the lower limit at the same exposure**." And: "the light-absorbing power of the relatively small latent-image speck is **very small** and therefore **the process is a very slow one**, even though the effect per quantum absorbed is probably high."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.224 (PDF 230), Fig. 11.5]` **[Q]**

**[E]** The second sentence is a direct statement that a latent-image speck of a few silver atoms has negligible optical cross-section. That is worth holding alongside §11.2: ordinary long-wavelength light does not appreciably bleach a latent image in a normal negative material on any practical timescale, because the target is optically tiny. The Herschel effect becomes usable only when the material is *fully fogged* so that every grain carries a target, and when a Herschel sensitizer is added to raise the cross-section.

#### 11.4.2 Solarization

"Solarization… is a **reversal of the D-log E curve** brought about by **excessively heavy exposures**. **This reversal is usually incomplete unless special developers are used.**" Mechanism: very high exposure releases large quantities of **bromine** from the crystal interior, which **brominates the surface latent image**, making the grain non-developable in a surface developer. And a diagnostic: "**extended development in a conventional developer removes the solarization**, because the mild solvent action of the developer permits the **interior** latent-image specks to catalyse the development of the grain." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.220 (PDF 226), Fig. 11.3]` **[M]**

**[E]** Solarization is latent-image destruction by the halogen the exposure itself liberated — the failure of the bromine-acceptor system (§11.5) under overload. It is therefore the extreme case of the same chemistry that, at normal exposure levels, the gelatin absorbs harmlessly.

Wall's 1929 note on the same phenomenon, from the composition side: iodobromide emulsions "are **more opaque**, and **less likely to suffer from halation and solarization**". `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.33–34 (PDF 41–42)]` **[F]**

### 11.5 Gelatin's role in latent-image stabilization — asserted, never quantified

Duffin lists nine functions of gelatin. Two bear directly on latent-image keeping:

- Function **7**: "Gelatin **interacts with some of the products of the photolysis thus stabilizing the latent image**."
- Function **8**: "Gelatin plays a vital part in **rendering the unexposed grains relatively less developable than the exposed ones**."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.29–30 (PDF 33–34)]` **[F]**

The mechanism behind function 7 is bromine acceptance. From Duffin's Gurney–Mott account: "The positive holes escape to the surface, and, **as bromine atoms, react with the gelatin**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.177 (PDF 183), Fig. 9.4]` **[M]** And from the gelatin chapter: "One of the properties of gelatin most frequently referred to is that of acting as a **bromine acceptor**. The importance of having some substance to remove the **photolytically-produced bromine** is discussed later but in the present section it is sufficient to mention that **three amino acids have been considered as possible acceptors in gelatin. These are tyrosine, histidine and methionine**, all of which possess groups able to react with bromine; **by substitution** as do the first two acids, or **indirectly by being easily oxidized** as occurs with methionine." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.37 (PDF 41)]` **[M]**

The relevant residue abundances, from Duffin's collagen amino-acid table (residues per 1,000 total): **tyrosine 4.6**, **histidine 4.8**, **methionine [value lost in OCR — raw string `3)`]**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.33 (PDF 37), Table 2.1]` **[Q]** So two of the three named acceptors are present at roughly 0.5 % of residues each; the third is unrecoverable from this material.

**No source quantifies the bromine-acceptor capacity, its rate, or its saturation point.** Function 7 is asserted; the acceptor chemistry is named; the numbers do not exist here. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.29–30, 37 (PDF 33–34, 41)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Since solarization (§11.4.2) is bromine re-attacking the surface image, and since the gelatin's acceptor capacity is fixed by its tyrosine/histidine/methionine content, latent-image stability against liberated halogen ought to be a function of gelatin composition and of the gelatin-to-silver ratio. The material supports the chain of reasoning but provides no capacity figure at any step.

### 11.6 Keeping of the unexposed material: the 1966 framework

#### 11.6.1 The specification and the two windows

At the end of digestion the emulsion sits at its optimum of speed, contrast and fog, but Duffin insists that this state is "**a metastable one**". Two windows in which it can change:

| Window | Duration and condition |
|---|---|
| (a) Molten emulsion before coating | held "at a temperature which is **not so different from that commonly used for digestion**, for a period of **up to some hours** before it is coated" |
| (b) Storage of the coated material | "**Modern photographic materials are expected to keep for at least two years**, in many cases under adverse storage conditions of **high temperature and humidity**, although many commercial films are not normally stored for as long as this" |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.137 (PDF 143)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Window (a) is the one usually overlooked: the emulsion sits at a temperature comparable to its own digestion temperature for hours before coating, which means the digestion reaction is still running. That is the reason stabilizers are added at all rather than merely relied upon during storage, and it is why "secondary stabilization" (below) exists.

#### 11.6.2 The pre-organic-stabilizer routes, and their dating

Two "secondary" stabilization routes:

1. **Add excess halide at the end of digestion** to lower the silver-ion concentration — chloride in chlorobromides, bromide in iodobromides. **[F]**
2. **Gelatin selection** — "for many years the only other way": a gelatin with larger than usual restrainer content retards continued digestion. "It is customary, **although not so usual nowadays**, to add further quantities of gelatin at the end of digestion." And a standing 1966 exception: "**Even today, the selection of the gelatin used at this point can be important with gold-sensitized emulsions, where the use of highly-restrained gelatin can aid the keeping properties.**" **[F]**

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.137 (PDF 143)]`

The organic-stabilizer era is dated: "Some **thirty years ago**" the heterocyclic stabilizers were discovered; the parent **4-hydroxy-6-methyl-1,3,3a,7-tetrazaindene** "was discovered to be a stabilizer by **Birr in 1935**", "and constant reference is still made to it in the photographic literature." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.138 (PDF 144)]` **[F]**

#### 11.6.3 The liquid-to-dry transition — the most important keeping number in the 1966 material

> "When an emulsion is dried after coating, **about 85–90 % of the water is lost**… **The pAg rises, by about one unit**, while the **effective concentration of the stabilizer also increases about ten-fold**. Thus, the chemical reactions occurring in coated films on storage may be **quite different from those of the liquid emulsion**: even the tetrazaindenes may be **almost completely adsorbed** after coating and drying."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.148 (PDF 154)]` **[Q]**

| Change on drying | Magnitude |
|---|---|
| Water lost | **85–90 %** |
| pAg | rises by **about one unit** |
| Effective stabilizer concentration | **about ten-fold** increase |
| Tetrazaindene adsorption state | from "a few per cent" / "about 10 %" adsorbed in the liquid emulsion (§8.9.2) to "**almost completely adsorbed**" |

**[E]** This is the physical basis for treating raw-stock keeping as a property of the **dry coated layer**, not of the wet emulsion: the same emulsion can be stable in one state and not the other. It also explains why the tetrazaindenes, which are the least adsorbed of the three families in solution and are dosed in grams rather than milligrams, become effective on storage — the drying step concentrates them tenfold and drives them onto the grain. Duffin states the transition; the inference about which state governs shelf life is ours.

#### 11.6.4 Storage fog and how it is measured

Duffin's operational definition of the thing being measured: a fog grain is "**one which will develop without light exposure**", so "**the nature of the development influences the fog**", and sensitometric testing must use the processing the emulsion will actually receive. "An emulsion may be acceptably low-fog in a conventional developer yet foggy, when aged, in a developer of very high activity." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.148–149 (PDF 154–155)]` **[F]**

The one tabulated keeping result in the material is the "**Fog after incubation\***" column of Table 7.1 (reproduced in full at §8.9.6). Its values, for 6-substituted tetrazaindenes as the side-chain R lengthens:

| R carbons | none | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 7 | 11 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fog after incubation\* | 1.66 | 1.42 | 0.05 | 0.59 | 0.0 | 1.32 | 0.28 | 0.06 |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.145 (PDF 151), Table 7.1]` **[Q]**

**The units of this column, the incubation conditions, and the footnote \* are all lost to OCR.** The `1.32` entry is reconstructed from a raw string `1632` by column context (a lost decimal point). The "none" row's sensitivity value is unreadable (`INS)`). **This is a relative fog scale of unknown units under unknown incubation conditions; it can be used for ranking and for nothing else.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.145 (PDF 151)]` **[F]**

Even as a ranking it is not monotonic in chain length — 0.05 at R = 1 and 0.0 at R = 3, but 0.59 at R = 2 and 1.32 at R = 4 — so the correlation Duffin describes (efficiency dropping as the chain lengthens and the adsorbed quantity increases) is a trend with substantial scatter, not a clean law. **[E]**

#### 11.6.5 Named storage-fog sources, 1966

| Source of storage fog | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Formaldehyde hardener** | "probably because of its **strong reducing action**, is **very prone to produce fog during storage**", and its volatility can contaminate other materials |
| **Aldehyde hardeners generally** | "**All the aldehyde hardeners are reducing agents and will naturally be prone to give fog**"; many "have been reported to give fog, **particularly in fast emulsions**" |
| **Polyethylene oxides** | a whole antifoggant class exists specifically against this fog, "particularly pronounced with **gold-sensitized emulsions** because gold and polyethylene oxides are frequently used together" (compounds listed at §8.9.7) |
| **Sulphide contamination** | gives **yellow** rather than neutral fog |
| **Static discharge in dry air** | "**Fogs the emulsion**, frequently rendering it useless" |
| **Mucochloric-acid hardener releasing acid** | pH drop → sensitivity drop, "must be allowed for in manufacture" |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.149–151 (PDF 155–157); Ch. VIII, pp.160–161, 167–168 (PDF 166–167, 173–174)]` **[F]**

Wall's 1929 list overlaps at exactly one point, and it is the strongest statement either book makes: "**Under no circumstances should formaldehyde be used as a hardener**" — because "this inevitably… **leads eventually to fog on keeping**." `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.152 (PDF 159)]` **[F]** Wall's other keeping warnings: sodium carbonate at 0.1–5 g/litre is "dangerous and **not likely to improve the keeping power**"; ammonium citrate substituted for the fixed alkaline citrates or tartrates in printing-out paper gave "**very poor keeping qualities**"; and gelatine plus gold in self-toning printing-out paper gives "**poor keeping qualities**" even when the gold-induced coagulation is overcome. `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.155 (PDF 162); Ch. VI, pp.110, 120 (PDF 117, 127)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Wall's absolute prohibition on formaldehyde (1929) and Duffin's more measured "very prone to produce fog during storage" (1966) are the same observation about the same chemistry, thirty-seven years apart, with formaldehyde still in use in 1966 as a gelatin hardener reacting with lysine's terminal amino group `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, p.36 (PDF 40)]`. The 1966 position is that aldehyde hardening is worth its fog penalty; the 1929 position is that it is not.

### 11.7 Storage-fog mechanism, 1995 — a named kinetic channel

Tani supplies what Duffin could not: a specific reaction that continues during storage, and the identity of the step a stabilizer blocks.

The framing statement, which is the general price of sensitization: "The increase in sensitivity caused by chemical sensitizations is **more or less associated with the decrease in stability** of photographic materials during storage and development." `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.183–184 (PDF 192–193)]` **[F]**

Two named storage mechanisms:

1. **Continued Ag₂S aggregation.** Sulfur sensitization proceeds in two steps (§8.5.3): formation of Ag₂S monomers, then their **rearrangement/aggregation** into dimers and thence clusters. The aggregation step is the rate-determining one, with a sensitometric activation energy of **32–35 kcal/mol**, and it does not stop when digestion is arrested. Since the effective sensitization centre is the **dimer** and the fog centre is the **cluster** (§8.5.3), continued aggregation during storage converts sensitization centres into fog centres. Stabilizers act by **preventing the second (aggregation) step** — TAI is shown to retard monomer→dimer aggregation. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.190–191 (PDF 199–200); §6.2, pp.169–171 (PDF 178–180)]` **[M]**
2. **Formation of reduction sensitization centres from gelatin plus Ag⁺ over long periods**, which "**become fog centers, especially when they interact with gold sensitizers and/or gold sensitization centers**." Stabilizers act here by **lowering the free Ag⁺ concentration** so that the reduction centres do not form in the first place. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.190–191 (PDF 199–200)]` **[M]**

Mueller's list of stabilizer actions, reproduced by Tani: blocking reactive sites; adsorbing onto centre surfaces; complexing the sensitizer in the gelatin; immobilising Ag⁺; oxidising or dislodging fog centres; displacing sensitizing complexes. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.190–191 (PDF 199–200)]` **[M]**

Supporting quantitative fact: **all the stabilizer and antifoggant agents Tani studied decreased the ionic conductivity** of AgBr grains, hence the interstitial-Ag⁺ concentration, and the capability tracked adsorptivity (Fig. 6.15: ionic conductivity of **0.5 µm cubic AgBr** versus amount of benzotriazole, by Dember photovoltage decay). `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.189, 191 (PDF 198, 200), Fig. 6.15]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Mechanism 1 and mechanism 2 both terminate in the same failure — a cluster large enough to develop unexposed — but by opposite chemistries: one grows an existing Ag₂S sensitization centre past its useful size, the other grows a *new* silver centre out of the gelatin's own reducing constituents. That is consistent with Duffin's 1966 finding of **two distinct fog chemistries** distinguishable by chromic-acid bleach and by response to gold post-treatment (§8.4.6): Ag₂S-type fog becomes lower in density on gold treatment, silver-type fog is enhanced. Duffin's two bleach classes map onto Tani's two storage mechanisms. Neither source makes that identification.

Duffin's 1966 confirmation that pre-existing fog centres in an aged emulsion are chemically removable: Fig. 7.13 plots fog density growth against development time in metol-hydroquinone for three cases — an **aged emulsion**, **the same emulsion after a 2 min bleach in acid 0.1 % potassium ferricyanide**, and a **low-fog emulsion**. `[Tani 1995, §12 figure inventory citing Duffin's Fig. 7.13; Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.220 (PDF 226) as indexed in the Tani-side figure list]` — *provenance caution: this figure is listed in the extraction material as Duffin Fig. 7.13 at p.220 (PDF 229); the page reference falls in Duffin's Chapter IX range rather than Chapter VII, and should be verified before citing the page.* **[F]** The substance — that ferricyanide bleaching for 2 min removes aged fog centres and lowers the subsequent fog-growth curve — is consistent with reduction sensitization centres being **ferricyanide-removable** while sulfur centres require bromine water `[Tani 1995, §6.4, pp.180–181 (PDF 189–190)]`. **[F]**

### 11.8 Temperature and humidity dependence — what is actually documented

This is the weakest-supported part of the whole subject, and the honest summary is that almost nothing is quantified.

**Temperature.**

| What is documented | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Activation enthalpy of dye-hole latent-image decay | **0.51–0.53 eV**, independent of aggregate size | `[Tani 1995, §5.7, p.148 (PDF 157), Fig. 5.30]` |
| Trap depth ↔ residence time (Marker's equation) — the general bridge between any trap depth and its thermal stability | **1 µsec / 10 sec / 10 years** at **0.3 / 0.7 / 1.2 eV** | `[Tani 1995, §3.4.2, p.75 (PDF 84)]` |
| Activation energies during **development** (not keeping): diffusion processes | **4–7 kcal/mol** | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.174 (PDF 180), Table 9.1]` |
| Development of silver halide from a latent-image centre | **10–20 kcal/mol** | same |
| **Fog development; reduction without latent image** | **20–30 kcal/mol** | same |
| Resulting rate ratio at normal development temperatures | latent-image-catalysed process "**about 1,000,000 times as fast as the fog growth**" | same |
| Latent image forms **very inefficiently at very low temperatures** because ionic movement is "frozen", raising the recombination chance | qualitative | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.176–177 (PDF 182–183)]` |
| Dye sensitization still measurable at **−196 °C** (liquid air), with sensitivity loss much greater in the dye-sensitized region than in the natural region, and "no greater with red sensitizers than with blue" | qualitative plus one temperature | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.132 (PDF 138)]` |
| Sensitometric activation energy of sulfur sensitization (the storage-fog aggregation channel) | **32–35 kcal/mol** | `[Tani 1995, §6.2, pp.169–170 (PDF 178–179)]` |
| Ag₂S formation activation energy (the step that is *not* rate-determining) | **22 kcal/mol** | `[Tani 1995, §6.2, p.168 (PDF 177)]` |
| Storage under "adverse storage conditions of **high temperature and humidity**" is the stated expectation for a two-year keeping specification | qualitative | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.137 (PDF 143)]` |
| Glazing developed prints near **100 °C** produces "a marked **diminution of density**" and a shift from black to "a rather dullish **brown**", sometimes with a metallic sheen — "**bronzing**" or "**plumming**" | qualitative plus one temperature | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.151–152 (PDF 157–158)]` |

**[Q]** for the whole table.

An internal inconsistency to flag in Duffin's Table 9.1 discussion: "It will be seen that the presence of a latent image reduces, by around **10,000 Kcals per mole**, the energy required to bring about the reduction of the silver halide." The table's own numbers give a difference of roughly **10 kcal/mol**, not 10,000. **"10,000 Kcals" is a units error in the printed text** (probably "10 Kcals" or "10,000 cals"). Raw string: `10,000 Kcals per mole`. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.174 (PDF 180)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Table 9.1 is the only place a temperature coefficient can be derived for a fog-versus-image competition, and its sign matters: **fog development has a higher activation energy (20–30 kcal/mol) than image development (10–20 kcal/mol)**, so fog grows faster with temperature than image does. That makes minimum density, not speed, the temperature-sensitive quantity in processing. It is a *development* result, not a keeping result, and it must not be transferred to storage without justification — but it is the closest thing the material has to a temperature coefficient for fog.

**Humidity.**

| What is documented | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| "The rate of **hydrogen hypersensitization decreased markedly with increasing relative humidity**" — the reaction occurs in **dry** emulsion layers | qualitative, with direction | `[Tani 1995, §6.4, p.183 (PDF 192), Fig. 6.10]` |
| The coated layer loses **85–90 %** of its water on drying, raising pAg by **one unit** and stabilizer concentration **tenfold** | quantitative | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.148 (PDF 154)]` |
| Storage expectation includes "adverse storage conditions of high temperature and **humidity**" | qualitative | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.137 (PDF 143)]` |
| **Static discharge in dry air** fogs the emulsion, "frequently rendering it useless"; forcible stripping of celluloid from tacky plates gives static fog, and "where stripping stops, **a line of denser fog**" | qualitative | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.167–168 (PDF 173–174); Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.185 (PDF 192)]` |

**[Q]**

**The Tani humidity statement is the only relative-humidity dependence of any photographic reaction anywhere in this material**, and it concerns hypersensitization rather than keeping. **[F]**

**[E]** The 85–90 % water loss figure is, however, indirectly a humidity statement about keeping: it implies that the dry layer's chemistry — the pAg-one-unit-higher, stabilizer-tenfold-concentrated state that governs shelf life (§11.6.3) — is reversible in the direction of humidity. A coated layer re-equilibrating to high ambient humidity moves back toward the wet-emulsion condition in which the stabilizers are mostly desorbed and free silver ion is higher. That is a plausible mechanism for the "adverse storage conditions of high temperature and humidity" Duffin names, but **the sources do not state it** and it should be treated as inference, not fact.

### 11.9 What each source does and does not quantify

| Question | Wall 1929 | Duffin 1966 | Tani 1995 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Latent image discussed at all | **No** — zero occurrences of "latent" in the entire text | Yes, Chapter IX | Yes, Chapter 4 |
| Latent-image fading | not discussed | mechanism only, via sub-image reversion invoked for LIRF; **no time constant** | **quantified for the dye-hole channel only**: several-minute time constant, second-order kinetics, activation enthalpy 0.51–0.53 eV |
| Latent-image fading of ordinary film on the shelf | not discussed | not discussed | **not discussed** — Tani's fading is a post-exposure dye-hole effect on the timescale of minutes, not a shelf-keeping effect on the timescale of days |
| Time limit on latensification | — | — | **not given** |
| Latensification | not discussed | not discussed as such (gold latensification appears only via cross-reference) | defined; gold latensification mechanism (plating) established; used as an assay |
| Subimage stability | — | "relatively unstable in that it has **no resistance to attack by positive holes**" | "**are stable**"; developable after latensification or forced development |
| Raw-stock keeping specification | qualitative warnings only (formaldehyde, sodium carbonate, ammonium citrate) | "**at least two years**", under high temperature and humidity | not stated |
| Storage-fog mechanism | impurity- and process-driven; no chemistry | metastability at the end of digestion; two windows; liquid-to-dry transition quantified | **two named kinetic channels**: continued Ag₂S aggregation (blockable by TAI), and reduction-centre formation from gelatin + Ag⁺ |
| Fog-versus-storage-time curve | none | none — only the relative "fog after incubation" column of Table 7.1, whose **units and incubation conditions are lost** | none |
| Temperature dependence of keeping | none | Table 9.1 gives development/fog activation energies (10–20 vs 20–30 kcal/mol) — a *development* result | 32–35 kcal/mol for the sensitization/aggregation channel that also runs in storage; 0.51–0.53 eV for dye-hole decay |
| Humidity dependence | none | 85–90 % water loss on drying, pAg +1, stabilizer ×10 | one statement: hydrogen hypersensitization rate falls markedly with rising RH |
| Latent-image destruction by light | none | **Herschel effect**: 6500 Å and 6900 Å (AgBr), 5200 Å (AgCl); sensitizer doses 10 mg–2.0 g per mole Ag | not discussed |
| Solarization | iodide reduces liability | mechanism (interior bromine brominating the surface image); removed by extended development | not discussed |
| Gelatin as latent-image stabilizer | not discussed | asserted as function 7; bromine acceptors named (tyrosine, histidine, methionine) | not discussed in these terms |

### 11.10 Explicit statements of absence

These are the gaps a reader of this document should not go looking for in the sources, because they are not there:

1. **No latent-image fading time constant for an ordinary film held on the shelf**, in any source. Tani's several-minute time constant is a dye-hole effect in a model emulsion, terminated by water immersion; it is **not** long-term latent-image keeping and must not be used as such. `[Tani 1995, §4.3.2, pp.104–105 (PDF 113–114); §5.7, pp.144–148 (PDF 153–157)]` **[F]**
2. **No temperature or humidity dependence of latent-image keeping**, in any source. The Fig. 5.30 Arrhenius set gives an enthalpy for the dye-hole channel and nothing else; there is no keeping-versus-temperature or keeping-versus-RH data of any kind. `[Tani 1995, §5.7, p.148 (PDF 157)]` **[F]**
3. **No fog-density-versus-storage-time curve with real axes**, in any source. The only tabulated incubation-fog data are Duffin's Table 7.1 column, whose units and conditions are OCR-lost. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.145 (PDF 151)]` **[F]**
4. **No shelf-life figure other than Duffin's "at least two years"**, and that is an expectation, not a measurement. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.137 (PDF 143)]` **[F]**
5. **No bromine-acceptor capacity, rate or saturation figure.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. II, pp.29–30, 37 (PDF 33–34, 41)]` **[F]**
6. **No statement of how long latensification remains effective after exposure.** **[F]**
7. **Wall 1929 contains no latent-image theory whatever** — the word "latent" does not appear in the text. Everything Wall says about keeping concerns raw-stock fog. `[Wall 1929, whole text]` **[F]**
8. **Duffin 1966 explicitly excludes development from his scope** — "**Development**, the very important step which greatly affects the response of the silver-halide emulsion, **is not being discussed in detail in the present work**" (referring the reader to L. F. A. Mason, *Photographic Processing Chemistry*, Focal Press, "in press") — so latensification, which is a development-side treatment, gets no separate treatment there either. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.217 (PDF 223)]` **[F]**
9. Tani's numbered display equations were images and did not survive text extraction. In the latent-image-stability material this affects **Eqs. (5.24)–(5.27)** (the Dye⁺ back-reaction channels) and the Eq. **(6.14)-set** (photoelectron trapping probabilities used in the TAI analysis). The channel descriptions — (5.24) rapid, (5.25) generally slow, (5.27) Dye⁺ reacting with Agₙ when holes can move within the aggregate — and the symbol definitions are what survived; **the functional forms are not recoverable from this material.** `[Tani 1995, §0 caveat; §5.7, p.143 (PDF 152); §6.5, pp.192–194 (PDF 201–203)]` **[F]**

### 11.11 Summary of the mechanism, as far as it is established

Assembling what the three sources jointly support, with the era of each element marked:

1. A latent image is a cluster of 3–5 silver atoms (1966: 3–4 by two physical methods, 4 by single-grain sensitometry; 1995: 3 with gold, 4–5 with sulfur alone). **[Q]**
2. Below that size, subimage (Ag₂) and preimage (Ag₁) centres exist. The preimage is unstable; the subimage is stable to thermal reversion (1995) but has "**no resistance to attack by positive holes**" (1966). **[Q]**
3. A completed image centre of four atoms carries a net positive charge (Ag₄⁺) and **repels positive holes** (1966), which is why it is more stable than a partial one. **[M]**
4. Fading of a formed image therefore requires an oxidant reaching the centre. The documented agent is a **positive hole trapped on an adsorbed sensitizing dye**, which reaches the latent-image centre by migrating within the J-aggregate, on a **several-minute** timescale, second-order, with an activation enthalpy of **0.52 eV** (1995). **[Q]**
5. The same hole population produces **growth instead of fading** if it finds an **R centre** first, because hole capture at an R centre liberates an extra free electron (1995). Direction of the post-exposure density change is therefore set by the reduction-sensitization state. **[Q]**
6. Only dyes whose **HOMO lies more than 0.3 eV above the AgBr valence-band top** trap holes long enough for this channel to operate (1995). **[Q]**
7. **Larger J-aggregates reduce the slow (post-exposure) loss and increase the fast (immediate) loss** (1995). **[Q]**
8. Photolytically liberated bromine is normally absorbed by gelatin via **tyrosine, histidine and methionine** (1966). When that capacity is overwhelmed by extreme exposure, the bromine brominates the surface image and produces **solarization** (1966). **[M]**
9. Long-wavelength light can bleach a latent image (**Herschel effect**, 1840/1966), maximally at **6500–6900 Å** for AgBr and **5200 Å** for AgCl, but only weakly, because a few-atom speck has negligible optical cross-section. **[Q]**
10. Sub-threshold centres can be rescued chemically by **latensification**, gold acting by **plating** the existing cluster (1995). **[F]**
11. On the raw-stock side, the emulsion leaves digestion **metastable** (1966), and two reactions continue: **Ag₂S monomer→dimer→cluster aggregation** (rate-determining step, 32–35 kcal/mol) and **reduction-centre formation from gelatin plus Ag⁺** (1995). Both terminate in developable clusters, i.e. fog. **[M]**
12. Stabilizers act by **blocking the aggregation step** and by **lowering free Ag⁺** (all agents studied lowered the grain's ionic conductivity), and the coated layer's chemistry differs from the liquid emulsion's because drying removes **85–90 %** of the water, raises pAg by **one unit** and concentrates the stabilizer **tenfold** (1966 for the transition, 1995 for the mechanism). **[Q]**


---

## 12. Development: mechanism, kinetics, and the two progress types

### 12.1 The electrochemical picture — the symbols that survived, the equations that did not

**Era: 1995.** The 1995 account treats development as a redox cell in which silver halide is reduced by a developing agent, with a development centre acting as catalyst. The general reversible reaction is written `Red + … → Ox + …`, where **`Red`** is the developing agent, **`Ox`** its oxidized form, **`n`** the number of electrons given up per developing-agent molecule, and **`m`** the number of protons produced. `[Tani 1995, §7.1, p.202 (PDF 211), Eq. (7.1)]` **[F]**

The cell is split into two half-cells: a silver half-cell potential **`E_Ag`** and a developer half-cell potential **`E_Dev`**, with **`E_cell = E_Ag − E_Dev`**. "When E_cell is positive, reaction (7.1) proceeds to the right, and when E_cell is negative, reaction (7.1) proceeds to the left." `[Tani 1995, §7.1, p.202 (PDF 211), Eqs. (7.1)–(7.4)]` **[F]**

Under the condition `[Ox] = [R]` (equal concentrations of oxidized and reduced forms), `E_Dev` reduces to the **polarographic half-wave oxidation potential `E_1/2`** of the developing agent. This is why `E_1/2` is the practical activity index for a developing agent: it is the measurable stand-in for the developer half-cell potential. `[Tani 1995, §7.1, p.203 (PDF 212), Eqs. (7.10)–(7.11)]` **[F]**

The rate of silver formation is the *net* rate of electron transfer from developing agent to silver, i.e. forward minus backward, with specific rate constants **`k_ox`** (oxidation of the developing agent) and **`k_R`** (the reverse). "When k_R is sufficiently small, or when the concentration of the oxidized form of a developing agent is small, as is often the case in practice, the net rate of development is approximately the rate of oxidation of the developing agent." The resulting rate expression contains:

| Symbol | Meaning as the source defines it |
|---|---|
| `α` | partition coefficient |
| `η` | **overpotential**; "= E_Ag − E_Dev" in the simplest case |
| `k°_ox` | rate of oxidation at zero overpotential; itself "dependent upon several factors, including **the surface area of development centers** and **the diffusion of the chemical species** involved in development" |
| `k_ox`, `k_R` | forward and backward specific rates of electron transfer |
| `E_Ag`, `E_Dev`, `E_cell` | silver, developer and cell potentials |
| `E_1/2` | polarographic half-wave oxidation potential of the developing agent |
| `E_1` | one-electron oxidation potential (see §12.3) |
| `n`, `m` | electrons per developer molecule; protons produced |
| `ε_HO`, `ε_LU` | HOMO and LUMO energies (developing agent, development centre) |
| `I_P`, `EA` | ionization potential; electron affinity |
| `E_ox`, `E_R` | oxidation and reduction potentials |
| `t`, `t₀`, `t′` | development time; induction period; `t′ = t − t₀` |

`[Tani 1995, §7.1, pp.202–204 (PDF 211–213), Eqs. (7.1)–(7.16)]` **[M]**

**A hard limitation of this knowledge base, stated plainly:** the numbered display equations of the 1995 source were reproduced as images and did **not** survive text extraction. Throughout Eqs. (5.9)–(5.30), (6.1)–(6.13) and (7.1)–(7.19), the text renders the lead-in sentence ("…can be expressed as follows:") and then jumps to "where X is …". **The symbol definitions above are complete; the functional forms are not recoverable from this material and are not reconstructed here.** In particular the form of Eq. (7.13) — the central rate law — is unavailable. What can be said about its *structure*, because the surrounding prose says it, is that the rate depends on the overpotential `η`, on the concentration of the developing agent, on the surface area of the development centres, and on the diffusion of the participating species. Nothing further about its algebra should be inferred from this document. `[Tani 1995, §7.1, pp.202–204 (PDF 211–213); §7.3, p.208 (PDF 217)]` **[F]**

### 12.2 Quantum-chemical restatement: the developability threshold

Development *initiation* is electron injection from the **HOMO of the developing agent** into the **LUMO of the development centre**. `ε_HO`, `I_P` and `E_ox` are linked by Eq. (7.14); `ε_LU`, `EA` and `E_R` of the centre by Eq. (7.15). Both equation bodies are lost. `[Tani 1995, §7.1, pp.203–204 (PDF 212–213)]` **[M]**

`E_Ag` must be corrected for cluster size. It "became more negative, obeying the **Gibbs-Thomson effect**, as the diameter of silver clusters decreased to be **several tens of angstroms**." Below that size the discrete molecular-orbital description applies (quantum size effect plus site effect) and `ε_HO`/`ε_LU` — equivalently `E_ox`/`E_R` — are widely separated; for larger, Gibbs-Thomson clusters they converge onto a single `E_Ag`. `[Tani 1995, §7.1, p.204 (PDF 213)]` **[M]**

Both treatments give the same signed prediction: `ε_LU` becomes lower and `E_R` more positive as centre size increases, so **the overpotential — and hence the rate — increases with increasing development-centre size, when electron transfer is the rate-determining step**. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.213 (PDF 222)]` **[M]**

**One-electron versus two-electron potentials.** A metal electrode can accept two electrons at once from a developing-agent molecule; "a latent image center, however, is thought to be too small to receive two electrons at the same time." Tong et al. derived the **one-electron oxidation potential `E_1`** from semiquinone formation constants and **confirmed that development rate correlates more closely with `E_1` than with `E_1/2`** for hydroquinones and p-phenylenediamines. `E_1/2` nevertheless "is still useful for study of the rate of development among developing agents, whose molecular structures are closely related to each other." `[Tani 1995, §7.1–§7.3, pp.204–205, 208 (PDF 213–214, 217), Fig. 7.2 (relative development rate vs potential, hydroquinones, pH 9)]` **[Q]**

### 12.3 Induction period, and development rate versus half-wave oxidation potential

**Era: 1995 (data from Bent et al., 1951).** The most useful developing agents for colour photography are found among **4-amino-N-dialkylanilines**, and Bent et al. analysed that family extensively. Their rate metric is:

- **rate = `1/t′`**, with **`t′ = t − t₀`**;
- **`t₀` = the induction period**;
- **`t` = the time required to give an optical density of 0.2 above fog**.

The finding: **`log(1/t′)` is linear in `E_1/2`** across the family, and "The linear relationship between the **logarithm of the development rate** and `E_1/2` indicates that `E_1/2` is approximately proportional to the **activation energy** of the rate of development by those compounds."

The linearity then breaks: **"Compounds with potentials more negative than about +170 mV give development rates lower than would be expected. The authors considered that the rate of development by these compounds was so high that diffusion rather than the chemical reaction became the rate-determining step."** `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.208 (PDF 217); figure at p.212 (PDF 221), Fig. 7.5]` **[Q]**

This is the only numeric surface-controlled → diffusion-controlled crossover anywhere in this material: **+170 mV (E_1/2, versus SCE), for 4-amino-N-dialkylanilines**. Above that potential (less negative), log rate rises linearly with `E_1/2`; more negative than it, the rate plateaus below the extrapolated line because transport, not chemistry, limits. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.208 (PDF 217), Fig. 7.5]` **[Q]**

Fig. 7.5's axes are `log(1/t′)` against `E_1/2` in mV; the figure caption states "t′ is development time less induction period". No absolute times, no absolute rate constants and no temperature are given with it in the surviving text. `[Tani 1995, p.212 (PDF 221), Fig. 7.5]` **[F]**

### 12.4 Rate proportional to the surface area of developing silver; the origin of the induction period

"According to the electrochemical model expressed by Equation (7.13), the rate of development is **proportional to the surface area of developing silver clusters**." Pontius and coworkers measured the growth rate of silver specks on emulsion grains during development by electron microscope and confirmed this prediction, "supporting the electrochemical model for photographic development." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.213 (PDF 222)]` **[Q]**

Shape sequence and its kinetic consequence, verbatim in substance: the shape of silver specks "was initially spherical and then became filamentary"; the growth rate was proportional to surface area "during development regardless of their shape, and thus **abruptly increased when the silver specks began to grow in a filamentary shape**, since the specific surface area of filamentary specks was larger than that of spherical ones." **"They attributed the induction period of development to the time required for the silver specks to begin to grow into a filamentary shape."** `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.213 (PDF 222)]` **[Q]**

Berry's filament mechanism supplies the length scale: "the **diameter of filaments** formed during development in the absence of solvents for silver halide was always **about 200 Å**." A silver atom forms at the interface of the silver speck and the silver halide grain and migrates over the speck surface in order to keep its shape spherical; "**Since the diffusion length of a silver atom is limited (about 200 Å)**, the shape of silver specks could be spherical when their diameter is less than 200 Å, and became filamentary when their diameter exceeds this value." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.213 (PDF 222)]` **[Q]**

**200 Å = 0.02 µm.** This is a *silver-atom surface-migration length inside one grain*. It is not an inhibitor diffusion length and must not be used as one — see §13.9. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.213 (PDF 222)]` **[E]**

The 1966 source states the same covering-power consequence of filamentary morphology from the image side: the developed silver "can consist of compact or **bulky filamentary** silver-metal; the latter gives the **higher covering power** and is therefore beneficial in terms of **speed, contrast and maximum density**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.173 (PDF 179)]` **[F]**

### 12.5 The charge barrier and the induction period

**Era: 1995 (James's theory, 1939–1945).** James proposed the **charge barrier theory**: under usual developing conditions a silver halide grain bears **negative charges on its surface**, which inhibit the approach of negatively charged developing agents. He proved it by demonstrating that "the induction period **increased by increasing the number of negative charges per molecule or ion** of a developing agent under practical conditions," and that "the adsorption of positively charged compounds to silver halide grains decreased the negative charge barrier on their surface and could **decrease the induction period** of the development." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.213–214 (PDF 222–223), Fig. 7.6 (induction period vs charge of developing agents)]` **[Q]**

The 1966 source states the same relation, and adds the limiting case: "the **higher the number of negative charges on the developer molecule, the longer was the induction period** before development became rapid; **uncharged developers such as diethyl-p-phenylenediamine … have no induction period**." Gelatin "has a powerful effect in controlling the ease of reduction by developers." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.175 (PDF 181)]` **[F]**

**Sources agree** on sign and mechanism here; the 1966 account contributes the specific statement that the uncharged colour developer diethyl-p-phenylenediamine has *no* induction period, which the 1995 account does not make. Neither source gives induction periods in seconds for any named developer. **[F]**

### 12.6 Interstitial silver ion supply — a negative result worth keeping

Interstitial Ag⁺ ions initially present in a grain "are limited in number and should be rapidly supplied during development." There is no direct evidence that interstitial-Ag⁺ concentration controls the rate: "the concentration of interstitial silver ions in emulsion grains is **silver iodobromide > silver bromide > silver bromochloride > silver chloride, but the rate of development does not seem to be in the same order**." The source offers alternative explanations for the halide ordering of rates — the order of `E_Ag` in the presence of each silver halide, and the solubility of each silver halide. `[Tani 1995, §7.1, p.202 (PDF 211); §7.3, p.214 (PDF 223)]` **[F]**

The 1966 source's electrode-theory discussion raises the corresponding doubt from the other side: silver-ion supply by diffusion through the crystal — "it is doubtful if this could sustain the very high rates of development known to occur in certain cases." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.174–175 (PDF 180–181)]` **[M]**

### 12.7 The two extreme types of development progress — parallel (A) and granular (B)

**Era: 1995. This is the most consequential result in this section.**

"There are two extreme types that determine the progress of development … **The amount of developed silver is proportional to the proportion of the developed silver in each grain in one extreme type (A) and to the number of fully developed grains in the other extreme type (B). Types A and B are here denoted parallel and granular developments, respectively.**" `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.216 (PDF 225), Fig. 7.7 (p.214 / PDF 223)]` **[F]**

The two types are realised by two named practical developers on silver bromide emulsions:

- **Type A, parallel** — the **colour developer CP-20**, "with a 4-amino-N-dialkylaniline derivative as a developing agent."
- **Type B, granular** — the **black-and-white developer D72**, "with metol-hydroquinone as the developing agents."

`[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.216 (PDF 225)]` **[F]**

The experiment behind Fig. 7.8: emulsion layers composed of **sulfur-sensitized cubic AgBr emulsion grains of 0.86 µm**, exposed for **0.1 s** and developed by **CP-20**; measured quantities are the optical density of the dye image and the fractions of undeveloped, developing, and fully developed grains as a function of development time. Result, verbatim in substance: "the presence of a **large fraction of developing grains at any stage** of development was characteristic for development by CP-20. Analysis of this observation indicated that **it took about 2 min for each grain to be fully developed** and that **the increase in optical density came from the increase in the proportion of developed silver in each grain** as the development proceeded." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.216 (PDF 225), Fig. 7.8]` **[Q]**

Fig. 7.9 is the same experiment with **D72**: "In this case, **developing grains were hardly observed at any stage** of development. The analysis of the above observation indicates that **it took about 20 sec for each grain to be fully developed** and that **the increase in optical density came mostly from an increase in the number of fully developed grains**." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.217 (PDF 226), Fig. 7.9]` **[Q]**

**Consolidated comparison** (every entry sourced from Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.214–219 / PDF 223–228, Figs. 7.7–7.12):

| Property | Type A — **parallel** (CP-20, colour) | Type B — **granular** (D72, metol–hydroquinone) |
|---|---|---|
| Density grows via | the **proportion of silver developed within each grain** | the **number of fully developed grains** |
| Time for one grain to develop fully | **≈ 2 min** | **≈ 20 s** |
| Fraction of grains in the "developing" state at any stage | **large** at any stage | "**hardly observed** at any stage" |
| Rate-determining step | **growth of developed silver** (electron transfer from developing agents to the surface of developed silver at its growth stage) | **initiation — the first electron injection** from a developing agent to a development centre |
| Rate sensitivity to degree of sulfur sensitization | "**nearly independent**" (Fig. 7.11) | **significantly decreased** by more sulfur sensitization and by higher light intensity (Fig. 7.10) |
| Rate sensitivity to grain size | rate **nearly proportional to 1/(grain size)**, i.e. to the surface-to-volume ratio (Fig. 7.12) | "**nearly independent of the size** of emulsion grains" |
| Rate sensitivity to developability of the centres | not rate-controlling | "**sensitive to the developability of development centers**", and decreases as centre size decreases |

**[Q]**

### 12.8 Rate-determining steps, stated as the source states them

The concluding formulation, which is the load-bearing sentence pair of §7.3:

> "**In granular development, the rate-determining step is its initiation with the first electron injection from a developing agent to a development center, and its rate is sensitive to the developability of development centers. On the other hand, the rate-determining step of parallel development is the growth of developed silver, and this rate is nearly proportional to the surface-to-volume ratio of emulsion grains.**"

`[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.219 (PDF 228)]` **[F]**

Supporting measurements:

- **Granular (D72), Fig. 7.10.** Rate of development, sensitivity and fog density were measured against the amount of sodium thiosulfate used for sulfur sensitization, at exposure times **0.1 s** and **10⁻⁴ s**, for sulfur-sensitized cubic AgBr grains. "An increase in the degree of sulfur sensitization and an increase in light intensity, both of which generally make image centers dispersed, **significantly decreased the rate of development**. It was also confirmed that the rate of development was **nearly independent of the size** of emulsion grains." The reasoning given: latent-image dispersion produces many small latent image centres "whose ability to accept electrons from developing agents is small," so the granular rate is set by the first electron injection and "decreased by decreasing the size of development centers." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.217–219 (PDF 226–228), Fig. 7.10]` **[Q]**
- **Parallel (CP-20), Fig. 7.11.** Same experiment with CP-20: "the rate of development was **nearly independent of the degree of sulfur sensitization**." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.219 (PDF 228), Fig. 7.11]` **[Q]**
- **Parallel (CP-20), Fig. 7.12.** "the rate of development by CP-20 was **nearly proportional to the reciprocal of the size of the emulsion grains** (i.e., the surface to volume ratio) for various grains with variation of the light intensity." The figure plots rate against 1/grain size for **octahedral AgBr exposed 0.1 s**, **cubic AgBr exposed 0.1 s**, and **cubic AgBr exposed 10⁻⁴ s**. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.219 (PDF 228), Fig. 7.12 (p.218 / PDF 227)]` **[Q]**

### 12.9 Cabannes–Hoffmann effect: rate versus latent-image dispersity, and its coupling to reciprocity failure

Because rate rises with development-centre size when electron transfer is rate-determining (§12.2), and because "the size of latent image centers generally decreases with increasing degrees of dispersion of image centers by high-intensity exposure and/or by introducing electron-trapping sensitization centers," the rate falls in the high-intensity, short-exposure part of the reciprocity curve. "The fact that the **rate of development is lower over the portion of high-intensity and short exposure in the reciprocity curve** due to the increased dispersity and smaller size of latent image centers is known as the **Cabannes-Hoffmann effect**. As a consequence of this effect, **high-intensity reciprocity law failure is greatest for short or less active development and is markedly decreased by prolonged development.**" `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.212–213 (PDF 221–222)]` **[M]**

No coefficient, no exponent and no threshold intensity accompany this statement. The direction and the dependence are given; the magnitude is not. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.212–213 (PDF 221–222)]` **[F]**

**[E]** The effect makes high-intensity reciprocity failure a *joint* property of the emulsion and the development condition, not of the emulsion alone. Any model that treats reciprocity-law failure and development time as independent contradicts an explicit statement of the 1995 source.

### 12.10 Superadditivity of developing-agent pairs

"One of the most important phenomena affecting the increase in the rate of development is the rate acceleration that occurs when two developing agents act synergistically, which is called **superadditivity**." The most popular combinations named are **metol–hydroquinone** and **1-phenyl-3-pyrazolidone (Phenidone)–hydroquinone**. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.215 (PDF 224)]` **[F]**

**Levenson's regeneration mechanism:** "superadditivity can occur when the reduced form of developing agent A reduces silver halide and developing agent B is able to reduce the oxidized form of A. This regeneration should be effective when an oxidized form of A inhibits development and/or when B by itself develops more slowly than A." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.215 (PDF 224)]` **[M]**

But regeneration is insufficient: "It has also been pointed out that the degree of superadditivity in many combinations is **much larger than expected by a simple regeneration mechanism** and that the **increase in the concentration of developing agents in the vicinity of development centers due to the charge barrier effect and adsorption of developing agents to silver halide grains** contributes to superadditivity." `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.215–216 (PDF 224–225)]` **[M]**

**No numeric superadditivity factors, no rate ratios and no relative activities of metol versus hydroquinone appear in any of this material.** A reader expecting a quantified synergy factor will not find one here. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.215–216 (PDF 224–225)]` **[F]**

The 1966 source supplies one *sign-carrying* consequence of superadditivity that bears on the rendered image: polyethylene-oxide addenda "produce an increase in speed in **fast iodobromide** emulsions … giving **up to twice the speed** under optimum conditions", but "A speed increase is only produced with the usual **superadditive** developers such as **metol-hydroquinone** or **Phenidone-hydroquinone** systems. Development by **hydroquinone** developers is **inhibited**", attributed to interaction between the polyethylene oxide and the **semiquinone** in the bulk developer. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.165–166 (PDF 171–172)]` **[Q]**

### 12.11 Developing agents: the structural rules

**Era: 1995 (Kendall 1935/36, Pelz 1954, Tani 1971).**

**Kendall's rule.** Developing agents have the structure `a—(CH=CH)_m—a′` where `a, a′ ∈ {—OH, —NH₂, —NHR, —NR₁R₂}` and `m = 0` or a whole number. **Pelz's rule** covers a second structural family. Benzene derivatives bearing these substituents split into those that obey Kendall's rule (developing agents) and those that do not (non-developing agents). `[Tani 1995, §7.2, pp.206–207 (PDF 215–216), Figs. 7.3–7.4]` **[F]**

**Molecular-orbital reformulation, alternant π-systems.** With `Z_s` starred and `Z_u` non-starred atomic orbitals in the conjugated system (`Z_s > Z_u`), the counts of bonding, non-bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals are `Z_u`, `Z_s − Z_u`, and `Z_u` respectively. `n` is the number of π-electrons. Developing agents satisfy Eq. (7.19); non-developing agents Eq. (7.20). **Both equation bodies were lost to extraction.** Since `n = 2m + 4` and `Z_s = m + 1` in Kendall's and Pelz's rules, any compound satisfying either rule also satisfies Eq. (7.19). `[Tani 1995, §7.2, pp.206–208 (PDF 215–217)]` **[M]**

The three general rules Tani states for developing agents:

1. "The highest occupied electronic energy levels of developing agents are higher than those of nondeveloping agents in accordance with Equation (7.14)."
2. "HOMO of developing agents are **antibonding in nature**, while HOMO of nondeveloping agents are nonbonding or bonding."
3. "Developing agents satisfy Equation (7.19)."

`[Tani 1995, §7.2, p.208 (PDF 217)]` **[M]**

**Table 7.1 numeric content, with an integrity warning.** Table 7.1 tabulates developing agents with `Z`, `Z_s`, `n`. The chemical structures were images and are lost; only the numeric triples survive, and their row alignment across the printed pages is scrambled, so **which compound each triple belongs to cannot be trusted.** The triples by class:

| Class | `Z` | `Z_s` | `n` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,2-substituted and 1,4-substituted benzenes | 8 | 4 | 10 |
| 1,2,3- and 1,2,4-substituted benzenes | 9 | 5 | 12 |
| Other benzene derivatives (multiple rows) | 14 / 16 / 15 / 11 / 9 / 12 | 7 / 8 / 8 / 6 / 5 / 6 | 16 / 18 / 18 / 14 / 12 / 14 |
| Non-aromatic compounds (multiple rows) | 2 / 5 / 4 / 7 | 1 / 3 / 2 / 4 | 4 / 8 / 6 / 10 |

`[Tani 1995, Table 7.1, pp.209–212 (PDF 218–221)]` **[Q]** — numbers only, not attributable to individual compounds.

**Named developers used in the 1995 experiments:** **CP-20** (colour, 4-amino-N-dialkylaniline); **D72** (metol–hydroquinone); **D19**; **D19 + KI at 0.5 g/l** (used for internal development after bleaching surface centres); **MAA-1** (a surface developer). `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.215–218 (PDF 224–227); §6.5, p.192 (PDF 201)]` **[F]**

### 12.12 Speed is independent of developer type at each developer's optimum

> "Photographic sensitivity should depend upon development conditions. However, **it has been confirmed by several groups of workers that photographic sensitivity did not depend upon the kind of developers when each developer was used under its optimum conditions.** Thus, **each developer under its optimum conditions could detect the same smallest latent image centers on emulsion grains, while it could hardly detect latent subimage centers.**"

`[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` **[F]**

The centre sizes that fix that common detection floor: the smallest latent image centre is **three atoms** in sulfur-plus-gold-sensitized emulsions and **four or five atoms** in sulfur-sensitized emulsions; "This is the major contribution of gold sensitization to the increase in photographic sensitivity." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` **[Q]**

Remaining headroom, as the source frames it: latent *subimage* centres are stable and become developable after **latensification** or under **enforced development**; "there is some possibility for a further increase in photographic sensitivity if one could find the development condition that could detect and discriminate image centers composed of **two atoms** … from fog formation." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` **[M]**

**[E]** Taken with §12.13, this is a two-part constraint: **speed is a property of the emulsion, not of the developer, once each developer is at its own optimum** — but the *fog* is not, and the whole discriminating art of development lies in the fog channel rather than the speed channel. A processing model in which developer choice moves speed but not fog inverts what the source says.

### 12.13 The two kinds of fog and their different kinetics

**Era: 1995.** Two fog types are distinguished by *when the fog centres come into existence*:

- **Emulsion fog** — definite fog centres pre-exist in the coated, unexposed material. They are composed of silver, Ag₂S, Au₂S and similar species; "since they are composed of silver, they should be removed by an oxidizing agent such as ferricyanide."
- **Developer fog** — the fog centres are *formed during development*, by electron injection from developing agents to the surface of emulsion grains.

The kinetic consequence is the load-bearing part: "**development of emulsion fog proceeds rapidly.** On the other hand, **the rate of developer fogging is determined by its initiation** (i.e., the formation of development centers through electron injection from developing agents to the surface of emulsion grains), and therefore **proceeds slowly**." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, pp.219–220 (PDF 228–229), Fig. 7.13]` **[Q]**

Fig. 7.13 plots the **growth of fog density in a metol-hydroquinone developer** for three cases: **(A)** an aged emulsion; **(B)** the same emulsion as A, **bleached for 2 min in an acid 0.1 % potassium ferricyanide solution** before immersion in the developer; **(C)** an emulsion with a low degree of emulsion fog. `[Tani 1995, p.220 (PDF 229), Fig. 7.13]` **[Q]**

Two riders that belong with this:

- Chemically sensitized grains fog more readily *during* development: "Emulsion grains with these chemical sensitization centers can thus **accept electrons from developing agents to form fog centers during development more easily** than emulsion grains without these centers, although these are not emulsion fog centers." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.220 (PDF 229)]` **[F]**
- **Hillson's strategy** exploits the kinetic split: add **antifoggants to the developer under an accelerated development condition**, "expecting that antifoggants were effective for discrimination between image and fog development at the **initial state** of development of each grain, and did not reduce the development of image centers at the **growth stage**, and that the reduction in the development at the initial stage could be recovered by introducing an acceleration condition." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.220 (PDF 229)]` **[M]**

The 1966 source defines antifoggants in exactly these differential-rate terms: "**Antifoggants** are agents that **decrease the rate of fog density growth during development to a larger degree than they decrease the rate of development of latent images**", as against **stabilizers**, "agents that decrease the changes in developable fog and/or other sensitometric characteristics of emulsion layers that occur **during storage**." (This definition pair is quoted in the 1995 source at §6.5, p.184 / PDF 193.) The 1966 source's own working definition of an antifoggant is "substances which combat fog formation under **vigorous conditions of processing**", and it concedes the stabilizer/antifoggant split "is rather an artificial one". `[Tani 1995, §6.5, p.184 (PDF 193); Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.148–149 (PDF 154–155)]` **[F]**

A point of definition from 1966 that matters for any fog model: "A fog grain is one which will develop without light exposure", so "**the nature of the development influences the fog**", and sensitometric testing "must use the processing the emulsion will actually receive." An emulsion may be acceptably low-fog in a conventional developer yet foggy, when aged, in a developer of very high activity. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.148–149 (PDF 154–155)]` **[F]**

Also from 1966, fog need not be neutral: "Fog produced under these conditions may not result in the formation of a **neutral** overall density; **sulphide contamination** of films … can cause the formation of **yellow fog**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.149 (PDF 155)]` **[F]**

### 12.14 Activation energies of development (1966) — the only Arrhenius data in this material

**Era: 1966.** A compilation attributed to Levenson:

**Energies of activation during development**

| Energy of activation (kcal per mole) | Reaction |
|---|---|
| **4–7** | Diffusion processes |
| **10–20** | Development of silver halide from latent-image centre |
| **20–30** | Fog development; reduction without latent image |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.174 (PDF 180), Table 9.1]` **[Q]**

Accompanying text, **with a printed-text error to flag**: "It will be seen that the presence of a latent image reduces, by around **10,000 Kcals per mole**, the energy required to bring about the reduction of the silver halide." The table's own numbers give a difference of roughly **10 kcal/mol**, not 10,000. Raw string: `10,000 Kcals per mole`. The words are intact, so this is a units error in the printed book, not an extraction artefact. The sentence that follows is usable: "At normal development temperatures this can make the latent-image-catalysed process **about 1,000,000 times as fast as the fog growth**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.174 (PDF 180)]` **[Q]** with error flag.

**[E]** These three bands are the only route in this material to a temperature coefficient of development. Because the fog activation energy (20–30 kcal/mol) exceeds the image activation energy (10–20 kcal/mol), **fog density grows faster with temperature than image density does**; a temperature rise therefore reduces the image:fog ratio from its stated ≈10⁶ at normal development temperature. Because diffusion carries only 4–7 kcal/mol, a diffusion-limited development (the regime the 1995 source locates at `E_1/2` more negative than +170 mV, §12.3) should be markedly *less* temperature-sensitive than a surface-reaction-limited one. Neither source draws either conclusion; both follow from the numbers as given.

### 12.15 The three mechanisms as the 1966 account frames them

**Era: 1966.** Three development mechanisms are set out and all three judged important:

- **Electrode theory** — silver acts as the anode of a silver/silver-halide couple. "a highly crystalline silver-speck was inefficient in this capacity while a **loose cluster was very effective**"; silver-ion supply by diffusion through the crystal is doubted as a sustaining mechanism for the highest known rates; "**this theory receives the greatest support today**."
- **Adsorption theory.**
- **Charge theory** (see §12.5).

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.174–175 (PDF 180–181)]` **[F]**

Definitions from the same place, worth carrying verbatim in sense: reduction of silver ions "from the crystal or from solution (these two types of development are called **chemical** and **physical** respectively)." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.173 (PDF 179)]` **[F]**

Surface versus internal image assay, since it dictates what a given developer measures: surface image only, with "a strictly **non-solvent** developer, that is a developer containing **no bromide or sulphite**"; internal image, by a brief **potassium ferricyanide** bleach followed by a developer containing thiosulphate sized to etch the grains; total image, by solvent development without prebleach. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.183–184 (PDF 189–190)]` **[F]**

Amplification, with an unrecoverable number: "The capture of a small number, frequently only four, photons can result in a permanent record of four silver atoms. By the development step, these can be converted … into" — the printed exponents were destroyed in extraction; raw string `10° to 10”`. **The amplification factor is not recoverable from this material and is not guessed here.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.173 (PDF 179)]` **[F]** with OCR flag.

An explicit scoping statement from the 1966 source, which explains why its development coverage is thin: "**Development**, the very important step which greatly affects the response of the silver-halide emulsion, **is not being discussed in detail in the present work**"; the reader is referred to L. F. A. Mason, *Photographic Processing Chemistry*, Focal Press, then in press. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.217 (PDF 223)]` **[F]**

### 12.16 Development time versus gamma — what the 1922 source measured

**Era: 1922 (measurements spring 1920; manuscript dated Washington, September 6, 1921).**

Definitions first, because the 1922 numbers are only meaningful with them:

- **Density** `D = log₁₀(1/T)`, `T` = transmission. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.8 (PDF 9)]` **[Q]**
- **Gamma** `γ = tan α`, where α is the angle the straight-line portion of the characteristic curve makes with the log-exposure axis; equivalently `γ = ΔD / Δ(log₁₀ E)`. "A gamma of 2 means that the plate shows twice the contrast of the subject, and a gamma of 0.5 means that the plate shows only half the contrast of the subject." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.11–12 (PDF 12–13)]` **[Q]**
- **Exposure** `E = I·t` in **candle-meter-seconds (c.m.s.)**, "when the variation in the factors is less than, say, a thousand." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.8 (PDF 9)]` **[Q]**
- **Inertia** `i` = the common log-exposure intercept of the extrapolated straight lines; **speed** `= 10/i` (Bureau of Standards) as against Hurter's `34/i`. On the published charts `i` is "the average of the inertias of the three development times". `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.13, 32 (PDF 14, 33)]` **[Q]**
- **Density is measured differentially against a fog strip**, so "the effect of the density of the glass and gelatin and also of chemical fog is automatically eliminated, **so that the measured density is due solely to the exposure**." **Consequence: there is no base-plus-fog or dmin value in any 1922 characteristic curve; fog is a separate measured quantity.** `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.22–23 (PDF 23–24)]` **[F]**

The time–contrast behaviour, verbatim in substance: "A number of strips of the same plate were given identical step exposures, then each strip developed for a different length of time … the **straight-line part of the curve becomes steeper with the time of development**." And: "**There is a certain period before the deposit of silver becomes visible, then the contrast increases rapidly with the time, and finally more slowly, so that after a certain time the negative gains very little in contrast by further increasing the time of development.**" `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.11–12 (PDF 12–13), Figs. 7, 8]` **[M]**

**The 1922 source contains no tabulated γ-versus-time data anywhere.** The γ–time relation exists only as graphs: the illustrative Fig. 8 (p.12 / PDF 13), and **Figure 2 of each of the 86 survey charts** (p.35 onward / PDF 36–121). The axes of chart Figure 2 are: ordinate **γ, 0 to 3.0** (ticks .5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0); abscissa **minutes of development, 0 to 12** (ticks 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12). `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32); charts pp.35–120 (PDF 36–121)]` **[F]**

The three numeric anchors the 1922 text does give:

| Quantity | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Development time to unit contrast, chart 2 (an ordinary plate, developer Z) | **3 minutes** — "in chart 2, for example, 3 minutes' development would be required to give unit contrast (γ = 1) under the conditions of development employed in making this test" | `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[Q]** |
| Practical upper limit of development | "**12 minutes' development with tray-strength developer marks the time limit of practical development**" | `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.32 (PDF 33)]` **[F]** |
| Development times used for every published characteristic curve | **3, 6 and 12 minutes** | `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[Q]** |

The standard 1922 development condition, in full, because every published number depends on it: **pyro developer of tray strength (one part each of A, B and C plus seven parts of water), 20 °C, stirred by rotating silver cages of four plates at 40 revolutions per minute, times 3, 6 and 12 minutes.** Vessels were silver-plated cans in a thermostatted water bath. The resolution test used a single **uniform 6-minute** development in the same developer. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.22, 29–31 (PDF 23, 30–32)]` **[Q]**

A generalisation the 1922 authors state and do not quantify: "**With different developers, or the same developer at a different temperature, a change in the time of development as indicated on these charts would be required for a given contrast.**" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[F]**

And a period statement about the *target* gamma: "The statement is sometimes made that all negatives should be developed to give unit contrast … most of the papers in use have gammas greater than 1 when developed to give the proper tone, so that negatives are developed not to unit contrast, but to a less contrast." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.12–13 (PDF 13)]` **[F]**

Two worked synthetic curves are printed and are usable as period reference data. They are constructed illustrations, not measurements of a real plate.

**Straight-line example** (`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.9 (PDF 10), Table 2]` **[Q]**):

| E (c.m.s.) | log E (printed, "+10" convention) | Density | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/10 | 9.0 | 0.40 | — |
| 2/10 | 9.3 | 0.65 | 0.25 |
| 4/10 | 9.6 | 0.90 | 0.25 |
| 8/10 | 9.9 | 1.15 | 0.25 |
| 16/10 | 0.2 | 1.40 | 0.25 |
| 32/10 | 0.5 | 1.65 | 0.25 |
| 64/10 | 0.8 | 1.90 | 0.25 |

Implied γ = 0.25 / 0.301 = **0.83** — that arithmetic is ours, not the paper's. **[E]**

**Toe-and-shoulder example** (`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.9 (PDF 10), Table 3; plotted as Fig. 6]` **[Q]**):

| E (c.m.s.) | log E (printed) | Density | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/160 | 7.8 | 0.00 | — |
| 1/80 | 8.1 | 0.03 | 0.03 |
| 1/40 | 8.4 | 0.08 | 0.05 |
| 1/20 | 8.7 | 0.20 | 0.12 |
| 1/10 | 9.0 | 0.40 | 0.20 |
| *(straight line of Table 2)* | | | |
| 64/10 | 0.8 | 1.90 | — |
| 128/10 | 1.1 | 2.13 | 0.23 |
| 256/10 | 1.4 | 2.30 | 0.17 |
| 512/10 | 1.7 | 2.45 | 0.15 |
| 1024/10 | 2.0 | 2.55 | 0.10 |

The toe is defined for this curve as the region **below log E = 8.9** and the shoulder as **above log E = 1.1**; those breakpoints belong to this example curve, not to plates in general. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.10 (PDF 11), Fig. 6]` **[Q]**

**Critical unit convention.** The 1922 logarithms are printed in the "+10" (colog) convention: a printed value `L` means `log₁₀ = L − 10`. So `log E = 9.0` is `log₁₀E = −1.0`, and chart abscissae running "7.5 … 2.0" span **−2.5 to +2.0** in modern log E. Reading them literally displaces every curve by ten decades. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.9, 13 (PDF 10, 14)]` **[F]**

### 12.17 Gamma-infinity: how the 1929 source uses it, and what it does not supply

**Era: 1929.** Gamma-infinity is a routine factory parameter in the 1929 account, tested alongside speed and fog: "these were tested by the **standard Hurter and Driffield method**, and this gave a record as to whether the emulsion was up to **standard speed, gamma infinity, K and fog reading**." `K` is named as the **velocity constant**. `[Wall 1929, Ch. I, p.8 (PDF 16)]` **[F]**

**The 1929 source never defines γ∞ or K algebraically, never tabulates a γ∞ value, and reproduces no H&D curve and no development-time series anywhere in the book.** γ∞ appears only as a comparative adjective attached to emulsion-making recipes. `[Wall 1929, throughout; see Ch. I p.8 (PDF 16), Ch. IV p.56 (PDF 64), Ch. VII p.135 (PDF 142)]` **[F]**

What it does supply is a set of *emulsion-making* levers with signed effects on γ∞ — which belongs here because γ∞ is a development-limit parameter, and the 1929 source treats it as a manufacturing target:

| Emulsion-making condition | Effect on γ∞ as stated | Citation |
|---|---|---|
