| Acid-boiled formulas generally | "rather a **low** gamma infinity" — suitable for portraiture, less for ordinary work; the boil-then-ammonia modification gives "not only faster plates but a **higher** gamma" | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.56 (PDF 64)]` **[F]** |
| Split-silver addition (only one-fourth of the silver first, remainder later) | "gives rather a **higher** gamma infinity" | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.75 (PDF 82)]` **[F]** |
| Sodium-halide plus sulphite formula | "very clean plates with **high** gamma infinity" — but the claimed extra fineness of grain could not be reproduced on repeated test | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.61 (PDF 69)]` **[F]** |
| Plener cold-digestion (stand 1–6 days at 10–15 °C / 50–59 °F) | "gives rapid emulsions with **high** gamma infinity, and **the colder the solutions during the mix the less the fog**" | `[Wall 1929, Ch. XIII, pp.222–223 (PDF 229–230)]` **[Q]** |
| Prolonged standing in the ice room | "does not give so much increase in speed as **increase of gamma infinity**" | `[Wall 1929, pp.81–82 (PDF 88–89)]` **[F]** |
| Acid emulsions afterwards treated with ammonia | "do ripen considerably, and also give **higher gammas**" | `[Wall 1929, p.82 (PDF 89)]` **[F]** |
| Fast-ammonia process X (three 20-hour ammonia digestions at 32 °C) | "fast but foggy", **low** gamma infinity | `[Wall 1929, Ch. XIII, p.226 (PDF 233)]` **[F]** |
| Boiling: actual temperature | "the emulsion does not actually boil; its temperature ranges from **95° to 98 °C (203° to 208 °F)**" | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.56 (PDF 64)]` **[Q]** |

The single fully-specified 1929 sensitometric data point, and the only one that pairs a developer, a time and a fog reading: Wall's slow sodium-sulphite emulsion (**0.25 parts Na₂SO₃ per 100 AgNO₃**, converted to ammonio-nitrate, digested **1 h at 43 °C (110 °F) plus 2 h at 27 °C (80 °F)**, set on ice) gave "regular, very clean … **speed of 22 H. & D.** with **high gamma infinity**, the **fog reading with ten minutes development with the standard pyro-soda developer being only 0.1**." `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]` **[Q]**

A useful negative result on blending, given as a worked case: an emulsion of **250 H&D with γ∞ = 1.3** mixed in equal volumes with one of **25 H&D with γ = 3** does **not** give speed 137 and gamma 2.15 — "The answer is in the negative; at least, that is the writer's experience. That there is an improvement by the admixture of the slower emulsion cannot be denied, but the result is not the mean." `[Wall 1929, Ch. VII, p.135 (PDF 142)]` **[Q]**

Cine requirements, as a statement of what γ∞ and K were *for*: "For positive work, the requirements for the emulsion are, a **high gamma infinity, with perfect freedom from fog and high velocity constant**. For negative emulsions, almost the same conditions are required, though such a high gamma is not essential." `[Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 92)]` **[F]**

**Sources disagree in scope, not in fact.** The 1922 source explicitly has **no** γ∞ concept, no development-rate constant, and no `γ = γ∞(1 − e^(−kt))` or equivalent; it reaches only "after a certain time the negative gains very little in contrast" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.12 (PDF 13)]`. The 1929 source treats γ∞ and a velocity constant K as everyday factory quantities but never writes them down `[Wall 1929, Ch. I, p.8 (PDF 16)]`. The 1966 source states no γ-versus-time relation at all, having deferred development to another volume `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.217 (PDF 223)]`. The 1995 source likewise contains no closed-form `D(t)` or `γ(t)`; its time-domain content is the per-grain completion times of §12.7 (≈2 min for CP-20, ≈20 s for D72) `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.216–217 (PDF 225–226)]`. **No time-gamma equation exists anywhere in this material; do not expect to find one here.** **[F]**

The pairing below is a positional re-interleaving. None of the four contains bromide as a standing ingredient; bromide is treated separately (§13.3). **Developers named in the 1929 source, with no composition given for the works test developer:** standard **pyro-soda** (the factory test developer, 10 minutes); **metol-hydroquinone** (used as a deliberately constant developer in Wall's chlorobromide image-colour series); **ferrous oxalate** versus **pyrogallol** (pyro "more suitable for emulsions rich in iodide than ferrous oxalate"; iodide-rich images "cannot be developed with ferrous oxalate"); **sodium quinone sulphonate plus sulphite** (a diagnostic developer — reduces AgCl but not AgBr); **metol 7 g / glacial acetic acid 28 ccm / water 6000 ccm** as a physical developer for phosphate papers; a pyrogallol-acid physical developer for Lippmann plates. `[Wall 1929, Ch. II p.24 (PDF 32); Ch. III pp.36–37 (PDF 44–45); Ch. V p.96 (PDF 103); Ch. VI pp.129, 134 (PDF 136, 141)]` **[F]**

**Developers named in the 1966 source:** **diethyl-p-phenylenediamine** as the colour developing agent, "acting as a **fairly low-energy developer giving fine-grain results**"; **Phenidone**-containing developers for diffusion transfer, chosen because they must be very fast; **metol-hydroquinone** and **Phenidone-hydroquinone** as the superadditive systems; plain **hydroquinone** as the non-superadditive contrast case; a **non-solvent** developer "containing no bromide or sulphite" for surface-image assay. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X p.191 (PDF 197); Ch. XI p.217 (PDF 223); Ch. VIII pp.165–166 (PDF 171–172); Ch. IX pp.183–184 (PDF 189–190)]` **[F]**

### 12.19 Temperature and agitation dependence — what exists and what does not

**Temperature.** The available facts, in full:

| Era | Statement | Class |
|---|---|---|
| 1922 | Every published characteristic curve, gamma-time curve and fog-gamma curve was measured at **20 °C**, in silver-plated cans in a thermostatted water bath. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.22, 31 (PDF 23, 32)]` | **[Q]** |
| 1922 | "With different developers, **or the same developer at a different temperature**, a change in the time of development as indicated on these charts would be required for a given contrast." No coefficient given. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` | **[F]** |
| 1922 | "In addition to the time of development, and **the temperature and concentration of the developer**, account must be taken also of the development characteristics of the plate used." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17)]` | **[F]** |
| 1966 | Activation energies 4–7 / 10–20 / 20–30 kcal per mole for diffusion / image development / fog development, with the ≈10⁶ image:fog rate ratio at normal development temperature (§12.14). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.174 (PDF 180), Table 9.1]` | **[Q]** |
| 1966 | "it is frequently customary today to process films at **elevated temperatures**, for instance in the rapid-processing methods used for quick access recording materials and the automatic processing machinery available for X-ray films" — the stated reason coating hardness matters. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.158 (PDF 164)]` | **[F]** |
| 1995 | Processing **temperature** is plotted against calendar year for colour negative films and colour papers, together with processing time and replenishment rate, with the number of processing steps annotated. `[Tani 1995, §8.2, p.237 (PDF 246), Fig. 8.2]` | **[Q]** via figure |

**A reader who expects a numeric temperature coefficient of development will not find one.** The 1922 source states no coefficient. The 1929 source states none. The 1966 source gives activation energies only. The 1995 source gives no development-temperature coefficient anywhere; temperature appears in it as ripening/digestion temperature, as measurement temperature, and as the processing-temperature trend of Fig. 8.2. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32); Wall 1929 throughout; Duffin 1966, Ch. IX p.174 (PDF 180); Tani 1995, §7.3–§7.5, §8.2]` **[F]**

**[E]** The only defensible temperature model derivable from this material is Arrhenius with the 1966 activation-energy bands: taking Eₐ = 10–20 kcal/mol for image development, the rate roughly doubles-to-quadruples per 10 K near room temperature, while fog at 20–30 kcal/mol rises faster still. The numbers are the source's; the Arrhenius application and the "double-to-quadruple" reading are ours.

**Agitation.** Two quantitative statements exist and they are both 1922:

- **"By proper rocking, the time of development may be cut in half of that required for no motion of the developer."** `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17)]` **[Q]** — a factor-of-two effect on time-to-a-given-contrast.
- "In developing it is important to **keep the rate and method of stirring constant** unless the negatives are examined for contrast." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17)]` **[F]**
- The published survey's own standard: test plates in **silver cages, each holding four**, "stirred in the developer by **rotating the cages at 40 revolutions per minute**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.22 (PDF 23)]` **[Q]**
- Tank development is recommended for consistency: "Tank development takes care of small differences in exposure without disturbing contrast ratios." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17)]` **[F]**

The 1995 source contains **no** processing-agitation data at all; agitation appears in it only as *emulsion ripening* agitation, never as processing agitation. The 1966 source gives no agitation regimes. `[Tani 1995, §7.1–§7.5; Duffin 1966, Chs. VII–XI]` **[F]**

### 12.20 Bromide restraint in development

Treated in full in §13.3, because bromide's action is the paradigm case of a development inhibitor. The development-kinetic core, stated here for completeness: the presence of potassium bromide in developer or emulsion makes **the inertia decrease as the time of development increases** — i.e. the straight lines of the development family no longer share a common exposure-axis intercept — whereas "typical development curves of clean working emulsions which are free from bromide show the straight-line parts intersecting in a point on the exposure axis for all times of development." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.15–16 (PDF 16–17), Fig. 10]` **[Q]** The 1922 source's own footnote to the inertia definition makes the same point as a precondition: the common intercept "always occurs, **provided there is no free bromide in the plate or in the developer** and that the plate does not fog badly." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14), fn.4]` **[F]**

### 12.21 Engineering conclusions on development

**[E]** **Type B (granular) development is a per-grain binary event and therefore carries counting statistics, while type A (parallel) is a partial-fill process.** In granular development a grain is either undeveloped or fully developed at any moment — the 1995 source reports that grains in the intermediate "developing" state were "hardly observed at any stage" — so density is proportional to a *count* of completed grains and inherits the variance of that count. In parallel development a large fraction of grains is partially developed at any moment and density is proportional to a *continuous fill fraction* per grain, which averages the per-grain fluctuation away. **Consequence: a colour-developed material and a metol-hydroquinone-developed material at the SAME density need not have the same noise statistics.** This conclusion is ours; the source supplies the two progress types, the grain-fraction measurements and the per-grain completion times, but draws no noise conclusion from them. `[derived from Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.216–219 (PDF 225–228), Figs. 7.7–7.9]`

**[E]** The rate-determining-step split implies two different *scaling* laws for development time. Parallel development scales with grain surface-to-volume ratio, so a finer-grained emulsion develops faster per unit volume and its time-gamma family shifts left with decreasing grain size; granular development is nearly independent of grain size but strongly sensitive to sensitization level and exposure intensity, so its time-gamma family shifts with the *latent-image* state rather than the geometry. `[derived from Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.217–219 (PDF 226–228), Figs. 7.10–7.12]`

**[E]** Speed and fog have different time constants and must not share one. §12.12 fixes speed as a property of the emulsion once each developer is at its optimum; §12.13 gives emulsion fog a *fast* development-time constant and developer fog a *slow*, initiation-limited one, on top of a time-independent pre-existing (ferricyanide-removable) fog offset. A model in which one development-time parameter scales gamma and dmin together therefore contradicts the source at three points: emulsion-fog kinetics, developer-fog kinetics, and the developer-independence of speed. `[derived from Tani 1995, §7.4, pp.219–220 (PDF 228–229), Fig. 7.13]`

---

## 13. Development inhibitors, accelerators, and edge/adjacency effects

### 13.1 Halide release during development, and why it acts locally

**Era: 1995.** Development releases **halide ions into the developer solution** as silver ions in the grain are reduced to silver; the reaction as written (Eq. 7.1) produces the oxidized developer form plus `m` protons, with halide liberated from the lattice. `[Tani 1995, §7.1, p.202 (PDF 211)]` **[F]**

The mechanism by which released by-products act *locally* rather than as a bulk developer property is stated as a diffusion-limited mass-transfer argument, and this single sentence is the whole physical basis of every adjacency phenomenon in this material:

> "One of the most popular chemical interactions between silver halide grains during development is the **chemical adjacency effect**, which is based on the **finite diffusion and mass transfer rates of development byproducts and developer**."

`[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230); the cited source for quantitative adjacency work is M. A. Kriss, in T. H. James (ed.), *The Theory of the Photographic Process*, 4th ed., Macmillan, 1977, Chapter 21]` **[M]**

Note carefully what species this names: **two** diffusing populations moving in opposite senses — fresh developer inward toward a developing region, and development-inhibiting by-products outward from it. The source does not reduce this to one length scale, and it gives no length scale at all. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[M]**

The 1995 source **does not** identify released bromide specifically as the adjacency inhibitor species, and offers no local-concentration model. It speaks only of "development inhibiting byproducts". `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[F]**

### 13.2 Iodide as a development retarder

**Era: 1995.** Iodide ions are named explicitly as a development retarder, and core/shell grain design is justified by the need to keep iodide away from the surface: double-structured grains place high-AgI silver bromoiodide in the core, "which is then covered with silver bromide **to inhibit the appearance of harmful photographic effects of iodide ions such as retardation of development**." No magnitude is given. `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1929.** The 1929 source states the same effect from the sensitometric side and adds its curve-shape consequence: "That a large proportion of iodide tends to give **thin negatives with a given time of development** is indisputable: that is to say, **iodide decreases the development velocity**; but **the same gamma can be obtained by prolonging the development**, and the author has always found that **increase of iodide prolongs the period of underexposure**, which in printing is the most valuable part of the negative scale." `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.42 (PDF 50)]` **[F]**

Quantities, quoted from Eder via the 1929 source, with the archaic fractional notation preserved:

| Iodide proportion | Stated effect | Class |
|---|---|---|
| **1/25 to 1/50** (i.e. 4 % to 2 % of the silver as iodide) | "produces an increase of the sparkle of the high-lights and a more delicate gradation of the negative, it **favors freedom from fog, delays development** and gives with sufficiently long development **more details in the shadows**" | **[Q]** |
| **about 1/12** (≈8 %) | "a considerable **loss of vigor** makes its appearance, which is **more noticeable with the oxalate developer than with pyrogallol**" | **[Q]** |
| Recommended for the acid boiling process | **3 to 5 per cent silver iodide** | **[Q]** |
| Cold emulsification process (Henderson) | "a greater content than **one to two per cent** is prejudicial" | **[Q]** |
| **10 %** | thin images, undevelopable with ferrous oxalate, density obtainable only with difficulty with pyro; "not commercially met with" | **[Q]** |

`[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.35–36 (PDF 43–44)]` — and note the 1929 author's own dating caveat on this passage: "It should be noted that the above passage was written in **1903**, and therefore some of the statements, particularly as to the fashions in emulsions, are hardly correct at the present time." `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.36 (PDF 44)]` **[F]**

The developer-dependence of the iodide effect is a real result and worth isolating: **"The pyro developer is more suitable for emulsions rich in iodide than ferrous oxalate."** Iodide-rich images "cannot be developed with ferrous oxalate" at all. `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.36–37 (PDF 44–45)]` **[F]**

### 13.3 Bromide as a restrainer — the three-era account

**Era: 1922.** The fullest quantitative treatment of bromide restraint in this material, and it is still only a figure plus four asserted signs:

> "Typical development curves of clean working emulsions which are free from bromide show the straight-line parts intersecting in a point on the exposure axis for all times of development. On the other hand, the presence of potassium bromide in the developer or emulsion produces a marked effect on the properties of photographic emulsions. **The inertia becomes less as the time of development increases** … The addition of potassium bromide is necessary with some developing agents, particularly **metol**. It **retards the appearance of chemical fog** and **permits the development of a higher degree of contrast**. However, **its presence produces a marked decrease in speed**."

`[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.15–16 (PDF 16–17), Figs. 10, 11]` **[F]** — *(the raw extraction reads "chemical jog"; read "chemical fog")*

Four signed effects, therefore: inertia falls with development time (breaking the common intercept); fog is retarded; attainable contrast rises; speed falls markedly.

The magnitude lives in Fig. 11 only, whose axes are recoverable: **ordinate "Plate Speed", ticks at 200 and 400** (so the plotted range spans roughly 200 to 400+ B.S. speed); **abscissa "K.Br.", 0 to 0.10 per cent, with a tick at 0.05 per cent**; three curves for three brands of plate, in **pyro developer of tray strength**. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17), Fig. 11]` **[Q]** via figure.

**Integrity flag on Fig. 11's curve labels.** The three curve labels were extracted as `Seed30`, `Seed 26`, `Seed23`. This is the only place in the 1922 paper where something reading as a trade name may have survived the deliberate anonymisation of the survey (M. A. Seed Dry Plate Co. plate grades 23/26/30 would fit). It is equally possible the extraction duplicated the word "Speed". **Uncertain; recorded, not relied on.** `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17), Fig. 11]` **[F]**

There is **no numeric bromide table** in the 1922 source. Fog-versus-bromide and gamma-versus-bromide are asserted, never tabulated. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.15–16 (PDF 16–17)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1929.** Bromide added to the *emulsion* rather than the developer, with quantities:

> "The purpose of the addition of the bromide is, of course, to **prevent fog in development** and also with the idea of **keeping the plates**. This it may do, but **if added in anything like large quantities it certainly slows the plates, that is increases the inertia of the plate with normal time of development.** Eder recommended the addition of from **one-tenth to three parts of potassium or ammonium bromide per one thousand**, the larger quantities being for a foggy emulsion."

`[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.154 (PDF 161)]` **[Q]**

Hydrobromic acid as an alternative: "a normal addition" is **5 parts of a 1 % solution per 1000 = 0.005 % HBr** — which the 1929 author calls "probably a negligible quantity". He also notes that residual lime from the washing water will neutralise it, "so that actually **calcium bromide** must exist in the emulsion." The practice "has fallen to a great extent into disuse, except possibly for transparency and paper emulsions." `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, pp.154–155 (PDF 161–162)]` **[Q]**

**Note the direction disagreement in sign convention, not in physics.** The 1922 source says bromide makes the inertia *decrease with increasing development time* (a change in the *slope* of the inertia-versus-time relation, Fig. 10) `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.15 (PDF 16)]`; the 1929 source says bromide *increases the inertia at normal development time* (a shift in the *level*) `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.154 (PDF 161)]`. These are compatible statements about different things — level versus trend — and are recorded here separately rather than merged.

**Era: 1966.** Bromide appears in the 1966 source only as a *diagnostic* variable, not as a restrainer with numbers: surface-image assay requires "a strictly **non-solvent** developer, that is a developer containing **no bromide or sulphite**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.183–184 (PDF 189–190)]` **[F]** The 1966 source contains **no bromide-restraint numbers at all**. `[Duffin 1966, Chs. VII–XI]` **[F]**

**Era: 1995.** Bromide appears only qualitatively, and only once in a processing sense: lith development requires "a very low concentration of free sulfite and **a suitable amount of a soluble bromide**." There is **no rate-versus-bromide-concentration data anywhere** in the 1995 source. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.222 (PDF 231)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1966, secondary stabilization by halide excess.** Related and worth keeping because it is the emulsion-side counterpart: at the end of digestion, excess halide may be added to lower the silver-ion concentration — "chloride in chlorobromides, bromide in iodobromides" — as one of two "secondary" stabilization routes, the other being selection of a gelatin with a larger than usual restrainer content. "Even today, the selection of the gelatin used at this point can be important with **gold-sensitized** emulsions, where the use of **highly-restrained gelatin** can aid the keeping properties." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.137 (PDF 143)]` **[F]**

### 13.4 Accelerators

**Era: 1966.** The best-documented development accelerators in this material are the **long-chain polyethylene oxides**, and the account is unusually complete because it names the chemistry, the quantities, the mechanism, the developer-dependence and the curve-region selectivity.

Requirement: "a long polyethylene-oxide chain containing **upwards of 20 individual units**" — against 6 to 8 units in ordinary non-ionic wetting agents. Two equally active classes: `R—(OCH₂CH₂)ₙOH` and `H(OCH₂CH₂)ₙOH`. Named products: **Texofor A1P** (R = C₁₆H₃₃, **n ≈ 23**) and **Carbowax 4000** (**n ≈ 90**), with the caveat that polymerization gives a distribution so n is an average. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.165 (PDF 171)]` **[Q]**

Effect and mechanism: "These compounds produce an increase in speed in **fast iodobromide** emulsions … giving **up to twice the speed** under optimum conditions. This is a **fairly recent introduction** to photographic technology and has played a part in the outstanding fast films of the present day." Initially believed to be chemical sensitizers, hence added before digestion, but "it seems most likely that they function as **development accelerators**"; Wood showed they do not desorb gelatin, are strongly adsorbed to the grain, and probably act "by **reducing the charge of the double layer surrounding the grain**, and thus facilitate the approach of the negatively-charged developing agents." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.165 (PDF 171)]` **[Q]**

That is the same charge-barrier mechanism the 1995 source attributes to positively charged adsorbates (§12.5) and to part of superadditivity (§12.10) — **the two eras agree on mechanism**, and the 1966 account supplies the speed magnitude (×2) the 1995 account does not. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.165 (PDF 171); Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.213–216 (PDF 222–225)]` **[F]**

Developer-dependence and the toe-selective consequence: "A speed increase is only produced with the usual **superadditive** developers such as **metol-hydroquinone** or **Phenidone-hydroquinone** systems. Development by **hydroquinone** developers is **inhibited**", attributed to interaction between the polyethylene oxide and the **semiquinone** in the bulk developer. "This behaviour has been applied by **Perutz** in a recent patent to improve the **contrast** given by emulsions used for **lithographic** purposes, **the effect being one of desensitization in the toe region of the characteristic curve**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.165–166 (PDF 171–172)]` **[Q]**

This is the only statement in this material that an addendum acts *selectively on one named region* of the characteristic curve. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.165–166 (PDF 171–172)]` **[F]**

One documented cost, since the same chemistry brings a fog liability: a whole antifoggant class exists specifically against fog from long-chain polyethylene oxides, "particularly pronounced with **gold-sensitized** emulsions because gold and polyethylene oxides are frequently used together." Active against it: cadmium and mercury compounds; acidic heterocyclics (3,5-dihydroxy-1,2,4-triazole, 2-guanidobenziminazole, 4,5-diphenyl-2-mercapto-oxazole, 5-mercapto-3-methyl-1,2,4-thiadiazole); non-salt-forming heterocyclics (2,4,6-triethylthio-1,3,5-triazine; the ester of 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole); phenols including bis-phenols and phenolic aldoximes such as salicylaldoxime; and polymers (polyvinylpyrrolidone and its vinyl-acetate copolymers, iodine complexes of polyvinyl oxazolidone). "Probably because of their fairly recent introduction, there is **no published work on how these substances function**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.149–151 (PDF 155–157)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1995.** The 1995 source's accelerator content is the **DAR (development-accelerator-releasing) coupler**, treated in §14.7 because its whole point is locality.

**Era: 1929.** Sodium carbonate added to the emulsion at **0.1 to 5 g per litre** gives "more details in the shadows and making the plates faster"; the 1929 author calls the practice dangerous for keeping. `[Wall 1929, Ch. IX, p.155 (PDF 162)]` **[Q]**

### 13.5 The chemical adjacency effect: border and fringe effects

**Era: 1995.** This is the source's complete edge-effect statement, and it is worth having in full because both signs are specified:

> "On development of a **knife-edge exposure**, the concentration of developer is higher and the concentration of development inhibiting byproducts is lower in the edge region than in the remainder of the high-exposure region, and **density develops more rapidly (the border effect)**. The development byproducts that flow into the low-exposure region of the knife-edge exposure can curtail development close to the edge, resulting in a **low-density region (the fringe effect)**. Chemical adjacency effects can take place **between emulsion layers in multilayer films, as well as within a single emulsion layer**, and can be controlled to improve image quality."

`[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[M]**

Read as a signed edge profile across a knife edge: on the **high-exposure side**, an *overshoot* of density near the edge (border effect), caused by locally higher developer concentration and locally lower inhibitor concentration; on the **low-exposure side**, an *undershoot* of density near the edge (fringe effect), caused by inhibitor by-products diffusing across into the low-exposure region. Both signs are stated; **no length scale, no edge-strength magnitude, no overshoot amplitude, no edge width, and no measured knife-edge profile appears anywhere in this material.** `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1966.** The 1966 source contains no adjacency or edge-effect treatment at all — an exhaustive keyword search of that book returns zero occurrences of "adjacency", "edge effect" or "interimage", and the subject index carries no such entry. Its nearest content is the lateral wandering of oxidized colour developer (§14.4) and the iodide-mediated cross-layer effect (§14.5), neither quantified. `[Duffin 1966, subject index pp.—(PDF 237–246); Ch. X, pp.194, 202–203 (PDF 200, 208–209)]` **[F]**

**Eras 1922 and 1929.** Neither source treats adjacency or edge effects. The 1922 source discusses **halation** and **irradiation** as sharpness-limiting mechanisms and quantifies neither; all its test plates were **backed with black shellac (lampblack in alcoholic shellac)** to suppress halation, so its published curves and scales are free of halation contributions that a user of an unbacked plate would see. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[F]**

### 13.6 Infectious development, and Anderson's one-parameter characteristic-curve family

**Era: 1995 (simulation published by Anderson, 1977).** The complementary interaction to inhibition: "the release of development byproducts that **initiate the development of neighboring grains that otherwise would not develop** (i.e., infectious development), or **inhibit the development of neighboring exposed grains**." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.221–222 (PDF 230–231)]` **[F]**

Anderson built a model of a developing grain with the adjacency effect included, and produced a family of characteristic curves indexed by a single dimensionless coupling constant **`c`**:

| `c` | Regime |
|---|---|
| **`c = 1`** | no adjacency effect |
| **`c > 1`** | **infectious development** — released by-products fog neighbouring grains |
| **`c < 1`** | **development inhibition** by released by-products |

`[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.221–222 (PDF 230–231), Fig. 7.14]` **[Q]** via figure

The signed trade-offs the source reads off that family, verbatim in substance:

> "**infectious development can be used to get increased sensitivity and gamma at the expense of increased graininess and decreased sharpness. This development inhibition provides an enhanced adjacency effect, and can be used to improve graininess and sharpness at the expense of sensitivity and gamma.**"

and, separately: "infectious development provides photographic materials with **high contrast and a short toe**." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.222 (PDF 231), Fig. 7.14]` **[Q]**

Fig. 7.14 is a **density versus log-exposure family, one curve per value of `c`**, `c` dimensionless. It is explicitly a **simulation**, not a measurement. `[Tani 1995, p.221 (PDF 230), Fig. 7.14 caption]` **[F]**

**Integrity flag.** A later passage cites "as shown in **Fig. 7.4**" where the content requires **Fig. 7.14**; raw string `as shown in Fig. 7.4.` Treat as a typographic or extraction error for Fig. 7.14. `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.234 (PDF 243)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Fig. 7.14's parameter `c` is exactly an "adjacency coupling strength", and it moves **speed, gamma, toe length, graininess and sharpness together, with fixed signs**. Anything that treats adjacency strength and characteristic-curve shape as independent parameters contradicts this family. That said, `c` is a simulation parameter with no stated physical units and no calibration against a measured edge profile, so it cannot be used to fix an absolute edge width or overshoot amplitude.

### 13.7 Lith (infectious) development chemistry

**Era: 1995.** "It is believed that **semiquinone**, which is formed by the reaction of **quinone with hydroquinone** in the vicinity of a developing grain, is so active that it initiates the development of a neighboring grain bearing a **latent subimage center** and produces materials with **high contrast and a short toe** in the presence of **a very low concentration of free sulfite and a suitable amount of a soluble bromide**. This is called **lith development** and is used to provide materials for the graphic arts." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.222 (PDF 231)]` **[M]**

A second infectious route: "The reaction of oxidation products from the development reaction with a **hydrazine** gives a substance that can fog a neighboring grain, providing photographic materials with high contrast and a short toe, which are used to produce materials for the graphic arts." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.222–223 (PDF 231–232)]` **[M]**

**Restricting the reach of infectious development is a stated design objective with no stated value:** "an idea to **restrict the range to which the infectious development starting from a grain could reach** was proposed to decrease the degree of the deterioration of the image quality by the infectious development." The reference given is a patent (K. E. Whitmore, WO 80/01614). So the finite reach radius is explicitly the designed quantity — **and no value for it is given.** `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.234 (PDF 243)]` **[M]**

**Era: 1966.** Infectious development is named as the one case in which grain-to-grain interaction occurs during development: "in an infectious developer where a **latent-image-bearing grain will initiate development and cause the reduction of those crystals near to it by chemical influence**." No chemistry, no range, no curve family. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.171 (PDF 177)]` **[M]**

**Era: 1966, the polyethylene-oxide litho route** is the alternative high-contrast lever and is quantified in §13.4: toe desensitization under a hydroquinone-only developer. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.165–166 (PDF 171–172)]` **[Q]**

### 13.8 The Eberhard effect

**The Eberhard effect is not mentioned in any of this material.** The 1995 source names the adjacency phenomena "border effect" and "fringe effect" only, and its index has no Eberhard entry across the pages searched. The 1966, 1929 and 1922 sources do not mention it either. A reader looking for the Eberhard effect by name will not find it here; the phenomenon it names is covered under the border/fringe account of §13.5. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230) and index; Duffin 1966, subject index (PDF 237–246); Wall 1929; Davis & Walters 1922]` **[F]**

### 13.9 Diffusion lengths and diffusion coefficients — the complete inventory, and the explicit absence

Every numeric length or transport quantity that exists in this material, so that the gap is unmistakable:

| Quantity | Value | What it actually is | Citation | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Silver-atom surface diffusion length** on a growing silver speck (sets filament diameter) | **≈ 200 Å = 0.02 µm** | metal-atom surface migration **inside one grain** | `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.213 (PDF 222)]` | **[Q]** |
| Filament diameter during solvent-free development | "always about **200 Å**" | developed-silver morphology | `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.213 (PDF 222)]` | **[Q]** |
| Onset of diffusion-controlled development | `E_1/2` more negative than **+170 mV** vs SCE, for 4-amino-N-dialkylanilines | a *potential* threshold at which transport overtakes surface reaction — **not a length** | `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.208 (PDF 217), Fig. 7.5]` | **[Q]** |
| Photoelectron diffusion range in a large sheet crystal, dye-induced | "photoelectrons induced by light absorbed by sensitizing dyes have been shown to **diffuse 40–50 microns in large sheet crystals**, i.e. as far as photoelectrons produced by light absorption by the halide" | a **single-crystal laboratory** number, orders of magnitude larger than any emulsion grain (0.2–2 µm) | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.131 (PDF 137)]` | **[Q]** |
| Latent-image speck displacement under ultracentrifugation | **3 microns in 10 minutes** at 40,000 rpm, radius 65 mm | an experimental *displacement* used to size the speck (3–4 silver atoms), not a diffusion length | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.172 (PDF 178)]` | **[Q]** |
| Dye-to-silver-halide separation steps (Langmuir–Blodgett spacer experiments) | van der Waals contact, then steps of **27 Å** | a spectroscopic spacer geometry | `[Tani 1995, §5.8, p.149 (PDF 158)]` | **[Q]** |
| Colour negative photosensitive-layer stack thickness | **about 20 µm total**, about 14 layers | the geometric envelope within which any lateral diffusion happens | `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]` | **[Q]** |
| Dry layer thicknesses | single emulsion layer **2–40 µm dry** (30–600 µm at the coating point); supercoats and filter layers **1–3 µm dry**; colour-material layers "**all of them 1–3 µm thick in the dry state**" | as above | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` | **[Q]** |

**The absence, stated in the words a project needs to read:** *this material contains no inhibitor diffusion length and no diffusion coefficient in µm or cm²/s.* No development-inhibitor diffusion length. No developer diffusion coefficient. No coupler-by-product diffusion length. No adjacency length. No edge width. No overshoot amplitude. The adjacency mechanism is attributed to "the finite diffusion and mass transfer rates of development byproducts and developer" with **zero** scale attached, and the only pointer to where such numbers live is Kriss, in James, *The Theory of the Photographic Process*, 4th ed. (1977), **Chapter 21** — cited by the 1995 source but not reproduced by it. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230), ref. 68]` **[F]**

**[E]** Do **not** press the 200 Å silver-atom figure into service as an inhibitor diffusion length. It is a metal-atom surface-migration length on a growing silver speck inside a single grain, three orders of magnitude below the layer thicknesses of the table above, and the 1995 source uses it only to explain why filaments are ~200 Å across. Likewise the 40–50 µm photoelectron range is a large-single-crystal result and cannot be used as a lateral spread in a coated layer; the 1966 source itself contrasts it against grain dimensions.

**[E]** What the material *does* license: the two-species picture of §13.1 (developer inward, inhibitor outward) implies two length scales in principle, not one, and the 1995 source separates the *scales of action* explicitly — DIR inhibitors are framed as acting on the **dye-cloud size around a single grain** (§14.6), while chemical adjacency is framed as acting across a **knife edge** (§13.5). Treating those as one bundled parameter loses a distinction the source draws.

### 13.10 Antifoggants and stabilizers as differential-rate inhibitors

**Era: 1995.** The definitions are precise, and they belong here because an antifoggant is an inhibitor selected for **kinetic selectivity**, not for potency:

- "**Stabilizers** are agents that decrease the changes in developable fog and/or other sensitometric characteristics of emulsion layers that occur **during storage**."
- "**Antifoggants** are agents that **decrease the rate of fog density growth during development to a larger degree than they decrease the rate of development of latent images.**"

`[Tani 1995, §6.5, p.184 (PDF 193)]` **[F]** — i.e. an explicit statement of a *ratio of two rate constants* as the design objective. The 1966 source's working definition is "substances which combat fog formation under **vigorous conditions of processing**", and it concedes the stabilizer/antifoggant split "is rather an artificial one". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.148–149 (PDF 154–155)]` **[F]**

Three families, with silver-ion affinity increasing down the list: **4-hydroxy-tetraazaindenes** (weak Ag⁺ affinity; TAI = 4-hydroxy-6-methyl-1,3,3a,7-tetraazaindene), **benzotriazoles**, and **mercaptoazoles** (very strong Ag⁺ affinity; PMT = 1-phenyl-5-mercaptoazole). Adsorptivity order: **mercaptoazoles > benzotriazoles > 4-hydroxy-tetraazaindenes**, and adsorptivity is pH-dependent, with the ordering capable of reversing between pH 5 and pH 10. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.184–189 (PDF 193–198), Figs. 6.11–6.14]` **[F]** *(The pKa and pK_sp tables for all three families, the per-gram-mole working quantities, and the surface-coverage arithmetic are stabilizer chemistry rather than development-inhibitor kinetics and are held in the stabilizers material, not repeated here.)*

The transport-side mechanism, which is the one that bears directly on development rate: **all agents studied decreased the ionic conductivity** — hence the interstitial-Ag⁺ concentration — of AgBr grains, and the capability tracked adsorptivity. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, p.189 (PDF 198), Fig. 6.15 (0.5 µm cubic AgBr vs benzotriazole amount, by Dember photovoltage decay)]` **[Q]** The 1966 source makes the inorganic counterpart statement: cadmium ions greatly decrease the concentration of interstitial silver ions, and "a considerable parallel" is suggested with the organic stabilizers. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.148 (PDF 154)]` **[F]**

**A result that contradicts the received view and must be recorded as such:** "It has generally been believed that stabilizers and antifoggants **decrease** photographic sensitivity, or at most do not change it. Tani has described a new photographic phenomenon …: **They actually can increase photographic sensitivity of emulsions with and without spectral sensitization.**" Among the measured contributing mechanisms: TAI increases **surface** sensitivity while decreasing **internal** sensitivity; photoelectron lifetimes lengthen with added TAI; the fraction of photoelectrons captured by sulfur sensitization centres rises; Dember photovoltage rises (higher photoelectron mobility from lower interstitial-Ag⁺); hole-trapping desensitization by cyanine dyes is reduced; and dispersion of latent-image centres is retarded — "sensitization by TAI was pronounced with **high-intensity exposures** and almost disappeared after **gold latensification**." `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.191–194 (PDF 200–203), Figs. 6.16–6.18]` **[Q]**

Two signed image-level consequences of stabilizer choice, from 1966, both bearing on speed:

- **Tetrazaindenes:** "as well as conferring great stability upon emulsions of many kinds, particularly those of high speed, **no speed loss occurs** when they are added; on the contrary **a slight speed increase is frequently detectable** … either on the addition of the stabilizer or after a short heat treatment." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.139 (PDF 145), Fig. 7.1]` **[F]**
- **Mercapto derivatives:** "Many of these mercapto derivatives, 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole is a well-known example, cause a **marked speed loss particularly in iodobromide emulsions** … they are quite useless in many high-speed commercial emulsions. On the other hand, 1-phenyl-5-mercaptotetrazole has far less effect on the speed of **chloride and chlorobromide** emulsions, at the quantities found to be effective, and is therefore commonly used in **paper** emulsions." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.141 (PDF 147)]` **[F]**

A dose-response trend from the same 1966 series, worth keeping because it is the only structure-activity number: as the tetrazaindene side-chain R grows from 0–3 carbons through 4–7 to 11 carbons, the tabulated sensitivity falls **21.5 → 20.5 → 19.0** — progressive desensitization with alkyl chain length — while stabilizing efficiency "**dropped as the carbon chain became longer and the quantity adsorbed increased**". *The table's three "Quantity" column sub-headings, the units of Quantity, the qualifier on the Sensitivity column and the footnote marker were all lost in extraction; the sensitivity trend is the reliable part.* `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.144–147 (PDF 150–153), Table 7.1]` **[Q]** with flag.

**[E]** For a processing model the operative content of this subsection is the definition: an antifoggant is a species chosen so that its inhibition of the *fog-initiation* rate exceeds its inhibition of the *image-growth* rate. That is a two-rate-constant object, and it is what makes Hillson's accelerated-development strategy (§12.13) coherent. A single "restrainer strength" scalar cannot express it.
---

## 14. Inter-image effects and layer interactions

### 14.1 What is quantified and what is only described — read this first

This section is thin by the nature of the sources, and the distinction between quantified and described must be drawn sharply before anything else:

**Quantified in this material:**
- The **geometry** of a colour multilayer: layer count, total thickness, per-layer thickness, grain areal density. `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12); Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]`
- The **stoichiometric difference** between masked and unmasked magenta coupling — 2 Ag⁺ versus 4 Ag⁺ per dye molecule. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.213–214 (PDF 219–220)]`
- Anderson's **one-parameter curve family** for adjacency coupling, which the 1995 source states applies between layers as well as within one. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.221–222 (PDF 230–231), Fig. 7.14]`

**Described only, with direction but no magnitude:**
- Chemical adjacency **between** emulsion layers.
- DIR-coupler and DAR-coupler action.
- Iodide-mediated cross-layer development inhibition.
- Layer-order rules.
- Interlayer (filter-layer) function.

**Absent entirely:** *no interimage gammas, no cross-layer coupling coefficients, no CMY interimage matrices, no measured interimage magnitudes of any kind for multilayer colour films appear anywhere in this material.* The 1995 source's index carries "interlayer effect" as a single page entry; the 1966 source's index has no interimage entry at all. `[Tani 1995, index and §8.1.2, p.234 (PDF 243); Duffin 1966, subject index (PDF 237–246)]` **[F]**

### 14.2 The multilayer geometry the effects act within

**Era: 1995.**

> "On a film base there are blue-, green-, and red-sensitive layers, which are coated one over the other. Moreover, each color-sensitive layer is composed of **high-speed, medium-speed, and low-speed sublayers**, which are also coated one over the other. A photosensitive layer in a typical color negative film is composed of **about 14 layers** with different functions and is **about 20 µm thick in total**. There are **12 million silver halide grains per square millimeter** and **more than 100 kinds of functional organic compounds** in a film."

The stock described is ISO 100 colour negative. `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]` **[Q]**

Companion accounting: an ISO 100 colour negative film has "about **1.2 × 10⁷** silver halide grains/mm² and **2 × 10⁷** equivalent pixels/135 format (36 × 24 mm²). Therefore, the area that corresponds to an equivalent pixel in this film is **43 µm²** and contains as many as **500 silver halide grains**." *(The extraction rendered "43 µm²" as `43 A2`; 864 mm² ÷ 2 × 10⁷ = 43.2 µm², so the reading is secure.)* `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)]` **[Q]** with OCR flag.

Coating tolerance, which bounds how tightly layers can be balanced against each other: "**A precision and uniformity containing 1–2 % variation is necessary** to achieve the desired abilities of photographic materials", with "simultaneous multilayer coating in the dark." `[Tani 1995, §1.2.5, p.10 (PDF 19)]` **[Q]**

**Era: 1966.** Thicknesses, which are the only per-layer dimensions in this material: "The thickness of an emulsion layer … varies widely with the type of material, between **30–600 µm at the coating point** which will then be **2–40 µm thick after drying**. **Supercoats and filter layers** are usually thinner than this, being **1–3 µm in the dry state**. **Colour materials** frequently contain a large number of layers, **all of them 1–3 µm thick in the dry state** and correspondingly thicker when wet." *(The extraction reads "1-3 mu" twice; from context this is µ, i.e. microns — a 1–3 mµ supercoat is physically absurd.)* `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` **[Q]** with OCR flag.

And a comparative statement: "The overall thickness of a modern **colour** film is **much less than that of a modern X-ray emulsion**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.202 (PDF 208)]` **[F]**

**[E]** The two sources are consistent: ~14 layers at 1–3 µm dry each is compatible with ~20 µm total. Any lateral-diffusion or cross-layer transport process therefore operates over a *vertical* budget of about 20 µm and a per-layer budget of 1–3 µm, and this is the only dimensional constraint the material supplies for interimage geometry.

### 14.3 The layer-order rule, with its efficiency rationale

**Era: 1995.** "the most sensitive grains should be in the position to capture incident light in advance of light absorption by other grains, **the emulsion with highest sensitivity should be at the top, followed by emulsion layers in the order of sensitivity**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1966.** The tripack order, from the top: **supercoat / blue-sensitive (undyed emulsion) / yellow filter layer / green-sensitive / red-sensitive / support** (film or paper). "The yellow filter layer protects the lower layers from the action of blue light to which they are also sensitive by virtue of their natural sensitivity; **this is usually yellow colloidal silver but may be an organic layer**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.195–196 (PDF 201–202), Figs. 10.1, 10.2]` **[F]**

When the yellow filter can be omitted, which is a genuine interlayer design decision: in negative-positive **print** material, "A **fast chlorobromide** emulsion may be used in the positive material for the two lower layers and in this case **it is unnecessary to include a yellow filter because the inherent blue speed of the green-sensitive and the red-sensitive layers is so much lower than the speed in the dye-sensitized region**." Similarly for Polacolor: "Polaroid make no reference to a yellow filter layer … however, the **yellow dye coupler is located beneath the blue-sensitive layer** and it is likely that this acts as a yellow filter." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.210–211 (PDF 216–217)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Note that the two sources give *different* ordering criteria, and they are not in conflict: the 1995 rule orders by *speed* (fastest on top, for photon-capture efficiency); the 1966 rule orders by *spectral record* (blue on top, because every layer retains intrinsic blue sensitivity and the blue record must be taken before the yellow filter removes blue). A real stock satisfies both — blue/green/red top-to-bottom, and within each colour record the high-speed sublayer above the low-speed sublayer.

### 14.4 Chemical adjacency between emulsion layers

**Era: 1995.** The one statement, and it is the same sentence that defines the within-layer effect:

> "Chemical adjacency effects can take place **between emulsion layers in multilayer films, as well as within a single emulsion layer**, and can be controlled to improve image quality."

`[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[M]**

The general framing that follows it: "The representative phenomena resulting from **interactions between silver halide grains** are **adjacency and interlayer effects** taking place during development. These phenomena are used as **methods for image processing** in silver halide photographic materials." Retardation by released substances "could **improve image quality at the expense of sensitivity and gradation** to some extent"; enhancement by infectious development "could **increase the apparent sensitivity at the expense of image quality**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.234 (PDF 243)]` **[M]**

So the *direction* of the interlayer effect, as the source gives it, is the same as the within-layer direction: inhibitor released in one region (here, one layer) suppresses development in its neighbourhood (here, an adjacent layer), trading sensitivity and gradation for image quality. **No cross-layer magnitude, coupling coefficient or spatial extent is given.** `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230); §8.1.2, p.234 (PDF 243)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1966.** The lateral-spread statement that is the closest 1966 analogue, and it concerns the *dye*, not the inhibitor: in chromogenic development "The dye is frequently formed at places which are **remote from the site where the silver-halide crystal is being reduced**. Indeed it is the general rule of many of these colour processes that there is **little connection between the grain pattern of the original silver-halide emulsion and that of the developed dye image**." Two candidate carriers are offered: the **quinone di-imine** itself, stabilized by resonance; or its hydrolysis to a **mono-imine** plus diethylamine, the mono-imine diffusing and regenerating oxidized developer elsewhere by reacting with an unoxidized developer molecule. **No diffusion distance is given.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.194 (PDF 200)]` **[M]**

Two related 1966 statements which are requirements rather than measurements: requirement (2) for a colour material is that dyes of the correct hue form in the appropriate layer "and **without appreciable sideways wandering in that layer**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.190 (PDF 196)]`; and for the soluble-coupler process, "In actual fact **some 'wandering' of the oxidized developer does occur** but substantially the desired reactions occur at the required points." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.202 (PDF 208)]` **[F]**

**[E]** The 1966 account identifies **one** diffusing carrier — the oxidized developer / quinone di-imine — as the cross-layer and lateral-spread species in colour development, and argues *against* tying colour-dye granularity to silver-grain geometry. That is a substantive constraint even without a number: in a chromogenic material the noise and the cross-layer coupling are dye-side, not silver-side, phenomena.

### 14.5 Iodide-mediated cross-layer inhibition — the one concrete interimage mechanism in 1966

**Era: 1966.** In Kodachrome-type processing, after the cyan and yellow layers have been developed, "The remaining **magenta layer is difficult to fog and develop because of the iodide, released during the development of the other layers, which has deposited on the crystals of this layer.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.203 (PDF 209)]` **[F]**

This is a *documented, named, directional cross-layer inhibition*: halide released by development in one layer migrates and adsorbs on grains of another layer, raising the threshold for their development. The remedies given are high-intensity light fogging, or chemical fogging — "a Kodak patent mentions the use of **potassium borohydride, KBH₄**", whose small BH₄⁻ ion "would be expected to **diffuse easily into the layer**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.203 (PDF 209)]` **[F]**

**No magnitude, no time constant and no distance are given.** But the mechanism is fully specified and it is chemically the same as the 1995 source's iodide-retardation statement (§13.2), and the same in kind as the released-by-product adjacency mechanism of §13.1. Sources therefore agree on the mechanism across a 29-year gap: **released halide inhibits development locally, and iodide is the worst offender.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.203 (PDF 209); Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` **[M]**

Related cross-layer transit problem, in a different process family: in Polacolor, unoxidized dye-developer from the red-sensitive layer must pass through the layers above it, and "**This could cause difficulties if exposed, but undeveloped, silver-halide grains were still present in these upper layers but these are avoided by correct balancing of the activities of the dye-developers and the rate of migration.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.208 (PDF 214)]` **[F]**

### 14.6 DIR (development-inhibitor-releasing) couplers

**Era: 1995.** The mechanism, as the source states it:

> "With regard to color development in the presence of DIR coupler molecules, **oxidation products of developing agents react with DIR coupler molecules to give dye molecules and development inhibitor molecules in the vicinity of a developing grain. The inhibitor molecules then depress the development of the grain, causing the formation of fine dye clouds around it. Thus, it is expected that DIR couplers provide fine images at the expense of sensitivity and gamma.**"

`[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.223–224 (PDF 232–233)]` **[M]**

Three things to hold onto here. First, the **inhibitor is generated stoichiometrically with the dye**, from the same reaction with oxidized developer — so inhibitor release is proportional to local dye formation, i.e. to local exposure. Second, the stated scale of action is **around a single developing grain** — the effect named is a reduction in *dye-cloud size*, not an edge overshoot. Third, the stated cost is **sensitivity and gamma**, and the stated gain is a **finer image**.

**Dating.** DIR couplers are dated by their primary reference: C. R. Barr, J. R. Thirtle and P. W. Vittum, *Photogr. Sci. Eng.* **13**, 74 (**1969**). `[Tani 1995, ref. 81, p.226 (PDF 235)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1966.** **There is no DIR-coupler discussion in the 1966 source.** This is expected — the primary DIR reference postdates it by three years — and it is worth recording as a dating anchor: a 1966-era colour material predates DIR couplers, so any 1966 colour account describes a material *without* deliberate development-inhibitor release. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.189–215 (PDF 195–221); Tani 1995, ref. 81]` **[E]**

**No magnitude of any kind is given for DIR action:** no inhibitor diffusion length, no dye-cloud diameter with and without DIR, no gamma reduction, no speed cost, no granularity improvement figure. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.223–224 (PDF 232–233)]` **[F]**

### 14.7 DAR (development-accelerator-releasing) couplers

**Era: 1995.** "DAR coupler molecules react with oxidation products of developing agents to produce **dye molecules and development accelerator molecules in the vicinity of a developing grain**, and provide **high sensitivity at the expense of graininess**." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.224 (PDF 233)]` **[M]**

The DAR is the exact sign-inverse of the DIR: same reaction topology, opposite local effect, opposite trade. Dated by refs. H. Kobayashi and K. Mihayashi, SPSE Annual Conference, Atlantic City, May 1985; and J. R. Jarvis and P. J. Twist, "The Effect of Development Accelerator Releasing Coupler on Color Negative Imaging Efficiency", International East-West Symposium II, 1988. `[Tani 1995, refs. 82–83, pp.226–227 (PDF 235–236)]` **[F]**

**[E]** DIR and DAR together map onto Anderson's coupling constant `c` (§13.6) with opposite signs — DIR is a designed `c < 1`, DAR a designed `c > 1` — and the trade-off signs match Anderson's family exactly: `c < 1` improves graininess and sharpness at the cost of sensitivity and gamma (DIR); `c > 1` raises sensitivity and gamma at the cost of graininess and sharpness (DAR). The sources never make this identification; it follows from their two statements placed side by side. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.222–224 (PDF 231–233), Fig. 7.14]`

### 14.8 Polymeric and diffusible-dye-forming couplers

**Era: 1995.** Two further coupler strategies aimed at the same dye-cloud-size objective as DIR, but geometrically rather than chemically:

- **Polymeric couplers** — "coupler molecules are combined with a polymer chain, made it possible to put **many coupler molecules in a small volume** and to form a **fine dye cloud**." Dated by ref. L. K. J. Tong, in James (1977), pp. 339–353. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.224 (PDF 233), ref. 84]` **[M]**
- **Diffusible-dye-forming couplers** — "could improve graininess by adjusting the **diffusibility of dye molecules**, and thus the **shape of the absorption spectra of dye clouds**." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.224 (PDF 233)]` **[M]**

**[E]** That last clause is a coupling that matters for any colour model: **dye diffusibility changes the absorption spectrum shape of a dye cloud.** Unwanted-absorption behaviour and lateral dye diffusion are therefore not independent knobs in a real stock — trading dye mobility for granularity also moves the effective spectral shape. The source states the coupling; it gives no spectra and no magnitude.

### 14.9 Interlayers

**Era: 1966.** The 1966 source names two non-imaging interlayers and states their function:

- The **yellow filter layer** between the blue-sensitive layer and the green-sensitive layer, "usually yellow colloidal silver but may be an organic layer", whose function is to protect the lower layers from blue light to which they remain sensitive by virtue of their natural sensitivity. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.195–196 (PDF 201–202), Figs. 10.1, 10.2]` **[F]**
- The **spacer layer** in the Polacolor receptor, between the dye-receiving layer and the alkali-neutralizing layer: alkali eventually seeps through the spacer, reacts with the acid reagent, producing water below the spacer which "will immediately open up the spacer layer enabling rapid neutralization" — a timed chemical shutter that stops the process and locks the dyes, and also "prevents any subsequent deterioration of the colour images due to alkaline oxidation in the print." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.208–210 (PDF 214–216), Figs. 10.19, 10.20]` **[F]**

Filter and interlayer thickness: **1–3 µm dry**, as for all colour layers. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` **[Q]**

**The 1966 source does not discuss non-filter interlayers or any interlayer function of the interimage kind** — no scavenger layers, no oxidized-developer scavengers, no anti-interimage barriers. The 1995 source states the layer count (~14) and the blue/green/red × three-speed-sublayer topology but "the identity and function of the remaining layers are never enumerated." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.189–215 (PDF 195–221); Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]` **[F]**

### 14.10 Masking as a layer-interaction tool

Masking is treated in full in §19.9 because it is a colour-reproduction mechanism, but it belongs here too because one masking route is explicitly a *cross-layer* speed rebalance rather than an in-layer chemical correction:

"There is a yellow filter layer in the negative and provided the sensitivities of the print layers are balanced (**the blue layer of the print material will have to be relatively faster or the exposing light give higher blue intensity**), the unwanted imagewise blue absorption will be completely removed." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.213 (PDF 219)]` **[F]**

That is a genuine interimage correction implemented in the *print* material's layer balance rather than in the negative's chemistry, and the 1966 source presents it as an alternative to the coloured-coupler route.

### 14.11 Absence inventory for this section

Stated explicitly so that a reader does not search for what is not here:

1. **No interimage gammas.** No layer-to-layer gamma coupling coefficients. **[F]**
2. **No cross-layer coupling matrices** (no CMY or RGB interimage matrix, no 3×3 of any kind). **[F]**
3. **No quantified interlayer effect magnitudes** for any real film. **[F]**
4. **No DIR inhibitor diffusion length**, no dye-cloud diameters, no measured DIR gamma or speed cost. **[F]**
5. **No measured knife-edge profiles**, within-layer or cross-layer. **[F]**
6. **No colour crossover data** — the term "colour crossover" does not appear in the 1966 source at all; the nearest content is layer-curve matching (§19.10). **[F]**
7. **No scavenger-layer or barrier-layer discussion.** **[F]**
8. The 1922 and 1929 sources predate multilayer colour entirely as a subject; neither contains any interimage content. Their multilayer content is confined to **"double coated (nonhalation)"** plate constructions, which the 1922 source treats as a *product class* (charts 21–23, 53–60, 67–68) with no discussion of interaction between the two coatings. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.34 (PDF 35)]` **[F]**

### 14.12 Engineering conclusion on interimage effects

**[E]** The material licenses exactly this much: interimage effects exist, are mediated by the same released-by-product diffusion as within-layer adjacency, act in the *inhibitory* direction for released halide and DIR inhibitors and in the *accelerating* direction for DAR accelerators, and trade sensitivity and gamma against graininess and sharpness with the signs Anderson's family gives. The vertical geometry within which they act is ~20 µm total, 1–3 µm per layer. **Every magnitude — coupling strength, spatial extent, gamma change, speed change — is missing from this material and must come from elsewhere.** The pointer the 1995 source itself gives for quantitative adjacency work is Kriss, in James (1977), Chapter 21. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230), ref. 68; §8.1.2, p.234 (PDF 243); Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159); Ch. X, p.203 (PDF 209)]`
