## 15. Sensitometry: definitions, and how they changed between eras

### 15.1 The four eras in this section, and what each source actually is

| Era tag | Source | What it is for sensitometry |
|---|---|---|
| **1922** | Raymond Davis and F. M. Walters, jr., "Sensitometry of Photographic Emulsions and a Survey of the Characteristics of Plates and Films of American Manufacture," **B. S. Sci. Pap. No. 439**, *Scientific Papers of the Bureau of Standards*, **Vol. 18** | The complete period definition set (density, opacity, transmission, exposure, characteristic curve, gamma, inertia, speed, scale, latitude, fog, resolution), the apparatus that produced the numbers, and a survey of 86 real American plates and films |
| **1929** | E. J. Wall, *Photographic Emulsions* | Factory sensitometric *practice*: H&D speed, gamma-infinity, the velocity constant K, and the fog reading, used as four routine acceptance numbers. No definitions, no curves |
| **1966** | G. F. Duffin, *Photographic Emulsion Chemistry* | Curve *shape* derived from grain populations; solarization; activation energies of development; explicitly defers development itself to another volume |
| **1995** | T. Tani, *Photographic Sensitivity: Theory and Mechanisms* | γ appears only inside the DQE definition; sensitivity↔resolving-power law; DQE loss budget. No characteristic-curve parameter values at all |

**Dating caveat on the 1922 source.** No publication year is printed anywhere in the document. The closing dateline is "WASHINGTON, September 6, 1921" `[Davis & Walters, B.S. Sci. Pap. 439, p.120 (PDF 121), final line]`; the measurements are earlier still — "In the spring of 1920 there was made for the information of the Government a confidential survey…" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.2 (PDF 3), §I.1]`; the GPO signature marks in the gutter read `90002°-22-2` … `90002°-22-8` (PDF 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112), whose "-22-" element is the printer's year-of-printing field, i.e. 1922. **The content should be dated 1920–1921; "1922" is a printing-mark inference, not a stated publication year.** Throughout this document the source is cited as "Davis & Walters 1922" for consistency with the printing marks. **[F]**

Printed-page ↔ PDF-page offset for the 1922 source: **printed page = PDF page − 1**, verified at PDF 14→13, 36→35, 96→95, 121→120. Several printed folios are OCR digit-reversed (PDF 62 shows "19" for 61; PDF 90 shows "68" for 89; PDF 107 shows "901" for 106) — artefacts, not real numbering. **[F]**

The 1922 paper's own three-part structure, from the title page: "Part 1 is a discussion of the general characteristics of photographic emulsions; part 2 describes the apparatus and conditions of testing as practiced at this Bureau; and part 3 gives data on practically all brands of emulsions (made in the United States) coated on glass and celluloid, **the trade names of the emulsions being omitted**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, title page (PDF 2)]` **[F]**

---

### 15.2 Density, opacity, transmission — 1922, verbatim

> "This definition is 'Density is equal to the common logarithm of the opacity.' Opacity is defined as the reciprocal of the transmission; and transmission, in turn, is defined as the ratio of the transmitted to the incident light. Thus if a portion of a negative transmits one-tenth of the light falling on it, its opacity is 10; and since the common logarithm of 10 is 1, its density is 1."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.8 (PDF 9), §I.4]` **[Q]**

Additivity of transmission in series, stated: "If a plate which transmits one-half be placed in front of a plate which transmits one-tenth the transmission of the two will be one-half of one-tenth, or one-twentieth." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.8 (PDF 9)]` **[Q]**

**TABLE 1.—Values of the Opacities and Densities for Certain Values of the Transmission** `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.8 (PDF 9), Table 1]` **[Q]**

| Transmission | Opacity | Density |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 1/2 | 2 | .3 |
| 1/10 | 10 | 1.0 |
| 1/20 | 20 | 1.3 |
| 1/100 | 100 | 2.0 |
| 1/1000 | 1000 | 3.0 |
| 1/10000 | 10000 | 4.0 |

*OCR damage flag:* the right-hand half of this table arrives as the raw run `100 / 1000 / 3.0 / 2.0 / 3.0 / 10000 / 4.0` — the values 2.0 and 3.0 are transposed/duplicated in the OCR stream. The reconstruction above is **forced by the definition** (log 100 = 2), i.e. repaired by arithmetic, not read from the page. **[F]**

---

### 15.3 Exposure and its unit — 1922

> "The term exposure is here understood to mean the product of the intensity of light by the time of exposure. This product, while not exactly constant, may be so regarded when the variation in the factors is less than, say, a thousand."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.8 (PDF 9)]` **[Q]**

The unit throughout is **candle-meter-seconds (c.m.s.)** — the chart abscissae read "LOG E C.M.S." and Table 2's footnote a reads "Candle meter-seconds". `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.9 (PDF 10), Table 2 fn.a]` **[F]**

Exposure steps are geometric: "Usually the exposures are proportional to 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64…" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.8 (PDF 9)]` **[F]**

---

### 15.4 The characteristic curve, toe and shoulder — 1922, verbatim

> "This curve giving the relation between density and exposure is known as the 'characteristic curve' of the plate. It is also called the 'H & D' curve after Hurter and Driffield, who were the first to state the relation between density and exposure. The underexposure part (below log E = 8.9) is called the 'toe.' The overexposure region (above log E = 1.1) is sometimes referred to as the 'shoulder.'"
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.10 (PDF 11), §I.4, Fig. 6]` **[Q]**

The two numeric breakpoints (log E = 8.9 and log E = 1.1) are properties of **the specific illustrative curve of Table 3 / Fig. 6**, not general constants, and they are printed in the era's "+10" logarithm convention (see §15.14, item 3): log E = 8.9 means log₁₀E = −1.1; log E = 1.1 means log₁₀E = +1.1. **[E]**

The H&D law itself, quoted by the 1922 authors from the original:

> "In a theoretically perfect negative, the amounts of silver deposited in the various parts are proportional to the logarithms of the intensities of light proceeding from the corresponding parts of the object."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.11 (PDF 12), quoting Hurter & Driffield; the paper's fn.3 gives the reference as "Journal of the Society of Chem. Ind.; May, 1890"]` **[F]**

> "That the density of a negative is proportional to the quantity of silver reduced by the developer has been corroborated by many independent investigators."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.11 (PDF 12)]` **[F]**

The operational consequence: "…it follows that the time of exposure should be such as to give densities on the plate which lie on the straight-line portion of the density-exposure curve." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.10 (PDF 11)]` **[F]**

---

### 15.5 Gamma / contrast — 1922, verbatim

> "The straight-line part of the characteristic curve continues downward until it cuts the exposure axis, makes an angle a with it. The contrast is then defined as equal to the tangent of angle a. This is called gamma (y), so that **y = tan a**"
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.11 (PDF 12), §I.5]` **[Q]**

*OCR note:* the Greek γ is rendered "y" throughout the scan and α as "a". The equation is **γ = tan α**, α being the angle between the extended straight-line portion and the log-E axis. Because both D and log E are dimensionless, this is identical in content to the modern γ = ΔD / Δ(log₁₀E). **[F]**

The 1922 interpretation of gamma values, verbatim:

> "Thus a gamma of I means that the ratio of the densities in the negative is the same as the corresponding ratio of the logarithms of the intensity of light coming from the subject… A gamma of 2 means that the plate shows twice the contrast of the subject, and a gamma of 0.5 means that the plate shows only half the contrast of the subject."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.11–12 (PDF 12–13)]` **[F]**

"Contrast" in the 1922 paper is used **strictly** as a synonym for gamma, never for a subjective or macro-contrast notion. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.11 (PDF 12)]` **[F]**

The period's own target-gamma commentary, which dates the practice:

> "The statement is sometimes made that all negatives should be developed to give unit contrast… most of the papers in use have gammas greater than I when developed to give the proper tone, so that negatives are developed not to unit contrast, but to a less contrast."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.12 (PDF 13)]` **[F]**

---

### 15.6 Inertia, and speed as its reciprocal — 1922, verbatim

> "It is observed in Fig. 7 that if the straight line portion of each development curve be continued until it cuts the exposure axis, all lines cut the axis in the same place. The value of the exposure at this point is called the 'inertia' of the plate. The faster a plate, the shorter the minimum time required to give an image, and hence the less its inertia. However, one's idea of speed is such that the greater the speed, the larger must be the number representing it, so that to indicate speed the reciprocal of the inertia is taken. This was Hurter's original idea, but to fit an actinometer of his design, he took **34/i** (34 divided by the inertia) which is the usual H & D number, as his measure of speed. The Bureau of Standards, however, has chosen **10/i** as its definition of speed."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14), §I.6]` **[Q]**

Two footnotes on the same page carry load-bearing qualifications:

- fn.4: "This always occurs, provided there is no free bromide in the plate or in the developer and that the plate does not fog badly." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14), fn.4]` — i.e. the common-inertia property that makes inertia a valid speed anchor **fails in the presence of bromide** (see §16.7). **[F]**
- fn.5: "The number 1/i would have been more logical, but 10/i was chosen so that all usual speed numbers might be represented by integers and the confusion of fractions be avoided." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14), fn.5]` **[F]**

Worked inertia reduction from the paper's own Fig. 7 `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14)]`:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| log i (printed, +10 convention) | 8.56 |
| log₁₀ i (modern) | −1.44 |
| i | 0.0363 candle-meter-seconds |
| 1/i | 27.5 |
| B.S. speed (10/i) | 275 |

*OCR / typographic damage flag:* the printed text reads "The reciprocal of 0.363 is equal to 27.5". **The number 0.363 is wrong by a factor of ten** — 1/0.0363 = 27.55, and 1/0.363 = 2.75. Raw string quoted: `The reciprocal of 0.363 is equal to 27.5`. The inertia is 0.0363 c.m.s. **[F]**

A second worked pair, from the unlabelled two-plate table beside Fig. 9. Raw OCR run: `I 0.0363 / Log i / i / 1/i / Bureau of Standards's speed / 8.42 8.77 / 0.0263 0589 / 38.0 17.0 / 380 170`. De-interleaved `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14)]`:

| Plate | Log i (printed) | i (c.m.s.) | 1/i | B.S. speed (10/i) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fig. 9, left | 8.42 | 0.0263 | 38.0 | 380 |
| Fig. 9, right | 8.77 | .0589 *(raw "0589")* | 17.0 | 170 |

Both check arithmetically: 10^(8.42−10) = 0.0263 and 10^(8.77−10) = 0.0589. **[Q]**

---

### 15.7 Scale and latitude — 1922, verbatim, and the authors' own warning

> "By scale is understood the range of light intensity that a plate is able to record correctly. **Latitude** is the variation which it is possible to make in the time of exposure and still retain a correct representation of the subject."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.13–14 (PDF 14–15), §I.7]` **[F]**

> "The scale is measured by the projection on the exposure axis of the straight-line part of the characteristic curve. The difference of the logarithms of the two extremes is taken, and the number corresponding is the scale."
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.14 (PDF 15)]` **[Q]**

That is: **Scale = 10^(Δ log E over the straight line)** — a plain intensity ratio, not a log range. Worked examples from Fig. 9, in the +10 convention `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.14 (PDF 15)]`:

- "0.90 − 8.78 = 2.12 = log of 132 for the first plate." (10.90 − 8.78 = 2.12; 10^2.12 = 131.8 ✓)
- "0.43 − 9.41 = 1.02 = log of 10.4 for the second plate." (10.43 − 9.41 = 1.02; 10^1.02 = 10.47 ✓)

**Internal inconsistency in the source:** the running prose says the right-hand plate "has a scale of **10.5**" while the equation on the same page yields "**10.4**". Both are recorded; neither is corrected. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.14 (PDF 15)]` **[F]**

Worked latitude: "If, however, the subject had an intensity range of 1 to 33, the plate [scale 132] would have a **latitude of 4** for such a subject; so that if I second were the shortest correct exposure, 4 seconds could be given and the plate would still show a correct tone representation." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.14 (PDF 15)]` — i.e. latitude = scale ÷ subject intensity range = 132/33 = 4. **[Q]**

The authors themselves flag the terminological clash with other writers of the period, in a footnote on their second page: "By some writers termed 'latitude.' As used in this article see definition, p. 13." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.2 (PDF 3), fn.1]` **[F]**

---

### 15.8 Fog — 1922, verbatim, and why it is plotted against gamma

> "It is well known that the density of chemical fog increases with the time of development and accordingly with the increase of contrast… Since the photographer must develop a plate to a certain contrast, what he wants to know is whether one plate fogs worse than another in being developed to a given contrast. **For this reason chemical fog in this work is plotted against the contrast (gamma) and not against the time of development.**"
`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32), §II.9]` **[F]**

The quantity plotted is "the values of the fog (exclusive of glass and gelatin)". `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.32 (PDF 33), §III.1]` — i.e. **1922 "fog" means chemical (development) fog only**; base density and safelight/age fog are outside the definition. **[F]**

The 1929 factory practice reduces fog to a single acceptance number read at a fixed development time: Wall's slow sulphite emulsion "gave a speed of 22 H. & D. with high gamma infinity, the fog reading with ten minutes development with the standard pyro-soda developer being only **0.1**." `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]` **[Q]**

---

### 15.9 Threshold — the 1922 paper does not use the term

**The word "threshold" does not appear in the 1922 paper.** What stands in its place is (a) the criticised "just visible image" speed method, quoted in full in §15.13, and (b) a statement of an induction period: "There is a certain period before the deposit of silver becomes visible" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.11 (PDF 12)]`. Neither is a numeric threshold criterion. **[M]**

Also absent: any fixed-density speed criterion of the modern type. The 1922 paper contains **no exposure index in the modern sense and no 0.10-above-Dmin style speed point**; speed is an extrapolated-intercept quantity (§15.6). `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.13–15 (PDF 14–16)]` **[F]**

For the 1995 era the same absence holds from the other direction: "ISO 100" and "ISO sensitivity" are used as labels and "ASA" as a figure axis unit, but **the ISO standard's speed point, its 0.10-above-Dmin criterion, and any ISO↔physical-quantity conversion are never given** in Tani. `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20); §1.4, p.19 (PDF 28)]` **[F]**

---

### 15.10 Gamma-infinity and the development constant K — a 1929 vocabulary; absent from 1922

**Gamma-infinity does not exist in the 1922 paper.** The term "gamma infinity", the symbol γ∞, and any limiting-contrast parameter are absent. The nearest statements are qualitative: "after a certain time the negative gains very little in contrast by further increasing the time of development" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.12 (PDF 13)]` and "12 minutes' development with tray-strength developer marks the time limit of practical development" `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.32 (PDF 33)]`. **No γ∞ value and no development-rate constant of any kind appears in the 1922 paper.** **[M]**

**By 1929 the two quantities are routine factory acceptance numbers, used without definition.** Wall's works test: "these were tested by the **standard Hurter and Driffield method**, and this gave a record as to whether the emulsion was up to **standard speed, gamma infinity, K and fog reading**." `[Wall 1929, Ch. I, p.8 (PDF 16)]` — four numbers per batch: H&D speed, γ∞, the development velocity constant K, and the fog reading. **Wall never defines γ∞ or K, gives no formula relating γ to development time, and reproduces no H&D curve anywhere in the book.** **[F]**

Every numeric γ∞ / speed / fog value in the 1929 source, collected:

| Emulsion / context | Speed (H&D) | Gamma / γ∞ | Fog | Developer & time | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Beginner's target, "slow negative emulsions" | **150–200 H&D** | — | — | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.30 (PDF 38)]` |
| Wall's slow sulphite emulsion (0.25 Na₂SO₃ : 100 AgNO₃; 1 h at 43 °C then 2 h at 27 °C) | **22 H&D** | "high gamma infinity" | **0.1** | standard pyro-soda, **10 minutes** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]` |
| Harris fast-ammonia formula (*Amer. Ann. Phot.* 1916) | "said to give a speed of **225 H. & D.**" | — | — | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. XIII, p.225 (PDF 232)]` |
| Wall's worked mixing example, fast component | **250 H&D** | **γ∞ = 1.3** | — | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. VII, p.135 (PDF 142)]` |
| Wall's worked mixing example, slow component | **25 H&D** | **γ = 3** | — | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. VII, p.135 (PDF 142)]` |
| "Fast-ammonia process (X)", 3 × 20 h ammonia digestions at 32 °C | "fast but foggy" | **low gamma infinity** | high | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. XIII, p.226 (PDF 233)]` |
| Acid-boiled formulas generally | — | "**rather a low gamma infinity**" — suits portraiture, less so ordinary work | — | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.56 (PDF 64)]` |
| Positive cine emulsion requirement | — | **high γ∞** *and* **high velocity constant**, plus freedom from fog | — | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 92)]` |
| Negative cine emulsion requirement | — | "not such a high gamma… essential" | — | — | `[Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.85 (PDF 92)]` |

**[Q]**

Wall's own worked non-additivity result is worth recording as a period fact about γ∞: given "an emulsion of 250 H. & D., with a gamma infinity of 1.3, and a slower emulsion of 25 H. & D., with a gamma of 3, will a mixture of the two in equal volumes give a speed of 137 and a gamma of 2.15? **The answer is in the negative**; at least, that is the writer's experience. That there is an improvement by the admixture of the slower emulsion cannot be denied, but the result is not the mean." `[Wall 1929, Ch. VII, p.135 (PDF 142)]` **[Q]**

**1966 and 1995 give no γ∞ either.** Duffin excludes development explicitly — "**Development**, the very important step which greatly affects the response of the silver-halide emulsion, **is not being discussed in detail in the present work**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.217 (PDF 223)]` — and no γ-vs-time or D-vs-time equation appears anywhere in the book. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX (PDF 177–194)]` Tani gives γ only as a symbol inside the DQE definition, with no value for any stock. `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25), Eq. (1.1)]` **[F]**

**Source disagreement to preserve, not average:** the 1922 Bureau paper deliberately reports *no* limiting-contrast parameter and treats development time as the independent variable to be plotted; the 1929 factory treats γ∞ and K as the primary emulsion descriptors and the D–log E curve as a means to them. These are two incompatible reduction schemes for the same measurement, seven years apart, and no source in this set reconciles them. **[E]**

---

### 15.11 The apparatus and conditions that give the 1922 numbers their meaning

Every 1922 number in §16 is conditional on the following. Change any of it and the numbers are not comparable.

#### 15.11.1 Light source and its colour quality

- Reference illuminant, verbatim: "…it was decided to reproduce in color **average yearly noon sunlight at the latitude of Washington** as the source of energy for the sensitometry of photographic materials." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.17–18 (PDF 18–19), §II.1]` **[F]**
- **No colour temperature, in kelvin or any other unit, is stated anywhere in the paper.** The illuminant is specified only by that verbal description plus the lamp-and-filter recipe below. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.17–18 (PDF 18–19)]` **[F]**
- Intensity at the plate: "In accordance with Hurter and Driffield, this is taken as **I candle meter (visual)**; that is, the light at the plate shall be equal in intensity to that of a source of i candlepower at a distance of 1 m." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.17 (PDF 18)]` **[Q]**
- Source brightness window: "The intrinsic brilliancy of the source should lie between **1 and 4 candlepower**…" — below 1 cp the working distance becomes too short for uniformity, above 4 cp the apparatus becomes cumbersome. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.17–18 (PDF 18–19)]` **[Q]**
- Lamp: "…adoption as a source of **6 to 8 volt Mazda C automobile headlight, operating on approximately 2.4 amperes**. A **Brooks's deflection potentiometer** is used in order to regulate the current accurately." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.18 (PDF 19)]` **[Q]**
- Colour correction: standardised by the Bureau's colorimetry section using "a **special blue glass filter**" so the light "closely approximat[es] the color of average noon sunlight"; visual candlepower and filter transmission were measured by the photometric section. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.18 (PDF 19)]` **[F]**
- Photometric chain, with numbers: **lamps without filter average 15 candlepower; filter transmission 18.2 per cent; average intensity of lamps seen through the filter 2.73 candlepower** (15 × 0.182 = 2.73 ✓). `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.18 (PDF 19)]` **[Q]**

#### 15.11.2 Sensitometer

Type: **rotating sector disk**, Davis's own design, covered by **patent No. 1,382,272, dedicated to the public**. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.18–22 (PDF 19–23), §II.2, Figs. 12–15]` **[F]**

- Disk: "contains **nine apertures**, the angle of each being **twice as great as the preceding** and having a radial length of **one-half inch**. The disk is **about 18 inches in diameter**, being twice the usual size in order to give greater accuracy of the small angles." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.18 (PDF 19)]` — nine steps at ratio 2, total range **512 : 1** across a strip. **[Q]**
- Drive: **1/8 hp shunt motor**, "speed control continuously from 0 to 1700 rpm", storage-battery supply; wheel timing checked against a **seconds pendulum clock** through telephone receivers and a chronograph. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.21 (PDF 22)]` **[Q]**
- The wheel sets both the graduated and the total exposure: "This sensitometer is distinctive in that the sector wheel gives not only the graduated exposure, but the total exposure as well," via an escapement timing device and an electrically operated shutter. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.21–22 (PDF 22–23)]` **[F]**
- Test strips: **1 1/8 by 5 inches**, three displayed radially, slid "up to within **2 mm** of the back of the sector wheel". `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.22 (PDF 23)]` **[Q]**

**TABLE 4.—Aperture Calibration in Fractions of 360°** `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.18 (PDF 19), Table 4]` **[Q]**

| Intended aperture | Actual aperture | Per cent error |
|---|---|---|
| 0.001953 | 0.00183 | −6.3 |
| .003906 | .00393 | +.6 |
| .007812 | .00770 | −1.4 |
| .015625 | .01553 | −.6 |
| .03125 | .03104 | −.7 |
| .0625 | .06238 | −0.2 |
| .125 | .1222 | −2.2 |
| .25 | .2502 | +.1 |
| .50 | .4997 | −.06 |

*OCR damage flag:* the two halves of this table are interleaved in the text stream. Raw run: `0.001953 0.00183 -6.3 / 0.0625 0.06238 / 003906 00393 +.6 / .125 1222 -0.2 / 007812 00770 -1.4 / .25 .2502 -2.2 / 015625 .01553 .6 / .50 .4997 +.1 / .03125 .03104 7 / -.06`. The de-interleaving above was validated by recomputing each per-cent error from its intended/actual pair — all nine agree. **Signs on rows 4, 5 and in the last column are inferred; minus signs were dropped by the OCR.** **[F]**

Standard run conditions actually used for the survey: **16 revolutions of the disk at 1 revolution per second, 16 s total exposure, 1 candle meter at the plate**, the nine squares receiving **8, 4, 2, 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 seconds**. "In case the 16 seconds' exposure did not include all of the toe and shoulder of the curve, shorter or longer exposures were made." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32), §III.1]` **[Q]**

Check on internal consistency: 0.4997 × 16 s = 8.0 s for the largest step; 0.00183 × 16 s = 0.029 s ≈ 1/32 s for the smallest. **[E]**

Intermittency, quantified as negligible: "…100 exposures of one-tenth second are not equivalent to a single exposure of 10 seconds. Tests showed this effect to be inappreciable (**not more than a few per cent and considerably less than the variation due to coating**) under the conditions used, namely, the number of revolutions of the disk **16**, the intensity of the light **I candle meter visual**, and comparatively slow rate of the wheel of **I revolution per second**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.22 (PDF 23), §II.2]` **[Q]**

**All plates in the sensitometric work were backed with black shellac** (lampblack in alcoholic shellac) to suppress halation. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32), §II.8]` — so every published curve, scale and speed is a **halation-suppressed** measurement, even for commercial plates sold unbacked. **[F]**

`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.33 (PDF 34), §III.1 "DEVELOPER FORMULAS"]` — "These are as recommended by different plate manufacturers." **[Q]**

All four are **pyro (pyrogallol) three-solution developers**. None contains bromide as a standing ingredient; bromide is treated separately (§16.7). **No metol or hydroquinone formula is given**, though metol is named in the bromide discussion. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.33 (PDF 34); p.15 (PDF 16)]` **[F]**

The 1929 source's works test developer is "standard **pyro-soda**", used for 10 minutes, and **its composition is never given**. `[Wall 1929, Ch. II, p.24 (PDF 32)]` **[F]**

#### 15.11.4 Development of the test plates

- Vessels: "**silver-plated cans** placed in a **water bath**, the temperature of which is kept constant by a **thermostat regulator** which controls the heating units through a relay." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.22 (PDF 23), §II.3, Fig. 16]` **[F]**
- Agitation: "The test plates are put in **silver cages, each holding four**, and stirred in the developer by **rotating the cages at 40 revolutions per minute**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.22 (PDF 23)]` **[Q]**
- **The full standard condition: pyro of tray strength (1+1+1+7), 20 °C, development times 3, 6 and 12 minutes, stirring 40 rpm.** Which of W/X/Y/Z was used is stated per chart. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32), §III.1]` **[Q]**
- Each published curve is "the **graphical mean of the density measurements of three test strips**". `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[Q]**
- Agitation sensitivity, quantified once: "By proper rocking, the time of development may be cut in half of that required for no motion of the developer." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17), §I.10]` **[Q]**
- Explicit transfer warning: "With different developers, or the same developer at a different temperature, a change in the time of development as indicated on these charts would be required for a given contrast." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[F]**

#### 15.11.5 Densitometer

- "The photometer used for measuring the density of the test strips is a **Martens polarization instrument**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.22–23 (PDF 23–24), §II.4, Fig. 17]` **[F]**
- **The measurement is differential against a fog strip**, and this is the single most load-bearing methodological fact in the paper: "One beam of light passes through the square a, the density of which is to be measured, while the other beam passes through the fog strip b. By this means, the effect of the density of the glass and gelatin and also of chemical fog is automatically eliminated, **so that the measured density is due solely to the exposure**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.22–23 (PDF 23–24), §II.4]` **[Q]**
- Illumination geometry: diffuse, "reflected from ground surface opal glass g, surrounded by ground glass o, o, outside of which are placed electric lamps (L, L) symmetrically arranged so as to give uniform illumination." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.23 (PDF 24)]` **[F]**
- "The angular readings of the polarization instrument are reduced to densities by means of a **table computed for the purpose**." **That table is not reproduced in the paper.** `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.23 (PDF 24)]` **[F]**
- Physical layout of the measured object, Fig. 18: "Test strip (slightly reduced) showing the nine densities due to exposure and the fog strip." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.27 (PDF 28), Fig. 18]` **[F]**
- **Visual-vs-photographic density caveat, verbatim:** "It may be remarked that densities measured visually do not represent photographic densities… The plates measured in this work are neutral in color, although developed with pyro, and the only results which may be affected materially by the difference between visual and photographic density are the values of the contrast, but in that case they still give reliable comparative data." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.23 (PDF 24)]` **[F]**

The 1929 source's only stated requirement on apparatus: "Accurate testing methods by the **sector wheel or neutral wedge**, with photometric readings of both plates and papers, are essential… only if… one single factor be varied in the next experiment." `[Wall 1929, Preface p.vi (PDF 6)]` **[F]**

#### 15.11.6 Spectrograph (colour sensitivity)

- Source: **100-watt tungsten lamp**, brightness held by rheostat at constant filament current; white reflector; ground glass; **slit 2 inches high**. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.24–25 (PDF 25–26), §II.5, Fig. 19]` **[Q]**
- Exposure wedge along the slit, from a rotating disk with variable aperture: "the exposure at the first line from the bottom is **one-quarter** that at the bottom; at the second line, **one-sixteenth**; at the third, **one sixty-fourth**; at the fourth, **one two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth**; and at the top, **one one-thousand-and-twenty-fourth**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.24 (PDF 25)]` — geometric ratio 1/4 per reference line, i.e. E(line n) = E_bottom × 4^(−n), n = 1…5. **[Q]**
- Optics: photographic lens → **replica of a diffraction grating** → "normal spectrum"; a screen bearing intensity and wavelength reference lines just in front of the plate; the red end of the plate "stained with a yellow filter dye to screen out the second order violet light". `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.24–25 (PDF 25–26)]` **[F]**
- **Colour-quality warning, load-bearing:** "The tungsten lamp is used without any correcting screen… the spectrograms do not represent rigorously the spectral sensitiveness of the plates to average noon sunlight, but rather to a light which is **deficient in the violet and blue**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.25 (PDF 26)]` **[F]**
- Wavelength axis: "The numbers give the wave length of the light in **millionths of a millimeter**" (mµ, i.e. nm), with ticks at 400, 500, 600. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.6 (PDF 7), Figs. 1–3]` **[F]**
- **Reproduction warning on the published spectrograms:** "the spectrograms on these charts are not in all instances true copies of the spectrograms on the original charts. The method of reproduction, zinc etching, is not well adapted to reproduce half tones… In some cases (the orthochromatic plates and films in particular), the sensitiveness in the yellow green is entirely lost. It is, therefore, advisable to judge the color sensitiveness by the filter factors only. **The charts without filter-factor data are blue sensitive only**, or so slightly color sensitive as to be of no practical value in this respect." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.34 (PDF 35), §III.2]` **[F]**

#### 15.11.7 Filter-factor apparatus

- Definition, verbatim: "A filter factor is the **ratio of exposure time required with a given filter to the exposure without a filter**; hence, to obtain the proper time of exposure when using a filter, the correct exposure time required without a filter must be multiplied by the filter factor in order to get an equivalent negative." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.25 (PDF 26), §II.6]` **[Q]**
- Method: two beams from a **standard metal filament lamp**, four mirrors plus two prisms, side by side on the test plate; the filter is inserted in one path and balance restored by moving the lamp; the inverse-square law gives the ratio — "the ratio by which the filter cuts down the intensity of the light is equal to the **square of the length of the path containing the filter divided by the square of the length of the other path**. The filter factor is the inverse of this ratio." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.25 (PDF 26)]` **[Q]**
- Geometry and range: **two paths each 1 m when balanced without a filter; lamp movement about 69 cm; measurable factor range 1 to 30**; filters must exceed 1/2 inch square; strips 1 1/8 by 5 inches, two filter factors per strip. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.25–26 (PDF 26–27)]` **[Q]**
- "The combination of lamp and filter is identical with that used as the standard source of this Bureau's sensitometer." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.26 (PDF 27)]` — so the factors are **sunlight-matched, i.e. outdoor factors**, not tungsten factors. **[F]**
- Chart convention: "The filters referred to by **letter are Wratten** filters. Those referred to by **name are Cramer** filters. In some cases where the value of the filter factor is **greater than 30 it has been omitted**." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.32 (PDF 33)]` — this explains the blanks in the survey tables of §16.13. **[F]**
- Validation: Fig. 21, "Photographs taken with and without filters. The exposure times with filters were adjusted according to the measured factors" — eight exposures on two plates developed together and printed on one sheet; "Had the negatives not been practically equal, it would not have been possible to secure prints of equal depth." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.28 (PDF 29), Fig. 21]` **[F]**
- **There is no filter transmission-vs-wavelength data anywhere in the paper.** The single transmission figure in the whole document is the sensitometer's own compensating filter at **18.2 per cent** visual transmission. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.18 (PDF 19)]` **[F]**

The eight Wratten filters, with the paper's own descriptions `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.7 (PDF 8), Fig. 4]`:

| Wratten | Name / description as printed | Effect noted |
|---|---|---|
| (none) | No Filter | — |
| **K₁** | Light Yellow | "Cuts down violet" |
| **K₂** | Medium Yellow | "Cuts down blue" |
| **K₃** | Deep Yellow | "Cuts … blue" *(OCR truncated)* |
| **G** | Orange | "Contrast filter" |
| **F** | Deep Red | "Contrast filter to photograph red as white" |
| **A** | Light Red | "for three color work" |
| **B** | Green | "for three color work" |
| **C** | Blue | "for three color work" |

*(The OCR interleaves these captions with the numbers 233, 242, 243, 244, 245, 246, 247, 248, 249 — laboratory negative numbers for the nine spectrogram strips of Fig. 4. The K₃ and G descriptions are truncated in the scan and are quoted as-is.)* **[F]**

"**Red filters can be used only with panchromatic plates**, while the others can be used on orthochromatic plates as well." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.5 (PDF 6), §I.3]` — this is why the orthochromatic charts carry only four Wratten factors. **[F]**

#### 15.11.8 Resolution apparatus

Full detail is in §18.1–18.2; the conditions in brief: **50 mm Zeiss Tessar at f/16**, test object of equal apertures and spaces back-illuminated, projected centre-to-centre spacings 0.012–0.030 mm, **development uniformly six minutes in pyro developer, tray strength**, examination at **100 to 300 diameters**, values the **mean of several observations by four different observers**. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–30 (PDF 30–31), §II.7, Fig. 22]` **[Q]**
