**Halation** — spread *via the support*: "A careful distinction must be made between irradiation and halation. Halation (which may be noticed in the 'halo' surrounding the image of a bright point of light against a dark background) is due to the **total reflection of light inside the glass or celluloid support**. The silver grains spread or diffuse the light in all directions. The light passes into the glass at all angles; that which strikes the second surface of the glass at less than the so-called critical angle of total reflection is largely transmitted, while that which strikes the second surface at an angle equal to or greater than the critical angle is all reflected back into the glass and its coating. It is this reflected light that causes the halo. **The size of the halo is determined by the thickness of the glass and its critical angle, which may be calculated from its refractive index.**" `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–30 (PDF 30–31), §II.8]` **[M]**

That last sentence is the closest any source in this set comes to a halation *model* — a geometric one, driven by support thickness and critical angle — **but no thickness, no refractive index, no critical angle and no halo radius is given for any material, and the calculation is never performed.** `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.30 (PDF 31)]` **[F]**

The 1922 remedies, verbatim: "Halation may be avoided by the use of **backed plates**, or by **surface development**. If the back surface of the glass plate is coated with a substance having practically the same index of refraction as glass, but containing light-absorbing materials, the light which would otherwise be reflected is absorbed, and halation thereby prevented. For this purpose **caramel containing burnt sienna or lampblack** is commonly used. A backing which dries quickly and which does not come off in the developer consists of **lampblack in alcoholic shellac**. All the plates used in the sensitometric work of this article were backed with the black shellac." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.30–31 (PDF 31–32), §II.8]` **[Q]** *(composition only; no optical density)*

And the film case: "Halation occurs in the same way with films, but since the **film support is thinner, the spreading is smaller**. A film is difficult to back for the purpose of preventing halation." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[M]**

**Note the methodological consequence, already flagged in §15.14 item 18: because every test plate was black-shellac backed, the 1922 resolution numbers are halation-suppressed values.** The irradiation and development-spread contributions remain in them; the halation contribution does not. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[E]**

### 18.4 Turbidity and light scatter in the emulsion layer — 1966 and 1995

The 1966 statement is the clearest in the set, and it contains a physics error that must be flagged:

> "Many modern emulsions are specifically designed to provide the highest possible definition or, to be more precise, **acutance**. One of the many means whereby the sharpness of a photographic image is decreased is by **scatter of the light by the emulsion grains, resulting in a spread of the image into adjacent areas**. The scattering of light is much higher at the blue end of the spectrum than at the red end, and is **proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength**."
`[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.164 (PDF 170)]` **[Q]**

**The printed exponent's sign is wrong.** Rayleigh scattering goes as λ⁻⁴, and the author's own preceding clause ("much higher at the blue end") requires the inverse power. Raw string as printed: `is pro- portional to the fourth power of the wavelength`. The words are intact in the scan, so this is a **book or typesetting error, not OCR damage**. **Use λ⁻⁴.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.164 (PDF 170)]` **[F]**

**[E]** With a λ⁻⁴ law, in-emulsion scatter at 400 nm is (700/400)⁴ ≈ **9.4×** that at 700 nm. That factor is our arithmetic from the corrected law; the source gives no scatter coefficient, no turbidity value and no point-spread width, so the factor describes only the *spectral ratio*, not any absolute spread.

The 1995 source gives the layer-level version of the same statement, coupled to absorption: "When the packing density is constant, the **fraction of incident light absorbed by the layers increases, and the image quality decreases with increasing thickness** of the layers." Tabular grains "increased [absorption] to a considerable degree when a high-speed color negative film was designed using tabular grains instead of conventional grains." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242)]` **[F]**

And the design constraint that follows: "A large number of fine and well-designed silver halide grains are **separately and randomly arranged in thin gelatin layers with a relatively low packing density to achieve fine imaging**. However, this arrangement prevents grains in these layers from absorbing incident light efficiently." `[Tani 1995, §1.2.2, p.9 (PDF 18)]` — thin layers and loose packing are the price of sharpness, paid in absorption and hence in speed. Table 1.1 of the same source lists "Short dynamic range" and "**Limited resolving power**" as explicit disadvantages of "Thin emulsion layers with many fine AgX grains". `[Tani 1995, Table 1.1, p.8 (PDF 17)]` **[F]**

A related 1995 datum on scatter in a *screen* rather than the emulsion, for contrast: an X-ray phosphor screen "benefits the above-mentioned system in having high sensitivity to X-rays, although it **deteriorates the resolving power of the system by scattering the emitted light**." `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.13 (PDF 22)]` **[F]**

**Neither 1966 nor 1995 gives a turbidity coefficient, a scattering cross-section, a point-spread function width, or an optical-density-per-micron figure for any emulsion layer.** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII (PDF 159–176); Tani 1995, §8.1 (PDF 237–245)]` **[F]**

### 18.5 Layer thickness and sharpness — the geometry numbers

These are the only physical lengths any source in this set supplies for a scattering or halation model.

| Quantity | Value | Era | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Emulsion layer at the coating point | **30–600 µ wet** | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` |
| Same layer after drying | **2–40 µ dry** | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` |
| Supercoats and filter layers | **1–3 µ dry** *(raw OCR reads "1-3 mu"; from context µ, not mµ)* | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` |
| Colour-material layers, each | "**all of them 1–3 µ thick in the dry state** and correspondingly thicker when wet" | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]` |
| Whole photosensitive pack, typical ISO 100 colour negative | "about **14 layers** with different functions and is about **20 µm thick in total**" | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12)]` |
| Relative thickness, colour vs X-ray | "The overall thickness of a modern **colour** film is **much less than that of a modern X-ray emulsion**" | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.202 (PDF 208)]` |
| Supercoat gelatin loading | "**10% or less of the amount of gelatin in the emulsion**" | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.166 (PDF 172)]` |
| Grain thickness (AgBr crystal) | **0.2–0.3 µ** | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.133 (PDF 139)]` |
| Support: glass plate thickness | **Not stated for any photographic plate.** Only "For the smaller size plates, also, **thinner glass is used**." The one quarter-inch figure in the book (6.35 mm, conv.) is a shop fixture, not a photographic plate | 1929 | `[Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.168 (PDF 175); Ch. XI, p.183 (PDF 190)]` |
| Support: optical properties of glass | **Absent.** "The book states no optical property of glass at all, and never mentions glass tint, greenness, base density, or transmission" | 1929 | `[Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.168 (PDF 175)]` |

**[Q]**

The thickness→sharpness link, stated three times across two eras:

- **1929, indirect:** coating thickness is judged optically against a lamp filament — for positive film "thickness must be such that the shape of the filament is entirely lost"; for negative film "the filament should be just discernible". `[Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.199 (PDF 206)]` **[F]**
- **1966, direct:** old plate practice at 300–400 g gelatin per gram-mole of silver "gives an emulsion layer which is **far too thick for present-day standards**; it would possess a slow rate of development, poor drying characteristics and **low sharpness**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.77 (PDF 83)]` **[F]**
- **1966, dated observation:** "This soluble-coupler process has been carried to a high level of perfection, for example in the latest **Kodachrome X**. The **sharpness is so good with the thinly-coated high-acutance films of today** that **8 mm movies can, at last, give acceptable definition**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.203 (PDF 209)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Combining the 1966 dry-thickness envelope with the 1995 pack thickness gives the working scale for any emulsion-side spread model in this set: a single black-and-white layer 2–40 µm, each colour layer 1–3 µm, a whole colour pack ~20 µm. Nothing in the set converts these lengths into a transfer function.

### 18.6 Acutance dyes — 1966, with the speed cost stated

The definition-by-use, verbatim: "Frequently, therefore, a dye, particularly a **yellow dye which absorbs blue light, tartrazine (18)** for example, is added to the emulsion to reduce the effects of this scatter. **Some speed loss must inevitably result** from the light absorbed by this addition, apart from any chemical desensitization which is always likely to occur. Nevertheless, many emulsions, **such as those used for aerial photography**, contain acutance dyes." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.164–165 (PDF 170–171)]` **[F]**

The 1966 book's most explicit statement of the sharpness↔speed trade, from the dye-bleach chapter: "High **tinctorial power** is obtainable in this system because the dyes are **molecularly dispersed** throughout the layer… This means that **only low coating weights of the dyes, and therefore of silver halide also, because the two must be in balanced chemical proportions, are needed, which means thin layers and high sharpness. This latter property is enhanced because the azo dyes function as fairly perfect acutance dyes, by reducing scatter in the emulsion layer of light in the wavelength region to which the emulsion is sensitive.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.207 (PDF 213)]` **[F]**

A consistent statement from the spectral-sensitization side: "**Only the dye adsorbed to the silver-halide grain is effective in conferring sensitivity** upon it… **Dye in the gelatin phase will only cause a filtering action** (see acutance dyes, Chapter 8) **and thus reduce speed in the region in which the dye absorbs light.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI (PDF 105–125)]` **[F]**

**[E]** These three passages together state a coupled (speed, sharpness) relation rather than two independent design choices: an in-layer absorber in the band the layer records buys MTF and costs speed, and via the dye:silver stoichiometric balance it also forces the layer thinner, which buys further sharpness and costs further absorption. **No source in this set quantifies the exchange rate — no stops per unit acutance-dye density, no MTF gain per unit optical density.**

**[F]** No acutance *measurement* appears in this set. "Acutance" is used in 1966 as a design goal and as the name of a dye class; there is no acutance formula, no measured acutance value, and no gradient-squared integral anywhere. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.164 (PDF 170); Ch. X, p.207 (PDF 213)]`

### 18.7 The 1929 antihalation practice — the era's treatment of the same physical problem

**Critical negative finding, stated first because it governs everything below: the 1929 source gives no quantitative statement of the magnitude, radius or spread of halation, and no figure for how much any remedy reduces it. There is no photometric halation datum in the book.** `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.83–84 (PDF 90–91); App., p.241 (PDF 248)]` **[F]**

The cause, as 1929 states it: "if the light could be prevented from penetrating right through the emulsion and glass there would be no halation" — i.e. halation is attributed to light traversing **emulsion and support** and returning, the same mechanism the 1922 paper describes geometrically. `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)]` **[M]**

The full 1929 remedy inventory:

| Measure | Statement | Class | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Backing the rear of the glass** | "The ordinary method of preventing halation is, of course, by coating the back of the glass with a non-actinic color; but this necessitates the handling of the coated plate, with possible chance of damaging the film of emulsion" | **[F]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)]` |
| **Backing formula, black, for panchromatic plates** | Yellow dextrin **80 g**; water **85 ccm**; heat till dissolved; mix in ivory sienna black **900 g**; phenol **15 g**. (The black is obtainable commercially as a water-ground paste.) | **[Q]** *(composition only; no optical density)* | `[Wall 1929, App., p.241 (PDF 248)]` |
| **Backing, ortho and ordinary plates** | "Use the same formula, but with **burnt sienna** ground in water" | **[Q]** | `[Wall 1929, App., p.241 (PDF 248)]` |
| **Desensitizing backing** | "Some commercial plates are backed with a thin layer containing desensitizing dyes, which diffuse into the developer, thus exerting their peculiar action. It is obvious that any of the desensitizing dyes may be used in this way." | **[F]** | `[Wall 1929, App., p.241 (PDF 248)]` |
| **Dyed subbing between glass and emulsion** | O. Magerstadt, Eng. Pat. 5,932/1893 — a preliminary gelatine coating stained with a non-actinic dye, **fuchsin** actually used; C. E. Pettit, Eng. Pat. 8,956/1893, the same idea. "Any acid red dye may be thus used, or a mixture of red and yellow dyes. **Acid dyes must be used… as they are more readily washed out of the gelatine.** Only a thin coating of the stained gelatine is required, **a five per cent solution being sufficient**." Candidate dyes: Congo red, carmine L, lanafuchsin SB, tolan red, with or without naphthol yellow or tartrazin | **[Q]** *(5 % dye-gelatine solution)* | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)]` |
| **Removability constraint on subbing dyes** | dyes that do not wash out "must be of such a nature as to be decolorized either by acid sulphite or other ready means, otherwise they would **seriously prolong the exposure in printing**" | **[F]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)]` |
| **Non-dye antihalation sub** | C. F. Oakley, Eng. Pat. 2,986/1895 — a **0.6 per cent solution of potassium permanganate in gelatine**, reduced in situ to "practically colloidal manganese hydroxide… an orange-brown color, that is very intense and **can not diffuse into the emulsion**"; removed by the ordinary acid fixing bath or by sodium bisulphite; "**it forms a better protection for panchromatic emulsions**" | **[Q]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]` |
| **Rationale for preferring a non-dye sub** | dyes "might lead to trouble because of partial **sensitizing or fogging action by diffusion into the emulsion layer**" | **[M]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.83–84 (PDF 90–91)]` |
| **Subbing applied to both sides of film** | "**Subbing is usually carried out on both sides of the film**, both to maintain flatness and also because the film will probably be coated on both sides, for example, **emulsion and anti-halation coatings** or double-side emulsion coating" | **[F]** | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)]` — 1966, quoted here because it is the structural complement to Wall's practice |

**The iodide-opacity argument — the 1929 emulsion-side route to the same end:**

- "Those containing iodide are more **opaque**, and less likely to suffer from **halation and solarization**." `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.33–34 (PDF 41–42)]` **[M]**
- Quoted from Eder, with a composition attached: "For landscape work bromo-iodide emulsions, **with three to four per cent of iodide**, are decidedly better than pure bromide emulsions, **because halation is less with the former** and small details against the sky are better differentiated." `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.35 (PDF 43)]` **[Q]** *(composition tied to halation; the effect itself unquantified)*

**[E]** The iodide-opacity argument is physically the *absorption* route rather than the *scatter* route: iodide raises the layer's own absorbance so that less light reaches the support to be totally reflected. It is thus the 1929 ancestor of the 1966 acutance dye (§18.6) and carries the same implicit speed cost, though Wall does not state the cost and in fact reports iodide as *increasing* sensitiveness after sufficient digestion. **Wall gives no figure for the opacity gain per per-cent iodide.**

**Double coating as an antihalation measure, 1929, with the marketing caveat:**

| Statement | Class | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| "Some of the non-halation, so-called double-coated plates, on the market are **merely coated with an extra quantity of emulsion, and not actually double-coated**" | **[F]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]` |
| True double coating, J. T. Sandell (Eng. Pat. 21,381/1891), "who actually coated **first a very slow, opaque emulsion and then on top a faster and more translucent one**" | **[F]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]` |
| Stated penalty of the thick or double coating: "**the longer time required for fixation, washing and drying**" | **[F]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]` |
| **No statement is made in the 1929 book about the effect of double coating on contrast or latitude.** Wall connects it only to halation control, coating thickness and processing time | **[F]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)]` |

Set that beside the 1922 survey, where "double coated" and "nonhalation" are used as synonyms in the contents list `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.34 (PDF 35)]`, and note that the survey's own double-coated classes do **not** show systematically better resolution numbers than the single-coated ones — ordinary double-coated charts 21–23 give R = 20, 27, 25 against R = 18–28 across the single-coated group. **The 1922 data therefore do not corroborate a resolution benefit from double coating, but recall that all test plates were separately black-shellac backed, so halation was already suppressed in both groups.** `[Davis & Walters 1922, PDF 56–58; p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[E]**

### 18.8 Antihalation in 1966 — the backing layer and its one spectral curve

The 1966 structural account, verbatim: "Although not a photographic layer, the **anti-halation layer** must be mentioned because it plays an important part in the photographic material. Every film, unless it is coated on both sides with emulsion as X-ray film, carries a backing layer of gelatin, or a substitute, designed to **prevent curl**… In colour film for example, this is frequently a **resin backing designed to be removed in processing**. Incorporated in this layer is a pigment or dye designed to **absorb light in those regions of the spectrum to which the emulsion is sensitive**. In **microfilms**, where complete absorption of the light transmitted through the emulsion layer is desired for **maximum sharpness**, the back coating is a **black-dyed resin**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.168–169 (PDF 174–175), Fig. 8.4]` **[F]**

The absorber and its curve: "One commonly-used substance is **colloidal manganese dioxide**, which is brown in colour and absorbing quite strongly at the violet end of the spectrum, dropping with increasing wavelength as shown in Figure 8.4." Prepared by reducing KMnO₄ with, for example, glucose in the presence of a suspending colloid such as gelatin. Fig. 8.4 axes: **Optical Density** on the ordinate (tick "0.5" legible, OCR'd as `° a`) against **Wavelength in Å** on the abscissa, ticks at **3500 / 4500 / 5500 / 6500**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.168–169 (PDF 174–175), Fig. 8.4]` **[Q]** *(axes only; no digitised values)*

Backing dyes named: triphenylmethanes — **crystal violet (28)**, **acid fuchsine (29)** — with the constraint "It is important that the dyes should reduce easily and that the products wash out of the gelatin backing layer"; plus a solubilized dye (30) and cyanine-type backing dyes (31), (32). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.168–169 (PDF 174–175)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Fig. 8.4 is the only antihalation spectral density curve in the entire source set, and its shape has a consequence worth recording: an MnO₂ backing is **strong in the violet and weak in the red**, so residual halation on such a stock should be **strongest in the red channel**. That inference is ours; Duffin does not state it, and the figure carries no digitised density values, so the magnitude of the red leak cannot be extracted.

Two more 1966 items belong to the same physical problem:

- Antihalation is the reason for double-side subbing, quoted in §18.7. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)]` **[F]**
- The 1966 book's earlier chapters contain **no** halation mechanism, optical model or numbers at all beyond the phrase "emulsion and anti-halation coatings" and the "Backing" label on Fig. 1.1; backing dyes and acutance dyes are deferred to Chapter VIII. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15); Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)]` **[F]**

### 18.9 Edge and adjacency effects in the spatial domain — 1995, mechanism only

The 1995 statement is the only treatment of the spatial *chemical* transfer function in this set, and it is complete as mechanism and empty as numbers:

> "One of the most popular chemical interactions between silver halide grains during development is the **chemical adjacency effect**, which is based on the **finite diffusion and mass transfer rates of development byproducts and developer**. On development of a **knife-edge exposure**, the concentration of developer is higher and the concentration of development inhibiting byproducts is lower in the edge region than in the remainder of the high-exposure region, and **density develops more rapidly (the border effect)**. The development byproducts that flow into the low-exposure region of the knife-edge exposure can curtail development close to the edge, resulting in a **low-density region (the fringe effect)**. Chemical adjacency effects can take place **between emulsion layers in multilayer films, as well as within a single emulsion layer**, and can be controlled to improve image quality."
`[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230); source cited as Kriss, in James (1977) Ch. 21]` **[M]**

So the two named phenomena are the **border effect** (overshoot on the high-density side of an edge) and the **fringe effect** (undershoot on the low-density side). **No length scale, no edge width, and no edge-strength magnitude is given.** `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[F]**

**[E]** The passage identifies **two** competing diffusing species — fresh developer flowing in and inhibitor flowing out — which means two length scales in principle, not one. It also separates two spatial regimes that a single "adjacency" parameter would conflate: the **grain-scale** dye-cloud size that DIR couplers act on (§17.5.4), and the **edge-scale** knife-edge effect described here. The source supports treating these as distinct mechanisms with distinct scales; it supplies neither scale.

**The Eberhard effect is not mentioned anywhere in the 1995 source.** The adjacency phenomena are named "border effect" and "fringe effect" only, and the index carries no Eberhard entry. `[Tani 1995, pp.122–254 (PDF 131–263) and Index]` **[F]**

The 1966 source's counterpart is a single sentence naming infectious development as the one grain-to-grain interaction at development: "in an infectious developer where a latent-image-bearing grain will initiate development and cause the reduction of those crystals near to it by chemical influence." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.171 (PDF 177)]` — and an exhaustive keyword search of that book returns **zero** hits for "adjacency", "edge effect" and "interimage". `[Duffin 1966, PDF 126–250 and Index PDF 237–246]` **[F]**

The 1922 source's counterpart is the phrase "**the spreading of the image in development**", listed as one of the three causes of resolution loss and never elaborated. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.29 (PDF 30)]` **[M]**

One length that must *not* be pressed into service as a spatial-spread figure: the 1966 report of photoelectron diffusion, "photoelectrons induced by light absorbed by sensitizing dyes have been shown to **diffuse 40–50 microns in large sheet crystals**, i.e. as far as photoelectrons produced by light absorption by the halide." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VI, p.131 (PDF 137)]` **[Q]** — this is a **large-single-crystal laboratory number**, orders of magnitude above any emulsion grain (0.2–2 µm), and it is evidence only that in-crystal photoelectron range is not the resolution-limiting term. Optical scatter and halation, not carrier diffusion, are what the sources name as the limits. **[E]** The same caution applies to the 1995 electron diffusion lengths in grains (0.4–2.3 µm) `[Tani 1995, §4.2 (PDF 96–100)]`: they explain the ~1 µm sensitivity-versus-size knee, not an emulsion transfer function.

### 18.10 MTF and resolving power — everything this set contains

**Resolving power is the only sharpness metric any source in this set quantifies.** `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.30 (PDF 31); Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20)]` **[F]**

The 1995 source supplies the one law relating speed to resolving power:

> "In 1970, Ooue summarized the relation between sensitivity and resolving power of various photosensitive materials that had been produced and studied by that time. This is illustrated in Fig. 1.7, in which sensitivity is expressed as **ASA** or the reciprocal of the exposure (**erg/cm²**) for imaging, and resolving power is expressed as the number of parallel **line pairs per millimeter** detected by photosensitive materials. **Ooue derived the equation used in the preparation of this figure by making the sensitivity proportional to the reciprocal of the resolving power squared.**"
`[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20), Figs. 1.7, 1.8]` — i.e. **S ∝ 1/(resolving power)², so S · R² = constant.** Fig. 1.8 is the same plot for materials in use at the time of writing, with sensitivity in **ISO** or 1/(erg/cm²). **[Q]**

And the envelope statement: "…silver halide photographic materials are the best photosensitive materials known from the viewpoint of sensitivity and resolving power, and form the **boundary region**, ranging from high sensitivity with low resolving power to low sensitivity with high resolving power." `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20)]` **[F]**

**[E]** S ∝ R⁻² implies that one stop of speed costs a factor √2 ≈ 1.41 in linear resolution. Note the scope Tani gives it: it is the empirical envelope of the **entire field of photosensitive materials**, not a within-brand or within-family rule, and it is a *family* trend. Use it as a sanity check across stock classes, not as a generator of per-stock numbers. The 1922 survey's own speed/resolution pattern (§18.2) is qualitatively consistent with it across two decades of speed.

**The one MTF-adjacent statement in the whole set, with its OCR damage:**

> "However, one line pair corresponds to two pixels in CCD. Thus, for comparison between CCD and color negative film, the resolving power of the former in Fig. 1.8 should be compared with the spatial frequency corresponding to **`\`** in the modulation transfer function of the latter, which is **nearly one half of the resolving power shown in Fig. 1.8**."
`[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20)]` **[Q]**

**OCR damage flag:** the fraction after "corresponding to" is lost and comes through as the single character `\`. Given the phrase "nearly one half of the resolving power" and standard practice, the missing value is very probably **½, i.e. the MTF = 0.5 point (f50)**. **But the raw string does not contain the value, and it is quoted here as `\` rather than filled in.** If the fraction is indeed ½, the statement gives **f50 ≈ 0.5 × (resolving power in lp/mm)** for colour negative film — the only route in this set from a resolving-power figure to an MTF frequency. **[F]**

Other frequency-domain and resolving-power figures in the set, for completeness:

| Item | Value | Era | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-silver benchmark: electrophotography with liquid toner development | sensitivity ~**1 erg/cm²**, resolving power **250–500 line pairs/mm** | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.13 (PDF 22)]` |
| Diffusion-transfer processing (instant films, photothermography) | "lose resolving power and gain real time processing" | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.13 (PDF 22)]` |
| Hard ceiling on resolving power | grain size cannot be smaller than molecules or polymers, which bounds silver halide against photopolymers | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, §1.2.3, p.10 (PDF 19)]` |
| Printing films | "required to provide very high gradation and image qualities that are unique to those films" | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.13 (PDF 22)]` |
| Sharpness in diffusion transfer | "the reduction on the catalytic nuclei in the positive sheet must be very fast otherwise **diffusion would spread out and produce unsharp pictures**" | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.219 (PDF 225)]` |
| MTF index scope in the 1995 book | index entry reads "modulation transfer function, **11**" — a single page, which is the passage quoted above | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, Index pp.245–246 (PDF 254–255)]` |

**[Q]**

### 18.11 ⚠ Explicit absences in the spatial domain — stated plainly

**No source in this set gives an MTF curve.** There is no plotted or tabulated modulation transfer function for any emulsion, layer, stock or class, in any of the four sources. The only MTF mention anywhere is the single sentence of §18.10, and it is a conversion remark, not a curve. `[Davis & Walters 1922; Wall 1929; Duffin 1966; Tani 1995]` **[F]**

**No source in this set gives an f50 figure.** No numeric MTF-50 frequency is stated for any material. The nearest is the conjectural reading of the OCR-lost fraction in §18.10, which would yield f50 ≈ 0.5 × resolving power as a *rule*, not as a value. `[Tani 1995, §1.3, p.11 (PDF 20)]` **[F]**

**No source in this set gives an adjacency-overshoot figure.** The border and fringe effects are named and their signs given, but no overshoot amplitude, no edge width, no undershoot depth and no length scale appears anywhere. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[F]**

**No source in this set quantifies halation magnitude or radius.** The 1922 paper states that halo size is determined by support thickness and critical angle and never performs the calculation or gives either quantity for a material `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.30 (PDF 31)]`; the 1929 book explicitly carries no photometric halation datum and no figure for how much any remedy reduces halation `[Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.83–84 (PDF 90–91)]`; the 1966 book gives an antihalation absorber's spectral shape but no halation model and no residual figure `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.168–169 (PDF 174–175)]`; the 1995 book does not treat halation at all. **[F]**

Further specific absences:

- **No point-spread function, line-spread function, edge-spread function or turbidity coefficient** for any emulsion layer. `[Davis & Walters 1922; Wall 1929; Duffin 1966; Tani 1995]` **[F]**
- **No acutance value and no acutance formula.** Acutance appears only as a design goal and as the name of a dye class. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.164 (PDF 170)]` **[F]**
- **No irradiation quantification** — the 1922 mechanism statement is the whole of it. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.29 (PDF 30)]` **[F]**
- **No quantification of "the spreading of the image in development"**, despite its being named as one of the three causes of resolution loss in 1922. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.29 (PDF 30)]` **[F]**
- **No resolving-power figure in lp/mm for any real photographic material** anywhere in the set. The 1922 survey gives spacings in thousandths of a millimetre under a countable-lines criterion (§18.2); Tani's Figs. 1.7 and 1.8 plot lp/mm on an axis but the extracted text carries no per-material values off it, and its quantitative resolving-power discussion sits at printed pp.10–14 as figures rather than tables. `[Davis & Walters 1922, PDF 36–121; Tani 1995, §1.3, pp.11–14 (PDF 20–23), Figs. 1.7, 1.8]` **[F]**
- **No relation between resolving power and density, gamma or development time** for any material. The only exposure-dependence statement is the unquantified 1922 "the greater the exposure the lower the resolution". `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.30 (PDF 31)]` **[F]**
- **No Callier coefficient and no specular-versus-diffuse density treatment** in any source, which matters here because a specular reading of a scattering layer is itself a spatial-domain quantity. The 1922 paper's visual-versus-photographic-density caveat (§15.11.5) is the closest approach. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.23 (PDF 24)]` **[F]**
- **No base or support optical data** — no glass tint, base density, refractive index, haze or transmission figure appears in the 1929 book, and none of the four sources gives a support refractive index despite the 1922 halation model depending on it. `[Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.168 (PDF 175); Davis & Walters 1922, p.30 (PDF 31)]` **[F]**


---

### 18.x The one bridge from resolving power to the frequency domain

⚠ Recorded because it is the **only** place in this source set where a spatial-frequency
description of film appears at all, and because our schema stores both a resolving power and an
f50. Comparing a CCD with colour negative film, the 1995 source states that a line pair
corresponds to two CCD pixels, and that "the resolving power of the former ... should be compared
with the spatial frequency corresponding to \u00bd in the modulation transfer function of the latter,
**which is nearly one half of the resolving power**". `[Tani 1995, §1.2, p.11 (PDF 20)]` **[Q]**

So: the frequency at which the film's MTF has fallen to 0.5 sits at roughly **half** the quoted
resolving power in line pairs per millimetre. That is a one-line, source-supported bridge between
a quantity these sources do give (resolving power, §18) and the quantity our `MTFSpec.f50_*`
fields hold.

Two cautions, both material:
- The relation is stated in passing, inside an argument about CCDs, with "nearly". It is not a
  measurement and no tolerance is given. **[F]**
- Resolving power depends on test-object contrast, and the sources quote low- and high-contrast
  figures separately (our schema mirrors this with `resolving_power_lp_mm_lowc` and
  `..._highc`). The 1995 statement does not say which contrast its resolving power refers to, so
  applying the factor of one half requires choosing one — and that choice is ours. **[E]**

Beyond this single sentence, the negative finding stands: **no source in this set plots an MTF
curve, tabulates an f50, or gives an adjacency-overshoot figure.** Tani's only other occurrence of
"modulation transfer function" is the subject-index entry pointing back to this same page
`[Tani 1995, Index, p.246 (PDF 255)]`. **[F]**

## 19. Colour materials

### 19.1 Colour development chemistry — the 1966 four-electron account

**Era: 1966.** The developing agent is **diethyl-p-phenylenediamine**. "It is used for that purpose, acting as a **fairly low-energy developer giving fine-grain results**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.191 (PDF 197)]` **[F]**

The mechanism, step by step as the source sets it out:

1. Diethyl-p-phenylenediamine loses one electron to a silver ion → a **semiquinone radical cation**.
2. In strong alkali the radical cation loses a proton → a **neutral radical**.
3. The neutral radical loses a second electron to a silver ion → the **quinone di-imine**, "the reactive species giving rise to the dye".
4. "All the colour-forming or colour-coupling substances are moderately strong acids and are converted into **negatively-charged ions** in an alkaline solution, all of them being strong enough to dissolve in aqueous sodium carbonate." The positive quinone di-imine reacts with the coupler **anion** → a **leuco** compound.
5. The leuco compound is "**very rapidly converted into the dye by the intervention of two more silver ions**, thus completing the process, and accounting fully for the equation."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.192–194 (PDF 198–200)]` **[M]**

So the **overall stoichiometry is four silver ions per dye molecule**, and the printed equations state it as such: the yellow coupling "reaction consumes **4 AgBr** and liberates **4 HBr**"; the magenta equation is shown as "**+ 4AgBr → + 4Ag + 4HBr**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.190–192 (PDF 196–198)]` **[Q]**

### 19.2 Colour development chemistry — the 1995 account

**Era: 1995.** The same chemistry, compressed and with different emphasis:

> "each color-sensitive layer with a corresponding color coupler and silver halide grains is developed in a color developer with **phenylenediamine compounds (PPD)** as developing agents. **A PPD molecule reduces two silver ions** and is converted into a **quinone diimine (QDI)**. A QDI then takes part in the formation of an image composed of a dye through an **intermediate compound** by reaction with a coupler."

`[Tani 1995, §1.1, pp.5–6 (PDF 14–15), Fig. 1.4]` **[M]**

Restated in the development chapter: "During development, a developing agent (PPD) oxidizes silver ions in emulsion grains to produce silver atoms and a **quinonediimine (QDI)**, and QDI reacts with a coupler to produce a dye molecule." The requirements placed on couplers are enumerated: "the **stoichiometry and coupling rate** of the reaction, and the **hue, fastness, and immobilization** of formed dye molecules." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.223 (PDF 232)]` **[F]**

### 19.3 The stoichiometry statements compared

**The two accounts give different numbers and they are describing different steps, so they must not be averaged.**

| Era | Statement | Step described |
|---|---|---|
| 1966 | "**4 AgBr** … + 4Ag + 4HBr" per dye molecule; four silver ions total, two to make the quinone di-imine and "**two more silver ions**" to oxidize the leuco compound to the dye | **overall**, developer oxidation *plus* leuco oxidation |
| 1995 | "**A PPD molecule reduces two silver ions** and is converted into a quinone diimine" | **the developer half only**, i.e. PPD → QDI |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.190–194 (PDF 196–200); Tani 1995, §1.1, pp.5–6 (PDF 14–15)]` **[F]**

The 1995 source's "two silver ions per PPD molecule" and the 1966 source's "four silver ions per dye molecule" are consistent if, as the 1966 source says, the intermediate leuco compound is oxidized by a second pair of silver ions — i.e. two PPD molecules' worth of oxidation per dye. **The 1995 source does not state the leuco-oxidation stoichiometry**, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the total of four. **[E]** — this reconciliation is ours; neither source states the comparison.

**A real, documented stoichiometric exception.** For a **coloured (masking) coupler**, the 1966 source states: "**It will be noted that only two Ag⁺ ions are involved in the formation of the dye molecule instead of the usual four**; there is no intermediate stage such as the substance [the leuco compound]." The azo group is expelled directly and the dye forms in one step. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.214 (PDF 220)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** That halving is a hard numeric constraint on any coupled silver/dye model: **a masked magenta layer's dye-per-silver ratio is twice that of the unmasked case.** For the same developed silver, a coloured-coupler magenta layer produces twice as much dye.

### 19.4 Couplers — the three colour classes and their chemistry

**Era: 1966.** All three from the printed equations and running text:

| Dye | Coupler chemistry | Silver consumed |
|---|---|---|
| **Yellow** | chain coupler containing **—COCH₂CONH—**, usually with benzene rings at each end | **4 AgBr → 4 HBr** |
| **Magenta** | **—COCH₂CN—** as an open chain, or as a ring; "this being the more commonly-used type", e.g. a **pyrazolone** | **+ 4AgBr → + 4Ag + 4HBr** |
| **Cyan** | a **naphthalene** derivative bearing a hydroxyl and commonly a carboxylic group | (same four-electron scheme); yields "greeny-blue dye … always referred to as a **cyan** dye" |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.190–192 (PDF 196–198)]` **[Q]**

**Chemical structures were line-art images and did not survive extraction** — the numbered coupler formulae came through as noise (e.g. `cHso-{ Couchco-mi-{” 0,`). The compound *classes* named in the running text, reproduced above, are the recoverable content. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.190–192 (PDF 196–198)]` **[F]**

The 1966 source's six design requirements for a colour material, quoted because they are the period's own specification of the problem:

> "1. Each of the emulsion layers must be sensitive to one of the three primary colours, blue, green and red. 2. The processing … must result in dyes of the correct hue being formed in the appropriate layer and **without appreciable sideways wandering in that layer**. 3. …moderate temperature and mild conditions… 4. The reactions producing the dyes must form these substances **in quantities proportional to the developed silver**. 5. …substantially free from coloured by-products or by-products which would generate colour on storage. 6. The dyes formed must be sufficiently light stable…"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.190 (PDF 196)]` **[F]**

Requirement 4 — **dye quantity proportional to developed silver** — is the assumption the masked-coupler exception of §19.3 modifies by a factor of two.

**Era: 1995.** Functional coupler families, with dates from their primary references: **coloured (masking) couplers** — Hanson & Vittum **1947**, Hanson **1950**; **DIR couplers** — Barr, Thirtle & Vittum **1969**; **DAR couplers** — Kobayashi & Mihayashi **1985**, Jarvis & Twist **1988**; **polymeric couplers** — Tong, in James (1977). `[Tani 1995, refs. 79–84, pp.226–227 (PDF 235–236)]` **[F]**

**[E]** These dates are a usable era key: a 1947-or-later colour negative can carry masking couplers; a 1969-or-later one can carry DIR couplers; a 1985-or-later one can carry DAR couplers. The 1966 source therefore describes a material with masking couplers but no DIR and no DAR.

### 19.5 Coupler-locating strategies, and their image consequences

**Era: 1966.** Three families, each with stated consequences for the rendered image. This is the most consequential part of the 1966 colour account because the *location* of the coupler determines dye purity, granularity and cross-layer behaviour.

**(a) Substantive couplers — Agfacolor, Ferrania, Gevaert.** Simple couplers would diffuse between layers or wash out, so they are anchored by "a **long carbon chain and a strongly acid group, usually a sulphonic acid**". Consequences, both negative and both stated explicitly:

- "**the dye is supposed to be fully dispersed through the emulsion layer but in practice there is a pronounced tendency to clump**";
- "the **severe interaction which frequently occurs between the gelatin and the colour coupler** which can cause an undesirable **increase in viscosity** of the emulsion layer and even cause **precipitation of the gelatin**."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.197–201 (PDF 203–207)]` **[F]**

**(b) Oil-dispersion couplers — Eastman Kodak; Ektachrome, Kodacolor.** The coupler is "ballasted with a large water-repellent oil-soluble group", dissolved in a solvent such as **tricresyl phosphate**, and emulsified in gelatin to give "a dispersion of small globules of the oily solvent"; the globules "are **similar in size to one another**" and to the silver-halide grains, and are mixed with the photographic emulsion. The dye forms **inside the globule** by diffusion of oxidized developer into the oily phase, the solvent being "nevertheless polar enough in nature to permit the ready acceptance of the quinone di-imine ion." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.199–201 (PDF 205–207), Figs. 10.8, 10.9]` **[F]**

**(c) Developer-soluble couplers — Kodachrome.** Simple couplers are carried in the processing solution and must be "of sufficiently small molecular size to **diffuse easily into the layers of a tripack coating** to effect satisfactorily rapid development, even in the lowest layer"; consequently three separate colour-development steps are required. The then-current sequence: black-and-white development → wash → **red exposure through the back** → cyan colour developer → **blue exposure to the face** (reaching only the top layer, the lower layers protected by the yellow filter) → yellow colour developer → **fog the middle layer** (high-intensity light, or chemically with KBH₄) → magenta colour developer → bleach out all silver. Red-dye migration between layers during the first development "is avoided by the choice of the appropriate red sensitizer and emulsion conditions designed to give it the maximum anchorage." A hard limitation is stated: **developer-soluble couplers are not used for negative-positive** — "it is quite impossible to devise means of obtaining the correct colour image in each layer." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.202–203, 211 (PDF 208–209, 217), Figs. 10.10–10.13]` **[F]**

**The dye-purity consequence, which is the payoff of the whole comparison:**

> "The **purity of the colour** produced by the dye, that is **the width of the absorption and the density of the maximum light absorption**, is very dependent upon the **molecular state** of the dye. **In solution the dye will give a high density and a fairly narrow band but in the solid state the dye will tend to give less pure colour from a broader band.** The oil-soluble coupler method gives a dye which is in solution and therefore produces **maximum colour purity**."

Verdict: "the overall quality produced by the formation of the dye in the small oil globules of the second type of process is generally **more acceptable**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.201 (PDF 207)]` **[F]**

**[E]** This is a statement about *band width and peak density as functions of the dye's physical state*, not about the dye's molecular structure. Two materials with the same coupler chemistry can therefore have different unwanted-absorption behaviour depending only on whether the dye ends up dissolved in an oil globule or clumped in gelatin. It is the same coupling the 1995 source states from the diffusibility side (§14.8).

**Bleach.** Both reversal and negative-positive processes finish with "a **ferricyanide/hypo** bleach", leaving the dye images only. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.198 (PDF 204), Fig. 10.7]` **[F]**

### 19.6 Layer order and interlayers in colour materials

Covered in §14.3 and §14.9. Summarised here for self-containment: tripack from the top is **supercoat / blue-sensitive / yellow filter layer (usually yellow colloidal silver, possibly organic) / green-sensitive / red-sensitive / support**, all colour layers **1–3 µm dry** `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.195–196 (PDF 201–202); Ch. VIII, p.153 (PDF 159)]`; the 1995 stack is **about 14 layers, about 20 µm total**, with each of the three colour records split into **high-, medium- and low-speed sublayers**, the most sensitive uppermost `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.3 (PDF 12); §8.1.2, p.233 (PDF 242)]`. **[Q]**

A UV-absorption function is assigned to the supercoat in colour prints: "In the case of colour images, particularly in prints, the supercoat can also contain a compound able to **absorb ultra-violet light. Ultra-violet is the most active radiation [in] fading of colour materials.**" Named UV absorbers include a thiazolidone related to the merocyanines, a colourless true cyanine, and a water-soluble derivative; "Many u.v. absorbers suitable for colour prints bear considerable structural resemblance to sensitizing dyes." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.167 (PDF 173)]` **[F]**

### 19.7 Reversal and negative-positive: the process-level differences that show in the image

**Era: 1966.**

- **Reversal fogging exposure** must be limited: it "must not be too heavy otherwise **some reversal occurs due to solarization**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.198 (PDF 204)]` **[F]**
- **Negative/positive spectral spread:** "In practice, the **hues of the negative dyes, and the spectral sensitivities of the positive material, are spread a little wider than those of reversal films so as to obtain better separation of the three records**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.211 (PDF 217)]` **[F]**
- **The print material is matched to the negative's dyes, not to the eye:** the print material's spectral sensitivities "must match those of the **dyes in the negative** rather than that of the eye", and there is no fundamental need for complementary pairing "as long as the light sensitivities of the material are matched to the absorption maxima of the negative images." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.211 (PDF 217)]` **[F]**
- **Tolerance for unwanted absorptions differs by process:** "In reversal materials this is not a very serious matter; by careful selection of the couplers, dyes may be chosen which are acceptable. **In a negative-positive process, however, the extraneous absorptions will cause serious colour degradation.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.211–212 (PDF 217–218)]` **[F]**
- **Sharpness, dated:** "This soluble-coupler process has been carried to a high level of perfection, for example in the latest **Kodachrome X**. The **sharpness is so good with the thinly-coated high-acutance films of today** that **8 mm movies can, at last, give acceptable definition**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.203 (PDF 209)]` **[F]**

### 19.8 Unwanted dye absorptions — the dye-impurity block

**Era: 1966.** The core statement, and it is the most useful colour-reproduction paragraph in this material:

> "The light absorptions of the three dyes forming the image are **not ideal**. The desired curves are shown in Figure 10.22; usually **the yellow dye is satisfactory, but the magenta and cyan dyes contain extraneous absorption in the blue region and green regions respectively** as shown in Figure 10.23. The effect of these additional absorptions is to add a **yellow hue to the magenta, and a red one to the cyan**, and thus to **degrade the reds and blues of the image**."

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.211–212 (PDF 217–218), Figs. 10.22, 10.23]` **[F]**

Read as a signed unwanted-absorption pattern:

| Dye | Principal band | Unwanted secondary absorption | Resulting hue error | Image consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Yellow** | blue | "usually … satisfactory" — none stated | — | — |
| **Magenta** | green | **blue** | adds a **yellow** hue to the magenta | **degrades the blues** |
| **Cyan** | red | **green** | adds a **red** hue to the cyan | **degrades the reds** |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.211–212 (PDF 217–218), Fig. 10.23]` **[F]**

**Era: 1995.** The same pattern from the coloured-coupler side: "In the absorption spectra of conventional magenta dyes, **main bands in the green region are always associated with sub-bands in the blue region, which make the color of the dyes impure**." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.223 (PDF 232), Fig. 7.15]` **[F]**

**Sources agree** on the pattern — magenta carries a blue secondary, cyan carries a green secondary, yellow is comparatively clean — across the 29-year gap. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.211–212 (PDF 217–218); Tani 1995, §7.5, p.223 (PDF 232)]` **[F]**

### 19.9 Masking couplers

**Era: 1966, discovery dated to the 1940s.** "an invention made at the same time at **Kodak and Ansco**; colour couplers of the required type had been prepared some years earlier." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.212 (PDF 218)]` **[F]** The 1995 source dates the primary literature: Hanson & Vittum **1947**, Hanson **1950**. `[Tani 1995, refs. 79–80, p.226 (PDF 235)]` **[F]**

**The mechanism, 1966 statement.** The coloured coupler carries a (usually colourless) group conferring absorption "in the same region as the unwanted blue absorption of the final dye image, and, therefore, **the coupler is now yellow**. This group is **expelled during the reaction** giving the dye." Two processes run concurrently across the exposure range:

- **in image areas** — oxidized developer plus the coloured coupler gives the magenta image, which carries its own unwanted blue absorption;
- **in non-image areas** — the blue-absorbing coupler simply remains, unreacted;
- **at intermediate exposures** — a mixture of the two.

"If the wavelength and intensity of the absorption are accurately balanced between the two parts, then, in terms of image, **only the magenta part remains**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.212–214 (PDF 218–220)]` **[F]**

**The mechanism, 1995 statement**, which is the same argument in one sentence: "On color development, a **yellow-colored magenta coupler loses its absorption band in the blue region, which is then compensated for by the sub-band in the same region of the formed magenta dye**. As a result, **the difference in the light absorption of the above coupler before and after color development appears only in the green region and can provide pure magenta color**." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.223 (PDF 232), Fig. 7.15]` **[F]**

**Chemistry, 1966.** The example given is a **4-arylazo-5-pyrazolone**, specifically **1-phenyl-3-methyl-4-phenylazo-5-pyrazolone**, existing in two tautomers; its anion reacts with the quinone di-imine to give the magenta dye directly "by expulsion of the azo group", via an intermediate, the expelled phenyl anion abstracting a proton from water to become benzene. And the cyan counterpart: "Similar azo derivatives of an **α-naphthol** behave as **magenta masks for the cyan** dye." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.212–215 (PDF 218–221)]` **[F]**

So the mask colours pair up as: **yellow mask for the magenta dye's blue secondary**; **magenta mask for the cyan dye's green secondary**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.212–215 (PDF 218–221)]` **[F]**

**How masking intensity is trimmed in practice — a continuously adjustable parameter, and the 1966 source says so explicitly:**

> "It is difficult to balance the intensity of the two blue absorptions. **Usually the modified coloured couplers possess higher blue absorption than the subsidiary maximum of the dye image**; this can be overcome by using a **mixture of coloured and uncoloured couplers which are identical except for the blue-absorbing group. In development the same dye will be formed from either of them and by balancing the proportion of the two substances the desired level of masking may be obtained.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.214 (PDF 220)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Masking strength is therefore a **continuous mix fraction** of coloured to colourless coupler, not a discrete design choice, and the 1966 source states that the natural coloured-coupler absorption is normally *too strong* — so real materials are typically under-masked relative to full coloured-coupler loading. The two-versus-four silver stoichiometry of §19.3 means the mix fraction also changes the layer's dye-per-silver ratio, which the source does not point out.

**The alternative masking route — layer-speed rebalance in the print material** rather than coloured couplers in the negative, is quoted in §14.10. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.213 (PDF 219)]` **[F]**

### 19.10 Colour balance, dmax and curve matching — the "crossover" content

**The term "colour crossover" does not appear in this material.** What exists is the underlying phenomenon: mismatch between the characteristic curves of the three layers, and the deliberate sacrifice of balance at one end of the scale. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.199 (PDF 205)]` **[F]**

**Era: 1966.** The two load-bearing statements:

> "In practice **many commercial films do not give a neutral colour at maximum density**; the completely fogged end of a film will often appear **deep green or deep violet** corresponding to insufficient magenta and cyan dyes respectively. **These areas are allowed to go out of balance in order to ensure that colour reproduction in the intermediate densities, in which the user is most interested, is correct.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.199 (PDF 205)]` **[F]**

> "Acceptable accurate colour rendering by this process is dependent upon the matching of **the maximum sensitivities of each layer, the absorption maxima of the dyes and the spectral sensitivity of the eye**, also taking into account the **colour temperature of the exposing and viewing illumination**. In addition **the sensitometric curves of each of the emulsion layers must be very accurately matched, otherwise in certain areas the density of colours will go out of balance.**"

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.199 (PDF 205)]` **[F]**

**[E]** Together these are a statement that per-channel curve mismatch is real, is deliberately non-uniform across the density scale, and is tuned to be smallest in the mid-densities — which is exactly the structure a crossover model needs. **No numbers accompany it**: no per-channel gammas, no dmax densities, no neutral-scale deviations. The direction is documented ("deep green or deep violet" at full fog, i.e. deficient magenta and cyan at dmax); the magnitude is not.

**A note on colour temperature.** The 1966 source names the colour temperature of exposing and viewing illumination as a determinant of colour rendering but gives **no colour-temperature values anywhere**. The 1922 source defines its own illuminant verbally — "**average yearly noon sunlight at the latitude of Washington**", realised as a 6–8 V Mazda C automobile headlight lamp at approximately 2.4 A behind a special blue glass filter — and **states no colour temperature in kelvin or any other unit**. Lamps without filter averaged **15 candlepower**, the filter transmitted **18.2 per cent**, and the average filtered intensity was **2.73 candlepower**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.199 (PDF 205); Davis & Walters 1922, pp.17–18 (PDF 18–19)]` **[Q]** — do not assume 5500 K or any other value for the 1922 illuminant.

### 19.11 Dye purity as a function of molecular state

Quoted in §19.5 and repeated here as a standalone fact because it is the only statement in this material relating absorption *band shape* to a physical variable: **in solution, high peak density and a fairly narrow band; in the solid state, less pure colour from a broader band**; oil-globule dye is in solution and therefore gives maximum colour purity; substantive couplers clump and degrade it. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.201 (PDF 207)]` **[F]**

The 1995 companion statement, from the coupler-design side: **diffusible-dye-forming couplers** "could improve graininess by adjusting the **diffusibility of dye molecules**, and thus the **shape of the absorption spectra of dye clouds**." `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.224 (PDF 233)]` **[M]**

### 19.12 Alternative colour systems in the 1966 account

These matter because their *image* properties differ from chromogenic materials in stated, signed ways.

**(a) Dye-bleach (Gasparcolor / Ilford; Cilchrome of CIBA).** A tripack with **yellow dye in the blue-sensitive top layer, magenta in the green-sensitive, cyan in the red-sensitive**, plus an optional filter layer; the dyes are **azo** dyes (–N=N–). After black-and-white development and fixing, a strong acid bath containing a silver-complexing agent (e.g. **thiourea**) and a catalyst (e.g. **2,3-dimethylquinoxaline**) dissolves the silver and reduces the dye where silver was:

```
Ag + HCl + NH2CSNH2  →  [Ag(SC(NH2)2)2]Cl + (H)
(H) + 2,3-dimethylquinoxaline  →  reduced quinoxaline
4 molecules of reduced quinoxaline + azo dye  →  quinoxaline + reduced azo dye
```

"where (H) is a nascent or very reactive hydrogen atom. **Each –N=N– group in the dye is reduced to –NH₂ H₂N–**, thus separating the molecule into two parts. In some cases the azo dye may contain **two –N=N– links in which case eight atoms of silver will be required for each dye molecule.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.205–206 (PDF 211–212)]` **[Q]**

Its two stated image consequences are an unusually clean speed/sharpness trade:

- **Speed cost:** "By the very nature of the system **each layer contains a dye which absorbs light in the same spectral region as that to which the layer is sensitive**. In fact **the whole coating appears black** … and **this reduces the overall speed**. … In the Gaspar layer, light absorbed by the azo dyes is **wasted** from the point of view of forming latent image." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.207 (PDF 213)]` **[F]**
- **Sharpness gain:** "High **tinctorial power** is obtainable in this system because the dyes are **molecularly dispersed** throughout the layer … This means that **only low coating weights of the dyes, and therefore of silver halide also, because the two must be in balanced chemical proportions, are needed, which means thin layers and high sharpness. This latter property is enhanced because the azo dyes function as fairly perfect acutance dyes, by reducing scatter in the emulsion layer of light in the wavelength region to which the emulsion is sensitive.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.207 (PDF 213)]` **[F]**

Also: azo dyes "are **more light stable** than are the **azomethines** used in the more conventional chromogenic development systems", and the verdict on the system: "The speed limitations derived from both the physics and chemistry of the tripack will probably **prevent it from being used in a negative system**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.206–207 (PDF 212–213)]` **[F]**

**(b) Dye diffusion (Polacolor).** Three emulsion layers, each with a **dye-developer** beneath it (cyan under red-sensitive, magenta under green, yellow under blue) — a molecule combining "the reducing part of a developing agent with a dye unit … effectively separated so that they are able both to act independently but move together." Alkali comes from pods; **oxidized** dye-developer is **immobilized**, **unoxidized** dye-developer **migrates** to the receptor. The receptor is **dye-receiving layer / spacer layer / alkali-neutralizing layer / base**, dyes held by a **mordant**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.207–210 (PDF 213–216), Figs. 10.17, 10.19, 10.20]` **[F]**

Its temperature behaviour is unusual and worth keeping for §20: "The degree of completion of the reactions occurring in Polacolor is controlled by carefully balancing the rates of the reactions. **As the temperature rises the diffusion rate of unoxidized dye-developer will increase but, at the same time, the interval before the reaction is terminated is correspondingly shortened, so that, unlike other colour products, the effect of temperature on the processing of Polacolor is not critical.**" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.210 (PDF 216)]` **[F]**

**(c) Named 1966-current colour products and processes**, useful as an era key: **Kodachrome** and **Kodachrome X** (developer-soluble coupler), **Agfacolor**, **Gevacolor**, **Ferrania**, **Gevaert** (substantive couplers), **Ektachrome**, **Kodacolor** (oil dispersion), **Gasparcolor** / Ilford and **Cilchrome of CIBA** (dye bleach), **Polacolor** (dye diffusion), **Technicolor** ("still used for movie films"), **Verifax** (Kodak document copying). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.189–217 (PDF 195–223)]` **[F]**

**(d) Historical dating from the 1966 account.** Clerk Maxwell demonstrated colour photographs at the Royal Institution "**more than 100 years ago**" (three black-and-white films behind three filters, projected through three filtered lanterns), and "This type of colour process is still used today for the preparation of many colour pictures via printing blocks"; the only commercial single-exposure three-filter product was "the **Dufay**-type product", by 1966 off the market. "The physics of the modern three-layer one-exposure colour process was worked out **by the year 1873 by De Hauron** but it was not until the **1930's** that it became possible to achieve one of his systems on a commercial basis." "It was in **1912 that Fischer** produced the brilliant series of reactions on which **every one** of the colour processes relying upon the formation of dyes is based today." And the enabling step: "it was not until the work on sensitizing dyes expanded rapidly in the **early 1930's** that it was possible to achieve sensitivities in the required positions." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.189–190 (PDF 195–196)]` **[F]**

### 19.13 Numeric dye absorption data — the explicit absence

**No numeric dye absorption data exist anywhere in this material.** Specifically:

- **No λmax in nm or Å** for any image dye, in any source. **[F]**
- **No peak densities, no half-band widths, no unwanted-absorption fractions.** The 1995 source explains the coloured-coupler mechanism (Fig. 7.15) but gives **no numeric unwanted-absorption fractions**. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.223 (PDF 232), Fig. 7.15]` **[F]**
- The 1966 source's Figs. 10.22 ("ideal" dye absorption curves) and 10.23 (actual dye absorption curves, showing the magenta's blue and the cyan's green secondaries) are the **only** carriers of the magnitudes, and their curves were images lost in extraction. What survives of them is the axis labelling: **ordinate "Density"; abscissa "Wavelength Å", ticks 4000 / 5000 / 6000 / 7000** (Fig. 10.22's last tick was extracted as "7060", read 7000). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.213 (PDF 219), Figs. 10.22, 10.23]` **[F]**
- Fig. 7.15 in the 1995 source likewise carries the magnitudes as images: it shows "the reaction of a colored coupler (A), the absorption spectra of a **conventional magenta dye** (B), and a **magenta dye formed from a colored coupler with increasing amounts** (C). The absorption spectrum of a **yellow-colored magenta coupler** is also shown by a dotted curve in C." `[Tani 1995, p.222 (PDF 231), Fig. 7.15 caption]` **[F]**

The one numeric absorbance figure anywhere near this topic is not an image dye but a **sensitizing dye**, and it is a ceiling rather than a spectrum: J-aggregates covering **65 % of an evaporated AgBr surface** (= **1.3 × 10⁻⁶ mol/m²**) gave **peak absorbance 0.09** with **half-width 283 cm⁻¹**, from which the source concludes "the absorbance of these dye molecules on a tabular grain is **too weak to absorb all incident photons in the panchromatic range (i.e., 600–700 nm)**." `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, pp.229–230 (PDF 238–239), Fig. 8.1]` **[Q]** *(a caption/text discrepancy is flagged in the source material: the caption names the dye as 3,3′-disulfopropyl-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine while the text names the panchromatic dye as 5,5′-dichloro-9-ethyl-thiacarbocyanine.)*

Two further absorption numbers, both about the silver halide rather than a dye, included because they bound per-layer efficiency: "The percent absorptions of a **cubic AgBr grain with an edge length of 1 µm at 420 and 460 nm are about 10 % and 1 %**, respectively", and "The incorporation of **3 mol percent of silver iodide into silver bromide increases the percent absorption at 460 nm by five times.**" The overall figure: "the percent absorbance of a high-sensitive photographic film is as low as ***[number lost in extraction]*** in the intrinsic (blue) region and **10–20 % in the spectrally sensitized region**" — raw string `is as low as\n\nin the intrinsic (blue) region and 10-20% in the spectrally sensitized region.` `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` **[Q]** with OCR flag on the missing blue-region value.

### 19.14 How the 1966 account differs from the 1995 account

A direct comparison, since the two are separated by 29 years and by purpose:

| Aspect | 1966 account | 1995 account |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | The colour *process* as an engineering system: chemistry, coupler location, layer construction, product families, masking. A whole chapter (Ch. X, pp.189–215). | Colour chemistry as one paragraph of foundational chemistry (§1.1) plus **functional couplers as image-processing devices** (§7.5). |
| **Development chemistry** | Full four-electron mechanism spelled out step by step; overall 4 Ag⁺ per dye; leuco intermediate named and its oxidation by "two more silver ions" stated. | Compressed: PPD reduces **two** silver ions → QDI → reacts with coupler via an intermediate → dye. Leuco stoichiometry not stated. |
| **Coupler families** | Organised by **where the coupler lives** — substantive, oil-dispersed, developer-soluble — with the dye-purity and clumping consequences of each. | Organised by **what the coupler releases** — coloured (masking), DIR, DAR, polymeric, diffusible-dye-forming — with the image-quality trade of each. |
| **DIR / DAR** | **Absent.** DIR's primary literature is 1969, DAR's 1985/88 — both postdate the book. | Central. Framed as parallel image processing during development. |
| **Masking** | Full mechanism, chemistry (4-arylazo-5-pyrazolones; α-naphthol azo derivatives for the cyan mask), the 2-vs-4 silver stoichiometry, and the coloured/colourless coupler mix as the strength control. | Same mechanism in one paragraph, with Fig. 7.15; no stoichiometry, no mix-fraction discussion. |
| **Unwanted absorptions** | Magenta carries blue, cyan carries green, yellow clean; serious in negative-positive, tolerable in reversal; Figs. 10.22/10.23. | "main bands in the green region are always associated with sub-bands in the blue region"; Fig. 7.15. |
| **Colour balance / dmax** | Explicit: many commercial films are non-neutral at dmax by design, sacrificed to keep mid-densities correct. | **Silent.** No colour-balance content; no dmax, no per-channel curves. |
| **Alternative systems** | Dye bleach, dye diffusion, Technicolor, Verifax all described with their image consequences. | Not covered. |
| **Framing of development** | A step "not being discussed in detail in the present work"; colour development treated as chemistry. | Development framed as **parallel image processing** — "each signal in each picture element is simultaneously subjected to image processing in a parallel fashion", contrasted with the serial processing of electronic imaging. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.224 (PDF 233), Fig. 7.16]` |
| **Numbers on dyes** | None (curves lost as images). | None (curves lost as images). |

`[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.189–215 (PDF 195–221); Ch. XI, p.217 (PDF 223); Tani 1995, §1.1, pp.5–6 (PDF 14–15); §7.5, pp.223–224 (PDF 232–233)]` **[F]**

**[E]** The two accounts are complementary rather than contradictory, and the split is chronological: the 1966 source is the authority in this material for *where the coupler sits and what the dye is like*, the 1995 source for *what the coupler releases and how that shapes the image*. Neither supplies a single numeric dye density. Any colour-reproduction model built from this material has complete mechanism and complete sign structure, and no spectra at all.
