### 20.2 The 1922 time–gamma data in detail

**Era: 1922.** Because this is the only measured time-gamma corpus in the material, its exact form matters.

The three published characteristic curves per material were developed for **3, 6 and 12 minutes** in **pyro developer of tray strength (1 + 1 + 1 + 7 parts)** at **20 °C** with stirring at **40 rpm**, and each curve is "the **graphical mean of the density measurements of three test strips**." Exposure: usually **16 seconds** total at **1 candle meter** at the strip, the nine sector-wheel apertures giving **8, 4, 2, 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 seconds**; "In case the 16 seconds' exposure did not include all of the toe and shoulder of the curve, shorter or longer exposures were made." `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[Q]**

Chart axes, all 86 materials:

| Chart figure | Ordinate | Abscissa |
|---|---|---|
| Figure 1 — characteristic curves (3, 6, 12 min) | **D, 0 to 3.0** | **log E in candle-meter-seconds, 7.5 to 2.0** in the "+10" convention (i.e. −2.5 to +2.0 modern) |
| Figure 2 — contrast-development curve | **γ, 0 to 3.0** (ticks .5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0) | **minutes of development, 0 to 12** (ticks 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) |
| Figure 3 — fog-contrast curve | **fog density, 0 to 1.0** (tick .5) | **γ, 0 to 4.0** (ticks .5 to 4.0) |
| Figure 4 — spectrogram | — | wavelength, ticks 400 / 500 / 600 mµ |

`[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.31–32 (PDF 32–33); charts pp.35–120 (PDF 36–121)]` **[Q]**

**What the printed alphanumerics per material are** — and therefore what is *not* in the time-gamma corpus as numbers: chart number, class caption, developer letter (W/X/Y/Z), **B.S. speed**, **scale**, **resolution number**, and filter factors. **No numeric gamma, no gamma-infinity, no inertia, no fog value and no development time to a stated gamma is printed for any of the 86 materials.** All of that exists only as curves. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.31–32 (PDF 32–33)]` **[F]**

The survey's own ranges, for scale: **speed B.S. 18 to 1050** using only unambiguous values; **scale 5 to 300**; **resolution number 12 to 28**. Developer X was used for every surveyed film (charts 72–83); W, X, Y and Z were all used on plates. `[Davis & Walters 1922, charts pp.35–120 (PDF 36–121)]` **[Q]**

**Two unit conventions that will corrupt any ingestion if missed.** First, **"scale" in 1922 is the antilog** of the straight-line log-E projection — a plain intensity ratio like 132 or 300, *not* a log range: `Scale = 10^(Δ log E)`, so "SCALE 300" means Δlog E = 2.48, about 8.2 stops. Second, **"latitude" in 1922 is subject-dependent and is not a plate property**: `Latitude = Scale ÷ (subject intensity range)`, expressed as an allowable multiplicative factor on exposure time; the worked example is scale 132, subject range 1:33, giving **latitude 4** — "so that if 1 second were the shortest correct exposure, 4 seconds could be given and the plate would still show a correct tone representation." The 1922 authors' own footnote concedes that other writers call their *scale* "latitude". `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.13–14 (PDF 14–15)]` **[Q]**

**And one that will corrupt any gamma comparison.** 1922 densities are **visual** (Martens polarisation photometer) and are measured **differentially against a fog strip**, so they exclude glass, gelatin and chemical fog. "It may be remarked that densities measured visually do not represent photographic densities … The plates measured in this work are neutral in color, although developed with pyro, and **the only results which may be affected materially by the difference between visual and photographic density are the values of the contrast**, but in that case they still give reliable comparative data." **1922 gammas are therefore visual-density gammas, offset from modern diffuse-density gammas by an amount the source does not state, and there is no dmin in any 1922 curve by construction.** `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.22–23 (PDF 23–24)]` **[F]**

### 20.3 Temperature: what can and cannot be built

Assembled from §12.14 and §12.19. **No source in this material gives a numeric temperature coefficient of development.** The available inputs are:

| Input | Value | Era | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Activation energy, diffusion processes | **4–7 kcal/mol** | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.174 (PDF 180), Table 9.1]` |
| Activation energy, development of silver halide from a latent-image centre | **10–20 kcal/mol** | 1966 | as above |
| Activation energy, fog development (reduction without latent image) | **20–30 kcal/mol** | 1966 | as above |
| Image:fog rate ratio at normal development temperature | **≈ 1,000,000** | 1966 | as above |
| Reference development temperature for all 1922 sensitometry | **20 °C** | 1922 | `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` |
| Processing temperature trend over calendar years, colour negative films and colour papers, with step counts annotated | figure only, no tabulated values | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, §8.2, p.237 (PDF 246), Fig. 8.2c]` |

**[E]** Applying Arrhenius to the 1966 bands gives the only temperature model this material supports: image density rate rises by roughly a factor of 2 to 4 per 10 K near room temperature (Eₐ 10–20 kcal/mol), fog rate by more (Eₐ 20–30 kcal/mol), and diffusion-limited steps by much less (Eₐ 4–7 kcal/mol). The consequences that follow, none of them drawn by the sources: raising development temperature **degrades the image:fog ratio**; a diffusion-limited developer — the regime the 1995 source places at `E_1/2` more negative than +170 mV — is **less temperature-sensitive** than a surface-reaction-limited one; and time/temperature compensation cannot be exact across the whole curve because gamma (image channel) and dmin (fog channel) do not share an activation energy.

**A documented counter-example worth keeping,** because it shows the compensation can be engineered away: Polacolor, where "**as the temperature rises the diffusion rate of unoxidized dye-developer will increase but, at the same time, the interval before the reaction is terminated is correspondingly shortened**, so that, unlike other colour products, the effect of temperature on the processing of Polacolor is not critical." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.210 (PDF 216)]` **[F]**

### 20.4 Agitation

Complete content, all 1922: rocking halves the time to a given contrast relative to no motion; stirring rate and method must be held constant; the survey standard was silver cages of four plates rotated at **40 rpm** in silver-plated cans in a thermostatted bath; tank development is recommended because it "takes care of small differences in exposure without disturbing contrast ratios." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.16, 22 (PDF 17, 23)]` **[Q]**

**The 1929, 1966 and 1995 sources contain no processing-agitation data.** In the 1995 source agitation appears only as *emulsion ripening* agitation, never as processing agitation. `[Wall 1929; Duffin 1966; Tani 1995]` **[F]**

**[E]** The single usable number is therefore a **factor of 2 in time between static and rocked development** at 1922 tray-strength pyro, 20 °C. Nothing in the material lets that be resolved into an agitation *rate* dependence, and the 40 rpm figure is a reference condition, not a data point on a curve.

### 20.5 Developer composition and type

The formulae are in §12.18 and the potential–rate relation in §12.3; the outcome-level links are itemised in the master table of §20.1. Three points that the table does not carry, and which are the substance of "developer composition" as a variable:

- **Developer type does not move speed, but it does move the mechanism.** Speed is developer-independent at each developer's own optimum `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]`, yet the same two developers that give equal speed give *different progress types* — CP-20 parallel, D72 granular `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.216 (PDF 225)]`. **[Q]**
- **The effect of an emulsion addendum can invert with developer type.** A polyethylene-oxide addendum gives up to ×2 speed with metol-hydroquinone or Phenidone-hydroquinone, and *inhibition plus toe desensitization* with hydroquinone alone. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.165–166 (PDF 171–172)]` **[Q]**
- **The effect of emulsion iodide content depends on the developing agent.** Pyro is "more suitable for emulsions rich in iodide than ferrous oxalate"; iodide-rich images "cannot be developed with ferrous oxalate" at all; and the loss of vigour at about 1/12 iodide is "more noticeable with the oxalate developer than with pyrogallol." `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.36–37 (PDF 44–45)]` **[F]**

**Developer concentration** is named as a governing variable — "In addition to the time of development, and the temperature and **concentration** of the developer, account must be taken also of the development characteristics of the plate used" — and is nowhere quantified beyond the 1 + 1 + 1 + 7 "tray strength" dilution of the 1922 formulae. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.16 (PDF 17); p.33 (PDF 34)]` **[F]**

### 20.6 pH

The pH content in this material is thin and almost entirely non-processing:

- In the 1995 development chapter, **pH enters only as an equation symbol** — through the developer half-cell ionisation constants of Eqs. (7.7)–(7.10), whose bodies were lost — and as the figure label "**pH 9**" on the chemical-development plot of Fig. 7.2. **There is no rate-versus-pH data.** `[Tani 1995, §7.1, pp.202–203 (PDF 211–212); Fig. 7.2, p.205 (PDF 214)]` **[F]**
- Coupler ionisation is pH-dependent in the 1966 colour account: "All the colour-forming or colour-coupling substances are moderately strong acids and are converted into **negatively-charged ions in an alkaline solution**, all of them being strong enough to dissolve in aqueous sodium carbonate", and the semiquinone radical cation "loses a proton **in strong alkali**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.192–193 (PDF 198–199)]` **[M]**
- **Emulsion**-side and **coating**-side pH effects are documented and quantified, and belong to manufacture rather than processing, but two of them terminate in a sensitometric outcome: chrome-alum hardening is "effective at the usual emulsion coating pH values, **about 6.0**, but far less effective at higher pH values" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.158–159 (PDF 164–165)]`; and mucochloric acid as hardener loses its acid grouping, which "causes an **appreciable drop in pH and thus sometimes in sensitivity**; this must be allowed for in manufacture" `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.160 (PDF 166)]`. **[Q]**
- Adsorption of stabilizers and antifoggants is strongly pH-dependent, with documented reversals of ordering between pH 5 and pH 10 (§13.10) — which matters because those agents' whole function is to bias the development-versus-fog rate ratio. `[Tani 1995, §6.5, pp.186–189 (PDF 195–198), Figs. 6.13, 6.14]` **[Q]**
- One curious 1966 kinetic result on pH, from the stabilizer side: with thiourea on gelatin-free AgBr in the presence of the tetrazaindene, the stabilizer **inhibits** silver-sulphide formation at high pH (about 8.0) but **actually accelerates** it at **pH 5.85** — "surprising because 5.85 is quite a normal digestion pH and is one at which the tetrazaindene is very effective as a stabilizer." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.147–148 (PDF 153–154)]` **[Q]**

**A reader looking for developer pH versus gamma, speed or fog will not find it in this material.** No source relates processing-solution pH to a sensitometric outcome numerically. **[F]**

The complete content, gathered because it is scattered:

It behaves identically with solvents such as cyanide to the red fog formed in the emulsion itself | 1929 | `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.42 (PDF 50)]` | **[F]** |
| Colour reversal and negative-positive processes both finish with a **ferricyanide/hypo** bleach, leaving the dye images only | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.198 (PDF 204)]` | **[F]** |
| Internal-image assay uses a brief **potassium ferricyanide** bleach followed by a developer containing **thiosulphate** sized to etch the grains | 1966 | `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.183–184 (PDF 189–190)]` | **[F]** |
| A **2-minute bleach in acid 0.1 % potassium ferricyanide** before development removes pre-existing silver emulsion-fog centres — the difference between traces A and B of the fog-growth family | 1995 | `[Tani 1995, p.220 (PDF 229), Fig. 7.13]` | **[Q]** |

X, pp.208–210 (PDF 214–216)]` | **[F]** |

**Explicit absences.** The 1922 source gives **no fixing, washing or drying specifications whatsoever** — a notable gap in a paper that specifies development to the revolution per minute. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.22, 31 (PDF 23, 32)]` **[F]** The 1929 source's extensive washing chapter concerns **washing the emulsion during manufacture**, not washing the processed film — its washing numbers (water not above 15 °C, 10–12 °C better; historic 12–18 hours in 1892 falling to 4–6 hours and in some cases 2–3 hours by 1929; Volhard sulphocyanide titration for the bromide endpoint) are manufacturing data and must not be read as processing data. `[Wall 1929, Ch. VIII, pp.144–145 (PDF 151–152)]` **[F]** The 1995 source gives no fixing or washing chemistry at all; its only processing-solution content beyond development is the replenishment-rate trend of Fig. 8.2b. `[Tani 1995, §8.2, p.237 (PDF 246), Fig. 8.2]` **[F]**

### 20.8 Fog and dmin as processing outcomes

Consolidated, because fog is the outcome the sources treat most carefully:

1. **Fog grows with development time and therefore with gamma.** The 1922 authors take this so seriously that they change the independent variable: "It is well known that the density of chemical fog increases with the time of development and accordingly with the increase of contrast … **For this reason chemical fog in this work is plotted against the contrast (gamma) and not against the time of development.**" The chart Figure 3 ordinate is fog density 0 to 1.0 against γ 0 to 4.0, "the values of the fog (exclusive of glass and gelatin)". `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.31–32 (PDF 32–33)]` **[Q]** via figures
2. **[E]** That choice is itself a modelling statement: the 1922 authors assert that the practically relevant question is *how much fog at a given contrast*, not *how much fog at a given time*, because "the photographer must develop a plate to a certain contrast". A fog model parameterised on time rather than on achieved gamma answers a question the 1922 source deliberately declined to ask.
3. **Fog has two kinetically distinct channels during development** — fast emulsion fog from pre-existing centres, slow initiation-limited developer fog — plus a **time-independent, ferricyanide-removable offset** of pre-existing silver fog centres. `[Tani 1995, §7.4, pp.219–220 (PDF 228–229), Fig. 7.13]` **[Q]**
4. **Chemical sensitization raises the developer-fog channel**: grains bearing sulfur or sulfur-plus-gold centres "can thus **accept electrons from developing agents to form fog centers during development more easily** than emulsion grains without these centers, although these are not emulsion fog centers." `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.220 (PDF 229)]` **[F]**
5. **Fog rises faster than image with temperature** (activation energies of §20.3). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, p.174 (PDF 180), Table 9.1]` **[Q]**
6. **Bromide retards fog** and **iodide favours freedom from fog**, both at a speed cost. `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.15–16 (PDF 16–17); Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.36 (PDF 44)]` **[F]**
7. **Fog is developer-dependent**, and an aged emulsion may fog only in a high-activity developer. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.148–149 (PDF 154–155)]` **[F]**
8. **Fog need not be neutral** — sulphide contamination gives **yellow fog**. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.149 (PDF 155)]` **[F]**
9. **Aldehyde hardeners can produce fog**: formaldehyde "probably because of its strong reducing action, is very prone to produce **fog during storage**"; many hardening agents "have been reported to **give fog, particularly in fast emulsions** … All the aldehyde hardeners are reducing agents and will naturally be prone to give fog." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.160–161 (PDF 166–167)]` **[F]**
10. **Static discharge fogs the emulsion**, "frequently rendering it useless", with the risk points named as reeling-up, unreeling for cutting, and withdrawal of sheets from boxes "if it occurs in a very dry atmosphere". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.167–168 (PDF 173–174)]` **[F]**

**[E]** A single scalar dmin driven by one development-time parameter cannot represent this. The material supports at minimum: a time-independent pre-existing offset (removable by ferricyanide), a fast-growing emulsion-fog term, a slow initiation-limited developer-fog term whose magnitude scales with sensitization level and developer activity, a temperature dependence steeper than the image's, and a non-neutral hue channel.

### 20.9 Granularity and sharpness as processing outcomes

**The signed statements exist; the magnitudes do not.**

Granularity:

- Infectious development (`c > 1`): **increased graininess**; inhibition (`c < 1`): **improved graininess**. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.222 (PDF 231), Fig. 7.14]` **[Q]** via figure
- DIR couplers: finer images (finer dye clouds) at the cost of sensitivity and gamma. DAR couplers: higher sensitivity at the cost of graininess. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, pp.223–224 (PDF 232–233)]` **[M]**
- Polymeric couplers pack more coupler into a small volume to give a **fine dye cloud**; diffusible-dye-forming couplers improve graininess by adjusting dye diffusibility. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.224 (PDF 233)]` **[M]**
- Colour developing agent: "fairly low-energy developer giving **fine-grain results**". `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.191 (PDF 197)]` **[F]**
- Chromogenic images are decoupled from silver-grain geometry: "there is **little connection between the grain pattern of the original silver-halide emulsion and that of the developed dye image**"; substantive couplers show "a **pronounced tendency to clump**", an unquantified dye-clumping noise source. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.194, 201 (PDF 200, 207)]` **[F]**
- **[E]** And from §12.21: granular (type B) development is a per-grain binary event carrying counting statistics, while parallel (type A) is a partial-fill process — so equal densities from a colour developer and from a metol-hydroquinone developer need not carry equal noise. `[derived from Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.216–219 (PDF 225–228)]`

**There is no quantitative treatment of granularity anywhere in this material.** No rms granularity, no Selwyn area, no σ-versus-density relation, no aperture specification, no signal-to-noise ratio. The words "granularity" and "graininess" do not occur at all in the 1966 source; the 1995 source uses "graininess" only inside the trade-off sentences above. The 1922 source has no granularity metric; grain enters it only through the resolution number and qualitative remarks. `[Tani 1995, index and §7.5, pp.222–224 (PDF 231–233); Duffin 1966 (zero keyword occurrences); Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–30 (PDF 30–31)]` **[F]**

Sharpness:

- Infectious development: **decreased sharpness**; inhibition: **improved sharpness**. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.222 (PDF 231), Fig. 7.14]` **[Q]** via figure
- Border and fringe effects are, by construction, a sharpness-relevant local density modulation across an edge — with no width and no amplitude given. `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.221 (PDF 230)]` **[M]**
- Diffusion transfer: "the reduction on the catalytic nuclei in the positive sheet must be **very fast otherwise diffusion would spread out and produce unsharp pictures**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.219 (PDF 225)]` **[F]**
- Excessive hardening interferes with developer penetration, and hardener choice changes "the influence of the hardened gelatin on the developed state of the image and thus its **covering power**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, pp.160–161 (PDF 166–167)]` **[F]**
- The 1922 resolution number is a *processing-dependent* measurement: the resolution test used **6 minutes uniform development** in pyro tray strength, and "It is found that **the greater the exposure the lower the resolution** of a plate." The number is a **spacing in thousandths of a millimetre — lower is better**: R = 12 was the best plate in the survey, R = 28 the worst, and "a resolution number of 18 means that the plate was able to resolve lines whose centers were **0.018 mm** apart." Test conditions: **50 mm Zeiss Tessar at f/16**, examination at **100 to 300 diameters**, values the "**mean of several observations by four different observers**", with the authors' own caution that "It is doubtful if consistent values by independent observers can be obtained until the method and exact procedure are better standardized." `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–32 (PDF 30–33), Table 5]` **[Q]**

**Resolution number to interval conversion, 1922** (`[Davis & Walters 1922, p.32 (PDF 33), Table 5]` **[Q]**):

| Resolution number | Interval (mm) | Interval (inches, conv. as printed) |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | 0.012 | 0.00047 |
| 14 | 0.014 | 0.00055 |
| 16 | 0.016 | 0.00063 |
| 18 | 0.018 | 0.00071 |
| 20 | 0.020 | 0.00079 |
| 22 | 0.022 | 0.00087 |
| 24 | 0.024 | 0.00094 |
| 26 | 0.026 | 0.00102 |
| 28 | 0.028 | 0.00110 |
| 30 | 0.030 | 0.00118 |

*(Flag: the printed list of projected spacings includes both 0.024 and 0.025 but no 0.026, while Table 5 lists 26; "0.025" may be a typesetting error for 0.026.)*

**No MTF, no f50, no spread function, no acutance measurement and no edge-overshoot amplitude exists anywhere in this material.** The 1995 source indexes MTF only to a page outside the mined range and resolving power to pages outside it; the 1966 source has none; the 1922 source has the resolution number and nothing else. `[Tani 1995, index; Duffin 1966; Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–30 (PDF 30–31)]` **[F]**

One relevant absence-adjacent 1922 caveat: **all test plates were backed with black shellac (lampblack in alcoholic shellac)** to suppress halation, so every published curve, scale and resolution number is free of halation contributions that a user of an unbacked plate would see. `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.31 (PDF 32)]` **[F]**

### 20.10 Colour as a processing outcome

- **Dye quantity is proportional to developed silver** (design requirement 4), so anything that changes developed silver changes dye density — with the coloured-coupler exception that halves the silver requirement (§19.3). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.190, 214 (PDF 196, 220)]` **[Q]**
- **The three layers' sensitometric curves must be accurately matched or "in certain areas the density of colours will go out of balance"**, and in practice balance is deliberately sacrificed at dmax — "the completely fogged end of a film will often appear **deep green or deep violet** corresponding to insufficient magenta and cyan dyes respectively" — to keep the mid-densities correct. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.199 (PDF 205)]` **[F]**
- **Cross-layer iodide release makes one layer harder to develop**, requiring a separate fogging step (light or KBH₄). `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.203 (PDF 209)]` **[F]**
- **Reversal fogging exposure level** must be limited to avoid solarization-driven partial re-reversal. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.198 (PDF 204)]` **[F]**
- **Where the dye ends up physically sets its band width and peak density** — in solution, narrow and dense; in the solid state, broad and impure. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.201 (PDF 207)]` **[F]**
- **Masking strength is a continuously adjustable mix fraction** of coloured to colourless coupler. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.214 (PDF 220)]` **[Q]**
- **Kodachrome-type processing sequence** determines which layer receives which dye, via back exposure, face exposure and chemical fogging between three colour-development steps; three separate colour developers are required because the couplers are in solution. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, pp.202–203 (PDF 208–209)]` **[F]**
- **UV is the most active radiation in fading of colour materials**, and colour-print supercoats therefore carry UV absorbers. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.167 (PDF 173)]` **[F]**
- **Azo dyes (dye-bleach systems) are more light stable than the azomethines** of conventional chromogenic development. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. X, p.206 (PDF 212)]` **[F]**

**No numeric colour outcome appears anywhere** — no dye densities, no λmax, no neutral-scale deviations, no per-channel gammas. See §19.13. **[F]**

### 20.11 Silver image tone as a processing outcome

Black-and-white image *colour* is treated as a commercially important, processing-dependent outcome:

- "In a black-and-white print material the '**colour**' of the developed silver is of very great commercial importance. By their nature, the chlorobromide emulsions used in **modern 'bromide papers'** give **warm-toned** images. Organic stabilizer-type molecules, in particular **benzotriazole** and related substances, when added to the emulsion, usually **in addition to a modern stabilizer**, change the **physical form of the developed image**, giving a **colder toned** image", "probably by modifying the surface nature of the developed grain." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, p.151 (PDF 157)]` **[F]**
- **Hot glazing** raises the developed silver "to a temperature **near to 100 °C**", producing "a marked **diminution of density**" and a change "from the good black obtained by the development procedure to a rather dullish **brown**", sometimes with a metallic sheen — "**bronzing** or **plumming**". Countered by adding 4,5-disubstituted-2-mercapto oxazoles or 2,5-dimercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole to the emulsion **or to the supercoat**; many such compounds form very sparingly soluble silver salts and are therefore strongly adsorbed to the image silver. `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VII, pp.151–152 (PDF 157–158)]` **[Q]**
- **Diffusion transfer** untoned "gives an **unpleasant yellow-brown image**"; toners are "**adsorbed to the surface of the silver image during growth and change its structure and surface reflectivity**." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. XI, p.219 (PDF 225)]` **[M]**
- The 1929 source's controlled experiment: image colour is set by **rate of development / rate of silver deposition**, not by exposure and not by emulsion composition. The series ran pure AgCl through 5, 10, 20 % to pure AgBr, exposures 1:1 to 1:1024 under a step plate of densities 1 to 3.01, with a **constant metol-hydroquinone developer** and three light sources (magnesium ribbon, Nernst lamp, incandescent gas). "Chapman Jones has also proved that the color of the image is dependent on the size of the silver particles." `[Wall 1929, Ch. V, pp.95–96 (PDF 102–103)]` **[Q]**
- Chloride and chlorobromide emulsions give "the extremely fine-grained image … **more like a stain than the normal silver image**." `[Wall 1929, Ch. V, p.91 (PDF 98)]` **[F]**

**No reflectance or spectral data accompany any of these tone statements.** The direction (warm ↔ cold, black → brown under heat, density loss with bronzing) is documented; there is no numeric tone or hue measurement in this material. **[F]**

### 20.12 Processing trends over time, and the 1995 forward view

**Era: 1995.** "Photographic processing with solutions containing numerous chemicals poses great problems for silver halide photography to meet demands such as the need for **rapid processing** and **environmental protection**. Extensive efforts are being made to develop **dry-processing** silver halide photographic materials as well as to improve the processing of conventional photographic materials. Remarkable progress is being made in dry processing by developing **photothermographic materials** based on silver halide photography and in conventional processing … especially by developing **minilab printer-processors** for rapid processing that meet environmental protection standards." `[Tani 1995, §8.2, p.236 (PDF 245)]` **[F]**

**Fig. 8.2** plots, against calendar year, for **colour negative films** and **colour papers** separately: **(a) processing time**, **(b) replenishment rate of processing solutions**, **(c) processing temperature**, with "The number in (c) refers to the **number of processing steps**." The trend directions are stated in the surrounding prose (rapid processing, environmental protection) but **no tabulated values survive**; the curves are images. Minilab references: Tokuda et al., **1986**; Suzuki et al., **1993**. `[Tani 1995, §8.2, pp.236–237 (PDF 245–246), Fig. 8.2]` **[Q]** via figure

**[E]** The three panels together are a statement that processing time, replenishment and temperature were driven jointly, with step count as a fourth, discrete variable — i.e. the four are not independent design choices, and a historical processing model that varies time alone against a fixed temperature and step count does not describe how the industry actually moved.

**Era: 1966.** The corresponding period statement: robust hardened layers are needed because "it is frequently customary today to process films at **elevated temperatures**, for instance in the rapid-processing methods used for quick access recording materials and the automatic processing machinery available for X-ray films." And on diffusion transfer: "The processing time is short and takes **between 10 seconds and 1 minute** in present-day materials." `[Duffin 1966, Ch. VIII, p.158 (PDF 164); Ch. XI, p.217 (PDF 223)]` **[Q]**

**Era: 1922.** The period baseline: **3 to 12 minutes** in tray-strength pyro at **20 °C**, with 12 minutes "the time limit of practical development". `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.31–32 (PDF 32–33)]` **[Q]**

**[E]** Read across the eras, development time for a normal camera negative moves from a 3–12 minute window at 20 °C in 1922, through elevated-temperature machine processing in 1966, to the minilab-era trend of Fig. 8.2 in 1995. This document contains no intermediate numbers, so the trajectory is qualitative between those anchors.

### 20.13 Absence inventory for this section

Stated explicitly, so that no reader searches this document for what is not in it:

1. **No γ-versus-time equation, no γ∞ value, and no development-rate constant.** Not in 1922 (explicitly absent), not in 1929 (γ∞ used as a factory term but never defined or tabulated), not in 1966 (development deferred to another volume), not in 1995 (no closed-form `D(t)` or `γ(t)`). `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.12 (PDF 13); Wall 1929, Ch. I p.8 (PDF 16); Duffin 1966, Ch. XI p.217 (PDF 223); Tani 1995, §7.3]` **[F]**
2. **No numeric temperature coefficient of development.** Only the 1966 activation-energy bands. **[F]**
3. **No agitation-rate dependence.** Only the 1922 factor of 2 between static and rocked, and the 40 rpm reference condition. **[F]**
4. **No developer pH → sensitometry relation.** **[F]**
5. **No numeric bromide table.** Only Figs. 10 and 11 of the 1922 source, and Eder's 0.1–3 parts per 1000 emulsion addition from 1929. **[F]**
6. **No developer-exhaustion or replenishment data**, beyond the unlabelled trend of Fig. 8.2b. **[F]**
7. **No fixing, washing or drying specification** for a conventional negative anywhere in the material. **[F]**
8. **No granularity metric of any kind.** **[F]**
9. **No MTF, f50, spread function, acutance measurement, or edge-overshoot amplitude.** **[F]**
10. **No inhibitor diffusion length or diffusion coefficient in µm or cm²/s** (see §13.9 for the full inventory of what does exist). **[F]**
11. **No numeric dye densities, λmax, or unwanted-absorption fractions.** **[F]**
12. **No characteristic-curve parameters for any real stock** in the 1966 and 1995 sources — no dmin, dmax, gamma, toe or shoulder values. The 1922 source has 86 stocks' curves but only as page images, with speed, scale, resolution number, developer letter and filter factors as the printed alphanumerics. **[F]**
13. **No Callier coefficient and no diffuse-versus-specular density treatment** beyond the 1922 visual-versus-photographic-density caveat. **[F]**
14. **No reciprocity-failure bounds as numbers** — no Schwarzschild exponent, no threshold intensities, no speed-loss magnitudes; the 1995 source supplies the *coupling* of HIRF to development time and activity (§12.9) without a coefficient, and the 1966 source supplies mechanism only. `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.212–213 (PDF 221–222); Duffin 1966, Ch. IX, pp.182, 186–187 (PDF 188, 192–193)]` **[F]**
15. **No print-stage or duplication modelling.** Colour paper appears in the 1995 source only as a curve in Fig. 8.2, and in the 1966 source as a product class with layer-order and speed-balance statements but no curves. **[F]**

Every date below is reproduced with the wording the source prints. Where a source hedges ("about", "mid-1920s", "the early 1950s"), the hedge is part of the datum and is preserved. Where the 1993/1996 IPI guide and the 2020 NEDCC leaflet give different dates or different accounts, both rows appear and the divergence is stated in §21.16 — they are never merged.
