### 21.2 Cellulose nitrate

**Composition.** "To make nitrate plastic in the first place, nitro (NO2) groups are grafted onto the long molecular chains of native cellulose." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] [F]

The 1966 account frames it as the parent of all flexible base: "The original flexible film base was prepared from cellulose nitrate, and was for many years the standard material. Although possessing many satisfactory features, such as excellent mechanical properties, this ester is highly inflammable and once ignited can supply its own oxygen to continue the combustion and is therefore very difficult to extinguish." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.47–48 (PDF 51–52)] [F]

**Attribution of introduction.** Duffin attributes the introduction to George Eastman without a date: "It was only the introduction of cellulose-nitrate film by George Eastman that led to the rapid growth in the popularity of photography" [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.47 (PDF 51)]. The 2020 leaflet supplies the month and year: "In August 1889, Eastman Kodak began selling the first photographic negatives on cellulose nitrate flexible film support." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)] [F]

**Formats never made on nitrate.** "No 16mm or 8mm motion picture film was manufactured on nitrate base." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)] The 2020 leaflet states this more broadly: "16mm, regular 8, and super 8 movie formats were considered amateur formats and were always made on a safety film base." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2), note E] [F]

**Physical properties as printed.** "Nitrate sheet film tends to have a very thick and rigid base." Film pack negatives, produced in the same sizes as sheet film, "used a much thinner and a very flexible based film. These negatives will feel like roll film." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2), notes B, C] No thickness figure in inches, mils or micrometres is given for nitrate in any of these sources. [F]

**Amateur roll nitrate curl.** "Amateur roll films were not marked but can be identified by their tendency to curl into very tight scrolls (later roll films were coated on both sides to prevent such curling)." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)] [F]

**Manufacturer scope caveat, printed explicitly.** "Unfortunately, Eastman Kodak is the only manufacturer that has supplied any dates on nitrate film production. These dates do not apply to other manufacturers' films, nor do they give an indication of when Kodak started selling safety films. For example, nitrate sheet film production ended in 1939, but Kodak began test marketing safety based sheet film sometime in the mid-1920s. For most formats, there was a carryover period when both types of film were made." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2)] [F]

**Optical properties.** No refractive index, transmission, tint or haze figure for nitrate base appears in any of these sources. Source silent. [F]

### 21.3 Cellulose diacetate

**Definition by acetyl content — the only chemical definition in these sources.** Fully acetylated cellulose triacetate "contains 44.8 % acetyl groups per molecule. In fact, fully acetylated material is not used for film base purposes owing to the preferred solubility of the less completely acetylated material: earlier cellulose acetates were only 40 % acetylated, called 'diacetate', while more recent products are 43 % acetylated and referred to as 'triacetate'." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.48–49 (PDF 52–53)] [Q]

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Acetyl content, fully acetylated cellulose triacetate | 44.8 % acetyl groups per molecule | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.48 (PDF 52)] |
| Acetyl content, "diacetate" | 40 % acetylated | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.48–49 (PDF 52–53)] |
| Acetyl content, "triacetate" | 43 % acetylated | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.48–49 (PDF 52–53)] |

[Q]

**Solvent consequence, and why it matters historically.** "Acetone can be used as the solvent of 'diacetate' but 'triacetate' is not soluble in that solvent and requires the use of methylene chloride." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.49 (PDF 53)] The corollary is a hard industrial gate on the triacetate transition: the introduction of the more highly acetylated base "was made possible only when methylene chloride became commercially available in large quantities." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] [F]

**Dates.** Diacetate is dated only by the 2020 leaflet: sheet film 1925–1950, roll film 1920s–1935; manufacturers "Agfa, Ansco, Dupont, Defender, Kodak" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. The 1993/1996 guide never breaks acetate down by chemistry in its history section; it states only that the guide's triacetate-derived data "apply as well to diacetate, acetate butyrate, and acetate propionate film bases" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.2 (PDF 2)]. The granular sub-acetate chronology is therefore single-sourced. [F]

**Handling behaviour.** "Material prepared from acetates with 43 % acetylation is less susceptible to physical deformation in handling." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.49 (PDF 53)] — i.e. the 40 % diacetate is, by this statement, the more deformation-prone of the two. No numeric deformation figure is given. [M]

### 21.4 Cellulose acetate propionate and cellulose acetate butyrate (the mixed esters)

**Composition.** The mixed esters replace some of the acetyl groups by propionyl and butyryl: the source names the substituent groups as `C2H5CO-` and `C3H7CO-` (the OCR of the source renders these as `C,H;CO-` and `C;H,CO`; the intended groups are unambiguous from the ester names). [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.51–52 (PDF 55–56)] [F]

**Why they were introduced — stated purpose.** "Acetopropionate and acetobutyrate bases were introduced as a means of improving these properties; both these bases possess lower water take-up and therefore smaller dimensional changes." The verdict in the same paragraph is blunt: "All these changes improve the properties only marginally and real improvements have been obtained only after the arrival of the polyester bases." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.51–52 (PDF 55–56)] [F]

**Dates.** Only the 2020 leaflet dates them, and it prints the names with two apparent typographic errors, reproduced here as printed: "cellulose acetate propiarate", sheet 1930–1945, roll 1920–1945, manufacturer Kodak; "cellulose acetate butynate", sheet 1935–present, roll cell printed "—", manufacturer Kodak [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. Note that the leaflet's running prose on the same page spells the second correctly as "cellulose acetate butyrate" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)] — so the table heading is the error, not the substance. [F]

**No water-uptake numbers.** Neither source gives a percentage water take-up, a hygroscopic expansion coefficient, or a dimensional-change percentage for any of the three esters. The comparison is ordinal only. Source silent where a reader would expect data. [F]

### 21.5 Cellulose triacetate

**Composition and acetyl content.** 43 % acetylated; see the table in §21.3. Fully acetylated material (44.8 %) is explicitly not used as film base [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.48–49 (PDF 52–53)]. [Q]

**Manufacture — process numbers.** Acetylation is carried out either in acetic-acid solution at **70 °C** with acetic anhydride and concentrated sulphuric acid as catalyst, "or better, by treating a suspension of cellulose fibres in methylene chloride at 45 °C" with the same reagents; "The completion of both these processes takes many hours." Back-hydrolysis to the required acetyl percentage uses aqueous sulphuric acid, "for example about 70 %", optionally as a two-phase process with the acetate dissolved in methylene chloride. Casting solvents named: methylene chloride with butanol, methanol or acetone. [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.49 (PDF 53)] [Q]

**Cellulose feedstock, and the shift in feedstock.** "Cotton is almost pure cellulose and for many years the primary source of cellulose for the preparation of film base, and paper, was from cotton linters, the scrap material remaining after the best cotton has been removed from the cotton seed and from rags. Today, however, cellulose is obtained almost entirely from wood pulp because modern methods of handling and purification of the cellulose make that source by far the cheapest." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.47 (PDF 51)] [F]

**Role in the chronology.** Triacetate is the base that replaced nitrate in 35 mm motion picture film in 1951 [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)], and the 2020 leaflet dates it 1945–present in both sheet and roll, made by "almost every film manufacture[r]" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. Note the four-to-six-year gap between the leaflet's 1945 introduction date and the 1951 motion-picture changeover — both sources are consistent with a staged, format-by-format adoption, and neither states that the two dates should be reconciled. [F]

**The "safety base" naming, and its afterlife.** Cellulose acetate is "the base originally called 'safety base' because it is non-inflammable and is, in fact, difficult to keep burning. Some modern films are still marked safety films, a legacy of the days when the user liked to be sure that he was not handling the very dangerous nitrate." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.48 (PDF 52)] This is a 1966 statement that the marking had already become vestigial. It bears directly on identification: because polyester is *also* marked "Safety Film", the marking alone does not distinguish acetate from polyester after 1955 (§21.13). [F]

### 21.6 Polyester (polyethylene terephthalate, PET)

**Composition and synthesis route.** PET is "chemically identical with I.C.I.'s Terylene fibre" (the source's OCR renders the company as `J.C.I.'s`). Route as printed: terephthalic acid → its dimethyl ester → reaction with ethylene glycol, with "a very small quantity of sodium metal or lead oxide" as catalyst → the bis glycol ester → polymer by heating under vacuum. [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.52–53 (PDF 56–57)] [F]

**Forming — the numeric process datum.** PET base is "extruded in a molten state at a high temperature, around 250 °C, and immediately after issuing from the slot it is stretched both longitudinally and laterally. The molecules arrange themselves regularly during this elongation and a short heat treatment then causes them to be stabilized in this form." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.52 (PDF 56)] [Q]

This biaxial orientation is the physical origin of the birefringence used to identify polyester (§21.13) — although note that neither source makes that connection explicitly; the orientation statement and the birefringence test are in different documents. [E]

**No plasticiser.** "No plasticizer is added to polyethylene terephthalate films because none is needed and this is another factor contributing to the increased dimensional stability." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] [F] This is a sharp material difference from acetate, which carries 12–15 % or up to 20 % plasticiser depending on the source (§21.10) — and it removes plasticiser exudation (§22.7) from the polyester failure list entirely.

**Physical properties as printed.** "The resulting film has very high physical strength and exceedingly low water take-up." "Dimensional stability is so high that the exacting field of colour separation can now be tackled using film instead of glass plates." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.52–53 (PDF 56–57)] "Polyester cannot be torn (except with tremendous effort) unless a nick or cut exists, while acetate and nitrate are fairly easy to tear." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] No tensile figure, modulus, elongation or water-uptake percentage is given in any source. [F]

**Named products, 1966.** "Kodak's Estar and Du Pont's Cronar are two very high quality bases of this type; the latter has even been introduced recently for X-ray film." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] [F]

**Shortcomings as printed in 1966.** PET is very hard to sub: it is "very insoluble and highly stable which makes simple etching or partial degradation almost impossible", requiring multiple-layer treatments with vinylidene chloride–itaconic acid or vinylidene chloride–ethyl acrylate–acrylic acid copolymers, "the latter being effective after an oxidation etching-treatment with permanganate", followed by normal acetate-type sub layers. Further: "polyester film is very prone to acquiring static and is also very difficult to splice … The latter factor is probably why it has not been used so far for cine films in spite of its high physical strength." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] [F]

The splicing obstacle is confirmed independently 27 years later: "The acceptance of polyester base in cinema films has been slowed somewhat by difficulty in splicing on traditional splicing equipment." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] [F] These two statements, from 1966 and 1993, agree on the cause and bracket the delay: in 1966 PET was not used for cine film at all; by 1993 its use "began to increase" in the 1980s "but it is still a small portion of the total film used" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)]. [F]

**Chemical stability — see §22.11 for the quantified 5–10× figure and the 500-year system claim.**

**A 2020 gap worth recording.** The 2020 leaflet names polyester as one of three broad film types and then treats it only as a test outcome — birefringent under crossed polarisers, negative to diphenylamine, floating mid-column in trichloroethylene. It gives **no polyester dates, no stability figure, and does not state that polyester replaced acetate** [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.1, 3, 4 (PDF 1, 3, 4)]. For a 2020 document this is a regression relative to the 1993/1996 guide, not an update. [F]

### 21.7 Other bases recorded in 1966: polystyrene and polycarbonate

**Polystyrene.** "Before the arrival of polyester bases, polystyrene was introduced by a number of manufacturers as a more stable base than triacetate." It is brittle unless melted and elongated (orientated). "Dimensional stability is achieved by the use of thicker base, and intermediate grade films on this base, for lower quality graphic-arts purposes, are still available." Copolymers with methyl methacrylate were also used. Subbing sequence: methacrylic acid–ester copolymers, then cellulose-nitrate layers, then gelatin layers. [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] [F]

Note the trade-off stated: dimensional stability bought with **thickness**, not with material stiffness. No thickness figure is given for polystyrene base. [F]

**Polycarbonate (Agfa).** Introduced specifically because it can be **cast** on existing film-casting machinery: extrusion, needed for polyester and polystyrene, "is expensive, and manufacturers are reluctant to abandon expensive film-casting machinery". Chemistry as printed: bisphenol A plus phosgene in alkaline solution, two-phase with a chlorinated solvent, giving a polycarbonate "with a molecular weight of about 100,000". It is "readily soluble in methylene chloride and gives good films of good dimensional stability, although not as stable as the polyesters." Subbing: a three-layer assembly — a vinyl or similar polymer on the base, then cellulose nitrate or partially hydrolysed acetate, then a gel sub. "Patents reveal that research is still going on." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.54 (PDF 58)] [Q]

Neither the 1993/1996 nor the 2020 preservation document mentions polystyrene or polycarbonate film base at all. Whether either survived into collections in quantity cannot be decided from these sources. [F]

### 21.8 Glass plates as the displaced base — the 1929 and 1966 positions

**1929.** Glass is still the primary base of the plate industry, and the source's coating chapters are built around it. What it says about the glass itself is remarkably thin:

| Property | What the 1929 source says | Class | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thickness of photographic plate glass | No figure is stated. Only: "For the smaller size plates, also, thinner glass is used." | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.168 (PDF 175)] |
| Thickness of carrier glass (a shop fixture, not a plate) | For mounting cut sheet film for flat coating: plate glass 20 × 16 in "should be obtained, one-quarter inch thick" (6.35 mm, conv.), "and the sharp edges ground off" | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.183 (PDF 190)] |
| Tint, colour, transmission, refractive index, haze | **Absent.** The source states no optical property of glass anywhere, and never mentions glass tint, greenness, base density or transmission. | — | — |
| Flatness / thickness variation | Handled mechanically, not specified: the Cadett coater uses a split, rubber-jointed silver distributing cylinder to accommodate unevenness of the glass; the Smith coater uses a swinging scraper that "adjusts itself to the thickness of the glass" | [M] | [Wall 1929, Ch. X, pp.170, 172 (PDF 177, 179)] |
| Plate sizes named | whole plate 6½ × 8½ in; double-half 6½ × 9½ in; quarter plate 3¼ × 4¼ in; English lantern 3¼ × 3¼ in; 4 × 5 in; 8 × 10 in; German machine maximum 18 × 24 cm | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. I, p.9 (PDF 17); Ch. X, p.168 (PDF 175)] |

**1966.** The reason glass was retained, and the reason it was lost, are both stated in one sentence: glass was "the only suitable material with sufficient planarity and of the desired degree of inertness to use as the base", and "The arrival of dimensionally-stable film base has resulted in the glass plate being finally displaced from its position of supremacy in the graphic-arts field. Today, only the most exact work and a number of scientific purposes, where the ability of glass to remain level without any other means of support, remain the realms of glass plates; in all other spheres film is the normal base for negative materials." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.47 (PDF 51)] [F]

The named agent of displacement is polyester: "Dimensional stability is so high that the exacting field of colour separation can now be tackled using film instead of glass plates." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] [F]

**One relevant later datum on glass plates.** Gelatin emulsions on glass "may suffer delamination from the glass support at RHs below 25%" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.19 (PDF 19)] — this is the reason a worked mixed-collection example in that source settles on 40 % RH rather than the drier optimum for acetate [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.5 (PDF 5)]. [Q]

### 21.9 Base manufacture and the numbers that come with it

**Casting (acetate).** Casting surfaces "must be exceedingly flat and polished because the whole thickness, which is usually between 0.003" and 0.01", of the base depends on the regularity of the cast layer". [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.50 (PDF 54)] The machine is either a very large drum, labelled **12–20 feet** in diameter on the source's figure ("Base-casting machines — diagrammatic", Fig. 3.1), or a flexible metal belt; surfaces are of copper, nickel "or, more recently, polished stainless steel"; "A copper surface must be coated with a renewable surface layer … and a gelatin layer is suitable"; the machine runs in a sealed air space with solvent recovery, and "after nearly one circuit of the moving surface the film base is tough enough to take off." Three stated precautions: static earthing; absolute freedom from dust; efficient solvent recovery "both from the economic standpoint and also to trap the poisonous methylene chloride." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.50 (PDF 54)] [Q]

**The band side / air side asymmetry — a structural fact of cast base.** "There are marked differences between the response of the two sides of the film, that in contact with the metal surface, the band side, and the open surface, the air side; this can cause curling of the film." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] [M] This is the only statement in any of these sources that gives a *mechanism* for intrinsic curl in cast base, as distinct from RH-driven curl or coating-driven curl.

**Casting in 1929, by contrast, is barely described.** The 1929 source refers to base manufacture only as "the dope casting and substratum machine", whose mandrels should be interchangeable with the coater's; **no casting wheel, drum, or solvent for the base itself is described** [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.194 (PDF 201)]. A trade advertisement in the same volume lists "Coating Machines for Raw Film (Band and Drum …)" — the OCR of the advertisement is corrupt at that point (raw string "Band and Drum MMJUMjQ") [Wall 1929, advertisement pages (PDF 266)]. So both the band and the drum route existed commercially in 1929, but the 1929 text does not describe either. [F]

**Base thickness — every figure in these sources, consolidated.**

| Base / format | Thickness as printed | Metric equivalent | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cellulose acetate base, general | "usually between 0.003" and 0.01"" | 76–254 µm (conv.) | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.50 (PDF 54)] |
| "Celluloid" cut sheet film | "the thicker celluloid films, about ten one-thousandths of an inch thick" (10 mils) | 0.254 mm / 254 µm (conv.) | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.182 (PDF 189)] |
| "Celluloid" roll film | Not stated; only "variation in thickness of the celluloid" is compensated by free-swinging mandrel bearings | — | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.195 (PDF 202)] |
| Nitrate sheet film | "very thick and rigid base" — no figure | — | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2), note B] |
| Nitrate film pack film | "much thinner and a very flexible based film" — no figure | — | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2), note C] |
| Microfilm on polyester | thinner than acetate — no figure; the stated benefit is "the possibility of using thinner supports, thereby increasing the number of images on each roll" | — | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] |
| Polystyrene | "Dimensional stability is achieved by the use of thicker base" — no figure | — | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] |
| Subbing layer | "only a few microns thick when dried down" | few µm | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] |

The 1929 cut-sheet figure of 10 mils sits at the top of the 1966 general acetate range of 3–10 mils, which is consistent with the 1929 source's own description of cut sheet as "the thicker celluloid films". All conversions marked (conv.) are ours, not the sources'. [Q]

**Raw sheet stock size, 1929.** Cut sheet film was supplied in sheets "approximately 50 by 21 inches" (127 × 53.3 cm, conv.); after trimming the irregular, "slightly cockled" edges the working area is "48 by 20 inches" (121.9 × 50.8 cm, conv.). The preferred working sub-size for flat coating was 20 × 16 in. [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.182–183 (PDF 189–190)] [Q]

**Splicing "celluloid", 1929 — a composition-by-inference datum.** The joining cement is celluloid 10 g, amyl acetate 330 ccm (the source's OCR prints "Amvl acetate"), acetone 670 ccm; scrape ⅜ in of each surface and clamp between steel plates at least ¾ in wide by 1/16 in thick. "In coating, the butt of the joint must be against the travel of the film … If this be reversed, the little ledge formed by the edge of the film causes streaks in the coating." [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.182–183 (PDF 189–190)] [Q]

**Motion-picture stock lengths, 1929.** "The longest length of motion picture film that is commercially available is four hundred feet and this is generally preferred to the two hundred feet lengths. These two are the standards, though it is possible to obtain one hundred feet lengths and even odd lengths." [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.209 (PDF 216)] [Q]

**Edge hardness, 1929.** "The edges of the celluloid are sufficiently sharp to cut through any plating in a very short time" — the coating roller must be solid silver, hard rubber or bakelite, never plated. [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.196 (PDF 203)] [F]

### 21.10 Plasticiser — composition and loading

Two sources give a plasticiser loading and they do not agree in either the figure or the basis of the percentage. Both are recorded.

| Statement | Figure | Basis as printed | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-volatile esters — octyl phthalate or tri-m-cresyl phosphate — "incorporated at a proportion up to 20 % of the acetate, prevents the base becoming brittle, probably by getting in among the chains of the polymer and assisting them to slide over one another" | **up to 20 %** | "of the acetate" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.49 (PDF 53)] |
| "Plasticizers make up about 12% to 15% by weight of the film." | **about 12 % to 15 %** | "by weight of the film" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)] |

[Q] The two are not formally contradictory — "up to 20 % of the acetate" is an upper bound on a resin-relative basis, "12 % to 15 % by weight of the film" is a typical value on a whole-film basis — but no source states a conversion between the two bases, and the difference should not be smoothed away.

**The two stated purposes of plasticiser, 1993/1996.** "Their main job is to slow down the rate of burning of the film, should it ever catch on fire. The awful tragedies that occurred because of the high flammability of nitrate film (fires that consumed film vaults, sometimes killing many people) made the photographic industry very careful about the burning properties of safety film. … The second function of plasticizers is to reduce the dimensional instability of film due to solvent loss or humidity change. All cellulosic films will shrink under dry conditions and expand under damp conditions; minimizing this behavior is an important role of plasticizer additives." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)] [F]

**The 1966 stated purpose is only the second one** — "prevents the base becoming brittle" [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.49 (PDF 53)]. The flame-retardancy rationale is absent from the 1966 account. Recorded as a divergence in emphasis, not a contradiction. [F]

**Nitrate also carries plasticiser.** "(Nitrate film also contains plasticizers that exude onto the surface as deterioration progresses.)" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)] [F]

**Polyester carries none** — see §21.6. [F]

### 21.11 Optical properties of film bases — what these sources actually contain

This subsection exists because the absence is as important as the presence, and because a reader coming to a knowledge base on emulsions and bases will expect refractive indices and transmission curves and will not find them here.

| Optical quantity | Status in these sources |
|---|---|
| Refractive index of any base (nitrate, any acetate, polyester, polystyrene, polycarbonate, glass) | **Not stated anywhere.** No source gives a refractive index for any base material. [F] |
| Spectral transmission of any base, fresh or degraded, at any wavelength | **Not stated anywhere.** [F] |
| Base optical density / base-plus-fog attributable to the support | **Not stated anywhere.** [F] |
| Base tint or colour of undegraded film | One statement only: nitrate is used in very small amounts as a subbing layer in acetate and polyester products, which in the diphenylamine spot test "may cause a very faint blue tinge to be seen in the support of the cellulose acetates and polyester", but this "does not appear to affect either the longevity or the safety of these materials" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. This is the single statement about a base tint of undegraded film in any of these sources, and it is offered as a test artefact, not as a photometric property. [F] |
| Haze / light scattering by base | **Not stated anywhere**, fresh or degraded. [F] |
| Birefringence | Stated for polyester, qualitatively: colour fringes "that resemble the colors formed by oil slicks on ponds" between crossed polarisers; "this phenomenon, known as birefringence, occurs only in polyester film" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)]; "polyester and other highly birefringent materials exhibit red and green interference colors like those seen on soap bubbles. Cellulose nitrates and cellulose acetates do not show these interference colors." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.3 (PDF 3)] No retardance value in nanometres, no fast-axis orientation, no wavelength. [F] |
| Edge light transmission | Stated comparatively only: "polyester film will transmit much more light than acetate or nitrate … Some light will pipe through the edges of the film with acetate, but polyester will look much brighter." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21), Fig. 20] Not quantified. [F] |
| Specific gravity / density | Ordering only, no values: in trichloroethylene "the densest—cellulose nitrate—will sink, while cellulose acetate will rise to the top. Polyester should remain floating near the center of the solution." With the caveat that "the specific gravities for cellulose nitrate and the cellulose acetates fall within a broad range" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. **No specific-gravity numbers are given.** [M] |
| Opacity of the *emulsion* affecting halation | Iodide-containing emulsions "are more opaque, and less likely to suffer from halation and solarization" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.33–34 (PDF 41–42)]; quoted from Eder, "For landscape work bromo-iodide emulsions, with three to four per cent of iodide, are decidedly better than pure bromide emulsions, because halation is less with the former and small details against the sky are better differentiated" [Wall 1929, Ch. III, p.35 (PDF 43)]. This is an emulsion property, not a base property, but it is the only place any of these sources ties a composition figure to a base-related optical effect. [Q] |
| Coefficient of thermal expansion; coefficient of hygroscopic expansion | **Not stated for any base.** Direction only: "All cellulosic films will shrink under dry conditions and expand under damp conditions" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)]. [M] |

The 1929 source is explicit in its own silence: the only base-optics statement of any kind in the whole volume is the halation mechanism, "if the light could be prevented from penetrating right through the emulsion and glass there would be no halation" [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)]. No numeric or qualitative optical property of the celluloid base is given anywhere in it. [F]

### 21.12 Dated snapshots: what a practitioner wrote in 1929 and in 1966

These are first-hand accounts, not histories, and their value is that they fix what was true and sayable at their dates.

**1929 — the word "cellulose nitrate" is not used.** The 1929 source uses only the trade word **"celluloid"** for the film support. It never writes "cellulose nitrate", "nitro-cellulose" or "nitrate base". Nitrate chemistry appears in the volume only as *pyroxylin*, in substratum and collodion-emulsion formulas, and the joining cement is celluloid dissolved in amyl acetate and acetone — which identifies the base as the classic camphor–nitrocellulose celluloid by composition rather than by name. [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.182–188 (PDF 189–195)] The chemical identification is inference from the formulas, not a statement in the source. [M]

**1929 — cellulose acetate is mentioned exactly once, and only in passing.** The single mention is a substratum-compatibility note: for the author's preferred celluloid substratum (gelatine 5 g; glacial acetic acid 50 ccm; water 10 ccm; methyl alcohol 1000 ccm), "**For cellulose acetate film, half the alcohol should be replaced by acetone**" [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.187 (PDF 194)]. The source gives cellulose acetate **no thickness, no optical property, no discussion of stability or flammability**, and never uses the words "safety base" or "non-inflammable". [F]

This is itself the historical datum: in 1929, in a full-length industrial manual on emulsion making and coating, acetate base warranted one clause about a solvent substitution. It is consistent with the 1993/1996 chronology, which puts large-scale acetate manufacture at the mid-1920s and acetate sheet film "in quantity in the late 1930s" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] — in 1929 acetate existed but was not yet the material an emulsion plant had to plan around. [E]

**1929 — flammability is never stated as a property of the base.** The only fire references in the volume are (a) ether substratum fumes, which are "a serious menace to the workmen, and also increase the fire hazard" [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.187 (PDF 194)], and (b) the coating-machine motor, which "must be fully enclosed and should comply with the specifications of the U. S. Government for motors of the explosion proof type" [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.202 (PDF 209)]. Both are implicit acknowledgements of a flammable-solvent and flammable-base environment; neither is a statement about base flammability. [F] Compare the 1966 source, which states nitrate's self-sustaining combustion outright [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.47–48 (PDF 51–52)], and the 2020 leaflet, which states that burning nitrate "cannot be extinguished" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)].

**1929 — the dimensional and static behaviour of celluloid in the plant.** These are the operational facts the 1929 source does give about base behaviour, and they are the earliest quantitative-adjacent record here of base-driven defects:

| Observation | Statement | Class | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Festoon depth and curl | deep festoon loops (10–20 ft) "cause curling and buckling of the celluloid"; a 9 ft shallow loop is much less likely to | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.190 (PDF 197)] |
| Over-drying | film blown dry at the tunnel entrance "has a tendency to become abnormally dry, with a consequent great tendency to curl and to the formation of static in reeling"; remedy: introduce hot air away from the tunnel end and let the film pass into "a cold and relatively damp region so as to allow it to cool off and become slightly damper" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.209 (PDF 216)] |
| Uncoated margin | an uncoated marginal strip at each edge "tend[s] to prevent undue curling at the edges during drying" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.203–205 (PDF 210–212)] |
| Slatted drying reels | "There is no chance for the celluloid to buckle or curl with this arrangement" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.203–205 (PDF 210–212)] |
| Web tension after the trough | unless the web is under extreme tension after the trough "there is a great tendency for it to buckle and the emulsion will run into uneven waves" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.189–190 (PDF 196–197)] |
| Static from forced stripping | stripping celluloid from tacky glass by force generates static electricity which "makes itself apparent on development as fog … particularly noticeable if a stoppage is made in the stripping, as a line of denser fog. How to completely prevent static is not known, but it is much lessened by leaving the plates to get thoroughly chilled, and stripping in a damp room." | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.185 (PDF 192)] |
| Drying-stick contact | "stick markings": a marked curve in the celluloid, and "frequently a thinner line due to the variation in rapidity of drying of the emulsion here" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.203 (PDF 210)] |
| Adhesion | "A gelatine emulsion has the greatest objection to adhere to celluloid. It will do anything but that, unless a substratum is used." | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.185 (PDF 192)] |
| Post-coating rest | "allow it to lie for a few days before use" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.210 (PDF 217)] |

**1966 — the acetate shortcomings section, verbatim, because it is the densest statement of base dimensional behaviour in any of these sources.** "When wetted, as occurs in processing, it 'takes-up' considerable quantities of water and when it dries it is with unequal shrinkage in different directions. This causes a marked change in size of the film and, therefore, a distortion. For so many purposes, this is of no consequence but for graphic-arts purposes, particularly in colour printing, this lack of dimensional stability makes triacetate quite unsuitable. These effects change with age, and re-wetting and re-drying cause still further dimensional changes. Also there are marked differences between the response of the two sides of the film, that in contact with the metal surface, the band side, and the open surface, the air side; this can cause curling of the film. The mechanical strength of acetate film also leaves something to be desired." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] [M]

Four separate claims are packed into that passage and each is worth isolating: (i) processing wets the base and the base takes up water; (ii) the dry-down shrinkage is **anisotropic** — "unequal shrinkage in different directions"; (iii) the behaviour is **age-dependent** — "these effects change with age"; (iv) the two faces of cast base respond differently, which produces curl. None of the four carries a number. [M]

**1966 — the secrecy caveat, which governs how far any 1966 industrial figure can be trusted.** The source states three times that the critical details are unpublished: "there is probably no other area of applied chemistry where the skill of the manufacturer has produced such sophisticated products while the published understanding of the process is so scanty … the very great secrecy which surrounds the truly critical steps of the preparation of the emulsions" [Duffin 1966, Preface, p.9 (PDF 13)]; "there is probably no other branch of applied science in which the manufacturer is less inclined to give away his secrets; all the large manufacturers are in possession of a vast amount of unpublished experience" [Duffin 1966, Ch. IV, p.62 (PDF 66)]. And on the science itself: "the science of photography remains far from a tidy one. One author still disagrees with another and interpretations of the facts, and even in some cases the facts themselves differ from worker to worker." [Duffin 1966, Preface, p.9 (PDF 13)] [F]

### 21.13 Identification methods and their diagnostic physical basis

| Method | Diagnostic property, as stated | Destructive? | Class | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Crossed polarisers (birefringence)** | "When polyester film is placed between two sheets of polarizing plastic and viewed by transmitted light, color fringes appear that resemble the colors formed by oil slicks on ponds. This phenomenon, known as birefringence, occurs only in polyester film. Acetate or nitrate film will not form bands of color in crossed polarizers." Described as "very useful in positively identifying polyester film". | No | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)] |
| **Crossed polarisers** | "polyester and other highly birefringent materials exhibit red and green interference colors like those seen on soap bubbles. Cellulose nitrates and cellulose acetates do not show these interference colors." Interference colours are "most apparent in clear areas"; badly deteriorated material is examined on a light table between two filters. The source includes build instructions for a mat-board viewer. | No | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.3 (PDF 3)] |
| **Edge light-piping** | "When viewed edge on (holding the reel up to a light source and looking through the spokes of the reel), polyester film will transmit much more light than acetate or nitrate … Some light will pipe through the edges of the film with acetate, but polyester will look much brighter." Requires film wound on a core or spoked reel. Relative, not quantified. | No | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21), Fig. 20] |
| **Edge printing — nitrate** | "Much nitrate base film is labeled on the edge with the word Nitrate, which certainly makes it easy to identify." | No | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)] |
| **Edge printing — "Safety" and the 1955 rule** | "Both acetate base film and more modern polyester base films are labeled with the words Safety Film. Films marked Safety which were manufactured prior to 1955 are definitely acetate, not polyester." | No | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] |
| **Edge printing — coverage limits** | "Many manufacturers stamped professional sheet films with an identification along one border. The words generally identified the manufacturer and the type of film: nitrate or safety. Unfortunately, not all manufacturers adopted edge printing identification. It wasn't done on either early nitrate negatives or on some roll film formats." | No | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)] |
| **Notch codes (Kodak sheet film)** | "A 'V' notch code (first from the edge) will identify pre-1949 Kodak sheet film as nitrate while a 'U' shaped notch (first from the edge) will indicate the Kodak film is acetate." Separately: professional sheet film negatives "will have notches on one corner. These notches are used by photographers to determine the emulsion side in the dark." Film pack negatives "lack a notch code, but may have a negative number, generally 1 through 12." | No | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.1, 2, 4 (PDF 1, 2, 4)] |
| **The copy trap — stated for both nitrate and acetate** | "Note that a nitrate negative may have been copied at some point and the edge printing from the original will appear on the copy. Therefore, just because you see the word 'nitrate' does not guarantee that it is." And for acetate: "just because you see the words acetate or safety does not guarantee your item is acetate." | No | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.1, 4 (PDF 1, 4)] |
| **Curl (as identifier)** | "Amateur roll films were not marked but can be identified by their tendency to curl into very tight scrolls (later roll films were coated on both sides to prevent such curling)." | No | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)] |
| **Base thickness / rigidity (as identifier)** | "Nitrate sheet film tends to have a very thick and rigid base." Film pack film is "much thinner and a very flexible based film. These negatives will feel like roll film." | No | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2), notes B, C] |
| **Tear resistance** | "polyester cannot be torn (except with tremendous effort) unless a nick or cut exists, while acetate and nitrate are fairly easy to tear." | Mildly | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] |
| **Deterioration appearance and odour** | "The nitrate will have sticky emulsions and lots of silver image deterioration, while the acetate will have channeling and smell of vinegar." | No | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)] |
| **Float test (specific gravity)** | Trichloroethylene. "The densest—cellulose nitrate—will sink, while cellulose acetate will rise to the top. Polyester should remain floating near the center of the solution." Procedure: "Place the sample in a test tube of trichloroethylene. Shake test tube so sample is completely immersed. Then observe the location of the sample in the liquid." Two stated confounders: "deteriorated acetate film may sink to the bottom just as nitrate film would"; and "the specific gravities for cellulose nitrate and the cellulose acetates fall within a broad range, which may cause materials to behave differently." **No specific-gravity numbers are given.** | Yes (needs a sample); toxic reagent | [M] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)] |
| **Diphenylamine spot test** | Diphenylamine in 90 % sulfuric acid; "cellulose nitrate turns a deep blue color. Cellulose acetate and polyester will not produce this color." One minute; confirm negatives with two more drops and another minute. Caveat: nitrate is used in very small amounts as a subbing layer in acetate and polyester products, which "may cause a very faint blue tinge to be seen in the support of the cellulose acetates and polyester", but this "does not appear to affect either the longevity or the safety of these materials." | Yes | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.3–4 (PDF 3–4)] |
| **Burn test** | "Cellulose nitrate burns quickly and has a characteristic yellow flame … only cellulose nitrate will burn downwards." Both acetates and polyester are "much less flammable". Burning nitrate "cannot be extinguished". Do not perform indoors. | Yes | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)] |
| **Age and historical context** | "Although several physical and chemical tests exist to identify film bases, most of the time the nature of the film supports in a collection can be determined by the age and historical context of the collection." | No | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)] |

**Diagnostic basis, summarised as physics.** Three of the non-destructive tests exploit genuinely different physical properties: birefringence (optical anisotropy from biaxial orientation of PET, per §21.6), edge light-piping (total internal reflection along the web, which the sources report as an empirical brightness difference without explaining it), and bulk density (the float test). The remaining non-destructive tests are documentary (edge printing, notch codes, dating tables) or symptomatic (odour, channelling, stickiness, curl, rigidity). The two chemical tests are destructive: diphenylamine detects the nitro group, and the burn test detects nitrate's self-sustaining, oxygen-supplying combustion — which the 1966 source describes as the material's defining defect [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.47–48 (PDF 51–52)]. [E]

**A stated limit on scope.** The 1993/1996 guide labels its own base history "only a general outline of historical trends; a full treatise on the history of film bases and methods to identify the various plastics is outside the scope of this publication." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.21 (PDF 21)] [F]

### 21.14 Subbing / substratum layers

Subbing is a base-side layer and belongs in this section. Two of these sources describe it in operational detail; the third does not mention it.

**Why it is needed — the 1966 mechanism.** "The final film base surface is non-polar in character … A photographic emulsion on the other hand is an aqueous suspension and this means that an emulsion would not spread evenly or adhere at all to such a film base. A further treatment, called subbing, is therefore necessary. This consists basically of coating a layer or a series of layers, only a few microns thick when dried down …" Composition: "water, gelatin, an organic water-miscible solvent such as ethanol or acetone, designed to effect some etching of the base, and a polymer similar to the base, such as extensively hydrolysed triacetate or even cellulose nitrate. Some subbing treatments involve successive layers becoming progressively more hydrophilic." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] [Q]

Note the composition datum that returns as an identification confounder in §21.13: cellulose nitrate is a legitimate constituent of subbing layers on acetate and polyester base, which is exactly why the diphenylamine test can give "a very faint blue tinge" on a non-nitrate support [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. Two sources, 54 years apart, agree on this point from opposite directions — one describing the recipe, the other describing the false positive. [E]

**Both sides.** "Subbing is usually carried out on both sides of the film, both to maintain flatness and also because the film will probably be coated on both sides, for example, emulsion and anti-halation coatings or double-side emulsion coating." [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] [F]

**Subbing polyester is a distinct problem.** See §21.6: PET is "very insoluble and highly stable which makes simple etching or partial degradation almost impossible"; it requires vinylidene chloride–itaconic acid or vinylidene chloride–ethyl acrylate–acrylic acid copolymer layers, the latter after "an oxidation etching-treatment with permanganate", before normal acetate-type sub layers can be applied [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)]. Polystyrene requires methacrylic acid–ester copolymers, then cellulose-nitrate layers, then gelatin layers; polycarbonate requires a three-layer assembly — a vinyl or similar polymer, then cellulose nitrate or partially hydrolysed acetate, then a gel sub [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.53–54 (PDF 57–58)]. [F]

**The 1929 formulas — the etching mechanism stated explicitly, and the glass/celluloid distinction.** The 1929 source is emphatic that subbing glass and subbing celluloid are different in kind. On celluloid, "the action of the substratum is rather an **etching** of the surface … not apparent to the naked eye, but it can be seen microscopically and also detected by the greater readiness with which a basic dye solution will penetrate such a surface" [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.186 (PDF 193)] — i.e. not a cement. [M] On glass, by contrast, the preferred sub "actually does form an infinitely thin film of cementing material" [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.186 (PDF 193)].

| Support | Formula / procedure as printed | Notes | Class | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Glass, older practice | potassium or sodium silicate (water glass) | "apt to fog the plates" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.163 (PDF 170)] |
| Glass, preferred | Gelatine 5 g; chrome alum 0.5 g; water 1000 ccm. Some use double strength plus 10 % alcohol. Dip the whole plate at 20°–25° C (68°–77° F), rack and dry | "The coating left on the glass is extremely thin, but quite sufficient to make the emulsion adhere well" | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.163 (PDF 170); Ch. XI, p.186 (PDF 193)] |
| Celluloid, early | Celluloid 2.5 g; ether 100 ccm; alcohol 900 ccm | "not very satisfactory" | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.187 (PDF 194)] |
| Celluloid, solvent type | Ether 625 ccm; acetone 375 ccm; glycerine 25 ccm | ether fumes are "a serious menace to the workmen, and also increase the fire hazard"; substituting alcohol risks "blushing" (a white surface) unless the drying temperature is high and the air very dry | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.187 (PDF 194)] |
| Celluloid, the author's best | Gelatine 5 g; glacial acetic acid 50 ccm; water 10 ccm; methyl alcohol 1000 ccm. Soak the gelatine in water plus acid, melt, then add the alcohol at the same temperature slowly | "**For cellulose acetate film, half the alcohol should be replaced by acetone.**" Suits all celluloid film, flat or roll. **OCR hazard: the raw string reads "melt to 55° C. (122° F.)", but 55 °C = 131 °F; one of the two figures is corrupt and neither should be relied on.** | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.187 (PDF 194)] |
| Cut sheet film, alternative | Pyroxylin 0.5 g; gelatine 0.5 g; glacial acetic acid 33 ccm; methyl alcohol 1000 ccm | applied with a cotton pad in Canton flannel, one light pass only — vigorous rubbing gives a smeary or streaky surface, "but no notice need be taken of this, as the marks will not show when coated with emulsion" | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.188 (PDF 195)] |
| Sodium silicate on celluloid | — | its virtue "probably lies in its alkaline nature, which slightly saponifies the extreme surface of the celluloid, but it is apt to fog the emulsion" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.185–186 (PDF 192–193)] |
| Invert albumen on celluloid | albumen 1000 ccm plus glacial acetic acid 15 ccm plus water 30 ccm, coagulated with 8 % caustic soda, washed 2 h, made up to 10,000 ccm with equal parts ethyl and methyl alcohol (dry albumen 150 g is equivalent to 1000 ccm fresh) | — | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, pp.185–186 (PDF 192–193)] |
| Tacky carrier layer (for mounting cut sheet on glass for flat coating) | Hard gelatine 58 g; golden (sugar) syrup 58 g; glycerine 86 g; chrome alum 0.8 g; water to 1000 ccm; melt at 50° C (122° F); 250 ccm per 20 × 16 in sheet; dries 3–4 days — "actually, of course, the coating never dries, but forms a tacky film to which the celluloid adheres firmly" | Carrier glass is ¼ in plate glass with edges ground | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. XI, p.183 (PDF 190)] |

Two of these carry an explicit image-level penalty and are carried forward to §23: the silicate subs are "apt to fog the plates" / "apt to fog the emulsion" [Wall 1929, Ch. X, p.163 (PDF 170); Ch. XI, p.185 (PDF 192)]. [F]

**A negative finding worth preserving.** No supercoat, top-coat, anti-abrasion or anti-stress layer is described anywhere in the 1929 volume. The only "extra layer" concepts in it are the antihalation sub, the baryta undercoat on paper, and backing on the rear of the glass. [F]

**The 2020 leaflet does not describe subbing at all**, except incidentally as the source of the diphenylamine false positive [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. The 1993/1996 guide does not describe subbing at all. Source silent. [F]

### 21.15 Antihalation backings

Antihalation layers sit on the base side of the film and their degradation behaviour is a base-side phenomenon, so they belong here rather than with the emulsion.

**What halation is, and why the backing is on the base side — the 1993/1996 footnote, verbatim.** "Halos are unwanted circles of light that show up around a bright object in the image — a street lamp in a night scene, for example. This is a disturbing, unreal effect caused by light reflecting off the film base during exposure. The gelatin coating on the back side of sheet films is a convenient place to put some dyes that would absorb this unwanted light and keep it from forming halos in the image." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12), footnote] [M]

**The 1929 mechanism, stated in terms of the support.** "If the light could be prevented from penetrating right through the emulsion and glass there would be no halation" — halation is attributed to light traversing emulsion *and support* and returning. [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)] [M]

**Critical negative finding, 1929.** The 1929 source gives **no quantitative statement of the magnitude, radius or spread of halation, and no figure for how much any remedy reduces it.** There is no photometric halation datum anywhere in the volume. [F]

| Measure | Statement as printed | Class | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backing the rear of the glass | "The ordinary method of preventing halation is, of course, by coating the back of the glass with a non-actinic color; but this necessitates the handling of the coated plate, with possible chance of damaging the film of emulsion" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)] |
| Backing formula, black, for panchromatic plates | Yellow dextrin 80 g; water 85 ccm, heated till dissolved; mix in ivory sienna black 900 g; phenol 15 g. (The black is obtainable commercially as a water-ground paste.) | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Appendix, p.241 (PDF 248)] |
| Backing, ortho and ordinary plates | "Use the same formula, but with burnt sienna ground in water" | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Appendix, p.241 (PDF 248)] |
| Desensitising backing | "Some commercial plates are backed with a thin layer containing desensitizing dyes, which diffuse into the developer, thus exerting their peculiar action. It is obvious that any of the desensitizing dyes may be used in this way." | [F] | [Wall 1929, Appendix, p.241 (PDF 248)] |
| Dyed subbing between glass and emulsion | O. Magerstadt, Eng. Pat. 5,932/1893 — a preliminary gelatine coating stained with a non-actinic dye, **fuchsin** actually used; C. E. Pettit, Eng. Pat. 8,956/1893, the same idea. "Any acid red dye may be thus used, or a mixture of red and yellow dyes. **Acid dyes must be used … as they are more readily washed out of the gelatine.** Only a thin coating of the stained gelatine is required, **a five per cent solution being sufficient**." Candidates named: Congo red, carmine L, lanafuchsin SB, tolan red, with or without naphthol yellow or tartrazin | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)] |
| Removability constraint | dyes that do not wash out "must be of such a nature as to be decolorized either by acid sulphite or other ready means, otherwise they would seriously prolong the exposure in printing" | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.83 (PDF 90)] |
| Non-dye antihalation sub | C. F. Oakley, Eng. Pat. 2,986/1895 — a **0.6 per cent solution of potassium permanganate in gelatine**, reduced in situ to "practically colloidal manganese hydroxide … an orange-brown color, that is very intense and **can not diffuse into the emulsion**"; removed by the ordinary acid fixing bath or by sodium bisulphite; "it forms a better protection for panchromatic emulsions" | [Q] | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)] |
| Rationale for preferring a non-dye system | dyes "might lead to trouble because of partial **sensitizing or fogging action by diffusion into the emulsion layer**" | [M] | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, pp.83–84 (PDF 90–91)] |
| Double coating as an antihalation strategy | "Some of the non-halation, so-called double-coated plates, on the market are merely coated with an extra quantity of emulsion, and not actually double-coated". True double coating: J. T. Sandell, Eng. Pat. 21,381/1891, "who actually coated first a very slow, opaque emulsion and then on top a faster and more translucent one". Stated penalty: "the longer time required for fixation, washing and drying". **No statement is made about the effect of double coating on contrast or latitude.** | [F] | [Wall 1929, Ch. IV, p.84 (PDF 91)] |

**1966.** Antihalation coatings are mentioned once in the base chapter, as one reason subbing is applied to both sides — "for example, emulsion and anti-halation coatings" [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] — and the layer appears as "Backing" in the source's schematic of a coated material [Duffin 1966, Ch. I, p.11 (PDF 15), Fig. 1.1]. **No optical density, dye identity, or spectral data for the antihalation layer appears in the base chapter**; backing dyes and acutance dyes are deferred to a later chapter on coating. [F]

**1993/1996 — the aging behaviour of antihalation dyes, which is the reason this subsection matters for §22 and §23.** "Still another consequence of vinegar syndrome is the appearance of pink or blue colors in some sheet films. This is caused by dyes incorporated into the gelatin layer on the back side. Such dyes are called antihalation dyes because they prevent halos in the image. These dyes are supposed to have been made colorless when the film was processed, but when acetic acid is formed during deterioration, the acid environment makes the dyes go back to their original pink or blue color. (Pink colors are found in some Kodak films, while blue colors are found in some Agfa and Ansco films.)" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)] [F]

This is a colour change in a base-side gelatin layer, driven by acid generated in the base, and it is optically real in transmission. It is manufacturer-specific — pink for some Kodak films, blue for some Agfa and Ansco films — and it is entirely unquantified: no density, no spectrum, no time constant. It carries forward to §23 as a boundary case. [F]

### 21.16 Where the 1993/1996 and the 2020 accounts differ on chronology

Both accounts are recorded above; this subsection states the divergences rather than merging them.

1. **Granular acetate chemistry.** The 1993/1996 guide declines to break acetate down by chemistry in its history, asserting only that its triacetate-derived data "apply as well to diacetate, acetate butyrate, and acetate propionate film bases" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.2 (PDF 2)]. The 2020 leaflet supplies a full table of diacetate, propionate, butyrate and triacetate with separate sheet and roll date ranges and named manufacturers [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. The sub-acetate chronology therefore rests on one source only. [F]

2. **When acetate roll film starts.** The 2020 leaflet dates cellulose acetate propionate roll film from **1920** and diacetate roll film from the **1920s** [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)]. The 1993/1996 guide says large-scale acetate manufacture "did not commence until the mid-1920s" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)]. The leaflet's 1920 propionate date is earlier than the guide's threshold. The two are not reconciled by either document. [F]

3. **When nitrate sheet film stops.** The 1993/1996 guide: sheet films on nitrate base are "uncommon after 1940" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)]. The 2020 leaflet, Kodak-specific: portrait and commercial sheet films ended **1939**, but film packs continued to **1949** [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2)]. The guide independently records the 1949 film-pack date [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)]. The 2020 leaflet attaches an explicit manufacturer caveat that the 1993/1996 general chronology does not carry (§21.2). [F]

4. **When nitrate stops altogether.** The 1993/1996 guide, writing in 1993: "nitrate film hasn't been manufactured for forty years" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15), footnote] — consistent with 1951–1953. The 2020 leaflet: "until the early 1950s" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)]. These agree. [F]

5. **Polyester.** The 1993/1996 guide gives dates, a stability multiplier, format-by-format adoption and the splicing obstacle. The 2020 leaflet gives **no polyester dates and no polyester stability figure**, and does not state that polyester replaced acetate. Temporally: the 1993/1996 text describes polyester as "still a small portion of the total film used" in motion pictures, and the 2020 leaflet does not update this — it says nothing about the post-1990s transition. **The 2020 document is therefore not a more current chronology; it is a narrower one.** [F]

6. **Terminology as printed.** The 2020 leaflet prints "cellulose acetate butynate" and, once, "cellulose acetate propiarate" in its table [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)] — evidently typographic errors for butyrate and propionate, and the same page's running prose spells butyrate correctly. Reproduced as printed and flagged. [F]

7. **A citation inconsistency worth recording.** The 2020 leaflet cites the IPI storage guide as "Reilly (1997)" for its cold-storage life-extension figure and links to the file `acetate_guide.pdf` [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.5, 6 (PDF 5, 6)]. The guide itself prints "© 1993 IMAGE PERMANENCE INSTITUTE" with "Minor revision 1996" immediately above the copyright line, and carries **no edition statement anywhere** [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.24 (PDF 24)]. The 1997 date in the 2020 leaflet does not match any date printed in the guide. Recorded, not resolved. [F]

**Provenance of the 1993/1996 guide, for the record.** Author line: "James M. Reilly • Director, Image Permanence Institute", Rochester Institute of Technology, 70 Lomb Memorial Drive, Rochester, NY 14623-5604 [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), cover (PDF 1)]. The research behind it began in **1988**, funded by the NEH Division of Preservation and Access, the NHPRC and Eastman Kodak, with film samples from Kodak and Fuji [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.24 (PDF 24)]. The 2020 leaflet's author line reads "Monique Fischer, Senior Photograph Conservator, Northeast Document Conservation Center", and the only date printed in it is "© 2020. Northeast Document Conservation Center. All rights reserved." — **no revision date, no "last updated" line** [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.1, 6 (PDF 1, 6)]. [F]

---

## 22. Acetate-base degradation and aging

### 22.1 The chemistry, and what distinguishes acetate from nitrate

**The shared vulnerability.** "Cellulose nitrate and cellulose acetate both share a built-in propensity to degrade; both these plastic materials are modified forms of cellulose, and both have a regrettable tendency to become 'un-modified' by the same kinds of chemical pathways." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] [M]

**Nitrate.** "To make nitrate plastic in the first place, nitro (NO2) groups are grafted onto the long molecular chains of native cellulose. As long as these side groups stay put, all is well. But in the presence of moisture, acids, and heat they tend to become detached, liberating the nitro groups. The nitro groups are very harmful substances to let loose — they are strongly acidic and strongly oxidizing in nature. They fade silver images and make gelatin soft and sticky; their highly acidic fumes rust film cans and embrittle paper enclosures." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] [M]

**Acetate.** "In acetate film the side groups are not nitro (NO2) but acetyl (CH3CO). As with nitrate, all is well as long as these acetyl groups remain grafted onto the cellulose molecules. Detachment of the acetyl groups also can occur in the presence of moisture, heat, and acids — only, in this case, free acetic acid is liberated. The acetic acid is released inside the plastic, but it gradually diffuses to the surface, causing a familiar sharp odor — the odor of vinegar (which in fact is a 5% acetic-acid solution in water)." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] [Q]

**Exclusivity, stated flatly.** "Vinegar syndrome is a problem that affects only cellulose acetate plastic materials." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] [F]

**How much acid.** "The amount of acetic acid that can be generated by degrading film is surprisingly large; expressing it in terms of teaspoonfuls of household vinegar, in advanced stages of deterioration there can be nine teaspoonfuls or more of vinegar for every four feet of 35mm movie film. A typical 1000-ft. can of 35mm film can generate enough acetic acid to be equivalent to 250 teaspoonfuls of household vinegar!" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] [Q]

| Quantity | Value as printed | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Household vinegar strength (the reference point for the odour) | 5 % acetic acid in water | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] |
| Acid generated, advanced stages | "nine teaspoonfuls or more of vinegar for every four feet of 35mm movie film" | as above |
| Acid generated, one 1000-ft can of 35 mm | equivalent to "250 teaspoonfuls of household vinegar" | as above |

[Q] Note that these are equivalences to *household vinegar*, i.e. to a 5 % solution, not to pure acetic acid. Neither figure is converted to grams or moles in the source, and the two figures are not mutually consistent as printed: nine teaspoonfuls per four feet scales to about 2250 teaspoonfuls per 1000 ft, not 250. The source offers no reconciliation; both figures are recorded as printed. [F]

**The trigger conditions are the same three variables throughout.** Moisture, heat and acids [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)]. The 2020 leaflet gives the same three plus external contamination: "When acetate base film is stored in a poor environment at high heat and humidity — or exposed to acidic vapors from nearby degrading film — it undergoes chemical reactions within the plastic support to form acetic acid." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] [M]

**Gas products released, by material.** Acetate collections "may release acetic, butyric, or propionic acids upon degradation" — the acid released tracks the ester used, which links this back to the mixed esters of §21.4. Nitrate releases "nitrogen oxides and/or nitric acid." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.20 (PDF 20)] The 2020 leaflet is more specific on nitrate: "Nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and nitrous dioxide are all released as gases from the decomposition of cellulose nitrate. In the presence of atmospheric moisture, these gases combine with water to form nitric acid." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2)] [M]

**And a clean baseline statement.** "As long as the acetate or nitrate film base is not deteriorated, there will be no acetic acid or nitrogen oxides in the film vault atmosphere." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.20 (PDF 20)] [F]

**The 1966 source records no degradation chemistry for acetate at all.** Its criticisms of acetate are dimensional and mechanical (§21.12), not chemical; it does not mention acetic acid release, vinegar odour, autocatalysis, or any aging mechanism of the base. Source silent — and this is itself a dated datum: as of 1966 the industrial account of acetate's shortcomings was about water uptake and dimensional stability, not about self-catalysed decomposition. [F]

### 22.2 Induction period and autocatalysis

**The shape of the curve.** "Acidity is at first almost non-existent, then for a long time builds up gradually, little by little. Then, after the acid level increases to a certain point, the increase suddenly becomes very rapid." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.13 (PDF 13), Fig. 17] [M]

**The induction period, and its environmental sensitivity.** "In the early stages (the induction period, before the sharp turn upward) there is little acid present, so the reaction rate is determined primarily by heat and moisture … environmental factors can influence whether the induction period is long (perhaps centuries) or short (just a few decades)." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.13 (PDF 13)] [Q] — the bracketing "perhaps centuries" versus "just a few decades" is the qualitative form of the prediction tables in §22.6.

**The autocatalytic mechanism, and its location on the acidity scale.** "The reaction is now feeding on itself — displaying what scientists call autocatalytic behavior … The acetic acid that is liberated as the acetyl groups split off catalyzes the removal of other side groups, and the whole process snowballs." The inflection is "called the autocatalytic point", and it is placed at **0.5 free acidity**. [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.13 (PDF 13)] [Q]

**The 2020 leaflet asserts autocatalysis for both materials, without numbers.** "Like cellulose nitrate, the deterioration of cellulose acetate is autocatalytic: once deterioration has begun, the degradation products induce further deterioration." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)] [M] Note that this extends autocatalysis to nitrate, which the 1993/1996 guide does not do in those terms — it describes nitrate's products as acidic and oxidising and says the resulting nitric acid "acts to further degrade cellulose nitrate film" only in the 2020 leaflet's wording [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2)]. [F]

**Cross-infection between films.** "Laboratory experiments show that acetic acid vapors are readily absorbed by fresh film, and this will lead to faster deterioration." Not quantified — no uptake rate, no partial pressure, no resulting change in predicted life. [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)] [M]

### 22.3 Free acidity — the guide's own metric

**What the number is.** "ANSI Standard IT9.1-1992 specifies the method used to obtain free acidity measurements." Free acidity "is not the same as a pH value. It represents the total amount of acid present in the film base", and the values "actually are derived from the volume of alkali that is necessary to completely neutralize the acidity of the film base." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.13 (PDF 13) and footnote] [F] The source does not state the units of the free-acidity number, nor the normalisation (per gram of base, per unit area, or otherwise). Source silent where a reader would expect it. [F]

| Free acidity | Meaning as stated | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| **0.05** | "the very low level of free acidity typically found in freshly manufactured films" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)] |
| **0.5** | the autocatalytic point. "the film will smell of vinegar, but it may not have any other symptoms of degradation and will be perfectly usable. However, it will degrade rather quickly from then on unless kept in low-temperature, low-RH storage" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), pp.13, 14 (PDF 13, 14)] |
| **1.0** | "film may smell of acetic acid, but it is still quite usable … the odor may be a little stronger" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.6 (PDF 6)] |
| **about 5.0** | "not until the free acidity reaches about 5.0 will changes (buckling, embrittlement) occur to render the film unusable" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.6 (PDF 6)] |
| **5.0–10.0, "sometimes even higher"** | "Advanced stages of deterioration (which are marked by very strong odor, shrinkage, buckling, and plasticizer exudation)" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)] |

All [Q]. The whole scale spans a factor of about 200 from fresh film to advanced degradation, and the usability threshold (about 5.0) sits an order of magnitude above the autocatalytic point (0.5). That relationship — vinegar odour arrives roughly ten-fold in acidity before unusability — is the single most important quantitative fact in this section, and it is the reason §23 is structured as it is. [E]

### 22.4 A-D strips

**As described in the 1993/1996 guide.** A-D Strips are presented as "A new tool to safely check your film collection for vinegar syndrome!", used to "Document the extent of vinegar syndrome / Determine when film must be duplicated / Check new acquisitions for deterioration"; "Safer, more accurate than 'sniffing'"; applicable to "all types of microfilm, cinema film, and pictorial film on acetate base" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)]. Elsewhere: "the use of diagnostic tools such as A-D Strips … may provide an idea of how far down the path of deterioration a particular film has already travelled" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.3 (PDF 3)]. [F]

**On A-D levels: the numeric scale is not defined in these sources.** The digits "0 1 2 3" appear adjacent to the A-D material on p.14 of the guide with no explanatory text, and **no source here defines what levels 0, 1, 2 and 3 mean, what free acidity each corresponds to, or how a level maps to a predicted remaining life** [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)]. A reader would expect that mapping and it is not here. Do not infer one. [F]

**As described in the 2020 leaflet.** "'A-D Strips' (acid-detecting strips) from the Image Permanence Institute at the Rochester Institute of Technology in Rochester, NY. They are acid-base indicator papers, which turn from blue to green to yellow in the presence of acid, and measure the extent of the acetate base support deterioration." Their stated use is "helping determine the amount of acid vapor present, and gain an overview of the condition of acid vapors in an entire collection." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)] [F] So the colour progression is documented — blue → green → yellow — but not calibrated to any number in these sources. [F]

### 22.5 Activation energies

**None of these sources states an activation energy, an Arrhenius pre-exponential factor, or any explicit kinetic equation for base degradation.** The predictions are presented only as tabulated years against temperature and relative humidity, derived from "the same kinds of predictive mathematical models … used on the accelerated-aging data" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)]. The 1966 source contains no aging kinetics for base at all. The 2020 leaflet contains none. [F]

This is an absence, not an omission on our part. An activation energy for vinegar syndrome cannot be sourced from this material, and must not be back-fitted from the tables in §22.6 and presented as though these sources supplied it. [F]

### 22.6 Predicted lifetimes — the quantitative core

**What is being predicted, exactly.** The prediction is "the period of time in years that would be required for fresh acetate film to start experiencing noticeable levels of vinegar syndrome; at the end of that period, the film would smell of vinegar but would still be usable" — i.e. the years to reach **0.5 free acidity** at constant temperature and RH [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), pp.2, 9, 14 (PDF 2, 9, 14)]. [Q]

**The experimental basis, and its worst-case character.** The predictions "were obtained from experiments in which the film was kept in tightly sealed foil bags, and so they represent a worst-case scenario" in which all the acid is trapped in the film. "Motion picture film is typically stored in closed cans, and sheet films are often kept in close quarters in a box or drawer. … Real-life storage may involve more opportunity for the acid to escape; if that is the case, it will take longer than predicted." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.3 (PDF 3)] [M] The magnitude of the trapping effect is never quantified — "If trapped, it greatly accelerates the rate of deterioration" carries no multiplier. [M]

**Instrument ranges.** The prediction wheel covers temperature **30 °F / −1 °C to 120 °F / 49 °C**; Side One covers RH **20 % to 80 % in 10 % increments**; Side Two covers RH **20 %, 50 %, 80 %** [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.4 (PDF 4)]. [Q]

**Table 22.6-A — fresh film, years to onset of vinegar syndrome (to 0.5 free acidity). Wheel Side One.**

[Q] The 70 °F / 20 % and 48 °F / 80 % pairing is the most useful single row here: it states an explicit trade-off rate — 22 °F of cooling buys the same life as 60 percentage points of drying, at that point on the surface.

**Explicit caution attached to these graphs, and it must be honoured.** "Don't try to 'read between the lines.' On this type of graph, interpolation between the lines is difficult because the time intervals are not uniform" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.7 (PDF 7)]. [F] Note that the 130 °F / 50 % row lies outside the wheel's stated 120 °F upper bound, so it comes from the contour graphs rather than the wheel.

The post-onset clock runs several times faster than the pre-onset clock at the same storage conditions. [E]

**Table 22.6-D — "Time Out of Storage Table": the combined effect of vault conditions plus time spent at an "office condition" of 75 °F (24 °C), 60 % RH. Column headings in the original are average days per year out of the vault. The cells below are those quoted in the source's running text, for a vault at 40 °F, 40 % RH.**
