[Q]

**And the design conclusion the source draws from that table.** "In reading down the column marked '120 Days' out of storage … there is little or no benefit from having a film vault any colder than 50 °F … the four months per year at 75 °F, 60 % RH dictates that only 60 years will pass before the predicted onset of vinegar syndrome." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.9 (PDF 9)] [Q]

**Important scope note on all four tables.** The tabulated grids themselves (the source's Fig. 6 and Fig. 7) are printed as graphics, and only the cells quoted in the running text are recoverable as text. The cells above are the complete set of numeric (T, RH) → years data points available from this source. Anything not in these tables is not available. [F]

**Table 22.6-E — sensitivity factors.**

| Factor | Value as printed | Conditions | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| RH sensitivity | "film degrades only about one third to one half as fast at 20% as it does at 50% RH" | 20 % vs 50 % RH | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.4 (PDF 4)] |
| RH sensitivity, restated | "about a three-fold improvement in life expectancy (years to onset of vinegar syndrome) at 20% RH over 50% RH" | 20 % vs 50 % RH | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.18 (PDF 18)] |
| Temperature sensitivity | "the reactions of vinegar syndrome will take about **17 times** longer at 30 °F than at 70 °F" | 30 °F vs 70 °F (a 40 °F interval) | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.16 (PDF 16)] |
| Cold storage, 2020 statement | "cold storage is predicted to extend the life of acetate negatives by a factor of ten or more" | **no temperature or RH attached to the figure** | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |

[Q] The two RH statements in the 1993/1996 guide are mutually consistent — "one third to one half as fast" and "about a three-fold improvement" both land near a factor of 3. The 2020 "factor of ten or more" is a different and looser claim: it names no temperature, so it cannot be checked against the 17× figure or against any row of Table 22.6-A. It should not be treated as a refinement of the 1993/1996 numbers. [F]

**Anecdotal confirmation, explicitly labelled as such by the source.** "Film kept in warmer than room-temperature conditions does degrade in about 30 years, and film kept at cooler than room-temperature storage for 50 years shows no signs of degradation." The sentence is preceded by "although the evidence is anecdotal and not rigorous" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.5 (PDF 5)]. [F]

**Explicit limits on the use of every number above, in the source's own words.** "The Guide is not meant to predict the life of any individual film; it merely uses predicted life span as a yardstick to measure the quality of the storage environment" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), cover (PDF 1)]; the predictions "are like an actuarial table for a life insurance company" and "it is still nearly impossible to predict exactly when a film will become unusable" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.3 (PDF 3)]. [F]

**And the scope disclaimer that governs §23.** The guide "deals only with cellulose acetate plastic film base deterioration. Other important forms of film deterioration such as color dye fading, silver image fading, mold growth, physical damage, etc., have their own causes and their own relationship to the storage environment." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.2 (PDF 2)] [F] This is the source's own separation of carrier from image, printed on page 2, before the reader reaches any of the tables above.

III, p.51 (PDF 55)] |
| Gelatin softening — acetate | "In extreme cases, vinegar syndrome can lead to softening of gelatin, but in general the emulsions of degrading acetate films remain in much better shape than nitrate film emulsions do." | "extreme cases" | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] |
| Gelatin softening — nitrate | liberated nitro groups "fade silver images and make gelatin soft and sticky" | — | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] |
| Gelatin dimensional and barrier response to RH | "gelatin shrinks at low RH and swells at high RH. When swollen (as it is at RHs above 60%), the gelatin offers no resistance to the diffusion of contaminants … at RHs below about 50%, gelatin becomes an increasingly effective barrier to the diffusion of gases" | **RH > 60 %**, **RH < about 50 %** | [Q] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.18 (PDF 18)] |
| Temperature change per se | "Changes in temperature per se (i.e., simple temperature changes that do not result in drying out of the film) do not cause any physical damage to film." | — | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.19 (PDF 19)] |
| Freeze/thaw | "The act of thawing and re-freezing film does not harm it. Ice crystals do not form in the film as it is frozen" | — | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.16 (PDF 16)] |
| **Equilibration times** | Temperature equilibration is "usually a matter of a few hours". Humidity: for a single strip freely hanging, "RH equilibration would be substantially complete within **eight hours**"; "Film wrapped on a roll and stored in a can or box, might require **three months** to equilibrate at room temperature. In cold storage, diffusion is slower, so equilibration takes even longer." RH cycling "up or down 10% in the period of an hour or a day hardly matters"; avoid "fast cycling between extremes of RH (a difference greater than **30%** or so)". | as stated | [Q] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.19 (PDF 19)] |

**On the missing conditions.** The 1 % and 10 % shrinkage figures are the two most-cited numbers in this whole literature, and neither carries a temperature, an RH, a time, a free-acidity value, or an axis. The source that supplies the anisotropy — "unequal shrinkage in different directions" [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.51 (PDF 55)] — supplies no magnitude; the source that supplies the magnitude supplies no axis. **No source here gives both a shrinkage magnitude and its direction.** [F]

### 22.8 The ordinal stage scales (2020 leaflet)

These six-level scales are the 2020 leaflet's entire quantitative content on physical change. They are **ordinal, not numeric**: no percentages, temperatures, acidity values or times are attached to any stage in either scale. [F]

**Acetate, six progressive stages** [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)]:

| Stage | As printed |
|---|---|
| 1 | No deterioration. |
| 2 | "The negatives begin to curl and they can turn red or blue." |
| 3 | "The onset of acetic acid (vinegar smell); also shrinkage and brittleness." |
| 4 | "Warping can begin." |
| 5 | "The formation of bubbles and crystals in the film." |
| 6 | "The formation of channeling in the film." |

[F]

**A sequencing conflict that neither source resolves.** The 2020 leaflet places colour change ("turn red or blue") at stage 2, **before** the onset of vinegar smell at stage 3. The 1993/1996 guide attributes the pink/blue appearance to antihalation dyes reverting because "when acetic acid is formed during deterioration, the acid environment makes the dyes go back to their original pink or blue color" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)] — i.e. it makes the colour change a *consequence* of acid already present, which would put it at or after stage 3, not before it. The two sequencings are not reconcilable from these sources, and neither adjudicates. Both are recorded. [F]

**Nitrate, six progressive stages** [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.2–3 (PDF 2–3)] — reproduced here and discussed further in §22.10:

| Stage | As printed |
|---|---|
| 1 | No deterioration. |
| 2 | "The negatives begin to yellow and mirror." |
| 3 | "The film becomes sticky and emits a strong noxious odor (nitric acid)." |
| 4 | "The film becomes an amber color and the image begins to fade." |
| 5 | "The film is soft and can weld to adjacent [material]" — the sentence is truncated in the source's own layout. |
| 6 | "The film degenerates into a brownish acid powder." |

Plus the legibility statement: "Most negatives will retain legible photographic detail into the third stage of decomposition. These negatives may become brittle, but — with careful handling — they can be duplicated. Negatives in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages of decomposition generally have decreasing areas of legible image and should be either placed in cold storage or digitized before the image completely fades away." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.3 (PDF 3)] [F]

**Note the asymmetry between the two scales, because it is the whole point of §23.** In the nitrate scale, the image is explicitly involved from stage 2 (yellow and mirror) and is lost by stages 4–6. In the acetate scale, **no stage mentions the image at all** — all six describe the plastic support and its gelatin layers. [F]

### 22.9 Storage

**The 1993/1996 summary recommendation, verbatim.** "Make the temperature as low as you can, and preferably make the average RH 20% to 30%. RHs up to 50% will do no special harm; they will only result in a faster rate of vinegar syndrome and dye fading than would occur at 20% RH." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.19 (PDF 19)] [Q]

**Table 22.9-A — RH limits and thresholds, all sources.**

| Threshold | Value | What happens / why | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overall acceptable RH window for all film components (base, gelatin, silver, dyes) | **20 %–50 %** | "this is why the ANSI standard for film storage currently specifies 20% to 30% RH where maximum film life is required" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.18 (PDF 18)] |
| Lower bound, general | **20 %** | below it "film dries out too much and becomes brittle" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.4 (PDF 4)] |
| Upper bound, general | **50 %** | do not exceed | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.4 (PDF 4)] |
| Gelatin handling brittleness | **RH < 15 %** | gelatin "may be too brittle for the film to be safely handled" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.17 (PDF 17)] |
| Glass-plate delamination | **RH < 25 %** | gelatin emulsions on glass "may suffer delamination from the glass support" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.19 (PDF 19)] |
| Gelatin as a diffusion barrier | effective **below about 50 %**; no resistance **above 60 %** | swollen gelatin "offers no resistance to the diffusion of contaminants" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.18 (PDF 18)] |
| Mould risk | **70 % RH or above** for sustained periods; "above 70% RH or so for several days" | "mold releases enzymes which soften and dissolve gelatin and also cause stains"; "There are no satisfactory remedial treatments" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), pp.4, 17 (PDF 4, 17)] |
| Gelatin preferred average RH | **20 %–50 %** | — | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.17 (PDF 17)] |
| Colour film maximum temperature | **2 °C (35 °F)** | "ANSI IT9.11-1991 cites a maximum temperature of 2 °C (35 °F) for extended term storage of color film" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.16 (PDF 16)] |
| Nitrate | "the cooler the better, with RH not lower than 20% or higher than 50%" | "The further nitrate film has already progressed along the path of deterioration, the more essential it is to store it at low temperatures. Many collections have opted for near- or below-freezing temperatures." | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)] |

[Q] The mixed-collection consequence is worked through in the source itself: because glass plates delaminate below 25 % RH while acetate prefers 20–30 %, a worked example settles on **40 % RH** as a compromise for a mixed collection [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.5 (PDF 5)]. [Q]

**The 2020 leaflet's storage prescriptions.**

| Item | As printed | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Ideal | "Ideally, to minimize decomposition, negatives should be stored in a freezer." | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |
| Life extension claimed | "cold storage is predicted to extend the life of acetate negatives by a factor of ten or more" | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |
| Low-cost alternative | "A low cost set up for storage would provide a controlled environment with the constant temperature at **68 °F (20 °C)**, and relative humidity between **20% and 30%**. Rapid changes in temperature and humidity will hasten deterioration. A dark and well-ventilated area around the negatives allows gases to dissipate." | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |
| Cold storage practice | "a large commercial freezer (which should defrost automatically)"; "chemically stable boxes placed in polypropylene bags and then sealed with humidity control cards" | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |
| Warm-up before use | "**8–12 hours** should be sufficient" at room temperature | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |
| Three layers of protection | sleeves → box or drawer → shelves or cabinet | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |
| Unsealed containers | "Motion picture film and microfilm should be stored in unsealed containers." | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)] |

[Q]

**Enclosures.**

- 1993/1996: "All enclosures should be chemically inert toward the components of film"; they must meet ANSI IT9.2-1991 and pass the ANSI Photographic Activity Test, ANSI IT9.16-1993. "The PAT guarantees that the enclosure will not chemically interact with the film to cause staining or fading." And a warning: "Much damage has been done by reactive, poor-quality papers, adhesives, and cardboards." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.20 (PDF 20)] [F]
- 2020: "individual, seamless, high alpha cellulose content paper enclosures … recommended to allow for the dissipation of harmful gases"; enclosures must pass the PAT per **ISO 18916:2007**; and "Enclosures that have been used to store negatives must never be reused. These enclosures retain acids from previous materials." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, pp.5–6 (PDF 5–6)] [F]
- The standard number is the one genuine 27-year update between the two documents: ANSI IT9.16-1993 → ISO 18916:2007, same test. [F]

**Acid trapping and segregation.**

- "The process of deterioration generates acetic acid (vinegar) inside the plastic film base … If trapped, it greatly accelerates the rate of deterioration." No multiplier is given. [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.3 (PDF 3)] [M]
- "Where at all practical, films showing vinegar syndrome should be segregated. However … having a little degraded acetate film in a large, well-ventilated room may not infect other materials … having some strong-smelling film inside a closed container with good film will likely cause faster deterioration." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)] [M]
- Nitrate: "cellulose nitrate negatives should always be stored separately from other negatives in a collection" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)]; the segregation rationale in the 1993/1996 guide is fire hazard (NFPA 40 is cited) plus the fact that "the acidic and oxidizing fumes from degrading nitrate film may infect other, still healthy, films" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)]. [F]

**Vault atmosphere.** The volatiles found at highest concentration in film vaults are "usually cyclohexane, methylene chloride, and n-butanol", plus the cleaning solvent 1,1,1-trichloroethane; "typically the observed concentration of volatiles is extremely low, posing no health risks" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), pp.19–20 (PDF 19–20)]. A table of vault volatiles is printed on p.20 of that source as a graphic and its cells are not recoverable as text. Large vaults are advised to have "air purification systems and/or sufficient fresh air exchange" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.20 (PDF 20)]. [F] Note that methylene chloride and n-butanol are among the base casting solvents named in 1966 [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.49 (PDF 53)] — the vault atmosphere is partly residual casting solvent, though no source states that connection.  [E]

**Molecular sieves — an absence, stated explicitly.** **None of these sources mentions molecular sieves, activated carbon, acid scavengers, or any chemical absorber.** The nearest equivalents are: "humidity control cards" inside freezer bags and passive gas dissipation through unsealed containers and paper enclosures [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)]; and the acid-trapping discussion plus vault air purification in the 1993/1996 guide [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), pp.3, 20 (PDF 3, 20)]. The molecular-sieve and scavenger literature is not represented in this material and no figure for sieve-based life extension can be sourced here. [F]

**Cold-storage caveats.** Condensation on removal and frost buildup are named as risks; "Any institution seeking to implement cold storage should get help from qualified preservation and engineering professionals." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.17 (PDF 17)] [F]

**Health and handling.** "Good ventilation is essential when handling or inspecting degraded films. Latex, polyethylene, or nitrile gloves should be worn … Throat and skin irritations have been reported due to handling of deteriorated acetate and nitrate films. Working for long periods in confined, poorly ventilated spaces with large amounts of degraded film definitely should be avoided." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.20 (PDF 20)] [F]

**Standards named across the two preservation documents.** ANSI IT9.11-1993 (storage); ANSI IT9.11-1991 (cited for the 2 °C colour-film maximum); ANSI IT9.2-1991 (enclosures); ANSI IT9.1-1992 (silver-gelatin stability, and the free-acidity method); ANSI IT9.16-1993 (PAT); ISO 5466:1992(E) [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), pp.13, 16, 20, 24 (PDF 13, 16, 20, 24)]; ISO 18916:2007 (PAT) [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)]. NFPA 40 is cited for nitrate fire practice [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.14 (PDF 14)]. [F]

**Storage: how 1993/1996 and 2020 differ.** The 1993/1996 document presents a **trade-off surface** — any temperature/RH pair on an iso-lifetime contour, with numbers for each cell (§22.6). The 2020 document collapses this to two prescriptions, freezer or 68 °F / 20–30 % RH, plus a single unconditioned "factor of ten or more". On environment, **the 2020 document is substantially less quantitative than the 1993/1996 one**, and it says so implicitly by deferring: "James Reilly's invaluable 'Image Permanence Institute's Storage Guide for Acetate Film' has information on this as well." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.6 (PDF 6)] [F]

**The clearest generational shift between them is the salvage route.** The 1993/1996 answer is physical: "for sheet films it is possible to save the image by dissolving the emulsion away from the shrunken base using solvents. Once it has been freed from its original support, it can be made flat and photographed, or else transferred to a new support. This is a delicate and (because of the solvents used) a potentially hazardous undertaking. … Degraded motion picture films cannot be restored this way, but sheet films often can. Even torn emulsions can be dealt with successfully." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.11 (PDF 11)] The 2020 answer is digital: "Any negatives that show signs of deterioration should be digitized as soon as possible", with the digital surrogate used for access "while the original remains in cold storage" [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.6 (PDF 6)]. The 2020 leaflet's reformatting section specifies "standard file formats, such as TIFF, with sufficient image resolution to capture a high level of detail", metadata, migration and redundant storage [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.6 (PDF 6)]. [F]

### 22.10 Nitrate decomposition stages and hazards

**Stages.** The canonical six-level scale is reproduced in §22.8. "Cellulose nitrate decomposition can be very rapid." [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2)] **No times, temperatures or acidity values are attached to any nitrate stage in any source here.** [F]

**The 1993/1996 guide gives no staged scale for nitrate at all.** Its nitrate content is chemical and comparative, and it is explicit about the data gap: "Does the Guide's data apply to nitrate? In a general sense, yes. Trends similar to those seen in the effects of temperature and RH on the rate of acetate deterioration are seen for nitrate deterioration as well. At this time, IPI has limited data on the behavior of nitrate films, so a wheel for nitrate does not exist." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)] [F]

**The nitrate accelerated-aging result, including its bimodality.** "IPI's 1988-1990 study of film-base deterioration included a **50-year-old sample** of nitrate motion picture film; its response to the storage environment (and therefore its predicted life expectancy) were much the same as that of acetate film." But: "Samples of nitrate seemed to divide into two groups: those that were in apparent good shape and performed similarly to fresh acetate, and those that were in apparent good shape but degraded very quickly in the accelerated-aging tests. Some of the nitrate film samples used in the research had slightly more acidity initially, and these degraded faster." A footnote fixes the sample age: "Since nitrate film hasn't been manufactured for forty years, all the nitrate samples were at least a half-century old." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)] [Q] The bimodality is reported but not parameterised — no proportions, no acidity values for the two groups, no separation criterion beyond "slightly more acidity initially". [M]

**Hazards.**

| Hazard | Statement | Class | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flammability | "The film was, and is, highly flammable, and it releases hazardous gases as it deteriorates. Large quantities of nitrate film have caused several disastrous fires." | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)] |
| Self-sustaining combustion | nitrate "once ignited can supply its own oxygen to continue the combustion and is therefore very difficult to extinguish" | [F] | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, pp.47–48 (PDF 51–52)] |
| Cannot be extinguished | "Cellulose nitrate burns quickly and has a characteristic yellow flame … only cellulose nitrate will burn downwards." Burning nitrate "cannot be extinguished". | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.4 (PDF 4)] |
| Historical fires, and the industry's response | "The awful tragedies that occurred because of the high flammability of nitrate film (fires that consumed film vaults, sometimes killing many people) made the photographic industry very careful about the burning properties of safety film. … The high plasticizer content of acetate films reflects a desire to make film as non-flammable as possible." | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)] |
| Most hazardous format, and its disposal | "Professional 35mm motion picture film is the most hazardous type. All nitrate 35mm motion picture film should be duplicated by an authorized laboratory. Then the nitrate motion picture film should be disposed of by the local fire marshal or a hazardous materials disposal service." | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2), note E] |
| Damage to neighbours | nitric acid "can destroy enclosures in which the negatives are stored. It can even damage materials stored in close proximity to the collection." | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2)] |
| Damage to cans and paper | nitro groups' "highly acidic fumes rust film cans and embrittle paper enclosures" | [F] | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.10 (PDF 10)] |
| Scale of loss | "Due to the inherent instability of cellulose nitrate, much of our photographic legacy from this period is disappearing." | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)] |
| Collection-level trigger | "A photographic collection that contains any flexible, transparent film negatives from the time period of 1890-1950 is very likely to contain at least some nitrate film. Since these negatives need special attention, they should immediately be separated from other negatives." | [F] | [NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)] |

**Nitrate also exudes plasticiser.** "(Nitrate film also contains plasticizers that exude onto the surface as deterioration progresses.)" [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.12 (PDF 12)] [F]

### 22.11 Polyester stability, and why it replaced acetate

**The stability claim, and its one number.** "Polyester film base is inherently more chemically stable than either cellulose nitrate or cellulose acetate. With nearly 50 years of manufacturing and keeping experience behind it, polyester film support has shown exceptional chemical stability and overall good physical performance. When there is a choice between polyester and acetate film supports, polyester is clearly the best one for archival use." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)] [F]

"Although polyester base is also subject to chemical deterioration (nothing lasts forever), accelerated-aging tests show that it will last **five to ten times longer than acetate** under comparable storage conditions. Such testing shows temperature and humidity dependence in polyester base deterioration, so good storage is still important." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)] [Q]

**No field failures reported as of 1993.** "To date, there have been no reported cases of chemical deterioration of polyester base in archival collections. When such deterioration does occur, brittleness and loss of tensile properties will likely be among the symptoms." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)] [F] Note that these are *predicted* symptoms, and that they are the same two symptoms as acetate embrittlement — but with no shrinkage, no acid odour, no plasticiser exudation (there is no plasticiser, §21.6) and no channelling mechanism named. [M]

**The system-level lifetime claim.** "Polyester base, gelatin emulsion layers, and the correct choice of image substance will yield a pictorial recording medium that should survive **five centuries or more at room temperature and moderate RH**." Conventionally processed silver images "are not equipped to withstand the slow attack of atmospheric pollutants" but "can be chemically treated to become virtually unalterable." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.15 (PDF 15)] [Q]

**And the limiting factor shifts.** For polyester, "the base may last long enough that the slow chemical deterioration of gelatin becomes the limiting factor in the survival of film." [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.17 (PDF 17)] [F] Gelatin's own chemical deterioration leads "to loss of strength and ultimately to softening and inability to withstand immersion in water", and is usually too slow to notice [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.17 (PDF 17)]. [M]

**Why polyester replaced acetate, format by format, as stated.**

| Format | Stated reason | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Cut sheet (X-ray, graphic arts, from 1955) | "good physical properties and dimensional stability were prime requirements" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] |
| Microfilm (rapid shift in the 1980s) | "the greater chemical stability of the base and the possibility of using thinner supports, thereby increasing the number of images on each roll" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)] |
| Colour separation / graphic arts (1966) | "Dimensional stability is so high that the exacting field of colour separation can now be tackled using film instead of glass plates" | [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] |
| Motion picture — **why it did not replace acetate faster** | "The acceptance of polyester base in cinema films has been slowed somewhat by difficulty in splicing on traditional splicing equipment"; and in 1966, "very difficult to splice … The latter factor is probably why it has not been used so far for cine films in spite of its high physical strength" | [Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.22 (PDF 22)]; [Duffin 1966, Ch. III, p.53 (PDF 57)] |

[F] The material reason is dimensional stability and chemical stability; the reason for the delay in cinema is a splicing-equipment constraint, stated independently by two sources 27 years apart.

**A comparison the sources do not make, and we should not fake.** No source here gives a polyester-equivalent of Table 22.6-A — there is no (T, RH) → years table for PET, only the 5–10× multiplier. Whether that multiplier applies uniformly across the temperature and RH range of Table 22.6-A, or only at some reference condition, is not stated. Source silent. [F]

## 23. Aging of the carrier versus aging of the photographic image

This section is the analytical point of §21–§22. It is kept deliberately strict, because the
temptation to convert a preservation fact into a rendering parameter is exactly the error that
would put unsupported numbers into the simulation.

The governing statement is the source's own scope disclaimer: the IPI Guide is about the
**plastic support**, and says so before the reader reaches any of its quantitative core
`[Reilly, IPI Storage Guide for Acetate Film, 1993 (rev. 1996), p.2 (PDF 2)]` **[F]**

### 23.1 List A — effects that act on the CARRIER only

| # | Effect | Evidence for placing it here | Class |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Base shrinkage, >1 % "real trouble" for cinema film, up to 10 % advanced | The source contrasts the two layers explicitly: "The acetate base gets much smaller, but the gelatin emulsion frequently does not (it isn't undergoing deterioration, so it stays the same size)" `[Reilly p.11 (PDF 11)]` | **[Q]** |
| A2 | Base embrittlement; "easily shatters with the slightest flexing" | Chain scission in the support polymer; no image change stated `[Reilly p.11 (PDF 11)]` | **[M]** |
| A3 | Free-acidity rise 0.05 → 0.5 → 1.0 → 5.0–10.0 | Measured "in the film base" `[Reilly p.13, p.14 (PDF 13, 14)]` | **[Q]** |
| A4 | Acetic-acid generation and vinegar odour | "released inside the plastic, but it gradually diffuses to the surface" `[Reilly p.10 (PDF 10)]` | **[Q]** |
| A5 | Plasticiser exudation as crystals or liquid bubbles | Additive migrating out of the base; visible "on either the base or emulsion side" but originating in the support `[Reilly p.12 (PDF 12)]` | **[M]** |
| A6 | Warping; buckling and channelling of the emulsion | Cause is in the carrier, the emulsion is the passive party — "something has to give" `[Reilly p.11, p.24 (PDF 11, 24)]` | **[F]** |
| A7 | Emulsion–base bond failure (delamination) | "the bond between the emulsion and base lets go in some areas, thus relieving the stress caused by base shrinkage" `[Reilly p.11 (PDF 11)]` | **[F]** |
| A8 | Humidity-driven expansion and contraction of all cellulosic bases | `[Reilly p.12 (PDF 12)]` | **[M]** |
| A9 | Curl and spoking at low RH; nitrate roll film in "tight scrolls" | `[Reilly p.17 (PDF 17)]`; `[NEDCC Preservation Leaflet 5.1, 2020, p.1 (PDF 1)]` | **[F]** |
| A10 | Polyester chemical stability, tear resistance, birefringence, edge light-piping | All carrier properties `[Reilly p.15, p.21, p.22 (PDF 15, 21, 22)]` | **[F]** |
| A11 | Casting-solvent evaporation from fresh base, and the small shrinkage it causes | `[Reilly p.11, p.19 (PDF 11, 19)]` | **[M]** |
| A12 | NEDCC acetate stages 3–6 — shrinkage, brittleness, warping, bubbles and crystals, channelling | All described as happening to "the film" / "the plastic support" `[NEDCC 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)]` | **[F]** (ordinal) |

### 23.2 List B — effects that reach the photographic IMAGE

| # | Effect | Evidence | Class |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | **Nitrate: silver-image fading** | "They fade silver images"; "Strong oxidants from nitrate may cause fading of silver images" `[Reilly p.10, p.20 (PDF 10, 20)]` | **[F]** |
| B2 | **Nitrate: image yellowing, mirroring, amber cast, progressive loss of legible image** | Stages 2, 4, 4–6 `[NEDCC 5.1, 2020, p.3 (PDF 3)]` | **[F]** (ordinal) |
| B3 | **Nitrate: gelatin ruined, soft and sticky** | "Ruined gelatin in degraded 35 mm nitrate motion picture film" `[Reilly p.10, p.17 (PDF 10, 17)]` | **[F]** |
| B4 | **Acetate: accelerated fading of SOME colour dyes** | "one effect of acetic acid generation in acetate film is to accelerate the fading rate of some color dyes in color film" `[Reilly p.10 (PDF 10)]`. ⚠ This is the **only** image-level consequence of acetate base degradation stated in either document, and it carries no factor, no named dye and no condition | **[M]** |
| B5 | **Acetate: gelatin softening in extreme cases** | "In extreme cases, vinegar syndrome can lead to softening of gelatin" `[Reilly p.10 (PDF 10)]` — hedged by the source itself | **[F]** |
| B6 | **Acetate: pink or blue colouration of the backing (antihalation) layer** | Optically real in transmission; caused by base-generated acid; located in a gelatin layer, not in the image record `[Reilly p.12 (PDF 12)]`; NEDCC stage 2 "can turn red or blue" `[NEDCC 5.1, 2020, p.5 (PDF 5)]`. **Boundary case** — acid from the carrier producing a colour change in a non-image gelatin layer | **[F]** |
| B7 | Image effects whose causes are **independent of the base**, recorded here because the documents are explicit that they are separate pathways: silver fading driven by RH and pollutants with temperature playing "only a limited role" `[Reilly p.16, p.18 (PDF 16, 18)]`; dye fading driven by T and RH, magenta surviving longest giving a purple cast, pre-1980 stocks "20 to 30 years at room temperature before fading becomes significant" `[Reilly p.16 (PDF 16)]`; mould stains and gelatin dissolution above ~70 % RH `[Reilly p.17 (PDF 17)]`; enclosure-caused staining and fading, addressed by the Photographic Activity Test `[Reilly p.20 (PDF 20)]` | | **[Q]** for the dye timescale, **[M]** otherwise |

### 23.3 List C — cannot be decided from these sources

Recorded as undecidable rather than guessed. Each of these is a question a simulation author
would naturally ask, and the honest answer from this source set is "not stated".

1. Whether acetate base degradation changes base optical **density**. No statement, no measurement, in either direction. **[F]** (absence)
2. Whether acetate base degradation changes base **colour or tint**. The documents give a colour change located in the *backing layer*, plus NEDCC's undifferentiated "turn red or blue"; neither says the acetate polymer itself discolours. Whether NEDCC's stage-2 colour is Reilly's antihalation mechanism or something else is not decidable from the texts. **[F]** (absence)
3. Whether degraded base becomes **hazy, cloudy or light-scattering**. Never mentioned in either document. **[F]** (absence)
4. The **magnitude** of the dye-fading acceleration caused by acetic acid — direction only `[Reilly p.10 (PDF 10)]`. **[F]** (absence)
5. The **magnitude** of the acid-trapping factor — "greatly accelerates", no multiplier `[Reilly p.3 (PDF 3)]`. **[F]** (absence)
6. Base **thickness change or refractive-index change** with degradation. Never mentioned. **[F]** (absence)
7. **Spatial statistics** of channelling, bubbles and crystals — size distribution, spacing, amplitude, frequency. Only photographs, plus the qualitative "typically in the center of the film" for liquid plasticiser bubbles `[Reilly p.12 (PDF 12)]`. **[F]** (absence)
8. Whether shrinkage is **isotropic**, or differs along versus across the web. The 1 % and 10 % figures carry no axis. **[F]** (absence)
9. Whether NEDCC's acetate stage order (curl and colour before odour) or Reilly's (acid first, then dye reversion) is correct. **The documents conflict and neither adjudicates.** Both are recorded in §22; they are not merged. **[F]**
10. **Activation energies** or any closed-form Arrhenius model. Absent from both — the predictions exist only as tabulated (T, RH) → years. **[F]** (absence)
11. **Spectral transmission** of nitrate or acetate base at any wavelength, fresh or degraded. Absent. **[F]** (absence)
12. Whether any of this affects a **scan**. Neither document discusses scanning optics; every connection to a scanner is inference, not source. **[F]** (absence)

### 23.4 Engineering assessment — what could legitimately reach a rendered frame

Everything in this subsection is **[E]** — our conclusion, not the sources' claim.

**Defensible.**

1. **Base material as an era/format validity constraint, not an image effect.** The chronology of
   §21 is the strongest usable deliverable in this whole area, not because base chemistry changes
   the look but because it constrains which stock, format and date combinations are historically
   coherent — 16 mm and 8 mm were never nitrate; a "Safety" marking dates a sheet film; polyester
   in still-camera roll film is late. Treat as metadata governing preset validity, never as a
   pixel operation. **[E]**
2. **Shrinkage as a geometric term.** The one aging effect with a real number attached to a real
   consequence: >1 % "enough to cause real trouble for cinema films", up to 10 % advanced
   `[Reilly p.11 (PDF 11)]`. Our pipeline already carries gate weave and misregistration, so a
   global shrink parameter over 0–10 % with a knee at 1 % is defensible. ⚠ But the source does
   not say what the trouble *is*, does not resolve shrinkage by axis, and gives no time or
   temperature dependence for shrinkage itself — only for the acidity that precedes it. This is a
   plausible range, **not a calibrated model**. **[E]**
3. **Surface deformation as a low-frequency geometry or focus field.** Channelling, warping,
   bubbles and crystals under the emulsion are documented and photographed. ⚠ The focus
   consequence is entirely our inference — neither document mentions focus, depth of field or
   scanning. And these are late-stage, visually catastrophic states: a frame with stage-6
   channelling reads as damaged material, not as "film look". Belongs in a damaged-archival-element
   preset, not in general film emulation. **[E]**
4. **Backing-layer pink/blue cast on degraded acetate sheet film.** The single stated,
   mechanism-explained, transmission-affecting colour change in either document. Format-specific
   (sheet film with a backing gelatin), manufacturer-specific, and unquantified — no density, no
   spectrum. Implementable only as a labelled artistic cast; do not present it as a base tint. **[E]**
5. **Nitrate image degradation as a distinct look.** Silver fading, mirroring, amber cast,
   progressive loss of legible image — genuinely image-level, and the only base-driven image
   degradation the documents support. Ordinal only, so a 1–6 severity scale with hand-authored
   looks is the honest implementation; there is nothing to calibrate against. **[E]**
6. **Colour dye fading with a magenta survivor.** Purple cast, magenta lasting longest, pre-1980
   stocks 20–30 years at room temperature `[Reilly p.16 (PDF 16)]`. Modellable as differential
   per-dye density decay with a rough timescale. ⚠ **This is not a base effect** — it appears in
   these sources incidentally and Reilly explicitly excludes dye fading from the Guide's scope
   `[Reilly p.2 (PDF 2)]`. Use it; do not attribute it to base aging. **[E]**

**Not defensible from these sources.**

7. ⚠ **"Vinegar syndrome" as an image effect: no measurable image effect is established in these
   sources.** This is the central honest finding of §21–§23, and it runs opposite to what a
   look-preset author would want. The source says: "the silver image is not faded to orange-red as
   is often the case in nitrate decomposition" `[Reilly p.10 (PDF 10)]` and "the silver image
   usually remains in good condition" `[Reilly p.13 (PDF 13), Fig. 18]`. The emulsion survives
   well enough to be floated off the ruined base and rephotographed `[Reilly p.11 (PDF 11)]`.
   A vinegar-syndrome preset that darkens, yellows or fogs the photographic image has **no support
   in either document and contradicts the source directly**. The only image-side consequences
   stated are the unquantified acceleration of some colour-dye fading (B4) and gelatin softening
   in extreme cases (B5). **[E]**
8. **Base haze or opacity — no support whatsoever.** Neither document mentions it. A "hazy base"
   parameter needs a different source. **[E]**
9. **Base yellowing changing base density for acetate — not stated.** Only nitrate is described as
   yellowing or ambering, and only ordinally. An acetate "yellowed base" parameter cannot be
   sourced here. **[E]**
10. **The entire storage-prediction apparatus** — the Wheel, the Time Contours, the Time Out of
    Storage table, the 17× and 3× factors, the 40 / 50 / 100 / 150 / 450-year predictions. These
    predict *when the carrier begins to smell of vinegar*, defined as reaching 0.5 free acidity
    `[Reilly p.2, p.9, p.14 (PDF 2, 9, 14)]` — at which point the source states the film "may not
    have any other symptoms of degradation and will be perfectly usable" `[Reilly p.14 (PDF 14)]`.
    There is no path from these numbers to a pixel. Do not build a "years of storage" control that
    changes image appearance on the strength of them. **[E]**
11. **A-D strip levels, free-acidity values, acid trapping, enclosure chemistry, segregation
    policy, vault volatiles, health hazards, PAT / ANSI / ISO conformance, cold-storage
    engineering, digitisation policy.** Zero image consequence. Preservation only. **[E]**
12. **Identification tests** (float, polarised light, diphenylamine, burn, notch codes, edge
    printing). Diagnostic procedures. The only two with any bearing on rendering are polyester's
    birefringence and edge light-piping `[Reilly p.21 (PDF 21)]`, and both describe how the film
    looks to someone holding it up to a light, not how a frame images. Birefringence is a real PET
    property that could in principle matter to a polarised-light scanner, but neither document
    connects it to image capture. **[E]**

### 23.5 Net summary

From roughly thirty pages of two authoritative preservation sources, the extractable
**image-level** content is: nitrate image loss (ordinal), colour dye fading with a magenta
survivor and a 20–30-year room-temperature timescale for pre-1980 stocks, an unquantified
acetic-acid acceleration of some dye fading, a format-specific pink/blue backing-layer cast, and
a shrinkage range of 1–10 % that can drive geometry. Everything else — including the entire
quantitative core of the IPI Guide — is about keeping the plastic alive. **[E]**

Cross-references: base chronology → §21; degradation mechanism and prediction tables → §22;
where the two documents disagree → §22 and item C9 above; what this means for our schema → §26.

## 23b. Sulfur sensitization measured: the traced sweeps (added 2026-08-27, task A2)

Tani Figs. 7.10 and 7.11 were traced from the source PDF at 200 dpi by local-ink-density peak
detection, calibrated on the printed axis ticks (x: −5 / −4 / −3 at 207 and 206.5 px per decade on
the two pages; y: panel frames at the printed limits). **Same emulsion, same sensitization sweep,
same 0.1 s exposure — only the developer differs.** That is what makes the pair decisive.

Emulsion: sulfur-sensitized cubic AgBr. Abscissa: log₁₀ of the amount of Na₂S₂O₃ used for
sensitization, mol per mol AgBr. `[Tani 1995, Figs. 7.10–7.11, pp.217–218 (PDF 226–227)]`

### 23b.1 Rate of development — the cleanest result in the whole source set

| log[Na₂S₂O₃] | **CP-20** rate, min⁻¹ (type A, parallel) | **D72** rate, min⁻¹ (type B, granular) |
|---|---|---|
| −4.05 | 0.769 | **2.681** |
| −3.74 | — | 1.074 |
| −3.68 | 0.779 | — |
| −3.63 | 0.788 | 0.794 |
| −3.55 | 0.740 | **0.639** |

**[Q] CP-20 is FLAT to ±3 % across the sweep (0.740–0.788). D72 falls by a factor of 4.2.**

That is the mechanism made visible. Granular development is rate-limited by the **first electron
injection** into a development centre, so dispersing the centres — which is what more sulfur does —
slows it. Parallel development is limited by the grain's own surface-to-volume ratio, which
sensitization does not change. It is the same distinction Fig. 7.12 shows from the other side:
parallel rate ∝ 1/d, granular rate independent of d.

**[Q] Light intensity acts the same way as sensitization, and only on the granular case.** The
10⁻⁴ s series in Fig. 7.10 (open symbols) runs **1.51 → 0.40 min⁻¹** and flattens — systematically
below the 0.1 s series at every point. Tani's text gives the shared cause: both a higher intensity
and a heavier sensitization "generally make image centers dispersed".

### 23b.2 Sensitivity — a peak in both, but a very different fall

| log[Na₂S₂O₃] | **CP-20** log S | log[Na₂S₂O₃] | **D72** log S (0.1 s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| −4.30 | 1.317 | −4.35 | 1.576 |
| −4.07 | 1.471 | −4.06 | 1.848 |
| **−3.69** | **1.755** ← peak | **−3.74** | **2.043** ← peak |
| −3.64 | 1.678 | −3.65 | 1.890 |
| −3.56 | 1.457 | −3.58 | 1.710 |
| — | — | −3.38 | 1.162 |

**[Q]** Both rise then collapse — over-sensitization destroys speed, and the optimum is narrow
(within ~0.3 decades of thiosulfate). But the fall is very different: **CP-20 −0.30 log** from peak
to the last measured point, **D72 −0.88 log**, nearly three stops.

⚠ **The two peaks differ (2.04 vs 1.76) and that is NOT a contradiction of the
developer-independence-of-speed rule** recorded in §24.1. That rule holds when each developer is
used **at its own optimum**; these two series are at one fixed development condition each. Recorded
so a later reader does not treat the gap as evidence against the rule.

### 23b.3 Fog

| | CP-20 (parallel) | D72 (granular) |
|---|---|---|
| least sensitized | 0.051 | ~0.02 |
| through the optimum | 0.056 → 0.065 | 0.03 → 0.06 |
| most sensitized | **0.107** | **0.351** |

**[Q] Granular fog rises about 4× at heavy sensitization; parallel fog roughly doubles and stays
under 0.11.** This is the mechanism §12 describes — sensitization centres act as electron traps and
therefore become developer-fog centres — measured, with the developer class deciding how much it
costs.

### 23b.4 What this changes for the database

* **It confirms the schema-v18 `DevelopmentProgress` field from a second, independent direction.**
  The field was justified on Figs. 7.8/7.9 (density versus grain-state fractions); these two figures
  reach the same split through development *rate*. `partial_fill_fraction` and
  `rate_size_coeff_um_min` are unchanged — 0.45 / 0.591 for parallel, 0.04 / not-applicable for
  granular.
* **It supports a `rate_sensitization_dependence` flag — and it is NOT proposed.** A per-stock
  sensitization level would be needed to use it, and `EmulsionSpec.sensitization` is empty on
  161 of 161 stocks with no source in existence that attaches it to a named commercial film (§27).
  A field nothing can fill is schema churn.
* **It sharpens B4 (two-component fog) without closing it.** The direction and the developer
  dependence are now quantified; the *rates* still are not, so B4 still needs a Dmin-versus-time
  series for one stock.
* ⚠ **It does NOT close the grain-size → graininess gap** (§24.2 item 1), which remains absent from
  all six sources.

## 23c. The sensitivity chronology measured: Tani Fig. 1.1 traced (added 2026-08-27, task A3)

Fig. 1.1 is the one figure in the source set that fixes the *whole* chronology on a single
quantitative axis, which is why §28.1 called it "the chronological spine of §2". Until now it was
cited only qualitatively. It is now traced.

**Method.** PDF page 13 was rendered at 600 dpi with `pdftoppm`, giving a 3422 × 5539 bitmap. The
plot is a single unbroken polyline; it was extracted by column-wise dark-run tracking, seeded inside
the curve at pixel (900, 1872.5) and run in both directions, accepting per column the ink run whose
interval lies nearest the previous ordinate. Vertical and near-vertical segments produce tall runs,
so a run taller than 18 px is resolved to its leading edge in the direction of travel rather than to
its midpoint — without that rule the two step transitions round off into ramps. The label text and
the five annotation arrows are dark too, and they are rejected because they never form a run
adjacent to the previous ordinate. 2246 columns were recovered, spanning the full plotted extent.

**Calibration.** Both axes were calibrated by least squares on the printed tick marks of that same
render, which are inward-pointing and were located by ink projection:

| Axis | Anchors (px) | Fit | Max residual |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year | 720 = 1830, 1010 = 1850, 1737 = 1900, 2470 = 1950 | year = 1882.5 + (x − 1484.25) / 14.582 | 2.4 px = **0.17 yr** |
| Sensitivity | 867 = 10⁴, 1166 = 10², 1462 = 10⁰, 1748 = 10⁻² | log₁₀ ISO = 1.0 + (1310.75 − y) / 146.95 | 4.3 px = **0.029 decade** |

⚠ The four decade anchors on the ordinate are **not** equispaced in the original artwork: successive
two-decade gaps measure 299, 296 and 286 px. That is draughtsmanship in the 1995 printing, not a
tracing artefact — the tick centroids are unambiguous to ±3 px. The linear fit absorbs it as a
±0.03 decade (±7 %) systematic, and every value below is quoted to that precision, not tighter.

Plotted extent: **1836.8 to 1990.8**, ISO **0.00135 to 1292**. Six orders of magnitude in 154 years.

### 23c.1 The curve is piecewise linear, and the vertices are the technology dates

A continuous piecewise-linear least-squares fit with free breakpoints converges on seven knots and
leaves an RMS residual of **0.017 decade (4.1 % in ISO)** over all 2246 traced columns — which is
below the calibration systematic, so the figure *is* a straight-segment construction and the fit has
recovered it rather than smoothed it.

| Segment | Slope (decade per 10 yr) | Speed multiplier per decade | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1836.8 – 1847.0 | +0.070 | ×1.17 | Daguerreotype plateau. Essentially flat |
| **1847.0 – 1851.5** | **+3.885** | ×7.7 × 10³ | **Development.** Vertical step: ×56 in 4.5 years |
| 1851.5 – 1871.0 | +0.074 | ×1.19 | Wet-collodion plateau. Flat for 20 years |
| **1871.0 – 1879.5** | **+2.007** | ×102 | **Gelatin, then spectral sensitization.** ×51 in 8.5 years |
| 1879.5 – 1905.0 | +0.072 | ×1.18 | Gelatin-dry-plate plateau. Flat for 25 years |
| 1905.0 – 1912.0 | +0.114 | ×1.30 | Transition |
| 1912.0 – 1935.0 | +0.371 | ×2.35 | Steepest *sustained* growth in the whole record |
| 1935.0 – 1990.8 | +0.224 | ×1.68 | Modern era. Continuous, and **decelerating** |

Vertex sensitivities, from the same fit: 1836.8 → ISO 0.00135; 1847.0 → 0.00159; 1851.5 → 0.089;
1871.0 → 0.124; 1879.5 → 6.3; 1905.0 → 9.7; 1912.0 → 11.6; 1935.0 → 82.6; 1990.8 → 1469 (the fitted
endpoint overshoots the traced endpoint of 1292 by 0.055 decade, because the final segment is very
slightly concave; where a number is wanted for 1990, use the traced value).

**Three plateaux and two steps.** This is the structural fact the figure carries and the reason it is
worth having as numbers: between 1836 and 1912 the record is not growth at all, it is *three flat
periods separated by two near-vertical jumps*. On the plateaux the material improves by a factor of
about 1.2 per decade — within the noise of the tracing. At the two steps it improves by ×56 and ×51
in under a decade each. Neither step is an emulsion-formulation gain: the first is the discovery that
a *latent* image can be amplified chemically, the second is a change of *binder* immediately followed
by the discovery that the binder can carry dyes. Both are cited in §2.3 and §5 from the text; the
figure is what makes them commensurable with each other and with the modern era.

**The modern era decelerates.** 1912–1935 runs at +0.371 decade per 10 yr; 1935–1991 at +0.224.
Tani's own text is consistent with this and explains it as the point at which raw sensitivity stopped
being the free variable: past a certain grain size, more speed costs granularity and sharpness faster
than it buys exposure latitude. This matters to us directly — see §23c.3.

### 23c.2 Traced values by decade

Read off the trace, not the fit, at the nearest traced column to each decade (all within 1 year):

| Year | ISO | Year | ISO |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1840 | 0.00142 | 1920 | 24.1 |
| 1850 | 0.0211 | 1930 | 53.7 |
| 1860 | 0.103 | 1940 | 105 |
| 1870 | 0.119 | 1950 | 182 |
| 1880 | 6.58 | 1960 | 296 |
| 1890 | 7.69 | 1970 | 521 |
| 1900 | 8.93 | 1980 | 873 |
| 1910 | 10.2 | 1990 | 1272 |

⚠ **What this axis is not.** The caption says only "photographic materials". Nothing in the caption
or the surrounding text states whether the ordinate is the *fastest material available* in that year,
a typical general-purpose material, or a specific product line; nothing states the measuring
standard, which cannot have been ISO before 1974 in any case; and nothing states whether the
pre-1880 points are ISO-equivalent reconstructions or contemporary measurements — they cannot be
contemporary, since ISO 0.0013 is not a number anyone measured in 1840. Treat the whole curve as
**one author's calibrated reconstruction of a trend**, [Q] in shape and [F] at best in level. It is
not a source of a speed value for any individual stock, and no profile in our database should ever
be given an `exposure_index` from it. `[Tani 1995, §1.1, p.4 (PDF 13), Fig. 1.1]`

### 23c.3 Cross-check against our own era ladder — and what it says about the last 30 years

The DQE guard added earlier this session bands stocks by class and era and evaluates
K = mid_slope² · EI / rms², a granularity-penalised speed proxy. For colour negative it produced,
without any reference to Tani:

| Era band | n | median EI | median rms | median mid slope | median K |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pre-1960 | 11 | 23 | 12.8 | 0.597 | **0.045** |
| 1960–89 | 21 | 100 | 12.0 | 0.529 | **0.219** |
| 1990+ | 38 | 200 | 4.6 | 0.573 | **2.676** |

**First cross-check — levels.** Taking the fastest *conventional* stock introduced in each decade in
our database (instant materials excluded, since Polaroid 410 at EI 10000 is not a camera-negative
emulsion) against the traced curve:

| Decade | Our fastest stock | EI | Tani Fig. 1.1 | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1920s | EASTMAN_ORTHO_1930 | 25 | 24.1 | 1.04 |
| 1930s | EASTMAN_SUPER_XX_1938 | 100 | 53.7 | 1.86 |
| 1940s | ILFORD_HP3 | 400 | 105 | 3.80 |
| 1950s | KODAK_TRI_X_400TX | 400 | 182 | 2.20 |
| 1960s | ILFORD_HP4 | 400 | 296 | 1.35 |
| 1970s | KODAK_RECORDING_2475 | 1600 | 521 | 3.07 |
| 1980s | KODAK_TMAX_P3200 | 1000 | 873 | 1.15 |
| 1990s | ILFORD_DELTA_3200 | 3200 | 1272 | 2.52 |

Median ratio **2.03**, and the log-slopes over 1920–1990 agree to +0.30 (ours) versus +0.25 (Tani)
decade per 10 yr. Two things follow. The agreement in *slope* is a real independent confirmation:
our era tagging and Tani's chronology are describing the same history, and neither contains a gross
error. The systematic factor of ~2 in *level* is expected and explicable — our `exposure_index` is
the manufacturer's rated speed, and the stocks that top each decade are precisely the push-rated
specialty emulsions whose true ISO is roughly half their name (Delta 3200 measures near ISO 1000,
TMAX P3200 near 800–1000). Corrected for that, the two curves sit on top of each other. **This is a
consistency check, not a calibration; nothing was adjusted to make it agree.**

**Second cross-check — and this is the substantive finding.** Our K ladder rises ×4.9 then ×12.2.
Tani's curve over the same two intervals rises only about ×6 then ×2. The K jump after 1990 is
therefore *not* a speed jump, and our own component medians say exactly where it comes from: between
1960–89 and 1990+, median EI rises ×2.0, median mid slope is flat (0.529 → 0.573), and median rms
granularity falls **12.0 → 4.6**, contributing ×6.8 through the 1/rms² term. Six of the twelve-fold
gain is granularity; two of it is speed.

That is the tabular-grain transition, and it means the DQE guard's era bands and Tani's Fig. 1.1 are
measuring two genuinely different things over the modern period: Fig. 1.1 tracks how fast the
*fastest* material got, our ladder tracks how clean a *given* speed got. They agree where the
industry was buying speed (pre-1960) and diverge where it started buying speed-per-grain instead
(post-1990) — which is the same story Tani tells in §7.3 and the same one the traced Figs. 7.8–7.11
tell about development efficiency. Fig. 1.1's own deceleration after 1935 is the first visible sign
of it.

**No database change follows from this trace.** It sets no parameter. Its value is that it converts
§2's chronology from a sequence of dated assertions into a curve with slopes, and that it gives the
DQE guard's era banding an external check it did not have before. Recorded as [Q] for shape and
slope, [F] for level, and explicitly **not** usable as a speed source (§23c.2).

Raw trace and calibration are in `doc/thirdparty/tani_fig1_1_raw_px.txt` (2246 rows).

## 23d. The 1920 American market measured: Davis & Walters Part III harvested (added 2026-08-27, task A5)

§28.1 listed two Davis & Walters items — the Part III survey charts and the time-of-development
figures — as "the only measured real-material sensitometry in the set". Part III is 86 pages, one
anonymous emulsion per page, each carrying a colour-sensitivity plot, a family of characteristic
curves, a time–gamma plot, filter factors, and a three-field data block. The three data-block fields
are now harvested for all 86.

### 23d.1 The method, and why the text layer was thrown away

The pages are rotated 90°, so the first step was a coordinate-space reconstruction: word boxes from
`pdftotext -bbox`, clustered by `xMin` into rotated lines, then read bottom-to-top. That recovers the
field labels reliably and gave a complete first-pass harvest.

**That harvest was then checked against 300 dpi renders of all 86 pages, and it failed.**

| Field | Pages with a value | OCR agreed with the image | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| B.S. speed | 86 | 58 | **67.4 %** |
| Scale | 81 | 80 | 98.8 % |
| Resolution number | 79 | 63 | 79.7 % |

⚠ **The B.S. speed errors are not garbage — they are silent leading-digit drops.** 330 → 30,
560 → 20, 650 → 10, 175 → 75, 355 → 55, 280 → 80, 215 → 20, 111's 355 → 55. Every one of those is a
number that would pass any range check, any plausibility check and any eyeball. Fourteen more pages
returned no speed at all, which is the harmless failure. The resolution errors are the same shape:
a two-digit value read as its second digit, usually `5`. **An unverified harvest of this table would
have produced a clean-looking dataset that was wrong on a third of its most important column.**

§29.3 already warned that "digits in the survey tables are the least reliable content in this entire
source set" and that "the page image should be consulted before the value is used". That warning was
written qualitatively; **it is now measured, and it was an understatement.** The values recorded in
`doc/thirdparty/davis_walters_1920_survey.txt` are the image-read ones.

The word fields — material class, emulsion type, developer formula letter — come from the text layer
and are *not* individually image-checked, because words survive this OCR far better than digits do
and because a misread class would show up as a nonsense category. Recorded as the weaker evidence
they are.

### 23d.2 What the three fields mean, in the paper's own words

Getting this right changes the sign of the main result, so it is quoted rather than paraphrased.

| Field | Definition as printed | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| **B.S. speed** | 10/*i*, where *i* is the Hurter & Driffield inertia. The paper explains the choice: "The number 1/i would have been more logical, but 10/i was chosen so that all usual speed numbers might be represented by integers and the confusion of fractions be avoided" | `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14), note 5]` |
| **Scale** | "By scale is understood **the range of light intensity that a plate is able to record correctly**" — a ratio, not a stop count, and explicitly the *correctly recorded* range, i.e. the straight-line portion | `[Davis & Walters 1922, p.13 (PDF 14), §7]` |
| **Resolution number** | "a resolution number of 18 means that the plate was able to **resolve lines whose centers were 0.018 mm apart**" — a **separation** in units of 0.001 mm | `[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–30 (PDF 30–31), §7]` |

⚠ **The resolution number runs backwards: SMALLER IS BETTER.** It is not lines per millimetre. Read
as lines/mm it inverts every conclusion below, and it is exactly the sort of unit trap that a harvest
which only captured the number would have walked into.

### 23d.3 The 86 emulsions

86 records: **73 plates, 13 films.** The survey is organised in blocks by class, each block sorted by
increasing speed — a structure that is itself a check, since a value that breaks the sort inside a
block is a candidate misreading. (No image-read value does.)

| Class | n | Median B.S. speed | Speed range | Median resolution number | Median scale, stops |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orthochromatic | 23 | 330 | 78 – 650 | 21.5 | 5.71 |
| Ordinary | 20 | 392 | 80 – 1050 | 21.5 | 6.32 |
| Panchromatic | 6 | 128 | 75 – 350 | 20 | 5.64 |
| Lantern slide | 6 | 33.5 | 18 – 45 | 14 | 3.45 |
| Transparency | 4 | 25 | 3.5 – 38 | 12 | 3.73 |
| Process (ordinary) | 4 | 40 | 7 – 60 | 16.5 | 2.70 |
| Roll orthochromatic | 4 | 295 | 155 – 400 | 22 | — |
| *(all 86)* | 86 | **235** | **3.5 – 1050** | **20** | **5.32** |

Whole-survey spread in speed is **300 : 1**. Four developer formulas are used across the survey — X
(36 emulsions), W (23), Z (11), Y (10) — which matters because a comparison across two of these rows
is a comparison across two developers unless the letters match.

### 23d.4 The speed/resolution trade-off, quantified from 1920 material

The paper states the rule qualitatively: "As a general rule, the faster a plate the larger will be
its grain size and the poorer its resolution, while the slower plates (such as lantern slides,
transparency, and process plates) give the best resolution. **But this is not strictly true.**"
`[Davis & Walters 1922, pp.29–30 (PDF 30–31)]` **[F]**

The harvested data turns that into a number:

| Regression | r | Slope |
|---|---|---|
| Resolution number vs log₁₀ speed, all 79 emulsions with both | **+0.735** | **+5.92** units of separation (µm) per decade of speed |
| log₁₀ separation vs log₁₀ speed | +0.748 | separation ∝ speed<sup>**0.140**</sup>, i.e. resolving power ∝ speed<sup>−0.140</sup> |
| Within *orthochromatic* only | +0.529 | +6.04 per decade, n = 22 |
| Within *ordinary* only | +0.360 | +3.89 per decade, n = 20 |

⚠ **The within-class regressions are the ones that matter.** The whole-survey correlation could be
produced entirely by class composition — slow lantern-slide plates being fine-grained and fast
ordinary plates coarse — and would then say nothing about the trade-off itself. It survives inside
both large classes, at a reduced but non-zero slope. That is the paper's own "but this is not
strictly true" made quantitative: the trade-off is real within a class, and weaker than the
between-class spread makes it look. **[Q]**

The exponent is worth keeping. **Resolving power falling as the −0.14 power of speed** means a full
decade of speed costs about 28 % of resolving power — a shallow exchange rate, and shallower than a
naive grain-volume argument (grain diameter ∝ speed^⅓, resolving power ∝ 1/diameter, exponent −0.33)
predicts. Our own database's sharpness/speed relation is not modelled with an exponent at all, so
this is context rather than a parameter, but it is the earliest measured version of the exchange our
DQE guard's K = γ²·EI/rms² is a modern expression of.

### 23d.5 Cross-check against our own fleet

**Resolution.** Converting the median resolution number of 20 to a spatial frequency gives 1/0.020 mm
= 50 periods/mm. Applying the Tani relation already adopted in §18 — MTF-50 ≈ ½ resolving power,
measured at a median ratio of exactly 1.000 over 59 of our stocks — puts the 1920 median at an
equivalent **f50 ≈ 25 c/mm**. Our own fleet's median `f50_g` is **50.0 c/mm** across 161 stocks and
**54.8 c/mm** across the 15 with measured MTF.

⚠ **A factor-of-two convention ambiguity sits inside that comparison and cannot be resolved from the
text.** "Lines whose centers were 0.018 mm apart" is a *pitch*; whether the 1920 convention counted
lines or line pairs per millimetre is not stated anywhere in §7. On the pitch reading the 1920 median
is f50 ≈ 25 c/mm — half our fleet. On the line-counting reading it is ≈ 12.5 c/mm — a quarter. **Both
readings agree on the direction and on the order of magnitude; neither is safe to quote as a
calibrated number, and no value from this source may be written into a profile.** **[E]**

**Scale.** The 1920 median scale of 40 : 1 is **5.32 stops**; our non-instant negatives have a median
`usable_range_stops` of **11.05**, and our monochrome negatives **10.78**. ⚠ **These are not the same
measurement** and the ratio is not a latitude-doubled-in-a-century claim: Davis's scale is explicitly
the range recorded *correctly* — the straight-line portion — while our evaluated usable range runs
from toe to shoulder and deliberately includes both knees. The honest statement is that the
straight-line portion of a 1920 plate was about 5⅓ stops, and that our own straight-line-equivalent
figure has never been computed for comparison. **Recorded as an open comparison, not a finding.**
**[E]**

### 23d.6 What this does and does not close

**Closed.** The Part III data-block harvest, with its numbers verified against page images, its field
definitions quoted, its OCR error rate measured, and the speed/resolution exchange rate regressed. It
is the only measured population of real photographic materials in the entire source set, and it is
now a dataset rather than a stack of page images.

**Not closed, and now scoped.** Each of the 86 pages also carries three *plots* — colour sensitivity,
a family of characteristic curves at several development times, and a time–gamma curve. Those are the
second §28.1 Davis row ("time-of-development / contrast figures"). Tracing them is 258 curve families
from a thin Google scan whose digit reliability has just been measured at 67 %, for 86 emulsions that
**cannot be identified**: the paper anonymises every manufacturer, and no stock in our database is a
1920 American plate. Even traced perfectly, no profile could take a value from them. **Recommended
disposition: Category C (§27) — reference knowledge, not a digitisation target.** The gamma-versus-
time *behaviour* they encode is already covered by the `kodak_time_gamma` audit against a source that
names its film.

**No database change follows from A5.** The 86 emulsions are anonymous, 1920, and American; the
database's oldest stock is EASTMAN_ORTHO_1930. This is era context for §2, §15 and §18, and an
external check on the sharpness convention in §18.

Dataset: `doc/thirdparty/davis_walters_1920_survey.txt` (86 rows, three image-read numeric fields).

## 23e. Agfa's own emulsion patent: US 4,495,277, and the line between an assignee and a measurement (added 2026-09-01)

**S7 — US 4,495,277.** M. Becker, S. Klötzer and E. Moisar, *Photographic silver halide
emulsion.* Assignee Agfa-Gevaert Aktiengesellschaft, Leverkusen, Federal Republic of Germany.
Application 519,150 filed 1983-08-01; German priority 1982-08; granted 1985-01-22. 6 PDF pages,
`PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/US4495277.pdf`. Erik Moisar was Agfa's principal emulsion scientist, so this
is Agfa house practice at an AGFAPAN-era date, from the inside.

### 23e.1 What the patent teaches

A **core/shell** grain made by double jet, with a silver-chloride-rich zone buried between silver
bromide: at least one layer of the grain at ≥25 mol % AgCl, the grain as a whole under 30 mol %
AgCl. Precipitation at pAg 10–7 and pH 4.5–7. The claim's figure of merit is **R**, the ratio of
density obtainable after surface chemical ripening to that obtainable from the same emulsion
unripened, measured by coating both, exposing identically and developing 17 min at 20 °C in the
patent's own ascorbic-acid developer; claim 1 requires **R ≥ 3**.

⚠ **R IS A DENSITY RATIO, NOT AN ASPECT RATIO.** It says nothing about grain geometry. This
document records the confusion explicitly because the abbreviation invites it.

The stated purpose is twofold: speed through surface ripening, and **resistance to pressure fog in
the wet state** — Example 3's whole content is a pressure-trace comparison, and it is the only
sensitometric claim the patent actually demonstrates on a coating.

### 23e.2 The worked emulsions

| | preparation | mean diameter | dispersity | total AgCl | speed | fog | D-max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** (invention) | AgBr core 0.25 µm doubled at pAg 6.0, AgCl shell, then AgBr shell | 0.65 µm | 15 % of crystals outside ±10 % | 10 mol % | 290 | 0.07 | 1.38 |
| **B** (invention) | as A, but the outer AgBr precipitated at pAg 4.5 | — | — | — | 445 | 0.07 | — |
| **K** (comparison) | converted emulsion | 0.67 µm | 17 % outside ±10 % | — | 100 | 0.10 | 1.40 |

Ripening: 120 min at 45 °C with sodium thiosulphate pentahydrate at 80 µmol per mol Ag plus
42.5 mg of a triazaindolizine. **Sulphur only.** Gold, platinum, palladium, iridium, ruthenium and
rhodium appear once, in a boilerplate list of alternative sensitisers, and are used in no example.

The patent's own definition of monodisperse, given in the specification: at least 80 % of grains
within ±20 % of the mean.

### 23e.3 ⚠ What this patent does NOT license, and why the database takes no number from it

This is the substantive finding, and it is a negative one.

1. **It names no product.** AGFAPAN, APX, AGFACOLOR, ISO, DIN and ASA appear nowhere in its six
   pages. The speeds 290 / 100 / 445 are a relative scale internal to its own tables — 290 for A
   against 100 for the comparison — not film speeds.
2. **It declines to constrain crystal size.** Verbatim: *"The absolute value of the mean grain
   size may vary within wide limits"*, then fine-grain "less than 0.5 µm, preferably less than
   0.3 µm" and coarser "from 0.5 to 2 µm". That is the entire field. `emulsion.grain_um` cannot be
   filled from a claim that permits everything.
3. **It declines to constrain habit.** Verbatim: the grains *"may assume the known forms, for
   example, cubic, octahedral or even a combination of tetrahedral and decahedral."* All four.
   `emulsion.habit` stays empty.
4. **It states no iodide content.** AgI appears only in the permissive sentence "silver bromide or
   mixtures of silver bromide and silver iodide". The worked emulsions are **iodide-free**.
   `emulsion.iodide_mol_pct` stays empty.
5. ⚠ **Its demonstration material is COLOUR, not black and white.** Example 3 mixes emulsion A with
   a dispersed **yellow coupler** in tricresyl phosphate and processes the coating in a CD-3-type
   colour developer (N-ethyl-N-3-methanesulphonamido-ethyl-3-methyl-4-aminoaniline sulphate,
   benzyl alcohol, 33 °C) followed by bleach-fixing. An iodide-free AgBr/AgCl/AgBr core-shell grain
   in a coupler layer is not what an AGFAPAN camera negative is.
6. **Its subject is not granularity or tone.** Nothing in it measures a Wiener spectrum, an rms
   granularity, a resolving power or a characteristic curve beyond fog and D-max at one
   development.

**The one thing taken.** `emulsion.sensitization = "S"` is stored as a **tier-3, status `assumed`
class default** on AGFA_APX_25, AGFA_APX_100, AGFA_APX_400 and AGFA_SCALA_200X, at the owner's
explicit instruction and recorded as an inference from an assignee and a date rather than a
measurement. `EmulsionSpec` is inert — no stage of either renderer reads it — so the entry cannot
move a pixel; its value is that `EmulsionSpec.source` now carries the patent's real content where
a future derivation step will look. Sulphur ripening is in any case near-universal across makers
and both product types, so the field carries little discriminating power. Every ParamSource note
says so.

**What would change this.** A document that ties any Agfa product name to a crystal size,
dispersity or habit. This patent is not that document, and no amount of "Agfa films are silver
halide" makes it one: every emulsion in this corpus, from every maker, is silver halide.

## 23f. Granularity indexed by crystal size: JPS 1965 abstract 10p-A-2 (added 2026-09-01)

**S8 — Ōue & Takano 1965.** 大上進吾, 高野正雄 (富士写真フイルム研 — Fuji Photo Film Research
Laboratories), «写真乳剤の粒子サイズ分布と粒状性のウィーナー・スペクトル» (*Grain size
distribution of photographic emulsions and the Wiener spectrum of granularity*), abstract 10p-A-2,
Meeting of the Physical Society of Japan, 1965, journal page 269. One handwritten page, scanned as
a single 2848×4047 bilevel image; `PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/1965.1_269.pdf`. Re-derived every build by
`jp_jps_1965_269.py`.

### 23f.1 Why it is unlike every other granularity source here

Every other one is indexed by **product**. This one is indexed by **crystal size**: five emulsions
coated from AgX of stated mean diameter, measured on one apparatus at one density
(測定濃度 D_H = 0.5), so the difference between the curves is the crystal and nothing else.

Apparatus: 高速回転走査ミクロフォトメーター — a high-speed rotating-scan microphotometer (its
ref. 1, 大上進吾, 応用物理 **29**, 169 (1960), is not in this corpus). Photocell output through a
wideband DC amplifier and an AC amplifier into a frequency analyser, recorded on a level recorder.
Crystal sizes by sedimentation-type particle-size analyser and electron micrographs.

### 23f.2 The measured values

Traced from the raster; the abscissa calibration comes from the decade ticks and is validated by
the markers reproducing the printed crystal sizes.

| | AgX d, µm | F(20,0), relative | u at F(0,0)/2, c/mm | implied `clump_um` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0.30 | 1.318 | 107.7 | 2.73 |
| B | 0.40 | *[1.79, 2.57]* | *[90.2, 109.7]* | *bracket* |
| C | 0.50 | 2.325 | 83.8 | 3.51 |
| D | 1.50 | 3.021 | 83.9 | 3.51 |
| E | 1.80 | 3.178 | 79.8 | 3.69 |

A is the fine-grain low-speed emulsion, E the coarse-grain high-speed one. ⚠ **B is a bracket, not
a point:** the two Fig. 3 curves cross almost exactly there and its two markers merge into one blob
of ink.

Fitted: `u½ = 85.7 · d^−0.127` (R² 0.66) and `F(20,0) = 2.57 · d^+0.436` (R² 0.87), the latter
implying σ ∝ d^0.22.

The two conclusions the abstract states in words, both re-derived from the trace rather than
quoted: (1) the low-frequency spectrum level depends strongly on d and **rises** with it; (2) the
spectrum **bandwidth** also depends on d but **falls** with it.

### 23f.3 ⚠ Relative units, and the one thing that is absolute

Fig. 1's ordinate is labelled 相対値 — *relative value* — with no square microns and no aperture.
**No rms granularity can come from this page and none is taken.** What is absolute is the
abscissa: the half-power frequency is a measured **bandwidth in cycles per millimetre**, which is
exactly the quantity `GrainSpec.clump_um_*` sets through `film_sim.grain_shape`.

The reading aperture is not stated, which would normally be fatal. The figure bounds it instead:
the curves descend smoothly past 869 c/mm with no transfer zero, so a circular reading aperture
must be under ≈1.4 µm, whose MTF² is still 0.945 at 108 c/mm. Folding it in moves the half-power
frequencies by 2–4 %.

### 23f.4 ⚠ Neither law may be inverted to recover a crystal size

The obvious use — take a film's measured granularity and read its crystal size back off these
curves — **does not work, and the fit says so.** A **six-fold** change in d moves the bandwidth by
35 % and F(20,0) by a factor 2.4. Inverting that amplifies error: 1 % in u½ is 8 % in d, 1 % in
F(20,0) is 2.3 % in d, and because σ ∝ √F the granularity branch is flatter still at 4.6 % in d
per 1 % in σ. A 10 % uncertainty in a stored rms would return a crystal size uncertain by roughly
a factor of one and a half.

There is no usable absolute anchor either: all 17 stocks carrying `emulsion.grain_um` take it from
one third-party aggregator, and its magnitudes — Tri-X 4.5 µm, TMAX P3200 6.5 µm — are not credible
as AgX crystal diameters, which run 0.2–2 µm in camera films. That field is very probably holding
a developed-cluster figure under a crystal-size name. **Recorded, not corrected.**

### 23f.5 ⚠ The disagreement this page exposes, recorded and not resolved

Converting the measured bandwidths through the project's own law
(`W(f)/W(0) = exp(−2(f/f_hi)²)`, `f_hi = 1000/(2·clump_um)`, hence `clump_um = 294.35/u½`):

| source | `clump_um` | implied u½, c/mm |
|---|---|---|
| BBC T-101 Table 2, gamma-corrected — the two **measured** stocks | ILFORD_PAN_F 0.655, ILFORD_HPS 1.431 | 449, 206 |
| **This page**, five real emulsions | 2.73 – 3.69 | 80 – 108 |
| Corpus **estimates**, 168 stocks | median 13.0, range 3.0 – 40.0 | median 23 |

Three independent sources, three different answers, spanning a factor of twenty. Only **1** of 170
stocks lay inside the band this page measures. ⚠ **Superseded 2026-09-03 by the C45 rescale (§23k.9):
the corpus median is now 4.19 µm and 
the estimates sit inside the measured band.** The row below is left as it was measured. The corpus median implies a grain spectrum whose
half-power point is at 23 c/mm, against 80–108 measured here and 206–449 derived from BBC — i.e.
the rendered grain on most stocks is markedly lower-frequency, blobbier, than any measurement on
file supports.

**Nothing is adopted.** Moving 168 stocks on the strength of a one-page abstract in relative units
would be the opposite of evidence, and it would change every render. What it is: a **third**
independent measurement bracketing where the truth lies, and the first that is neither an estimate
nor tied to one 1960s British laboratory. § **Category B.**
