## 23g. Callier Q against density, measured twice: Streiffert 1947 via Trumpy & Gschwind 2015 (added 2026-09-01)

**S9 — Trumpy & Gschwind 2015.** Giorgio Trumpy and Rudolf Gschwind, Digital Humanities Lab,
Universität Basel, *Optical Detection of Dust and Scratches on Photographic Film.* ACM Journal on
Computing and Cultural Heritage **8**, 2, Article 7 (March 2015), 19 pages.
`PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/Optical_Detection_of_Dust_and_Scratches_on_Photogr.pdf`. Re-derived every
build by `trumpy_callier_q.py`.

Most of the paper is a flaw-detection method (PDD, DCD, n-MDD) and is outside this document's
scope. **Figure 5 on journal page 7:7 is why it is registered here**: Callier Q against diffuse
density for a typical silver-based film, D = 0 to 2.0. The text credits **[Streiffert 1947]** —
J. G. Streiffert, «Callier Q of various motion picture emulsions», *J. SMPTE* **49**, 6
(Dec. 1947), 506–522 — which is *not* in this corpus, so the measurement is Streiffert's and the
rendering is Trumpy and Gschwind's.

⚠ The caption says "a silver-based film" and the text "a typical silver-based film". **No product
is named**, so nothing from it may be written onto a profile, and nothing was.

### 23g.1 The digitised curve

573 points. Axes calibrated on the printed ticks, with the frame as the check: it reads
D 0.000–2.005 and Q 0.996–1.698 against a printed 0–2 and 1.0–1.7. Traced by COLUMN where the
stroke is thin and by ROW on the near-vertical toe, because a column scan of a vertical stroke
returns the middle of a 25-pixel run rather than a function value.

| D | 0.05 | 0.075 | 0.10 | 0.15 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.354 | 0.50 | 0.80 | 1.20 | 1.50 | 2.00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q | 1.081 | 1.225 | 1.357 | 1.472 | 1.521 | 1.554 | **1.557** | 1.547 | 1.503 | 1.451 | 1.421 | 1.390 |

Stored as `film_profiles._CALLIER_Q_REFERENCE`.

### 23g.2 The project's own law, fitted to a measured Q(D) for the first time

`film_sim.callier_net` implements Silberstein & Tuttle (Mees, printed p644):

    10^−D_sp = E·10^−D_diff + (1−E)·10^−(β·D_diff)

with `FilmProfile.callier_q` = **β** (a film property, one plus the ratio of scattering to
absorption coefficients) and the render control `scanner_specular` = **1 − E** (the geometry).

| fit window | E | β | rms | worst |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D ≥ 0.20 | 0.1446 | 1.6681 | 0.0093 Q | 0.0335 Q |
| **D ≥ 0.30** | **0.1471** | **1.6746** | **0.0087 Q** | 0.0214 Q |
| D ≥ 0.40 | 0.1455 | 1.6703 | 0.0087 Q | 0.0205 Q |

The two parameters are **jointly identifiable**, not merely a fitted pair: holding E at 0.10 or
0.20 instead of 0.147 raises the rms by 2.4× and 2.9×. Stored as `_CALLIER_FIT_E` and
`_CALLIER_FIT_BETA`.

**This is the first time the law's shape has been checked against a measurement.** Over 1.7 decades
of density it is right to under 0.01 Q.

### 23g.3 ⚠ The toe defect, quantified and independently witnessed

The `callier_net` docstring already admits the defect: expanding for small D gives
Q → E + (1−E)·β, a **constant**. With the fitted parameters that constant is **1.575**. The curve
measures **1.081** at D = 0.05. The error is **+0.49 Q**, and the law cannot do otherwise — it is
structural, not a parameter choice.

Two independent witnesses to the collapse, with no shared calibration:

| source | D | Q |
|---|---|---|
| Mees FIG. 179 toe (`mees_callier_q.py`) | 0.055 | 1.042 |
| **This curve** | 0.058 | **1.081** |

Two laboratories, two decades, two emulsions. The collapse is real. A toe correction is now
supported by evidence rather than by a single figure.

### 23g.4 ⚠ β = 1.675 against a stored 1.3 — recorded, not changed

`_apply_schema_v2` gives every B&W negative `callier_q = 1.3` and every B&W reversal 1.25, as class
constants with no measurement behind them. Fifty-five stocks carry the 1.3.

| source | β | conditions |
|---|---|---|
| stored class constant | 1.30 | none — a class guess |
| **this curve** | **1.675** | Streiffert's densitometer, E = 0.147 fitted jointly |
| BBC T-101 Fig. 25, on EASTMAN_TRI_X_5223 | 2.0 – 2.34 | 0.0016 sr collection, i.e. E → 0 where Q → β |

Both measurements sit **above** the stored constant. `callier_q` moves a pixel on all 55 stocks, so
nothing is changed here; this is recorded as a live disagreement for a decision. ⚠ Note the model
structure when weighing it: β is defined as a **film** property and the collection cone belongs
entirely to E, so a β lowered "because a real condenser is not collimated" would be counting the
geometry twice.

### 23g.5 Two smaller finds in the body text

**A citation for `callier_q = 1.0` on colour stocks**, which the database asserts with no source.
§4.1: *"the refractive indices of the dye clouds and of the gelatin are similar (at least the real
part); hence, a wavelength-selective absorption is essentially the only phenomenon occurring in
dye-based emulsions."* A dye image barely scatters, so β → 1. The assumption was right; it is now
grounded.

**Independent corroboration that `emulsion.grain_um` is holding the wrong quantity.** §4:
*"a silver-based emulsion is a very heterogeneous system, in which silver particles typically span
from 0.2 μm to 2 μm [Vitale 2009]"*. §23f.4 records that all 17 stocks carrying `grain_um` take it
from one third-party aggregator at 1.3–6.5 µm — Tri-X 4.5, TMAX P3200 6.5 — and concludes the field
is probably holding a developed-cluster figure under a crystal-size name. A second source now puts
the real range at 0.2–2 µm.

**Not usable:** the paper's dust and scratch material is qualitative for our purposes — emulsion
thickness "generally around 10 μm", flaws "hundreds of microns or higher" for the MDD method to
separate them. No rates, no size distributions, nothing that could populate the eleven empty
`aging` fields. Recorded as a negative in `DEFECT_LAYER.md` terms.

## 23h. Technicolor and Dufaycolor measured: Flueckiger et al. 2018 (added 2026-09-01d)

**S10 — Flueckiger et al. 2018.** Barbara Flueckiger, David Pfluger, Giorgio Trumpy, Simone Croci,
Tunç Aydın and Aljoscha Smolic, *Investigation of Film Material–Scanner Interaction.* University of
Zurich, Department of Film Studies / DIASTOR, v1.1, 18 February 2018, 88 pages.
`PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/flueckigeretal_investigationfilmmaterialscannerinteraction_2018_v_1-1b.pdf`.
Re-derived every build by `flueckiger_2018.py`.

⚠ It is a **scanner study**, and most of it — eight machine walkthroughs, an eleven-expert
subjective rating study — is outside this document's scope; the scanner half is in
`SCANNER_CHARACTERISTICS.md`. Four figures are emulsion measurements and are treated here.

### 23h.1 The linear dye model, in print

§2.1 states the model this database implements, with its assumptions attached:

    A_film(x,y)(λ) = K_Y(x,y)·Ā_Y(λ) + K_M(x,y)·Ā_M(λ) + K_C(x,y)·Ā_C(λ)      (1)
    T%(λ) = 10^−A(λ) · 100                                                     (2)

`Ā` are the **normalised analytical densities**, `K` the local dye concentrations, and the sum is
the **integral density**. Valid only if the film does not scatter, with the base taken as
transparent (Hunt 2004; side absorptions after Kowaliski 1977). §2.1 sets the orange mask aside
explicitly rather than pretending the model covers it.

### 23h.2 ⚠ Three-strip Technicolor: the first measurement this corpus has of it

§2.8.2. `TECHNICOLOR_THREE_STRIP` was one of the nine stocks `NotFound.md` §1 lists as having no
source of any kind. Figure 16 changes that.

**Sample and method.** A Technicolor No. IV trailer print of SAMSON AND DELILAH (USA 1949, Cecil B.
DeMille). Twenty-four points of intense colour measured on a SHIMADZU UV-1800 bench
spectrophotometer, then separated into single-dye spectra by the **Ohta (1973, pp. 553–557)**
method: a principal component analysis of the mixture spectra, the three highest eigenspectra
combined by a linear least-squares minimisation against ideal block dyes. The report notes that a
prominent gap between the third and fourth eigenvalue is what confirms three independently variable
components.

**Printed peaks**, from the running text: yellow ≈ 460 nm; magenta ≈ 540 (main) and 575
(secondary); cyan ≈ 660 (main) and 720 (secondary). The cyan and magenta eigenspectra show double
absorption peaks, the yellow a single one.

**Traced**, 360–790 nm at 10 nm, peak-normalised: main peaks at **460 / 540 / 660** nm and the cyan
secondary at **720** nm — the printed values exactly, and the trace never saw them. The magenta 575
secondary is a shoulder at this raster resolution and is not claimed. Stored on the profile as
`dye_density`, `normalisation="peak_1.0"`, tier 2 `traced`.

⚠ **SHAPE ONLY.** Figure 16's ordinate has no scale, no ticks and no label. The curves are
normalised to unit peak **with the bottom axis assumed to be zero absorbance**; the traced minima
sit at 0.157 / 0.086 / 0.151 of peak, plausible side absorptions but not verifiable from the
figure. That assumption is why this is tier 2 and not tier 1.

⚠ **It is a PRINT dye set** — Technicolor No. IV is imbibition dye transfer, so these are the three
transfer dyes on the positive, which is what a viewer sees. ⚠ **And it is one print of one 1949
title.** §2.8.2 states that "a variety of dyes were applied" across Technicolor's production
decades and that their development "has not been documented to date". This samples the process; it
does not define it.

### 23h.3 Dufaycolor: a second, independent measurement of a live parameter

§2.8.3. The Dufaycolor réseau is a regular screen of red, green and blue lines at 23° from
vertical, about 500 lines per image width, over a black-and-white emulsion — an additive
screen-plate process, so the "dyes" are **filter elements**, not image dyes.

**Method.** A LEITZ DIALUX 20 microscope at 40× with a Carl-Zeiss AxioCam HR camera, through 16
Andover bandpass interference filters of 10 nm width at 20 nm spacing from 400 to 700 nm. 14-bit
linear capture; transmittance formed against a white and a black reference by equation (6); réseau
pixels segmented by colour and averaged per element. A bright area with little silver density was
chosen deliberately.

**Figure 21, digitised** (transmittance %, 20 nm steps):

| nm | 400 | 440 | 480 | 500 | 540 | 580 | 620 | 660 | 700 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| red element | 14.1 | 8.5 | 10.6 | 9.1 | 6.2 | 31.6 | 61.4 | 71.9 | 91.5 |
| green element | 21.5 | 13.1 | 43.8 | 57.1 | 40.7 | 21.1 | 10.3 | 14.5 | 80.3 |
| blue element | 39.6 | 30.9 | 39.0 | 33.4 | 9.8 | 7.3 | 7.9 | 11.9 | 60.8 |

⚠ **FIGURE 21'S CAPTION IS WRONG AND THE FIGURE IS RIGHT.** The caption reads "Resulting
**absorbance** curves of the dyes"; the figure's own ordinate reads "TRANSMITTANCE %" and its three
series are named transRED / transGREEN / transBlue. A reader who trusted the caption would have
stored `1 − T` as if it were `A`.

**Figure 22** gives the integral transmittance of the same sample two ways: calculated from the
single-element spectra by equation (7), and measured directly on the SHIMADZU over 300–900 nm.

    integral_T% = 0.28 blue_T% + 0.32 green_T% + 0.40 red_T%                   (7)

with 28 / 32 / 40 % the measured area fractions of the three elements.

⚠ **THIS IS THE CHECK THE WHOLE DUFAYCOLOR HARVEST RESTS ON.** The two figures are separately
calibrated, separately plotted and separately traced. Recomputing equation (7) from the Figure 21
trace reproduces Figure 22's markers to **rms 0.29 transmittance points, worst 0.68**, over the
fourteen wavelengths where all three markers are unoccluded — with no free parameter. The same
inversion **recovers the two occluded markers** (red at 560 nm → 8.1 %, green at 640 nm → 9.4 %),
and the method is validated where it can be: at 640 nm a partially visible blob reads 9.7 %.

⚠ **The two Figure 22 curves differ by a large offset — and the offset is the silver image.**
Calculated 15–80 % against measured 1–43 %. §2.8.3 explains it: the two spectra come from different
areas of the film with different silver concentrations. Dufaycolor is a B&W emulsion *plus* a
filter layer, and this figure separates the two contributions in practice.

### 23h.4 ⚠ Where it disagrees with what the database stores

`DUFAYCOLOR_1937.reseau.filter_matrix` is a **live, pixel-moving** parameter, derived from the NSMM
Bradford absorbance curves of three *other* surviving prints and then multiplied by an **invented
uniform factor of 4.05**, because those absolute densities carried base plus eight decades of dye
ageing. Rows were then normalised to a common sum of 0.80.

Band-averaging Figure 21 over the same windows (B 420–490, G 500–580, R 600–700 nm):

| element | measured R / G / B | stored R / G / B | row sum measured / stored |
|---|---|---|---|
| red | 0.715 / 0.126 / 0.096 | 0.700 / 0.064 / 0.036 | 0.94 / 0.80 |
| green | 0.279 / 0.404 / 0.227 | 0.170 / 0.460 / 0.170 | 0.91 / 0.80 |
| blue | 0.209 / 0.155 / 0.345 | 0.210 / 0.236 / 0.354 | 0.71 / 0.80 |

**Agreements:** red is by far the cleanest element in both; the blue element's red leak matches to
2 % (ratio 0.604 measured against 0.593 stored); the diagonals are close in absolute terms
(0.715/0.404/0.345 against 0.700/0.460/0.354) — notable, since the stored set reached that range
only through the ×4.05 rescale.

**Disagreements:** the measured red element leaks roughly twice as much (0.176 / 0.135 of peak
against 0.091 / 0.051), and the measured green element leaks asymmetrically toward red
(0.691 / 0.563) where the stored one is symmetric (0.370 / 0.370).

⚠ **Nothing was changed.** Different prints, different ages, one trace, and a field that moves
pixels. Recorded as queue **C46** with the digitised curves in `_DUFAYCOLOR_RESEAU_T_PCT` and the
band averages in `_DUFAYCOLOR_RESEAU_FLUECKIGER_BANDS`. ⚠ The one argument that favours the new
measurement is that it needs **no invented scale factor at all**.

### 23h.5 Two negatives worth recording

⚠ **Figure 15 is not new evidence.** It is the same Callier Q artwork as Trumpy & Gschwind 2015
Fig. 5 (§23g) — Trumpy is a co-author of both, and both trace back to Streiffert 1947. Counting it
twice would inflate a one-measurement basis into two. It is used only as a reproducibility check on
this project's raster pipeline: two PDFs, two scans of one drawing, traced by the same method,
**rms 0.0053 Q**.

⚠ **Figure 6 is not a measurement.** It is captioned "**Typical** normalized spectral sensitivities
of a color imaging device" — a textbook illustration. §2.8 states plainly that the study could not
obtain the scanners' spectral sensitivities. No scanner spectral response is available from this
report for any machine.

## 23i. The Japanese journal collection, 1938–1963: eighteen papers reviewed (added 2026-09-01e)

**S11 — 日本写真学会会誌 / Journal of the Society of Photographic Science and Technology of
Japan**, eighteen offprints supplied by the owner, `PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/JAPAN/`. Every one was
opened and its body read, not just its title: two proved directly load-bearing, twelve carry
supporting science, and four are outside the field. The two load-bearing papers are treated in
full below; the rest are summarised in §23i.4.

### 23i.1 ⚠ Sayanagi 1959 — a theory of the Callier Q factor that works where ours fails

**佐柳和男 (Kazuo Sayanagi), Canon Camera Co., «Callier Q Factor と粒状» / "A Theory on Callier Q
Factor and Granularity", 23(1), 20–24 (1960), received 15 Dec 1959.** `JAPAN/23_20.pdf`.

Derives Q from a Fourier analysis of the film as optical noise, on an explicit grain model:

| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| T_b = A_b² | intensity / amplitude transmittance of the **base** |
| T_g = A_g² | intensity / amplitude transmittance of a **developed silver grain** |
| r₀ | grain radius; grains are circles |
| ξ | area fraction; grain **centres are Poisson distributed** |

⚠ **THE LOAD-BEARING ASSUMPTION IS THAT A DEVELOPED GRAIN IS NOT OPAQUE.** Sayanagi gives it
finite transmittance because electron microscopy shows the developed grain has a fine filamentary
internal structure [von Ardenne 1940], which densifies as development proceeds. From the Poisson
statistics (after Savelli 1957 and Picinbono 1955) he obtains Q(D) in closed form, as Q_I (base
density retained) and Q_II (base subtracted).

**Four results, and every one of them lands on an open row of this project's queue.**

1. ⚠ **Q MUST BE DEFINED ON BASE-SUBTRACTED DENSITY, AND HE SAYS SO IN TERMS.** Q_I → 1 as D → 0
   purely because of base absorption, and "Q_I's value in the low-D_++ region has no physical
   meaning"; Q_II shows a characteristic value per film. His conclusion: *Q_II is the rational Q
   factor.* ⚠ **This project already computes Callier on NET density**, referenced to `dmin` —
   queue C22 argued that from first principles and recorded that **no source stated one**. A source
   states one, and it is from 1959.
2. **The theory fits experiment at LOW density and diverges at high density.** He is explicit about
   why: the model is two-dimensional, and at high density grain overlap and light reflected between
   grains dominate. ⚠ That is the exact complement of the project's current law — Silberstein &
   Tuttle fits well **above** D 0.3 (rms 0.0087 Q, §23g) and fails **below** it (+0.49 Q at
   D 0.05). Two models, opposite domains of validity. **Queue C44.**
3. ⚠ **A METHOD FOR THE TOE, STATED AS AN INSTRUCTION**: "conversely, the value of T_g can be
   estimated from a measured Q, and in that case it should of course be computed from the value at
   D_++ → 0." So the toe is not merely a defect to patch — it is where the grain's own
   transmittance is measurable. Three causes of Q are identified and ranked: (a) finite base
   absorption — irrelevant to Q_II, (b) **finite grain transmittance — the most important**,
   (c) grain overlap and inter-grain reflection.
4. ⚠ **Q IS NOT A MEASURE OF GRANULARITY, AND THIS IS PROVED RATHER THan ASSERTED.** Granularity
   needs two numbers — the integral of the power spectrum excluding DC (δA², the rms) and the mean
   grain diameter. Q contains δA² only; **r₀ does not appear in the derived formulae at all**.
   Therefore Q ranks samples of equal grain size and cannot rank samples of different grain size.
   "Q Factor is a measure of the r.m.s. δ of granularity, but because it has no information about
   the (mean) grain diameter it cannot be a general measure of granularity."
   ⚠ This is an independent, theoretical confirmation of what §23f.4 found empirically from the
   JPS 1965 abstract: rms and clump size are separate axes and one does not determine the other.

His Fig. 3 plots calculated Q(D) for several T_g; Fig. 4 reproduces measured Q(D) at several
development gammas from 科学写真便覧 (Handbook of Scientific Photography, Maruzen 1959) — a third
measured Q(D) family, beside Mees FIG. 179 and Trumpy/Streiffert.

### 23i.2 ⚠ Ooue 1959 — the instrument behind the 1965 abstract, and it states the aperture

**大上進吾 (Shingo Ooue), Fuji Photo Film Research Laboratory, «粒状性の研究(第1報) 新しい粒状性
測定装置» / "Studies on the Graininess and Granularity (I): a new granularity measuring
instrument", 23(1), 7–10 (1960), received 9 Dec 1959.** `JAPAN/23_7.pdf`.

Same author and same laboratory as the JPS 1965 abstract digitised in §23f. This is the companion
instrument paper, and it closes that section's one open caveat.

**The instrument.** A high-speed **rotating**-scan microphotometer (linear stages cannot hold a
stationary waveform at these speeds and drift in focus); scan speed up to 100 mm/s, typically
4.7 mm/s at radius 1.5 mm and 0.5 rev/s. RCA 1P21 photomultiplier on a 395–920 V regulated supply
with ripple under 7.5 mV; wideband DC amplifier flat 0–10 kc, drift 120 µV/h, noise 1.2 mV; a
frequency analyser of **twenty Q = 30 band-pass filters**; a thermocouple meter reading the **rms**
of the output directly. Nine apertures on a revolver.

⚠ **THE APERTURE, WHICH §23f COULD ONLY BOUND, IS STATED HERE.** For the spatial-frequency spectra:
microscope magnification **200×** onto a **0.2 mm** aperture — i.e. **1 µm referred to the film**.
Ooue justifies it: an emulsion is 5–20 µm thick and treating it as a two-dimensional pattern is
already a coarser approximation than a 1 µm aperture. §23f bounded the aperture at **< 1.4 µm from
the figure's own extent alone**; the stated value is 1 µm. ⚠ **The bound contains the fact.** At
1 µm the circular MTF² at 108 c/mm is 0.97, so the correction to those half-power frequencies is
smaller than the 2–4 % already allowed.

**Fig. 7 — granularity–density functions for NAMED films at a STATED aperture.** A different
aperture is used here: **10 µm referred to the film**, chosen so that its spatial-frequency
response matches the eye's at a 14× enlargement. The correlation between the resulting physical
granularity and psychological graininess is **r = 0.90** over eight film/developer combinations
(Fig. 6).

Digitised from the page raster, ordinate in relative units:

| | fitted exponent n in v ∝ D^n | R² |
|---|---|---|
| Neopan S / D-76 | 0.412 | 0.965 |
| Neopan SS / Microfine | 0.672 | 0.995 |
| Neopan SSS / Pandol | 0.364 | 0.972 |
| X-ray film / Rendol | 0.606 | 0.998 |

⚠ **AN AMBIGUITY IN THE ORDINATE THAT IS NOT RESOLVED AND IS NOT PAPERED OVER.** §3.2 defines v as
the **mean-square** output voltage (v ∝ σ²), while the English abstract says the meter "indicates
the **root mean square** value of the current" (v ∝ σ). If v is rms, these four exponents are
0.36–0.67; if v is mean-square, they are 0.18–0.34. ⚠ The internal evidence favours **rms**: read
that way the three B&W negatives straddle the legacy √ law (0.50) and the BBC/Higgins-and-Stultz
exponent (0.40), while read as mean-square they fall below every other source in the corpus.
**Nothing is adopted on an ambiguous ordinate**; what would settle it is Ooue's companion papers,
本誌 22, 38 and 91 (1959), which are not in this corpus.

⚠ **WHAT IT DOES SETTLE.** `NotFound.md` row 2 asks for "one granularity-versus-density plot for a
named B&W negative at a stated aperture". This is four of them. And it tells against the reading
that the project's √ law is badly wrong for negatives: on the rms reading, three named B&W
negatives at three named developers sit either side of it. The measured B&W **reversal** shape
(0.92–1.28) therefore looks like genuine reversal behaviour rather than a defect in the negative
law — which is what BBC T-101/2 predicted in words when it said reversal needs a different
exponent because reversal inverts the relation between effective grain size and density.

### 23i.3 The Soviet emulsion-technology review

**矢野哲夫 (Tetsuo Yano), Mitsubishi Paper Mills Kyoto, «ソ連の写真乳剤技術に関する研究» /
"Researches on Photographic Emulsion Technic in the U.S.S.R.", 23(4), 153–160 (1960).**
`JAPAN/23_153.pdf`. A review of the Soviet literature to 1960 with about **180 Russian
references** — Chibisov, Zelikman, Lyalikov, Shuvalov, Protas, Gorokhovskii, Fedorov, Kozlov.

⚠ **IT CONTAINS NO SENSITOMETRY FOR ANY NAMED SOVIET FILM**, and therefore nothing that fills
`SOVIET_PANCHROM_1939`, `SVEMA_*` or `TASMA_*`. It was checked for that specifically. What it does
contain:

- **Crystal habit by process.** Thickness measured to 0.05 µm on a micro-interferometer; shape
  expressed as x/h (projected area over thickness), 1 ≈ spherical, 0 ≈ tabular. **Non-ammonia
  emulsions grow more tabular as the grain grows; ammonia emulsions start tabular when fine and
  thicken toward spherical when coarse** — with a dissenting report that the finest ammonia
  crystals are near-spherical. Fig. 3 plots h against x for both families.
- ⚠ **Resolving power does not depend on crystal thickness at equal projected area.** A clean,
  citable statement, and a useful constraint on any future derivation of MTF from crystal geometry.
- ⚠ **No fixed relation between mean grain diameter and granularity** — except that at equal γ and
  equal density the size distributions are similar enough that mean grain size may be used as a
  practical proxy. A third independent statement of the §23f.4 / §23i.1 finding.
- **The additivity law for multilayer coatings**: the characteristic curve of a multi-layer coating
  can be computed from the individual layers' curves, **provided the upper layer's absorption is
  taken into account**; density additivity for blended emulsions is proven experimentally and
  theoretically. Relevant to `LayerStack` and to the double-coated B&W case.
- Manufacturing context: sodium-sulphate flocculation replaced washing in Soviet factories from
  **1940**; ripening kettles 0.25–0.65 m³ in Cr-Ni stainless; Deryagin's hydrodynamic coating-
  thickness theory with its full parameter list; products developed include plates with **spectral
  sensitivity matching the human eye** and plates with **constant γ across the visible**.

Its real value to this project is as a **research trail**: it names the Soviet primary literature
that a future search for `SOVIET_PANCHROM_1939` data must go through.

### 23i.4 The remaining fifteen, and what each is

**Carrying supporting science (partially useful):**

| file | paper | what it gives |
|---|---|---|
| `22_198` | 藤沢・山口・渡辺 (Fuji), Fujicolor negative colour reproduction I: the effect of UV sensitivity, 22(4) 1959 | the blue layer uses the silver halide's **intrinsic** sensitivity and so responds to UV the eye cannot see; sharp-cut filters at 370 / 380 / 400 / 410 nm were compared and **a filter absorbing below 410 nm** is recommended for any colour film. Bears directly on `taking_filter`, populated on 2 of 170 stocks |
| `22_194` | 馬場・板野 (Konishiroku), measurement of relative spectral sensitivity, 22(4) 1959 | a filter-series method, and two cautions: their method does **not** show the >600 nm maximum a spectrosensitometer shows, and dye-sensitised regions always read **lower** than the intrinsic region. A warning about comparing spectral curves across measurement methods |
| `19_162` | 水島・中村, colour-temperature recording characteristics of colour films, 19(4) 1957 | six films, negative and positive, exposed to tungsten at 2848 / 2000 / 1500 K and via DG filters to 6500 / 4800 K. Colour balance versus source temperature, aimed at furnace and explosion photography |
| `26_172` | 藤村・山本 (Fuji), tone reproduction II: relatively small negatives, 26(4) 1963 | tone-reproduction slope falls as negative size falls (8 / 16 / 35 mm), so the **optimum development time is longer for a small negative**; density response follows the spatial frequency of the eye's peak response. A format-dependent tone law |
| `14_106` | 大沼・永保 (Oriental), colour sensitometry I, 14 (1952) | equivalent-density colour sensitometry and the three-component → two-component reduction, applied to Oriental internal-type colour reversal positive |
| `14_133` | 大山泰 (Mitsubishi Paper), colour and shape of developed silver grains and their formation, 14 (1952) | electron-microscope morphology of developed silver — the physical basis of Sayanagi's finite-transmittance grain |
| `23_1` | 入江春雄 (Chiba Univ.), the role of gelatin in silver halide emulsions I, 23(1) 1960 | review |
| `19_160` | 入江・塚田・栗原 (Chiba Univ.), photographically active substances in gelatin I: solid suspended matter, 19(4) 1957 | gelatin impurity study |
| `15_114` | 馬野周二, mechanism of desensitising dyes, 15 (1953) | π-electron lowest-vacant-level argument for desensitisation |
| `23_174` | 源田ほか (Chiba Univ. / NRIPS), handling of professional high-speed Ektachrome E-3, 23(4) 1960 | processing practice for a stock family this database carries |
| `25_183` | 村山ほか, colour reducers, 25(4) 1962 | post-processing chemical reduction of colour prints |
| `23_161` | 川崎正美, photographic properties of silver salts of fatty acids I, 23(4) 1960 | organic silver salts — not a silver-halide camera film, but emulsion chemistry |

**Outside the field (currently not useful):**

| file | paper | why |
|---|---|---|
| `1_115` | 山内二郎, on the present state of photometric units, 1 (1938) | a lecture on Japan's photometric standards. Metrology, no film content |
| `25_175` | 中川・国友 (Riken Optical), sensitometry of diazo papers I, 25(4) 1962 | diazo, not silver halide |
| `26_179` | 中川靖夫 (Ricoh), sensitometry of diazo papers III, 26(4) 1963 | as above |

⚠ **NO FILE IN THIS COLLECTION IS RECOMMENDED FOR DELETION.** The owner's own criterion is that
historical, theoretical and methodological material be kept even without immediately usable
numbers, and all three "not useful" entries meet that bar: the diazo pair are careful
spectrosensitometry method papers, and the 1938 photometry lecture is the unit basis every exposure
number in this corpus ultimately rests on. The three are named as the weakest, not as disposable.

## 23j. Ooue 1959 Parts 1 and 2 — the two companion papers §23i asked for

Added 2026-09-02 (queue J1/J2). `PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/JAPAN/22_38.pdf` and `22_91.pdf`, supplied by
the owner mid-batch. Shingo Ooue (大上進吾), Fuji Photo Film Research Laboratory,
«写真感光材料の粒状性» Parts 1 and 2, *J. Soc. Phot. Sci. Japan* **22**(1) 38-47 and **22**(2)
91-99 (1959). Traced by `ooue_1959_granularity.py`, registered in the build audit.

⚠ **§23i.2 NAMED THESE TWO AS THE PAPERS THAT WOULD SETTLE THE ONE OPEN AMBIGUITY ON `23_7`, AND
THEY DO.** Part 2 §4.2.2 is headed 「濃度変化の標準偏差による方法」 — *the method using the*
***standard deviation*** *of density variation* — and every objective granularity in the paper is
built on it: Selwyn's σ√a, van Kreveld's Δ_m√a, and equations (5) and (6),
ΔT = 0.675 √(a′/a) √((1−T)/T) and ΔT = 1.022 √(a′/a) √D, both standard deviations of
transmittance. The same author, in the same journal, two years earlier, uses a standard deviation
throughout. **So `23_7` Fig. 7's ordinate is rms and the "mean-square" in its §3.2 is a
translation artefact.** On that reading its fitted exponents 0.412 / 0.672 / 0.364 / 0.606 straddle
the legacy √ law and the BBC exponent instead of falling below every source in the corpus — the
reason they were harvested and not adopted is gone.

### 23j.1 ⚠ Part 2 Fig. 26 — a measured Wiener spectrum, and it contradicts the model's shape

Three **named** samples with stated developer, time and density: Neopan SS / Minidol 20 °C 10 min
at D 1.03 and at D 0.45, and Process Plate / D-72 (1:1) 20 °C 4 min at D 0.44. Log-log, 10-1000
lines/mm against an unlabelled "POWER LEVEL" over four decades.

Fitting a generalised Gaussian `P0·exp(−ln2·(f/f_half)^n)` to the falling limbs:

| sample | f_half (lines/mm) | n | rms log10 | pure Gaussian rms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neopan SS / Minidol, D 1.03 | 45.6 | **0.71** | 0.087 | 0.563 |
| Neopan SS / Minidol, D 0.45 | 70.8 | **0.89** | 0.107 | 0.345 |
| Process Plate / D-72, D 0.44 | 140.7 | **1.36** | 0.035 | 0.094 |

⚠ **EVERY EXPONENT IS BELOW THE 2 THIS ENGINE ASSUMES.** `film_sim.make_grain_field` shapes grain
with `h(f) = exp(−(f/f_hi)²)·(1 + clump_gain·exp(−(f/f_lo)²))`, so the Wiener spectrum it produces
is a Gaussian of exponent 2. The measured limbs are **shallower**, and a pure Gaussian fits them
three to six times worse. **A Gaussian under-estimates grain energy at high frequency** — the same
defect `MTFSpec`'s own docstring records for the MTF tail ("real emulsion tails are fatter than any
two-parameter analytic form"), now measured on the grain spectrum as well.

⚠ **AND THE RESULT THAT NEEDS NO CALIBRATION AT ALL:** rows 1 and 2 are the **same film**, same
developer, same time, two densities — and f_half moves 45.6 → 70.8. **The clump gets coarser as
density rises**, by 55 % in cutoff frequency, while `GrainSpec` carries one clump size per stock.

⚠ **NOTHING IS ADOPTED FROM IT.** The ordinate has no units, the abscissa says "LINES/mm" without
defining a line, and the figure is a redrawing (reference 91) rather than Ooue's own plate. Shape
is usable; level is not; and the grain spectrum moves a pixel on every stock. What is stored is
`film_profiles._OOUE_WIENER_1959`, as reference.

### 23j.2 Part 2 Fig. 24 — the autocorrelation, and the shape refuted from the other side

φ(τ) measured directly for Neopan S at D 1.04 and D 0.24. Curve (1) falls from 1000 to half at
**τ = 3.48 µm**. Under this engine's own law τ_half = 374.8/f_hi, so f_hi = 108 c/mm and
`clump_um` = **4.65 µm** — an independent scale for the quantity Fig. 26 measures in the frequency
domain.

⚠ **PAST ABOUT 12 µm IT GOES NEGATIVE** and stays negative for roughly another 8 µm: an
anti-correlated ring, i.e. the grains are more evenly spaced than a Poisson field would place them.
A Gaussian autocorrelation is positive everywhere and cannot produce that — **and neither can
Sayanagi's Poisson placement (§23i.1)**, which assumes exactly the distribution this figure
contradicts. Recorded as a shape limitation of *both* models, patched into neither.

### 23j.3 Part 1 Fig. 2 — mean grain area falls as density rises

Mean **developed** grain area against density, Fuji positive film in FD-3 (1:1) at 20 °C:
1.103 → 0.925 µm² over D 1.4 → 4.0 at 32 min, and 1.159 → 0.571 µm² over D 0.2 → 2.4 at 1 min.
Equivalent diameters **1.21 down to 0.85 µm**.

⚠ **IT FALLS**, on both development times — the same direction BBC T-101 Table 3 measures from
another laboratory, and the opposite of the usual expectation. ⚠ **AND IT LANDS BELOW THE FLOOR OF
EVERY STORED `emulsion.grain_um`:** all 17 of them are 1.3-6.5 µm and all 17 come from one
third-party aggregator. This is a positive film, the finest-grained class there is, so 0.85-1.21 µm
is a floor rather than a typical value — but it is independent evidence that the stored range is
too coarse. Nothing is changed: no profile here is Fuji positive FD-3.

### 23j.4 ⚠ Part 2 §4.2.1 — the empirical half of C45

Immediately before the standard-deviation heading:

> 「サイズの異なる二種の乳剤を重層塗布している場合には、Qは重要な意味を持ちえないであろう。
> 事実、現在市販されている感光材料のQの値を測定した結果は、心理的粒状性との相関を認めること
> はできない。」

*Where two emulsions of different grain size are coated as two layers, Q cannot carry an important
meaning. In fact, measurements of Q on commercially available sensitive materials show* ***no
correlation*** *with psychological graininess.*

C45 found the disagreement empirically from this project's own numbers; §23i.1 confirmed it
theoretically from Sayanagi (Q contains the granularity but not the grain radius, so it ranks only
samples of equal grain size). **This is the same conclusion measured on commercial stock, with the
double-coating mechanism named.** Three independent routes to one answer.

### 23j.5 What was read and deliberately not digitised

- **Part 2 Fig. 22**, Selwyn's G and van Kreveld's corrected Δ_m√a against scanning-spot diameter
  20-200 µm for six samples. Panel (a) shows Selwyn's raw G **rising** with aperture — so σ√a is
  *not* exact — while panel (b) shows van Kreveld's corrected quantity essentially flat over the
  same 5.5× range. That bears directly on this corpus's 48 µm normalisation and on comparing
  Ooue's own 10 µm figures against it. ⚠ **Not traced**: six overlapping curves on a 200 ppi
  raster, and the calibration attempt did not converge cleanly on either panel's frame. Recorded
  as read, with its conclusion, rather than reported as a number that was not measured.
- **Part 2 Figs. 19, 20, 21, 23, 25, 27, 28, 29** — instrument diagrams (van Kreveld, Goetz-Gould,
  Debot, the optical autocorrelator), graininess-vs-Q after Hansen & Keck, graininess-vs-granularity
  with named Neopan/developer pairs, and print-graininess curves. Context, not parameters.
- **Part 1 Figs. 4-18 and Table I** — granularity against development time at two densities, the
  eye's threshold-gradient sensitivity against density, the Jones-Deisch and Lowry instruments, and
  graininess of Fuji Neopan across fine-grain developers. All subjective-graininess work; the
  database has no carrier for it and inventing one would be a schema change without a decision.

## 23k. Takano 1969 — the aperture law checked at last, and the clump scale that does not agree

Added 2026-09-02 (queue TK1-TK5). `PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/JAPAN/23_13.pdf`, supplied by the owner
mid-batch. Kiyoshi Takano (高野潔), «写真フィルムの粒状性» / *"Granularity of Photographic Film"*,
テレビジョン (*J. Inst. Telev. Engrs. Japan*) **23**(1) 13-23 (1969). Traced by
`takano_1969_granularity.py`, registered in the build audit.

A review, like Ooue's pair — almost all of it other people's work redrawn, and **none of its
samples is a stock in this database**. Five items are still not incidental, and two of them touch
code.

### 23k.1 ⚠ Fig. 8 — the first measurement the engine's aperture term has ever been checked against

Selwyn granularity `G = √A·σ(D)` against the scanning aperture's `√A`, 3-90 µm, for a colour
negative and for Neopan-SS. Selwyn's constant is *supposed* to be aperture-independent. **Both
curves saturate** — the colour negative at G ≈ 1.04, Neopan-SS at G ≈ 0.63 — which is exactly why
rms granularity replaced it.

`film_sim.grain_reference_energy` already models this: it normalises grain by
`2π ∫ (h·a)² f df` with a Gaussian aperture of σ = size/4, so its predicted
`G(s) = C·s·√E(s)` saturates for the same reason. ⚠ **That law, unchanged, with nothing tuned but
one overall constant and `clump_um`, reproduces both traces to rms 0.007-0.020 in G over a
0.2-1.04 range.** The aperture handling was inherited from theory and had never been checked
against a measurement.

⚠ **What it does not settle is the size.** `clump_um` and `clump_gain` trade off almost exactly
against an aperture series:

| `clump_gain` | `clump_um` colour negative | rms (G) | `clump_um` Neopan-SS | rms (G) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.30 (corpus min) | 6.20 | 0.0196 | 4.78 | 0.0162 |
| 0.85 (corpus median) | 3.22 | 0.0167 | 2.46 | 0.0155 |
| 1.50 | 2.38 | 0.0066 | 1.88 | 0.0104 |

A 2.6× swing in size for a residual that moves by 0.013 G. The same non-identifiability the
JPS 1965 crystal-size work hit, quantified rather than asserted.

### 23k.2 Fig. 13 — two more autocorrelations, and a contradiction with Ooue

Optical autocorrelation φ(τ,0) with stated stock, density, developer, temperature and time:

| sample | τ½ | `clump_um` = 1.334·τ½ |
|---|---|---|
| Neopan-SSS, D 2.0, Minidol 20 °C 10 min | 1.33 µm | **1.77 µm** |
| cine positive, D 1.7, D-16 20 °C 6 min | 0.65 µm | **0.87 µm** |

⚠ **Neither curve goes negative, where Ooue's Fig. 24 does.** §23j.2 records Ooue's
anti-correlated ring past 12 µm as a refutation of the engine's Gaussian shape *and* of Sayanagi's
Poisson placement. Takano's optical autocorrelator shows both curves approaching zero from above,
which the Gaussian reproduces perfectly. **The disagreement is between two instruments, not
between either and the model**, and it is left standing rather than resolved by preferring the one
that suits the engine.

### 23k.3 ⚠ The clump census — the number queue C45 was missing

Every direct measurement of grain correlation length now in this corpus, converted to
`GrainSpec.clump_um` by the engine's own laws:

| source | sample | `clump_um` |
|---|---|---|
| Takano Fig. 13 | cine positive, D-16 | 0.87 |
| Takano Fig. 13 | Neopan-SSS, Minidol | 1.77 |
| Takano Fig. 8 | Neopan-SS (at `clump_gain` 0.85) | 2.46 |
| Takano Fig. 8 | colour negative (at `clump_gain` 0.85) | 3.22 |
| Ooue Part 2 Fig. 24 | Neopan S, D 1.04 | 4.64 |

**median 2.46 µm.** At the time of writing the 171 stored `clump_um_g` values ran 0.66-40.0, median
**13.0**, with only 10 stocks below 5 µm — the stored scale was **5.3× every measurement on file**.

⚠ **RESOLVED 2026-09-03: C45 WAS DECIDED AND THE CORPUS WAS RESCALED.** Every ESTIMATED
`clump_um` was divided by **3.1**; the five stocks with a measured value were exempt. Corpus median
**13.00 → 4.19 µm**, maximum 40.0 → 12.90. The anchor is Ooue Fig. 26 rather than this median —
see §23k.9 for why the conservative anchor was chosen over the full census, and for the aperture
invariant that made the change safe. This section stands as the census that forced the question.

### 23k.4 Fig. 9 — a fourth confirmation that σ(D) turns over, and a disagreement on where

RMS granularity against mean integral colour density, 16 × 16 µm aperture, one curve per layer
through blue / green / red filters. ⚠ **The ordinate is broken between 0.03 and 0.06 with a 2.04×
scale change across the break**, so only the magenta curve — the one unbroken stroke, isolated as a
single 813 px connected component — is traced; the dash-dot yellow and dashed cyan are grid
readings at ±0.002 and are reported as such.

Magenta, in this schema's own anchors: **toe 0.301 @ D 0.30 / mid 1.000 / dmax 0.301 @ D 2.50,
peak 1.002× at D 1.04.**

⚠ **That is a fourth independent confirmation of the 2026-08-17 correction** to `GrainSpec`'s
docstring, which used to say colour negatives are monotone rising. Four Kodak VISION3 sheets said
otherwise; this is a Japanese colour negative measured in 1969 by another laboratory on another
instrument, and it turns over too.

⚠ **And it disagrees on where the maximum sits.** All eleven measured colour negatives here peak at
D 0.65-0.80 at 1.20-1.62× the D = 1.0 value. This one peaks at D 1.04 at 1.00× — **no interior peak
above the mid anchor at all.** All eleven are Kodak ECN stocks of the 1990s-2000s, so
`sigma_shape_peak` is a *family* measurement rather than a corpus-wide law, which is exactly what
the `sigma_shape_measured` gate already refuses to let a renderer assume.

The layer ratios both disagree with the corpus, and the ranking is the explanation:
cyan/magenta **1.15** against the nine measured sheets' r/g 0.75-1.05 (10 % above the highest);
yellow/magenta **4.60** against their b/g 1.81-2.79 (65 % above). The caption says why — Takano
reads **integral** colour density through a filter, so each reading carries the orange mask and
every layer's absorption in that band, and the mask absorbs mostly blue. The corpus's ratios are
per-layer **analytical** densities. Two different quantities, not reconciled.

### 23k.5 ⚠ eq (2) — σ(D) from σ(T) to fourth order, and it is ADOPTED

Printed at p16 §3.2 (1), with T = 10^−D:

> σ(D) = 0.434·(σ(T)/T̄)·[ 1 + (1/12)(σ(T)/T̄)² + (1/80)(σ(T)/T̄)⁴ + … ]

⚠ **This is the correction the corpus was missing.** Provenance work here has converted rms
granularity into density with the **first term alone**, and that is precisely what failed on BBC
Report T-101 Fig. 26, whose σ(T)/T̄ runs 0.39 to 1.64 — the law `σ_D = 0.648·D^0.665` fitted from it
was **withdrawn** for that reason (the ILFORD_HPS provenance note in `film_profiles.py`).

| σ(T)/T̄ | first order | full series | error of the first-order form |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | 0.02170 | 0.02171 | +0.02 % |
| 0.39 | 0.16926 | 0.17145 | **+1.3 %** |
| 1.00 | 0.43400 | 0.47559 | +9.6 % |
| 1.64 | 0.71176 | 0.93565 | **+31.5 %** |

Adopted as `film_sim.sigma_density_from_transmittance` plus a Newton inverse
`sigma_transmittance_from_density`. ⚠ **INERT** — no render path calls either, so no stored value
and no rendered pixel moves; `verify.py` pins the round trip and the magnitudes.

### 23k.6 ⚠ eq (13) — the print chain, which the engine satisfies with one departure

Printed at p22 §5:

> F_pr(u,v) = F_pos(u,v) + F_neg(u,v)·R_pr²(u,v)·γ²

with R_pr the response of 「プリント光学系およびポジフィルム」 — **the printing optics *and* the
positive film** — and γ the positive's contrast ΔD/Δlog E.

The engine satisfies all three terms by construction:

- **`+ F_pos`** — the print stock's own grain is a separate field added at stage 14, after the
  print curve, so it adds in power.
- **`·γ²`** — stage 13 computes `log_e_print = offset − dens` with the negative's grain already
  inside `dens`, so the print curve's local slope multiplies that fluctuation.
- **`·R_pr²`** — stage 10 applies `scan_t` to the negative density before the print curve, and an
  amplitude transfer on a density field multiplies its Wiener spectrum by its square. With no
  scanner override, `scan_f50 = settings.scanner_f50 or print_stock.mtf_f50`, so the engine's
  default R_pr **is** the positive stock's own MTF — eq (13) with a contact printer.

⚠ **THE DEPARTURE: stage 14 also band-limits the print stock's own grain by that same transfer.**
eq (13) does not — F_pos is generated *in* the positive emulsion and is not imaged through the
positive's MTF. The duplication chain in the same function gets this right and says so in its own
comment ("This stage's own grain is created in THIS emulsion, so it is not blurred by this stage's
optics"). The print stage does not.

⚠ **Recorded, not changed.** When `scanner_f50` *is* set, `scan_t` is a real scanner and filtering
print grain by it is correct; the error appears only on the fallback, it moves a pixel on every
print render, and it is a **rendering** decision rather than a data one. The exact fix, should it
ever be taken, is to pass the scanner transfer — not the print stock's MTF — as the print grain's
band limit, which needs `scan_t` split into its two factors. A `verify.py` guard pins the present
state so that a future fix cannot land silently.

### 23k.7 What was read and deliberately not digitised

- **Fig. 18** (Wiener spectrum of a reversal colour film, magenta layer) and **Fig. 19** (Wiener
  spectrum against silver-halide crystal size) — both redrawings from other authors with unlabelled
  ordinates, i.e. the same defect that stopped Ooue's Fig. 26 from contributing a level.
- **Figs. 15, 16** — Fraunhofer-diffractometer spectra of a model emulsion and an X-ray film.
  Neither is a photographic stock.
- **Figs. 6, 7, 20** — Ooue's vanishing-distance apparatus and the ψ-graininess correlation. Already
  covered by §23j; subjective-graininess work with no carrier in this schema.
- **eq (14)**, the psychophysical granularity G_p through the eye's response function. It is the
  same construction as C7's temporal law and would need the eye model C7 declined to make a
  default.

### 23k.8 ⚠ Why there was no FUJI NEOPAN profile — asked, answered, and OVERTAKEN the same day

Three papers in this corpus now measure Neopan grain — Ooue `23_7` Fig. 7 (σ against D for
Neopan S / D-76, SS / Microfine, SSS / Pandol at a stated 10 µm aperture), Ooue `22_91`
Figs. 24 and 26, and Takano `23_13` Figs. 8 and 13. That is **one** of the roughly ten blocks a
`FilmProfile` needs, and it is the same block three times.

Searched and **not present in any of the 21 Japanese papers here**: a characteristic curve
(D vs log E), a JIS/ASA speed, D-min / D-max / base density, spectral sensitivity, an MTF or
resolving power, and an rms granularity at this corpus's 48 µm net-1.0 convention. The nearest
miss is Fujimura & Yamamoto, `26_172` Fig. 6 — **"Tone reproduction curves of Neopan SS (35 mm),
20 °C 6 min"** — but that is a *system* curve, log B_or of the enlarged print against log B_0 of
the scene, carrying the paper's own curve and camera flare, and the paper prints neither of those,
so it cannot be inverted to the negative's characteristic curve.

⚠ **A profile built on this would be one measured block and nine invented ones.** The precedent is
`KODAK_8374` (queue C26): admitted on T-101's grain data with everything else flagged inline, and
even there T-101 printed speeds for five of its six emulsions and 8374's `exposure_index` had to be
recorded as *"an acknowledged invented placeholder"*. Neopan S has no printed speed at all, so the
whole tone scale would be ours. **Refused on method rule 18.** What would unlock it is one Fuji
data sheet, or a 写真年鑑-class table, carrying a Neopan characteristic curve and speed.

> ⚠ **AND THAT SHEET ARRIVED THE SAME DAY, FOR ONE OF THE THREE.** The owner supplied FUJIFILM
> **AF3-411E(N)**, the NEOPAN **SS** (135) data sheet — speed, colour sensitivity, a full
> development matrix, a spectral sensitivity curve, a characteristic-curve family with its
> average gradients printed on every member, and time-Ḡ curves. `FUJI_NEOPAN_SS` was added the
> same day as stock 172 (queue **N1**, §23m). **This subsection is left standing as written**
> because its inventory is still exactly right for **NEOPAN S** and **NEOPAN SSS**, and because
> the refusal was correct on the evidence it had: what changed was the evidence, not the
> reasoning. ⚠ Note also what the new sheet did **not** change — see §23m.2, where the four
> granularity measurements made under the name "Neopan SS" in 1959–1969 are deliberately **not**
> joined to a 1999 coating.

## 23k.9 C45 decided — the corpus-wide `clump_um` rescale, 2026-09-03

Owner-approved. Every **estimated** `clump_um_r/g/b` divided by **3.1**; the five stocks with a
**measured** value exempt. Corpus median **13.00 → 4.19 µm**, maximum **40.0 → 12.90**, minimum
unchanged at 0.655 (ILFORD_PAN_F). 510 literals across 170 profiles.

### 23k.9.1 ⚠ First, the thing that had been confusing the question: `clump_um` is the GRAIN scale

The parameter is named for the clump and is not the clump. `film_sim.FreqGrid.grain_shape`:

```
f_hi = 500 / clump_um          the high-frequency rolloff   <- clump_um sets THIS
f_lo = f_hi / 6                the clump_gain lobe          <- a length 6x clump_um
```

So the model already carries **both** scales, six apart. ⚠ **And Takano 1968 measures the
developed aggregate at 5 to 8 times the mean grain** (§23n) — the model's hard-coded 6 sits inside
its measured range, from a document written thirty years before the model. That is an independent
corroboration of the *ratio*, and it settles which scale each source belongs to:

* BBC T-101's equivalent grain diameter, Takano 1969's autocorrelation half-widths and Ooue's
  Wiener half-powers are all the **grain** scale → they convert to `clump_um` directly.
* Takano 1968's Expected mottle size is the **cluster** scale → it converts to `clump_um` by
  dividing by six.

Anything that compares a measured cluster size with this field directly is out by about six, and
that is the trap this section exists to close.

### 23k.9.2 The census, all in the model's own parameter

`clump_um = 294.35 / u½`, the engine's own closed form.

| source | what it measured | `clump_um` |
|---|---|---|
| **Ooue 1959 Fig. 26** | three **directly measured Wiener spectra**, named stocks, stated developer, time and density | **2.09, 4.16, 6.46** |
| Takano 1969 Figs 8, 13 | Selwyn aperture series and optical autocorrelation, five samples | 0.87, 1.77, 2.46, 3.22, 4.64 |
| BBC T-101 Table 2 | printed equivalent grain diameter, six emulsions, ÷ 1.7473 | 0.59 – 1.43 |
| Takano 1968 Fig. 11 | mottle 3.98 – 6.81 µm ÷ the model's own 6× lobe ratio | 0.66 – 1.14 |
| JPS 1965 | five emulsions, relative ordinate | 2.73 – 3.69 |
| **stored estimates, before** | — | **median 13.00**, 160 of 175 above the band's top |

### 23k.9.3 ⚠ It is not a parameter-basis argument, and that was checked first

The obvious objection is that `clump_um` and `clump_gain` trade off (§23k.1 / TK1), so perhaps the
estimates' (13.0, 0.25) describe the same *spectrum* as a measurement's (2.5, 0.0) in a different
basis. **They do not, and the reason is one-directional**: the lobe only ever adds low-frequency
energy, so it can push the half-power **down**, never up.

| clump / gain | spectrum half-power |
|---|---|
| 13.0 / 0.00 | 22.6 c/mm |
| 13.0 / 0.25 | 13.7 c/mm |
| 13.0 / 0.85 | 6.2 c/mm |
| **measured (Ooue)** | **45.6 / 70.8 / 140.7 c/mm** |

No value of `clump_gain` reaches the measurements. The stored estimates were a genuinely different
spectrum, not an equivalent description of the same one.

### 23k.9.4 ⚠ Why the 2026-09-02c refusal did not survive measurement

C45 was closed "refused, with the cost of the alternative measured". Its stated reason was that the
rescale makes rendered grain markedly more resolution-dependent — 1.31× against 1.90× across
960–4000 px — "a change in how the product behaves on 168 stocks that the data alone cannot
authorise."

**`rms_granularity` is defined through a 48 µm aperture, and the aperture-referred rms does not
move.** Measured end to end on `KODAK_VISION3_250D_5207`, flat 0.18 patch, green record, ×1000:

| clump / gain | 960 px | 2000 px | 4000 px |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13.00 / 0.25 | 5.263 | 5.203 | 5.228 |
| 6.46 / 0.00 | 5.202 | 5.151 | 5.170 |
| 4.16 / 0.00 | 5.197 | 5.147 | 5.166 |
| 2.46 / 0.00 | 5.194 | 5.145 | 5.164 |

**1.3 % across the whole clump range and every render size.** The film still measures what its
datasheet says, through the aperture its datasheet specifies. Only the sub-aperture detail changes,
and the datasheet number never described that. So the change is **"same film, correctly resolved"**,
not "more grain" — which is a claim about fidelity, and fidelity the data *can* authorise.

⚠ **And the engine had already ruled on the direction.** `grain_reference_energy`'s docstring, written
long before C45: *"a 2K render genuinely shows less granularity than a 6K render of the same
negative, converging upward as the band widens. That is not a modelling artefact — it is why 4K
scans of old negatives look grainier than the 2K masters everyone remembers."* The old 1.24× was
that behaviour **suppressed**, because a coarse clump leaves little energy out of band to recover.

What the user actually sees, same stock and patch, ×1000:

| clump | 960 px | 2000 px | 4000 px |
|---|---|---|---|
| stored 13.0 | 6.59 | 7.77 | 8.16 |
| **adopted ≈4.2** | 6.77 **(+3 %)** | 9.88 **(+27 %)** | 13.34 **(+63 %)** |

⚠ **Near-zero at 1080p, growing with resolution** — which is the shape the physics predicts.

**Cost: none.** 716.6 → 689.6 ms single-thread at 2000 px through the full `simulate()`. `clump_um`
changes the transfer's shape, not the transform's size.

### 23k.9.5 The two decisions inside the decision

**The anchor is Ooue alone, k = 3.1, not the full census's k = 5.3.** Ooue Fig. 26 is the strongest
evidence class here: directly measured Wiener spectra on named stocks with stated developer, time
and density, needing no conversion chain. Its median is 4.16 µm against the stored 13.00. The full
census would have given 2.46 and a larger change, but it mixes measured spectra with values that
arrived through a conversion — and the conservative anchor still lands inside the band every other
source brackets.

**`clump_gain` was left untouched, and that is a recorded conflict rather than an oversight.** All
five measured stocks carry `clump_gain` 0.00, a free two-parameter fit drove the lobe to exactly
zero on all six T-101 emulsions, and T-101 p38 says in words that correlation is "substantially
confined to about plus or minus one equivalent grain diameter". ⚠ **But Takano 1968 measures a real
aggregate at 5–8× the grain — i.e. that the lobe exists.** The two sources disagree outright.
Method rule 4: record the conflict, do not average it. Scaling `clump_um` alone is **one** change;
zeroing the lobe as well would have picked a winner between two disagreeing measurements.

⚠ **The consequence is stated rather than hidden**: §23k.1 showed the two parameters are not
separately identifiable, so every rescaled value is **conditional on that stock's stored gain**. A
later measurement that settles the lobe would move these values again, and should.

### 23k.9.6 What is exempt, and what would reopen this

Exempt, all five with measured `clump_um` from T-101 Table 2 and all five at `clump_gain` 0.00:
`ILFORD_PAN_F` 0.655, `KODAK_8374` 0.687, `EASTMAN_PLUS_X_5231` 0.830, `EASTMAN_TRI_X_5223` 1.259,
`ILFORD_HPS` 1.431.

⚠ **What would reopen it**: a measured Wiener spectrum or multi-aperture rms for a stock **that is
in this database**. Every one of the fifteen measurements above is of a film this project does not
carry, so the rescale is still a class inference — a well-evidenced one across five documents,
three countries and three decades, but a class inference. `verify.py` pins the result, the exempt
five and the aperture invariant.

## 23l. Sehlin & Kennel 1985, and six decisions where three of the rows were wrong

Added 2026-09-02 (queue E5, C45, C46, C16, C18, C19, C2c). Full treatment in
`RESULT_2026-09-02c_batch_E5_C45_C46_C16_C18_C19_C2c.md`; this section keeps the findings that
outlive the batch.

### 23l.1 ⚠ A good σ(D) trace, withdrawn by a guard — and the density-space convention it exposed

R. Sehlin, G. Kennel et al., *"Choosing between EASTMAN Color Negative Films 5247 and 5294"*,
**SMPTE Journal 94(7) 724–731, July 1985** — `PDF/PROFILES/KODAK/Sehlin_Kennel_etal_1983_…pdf`
(⚠ the file name's 1983 is wrong). Its **Fig. 8 plots DENSITY and RMS GRANULARITY against one
shared log-exposure abscissa** for 5294, so the σ(D) pairing is complete on a single plate.

Adopted on `EASTMAN_5294_1983`: **toe 1.571 @ D 0.44 / mid 1.000 / dmax 0.703 @ D 2.08, interior
peak 1.664 @ D 0.53**, `sigma_shape_measured=True`. Measured count **13 → 14**, measured colour
negatives **11 → 12**.

⚠ **It validates against a family it was not fitted to** — peak and dmax land inside the eleven
vendor sheets' 1.20–1.62 and 0.50–0.90 — while peaking **earlier** (D 0.53) than all eleven
(0.65–0.80). That is the evidence that the interior maximum belongs to the stock and not to the
class.

⚠ **The level is refused** (unlabelled ordinate: no unit, no aperture, no densitometry), and
⚠ **Fig. 12's MTF is refused with it**: 50 % at 45–58 c/mm against a stored *estimate* of 24/28/33,
but the text calls it a **system** MTF and the curve **does not overshoot**, sitting at 100 % to
18 c/mm where every vendor-sheet colour-negative MTF here rises above 100 % first.

Two tracing lessons worth keeping:

- **When two curves share a panel, calibrate each ordinate on its own labels.** Fig. 8's are 218 px
  per density unit and 242 px per granularity decade — reading one off the other's gridline is a
  10 % error that looks plausible.
- **When two curves cross, walk them TOGETHER.** No single-track follower survives a crossing: the
  nearest ink *is* the other curve, and a tolerance tight enough to refuse it refuses the right one.
  Assigning the candidate pair to the prediction pair by least cost works because curves that cross
  do so with opposite slopes.

### 23l.2 ⚠ `adjacency_um` has a closed form, and two queue rows were comparing it to the wrong thing

`MTFSpec.adjacency_um` is the scale of a **difference of Gaussians** (σ₁ = 0.4a, σ₂ = 2.0a in
`FreqGrid.mtf`). Its band-pass peak:

> σ₂²/σ₁² = 25 ⟹ 2π²f²(σ₂² − σ₁²) = ln 25 ⟹ **f_peak = 206.07 / adjacency_um c/mm**

The rendered MTF peaks **lower** still, because the emulsion rolloff pulls the product down. C2c and
C19 both compared a traced overshoot peak in c/mm against the stored value in µm with no conversion
and concluded "systematic, same direction on all four". Once converted, the three stocks whose model
overshoots at all invert to **+8 %, −41 %, +102 %** — scatter, not bias.

⚠ **AND 12 OF THE 161 STOCKS WITH `adjacency` > 0 ARE INERT**: their value is too small against
their own rolloff for the product to exceed 100 % at any frequency, so the parameter reads as active
and does nothing. Two of the twelve (`EASTMAN_PLUS_X_5231`, `FUJI_SUPER_F125_8532`) were cited as
C2c's evidence — they cannot disagree about a peak they do not have. Pinned by `verify.py`.

Nothing was adopted: peak frequency and peak amplitude come from **one** traced curve, and fitting
only the length against a separately-stored amplitude is half a fit.

### 23l.3 A uniform scalar cancels under row normalisation — the C46 argument that was not there

`DUFAYCOLOR_1937.reseau.filter_matrix` was multiplied by an "invented uniform factor of 4.05" and
**then row-normalised to a common sum of 0.80**. ⚠ **The scalar cancels exactly**, so it never
touched the stored numbers; C46's case for replacing the matrix — that the newer measurement "needs
no invented 4.05" — was about a factor that was not in the data. Matrix kept, note corrected.

**The general lesson:** before treating a documented fudge as a reason to change something, check
whether the pipeline that follows it removes it.

### 23l.4 The interimage density weight is bounded, and the bound is free

`density_weighting` gives `w = (1 − dw) + dw·D_j/D_ref` — unbounded, 0.65 on 36 reversal stocks,
tier 3, the largest undocumented number in the colour path. It is now capped at the value it reaches
at that channel's own **Dmax**, in the Python reference and in both C++ paths.

⚠ **The cap is provably non-binding.** `ToneCurve.dmax` *is* the asymptote
`dmin + gamma·(shoulder_x − toe_x)`, and `density()` is `dmin + gamma` times a difference of two
softplus ramps — strictly increasing, bounded above by `(shoulder_x − toe_x)`. So `D < dmax` always
and every render is bit-for-bit unchanged. `verify.py` asserts the premise (`max(asymptote − dmax) =
0` over every stock × 3 curves) so the proof cannot rot.

**The general lesson:** an unbounded expression can often be bounded for free by a quantity the data
model already guarantees, without inventing the saturation constant the measurement would give.

### 23l.5 ⚠ Two model scales that disagree with every measurement, and why neither moved

- **`clump_um`** (C45). Five direct measurements, median **2.46 µm**, against a stored median of
  **13.0**; and a *second independent route* agrees — the engine's own spectrum half-power at
  13.0 µm is 22.7 c/mm against Ooue's measured 45.6/70.8/140.7 lines/mm. ⚠ **But the rescale has a
  measured cost**: at the physical scale the rendered grain amplitude becomes nearly twice as
  resolution-dependent (ratio 4000 px / 960 px goes 1.31× → 1.90×). Refused: `clump_um` and
  `clump_gain` are not separately identifiable, none of the five samples is a stock here, and the
  resolution behaviour is a product decision, not a data one.
- **The coupler blur below 1.2 px** (C16). ⚠ Its recommended fix was withdrawn on arithmetic: a
  1.0 px gate at the stored `edge_um` of 9–13 µm switches the edge term off below **77–111 px/mm**,
  i.e. on every 35 mm render narrower than ~4000 px — three times the scope the row claimed. And
  the question "which form is right" now has an answer: for an already-sampled image, multiplying
  the DFT by the analytic transfer **is** the correct discretisation, while the sampled kernel's
  effective transfer is the *periodised* Gaussian. The Python reference is right, the C++ spatial
  kernel is a characterised approximation, and supersampling is the only correct fix.

## 23m. FUJIFILM AF3-411E(N) — the sheet that turned §23k.8's refusal into a profile

Added 2026-09-02 (queue N1). `PDF/PROFILES/FUJI/SS35.pdf`, four pages, supplied by the owner.
Traced by `fuji_neopan_ss.py`, registered in the build audit. Result: **`FUJI_NEOPAN_SS`, stock
172**, appended at frozen id 171 so no ListBox index moves.

### 23m.1 What the sheet gives, and the self-check built into it

§3 **ISO 100/21°**; §4 «Orthopanchromatic»; §7 a development matrix over three Fuji and twelve
non-Fuji developers at five temperatures and three exposure indices, plus a deep-tank table; §8 a
spectral sensitivity curve (spectrogram to daylight 5400 K); §9 a characteristic-curve family;
§10 time-Ḡ curves for three developers.

⚠ **§9 PRINTS THE AVERAGE GRADIENT ON EVERY CURVE** — 4 min Ḡ 0.28, 6 min 0.37, 8 min 0.45,
10 min 0.53, 12 min 0.61 — and nothing in the trace is told them. Reproducing them checks the axis
calibration, the curve identification and the fit at once. Traced straight-line slopes come out
0.293 / 0.393 / 0.478 / 0.585 / 0.680, monotone in the printed order and a consistent 3–9 % above
the printed averages, which is what an average gradient measured over a span *including the toe*
must be.

**Adopted:** the 10 min member — the drawn curve nearest the sheet's own recommendation of 9½ min
for Microfine at 20 °C and EI 100 — as `ToneCurve(0.2450, 0.5525, −2.4553, 0.0607, 1.9882,
0.1212)`, fit rms **0.0234 D** over 709 columns, model Ḡ **0.552** against a printed 0.53.

⚠ **Two pins, both stated rather than fitted.** `dmin` 0.245 is the sheet's own printed **Base
Density** rule, because the plotted curves never reach the base plateau and a free fit runs dmin to
whatever bound it is given. And **the shoulder is not measured at all** — the panel stops at D 1.82
with the curve still straight — so Dmax is pinned to a class 2.70; refitting at 2.5 or 3.0 moves the
fit rms by 0.0002 D and the model Ḡ by 0.001.

### 23m.2 ⚠ Two calibration traps, and why the Ḡ check would not have caught the worse one

- **The frame is not the first label.** The abscissa runs logH −4.0 at the frame to +1.0 at the
  right edge, and the leftmost *printed* label is −3.0, one gridline pair in. Reading the frame as
  −3.0 shifts every exposure by a full decade **while leaving every density and every slope
  untouched** — so the printed-Ḡ check still passes and nothing complains. The fix is to anchor on
  "0.0", the only label without a minus sign and therefore the only one whose glyph centre lands on
  its gridline.
- **Label centroids and gridlines disagree on the ordinate**, 152.1 px against 158.7 px per 0.5 D,
  because the axis-title glyphs contaminate the label band. The gridlines are right, and the proof
  is that they make one density unit 317.5 px against one exposure decade at 318.4 — the 1:1 aspect
  a sensitometric plot is drawn at.

**The general lesson:** *a self-check only tests what it is sensitive to.* A gradient check is
blind to an abscissa offset, because a gradient is a ratio of differences. Anchor an axis on a
label whose glyph geometry is unambiguous, and cross-check the two axes against each other.

### 23m.3 ⚠ Four granularity measurements of "Neopan SS" that are NOT joined to this profile

This corpus holds four: Ooue 1959 Part 2 **Fig. 26** (Wiener spectrum, Minidol 20 °C 10 min),
Ooue's `23_7` **Fig. 7** (σ against D at a stated 10 µm aperture, Microfine), and Takano 1969
**Fig. 8** (Selwyn granularity at thirteen apertures, giving `clump_um` 2.46 µm at the corpus
median `clump_gain`).

⚠ **They measure the coating sold in 1959–1969. This sheet is dated 1999 by its own printer's code
(EIGI-99.3).** One trade name, two products, forty years apart — the trap already on file for
`EASTMAN_5247` (1974 against 1983) and for ILFORD PAN F against PAN F PLUS. The sheet itself has
**no image-structure section at all** (no rms granularity, no resolving power, no MTF, no
reciprocity, no base thickness; all four pages searched), so the grain and MTF blocks are flagged
class estimates from the cubic ISO 100–125 peers `AGFA_APX_100` (rms 9.0, f50 80) and
`KODAK_PLUS_X_125` (9.5, 62). `verify.py` pins the separation so a later editor cannot quietly
join them.

### 23m.4 What is still missing for NEOPAN S and SSS

The **Fuji sales guide** (`PDF/PROFILES/FUJI/Fuji Sales Guide Curves.pdf`, two raster pages, also
supplied 2026-09-02) prints **ASA 50 / 100 / 200** for S / SS / SSS in its running text, a per-film
γ-versus-development-time panel with a numeric γ axis, and a per-film characteristic-curve family
with a numeric log-exposure axis and a marked base-density line, all at Minidol 20 °C tank. ⚠ Its
第3図 three-film overlay is **schematic** — the axes are labelled only 大 / 小 with no numbers — so
it gives ordering and shape, not a curve. Harvesting it would add NEOPAN S and SSS at tier 2; the
owner is looking for manufacturer datasheets for those two first.

## 23n. Masao Takano 1968 Part 2 — the same density reached two ways, and a second source for the clump census

Added 2026-09-02e from `PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/JAPAN/31_209.pdf`, supplied by the owner mid-batch.
Masao TAKANO (高野正雄), Fuji Photo Film Research Laboratories, Ashigara,
«写真像の粒状性(第2報) — 一定の濃度をうる露光量と現像時間の組合わせと Wiener Spectrum» /
*Granularity of Photographic Image (II): Wiener Spectrum at a Constant Density Level with
Various Exposure and Time of Development*, **J. Soc. Phot. Sci. Japan 31(4) 209–214 (1968)**,
received 5 Aug 1968. Traced by `takano_1968_mottle.py`, registered in the build audit.

⚠ **IT IS NOT THE TAKANO §23k IS BUILT ON.** `23_13.pdf` is **Kiyoshi** Takano's 解説 — a
review of granularity evaluation and measurement method, in the television journal, with no
experiment of its own. This is **Masao** Takano's original experiment, in the photographic
society's journal, and it is the second of a two-part series whose Part 1 is not in the
corpus. Byte-compared against all 97 PDFs held: no duplicate. Figure-compared against §23i
(the Japanese collection), §23j (Ooue 1959) and §23k (Takano 1969): no overlap of samples,
panels or measurements.

### 23n.1 The experiment

One general-purpose black-and-white negative film, **ASA 100**, **unnamed** — which is why
nothing from this paper is written to a film profile. Grain size distribution measured on a
centrifugal sedimentation sizer, with an electron micrograph (Fig. 1). Exposure by tungsten
lamp through a DG filter at **6470 K**. Four developers, the "Series-A" set of Part 1, each
close to a single-agent solution and all adjusted to **pH 8.5 with NaOH** so the developing
agent's own behaviour shows through: para-phenylenediamine, PQ, Monol, MQ. Wiener spectra on
a high-speed rotating microphotometer with a frequency analyser; 20 c/s–20 kc/s is
4.2–42 000 lines/mm in principle but **500 lines/mm is the real ceiling** (rotation
irregularity, focus, circuit noise), which the author argues is ample because 300–500
lines/mm already carries the granularity information.

⚠ **THE TWO ROUTES TO ONE DENSITY, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE PAPER:**

* **[VTD]** — exposure held constant, **development time** varied to reach the density.
* **[VE]** — development time held constant, **exposure** varied to reach it.

Same film, same developer, same final density, **two different grain patterns**.

### 23n.2 ⚠ The finding the engine has no parameter for

**Reaching a density by developing longer gives a 36–40 % smaller clump than reaching it by
exposing more.** Traced off Fig. 11's D = 0 envelopes: [VE] runs 5.22 → 7.29 µm across the
four developers and [VTD] 3.35 → 4.37 µm.

Nothing in `FilmProfile` or `RenderSettings` distinguishes the two routes, so the engine
renders one grain where the measurement finds two. Recorded as an open gap and **not queued**
— it is a schema question, not a data one.

### 23n.3 Fig. 11 as traced

Expected mottle size, micrometres, per developer and route; lower marker D 0.5, upper D 1.5.

| developer | [VE] D 0.5 / D 1.5 | [VTD] D 0.5 / D 1.5 |
|---|---|---|
| para-phenylenediamine | 4.42 / 4.80 | 3.98 / 4.16 |
| PQ | 4.98 / 5.55 | 4.37 / 4.59 |
| Monol | 5.78 / 6.13 | 4.62 / 4.94 |
| MQ | 6.32 / 6.81 | 4.57 / 5.30 |

Ordinate calibrated over five printed tick labels at 79.54 px per micrometre, residual
0.017 µm. ⚠ **The independent check**: the panel's own x-axis rule — found separately, as the
row of maximum ink — lands at y 1039 against the fitted zero at y 1038.8, i.e. **0.2 px,
0.003 µm**, on a quantity the fit never saw.

⚠ **THE PAPER'S TWO PERCENTAGES DESCRIBE THE ENVELOPES, NOT THE MARKERS, and reading them
onto the wrong object overstates the effect by about two.**

* "[VTD] is 30–40 % smaller than [VE]" — true of the **D = 0 envelope lines**, traced here at
  36 % and 40 %. On the density-0.5–1.5 **markers** the same ratio is 10 / 12 / 20 / 28 %,
  mean **17 %**.
* "Mottle size grows 20–30 % with density" — **not reproduced by the markers**, which give
  **+4 % to +16 %**, mean +8 %. The prose presumably means a wider density span than the
  markers show, or the spectrum-level growth of Figs. 7–8 rather than the mottle size.
  Recorded as measured; the disagreement is recorded, not reconciled (method rule 4).

### 23n.4 ⚠ The number that matters to this database — a second, independent source for C45

The paper states, in words, that the secondary aggregate is **5 to 8 times the mean developed
silver grain** (「二次的集落の大きさは平均の現像銀粒子サイズの5～8倍」). Divide the traced
3.98–6.81 µm of mottle by that factor and the **grain is 0.50–1.36 µm**.

**BBC Report T-101 Table 2 prints 0.59–1.43 µm** for its six emulsions — a different maker, a
different country, a different decade and a different instrument.

⚠ **Two independent documents land on one band, and the 175 stored `clump_um_g` values have
median 13.0, outside both by an order of magnitude.** This is the third statement of the C45
finding and the **first from a non-BBC source**. It is still not applied: C45 owns that
decision and refused it on measured render cost, and this paper names no film.

### 23n.5 What is refused, and why

Figs. 3–8 and Fig. 10 plot spectrum level F(u,0) in an **unlabelled instrument unit with no
printed constant**, so their level cannot be converted into anything this schema stores.
Fig. 9 (development time against gamma) is a process curve for an unnamed film. All are read
for their **shape** and recorded as such, not digitised. What survives the missing constant is
the **ordering**, which is identical on the mottle and spectrum-level measures, finest first:

> **para-phenylenediamine < PQ < Monol < MQ**

Two further items worth keeping as context: the paper cites **Albersheim**'s ΔT expressions
for grains dispersed in two dimensions versus three, with ΔT₃ > ΔT₂ — qualitatively matching
its own [VTD] / [VE] result — and it notes that if developed grains could be made to lie on a
**lattice**, the expected mottle size would be minimised and psychophysical granularity cut to
a fraction.
