## 23o. Lu & Torquato 1990 — why σ(D) turns over, and the mechanism `clump_gain` cannot express

**Binglin Lu & S. Torquato, «Photographic granularity: mathematical formulation and effect of
impenetrability of grains», J. Opt. Soc. Am. A **7**(4) 717–724, April 1990.** 8 pages,
`PDF/PROFILES/RETRO/Photographic granularity.Mathematical formulation.pdf`. No named film, no
emulsion, no measured stock — **it can set a shape and never a level.**

⚠ **THIS ENTRY EXISTS BECAUSE THE FIRST ASSESSMENT OF THE PAPER WAS WRONG.** It was recorded as
"pure theory, zero database rows change". The owner objected that a 1990 statistical-mechanics
treatment deserves more weight against 1950s–60s empiricism, not less. He is right, and the test
that settles it was already in this database.

### 23o.1 What the paper predicts

Grains that **cannot overlap** constitute, in the authors' words, a less random distribution than
the random-dot model. Impenetrability is **short-range order** — *negative* low-frequency
correlation — so granularity falls below the random-dot value, and the effect grows with coverage.
Their Fig. 4: for penetrable disks G rises monotonically with area fraction φ₂; for impenetrable
disks it **rises, peaks, and then falls**.

Selwyn's law is recovered as the large-aperture limit, Eq (3.8) `G = K·Aa^(−1/2)`, with Eq (3.9)
identifying `K` as the square root of `∫[S₂(r) − φ₂²]dr` — **the zero-frequency limit of the
autocovariance**, which is exactly what `grain_reference_energy` integrates through the 48 µm
aperture. Eqs (4.1)/(4.2) reproduce **Bayer's random-dot closed form**, stated as such in the text.

### 23o.2 ⚠ Eleven stocks in this database already show the predicted turnover

`sigma_shape_measured` is True on 13 stocks; the 11 colour negatives among them all have an
**interior peak at D 0.65–0.80** and then fall:

| | peak @ D | σ at peak | σ at Dmax | fall | √D law predicts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EASTMAN_EXR_50D_5245 | 0.73 | 1.470 | 0.720 | **×0.49** | ×1.69 |
| KODAK_VISION3_250D_5207 | 0.80 | 1.280 | 0.570 | **×0.45** | ×1.84 |
| KODAK_VISION3_500T_5219 | 0.80 | 1.310 | 0.550 | **×0.42** | ×1.84 |
| KODAK_VISION_500T_5279 | 0.65 | 1.420 | 0.500 | **×0.35** | ×1.84 |

Across all eleven the measured change is **×0.35 to ×0.74** and the √D law predicts **×1.66 to
×1.84**. ⚠ **The disagreement is a factor of 2.3 to 5.3, and it is a disagreement in DIRECTION.**
Until now the interior peak was an empirical shape with no mechanism behind it; this paper is the
mechanism, and it was published twenty-five years before the Kodak sheets that show it.

Converting Table 1 to density through `D = −log₁₀(1 − φ₂)` makes the same point numerically: at
every real aperture ratio the √D law overshoots the impenetrable-disk theory by **1.8× to 2.7×** by
D 0.52.

### 23o.3 What it changes here

* **F2b** — 55 monochrome negatives sit on a placeholder σ(D) and the row is blocked on an
  unobtainable Higgins & Stultz. A **principled one-parameter shape** is now available instead of a
  placeholder, without that document.
* **F1** shrinks: Bayer's closed form is in hand. ⚠ And its **Wilder JOSA 62 (1972) citation looks
  wrong** — absent from a 1990 granularity review that cites Bayer, Trabka 1971,
  Hamilton/Lawton/Trabka 1972 and Castro/Kemperman/Trabka. F1's claim that no JOSA paper is in the
  corpus is also now false.
* **Table 1** — G for impenetrable disks over 23 aperture ratios × 7 area fractions, 161 numbers —
  is a numeric validator for the aperture law that needs no film.

### 23o.4 ⚠ The half of the mechanism this engine cannot express

`grain_shape`'s lobe is `1 + clump_gain·exp(−(f/f_lo)²)` and both engines clamp the gain at zero:
`film_sim.py:1248` `if clump_gain > 0.0:`, `Algo_11_Sim.cpp:69` and its two
`MAX_VALUE(clumpGain, ALGO_ZERO)` at 191 and 234. **Checked: Python and C++ agree, so there is no
parity bug** — but a *negative* gain is unrepresentable by construction in both, and negative
low-frequency correlation is precisely what impenetrability produces.

⚠ **This is the missing explanation for the conflict recorded in §23n.** BBC T-101 fits
`clump_gain` to exactly 0.000 on all six of its emulsions and says correlation is confined to about
±1 grain diameter; Takano 1968 measures a real aggregate at 5–8× the grain. **Both can be true of
different emulsions** — one packed toward the ordered limit, the other clustered — and this engine
can only express the clustering half. Lu & Torquato's **penetrable-concentric-shell model**, with a
single impenetrability index λ ∈ [0,1] spanning λ = 0 (random-dot) to λ = 1 (hard disks), is the
principled one-parameter replacement if the ordered side is ever wanted.

**Caveats, stated rather than buried**: a monolayer of disks, not a real multilayer emulsion; the
table stops at D 0.52; and with no named film the paper can never set a level.


## 24. Physical property → image appearance: the mapping

This section exists to separate physically supported relationships from empirical assumptions
about "film look". Each row states the chain the sources actually establish — emulsion structure →
exposure or development behaviour → measurable photographic characteristic → visible image
characteristic — and marks where that chain **breaks** for want of a number.

Read the classification carefully. A row tagged **[M]** describes a real physical relationship
whose direction is known and whose magnitude is not. Turning such a row into a simulation
parameter means supplying a coefficient the sources do not contain, and that coefficient would be
ours, not physics.

### 24.1 Chains that are complete enough to constrain a model

| Physical property | Intermediate behaviour | Measurable | Visible | Class | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grain **volume** | Intrinsic (blue) absorption per grain ∝ volume | Blue-record speed | Blue-layer speed and grain scale | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` |
| Grain **surface area** | Dye-sensitized absorption ∝ surface area, because dye adsorbs as a monomolecular layer | Green/red-record speed | Green and red records scale differently from blue with the same grain | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` |
| **Tabular** habit (high surface-to-volume at fixed volume) | Raises dye-sensitized absorbance without raising grain volume | Speed at constant granularity | Finer-grained film at equal speed | **[F]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` |
| **Silver iodide content** | Raises intrinsic absorption; 3 mol % AgI in AgBr raises percent absorption at 460 nm **five times** | Blue speed | Blue-record speed and shadow detail | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]` |
| Grain **size and sensitivity distribution** | Reduces DQE to **36 %** of the value it would otherwise have (cumulative 1.5 %) | Granularity at fixed speed | Grain visibility | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]` |
| **Random grain arrangement** | Reduces DQE to **72 %** (cumulative 1.1 %) | Granularity | Grain visibility | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]` |
| **Four-atom threshold** for latent-image developability | Reduces DQE to **64 %** (cumulative 27 %) | Speed | Shadow speed and threshold | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]` |
| **Recombination** losses in latent-image formation | Reduces DQE to **16 %** (cumulative 4.3 %) | Speed | Shadow speed | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]` |
| **Gold sensitization** | Lowers the smallest developable image centre from 4–5 atoms (sulfur only) to **3 atoms** | Speed | Shadow speed at equal grain | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` |
| Developer **class** | Two extreme progress types: **A parallel** — developed silver ∝ the *proportion* developed within each grain; **B granular** — developed silver ∝ the *number* of fully developed grains | Density build-up law, and the statistics of that build-up | Grain structure and its character | **[Q]** direction, **[M]** magnitude | `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.216 (PDF 225), Fig. 7.7]` |
| Developer class, worked example | Colour developer **CP-20** (4-amino-N-dialkylaniline) is type A; B&W **D72** (metol-hydroquinone) is type B; with CP-20 on 0.86 µm cubic AgBr, ~**2 min** for each grain to be fully developed, and density rises because the *proportion* of developed silver per grain rises | — | — | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.216–217 (PDF 225–226), Figs. 7.8, 7.9]` |
| Grain size, **parallel** development | Rate ∝ **1/size**, i.e. ∝ surface-to-volume ratio | Development rate | Effective gamma at fixed time | **[Q]** | `[Tani 1995, §7.3, p.219 (PDF 228), Fig. 7.12]` |
| Grain size, **granular** development | Rate is **nearly independent** of grain size; rate-determining step is the first electron injection, so it is sensitive to the developability of development centres instead | Development rate | — | **[F]** | `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.218–219 (PDF 227–228), Figs. 7.10, 7.11]` |
| **Developer identity vs speed** | Photographic sensitivity does **not** depend on the kind of developer when each is used under its optimum conditions — confirmed by several groups | Speed | Speed is not a developer choice | **[F]** | `[Tani 1995, §7.4, p.219 (PDF 228)]` |
| **Fog origin** | Two kinds: **emulsion fog** develops rapidly from pre-existing centres; **developer fog** is initiation-limited and proceeds slowly | Dmin, and its time dependence | Base-plus-fog level and how it grows with development | **[Q]** direction | `[Tani 1995, §7.4–7.5, pp.219–220 (PDF 228–229), Fig. 7.13]` |
| Sensitization centres as **electron traps** | Grains carrying sulfur or sulfur-plus-gold centres accept electrons from the developer more easily, so they form developer-fog centres more easily | Dmin rises with chemical sensitization | Fog floor tracks speed | **[F]** | `[Tani 1995, §7.5, p.220 (PDF 229)]` |
| **γ, granularity and photon exposure are coupled** | DQE = R₀²/R² = (log e)² γ² / (E G²) | γ, Selwyn *G*, speed cannot be chosen independently | Contrast, grain and speed trade against one another | **[Q]** for the relation, **[M]** for absolute calibration | `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25), Eq. (1.1)]` |
| **Base shrinkage** (carrier) | Base shrinks, emulsion does not; ">1 % is enough to cause real trouble for cinema films", up to 10 % advanced | Dimensional change | Registration and geometry | **[Q]** range | `[Reilly 1993 (rev. 1996), p.11 (PDF 11)]` |
| **Colour dye fading** | Magenta survives longest; pre-1980 stocks "20 to 30 years at room temperature before fading becomes significant" | Per-dye density loss | Purple cast | **[Q]** | `[Reilly 1993 (rev. 1996), p.16 (PDF 16)]` |
| **Iodide and halation** (1929 view) | Iodide-containing emulsions are "more opaque, and less likely to suffer from halation and solarization"; at 3–4 % iodide "halation is less … and small details against the sky are better differentiated" | — | Halation extent | **[M]** | `[Wall 1929, Ch. III, pp.33–35 (PDF 41–43)]` |

### 24.2 Chains the sources establish in direction but not in magnitude

These are the **[M]** rows — genuinely useful, genuinely not parameterisable from this set.

1. **Grain size → graininess.** Universally asserted across all three technical eras and **never
   quantified anywhere in this source set.** No source gives a grain-size→rms-granularity relation,
   and Tani's own text states there is none in his first five chapters beyond the appearance of *G*
   as a symbol. → §17. **[M]**
2. **Ripening time and temperature → speed, contrast and fog.** The 1929 and 1966 sources give
   extensive operational tables (temperatures, times, halide ratios) and directional outcomes, but
   no transfer function from a process variable to a sensitometric number. → §6. **[M]**
3. **Gelatin batch → speed and fog.** A documented and industrially significant source of
   stock-to-stock variation in both 1929 and 1966; magnitude never stated. → §7. **[M]**
4. **Emulsion turbidity and layer thickness → sharpness.** The mechanism (light scatter within the
   coated layer) is described; no MTF, no scatter length, no thickness→sharpness coefficient. → §18. **[M]**
5. **Acetic acid → colour dye fading rate.** Direction stated, no factor, no dye named, no
   condition given. → §23 B4. **[M]**
6. **Development type → grain statistics.** Our own inference (§24.3) is that type B implies
   per-grain binary statistics and type A implies partial-fill statistics; the source states the
   two *progress laws* but does not state a noise consequence. **[E]** for the noise step.

### 24.3 Engineering conclusions we draw from §24.1 — flagged as ours

1. **Speed and granularity are not independent parameters.** Eq. (1.1) makes γ, *G* and photon
   exposure one relation, and two of the five DQE loss terms — the grain size/sensitivity
   *distribution* term (36 %) and the random *arrangement* term (72 %) — are precisely the terms a
   grain-noise model represents. A database that lets `exposure_index`, `GrainSpec.rms_*` and
   `ToneCurve.gamma` be set fully independently can express combinations that are physically
   impossible. This is a candidate for a **verification guard**, not a new field. **[E]**
2. **Grain noise statistics should differ by developer class, not only by stock.** Type B granular
   development is a per-grain binary event, which implies counting statistics over the number of
   fully developed grains; type A parallel development is a partial-fill process, which implies a
   less quantised, lower-variance build-up at equal density. Our `GrainSpec` carries one
   σ-versus-density shape per stock and no notion of the developer's progress type. If this is
   right, colour-negative grain (colour developer, type A) and B&W MQ-developed grain (type B)
   should not share a noise model. ⚠ The source supports the two progress laws; the noise
   consequence is our inference and would need validation. **[E]**
3. **Per-record grain scaling should differ between the blue record and the green/red records.**
   Intrinsic absorption scales with grain *volume*, dye-sensitized absorption with grain *surface
   area*. For a given grain population the blue record and the minus-blue records therefore sit at
   different points on the speed/grain trade-off. Our schema already has per-channel `rms_r/g/b`
   and `clump_um_r/g/b`, so this is expressible — it argues that those per-channel values should
   not be set equal by default. **[E]**
4. **The development family should not move speed.** Since sensitivity does not depend on developer
   type at each developer's optimum, a time–gamma family should move γ and Dmin but leave the speed
   point alone. Worth asserting as a guard on `ProcessingFamily`/`DevelopmentPoint` data. **[E]**
5. **Dmin has two components with different time dependence.** Emulsion fog develops rapidly;
   developer fog is initiation-limited and slow. A single Dmin value per stock cannot express a
   development-time series correctly. **[E]**
6. **The "wrong shape" finding.** The most valuable thing this source set gives us is not a value
   but a shape check: several of our parameters that are currently set independently are
   physically one quantity (see §26 items B1 and B2). That is the same class of defect as the
   `adjacency` / `edge_strength` / `edge_um` / `radius_um` problem already recorded in our queue. **[E]**

---

## 25. Category A — immediately usable in the existing database

**Honest finding: this category is empty of database writes, and that is the correct outcome.**

The criterion for category A is a value that can be represented in the existing schema *and*
attached to a specific profile with a technically justified role in the current algorithm. Applying
that criterion strictly:

| Candidate | Why it does not qualify as a write |
|---|---|
| Grain sizes, iodide contents, aspect ratios, sensitization types | Real numbers, but none is attached to a stock in our database. They characterise research emulsions and generic 1929/1966/1995 practice. Writing them against a named profile would be fabrication. |
| Davis & Walters 1922 survey data | Real measured sensitometry of real materials — but the authors deliberately **omitted the trade names**, the materials are ~1920 plates, and none corresponds to a profile we model. Recorded in §16 as a dated snapshot. Per the agreed plan, any period profiles derived from it are deferred so that a single `film_enum.hpp` renumber can cover them together with the five pending PORTRA additions. |
| `AgingSpec.shrinkage_pct` | The 1–10 % range with a knee at 1 % is now genuinely sourced `[Reilly p.11 (PDF 11)]` — but it is a property of *a degraded physical element*, not of a film stock. No stock in our database has an age or a storage history. It belongs to a damaged-element preset, not to a stock profile. |
| `DyeStabilitySpec` | Reilly's 20–30 years at room temperature for pre-1980 stocks, with magenta surviving longest, is a **class** statement about pre-1980 colour materials. Our method rule against deriving a class estimate from insufficient sampling applies, and the field set is per-profile. Recorded in §22–§23 for use when a dye-fade preset is designed. |
| `AgingSpec.base_yellowing_d` for acetate | ⚠ **Negative finding, and it was ACTED ON — see §26 B7.** Neither preservation source states that the acetate polymer itself yellows or changes density; only nitrate is described as yellowing, and only ordinally. ✅ **Audit run 2026-08-27: 0 of 161 profiles carry a non-zero value**, so there was nothing unsourced to withdraw. A guard now pins the field to zero on **every** profile — not just acetate ones, because no base-material field exists to select them (§26 B8). Still not a Category A *write*: the outcome was a guard, not a value. |

**What was therefore written to the database in this pass: nothing.** Forcing any of the above
into an existing field would violate the project's own standing rule against writing values the
sources do not support, and would be the same class of error as the tungsten-exposure-index
incident already recorded in the project history, where a filter factor was nearly written into a
film field.

⚠ **THAT CONCLUSION STILL STANDS, AND IT IS NOT CONTRADICTED BY WHAT SHIPPED SINCE.** Updated
2026-08-27. Schema v16–v18 added `PushSpec`, `EmulsionSpec`, `ThirdPartyObservations`, `ParamSource`,
`ProcessVariant` and `DevelopmentProgress`, and values were written into several of them. **None of
that is a Category A write.** Category A means *an existing field, on a specific stock, with a
justified role in the current algorithm*. Every one of those additions is a **new** field, all of
them inert on the render path, precisely because the corpus gave us facts the existing schema had
nowhere to put. **The empty Category A table below is still the correct answer**, and the honest
summary of the whole exercise is: the emulsion corpus changed what the database can *record*, and
changed nothing about what it *renders*.

~~**One schema addition is proposed rather than implemented** — see §26 B1 — because it touches
`ProcessingSpec`, which is adjacent to the two schema decisions already pending in the
digitisation queue (the aim-density field and the alternate-EI curve-set structure). Landing three
overlapping schema changes in three separate passes would produce three migrations where one would
do.~~
✅ **Implemented after all, and the batching argument was honoured.** B1 landed in **v18 together
with `ParamSource` and `ProcessVariant`** — one migration, not three. The two digitisation-queue
schema decisions (aim-density shape, alternate-EI curve sets) are **still open and still deliberately
held**, so the reasoning above remains live for those two.

### B1 — Development progress type on the processing record ✅ **SHIPPED**

> ✅ **BUILT 2026-08-27 as schema v18.** `DevelopmentProgress` landed on `ProcessingSpec` exactly as
> proposed below, together with two fields the proposal did not anticipate needing:
> `partial_fill_fraction` and `rate_size_coeff_um_min`, both of which came out of tracing Tani
> Figs. 7.8–7.12 rather than out of the prose.
> **Set on 9 stocks**; `UNKNOWN` on the rest, so every other profile renders bit-identically.
> **Guard G-PROGRESS** enforces the physics the figures established: it **rejects a 1/d rate
> coefficient on a GRANULAR stock**, because granular development rate is nearly independent of
> grain size and a 1/d coefficient there is a category error, not a tuning choice.
> The measured constants are in §23b: parallel (0.45, 0.591), granular (0.04, 0.0).
> ⚠ **Reach is limited by something the proposal did not foresee** — progress type is a property of
> the **developer**, not the emulsion (Tani proves it by getting both types out of the *same*
> emulsion with CP-20 and D72), and most profiles do not record which developer their curves were
> made with. Widening past 9 stocks is a developer-identity problem, not a physics problem.

~~**What:** an enumerated field recording whether a developer produces type A (parallel) or type B
(granular) development.~~
**Proposed representation:**
```python
class DevelopmentProgress(Enum):
    UNKNOWN  = 0    # default; nothing changes
    PARALLEL = 1    # type A: developed silver ∝ proportion developed within each grain
    GRANULAR = 2    # type B: developed silver ∝ number of fully developed grains
```
on `ProcessingSpec` (and, if the family is the better home, on `ProcessingFamily`), defaulting to
`UNKNOWN` so that every existing profile renders bit-identically until a value is set.
**Source:** `[Tani 1995, §7.3, pp.216–219 (PDF 225–228), Figs. 7.7–7.12]`, including the worked
identification of CP-20 as type A and D72 as type B.
**Why it matters:** it is the only source-supported reason we have found for two stocks with the
same rms granularity to *look* different in their grain. It also carries the rate law: parallel
development rate ∝ 1/grain size, granular development rate nearly independent of grain size.
**What is needed beyond the field:** the noise consequence (§24.3 item 2) is our inference and
needs validating against a real scan before any renderer uses it. Codegen impact: mirror in
`cpp_codegen.py`, append at the end of the struct so the aggregate-initialiser prefix is preserved.
~~**Blocked by:** nothing technical; deliberately held for the combined schema revision.~~
⚠ **Superseded.** It was not held. It shipped in v18 alongside `ParamSource` and `ProcessVariant`,
which is the combined revision the sentence was waiting for.

### B2 — A verification guard coupling γ, granularity and speed ✅ **SHIPPED**

> ✅ **BUILT 2026-08-27 as guard G-DQE.** The calibration problem the proposal identified was real
> and was solved by **not** converting to Selwyn's *G* at all. Instead the guard evaluates the
> dimensionless proxy **K = mid_slope² · EI / rms²** and compares each stock against the median of
> its own **class and era** band, failing at a 30× deviation.
> ⚠ **The banding is the whole trick.** Ungrouped, the guard flagged 14 outliers — all explicable
> (Polaroid print-like materials, 1940s stocks, the 5285 reversal). Banded by class and era it
> flags **two**; reading evaluated `mid_slope` instead of the stored `gamma` coefficient takes it to
> **zero, with no exception list at all**. An earlier `_DQE_KNOWN` allowlist was **deleted**, and its
> deletion is the point: a guard needing an allowlist on its first run is usually measuring the
> wrong quantity.
> ⚠ **It found a real defect in this document's own neighbourhood, and then a false one.** It
> flagged `KODAK_EKTACHROME_100D_5285` at 50× its class median; that was **my error, not the
> profile's** — for that curve `gamma` is a softplus model coefficient, not a slope. Withdrawn, and
> `ToneCurve` gained evaluated `mid_slope`, `usable_range_stops` and `is_degenerate` as a result.
> **Unplanned dividend:** the class/era medians independently reproduce Tani's Fig. 1.1 sensitivity
> history from our own data — colour negative K = 0.045 → 0.219 → 2.676. §23c.3 decomposes it and
> shows the post-1990 jump is **granularity, not speed**.

~~**What:** a check, not a field.~~ Eq. (1.1) makes γ, Selwyn *G* and photon exposure one relation with
DQE clustering at 1–2 % for real films.
**Source:** `[Tani 1995, §1.4, p.16 (PDF 25), Eq. (1.1)]` and the loss budget at
`[Tani 1995, §8.1, p.228 (PDF 237)]`.
**Why it matters:** our database currently allows a stock to be fast, contrasty and fine-grained
simultaneously in ways no emulsion achieves. A soft guard that flags profiles falling outside a
plausible DQE band would catch data-entry errors of exactly the kind this project keeps finding.
~~**What is needed:** a calibration of *G* against our `rms_*` convention. Selwyn's constant is
defined through σ_D·√(2a); our `rms_granularity` is a manufacturer's aperture-specific figure.
The conversion must be established before the guard can be numeric rather than ordinal.~~
⚠ **Superseded, and the reasoning was wrong in a useful way.** The conversion was never needed. A
*relative* guard comparing like with like inside a class/era band never has to know the absolute
constant, because the convention cancels. Reaching for the absolute calibration first would have
blocked a guard that works.

### B3 — Per-record grain scaling from the volume/area distinction ★ medium-high
**What:** default per-channel `rms_r/g/b` and `clump_um_r/g/b` that are *not* equal, reflecting
that the blue record's absorption scales with grain volume and the minus-blue records' with grain
surface area.
**Source:** `[Tani 1995, §8.1.1, p.229 (PDF 238)]`.
**What is needed:** the ratio. The source gives the two scaling laws and the absorption figures
(cubic AgBr 1 µm: ~10 % at 420 nm, ~1 % at 460 nm; 3 mol % AgI raises 460 nm five-fold) but not a
granularity ratio. Needs either a derivation with stated assumptions or measurement.

### B4 — Two-component Dmin with distinct development-time behaviour ★ medium
**What:** separate the fog floor into an emulsion-fog term (fast, from pre-existing centres) and a
developer-fog term (slow, initiation-limited).
**Source:** `[Tani 1995, §7.4–7.5, pp.219–220 (PDF 228–229), Fig. 7.13]`.
**Why it matters:** a development-time series cannot currently be represented correctly, because
one Dmin per stock has no way to grow at two different rates. This interacts with the pending
alternate-EI schema decision.
**What is needed:** measured Dmin-versus-time for at least one stock; the source gives the
mechanism and the ordering, not the rates.

### B5 — Emulsion structural parameters as a new record ✅ **SHIPPED**

> ✅ **BUILT 2026-08-27 as schema v17.** `EmulsionSpec` carries exactly the proposed fields —
> `grain_um`, `size_sigma_log`, `habit`, `aspect_ratio`, `iodide_mol_pct`, `sensitization`,
> `coated_um`, `source` — with controlled vocabularies for habit and sensitization, a 20 µm ceiling
> on grain size, and `aspect_ratio` legal only on `tabular`. **Populated on 17 stocks**, inert
> everywhere, so a v17 database renders bit-identically to v16.
> ⚠ **`EmulsionSpec.grain_um` IS NOT `GrainSpec.clump_um_*`, AND ALIASING THEM WOULD BE A REAL BUG.**
> `grain_um` is a mean *crystal* diameter; `clump_um_*` is a mean *developed clump* diameter, which
> depends on development gamma and density — the BBC T-101 work in §17 measures the clump shrinking
> 20 % across the tone scale of one film. One is what the emulsion is; the other is what the
> developer made of it.
> ⚠ **The objection below was answered by a source arriving, exactly as predicted.** The proposal
> said the record becomes worthwhile "the moment a source with per-stock crystal data enters the
> corpus". A vendor publication did, for CineStill 800T, and the field had somewhere to go.

~~**What:** a new `EmulsionSpec` carrying mean grain size (µm), size-distribution width, habit
(cubic/octahedral/tabular), aspect ratio, iodide mol %, and sensitization type.~~
**Source:** the physics is throughout §4–§8; representative numbers exist for research and generic
emulsions.
**Why it matters:** it is the natural home for everything in §24.1 that is currently unrepresentable,
and it would let the grain and speed models be *derived* rather than typed in.
~~**Why it is not implemented:** we have no per-stock values for any stock we model. Adding an empty
record would be schema churn. It becomes worthwhile the moment a source with per-stock crystal data
enters the corpus.~~
⚠ **Superseded — the condition in the last sentence was met.** ⚠ But note what did **not** change:
per-stock **habit, iodide, aspect ratio, sensitization type and coated thickness remain Category C**
(§27) and are still unavailable for every stock we model. The record exists and is mostly empty, and
that is the honest state — an empty field with a defined meaning is not the same as a filled one.

### B6 — Reciprocity: intensity-dependent nucleus count ★ medium
**What:** the high-intensity branch of reciprocity behaviour follows from a nucleation rate ∝ I².
**Source:** Tani 1995, chapter 4 — the form is source-supported.
**Why it is only B:** ⚠ no Schwarzschild exponent, no threshold intensity in absolute units, no
exposure-time bounds beyond a 10⁻⁴ s / 1 s pair used as a figure's metric, and **no temperature
dependence of reciprocity failure anywhere in the book**. Our `ReciprocitySpec` already has
`schwarzschild_p_r/g/b` and `onset_s`; this source constrains the shape but supplies no coefficient.

**What:** audit the database for non-zero `base_yellowing_d` on acetate-base profiles.

`[NEDCC 5.1, 2020]` describe yellowing only for **nitrate**, and only ordinally. → §23 C2.

withdraw and nothing to cite — the correctness gain the item predicted was already banked, by

⚠ **It was clean by accident, not by construction, and that is now fixed.** Nothing prevented a
future edit from introducing one. A guard (**G-YELLOW**, `verify.py`) now asserts the field is zero on
**every film profile AND on all 11 print stocks** — the print stocks carry their own `AgingSpec`
since schema v12 and this item as originally written had not accounted for them — with the evidence
attached: neither preservation source states that any base yellows except
**nitrate**, and for nitrate only ordinally, as a stage in a degradation sequence with no density
attached. ⚠ **The guard cannot say "acetate", because there is no base-material field** — see B8,
which is the item that would supply one. Pinning the field to zero everywhere is the stronger

### B8 — Base material as a preset-validity constraint ★ small, metadata only
**What:** record base material and its date window so that stock/format/date presets can be checked
for historical coherence (16 mm and 8 mm were never nitrate; "Safety" markings date a sheet film;
polyester in still roll film is late).
**Source:** §21 chronology, from `[Reilly 1993 (rev. 1996), pp.21–22 (PDF 21–22)]` and
`[NEDCC 5.1, 2020, p.2 (PDF 2)]`.
**Why B not A:** it is metadata governing preset validity, never a pixel operation, and it needs a

## 27. Category C — reference knowledge only

Retained in this document because it is technically valid and explains the material, but not
appropriate for the simulator. Each entry states why.

| Content | Where | Why not in the simulator |
|---|---|---|
| Silver halide solubility products, pAg control, lattice constants, Frenkel and Schottky defect chemistry, interstitial silver-ion mobility | §4 | Two or more causal steps below any image-level quantity. No measurable image effect is established from them in these sources. |
| Sensitizing-dye chemistry — J-aggregates, redox potentials, supersensitization mechanisms, individual dye identities | §9 | Our spectral model consumes measured sensitivity curves. Dye chemistry explains where a curve's peak comes from; it does not predict the curve. |
| Stabilizer and antifoggant chemistry, dose ranges in g or mg | §8, §13 | Manufacturing control variables. Their image effect (fog suppression) is already represented as Dmin. |
| Gelatin classes, setting and melting points, water absorption, natural-sensitizer content | §7 | Manufacturing variable. Its documented image effect — batch-to-batch speed and fog variation — has no magnitude in any source, so it cannot be modelled; it is, however, the honest explanation for why nominally identical stocks differ. |
| 1929 emulsion recipes, coating-machine geometry, drying-tunnel engineering, baryta-paper preparation | §3, §6, §21 | Historical manufacturing record. Valuable for understanding period materials; outside a renderer's scope. |
| Development-agent electrochemistry — half-wave potentials, Z / Zs / n orbital counts, superadditivity | §12 | Explains *why* developers differ. What the renderer needs from it is B1, and that is one enumerated field. |
| Non-conventional processes | §12, §20 | Outside scope. |
| The entire IPI storage-prediction apparatus: the Wheel, time contours, the Time Out of Storage table, the 17× and 3× factors, the 40/50/100/150/450-year predictions, A-D strip levels, free-acidity values | §22 | These predict **when the carrier begins to smell of vinegar** (0.5 free acidity), at which point the source states the film "may not have any other symptoms of degradation and will be perfectly usable". There is no path from these numbers to a pixel. → §23.4 item 10. |
| Enclosure chemistry, PAT / ISO 18916, segregation policy, vault volatiles, health hazards, cold-storage engineering, duplication policy | §22 | Preservation practice. Zero image consequence. |
| Davis & Walters Part III's 258 plotted curve families — colour sensitivity, characteristic-curve families at several development times, and time–gamma — for all 86 emulsions | §23d | **Added 2026-08-27 (A5).** The plots are real measurements, but the emulsions are **anonymous by the paper's own design** and are 1920 American plates; our oldest stock is 1930. No profile could take a value from them even if every curve were traced perfectly, and the time–gamma behaviour is already covered by the `kodak_time_gamma` audit against a source that names its film. The *data-block* fields (speed, scale, resolution) WERE harvested and are Category A-adjacent era context — see §23d. → §23d.6 |
| Base identification tests: float, polarised light, diphenylamine, burn test, notch codes, edge printing | §21 | Diagnostic procedures for a person holding film up to a light. Polyester birefringence and edge light-piping are real optical properties but neither source connects them to image capture. |
| Vinegar syndrome as an *image* effect | §23 | ⚠ Not merely unsupported — **contradicted**. The source states the silver image "is not faded to orange-red as is often the case in nitrate decomposition" and "usually remains in good condition", and that the emulsion survives well enough to be floated off the ruined base and rephotographed. A vinegar-syndrome look preset that fogs or yellows the image would be inventing an effect the authority denies. |
| Base haze or light scattering with age | §23 | Never mentioned in either preservation source. Needs a different source entirely. |

Two book errors found (mean ÷10; a composition pair summing to 92.6, which is impossible on complementary columns) and the corrected figures, plus the first thickness estimate the corpus supports (21.9 µm dry), are in §3.3.1a | **done** |

## 29. Provenance and source-integrity register

### 29.1 Page-offset map

**Re-derived by measurement, 2026-08-27.** The earlier version of this table was written from
spot checks and stated the change-over points as approximations ("up to ~p.55", "from ~p.80").
That was not good enough to validate a citation against, so the whole map was rebuilt: every page
of all four books was passed through `pdftotext -layout`, the printed folio was read out of the
running head or page footer, and the offset was computed per page. The ranges below are exact, not
approximate, and the boundaries are the pages where the offset actually changes.

| Source | Offset (PDF = printed + Δ) | Range in printed pages | Evidence for the boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tani 1995 | **Δ = +9**, uniform | all, pp. iii–254 | 244 pages carry a legible running-head folio and every one of them gives +9. No boundary exists |
| Duffin 1966 | **Δ = +4** | pp. 6–71 | PDF 75 footer reads `71` |
| Duffin 1966 | **Δ = +6** | pp. 73–245 | PDF 79 footer reads `73`. PDF 76–78 carry no folio: two unnumbered plate leaves plus one blank were bound in, which is what shifts Δ by +2. p.72 falls inside the insert and cannot be addressed by offset — cite it by content |
| Wall 1929 | **Δ = +8** | pp. 2–65 | PDF 73 head reads `NEGATIVE EMULSIONS 65` |
| Wall 1929 | **Δ = +7 or +8** | pp. 66–69 | ⚠ **ambiguous.** PDF 74, 75 and 76 carry no legible running head, and they have to hold four printed pages (66–69) in three PDF pages, so one printed page is absent from the scan. Which one is not determinable from the text layer. Cite this range by content, not by PDF number |
| Wall 1929 | **Δ = +7** | pp. 70–252 | PDF 77 head reads `70 PHOTOGRAPHIC EMULSIONS`; PDF 259 head reads `252 PHOTOGRAPHIC EMULSIONS` |
| Wall 1929 | **Δ = +6** | pp. 254–260 | p.253 is absent from the scan (§29.3), so everything after it moves up one. PDF 260 head reads `254 ; PHOTOGRAPHIC EMULSIONS`. **No citation in this document falls in this range** — the highest Wall page cited is 251 |
| Davis & Walters 1922 | **Δ = +1**, uniform | pp. 1–120 | PDF 3 head reads `2  Scientific Papers of the Bureau of Standards`; PDF 32 head reads `… Sensitometry of Photographic Emulsions   31`. ⚠ The plate pages at PDF 36–121 each carry their own plate number in a rotated caption; those numbers are **not** folios and will produce a false Δ ≈ +35 if an automated check treats them as such |
| Reilly IPI 1993 | **Δ = 0** | pp. 1–24 | separate 24-page PDF (`acetate_guide.pdf`) |
| NEDCC 5.1 2020 | **Δ = 0** | pp. 1–6 | separate 6-page PDF (`5_1_FilmBaseGuide_2020.pdf`) |

**Audit result.** All 2242 `p.N (PDF M)` pairs in this document were checked against the map above.
Nine occurrences, six distinct pairs, were wrong and have been corrected:

| Citation | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Duffin, Ch. IV, p.61, Table 3 | PDF 67 | **PDF 65** |
| Duffin, Ch. VI, pp.125–126, Fig. 6.8 | PDF 131–133 | **PDF 131–132** |
| Duffin, Ch. IX, p.220 | PDF 229 | **PDF 226** |
| Tani, §5.3, pp.124–126 (×2) | PDF 133–134 | **PDF 133–135** |
| Tani, §6.2, pp.171–172 (×2) | PDF 180–182 | **PDF 180–181** |
| Tani, §6.5, pp.186–189 (×2) | PDF 195–199 | **PDF 195–198** |

Every one is an end-of-range slip of ±1 in a page range, except the three Duffin singletons, which
predate the discovery that Duffin has two offset regimes. No citation pointed at unrelated content;
all nine landed within one page of the right place. The check is reproducible: the folio for a
printed page *p* must appear in the running head or footer of PDF page *p* + Δ.

⚠ **A page-range citation must be validated at both ends.** Six of the nine errors were correct at
the low end and wrong at the high end, because the range was extended by counting rather than by
reading the folio of the last page.

### 29.2 Bibliographic details as printed
Full details are in §1.1. Publication years were taken from the documents themselves, not from
filenames: Tani from the OUP title page ("1995"); Duffin from "© 1966 FOCAL PRESS LIMITED …
Printed in Hungary 1966"; Davis & Walters from the dateline (Washington, 6 September 1921) with GPO
marks reading "-22-"; Wall from "COPYRIGHT, 1929 BY AMERICAN PHOTOGRAPHIC PUBLISHING Co."; Reilly
from the IPI leaflet's own © statement; NEDCC from the leaflet's © 2020.

### 29.3 OCR and source-integrity register

⚠ **Tani 1995 — every numbered display equation is image-only.** The text layer reads
"…is defined as follows:" followed by a blank line, then the symbol definitions. This affects
Eqs. (1.1)–(1.3), (2.1)–(2.3), (3.1)–(3.23), (4.1)–(4.9), (5.1)–(5.9) and (7.1)–(7.13). Tables 5.1
and 5.2 (dye absorptions and structures) are likewise image-only — captions survive, contents do
not. Table 3.1 survives but is column-scrambled.
**Mitigation applied:** the equations quoted in this document were recovered by rendering the
relevant PDF pages as images at 170 dpi and reading them directly. Eq. (1.1) (the DQE relation) was
recovered this way and is quoted in §17 and §24.1 exactly as printed. The remaining equation bodies
were **not** recovered and are recorded in the body of this document as symbol lists with their
stated behaviour, never as reconstructed formulae. Nothing in this document is an inferred equation
presented as a quotation.

**Recurring OCR substitutions in Tani 1995**, to be aware of when re-checking a number:
`/^m`, `/xm`, `/am`, `/jum`, `fjum`, `/«n`, `^m` all = µm; a bare `A` after a number is sometimes Å
and sometimes µm² (the "43 A2" case is µm²); `106` = 10⁶; `l` ↔ `1`; `S` ↔ `5`; fraction glyphs
(½, ⅔, ⅓) are lost and appear as `f`, `§`, `\`.

**Duffin 1966** — the dust-jacket page (PDF 2) is heavily garbled; body text is sound. Equation
survival is recorded per item in §4–§8.

**Davis & Walters 1922** — thin Google OCR, ~858 characters per page average. Digits in the survey
tables are the least reliable content in this entire source set and every uncertain digit is
flagged at its point of use in §16. Where a table's numbers matter, the page image should be
consulted before the value is used.

**Wall 1929** — generally clean. Two known losses: Fig. 34 (drying-stick profile) and the
collodio-chloride baryta table on p.253.

⚠ **p.253 is not an OCR failure — the page is not in the scan.** This was checked directly on
2026-08-27, because the earlier wording ("missing from the OCR … would have to come from the page
image") implied the content was recoverable by re-rendering, and it is not. Three findings settle it:

1. PDF 259 carries the running head `252 PHOTOGRAPHIC EMULSIONS`, and its text ends
   *"For collodio-chloride emulsions the following coatings are given in tabular form:"* followed by
   the digitiser's own literal annotation **`(Table on 253 missing)`**. The scan flags its own gap.
2. The next PDF page, 260, opens on `254 ; PHOTOGRAPHIC EMULSIONS`. There is no PDF page between
   them. The folio sequence runs 248, 249, 250, 251, 252, **254** — printed page 253 has no image
   in this file at all.
3. Consistent with that, the offset drops from Δ = +7 to Δ = +6 at exactly this point (§29.1),
   which is the arithmetic signature of one absent leaf rather than a blank or unreadable one.

An earlier reading of PDF 260 was briefly misled because that page carries **two** folio strings
(`254 ; PHOTOGRAPHIC EMULSIONS` at the top and `' APPENDIX 255` further down), which looks like a
two-page spread and would have explained the gap innocently. It does not: PDF 259 is a single page
whose text layer runs on into the head of the following one, which is a text-layer boundary artefact
of this scan and not evidence of a spread.

**Status: closed as permanently unavailable from this source.** Obtaining the table requires a
different copy of the 1929 book. Nothing in this document depends on it — no coating-weight figure
in §3 is drawn from p.253, and the collodio-chloride coating weights we do quote come from the
Tappen & Rekaschow table on p.157 (PDF 164).
One internal arithmetic inconsistency is the **book's own, not OCR**: the mean coating weight on
p.158 (PDF 165) divides a sum of nine values by ten. Both the book's figure and the true mean of
the nine are given in §3.

**Reilly IPI 1993 and NEDCC 5.1 2020** — clean digital text.

### 29.4 Method rules this document was built under
Carried over from the project's digitisation method, and applied here:
record conflicts rather than averaging them; never derive a class estimate from an insufficient
sample; skip loudly rather than silently; and keep the classification of fact, quantified fact,
mechanism, engineering conclusion and speculation visible on every item so that a later reader can
tell which is which without returning to the sources — which is the whole point, because the
sources will no longer be there.
